I am still not done with this game but I think I can safely say that this is one of the best collections of puzzles you can experience in a game, probably period.
Unconcerned with trivial concepts like conventional gravity and the laws of physics, this game, even in its crazier moments, never ends up feeling obtuse or alienating, but rather challenging and enticing. If one feels completely overwhelmed by a particular puzzle, oftentimes the best way to go is to leave the game, get some rest, let your brain do the work, and come back to it fresh the next morning, and more often than not it will solve itself.
Fortunately, thanks to its very well made undo feature (that also works to undo a restart by the way !), it encourages experimentation and as a result never feels frustrating. Even better, the beautiful ambient score (on more than one occasion reminiscent of artists like Steve Roach, for example) ensures that the experience is often more soothing than stressful : unlike a lot of puzzle games, there is no stress element in English Country Tune, no timer, no lives, no limited continues. It's just you and a bunch of extremely well-designed, unique puzzles.
Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys a good brain teaser.

Gameplay consists of turning off a screen/ field of tessellating geometric figures that are in a “steady state,” or fixed repeating pattern. Here, you simply choose how many and where you want to place the shapes and then start the program running to see if it works. I started in Hard mode, because there is only Hard and Harder, or the Simulation mode which works like a sandbox. Of course, after struggling with that for a few minutes, I moved to the Simulation mode where you have more freedom with where you can place the pieces on the field. It was there I began to really understand the game.
Basically, you have a marked segment of the field for dropping in shapes on the Hard mode, and they must be placed in such a way as to have an effect on all the figures already on the screen. On the other hand, the Simulation mode allows you to interact directly with the figures already on screen, to see how they are changed when a figure you place hits them. This directs your thinking.
You turn on the game and before long you find yourself mesmerized with just watching the effects the shapes you add to the field have on the whole process. After some time and experimentation, you realize you’ve actually begun to see how the program is “thinking.” It’s a definite lightbulb feeling.
Bacteria is an incredible game! I spent 4 hours in a single setting on this. It has a lot to offer for people who like to just jump into a puzzle with no preconceived ideas or splash screens. And, the achievements drop pretty quickly once you figure out the idea. I got the first four of six achievements in the first four hours.
Normally I've felt like a game couldn't do without words... text... but I have to say in this case the wordlessness is a major asset. There is nothing to get in the way or distract from the simple concept of the geometric patterns and the AI’s plan. In that way, it is similar to logic and/or strategy games, like Frozen Synapse, where you make your moves and then see the results, then try again.
It's an awesome game... one that I will probably spend quite a bit of time in I can tell already. And, the card art is definitely original and something I’ve enjoyed collecting. And, right now at $0.88 it’s well worth the price.

The graphics are presented on an interface that resembles the old cathode ray tube (CRT) design monitors, with a convex screen. The puzzle pieces look something like pentomino figures, being simple geometric shapes. The music is ambient space age music, very relaxing. The dlc includes the soundtrack and a selection of various bacteria backgrounds, as well as a mini game that takes you further into the “Game of Life” idea Bacteria is based on. I’ve enjoyed it so much, I grabbed a couple of copies of the game and dlc to give away over on Steam Gifts, so look for the giveaways on my page as soon as they add them.
* Presents an array of difficulty choices to make the game accessible from the start.
* Nostalgic look of old DOS screens
* Reminiscent of Games programmed in BASIC language
* Nerdy geometric component of recreational Math
*No narrative
*No words
*Not even the sound of your own inner voice :D
If you like pattern mathematical games like pentominoes, or Izzi , or if you spent hours  trying to decipher a coding language, or just love the way computer AI “thinks,” then this open puzzler is for you.

Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is a platform, adventure game that takes place in the harsh climate of the tundra while facing a catastrophic blizzard that perpetually weighs you down as you trod through the frozen tundra in order to stop the blizzard from destroying your village. You play as a girl named Nunu and her companion, an all-white coated Artic fox. Fox were believed to bring joy and be excellent companions in the Alaskan climate to guide and aid people away from danger.  You use what is called a Bola which is an ancient weapon that was used by Native American tribes to hunt for duck which an elderly man humbly gives you, the bola, as a reward for finding his drum he lost. Drums are considered the pinnacle and way of life of Native American tribes, the Iñupiat.  The spirituality and belief in pantheism, that all living things and animate objects possesses a soul and a nature of some type is represented in the early parts of the game through spirits controlled by the fox that helps you get to heights, ledges, platforms, cliffs, ladders and hills you are unable to reach normally in the game playing as Nunu.
Nunu is an emotional, devastated and vivacious girl. How would you feel if in real-life you were from a native tribe and someone who was a foreign alien, unwelcomed as an adversary, destroyed your hometown including all women, men and children alike? You would be distraught just like Nunu is at times. Nunu is at a loss because this fox seems to be her one and only companion. We don't know the whereabouts of her parents nor if she has any siblings.
Never Alone is based around a true and real tale of Native American tribes, Alaskan natives to be more specific whom have experienced severe forms of climate change throughout the aging of glaciers and a great devastation of a blizzard in which at the beginning of the game has been coming from an unknown source. You will battle your way through your adversaries of an opposing tribe wanting to take you hostage, attempting to kill you, forcing you to always be on the run from imminent danger.
This game has much heart and dedication towards being a true to life amalgamation of Native American cultures.
Along the way they have this very unique feature called cultural insights. Cultural insights are history behind the developers and publishers covering history of the Alaskan people mostly talked about called the Iñupiat. We learn through this about their weapons, way of life, spirituality, heart of their community, sharing, management of resources, simplistic; primitive way of life and about the various types of people and philosophies that the community holds dear to them. The presentation of the cultural insights is illustrated through descriptive imagery of photos of their heritage and way of life. There are interviews in the form of a documentary in order to educate the gaming community whom may have not known anything prior about foreign cultures and the way in which the Alaskan natives and Native Americans live. Usually we are too caught up only within our own society, we forget of the primitive and more simplistic ones out there that care more about resources than how much entertainment we have, wealth we accumulate in our life and our own accolades. This brings a mist of fresh air in a gaming culture that in the present day have resorted to liking more simplistic games that are considered fun and mindless entertainment rather than the latter being educationally based.

I am calling the climate and real-time weather effects a real-time environment trajectory system because the weather is so perfectly done throughout this game with precise timing and accuracy that it becomes a 1:1 ratio relating to real-life mechanics. What I mean by this is as the blizzard blows from the east, it perfectly breaks for just the right duration of time giving you only a second to breathe before having to get up again trudging your way through the unforgiving blizzard storm. It will usually start from the east, give you a small breather, then, it picks back up steadily at full force in the West. The trajectory part of this feature is used when you need the precise angle pointed at a certain degree and angle in order to make it to new platforms and later in the game, new ladders. That is, you have to use the environment to your advantage because some jumps you can't make until the storm carries you towards that next platform, ladder or step you need to reach. The end goal becomes to restore back your village and the environment by protecting your Alaskan Native American people by defeating and defending against all your enemies.
Story: The story is magnificent, superb. Although the voice acting in Never Alone is good, I do have one criticism. The primary disadvantage I see within the voice acting is I wish it was more in the old-fashioned documentary style. It would make the game's story more enticing, intriguing if the voice acting was more in a documentary format like the cultural insights were.
The last feature we will be discussing is the single player co-op feature:
Single player co-op:
Sometimes you will see modern platformers implement a method in which you have to control both characters at different times when placed in different situations. You have to work together in order to get certain tasks done. For instance, the main character Nunu can move heavy crates while the fox is good at jumping. Use what skills you have to your best ability. The fox is the only one that can control these spirits which guide and levitate you to new heights and to new places. It reminds me of the co-op system used much like the horror game Resident Evil Revelations 2 when I used to play horror games.
Controls:
The controls are smooth, fluid, responsive and accurate. I recommend like in all platformers to use a gamepad to get the best results and experience when playing.
Graphics:
Beautiful, lust and gorgeous visuals reminiscent of Journey by Thatgamecompany. The wind and lush snowy tundra reminds me of the antithesis of its climate in Journey. The only graphical glitch you may experience time to time is wall glitching only when falling under a platform usually when instead you are supposed to die instantly. Sometimes your character will just be stuttering back and forth. If you experience this, it is very easy to continue where you left off from your last checkpoint. Although I did encounter this when falling off of some edges where I did not immediately die, it is only a minor glitch and will not dissuade your experience.
The Good & Bad:
Positive aspects:
•Gorgeous Visuals
•Amazing, breathtaking emotional experience from cultural insights to the story
•Excellent use of Phenomenology in use of perception, visual stimulation and story cues
•Awesome Native American Alaskan Iñupiat background information
•No major technological glitches, bugs
•Timeless and short
Negative aspects:
•Could have better voice acting in documentary vocal form
•It could have a better artificial intelligence design where they could have used prompt commands like follow, stay, be careful and of course a hug command where it would be possible to pat the fox on the head when the fox has done a good job.
Overall: 10/10- Amazing
Key:
1-3 = poor
3-5 = ok
6-7= good
8-10 = amazing

Stories Untold is an anthology horror game that blends a few genres; namely text adventure, and walking simulator. It is a four part episodic that tells a singular foray into mental health, forgiveness, psychosis and a few other mental tropes. I wish it wasn't! -- more on that later -- But I absolutely adore anthologies. I've seen everything from Hitchcock Presents to Twilight Zone to Tales From the Crypt to reading dozens of written versions, including comics. Digestable, microscopic horror stories is the way that I properly appreciate the genre as a whole (Lovecrafitan short/flash fiction is my standout favorite.)
That out of the way, Untold hit the mark a few times and missed in others. Ultimately given the price, that it can be completed in one setting, and that it can be unremarkably unsettling, I recommend it for the price given.
Pros
*Well written, cohesive narration even if it wasn't to my taste.
*Chapter 3 astounds as a wonderful little gem of pure, slow burn horror.
*Interface and graphics are surprisingly polished at times, except for walking segments.
*Music is wonderful. Reminds me of Stranger Things.
*Game is at it's best in 2 & 3 when you are controlling puzzles, not writing your moves into a terminal.
Cons
*Walking simulator aspects are almost amazingly bad.
*Low-vocabulary and ridiculously short CYOA elements render them almost pointless.
*Everything is too short, and the overall ending is a lackluster Sanitarium nod.
Chapter 1: The House Abandon
Chapter 1 is the demo to the game, and is also probably the nestegg which created this whole project. You sit down at an ancient little commodore spinoff and play a CYOA text adventure. It is very easy and routine, almost hum-drum, in controls. But the main issue I struck up with was that the vocabulary is so limited. Look around, Leave, etc are very specific. You can't say "Look around me" or "Leave the Car", you need to use "Look Around" and "Exit Car", etc. Besides for this, Abandon does a fantastic job of ramping up the tension as the little adventure continues and has a clever, although predictable, ending.
Chapter 2: The Lab Conduct
In what I originally felt was a playable SCP, I was happy to see so many systems and puzzles at my fingertips. Felt like a controlled surgeon simulator and I was excited to do more than just type. Unfortunately for me, and you, this chapter winds up being as linear as can be. Hell, even the manual is laid out in a way that gives you instructions one at a time in the proper sequence with which you'll be using the tools to fiddle with -- and eventually release -- the artifact therein. I won't spoil the ending, but what happens during the closing act of this Chapter is hairbrained nonsense that felt like a ripoff of a Star Trek concept and was bonkers in execution. Bright lights, loud noises, Shadows of Chernobyl Ending Cutscene style montages, etc. It was disorienting, clumsy, and frustrating and I just wanted it to end.
Chapter 3: The Station Process
Let me get the negatives out of the way, the walking section sucks and going back and forth to the microfilm is frustrating. Two tips; one, you can zoom in and zoom out and adjust focus with the tiny thumb-sliders under the manual. Two, just look up the guide for when it starts beeping at you because you won't be bothered to figure out Morse Code on the spot for a game because it asks you to.
The tension in this chapter is terrific. The concept is stark and creepy, reminiscent of The Thing to me. You're a radio operator in the arctic and an extinction level event might have begun, and it's up to you to relay codes from your ferry station out to the world that needs it -- be it ships, military, civilians, etc. You can kind of guess and articulate what the codenames, lingo, and frequencies all mean with deduction as the story goes on. It's not a hard nut to crack, but it's a tense one. I just wish a few things were different here. First, a manual would have made more functional sense in a gameworld than the micro film. Some features the MF has aren't utilized, namely slides, and spinning the damn thing is never used and it just irritated me when it did do that via the dial. The walking simulator, and the obvious "scares", were also dumb. This story should have been tripled in length, filled with more lore, had more communication and expanded upon the feeling of impending doom a lot more than the slice it did.
I also would suggest to the developers that right here is an organic time to play with your text adventure. Our mic was cut off, I was happily expecting to be able to type my replies instead to my friends and was wholly let down.
Chapter 4: The Last Session
This is an amalgamation of all the previous chapters and isn't quite worth discussing. It's kind of lousy, and my interest dropped off to a point where I just beat it to beat the game.
-------
My closing comments are this. I am impressed with the atmosphere, delivery of new mechanics, visual polish, wonderful audio and above average writing. From a horror enthusiast, I will tell you this; the game needed more story, a more meaningful exploration of the text adventure system, Chapter 3 could be it's own game, and there is no reason to me why an anthology has to be cohesive. For $10 and about 2 hours of game, you can't go wrong for a bite sized experience this October. I hope to see the devs get enough sales to make Untold 2, where they can properly explore a semi-full game with each mechanic without bleeding into each other. I want to see a long House Abandon, a long SCP style Government Experiment, a grueling and tense story-first narrative of being a radio operator, and let's lose the ending and find a good new forth chapter shall we?

Honestly the game balance is very poor. There are some classes with Massive advantages and very few disadvantages if any specifically Warden, Warlord, and Centurian. Some classes have virtually no advantages and are behind from the outset. The game design is stuck somewhere between brawler and fighting game, and becuase it couldn't pick it has all the weaknesses of both without many of the advantages of either. It's the worst of both worlds.
There are mechanics that care entirely about your reflexes with response timings of 200ms or faster. this is literally faster than human reaction speeds so you do have to predict them. A casual game this is not, it is very much designed and built around a hardcore base but also doesnt' have the gumption to focus on that either and the endgame isn't that wild in a way that a game like streetfighter or tekken might be.
The arenas are Littered with Instant enviromental death with a number of characters seemingly designed to exploit these instant death traps even in 1v1 modes. This, for a fighting game, is like the underbarrel grenade launcher in a FPS, but in a game that pretends to be more skill based and shouldn't need that becuase it in theory has actual matchmaking. However the player base is virtually nonexistant so fair matching basically doens't happen at this point. if you are a new player you're going to run into a brick wall most likely.
Furthermore there's a cash shop meaning it has internal microtransactions as well in a premium game, this is unacceptable and a blot on an already dalmation-patterned game
So with a fairly low skill ceiling and a weird at best game balance where the character that appeals to you may put you at a very large perminant disadvantage I can't really recommend this game to anyone. 1/10, great concept stops it from being a 0 but a poor attempt in basically every way for any audience.

Why do I even bother? I've done this three times already, do I need to keep writing new introductions to every Jackbox review? Whatever, this is still a good game.
FIBBAGE 3: Yeah, we get it. It's Fibbage. We've already done this twice before. Not to say the game is bad... I mean, the new music and art style are AMAZING and the more updated questions are an improvement, but I feel they should have gone with Earwax 2 or Quiplash 3 instead of this. Fibbage was a great game, but this is unfortunately the worst in the pack.
FIBBAGE: ENOUGH ABOUT YOU: I know this is technically an alternate game mode, but the pack claims to have "five-and-a-half" new party games, so it gets its own section. At the start of the game, everyone answers questions about themselves. From there, it's basically Fibbage, but about the players. I also like the truth-or-lie lightning round at the end. Speaking of lightning, though... that's how long the game is. Fibbage: EAY goes by way too quickly. Only one question per player and a lightning round. That's it. No extra time. The rest of it is pretty decent, but I need to warn you of something. If you want to give EAY a try, do it with friends or streamers. It's not very fun when your family already knows everything about you.
SURVIVE THE INTERNET: Whoo boy, do I love this one! The concept? Hilarious! The art style? Nostalgic as all hell. The music? Don't even get me started on its majesty. Survive The Internet is my favorite in this pack, as well as the favorite of the rest of my family. The game's objective of twisting opponents' words is... actually too true... BUT WHATEVER, IT'S JACKBOX! I was worried the game would be boring with only 3 people, but the game includes Gene the A.I. character to add some randomness to the mix. I have only one complaint about the game: the final round. Sure, the photo captions give you infinite freedom, but the photo selection is VERY weak. I get a question and only two photos from the gallery to choose from? Really?! The rest of the game is pretty fun, though, so it's more than excusable. If you're planning on buying this pack, START WITH THIS GAME.
MONSTER SEEKING MONSTER: This one may seem complicated at first, but once you understand it, it's really fun. This game is really out there when it comes to Jackbox. Live texting? Monsters dating?! The Audience being an 8th player and collectively being ABLE TO WIN?!?!?! Yeah, sure, why not? The texting mechanic is really cool, and there's even a block button for playing on streams with possible trolls. YOU DON'T KNOW (JACK) HOW HANDY THIS LITTLE BUTTON WAS. And the monster powers... they are a very unique range. Some like the Werewolf absolutely SUCK while others like the Invisible Person can prove to be very useful. Also, the Zombie is hella O.P. Just wanted to let that be known. A common trend I've seen is Twitch users adore this game, but my family doesn't like it as much. Oh well. If you can find a group of friends that enjoy stupid games like this, have a ball.
BRACKETEERING: Quiplash with gambling and a tournament format. No, really. It's literally Quiplash with gambling and a tournament format. That doesn't mean it's bad, though. The responses people can come up with get huge laughs from me, especially during the Blind and TRIPLE Blind Bracket rounds. The 16-player support is absolutely AMAZING, since Jackbox hasn't added more than 8 players since Lie Swatter! (Yeah, I know about the 10K Audience members, but that feature doesn't really count...) This game also receives OPPOSITE love than MSM, from what I've seen. Twitch users, the MAIN DEMOGRAPHIC for this one, hate this game, but my family absolutely loves it. Oh well. If you love Quiplash, give this one a try. You won't be disappointed.
CIVIC DOODLE: When I first saw this game, I was confused and annoyed. "They're making a Jackbox game out of the draw-something-and-other-people-add-onto-it game? How could you possibly make that fun?!" After playing it for the first time, though... I can now think of at least 10 ways they made it fun. Not only are the art possibilities endless, but the titles you can give the finished murals can be just as messed up. The emojis are a great way to earn bonus points and keep the non-drawers entertained with judging the on-screen drawings... or just spam the purple bananas (eggplants) until one racks up OVER A HUNDRED of them. Yeah, I've done that on more than one occasion... The final round is also really intense when EVERYONE draws at once, collaboratively drawing a face, family, or pet. The game would be one of my favorites... if it wasn't so freaking long. Seriously, I've gotten over Tee K.O.'s length, but this just drags along. It even seems LONGER than Tee K.O. sometimes, which SHOULD BE IMPOSSIBLE. The game does remove a round if enough players join in, in order to balance the time a bit more, but 5 players seems to be the sweet spot of time elongation. I really like this game, but DO NOT play it if you're in a time crunch.
To conclude, games like Quiplash will be missed by us Jackbox fans, but Survive The Internet (not putting it by its accidentally disgusting acronym, LOL) and Bracketeering will definitely mend the void, along with the other games in this fourth pack. Here's to Quiplash 3 and some awesome new ideas in Party Pack 5! Cheers!

So far I like this software a lot and have been enjoying it :)
Cons:
-Although there is a fair amount of variety in the tiles available, this program could definitely benefit from more tiles & objects (this would make it much more versatile). I would suggest less of a focus on making slightly different versions of the same type of object (e.g. 5 different workshop table layouts; 3 different armory table layouts), and more of a focus on different types of objects (e.g. singular weapons, curtains, villager hut icon, jewelry, pile of garbage, white puddle - so it can be readily tinted to serve as blood, water, acid, etc. as needed - I'd love to see any and all of these things). It is nice to have the slightly different versions of the same type of item, but I would personally prioritize variety in the types of items over variety in the styles of a particular item.
-The art style is inconsistent. This is both a pro and a con in that, if you don't like one style, there are others to choose from. On the other hand, while some objects overlap between sets, there are other objects that you'll only find in one set (thus having to use an inconsistent art style if you want that particular item on your map). This doesn't matter too much to me, since it still serves my needs quite well, but I could see this being an issue for less casual gamers :)
Pros:
-It is easy to pick up and use (not too much of a learning curve)
-You can make a variety of different maps (which look decent) quickly and easily
-Has tiles & objects that are useful for making world maps as well as for making individual houses and outdoor (e.g. cave, forest) settings
-Appears to be updated roughly once a month as of this writing - which is to say that the creator(s) are attentively continuing to develop this product.
-From what I've seen, the creator(s) are responsive to the issues brought up in the discussion boards for this product (e.g. the undo button issues, which have been fixed)
-You can customize effects layers to change the portrayal of each item (or multiple items, as you can save your effect layer combinations) with regard to shading, tint, sharpness of edges, and inner/outer glow. You can also flip things around and shrink/enlarge them, which adds further variety of objects.
-Quick and easy exporting of completed maps to Fantasy Grounds
Overall, this is good software for the quick and easy construction of simple virtual tabletop gaming maps and I would recommend it to non-professionals like myself (i.e. GMs who just need some software to make some quick maps). With the addition of more content (objects and tiles), this software could easily be bumped up to fantastic.
*Side note: I notice some of the other reviews mention objects they place "randomly disappearing". Highlight the object you want to see and click "top" under layers (right side of screen). My wager is that the things aren't actually going anywhere; the program just thinks you want them underneath what is already there. Designate the object you want on top as part of the "top" layer so that the program understands where you want it. Hope that helps :)

It's coming up to Halloween so I was digging into my games library for something a bit spooky to get me in the mood. Stories Untold caught my attention and I started to play it – and didn't stop until I had completed it.
I'm old enough and ugly enough to remember the golden era of text adventures. One of my first ever games was the 1982 BBC Micro release of The Philosopher’s Quest which both hooked me and flummoxed me in equal measures and is, without question, one of the games that turned me into the gamer I am today. (I never did get past the gorgonzola) When I began Stories Untold I gleefully dove into the old habit of ‘using’ ‘pulling’ ‘opening’ and attempting to look at everything even vaguely mentioned in the text and loved every second of it!
This game managed to be nostalgic, clever and original all at the same time, which is a hard balancing act for anyone to accomplish. The puzzles were straight forward and challenging in equal measure, with a couple being downright devilish. Add to that a really atmospheric soundtrack and some excellent voice-acting and you’re on to a winning gaming experience and I would, unreservedly, recommend this game.
It does, unfortunately, have one (for me rather major) downside. Without giving away spoilers, you spend quite a lot of the game either having a light-source pointed at you or looking into bright lights, which were incredibly uncomfortable. Similarly there were a couple of times you were required to use onscreen manuals that contained the information required to progress and seemed to have no zoom function, other than a slight right-click which made very little difference. While this product stays on it current state, i must say to avoid it like the plague, but keep an eye on it for it may become one of the best softwares around for mapping.

Pros:

I first bought X-Note years ago, and it was the first Visual Novel that I downloaded on my computer.  I was really excited when I heard about old buyers receiving steam keys for the game.  Even now, I still love X-Note and look back on it fondly.
(My personal favorite character of the three boys is Oure because of his purity and gentleness.  In such a chaotic and enigmatic plot, Oure's dreamy qualities are beyond endearing!)
That aside, Zeiva Inc. weaves together an exciting adventure with a captivating story, filled with mysterious secrets, developed characters, and even unexpected romance.  As the player progresses through the story, playing through each character's route, the story becomes more and more clear.
The artwork improved dramatically from the original v1.0 release.  While some scenes are proportionally awkward, the vibrance and atmosphere compensate for any shortcomings in the piece.
The music is soothing.  My favorite piece is titled, "Broken" which plays during many climactic scenes.  The pianos in the composition suit the overall mood of the game.
One downside to mention is the saving feature.  After each chapter, a code is given based on the choices the player has made.  Thus, players must keep track of their codes if they want to load their progress.  I remember I had dozens of them written in my notebooks!
Even with a few grammar mistakes - English is not the developer's first language - X-Note explores paranormal and psychological activities.  While X-Note isn't perfect, it continues to be a Visual Novel that I will never forget.

The Darkness II is a very entertaining FPS held together by a great horror story that deftly mixes mafia crime with the supernatural in an original way.
What the game does really well:
1. The characters.
This game boasts excellent voice acting. In addition, the way the characters gesticulate and express themselves facially brings them to life. Pretty much all the characters are eccentric, distinctive and likeable. It's a shame the game is so short as it feels like you don't get enough time to really love them, e.g. like you do in the mass effect games.
2. The story.
Whilst following an arc you've probably seen a few times before, the plot, pacing and structuring is very neatly done. The tragedy, comedy, romance, mystery and revenge elements hit the spot. Just great writing.
3. The FPS combat is unique and a lot of fun. A lot of variety and interest is added due to the darkness powers. I also like how the upgrades make a meaningful difference to your gameplay style.
On the downside, and as others have noted, this game is quite short, and quite easy even on the hardest difficulty. The lack of challenge, particular in the last levels makes the experence feel a bit antii-climatic.
To end, fans of games with good stories will love this. This is a high quality game that's fun to play and deserves a third installment (and a PC port of the first game would be welcome)

Long version:
Ever wanted to be mafia's don? Or to have cool supernatural powers? Or just to be able to rip hearts out of your enemies chests?
The Darkness II is a neat short game which has it all: you are Jeckie Estacado - head of old style crime family (like in Godfather) posessed by the most evil force imaginable - the Darkness. , and starts shooting gallery in the restaurant house. Now it all starts again.
As for boring stuff: TD2 is a great FPS game. Shooting mecanics are good, there is a lot of weapons to choose from. No explosives though, but who needs them, when you can slice and dice enemies with your snake-like arms or create a goddamn blackhole?
Including RPG element was a good choice: skill tree was really needed in the previous game. It really lets you express you "killer machine" potential.
And for the record: it's really gory. Like Shadow Warrior kinda level. Ripped out hearts, cut off limbs and such.
In the end of the day TD2 really nice solid gaming experience. It can be action packed or drama filled. It can be really deep. I really enjoyed it through and through. Shame there is no sequel.

THE DARKNESS II is a terrific little game. I say little because the main campaign is somewhat short, (6–8 hrs, depending on how you play) although it is supplemented by a number of small campaigns that can be played alone or as online coop. But this lack of content is more than compensated for by the quality of what you do get. The best thing about TD2 is the combat, which incorporates some of the most enjoyable features and mechanics I’ve encountered in a game. The demon arms that Jackie sprouts when he engages The Darkness are great fun to use. You can grab, dismember, and disembowel enemies with ease. You can whip, slash, and decapitate. You can also throw all manner of objects, and it’s especially satisfying to impale enemies with scaffolding poles or to cut them in half with a car door. The weapons are pretty good too, and channelling The Darkness through dual-wielded pistols is as cool as gunplay gets. You’re also accompanied by a side-kick, in the shape of a hilarious Darkling, who farts and wisecracks while jumping on enemies and beating them around the head. What more could you want? Well, there’s a decent story behind the action and the voice acting is good throughout. The art style is similar to that of the Borderlands series and is perfectly suited to a comic book adaptation. On the downside, it is, as already mentioned, rather short. Also, when playing the additional maps you play as different characters, none of whom have the demon arms (although they do have the darkness and can channel it through various weapons), and consequently they do not offer quite as much fun as Jackie does. Nevertheless,  TD2 is enjoyable throughout and I highly recommend it. 4/5

The game is fairly simple, its one of those games where having a microphone is a big advantage, there is no side chat meaning you cant type. Voice is the only means of communication, consider buying a microphone before playing this game otherwise you may find it frustrating, one game item is the walkie talkie that allows players who have found the item to chat VoIP with anyone else who has the item you can also chat to people in close vicinity to you (you can talk to someone in your vicinity who has a walkie talkie so they may use it on others who have a walkie talkie in game). At the end of every game you will be awarded points depending on how well you did in game, this will allow you to roll perks.
Rolling perks is a very random process and almost every attempt will result in something different. Each perk has a main attribute (like 25% reducing fear) and also a disadvantage. You roll usually between 1-25% for the primary advantage and 1-10% for the disadvantage (like 10% less stamina). If you roll a really bad perk you are able to recycle them for points to try for something else. Perks are rated by a legendary system meaning some are common others are rarer, the rarity is based on the advantage vs disadvantage not by the skill itself (each skill has a different power,) meaning common perks can be very valuable. You can have the same perk equipped on as many counsellors as you like so there is no need for duplicate perks. Rolling for perks is fairly decent and you will be able to come up with a few builds for each character even if you only roll averagely. But the really rare (red ones) are pretty sweet.
It cost 500 points to roll a perk, there is not p2p option, all points are awarded based on what you did in game. Bonus points are awarded per level.
You can also spend points on 'kill skill's' for Jason there are many to unlock and even more in game based context kills which are basically environmental. They are all unlocked from the start they are great and you can see people put a lot of effort into them. They are things like slamming heads in doors, stamping someone's face into a fire repeatedly and pinning people to trees. Now that I think about it pretty much the entire environment can be used to kill someone. Its quite amazing, where they got the ideas from I simply could not even imagine, the violence involved. They must have had a 'brutal killing dictionary' or some such thing.
New Jason skins are awarded every level or so with a new look, new weapon, new strengths and weakness'. You also unlock new counsellor's every few levels. They have different clothing each having 3 different sets of clothing to begin with pants, tops and shoes. The clothing sets can be mix and matched.
Currently there are 3 maps, A lot of players are really strong at Jason. But the real fun is to be had in co-op as a counsellor, yes its difficult but its supposed to be hard you can score highly and not escape just by being useful before dying, so there's not to much to whine about.
The main point to the game is to survive Jason. The game ends after 15 minutes automatically so you can attempt to hide from Jason, mostly people hide to reduce fear which is one of the means Jason has to detect you (fear is raised by finding bodies and other scary stuff Jason does.) You can call the cops and after 5 minutes escape to them (this requires you to fix the fuse box, which requires a fuse, then you have to call them, its harder than it sounds.) There are 3 vehicles that require certain parts to be able to use then you may use these to escape with 2 or more of the players depending on the vehicle you fixed. The only problem is Jason is super hard and can stop a car by punching it.
Do I like this game, yes. Its a super idea in a totally original environment. I hope you understand this is an honest review, I don't believe in the recent spate of interweb rumors concerning 'loss of constitutional rights.' Its fairly normal internet stuff I just hope you see through it as gossip and recognise this game is pretty decent. The only down side I would say this game has is the same with all co-op games and that is the company you end up having to play with, some players do manager to sabotage games by grouping up and playing with Jason to 'power level' all be it somewhat clumsily, it can be a pain and fairly tedious (obviously they are not supposed to do that, but its a fairly large oversight in the games mechanics and should be mentioned.) Also some players like to be annoying and they experience a fair amount of success.
To sum up the game briefly, its a game like any other, and it has shady areas sure, some dodgy moment's like weird animations, It feels fairly clumsy and cheap sometimes, particularly driving a vehicle. After playing a while you kind of get used to it. You can have a lot of fun and it has a decent perk system with genuine golden moments and its not in development so the game is fairly trim.
You can have a lot of fun for well over 50 hours here, if that's worth £30 to you then by all means ignore the gripers.

In my opinion:
- Graphics: enjoyable, big maps with a beautiful decor: huge buildings, ruins, hills and so on.
- Atmosphere: smokes, dark, anomalies. Represent the pure post-apocalyptic sphere.

Overlord is in the simpliest words a small,tactical slaughter fest with a short simple story. The game is fairly old and isn't the best looking title however that is not what the game is about. It's about going around with your horde of minions and killing everything insight. The game has a little sense of humour which is fairly light and is not that difficult and you can simply send waves after waves of minions to beat enemies. The game has a very linear range of minions Brown(basic starting units mainly for straight up fighting), Reds (Putting out fires and ranged units), Greens (Stealth weak units which can remove poisonous  plants) and finally Blues (weakest unit with the abilty to revieve fallen minions). You must unlock the Reds first then it is up to you if you want to unlock the greens or the blues. I perfer to unlock the Greens then the Blues as i perfer the Greens. The game has you go around killing "Heroes" who have fallen to evil. The heros are a Halfing King, an Elf hero (who has became a tree), Paladin, a Dwarf king, a huge warrior and a Wizard. The game then decided what ending to give you depending on your corruption level (if you have been evil or not during the game). That's it really other than you can forge three types of linear iteams (armour,helmet and weapons), fight fallen enemies in a dungeon, upgrade your tower (no really need to) and collect relics (statues to upgrade health and mana as well as unlock new spells). So to me Overlord is a fun simple game worth yout time and money as it is enjoyable and relaxing.

I recommend this game.

As an avid fan of Stardrive 1, I had high standards coming into Stardrive 2. I was surprised to find that the game had changed from a real time strategy to a turn based format, although space combat still happens in real time. The turn based format does not hamper the game flow however, and Stardrive 2 is just as fun as it's predecessor in terms of a space 4X Game.
Pros:
-Diplomacy system is greatly improved from SD1
-Space combat is simple, but effective. Your ships will have multiple weapons and can engage multiple targets at the same time.
-Ground combat is now a turn-based system, unlike SD1's "Land troops on a planet and cross your fingers" system.
-Ship Building has been simplified but still very easy to grasp.
-Unique missions and events featuring neautral factions keep the game interesting.
-Interesting and diverse factions with different personalities. Factions with similar personality traits get bonuses in diplomacy.
Cons:
-The game can be very hard for players not familiar with the genre.
-The game does not tell you if a planet is sitting idle and not constructing anything. This results in lost production so it's important you keep your build queues full.
-Less ability for automation compared to SD1. For example, you cannot tell your scouts to Auto-Explore, or your ships to defend an area.

Usual review caveats - The "Yes/No" recommend system on Steam is extremely simplistic. I'll try to cover both good and bad elements of the game and readers can make their own decision.
Edit: Decided to cut down the review to something a little more succinct.
Bugs and some dodgy design aside, let's cut to the chase. If you want a Master of Orion 2 clone, with a fair amount of bugs (although Zero has been working on resolving them), then great! Buy it, you'll probably like the game a lot.
If you're looking for Stardrive, which was a flawed, but an extremely fun and novel mixture of RTS and 4X with some Master of Orion character with some especially amazing ship design mechanics and that gave you the feeling of running a living and breathing real time empire, with some additions and improvements, then don't buy it, because like me, you'll hate it. This isn't really Stardrive 2, it's a MoO2/Stardrive inspired typical 4X.
Don't get me wrong, I love 4X games, but why buy one that is basically a reskin of a 20 year old game with mechanics that have long been improved on and, quite frankly, surpassed in every way? Be nostalgic all you like, but after a few rounds on any of Amplitude's 4X's, this is going to feel bland as grey buttons.
I feel for Zero, I really do. SD1 got pilloried for never really becoming a final product. A lot of it was unjustified - typical Reddit gamer entitlement that makes you ask - 'When you got 150 hours out of a game, how can you justify being so upset?' really buried it. SD1 was ambitious, new, and with a little TLC and maybe a larger design team, could have got closer to it's full potential. SD2 felt like that was that opportunity, but instead ditched everything that was innovative and played it safe.

Honestly the game balance is very poor. There are some classes with Massive advantages and very few disadvantages if any specifically Warden, Warlord, and Centurian. Some classes have virtually no advantages and are behind from the outset. The game design is stuck somewhere between brawler and fighting game, and becuase it couldn't pick it has all the weaknesses of both without many of the advantages of either. It's the worst of both worlds.
There are mechanics that care entirely about your reflexes with response timings of 200ms or faster. this is literally faster than human reaction speeds so you do have to predict them. A casual game this is not, it is very much designed and built around a hardcore base but also doesnt' have the gumption to focus on that either and the endgame isn't that wild in a way that a game like streetfighter or tekken might be.
The arenas are Littered with Instant enviromental death with a number of characters seemingly designed to exploit these instant death traps even in 1v1 modes. This, for a fighting game, is like the underbarrel grenade launcher in a FPS, but in a game that pretends to be more skill based and shouldn't need that becuase it in theory has actual matchmaking. However the player base is virtually nonexistant so fair matching basically doens't happen at this point. if you are a new player you're going to run into a brick wall most likely.
Furthermore there's a cash shop meaning it has internal microtransactions as well in a premium game, this is unacceptable and a blot on an already dalmation-patterned game
So with a fairly low skill ceiling and a weird at best game balance where the character that appeals to you may put you at a very large perminant disadvantage I can't really recommend this game to anyone. 1/10, great concept stops it from being a 0 but a poor attempt in basically every way for any audience.

A good, solid fighting game at it's core, with some interesting ideas, but it is ruined as your progress by the abilities granted from end game gear. It becomes less about talent and more about who can pop their revenge or abilities most. Some of the balancing decisions are questionable as well and game mechanics break down as a result i.e. increasing a characters speed so that some of their standard attacks are too fast and unblockable.
Single player campaign feels more like a continued tutorial as well. Not very engaging. I only made it 1/3 through. Story is bland and the dialogue can be cringe worthy, and at times even laughable. The over delivery of cliche phrases gives it a B movie feel.
Probably not worth $60, but if you have a chance to play, I recommend sticking to game types that don't allow gear bonuses. Especially if you're starting out fresh.

No Code and Devolver Digital have made something fantastic here, with a wonderful mix of new and old.

I gave this a quick test to see how I liked it and threw together a 80x80 dungeon map for a game without any fuss.  There isn't a lot of included content yet, but the workshop fixes that up (highly recommend tops collection).  You can import your own assets as well.  Overall, I found the software to be extremely easy to use, but not nearly as powerful as something like MapTool from RPTools.  I'll probably end up using this for most maps now just because it's so quick.  The export feature works extremely well.
I saw reviews talking about crashes and lag, but I didn't experience any of that.  I've got an SSD, 16gb of ram, and i5 4760K (mediocre CPU).  I doubt GPU factors much into things, but I've got a 1060 GTX.  It could be they fixed the issues, or maybe the issues are related to hardware limitations on some machines.  I don't know.  It works great for me.
I saw a review complaining about the lack of layers.  There are layers now.  The organization is a bit clunky and weird.  Everything you draw or place becomes its own layer.  You can select a bunch of objects and group them.  It doesn't seem possible modify something in a group individually.  Modifactions effect the whole group then.  So their layers implementation isn't like you're used to in most applications.  Most map editors have layers like 'background, objects, tokens, drawing, ect'.  In this one, layers are individual pieces of drawing or objects, or groups of those items.  It makes it tedious to go back and edit something.  I wish we could create custom 'layers' that obects, draws, or groups could be organized into... like catagories that could expand.  If we could name groups and expand them like catagories to modify individual elements, that would be good as well.  MAYBE those exist already and I haven't used the tool long enough to figure it out.  Anyway, I don't think any of that will be a problem unless you're working on a huge map.

This is an interesting game.  It is free to play, but like most games of that ilk it is pay to win.  I have been playing for a while (if you saw how many blueprints I have you would know that) and still enjoy the game, but there are many aspects that are a problem.  The first is that of noobs.  The amount of time that it takes for a noob to get anywhere is quite long.  Some of the basic items that require research and build should be reduced significantly.  Second is related to this.  That of build times for any new items.  The time it takes to build a new ship is quite long (some may take upwards of a month) and since you can only build one ship at a time, that is quite bad.  The third item is that of the speed of which new items come into the game.  New items have been coming in faster and faster.  So since it takes so long to build some of the previous ships, you never have time to build the new ships.  The only way around all of this is to spend money and while I have spent a little, I am not really considering putting much into this game since money doesn't go very far in the game.
I really do wish I could recommend the game, but unless the build times can be resolved, I cannot recommend this game to a new player.

As you may know, The Jackbox Party Packs are only good if you have a big enough group to join along.
In regards to the games within the fourth pack, it's mostly tailored for Twitch streamers and the need for a decent sized audience. It has less to do with trivia and relies on the players to give original content. Jackbox Games can only bring so much to the table, so it's up to the players to bring the entertainment.
There are no single player games, and you'll need a minimum of 3 players for all but Fibbage 3, which allows for two to start a game.
Here are a few things to know about the games:
- Fibbage 3: Still just as fun, fresh look, and the only game that supports a minimum of two players.
- Monster Seeking Monster: Play this around your friends if you dare, but not with family. That would be awkward. Popular game in streams. Catchy music and very unpredictable. Also, the 8th player is the audience.
- Survive The Internet: Confusing at first, but a good game to play. May not be as popular as the others in the pack.
- Bracketeering: Geared towards online streams and a large audience. Good luck trying to find 16 players in the same room...
- Civic Doodle: If people are willing to draw, this game is extremely fun. Music is fun and fits the game perfectly.
JBPP4 may not have another edition of Quiplash, but it does what it can to stir up some fun. If you are the type to want to start a party when others won't, this is for you.
Bonus note: you can buy the soundtracks for JBPP3 and JBPP4, or stream it in Spotify.

I really want to like this program, it's helped me out in a jam when I needed a quick map for something specific, but in its current state I spend 80% fighting it. I frequently lose the ability to place new objects, having to restart the program frequently. One would assume you'd just need to deselect the current object but that doesn't work (and I had to actually google how to deselect something as it's that unintuitive). The lack of layers really makes it frustrating to build anything complicated, as half the time you try to place something new you end up picking it up and screwing it up or somehow changing the texture of something you've already placed. The move tool is hilariously broken, the object you're trying to move always ending a random distance from where you actually dropped it, seemingly chosen by some divine phenomenom not for mortals to understand. While I'm not expecting a massive amount of textures and objects to use as a base, the ones it starts with are seriously lacking. I don't remember how much I paid for this, but it probably was too much.
Wouldn't recommend, unless you only need to make quick square rooms.

Yes. Yes I got it. I even saw it coming, but being well-telegraphed doesn't make a lousy writing trope any less bad.
And it's a shame that it wound up this way; I was a fan of The House Abandon and was excited for there to be three more episodes.  There's a lot of incredibly clever game design at work here.  I could have even swallowed the cliche 'twist' if they had more restraint and left it as nothing more than clues and subtext, leaving it for the player to figure out for themselves.
It's not a total loss and I wish that Steam had some sort of middle-ground option when it comes to these reviews.  I'm mad because I was really enjoying the game until it went full bore on explaining itself and fizzling all the atmosphere and intrigue that it had built up.

Overlord has interesting game mechanics that enables you to command an army of his own to defeat enemies. The Overlord himself is quite weak while the character building is mainly focus on the minions the player command. This tests the your ability to strategize your minion types and how well you control them. It makes the game quite fun when you overcome a challenge that overwelms both you and your army. But I wouldn't recommand (or try to get it at discounted price) because of some major (imho) flaws.
I am 8 hours into this game while writing this review. That is because this game makes you run around way too much. It feels like this game is designed to deliberately waste your time. First of all, there is no map feature. No compass of any sort. I sometimes agree that map is distracting in a HUD, but this game requires you countless times to obtain a specific item (those ♥♥♥♥ing sticks) in a dungeon in order to progress to the next part. Without a map, you will make a wrong turn occasionally. Sometimes you are just completely lost and you have to go through every room to find the place you want to go. There should at least be some kind of indicator for me to find my way back to my objectives, but there is none.
The WORST THING about this game is how useless the waypoint gates are. They are completely not accessible at all. It's like a handicap parking stall with only enough space to park a small hatchback. Seriously, it makes me mad everytime i see one waypoint because they are useless. Unlike waypoints in other free roaming rpg games, you cannot use them to travel freely between waypoints. It's only use is to take you back to your tower (home). Well wtf, now they just waste my time for no reason. But wait, it's EVEN WORSE than that. From your tower, you can only teleport to major towns (which so far I only have three) and the last visited dungeon. The lifeforces (used to summon minions) are area specific, so when you run out, even when you know where to find them, you cannot go there directly. You have to teleport one of your major waypoints (which all of them are super far away from the location you want to go) and WALK. This is very serious, this is like the game breaking flaw that might render this game unplayable.
Finally, the puzzles in the game are quite dull (so far). Feels like a cookie cutter design. It follows a formula of: you can't pass area until you get the red minion. You get the red minion, but look this green gas will require you to get the green minion to pass. so on and so forth. Even after I unlocked all 4 minions, the puzzles are still boring.
This game is not bad by all means, but it could use a lot of serious work. Now I feel really relucant to continue playing because I feel this problem will add onto itself when I unlock even more playable areas. I really don't want to waste time doing things that make me not enjoy the game. Plus that old imp is just ♥♥♥♥ing annoying. Try it out if you have the $$$ since its not that expensive, but if your serious about how your time is spent, stay the heck away from this.

X-note is a visual novel that doesn't seem to be much at first...but ends up being a decent playthrough. I have a few facts and opinions to share about this game.
Pros:
+Good artwork
+Good audio quality
+The game has a full-screen option that actually looks good!
+Pressing "Esc" will just put the game into windowed mode. IT WON'T EXIT THE GAME!!! :D
+Very few errors grammar-wise
+The characters are interesting
+The ending is pretty good (well...the actual ending)
+The game is fairly short, which I like for a visual novel
+Fairly inexpensive game
+Has an "Extra Gallery" to reward those people that get all the endings :)
Cons:
-Sometimes the audio cuts out suddenly when advancing to the next scene.
-There are quite a few "repeats" of scenes...same dialogue, etc.
-The game is sort of confusing sometimes. For instance, it took me multiple tries to get to the ending that is the best ending (there's no other ending that anyone could possibly want...trust me. The good ending is the best ending).
-Sometimes the game will just decide to end, simply because you didn't put enough points into a certain ability.
-The other endings...they...well, they suck. Really, they do.
-Pressing "X" on the game's menu will not exit the game. It will lead you back to the main menu. Pressing "X" again will just reload the main menu...you actually have to exit the program by clicking the "x" that your OS uses.
-Sometimes the music....is just lol....
Overall, I recommend X-Note. It's worth a play. I'd recommend getting it at humblebundle while it's still $1. However, it's definitely not worth $20...I'd try and get it on sale for $5 or lower. Hope this review helped!

Ah, X-note. I started playing this game because of Area-X, and before I played Rexus' path I realized I didn't want to be spoiled for X-note and thus downloaded it to play.
My recommendation for doing the routes: Yuon - Oure - Anon. Even Zeiva recommends doing Yuon's route before Anon's. The way I see this: Yuon's route establishes the game to an ending; Oure's route changes a few things in Yuon's route (kind of like a what if, but don't worry, doesn't change the plot), while Anon's route answers quite a lot of questions and mysteries that this game contains.
What I liked:
- mini-games were related to the story plot
- the artwork - anyone who likes Japanese artwork will like this one
- the story plot was nice, although interestingly you don't find out the mysteries all in one path (perhaps a smart move by Zeiva to get people to replay routes), although
- the characters, while at first glance look similar to otome archetypes, are actually deconstructed (to some extent) in their routes, especially Oure and Anon. Much props to this, but then since Zeiva had intended to parody the archetypes in the first place it's really not that big of a surprise. Special mention goes to Anon; I didn't think much of him initially, and even during Yuon and Oure's paths, but his path certainly surprised me. A pleasant surprise, don't worry.
- the music was appropriate
What I disliked:
- the minigames were somewhat difficult when you try to max out the stats, and it gets ever more tedious and frustrating when you replay routes to see other endings. Much as I like how the minigames are integrated into the story plot, it also makes me grind my teeth to have to play Psychokinesis III for the Xth time (pun not intended). Although, with the save/load function, it does make it easier - I shudder for those that played V1 of this game.
- Loil.
All in all, while I did enjoy X-note, I still found Area-X to be superior. And I'm saying this as someone who has only played 2 routes in Area-X (Belph and Yuras), while I've completed all 9 endings for this game. This isn't a bad thing; Area-X being newer and better, means that Zeiva is improving with time, which is always a good thing. Though, that being said, it remains a debate whether getting this game at $20 is worth it. My opinion? If you enjoy OELVN, and otome games (but beware that while romance is an aspect, it isn't as overwhelming as other otome VNs, like those of Voltage and NTT Solmare, for instance), and mystery and paranormal aspects, then get this; but if you're on a budget, you might want to consider other offerings.

The first time I tried to play this game, it annoyed me a bit. Most beautiful atmosphere, sure. But the camera movements were lagged and inventory interface was downright annoying. I gave the game an hour or so, declared it as "meh" and quit to complete it for achievements on a later date. That was before I managed to get into the house. After my success, I learned that I couldn't be more wrong.
is a tragedy, adorned with a love story, a murder, a forgotten promise and the cult of the Sacred Feminine. Our protagonist is an esteemed professor of history who gives lectures at a university in Italy. Important to note that he is specialized in mythology and folktales - because this is where social sciences tend to present complications fitting for a horror story. Life goes pretty much ordinary - aside some vaguely disturbing and symbolic dreams that he has been having - until he finds an envelope in his closet which leaves him with a sense of uneasiness. He avoids the envelope like the plague until his assistant conveniently spills tea over it, making opening the thing a priority. Then, he discovers photos of him in places that he has no memory of visiting. And the implication of a woman being there. He takes a pause, and mumbles to himself: "Anna, how could I forget you, my love".
We learn all this information from our professor's notes, meeting him the first time where he stands outside of an abandoned country house in a secluded valley. This is the house that he's been dreaming of, and he intends to discover more about it at any cost. I warn you: this is a "be careful what you wish for" scenario and it includes many disturbing symbolic imagery, knowledge of the occult, and the versions of folktales that Disney wouldn't even touch with a 10 foot pole. So keep reading if you are interested in a kind of dread that Lovecraft would be much proud of.
I wouldn't like to exaggerate anything, but the atmosphere is really marvelous and effective. Every detail is carefully put together to arrange the correct mood, empowered with symbolisms and background noises. Drawings and writings on the wall, lights flickering and beaming on furniture, random events and paranormal occurrences within the house makes you tiptoe, and jump at the tiniest of changes in setting. Yes, there are jump scares, but on contrary to a brutally gory display which we are used to, such events are presented elegantly with the usage of either uncanny symbolisms - concerning many, many weird puppets - or the usage of partial objects that would poke your unconscious with a needle like
did back in the day. All of this is accompanied by the most beautiful soundtrack, full with suspense and emotion.
As for story, all events center the cult of the Sacred Feminine, where female force is idolized like a deity, or even a paranormal entity. I was astonished at the amount and authenticity of lore accumulated in this game. Story and atmosphere combined with the theme of survival horror, I think Anna as a more female oriented version of
. We have a flaw in memory, an abandoned settlement with occult on goings, appearances of most strange and disturbing phenomenon and a mystery to solve at all costs, mostly to our own inconvenience.
As for gameplay itself, there are much that lacks, I won't lie. There are books to collect and learn from, intuitions to combine, items to gather and puzzles to solve. Both without a basic background on at least mythology and an understanding of societal belief, the game would feel plain. Puzzles and most items do make complete sense only if you are already familiar with pagan customs. It is a feast to the ones who are interested in the lore, but I'd advice to skip this game for the casual horror game player.
If we are to be straight with the negative, controls do suck. Okay, you cannot go wrong with the tradition of WASD, but camera controls lag horribly, and mouse sensitivity is abhorrent. You basically go pixel hunting to grab something you are interested in, and I have been stuck with inventory bugs that makes it impossible to go through your documents for more than once. You save. You quit the game. You restart, reload. This is a thing now. Sorry.
Still, if you are persistent enough to endure controls - you get used to it as a nagging spouse after a while - and set aside the 3rd Party DRM that belongs to Kalypso, it is a good game. As a market strategy, a 3rd Party DRM is a really bad call and I've read there are issues of lost CD Keys about this game too. If you are interested, I advise to play the game in a 3-4 days period, complete everything and get done with it, for being on the safe side.
Is it worth all this trouble? Most would say definitely not, but I'm still glad that I was stubborn enough to go through with it. The true ending - it has 8 different endings depending on different courses of action you may take - baffled me and made complete sense for me. I gulped down the rest of my coffee and shed a tear, knowing what this whole ordeal was about. A tragedy, a warning, a mistake to be corrected, a demon to be faced... Call it whatever you may. On a last word, I loved it. I loved Anna, the Sabot Maker and our poor professor. I hope you'd give them a chance to haunt your subconscious too.

This is my very first review.
The premise of this game was rather intriguing. You control little little minions to do your biding, ala pikmin style. Except you're evil. Really evil. There is even a mechanic where if you go out of your way to do evil things, such as kill peasants, you receive a certain percentage of corruption. This corruption ultimately determines a 100% chaotic ending, or a good ending. If you lean towards being good, the appearance of the overlord changes. If you however choose to do evil deeds, such as kill NPCs, your appearance will also change. Spikes grow out of your armor and the overlord emits an unsettling red glow.. As charming as this all was, many things brought down my experience with this game.
1. Combat & Controls. Oh dear, the combat. It feels quite clunky. Especially how the overlord swings his weapon. It feels as though it doesn't have much weight to it. You have one standard combo. Also, attack is bound to the spacebar with no way to rebind keys! In no way is this acceptable! I would prefer to attack with my left mouse button. I know that the minions are supposed to fight for you, however, I would at times like to do some fighting of my own. Controlling the minions wasn't so bad at first, until I was controlling a large swarm of them. The clunkyness of the controls becomes evident later on as you gain access to more minions. You are however able to split them up into groups, which helps to a certain degree, but I still had issues when I would have 30-40 of each, all trying to collect something or kill a big monster. It felt like attempting to control a mouse through a maze that has a strong will of its own. You want it to do this, or go this way, but it just won't obey.
2. Graphics: Being a seven-year-old game, it will of course not look as gorgeous as modern games. The art style is charming and fits a comical fantasy world such as this. I find certain character models to be humorous, especially the halfings. There are graphical issues, though. All of which I will mention below under the bugs section.
3. Level-design: This aspect of the game really affected my enjoyment. Areas were quite large, thus requiring much backtracking. One of my main gripes in any game is excessive backtracking. About halfway through, I was in a forest. Without giving away any major spoilers, the task at hand was to take down some roots connected to a peculiar tree. Halfway through this ordeal, I had to go to an entirely new area to gain new minions just so I could progress in the previous aforementioned area. While it is nice to be introduced to new areas, having to move onto a new one abruptly was jarring.
4. Characters & Story: I wish the overlord could speak. It would make for some interesting situations. While some interactions are amusing, most of the characters are forgettable, annoying, or just plain cheesy. As for the story, you are given quests for each area with more quests given to you along the way, which all contribute to a story in each area. Which, in turn, contributes to the overarching story of the big evil baddy conquering the world. There however isn't much to the story, nor much depth. A shame since a story is a big aspect when it comes to the overall experience of a game such as this.
5. Bugs: This is what truly broke my experience with the game. At times there would be graphical glitches. Parts of the ground would't render properly as well as walls. There were Random crashes aplenty as well as random slowdowns on a high-end computer. Then came the infamous elevator bug
Elevator Bug: In order to progress in a later part of the game, you are required to find two missing levers to complete a rotating wheel. This wheel is used to raise an elevator. With the levers found, I directed my minions to move the wheel. The elevator arose. But something was wrong. When I tried to go inside, it would not go to the next area. I tried leaving the area, going back to the tower, even exiting the game and going back. Nothing worked. While not everyone may encounter this bug, is it one I encountered that stifled my ability to even finish the game.
Sidequest Bug: For contribution to the 100% chaotic ending, there is a sidequest in the starting area where you have the option to capture maidens for your tower. You must capture 10 of these maidens spread throughout the area. After finding 7/10, I came upon the next two. So I did what any overlord would do: Swarm them with 50 minions and have them carry her to the nearest portal! Muahaha! But, something was wrong. My minons carried both maidens to one specific spot and then they wouldn't budge. I ordered different minions to carry them. I captured them out of order. I exited the game and went back in. No matter what, they would always carry them to the same spot and not move. Thus, I was unable to finish the sidequest.
TLDR Version:
While this game starts out enjoyable with many quirks and amusing moments, it is full of many issues. Most of which become prevalent as your progress. The incessant bugs, controls, excessive backtracking, lack of intriguing characters and story as well as repetitiveness ultimately bring this game down. I unfortunately cannot recommend this game.

It's a great 4x strategy game. If you like things like empire management, designing ships, tech trees(not quite a tech tree but something better imo), and some good old real time tactical spaceship combat then this game might be for you. There's just one thing you might want to consider before buying it. Do you like a challenging game that has a lot of depth that is hard to learn and hard to master?
At first I found the game very frustrating. The first half a dozen games I played ended in utter failure. In my first couple of games the AI got a huge lead and dominated me. I did better in the next two and managed to compete with  and beat some of the AI empires but one still got a lead in the end and beat me. The last two I was doing well and it looked like I was going to come out on top but I ended up making a huge mistake and it ended up setting me back enough that I lost. I'm on my seventh try right now and I think I might actualy win this one though I'm not certain as I suffered a fairly big set back before I decided to turn in for the night.
A lot of peopel would be upset by this kind of experience and I can understand why. It's very frustrating to be beaten so badly and wonder how things could have gone so wrong. It can feel down right oppressive and if you don't enjoy a challenge then it is certianly overwhelming, but the thing that has made it all worth it to me and the reason I am recommending this game is because I'm getting better each time I play and I'm enjoying more each time I play too. The game has a lot of depth and I've only scratched the surface so far but each time I play I understand more about how the game works. I'm not confused as to why I lost so badly in my first couple play throughs now. I now understand the mistakes I made and I won't be making them again.
The game is not easy to learn and that is going to scare a lot of people away but it's very rewarding for the persistent. If you play this game you are probably going to lose pretty badly on your first games and that's a tough sell for most people. However, if you stick with it and keep playing you will find enjoyment in this game and won't regret the purchase.

EDIT:
After playing all the way through a game twice, I find it really worth the money. However there *is* one issue with planet management I see in late game - there are just too many structures I want to *build on each new planet*. Right now I avoid colonizing additional planets just because it would bring low benefit for much clicking - which is a wrong choice strategically.
A very nice solution I've seen in one of the fan-made old civ games is - *templates*. Imagine there are cca 4-5 templates defined (template 1, template 2, T3, T4, T5) and *the player choses what this template will build*. After that a planet can be assigned to 'build' "template 1" and will start filling it's queue with stuff that is in template 1's queue.
Now the obvious advantage of this approach over ministers is that player has complete control over what his planets are building, while *saving tons of clicking*. Plus when a new building is unlocked, there's nothing easier to add it to template 1 and have all planets using it build it.
Example of this template approach can be found in an old fan civ game "C-Evo"->menu->macro management->city types.

I really love this game. I got it a while back and rage quit because of a particularly hard boss. I just came back to it recently and it was a blast. I'd love to explain it more in-depth, but I'm a terrible writer, so I'll just list the pros and cons:
PROS

-engaging combat
-varied bosses
-surprisingly deep skill system
-item crafting
-lots of optional activities (fishing, housing, sidequests, etc.)
-really good pixel art
-full controller support
-cool area specific gimmicks
-works great in singleplayer and multiplayer
-endless mode for an extra challenge
-amazing sprite animation
-active developers
-good as a parody and a stand alone experience
CONS
-severe difficulty spikes
-stuck in early access
-only 3-4 few unique enemies per area
-a few too many crashes
-story is somewhat lacking

I think this was one of TellTale's first games, along with BTTF. As with that game, I will say that this is a very linear game, unlike their later attempts. If you're expecting the same choices and branches, you will be disappointed.
Tales of Monkey Island is... different from the older Monkey Island games, holding a very strange position in the franchise. This is, I suspect, the first game that wasn't made by LucasArts. Many of the people from the original games are involved, but there is a strangeness about the game that wasn't in the others.
The graphics aren't bad. If you've seen any other TellTale games, you'll know what they're like. The art direction is reminiscent of Curse of Monkey Island which is no bad thing. Voice acting is top-notch as always, with Alexandra Boyd, Earl Boen and Dominic Armato doing splendid work as Elaine, LeChuck and Guybrush. Music isn't bad, with some eerie voodoo music tied in with the usual Monkey Island themes.
Tales of Monkey Island, however, seems to rely very much on shock value, going to places where none of the previous games had gone to. The humour is still there, as are the quips and the fun puzzles. But it's darker, particularly the final episode, and while it did its job in shocking me when I first played the game, it's a bit jarring now that I know it's coming (and I'm in a position to compare it with Curse of Monkey Island).
Tales of Monkey Island is significantly better that the Remastered versions of the first two games (which I returned because of how uncanny valley I found the graphics), but not as good as Curse of Monkey Island. I'd rate it at about the same level as Escape from Monkey Island, which I rather enjoyed, but found a bit frustrating because of the inventory controls.
There's a pretty blatant sequel hook at the end, I wonder if anything will ever come of it. I have yet to see TellTale bring out a second season of any property.

I got major stuck on each game at least once--I don't mind this a bit!  I think the games were balanced and had a good mix of difficult and easy puzzles.  The gameplay is pretty repetitive from episode to episode.  Almost inevitably you have to cook up some sort of voodoo concoction to save the day against impossible odds.
Very piratey, endearing characters, great voice acting, what's not to love?
The ending of Rise of the Pirate God was great--I really enjoyed it, at least.  It was great because the events the characters had to get through to get to that point made the right mix of tension and drama.  You end up rooting for Guybrush, and caring for Morgan, and becoming involved in the story.
Each episode was about 4.5 hours for me.  It's a fun adventure series you can step away from and come back to if you want puns, great facial expressions, witty dialogue... somewhat awkward circumstances, and of course, voodoo ingredient hunting.
