Essi have paranormal skills, that we, as players, will have to train in order to move story forward and get different endings. When Essie was a child, her mother died. It was considered murder, but the culprit was never found. She left her daughter USB called "X-Note". Essi believe that it may be the key to solve the mystery. She is contacted by Yuon - student of very special school (Xen Institute), who is fully aware of her skills. He ask Essi to help him solve the mystery of suicide one of the founder of Xen Institute. All of it seems to be linked to her mother's death.
Game was created on Adobe Flashplayer and although this program works well with classic dating simulators, it isn't best choice for visual novel. I encountered issues with save files. I played Overlord back when it first came out, and remembered enjoying it quite a bit. I was excited to see it on sale here on Steam with its addon and sequel, so I picked them up dirt cheap.
The game is pretty fun, with the story being staged with you in the role of the villain out to subjugate any and all you come in contact with. You get the option to choose between good and evil, but it's more accurately evil and really,
evil. The game play is fun, though a bit frustrating when you can't quite find how to get to the next area. I realized how much I've come to rely on the objective markers in newer games (Skyrim and such), when I had to actually think about where to go. Once you get all four minion types, the game really starts to move, because more paths to success are open to you.
The primary negative to the game, I feel, is the minion control when using the keyboard and mouse. Controlling minions is often clunky, especially if you are standing just a bit too close to something you want them to interact with. It is exceedingly difficult to control the minions when they have to lure enemies to certain places or take timed explosives to certain points before they detonate (both happen a lot late in the game). It was really hard to move around while directing a minion, which made a couple of challenges lose their entertainment value quickly.
Besides those few specific examples, however, I found the game to quite fun all these years after my first playthrough. The graphics are dated, and the story is very shallow, but it was worth the couple of bucks I spent on it. Just remember you are playing an older game when you start!
Edit: It was mentioned in comments that I might need to note that my hours recorded playing are inaccurate. I have a tendancy to leave games running overnight while I'm sleeping or while I'm at work, so the hours logged never match my actual hours played by a long shot. Do NOT expect to get over 300 hours of playability out of this game. I have no idea exactly how many hours I've put in.

Anna is one of those first person exploration games that does not have a protagonist with an array of weapons; there are no boss battles, no multiplayer and no high-budget cutscenes connecting one stage to another. It does not mean that it is a bad thing. Quite the contrary - considering its low budget nature Anna is quite a beautiful game; its sound and music are equally good.
The story revolves around a professor who is haunted by an image in his dreams - a sawmill that is constantly calling him. He finally decides to set out and seek out the answer - Anna seems to be the name of the woman calling him and while the house is surrounded by a forest and spacious, green garden upon entering the game's tone immediately changes to something much, much darker. Our hero begins to hear more voices and here the game focuses on puzzle solving till the very end.
While the game is similar to a certain degree to Amnesia its psychological / horror nature is very far from it. There are some jump scares here and there but those of you already familiar with Amnesia may find these quite boring. However, the puzzles are interesting and the many books we find in the house give us the background of an interesting story. As for the puzzles: it is difficult to know sometimes what to do - the inventory can easily become filled with items and objects can be used not just with our surroundings but their combination is a must, too.
The Extended Edition is an upgrade the game received and the only version of the game that can be purchased. One of the new concepts introduced was the sanity meter - again, something reminiscent of Amnesia. Still, while wandering aimlessly and not knowing what to do I could not manage to completely go insane. I understand it would have given an extra ending (the game has 8 different endings, by the way).
Anna is a bit rough around the edges - its narrative is not the best and the puzzles could have been a bit easier. The sanity meter is good but as we cannot die we do not really have a sense of threat while searching for Anna in the abandoned household. Also, the Extended Edition could have had an upgrade to its interface as it isn't exactly user friendly.
Nevertheless, Anna is an interesting adventure game and while I said it is one of those first person exploration games here we have more focus on puzzle solving so bear this in mind when purchasing it. I recommend it if it is on sale and remember you can always use a Steam guide if you get lost in the narrative / puzzle solving like I did!
PS: The game requires a Kalypso account to be created otherwise it cannot be launched!

This is an all around good game. The art is fantastic and the music is nice. Well, the music is good, but it also sort of fades into the background while playing. The story is interesting and changes depending on the route you're taking making each play through less same-y.
When it comes to playing the game it's both straight forward and not at the same time. There's a reason there are
on the creator website and it's because you'll probably get only bad endings without them. They're official and mostly spoiler free, doing little but say what choices to make and what skills to raise by when.
The actual gameplay is simple, every day you play a minigame to raise one of three psychic abilities and every so often you pick between choices, standard visual novel stuff. The minigames start off simple and grow harder as the story progresses, but you can save before trying, and fail a few times in a row before you have to either reload a save or fail for the day.
One thing that is fairly lacking is how the abilities play into the game. You have to have certain abilities at certain levels to proceed and each love interest (Yuon, Oure, and Anon) has one that is extra important to their route. Otherwise, they aren't tied to the game. Skill level doesn't change dialogue, add extra scenes (except one additional scene after each LI's good ending), or require you to actually use them. Fairly anticlimactic really.
As I said before, there are three love interests: Yuon, Oure, and Anon. I've gone through each of their routes, obtaining both their good and bad endings. I really enjoy all of them and recommend saving Anon for last. While you have to go through the same basic story to get through each route, the overall story you see changes a lot depending upon the route you're taking. It's both good and bad that you can't skip through already seen text, as there's little to the game that is superfulous and not plot related. However, going on your fourth time through it can get a little annoying with reading the stuff you just read thirty minutes ago again.
To simplify things I'd make
, before making any choice, one for each LI (preferably one save per page), then again at the
to let you go for both their good or bad endings. And really, use the
. Do yourself a favor.

I find this to be a great game, but there are some issues. For one, there's no voice acting. This game could heavily benefit from voice acting in that it's very quiet, other than the amazing soundtrack. Secondly, the video options menu is painfully limited. You have the option to swap between preset video qualities ranging from "Fastest" to "Best," but they have no description of what changes what. You have your average AA options, 0-8 evens. You can set V-Sync and Fullscreen. Lastly you can change resolution. That's it, except for the option to turn off GNN, which it provides no explanation of. The only audio options you get are sliders for FX and Music, but no more. Not even a keybind menu.
Unfortunately, you are also left in the dark when it comes to information on ships, at least from what I can see. When lookign at the ships I can construct, I am not given any explanation of what they are or what they can do. The best I can do is guess based on the name.
The positives include great combat. It's easy to learn and very fluid. You can even go so far as to change the engage distance on individual ships, something that I haven't found before. Granted, I've never really played 4x games too often.
Another positive is the interface. The interface is neat and well designed, and allows for quick access to many things, with preset shortcuts to certain menus. I also found the art style for most things to be very beautiful, and even animations for the characters are present.
Overall, I would give this game a 7/10, and I recommend it to any who like the 4x genre.

You'll be seeing a lot of "negative" reviews that say this game is too hard.  Ignore them.  These people are terrible at strategy games.  I won my first game on easy, which, while challenging at the beginning when I had no idea what to do, quickly lived up to its name.  As I write this, I'm currently blazing through my first normal game as a cybernetic civilization where I basically wasted my first 60 turns doing jack squat.  If this game is too hard for you, go play baby's first tbs, the garbage known as Civilization V.
That being said, I was originally wary of this game.  StarDrive 1 was a bundle of broken promises and not a very good game, and made me wary of anything with an 'early access' label on it.  To this day I'm still annoyed at just what 'could have been' if the game had ever actually been finished.  I was never going to buy this game, but I saw that it had gone from real time to turn based and talked to a few people with decent amounts of played time, and decided to try it out.  I was not disappointed.  It is a good game.  Not a spiritual successor to MOO2, but it comes bloody close.  With a little more work and polish (or even a single, well made expansion pack) this could be the game moo fans have been waiting for.
Just remember this -  mass drivers.  Mass drivers everywhere.

Potential to be the most fun and epic multiplayer survival game. However, development has overlooked some severe game breaking things that should've been fixed already. Here's a short list:
(1) Objects becoming bugged. You die with the keys on you, they get "lost" so nobody can pick them up even if they can see it on the ground. You die while putting the battery in the car, the battery gets stuck on the hood of the car and nobody can pick it up. The game is full of stupid bugs like this that just shouldn't happen.
(2) Jason going into combat mode can block flares, firecrackers, traps. Remove the "stun immunity" from combat mode blocking. Just make it a straight damage reduction. Problem solved.
(3) Hiding places (beds, closets, tents, etc.) are useless. This could make the game great but it doesn't. Except the humorous moments when you are already dead and spectating and watch some dumb noob try to hide from Jason just to die 5 seconds later.
(4) It's pretty rare for any quick play match to not have at least 1-2 losers quit as soon as the match starts because they didn't get picked as Jason. Put a 15 minute penalty on anyone leaving a match before they die. Give disconnected players a chance to rejoin a match. This isn't complicated.
(5) Tommy Jarvis bugging out on spawn. Can be extremely frustrating for both the counselors and the Jason player when everyone is dead but a Tommy character is "alive" though not controlled by anybody.
(6) Combat glitchy. Attack distances need tweaking. Should be able to adjust attack angle all during the swing. It's too easy for a Jason player to backpedal or sidestep and counter.
(7) Jason completely immune to damage when stunned. Would make it much better if counselors could keep smacking him around, and if he could struggle back but not grab people while recovering from a stun.
(8) Chase mechanics. Something needs to be adjusted here. Maybe give Jason a 5% base movement speed and give counselors 10-15% more stamina. Make him rely more on knife shots to slow people, and his OP shift to catch up to them and his morphing to jump ahead of them. As it is, high stamina + speed characters can outrun Jason indefinitely with the right perks, and the slow fat kids are too easy to run down.
All this being said... this game has tons of potential. It's VERY fun at times. If you have a group of friends and decide that Jason should only be allowed to kill people by environment kills, it becomes a very good experience.
Or if you play like me and when you spawn as Jason, spend the first few minutes setting up traps, breaking windows, knocking out power, and taking a few knife shots or axe swings at the counselors but not actually trying to kill them, they get a real chance to fight back and survive and make it a fun match. It's far too easy for Jason to kill a player in the first 30 seconds of the match because they were unfortunate enough to spawn right next to the 4-seater or the fusebox.
If this game's dev team gets serious about fixing the broken elements of the game, it's gonna be great. As it is, this game should've never been released even as an "Alpha" game. However, the kill animations, the friends you can make in game (actually some pretty cool people out there), and the fun you can have trolling squeaky teenagers with negligent parents that let them play this game, totally worth $40.

One of the best 4x games to come out in a long time. SD2 has phenomenal game design philosophy...in Most parts.
THE GOOD
Ship design:- This is by far the best ship building feature off of any 4x game excluding the original which manages to outdo this one just ever so slightly. You manage everything within your ship in a FUN way. This is the problem with a lot of other 4x games with ship building, they add a ton of things you can do, but it doesn't feel fun. You're just moving numbers about. In SD", you get to see exactly where your components go, why they go there is completely up to your combat logic. You want to create massive artillery ships with weak armour and then create some up close and personal heavy shielded and armoured heavy hitters to protect the artillery? Easy. Then when you've built your ship with a specific class in mind, you get to see how it plays out in battle.
Combat:- Superb combat. The action takes place as an RTS. You get to build your fleet in factories after you're done designing it, then put them together in a fleet. When that fleet meets an enemy fleet, you enter into an RTS strategy map where you can plan out your manoeuvres in real time or with a pause function. There is some UI issues which I'll go over in "THE BAD" section. My only other complaint besides the UI is that there really isn't anything to interact with in these battles. An asteroid battle or having to battle over your home planet, trying to make choices of attacking the ships that can kill your ships, or attacking the bombers that can kill your population would make an excellent addition to the ship combat. As it stands it's awesome, but with a few wasted oportunities.
Events:- Another thing that SD2 outclasses everything else on. Events make you feel like you're really managing your empire. In most 4x games you see something on the map, get the reward and off you go to the next one. In SD2, you can find things that intertwine within other concepts of the game. For example, you can find a world where dinosaurs live in. So you now get a new research project to mount guns on the dinosaurs... There are quests you can find, the usual $50 from every other 4x game, and events that  happen because of your own doing. Create too much pollution on a farm world and your crops are dust for a few turns. Build a ship production line on a lava planet and you might just find a new way to make hulls more durable using that planet's natural resources. Events make the universe come alive and it follows choices and consequences in a logical and believable way for the player.
Tech:- At first I was disappointed with the tech tree. I've been let down so many times in 4x games before, that when I saw videos of it pre-release, I just thought there wasn't enough there. Well I was wrong. The choices you make in tech are really meaningful. You have to pick one tech out of a couple of choices and you never get to pick the other tech again. You can trade for it with other empires, or steal it from them using spies, or taking over their planets with a specific trait or tech. This makes trading for tech pretty important. But even though you never research all the techs, there are so many that you will be researching for days. You also get new techs that come up due to events in the game. Found a strange asteroid? Tow it back to earth for a new research project. Colonized a planet with a specific negative attribute? New tech (My only complaint is that these don't exist for every planet with negative attributes). Found a wormhole next to a research planet? New tech. You get the point. I really hope that this feature gets expanded on in a future update though.
THE BAD
UI:- There needs to be a more user friendly interface. It does a lot of stuff right, like showing information most of the time for example, but in combat, it fails miserably. Why can't you highlight all of your ships and have their powers show up at the bottom so you can click on all of them instead of each one individually? Same with troops. Why do I have to waste time loading combat with my scout, just to wait for him to retreat? Why can't you drag all of your ships and place them in a different location before the battle starts (or even save a formation for your fleet?!?!??) Why can't you click on an enemy troop with your troop selected for an automatic attack with your main weapon? Why can't your melee troops auto run and then attack when you click on an enemy soldier with your troop selected? Things like this are just not acceptable in this age of gaming. An almost catastrophic oversight in SD2.
Ground Combat:- This is not fun. It's OK, but it's not fun. Most of the problems come from the UI. So once that's fixed, we can begin to enjoy the simplistic nature of this minigame. Maybe an expansion should really concentrate on adding more to this mechanic.
AI:- the AI cheats. We all know this. The problem is that they don't play by your rules. I hate this sort of mechanic in games. I like the AI to play by my rules, not for them to get bonuses while we get gameplay mechanics. It's much harder to balance a game this way and I feel like this was a bad but maybe forced decision by the developer.
Generation Options:- There just isn't enough options for generating your galaxy right now. No slowing down tech or production options, only 100 planets, not being able to add custom races to go over the 8 AI limit. A missed opportunity here.
PERSONAL STATEMENT ON DIFFICULTY
I don't really feel like the game is too hard right now. I play it on hard as the humans and I'm doing pretty well. I feel like deployable shields are OP in ground combat. It's got to a point that I just don't lose soldiers anymore. My under tech'd ships are doing their job just fine because they have shields and a good formation with strong artillery, and the enemy doesn't do that. They get some missile throwers but it's just not enough when I have big massive cannons that start attacking them before they're even in range. I really don't see why everyone is making a big deal about the difficulty. Start off with building as many small ships as your empire can handle for free, then defend with them (for medals) until you get shields. Build 2 artillery ships with little armour, and 3 frontline armoured ships. All 5 ships with shields. That's enough to defend against any attack through most of the early game (safe till at least 2 fifths of the way through). I know the humans get some pretty powerful ship traits, maybe this is why I'm not finding it difficult.
FINAL VERDICT
This game is awesome. I've not been able to put it down since it came out. I know it was made mostly by just one man, but I'm not paying to appreciate the awesome talents of one man creating an awesome game, I'm paying to play an awesome game. And I can't say I'm displeased with that. I got a nice discount for owning the first game, but I would still recommend it even if it is full price. Just know that there are parts of the game that will feel unfinished. Specially the UI. As it stands, it never really prevents the fun parts from being fun. It's still a masterpiece, a slightly flawed one though. 8.5/10
MESSAGE TO ZERO (Maker of SD1+2)
Make DLC for this game. I waited a long time for SD1 DLC. Don't disapoint us, we all want to throw our money at you for DLC.

As for connections, yes I do encounter the occasional annoying interference that can come with P2P connections, but its not as pervasive in my experience as many make it sound (and I have a pretty iffy internet sometimes.) In fact, the only time I ever really suffered bad connection is when I was using bluetooth to connect my xbox controller, and that stopped as soon as I switched to wired connection. I only really do duels in PvP, and yea, I've encountered a couple salty people, but I just be nice to everyone I meet and 95% of the time it works. My biggest criticism would be the accumulation of Steel, it is quite an arduous process. Your main source without buying it is daily orders which amounts to only 800 a day from those alone. Yes contracts give a small amount but not alot to really make a great difference with how much steel things like emotes and outfits cost. My feeling there is that maybe there ought to be contracts that give large amounts of steel and small  amounts of xp (essentially flipping the roles.)
Bottom Line-
No, this game is not for everyone. If you prefer hardline rpg or MK style fighting games, this may not be for you. But if you want something new and exciting with learning curves galore and an overall fun game to play with friends. Then you have found a great game.

As many a reviewer has said, I wish there was a neutral option, as the game isn't bad, it's just not what it appears to be.
The cartoony graphics and action RPG like gameplay suggests that this would be a causal experience but it seems that's not the case, at last in solo play. Even the inaccurate aiming and controls overall suggest this isn't a game that requires a whole lot of skill. However the game is very hard, especially during boss battles. You take huge amounts of damage and the only way to heal is by picking up health globes dropped by fallen enemies. The issue with this system is they only seem to drop when you're at low health and during boss battles, they don't drop at all. This mean you cannot heal during an entire boss battle. It took me 6 tries just to take down the second boss.
If this were a hardcore souls-like game, that'd be fine but that's not the case here. The controls don't allow for fine aim or perfect movement, causing you to often take damage or miss attacks, something you can't afford to do when a boss will kill you in only 5 or 6 hits. If you're into very challenging games, then this may be the game for you. However if you're like me and you saw the silly graphics and causal looking gameplay and thought it'd be an easy game to sit back and mess around with, you'll be disappointed.

I have only played this for a couple of hours but I know enough to get a solid impression. As someone who has played Worms 3D on the Playstation 2 and enjoyed it as a kid... I have to say this is disappointing.
Firstly, the things that I enjoyed doing as a kid are all there. That being, the ability to make a few teams, and then a game mode where all the weapons are unlocked with no restrictions. Yes you are able to do this, but it may at first look like there is no way to impliment this in to a CPU game mode, but it turns out "game mode" is different to "game style" with the style being the mode you have created. It's odd, but at least it is in there. So other than re-creating a bit of childhood fun I used to have when I was 10 years old...this game is pretty useless, and I would say it is unfinished.
Firstly, there is not a lot of weapon variety in this game compared to other titles I have played in the Worms franchise (The DS version Armageddon comes to mind) which is a shame. And there is nothing particularly as wacky as the other games. Also, half of the sound effects from Worms 3D are completely GONE. And there is a lot less variety in the voices for your worms. The campaign modes are short as well. It has a new campaign (Which is either new to this game or was in Forts: Under Siege) and the campaign from Worms 3D. The Worms 3D only has SEVEN missions, and the new campaign has FOUR. And with each mission taking about 10-15 minutes to beat, that makes the game about 2-3 hours long. There are challenge modes and an online mode, but the online is dead and the challenge missions are pointless with no reason to play them at all unless you REALLY care about pointless score which you can't compare to anyone because there is either no option for leaderboard (I couldn't find one) or there is and no one is using it because no one is playing this game.
Only play this if you played Worms 3D and/or Worms Forts: Under Siege on the PS2, just to get a nostalgia rush. But even then you won't be playing the game for very long. I mean, I've put just under 2 hours in and I don't really want to play this anymore.

One of the most frustrating and deceptive games I have ever tried to play.
I didn't realize it was a game simulating you sitting at a computer playing a game.. but it still seemed fun.
My frustration is that the game is text-based... and it takes about 45s for it to load one screen with about 2 sentences... then you type 'open' or something similar and it takes another 45s or more to load a small amount of text.  So I thought maybe my graphics are slowing it down, so I turned them down... then I was forced to watch the intro again, watch the director and writer and producer put their names up, watch the slow 8-bit game menu load (want to hear the most annoying sound in the world?  It is this game's opening menu) ... then finally learn that the text is still about 2 letters a second.  No way I can play a game THIS slow.
This game is deceptive at it's core.  It is obviously ripping off the whole 'Stranger Things' vibe, and even copies the cover art almost exactly.  This should be your first clue that there is no real content here.  Fire up the game and what do you get... a game that simulates you sitting at a computer playing a clunky text-based game. Yes, it is a clunky text-based game that comes at you 2 sentences at a time and sits in a nicely polished shell of a game that is really just a picture of your computer and keyboard.
UPDATE:
Just a heads up, I tried it again... definitely, DEFINITELY not worth more than a dollar for this game.
Small spoiler for the first 5 minutes of gameplay:  You arrive in a car at a house... it takes about a minute for it to type that to you.  Your dad said open the glovebox before you exit.  I exited before opening the glovebox and spent the next 2 minutes reading about how the house sits next to trees... then I went back in the car to open the glovebox and guess what???  The game starts typing out that I just pulled up to a house and dad says to look in the glovebox.  There is literally nothing to this game but a small, forced story that totals probably 5 pages on paper.

Really glad I purchased this, despite some of the negative reviews. I have not had a single crash, even after making some quite large (50x50 tiles) and complex maps. It does take some getting used to how everything works and I recommend watching the 10min video a few times.
Not understanding 'layers' would seem to explain some people thinking objects have dissapeared, when actually there just hidden by a layer above and you just need to drag one of the layers to a new position (or use the 'To Top' button etc). The author has added an 'Undo' feature which works as expected, either using buttons or ctrl-z.
You can also import custom art, although its best to do it manualy and you need to understand the folder structure. See this link...
Only thing that does not work for me is scaling an object after you have placed it, although scaling it before placement works fine. Was also confused for a while until I realised your brushes are filtered depending on which tool you have selected.
Anyway, once you understand all the different features, this is a powerfull tool for creating very nice looking maps plus it has easy export options for popular formats (like Roll20). I give it 9 out of 10.
EDIT - Developer replied and scaling tool is meant for resizing rooms and does not affect objects by design.

Here's the run down: X-Note is a visual novel created by Zeiva Inc. You play as Essi, a psychic who's mother died ten years previous to the game, leaving her only with a USB flash-drive with a locked folder on it called "X-Note". Essi is approached by a young man named Yuon and invited to join the Xen Institute to investigate a murder and a disappearance that may be somehow connected to her mother's death and the X-Note. Essi accepts, and the mystery begins.
Before you even play, there's one thing you should know: Bad endings seem rather inevitable without a guide. When a bad ending occurs, most likely you will have to replay the entire game over again. This happened to me on two occasions, and it does get very tiresome. If you want to go forth straight to get the endings you desire, you're better off using a guide. Though if you prefer going on your own, by all means, you should play without a guide.
As a VN, the game is primarily text with quite stunning but unique artworks, with a few choices popped in here and there, plus mini-games to up your psychic powers (which I will talk about later). Sometimes the choices don't matter. Most of the time, they do matter and lead to a bad end if you don't know who's route you're going for. However, the routes themselves are quite short. You'll spend roughly an hour to an hour and a half going through one, depending on how much you struggle with the mini-games.
There are three guys in the game you can go for: Yuon, Anon and Oure. I've only gone through Yuon's and Anon's, but they were both really great stories. I especially liked Anon's, for reasons I will not spoil. I do intend to go through Oure's, as there are still things I have not learned and you don't find out every mystery in just one play through which is what I really like about this game. It adds to the replayability and enhances the mystery. To be warned, there are some things are easily predictable in this game. But other times, I was pleasantly surprised and shocked to learn what this mystery had in store.
Another key factor of this game is pretty much your "skills" of the game. Essi's psychic powers. You have the option to choose between Psychokinesis, Clairvoyance and Telepathy. Generally, one power is more helpful in certain playthroughs, depending on which guy you're going for. However, you're still going to want get them all up to max by the end of the game. I think the powers were a little bit of a let down mostly, as your character didn't change really whether you specialised in one form more than the others. There were not really any scenes where the outcome seemed to change drastically by what you had powered up more. I think this game could have improved a lot more if it had more focus on the psychic powers. They were critical in the big picture, just not to certain scenarios.
To achieve these powers you must go through different little minigames (such as memorising and clicking at the right time) which grow to be quite challenging as the game goes on. They were quite fun, but at times I admit that I grew frustrated with them.
If you can get this game on sale, like me, go for it. I still find that it is worth twenty dollars however, even if it is a little short.
Overall, X-Note is a really a fun game, with a good mystery and some rather dark scenes within. You feel for the characters, some more than others, and Essi turned out to be an interesting protagonist, with her own quirks and interests (like obsessing over the colour black and drinking straight black coffee). The music is rather basic in my opinion, but nice to listen to and not annoying and repetitive. All the music sets very certain tones for the scenes, which kind of reassured me about what was going to happen next. The story is well written with lots of incentive to go through all three routes, the artwork is unique but lovely in my own personal opinion, and I'm pretty excited to keep playing and go for Oure's route.

X-note is a game I have been following since the demo was released on Zeiva's deviantART page some number of years ago (the demo is also available for free off of Zeiva inc's webpage:
. Seeing the full game now available on Steam was exciting and I was not disappointed.
The graphics, the characters in particular, were all very pretty and cohesive in style.  Atmospherically, the combination of horror themes, music and lighting were done well and used sparingly to create dramatic effect during those scenes.  The music was mixed frequently to help break the monotony of background sounds on a loop; plus the music was better than anticipated going into the game.  As a note, there is no audio for the dialogue and narration.
Gameplay wise, the game relies on both choices and mini games which boost stats.  There are only 3 stats and only one can be trained via mini game per day.  The mini games are doable without being overly difficult for the casual player.  If you were to get a bad ending due to stats, the game gives helpful advice as to what to do for next time so it eliminates the need to go hunting online for a walkthrough.  There are 9 different endings, and each ending adds something to the overarching storyline.  My only critic of the game is that each path is relatively short and can be completed in roughly an hour.  However, the story is interesting, emotional and I look forward to the sequel Area-X.
One nice thing to note is that anyone who has already purchased this game off of Zeiva inc's website may obtain a free steam code by e-mailing them the e-mail address that they purchased the game with.  It's hard to think of any other company that would do this.

The cartoony graphics and action RPG like gameplay suggests that this would be a causal experience but it seems that's not the case, at last in solo play. The issue with this system is they only seem to drop when you're at low health and during boss battles, they don't drop at all. This mean you cannot heal during an entire boss battle. It took me 6 tries just to take down the second boss.
If this were a hardcore souls-like game, that'd be fine but that's not the case here. The controls don't allow for fine aim or perfect movement, causing you to often take damage or miss attacks, something you can't afford to do when a boss will kill you in only 5 or 6 hits. If you're into very challenging games, then this may be the game for you. However if you're like me and you saw the silly graphics and causal looking gameplay and thought it'd be an easy game to sit back and mess around with, you'll be disappointed.

I'm a bit confused why the reviews are so fanatically positive, they refuse to address the elephant in the room. I know we all like Frictional and Amnesia, but people are really blowing smoke up their♥♥♥♥♥ So far this game has been extremely walking simulator-y. You run until you come across an enemy area, crouch through it, then go back to running around turning power on and unplugging stuff. Oh, and reading computer terminals and iPads for passwords or to know which power to turn on.  (BTW, they can build a geothermal power plant underwater and superintelligent AI but can't get their tablets thinner than 6 inches thick? Or put more than notes and pictures on them? WTF? The dumbed down interactions with any kind of computer or engineering equipment completely ruined any kind of immersion for me personally) That's seriously as much gameplay as there is.
The good parts, the Sci-Fi and plot is creative, the atmosphere and sound design is creepy, the lack of HUD is immersive and functional, the way you interact with the world is cool, and the philosophical questions raised are all well done. Overall it's enough to make my review about neutral. If it was a book or movie instead, I'd be all about it.
But again there just isn't much gameplay, the most you can do is pick up items to learn the story, occasionally unplug or power something, and interact with computer terminals. Literally. The enemies are infrequent, simplistic, and easy to run away or hide for a second from. The experience is light-puzzle, linear adventure game with ambient horror thrown in, but nothing is ever truly a threat or even difficult.
It's definitely becoming a chore to keep coming back to this game. Hopefully the gameplay progresses to something more compelling, or the conclusion is enough to justify all the slogging. I really feel like Soma would've been much better presented as a movie or short film instead of a video game.
edit : I finally finished..... the ending that was supposedly so mind blowing.... fell flat on its face. I was expecting something that would wrap up the entire story leading up to it, or some kind of deep philosophical insight would be enraptured to me... but it was exactly the ending that logically should happen. And even worse is the post-credit ending, which completely ruins any decency of the ending that they chose to go with.... I'm impressed at how such existential ideas were presented and made so popular among gamers but overall I felt let down by the pay off, especially the way people were hyping it. And also that none of your choices really matter in the end. I'll say it over and over again, I wish this was made into a movie instead of a game. The story and sci-fi is interesting but there just isn't enough gameplay to justify making it into a game. I think a lot more could've been done with it in the form a film.
This is the last time I play through a game just to get to the end. If you aren't enjoying Soma by hour 3 or 4 I don't think you'll like the rest of it. Go with your gut on this one. If you're into it you'll love it more as the story goes, if you don't you'll grow to despise it.

In all honsety, I'm putting this game up there with the expert mode of super monkey ball. It's just insanse. It does share the tools that made smb great though, you can instantly restart a level with the press of the button, when you fail, and failing will come often here, you also get the turn back by one move feature, which is great for experimenting when your not sure , powering through with trial and error, or salvaging a run on one of the later puzzles. Together these make the game bearable.
You play as a square which flips from space to space, but it throws new things at you constantly. One of the most notable, is that gravity is determined in the direction that you move, and only for things you come into contact with, which is one of the hardest conceptual challenges I've faced in a long time. You'll have to deal with the cube based nature of the game on another level when you are asked to "cut' specific shapes into your square, using a raised platform to flip right, on top of it, and back down to present a different face to be cut.
Gameplay is pretty varied, and the game is semi non linear, as the unlocking process branches out early in the game, giving you some things to come back to if you are stomped to hard. For example, you can choose to work on whale after beating larva, or go straight to advanced larva, and later you can choose  (freely, you get them all at once)between planting, half sided, and Larva+Whale, and planting itself leads to a further choice of advanced planting and garden.
Every new level brings something new to the table, and every one of the advanced levels turned out to not just be a "more of the same but super long now" but to creatively ask you to do something different. Also intereactions between the gravity ball from larva and the whale thing... turn out to be absoultely insanse.
This game is pretty much  the benchmark for undiscovered gems for anyone who loves playing puzzles. It is almost entirely clever, and has an unusually amount of content for this genre of game. The time saving features make it seem fair. It does have a few sour spots... a handful of levels literally cannot be done in less than 7+ minutes, ramping  up already crazy difficulty on an artificial level. They are very rare and unlikely to be encountered by anyone less than 15 hours in, or 9 if you have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of experience.
This game will be in your libraray for an insanely long time if you have the will to beat it. The graphics... grow on you after a while. While you are in some kind of geometrical nighmare puzzle world, the background is like a petri dish under a microscope with cell things just floating around or idling in place, and the level selection just looks amazing, although it is a bit unwieldy.
If you think you have become the god of all things puzzle;that you will never be beyond a weekend stand to learn the mechanics of some new gimmick game and master it : then English Country Tune will be your final trial before you can ascend to a higher plane. And it might just put you in your place.

♥♥♥♥ing hell, this one's a doozy. Strap yourself in, kids.
First of all, the premise is amazing. 7 players running around while a serial killer hunts them down is fun, but Dead by Daylight already did that. Unfortunatly, that game's a DLC riddled grind-a-thon in which you'll be used to scrub the floor by players that have played the game for two billion years. What really sold this game for me was the Friday the 13th branding. That was what got my interest peaked. Playing as a stock killer from Dead by Daylight was a bit underwhelming, but Jason mother♥♥♥♥ing Voorhees running around Crystal Lake spilling people's insides out all around the place? ♥♥♥♥ing sold.
Although I didn't back the game on Kickstarter or Backerkit, I kept a careful eye on it, and when it released I got it as soon as I could. But then my first problem with the game arrised before even buying the bloody game.
$39.99 US ♥♥♥♥ing dollars. Not an amazing start. Now, I had no trouble coughing up the money, but here's the thing, This game getting the licence to a movie franchise might trick you into think that they are big buck publishers who have the resources to make a really good game. In reality though, this game was the result of a bunch of indie developers asking for the license. A bit rare for indie developers to get a hold of the rights to a movie franchise, But the Friday the 13th films are a load of B movie horror films that weren't very well received by critics, So as you could guess, not many people were quite begging for the rights to them.
So with that in mind I went off and bought the game, installed it, and got started. And I thought it was really good. Not amazing, but pretty good. The first thing I liked was the customization system. First, the you don't actully buy clothes or anything. You could have alternative clothing, but you'd unlock them as you level up, which i thought was a great idea. Second was the perks. There are three perk slots that you could use to equip perks, and the way you got perks was by earning currency called CP, which you get just by playing the game. Then you use the CP to "roll perks", which acts like a slot machine, where you'd get random perks with different levels of quality. You could get a perk that increases your running speed by 5%, and later on you'd roll the same perk, but this time with a 18% running speed increase, which I thought was another amazing idea. You could also use your CP to buy different kills for Jason to use, which was also really cool. Otherwise, CP dosen't serve much else of a purpose.
Then, you have different counselors that you can play as. Each one has their own different skills, Some may be good at hiding from Jason, some may be better at repairing vehicles, or maybe some can run faster than others, or can regenerate their stamina faster. I thought this was another great idea. And the other great part is Jason. Not only do you get to play as him, you get to play as every single Jason that has appeared in the film series, except for the one from Part 4, Part 5, and the spinoff films. You can choose to play as the Jason that appeared in Part 3, or the one that appeared in Part 6. The best part is that each Jason has strengths and weaknesses, just like the counselors. Some can swim faster, some can teleport faster, some can break down doors faster, or some can deal more damage when the attack the counselors with weapons. The only problem I have with it is that you have to level up and unlock the counselors and Jasons, I thought that they should be unlocked from the start, but then I suppose then there would be nothing to work towards.
Now we get to the good stuff. The counselors have got many different ways of escaping, whether it be by calling the cops, repairing and starting the car or boat, or even killing Jason by filling the given criteria. They can use weapons to stun and damage Jason, and distract him so that the objectives can be done. Jason's job is to kill all those promiscous teenagers before they escape. He can place traps on the objectives, and he can throw knives at them to injure his victims and slow them down. Then he can use his abilities to catch his prey, and finally, he can choose to slice his victims to death with his weapon, or he can grab them and execute an amazing looking kill animation. Playing as both counselor and as Jason is always a ton of fun, and I enjoy playing both immensely.
So, TL;DR, the gameplay is awesome, and I really enjoyed it. For a while. But with that out of the way, my only issue with the gameplay is that everything is locked in animations. Jason's kill animations sort of get a pass, but everything else is a bit tedious. Instead of just making a jump/vault system so you can hop in and out of windows with ease, or just pressing a button so that actions can be done with just a single press, you have to do a 2 second animation to open a window, and a two second animation to go through the window. And barricading the door isn't just "press a button and the door will be locked", it's "Go and hold the E key for 1 second and then you'll do this animation which takes half a century to finish because what the ♥♥♥♥ does convenience mean?". It could be on purpose to add a little more challenge, but if I were running from a serial killer, I wouldn't bolt for a window and then calmly open it and climb in at a leisurely pace like an eighty year old grandma, you know what I mean?
Anyway, the gameplay is great, although it does get a bit stale after a while. The music sounds pretty much exactly like it did in the movies, the three maps are really big, open and fun to explore, as well as looking exactly like they do in the films, and is a great homage to the underground horror series it sets out to honor. I'd give it a 7/10, maybe even an 8/10 if they add new counselors and new Jasons, and if that singleplayer mode that they talk about ever gets released, i'd bump it to an 8.5, or if it's exceptionaly good, a 9/10.
Overall, A 7/10, a great game to play with friends, probably worth about $30 bucks overall.

Personally I do enjoy this game and while this game certainly does have its ups and downs, I am not here to praise or criticize this game. I am here to offer a phenomenal 4 Cheese Ravioli recipe!
Here are the ingredients you will need!
Ravioli Dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 pinch salt, 1 teaspoon olive oil, 2 eggs, 1 1/2 tablespoons water.
Ravioli Filling: 1 (8 ounce) container ricotta cheese, 1 (4 ounce) package cream cheese, softened, 1/2 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, 1/2 cup provolone cheese, shredded, 1 egg, 1 1/2 teaspoons dried parsley.
Pesto-Alfredo Cream Sauce: 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 cloves garlic, crushed, 3 tablespoons prepared basil pesto sauce, 2 cups heavy cream, 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, 1 (24 ounce) jar marinara sauce.
1. Mound the flour and salt together on a work surface and form a well. Beat the teaspoon of olive oil, 2 eggs, and water in a bowl. Pour half the egg mixture into the well. Begin mixing the egg with the flour with one hand; use your other hand to keep the flour mound steady. Add the remaining egg mixture and knead to form a dough.
2. Knead the dough until smooth, 8 to 10 minutes; add more flour if the dough is too sticky. Form the dough into a ball and wrap tightly with plastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
3. While the dough is resting, prepare the ravioli filling. Combine the ricotta cheese, cream cheese, mozzarella cheese, provolone cheese, egg, and parsley and mix well. Set the filling aside.
4. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and pesto sauce and cook for one minute. Pour in the heavy cream, raise the heat to high, and bring the sauce to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the Parmesan cheese and stir until the cheese melts. Remove the pan from the heat and keep warm.
5. Meanwhile, in a separate saucepan, warm the marinara sauce over medium-low heat.
6. Preheat an oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water to make the egg wash.
7. Roll out the pasta dough into thin sheets no thicker than a nickel. To assemble the ravioli, brush the egg wash over a sheet of pasta. Drop the filling mixture on the dough by teaspoonfuls about one inch apart. Cover the filling with the top sheet of pasta, pressing out the air from around each portion of filling. Press firmly around the filling to seal. Cut into individual ravioli with a knife or pizza cutter. Seal the edges.
8. Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Stir in the ravioli, and return to a boil. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the ravioli float to the top and the filling is hot, 4 to 8 minutes. Drain well.
9. Grease a baking sheet. Place the cooked ravioli on the sheet pan and bake in the preheated oven until brown, about 4 minutes.
10. To serve the ravioli, divide them among four warmed serving bowls. Drizzle the marinara sauce over the ravioli and then top with the cream sauce.

Here is the short version of this review: game is priced too high and should be half of what it is currently priced at, too many game breaking bugs that have been persistent since launch, game is repetitive with little to no change in gameplay between matches, and the game's combat system is flawed and sluggish with poor hit detection.
Now, let's dive into each of these points:
Price: The game does not have enough replayability to be priced at 40$ the game does not change enough between matches and due to the innumerable number of bugs and glitches this game is not worth the price, I personally like to get at least an hour for each dollar i spend on the game, and for the first ten to twenty hours the game was fun, i admit but then it just gets boring and repetitive. And all of those hours were spent in lobbies with friends and to be honest i can't imagine playing this game without them without being bored to tears.
Bugs: the game has game breaking bugs that have been in the game for as long as the game has been out, for example when a counselor dies and his items are left behind they bug out and disappear into the ground to where they died never to be used again. These items are key to the counselors survival and so no items no survival. Another bug is how if Jason is blocking while walking onto a bear trap then it becomes stuck onto his foot and he can then no longer be trapped, so there goes one of the counselors main forms of defense.
Repetitive: there is little to no difference in each game aside from which Jason is played, the maps are so similar its ridiculous most people cant even tell between them, let alone care about which map is being picked. They all feel the same as well with little to no variation the only thing that makes the maps feel different is if there is goint ot be 2 cars or a car and a boat, otherwise there realy isnt any difference in the maps that makes them feel different. Additionally, there isn't even much variation in Jason's since most people play the same one's since there are just some better choices than others and i understand that in a game that implements a system that has differing characters with differing strengths that that is to be expected but it just leads to more repetitve gameplay.
Combat System: I'm going to preface this by saying that i understand that given the game is based on the f13 series and that Jason is supposed to be able to kill counsellors easily but since this is a game and not a movie there need to be adjustments, such as making it so Jason is not able to kill so quickly in rapid succession. Jason's grab range is also broken af and he can grab you from 5 feet away which is kinda bs. The counsellor's system isn't much better either since the hitboxes in the game are broken as all heck as well. And when trying to escape since there isnt any vault or anything like that if you get stuck on a rock that is maybe half a foot tall then you will get stuck and you will die.
Overall: Game is not good for long term play imo, playing wihtout friends is not nearly as fun and since there are numerous bugs and problems I'd advise stearing clear of this game at least until either ALL of the games problems are fixed or until there is a price drop, either way i'm pretty sure I'm done with this game.

English Country Tune, an inexplicably-named geometrical, abstract puzzle game. First of all, the soundtrack isn't English or Country... though it is a tune (albeit not an amazing one). And while this review may have started negatively, my opinion of English Country Tune is anything but. Simply because it is a very good puzzle game and that it's everything it's aspiring to be. The puzzles are based on those movement or arranging puzzles where you have to move certain objects to certain locations (some further research lead me to a style of puzzle called Sokoban).
Overall, the game has the feel of an end of degree, final project except for one difference. The gameplay and level design is actually well-refined with a lot of thought and time going into each level. The harder puzzles have only one solution with only an undo button and reset button to help you through (or help you backtrack). The graphics are rudimentary and there is no initial instruction in the menu screen. It took me a while to work out how to access the puzzles. And while the graphics are basic, they are perfect for this game.

To tell you the full scope of what this game can bring you, let me tell you a story. A story of conquest, Pollop treachary, and human insubordination
The United Federation of Planets, my fledling creation, had reached it's third star system of colonization. We made first contact with the Draylock council. War soon broke out but was ended with the successful defense of Earth. They were forced into peace and eventually became lucrative trading partners. Galactic tensions were high between the many newly discovered aggressive empires, such as the Chukk and Rayleh. I soon discovered a small spacefaring civilisation of the Pollop race. They were peaceful and docile so I let my guard down on them.... a huge mistake.
They sent a colony ship to my homeworld system and claimed a colony on a small world with the "beautiful" trait, which I had overlooked due to it's ironic toxic nature. Enraged they had the audacity to pull such a move, I sent a task force to bombard the planet out of existence... My second mistake. Thinking I was safe I continued to focus on the other larger, aggressive empire.
Suddenly alerts begin blaring as an enormous Polop fleet enters my outer space and begins making a beeline straight for Earth. I rallied the fleets but only about 2/3 of my forces made it to the homeworld in time. They has at least 8 cruisers with an absolute swarm of fighters. They tore through the orbital defences in a matter of minutes and outnumbered our ground forces 2:1. Earth was lost. And soon the Federation was left with but one colony.
Our last colony of Epsilon was kicked into overdrive mode and started pumping out a fleet, with a new flak cruiser to combat the plant swarm. The Pollop invasion fleet finally made to to Epsilon, as the fate of the Federation and Humanity as a whole rested on this battle. After a long and drawn out battle the human fleet remains victorious, and prepares immedately to reclaim the homeworld.
The fleet jumps out of warp and engages the Pollop fleet. Lasers and missiles are flying all over, Pollop swarms and human fighters battle it out zipping around the cruiser slug fest, with flak rounds detonation all over. With the destruction of the new enemy starbase, human forces plant their boots on the ground to reclaim what is theirs. After a lengthy ground battle the Pollop forces cannot withstand the human combat prowess and determination. The victory fleet went around to reclaim all our colonies and is preparing to take the fight back to Pollop space...
All in 8 hours of non-stop gameplay. This is the kind of story you can create for your empire. The challenges you will face and how you can overcome them using strategy and wit. Fleet variation and devised roles are crucial, as opposed to two walls of ships slugging it out as seen in games like Sins.
The AI's are good and difficult, but not impossible to take on. The game is so much like MOO2 it's rediculous, but in no way is this a bad thing. Spectacular visuals, awesome gameplay and the games create their own narrative. All complemented with the amazing and very suiting soundtrack.
The only things are that ground combat could use a little more polish and depth. Persistent debris would also be cool in the tactical battles.
Overall an epic edition to the 4X sub-genre, and truely the spiritual succesor to Master of Orion.

The game is based on nice story where a girl along with a fox set out on a journey leaving her village and family behind.
Little fox is her one and only best friend. Together they both encounter all the life threatening situations beginning with the polar bear and eventually end on ice-made blizzard-creating Giant man.
Both the fox and Nuna tackle things differently. The game can be played as co-op or even solo. I went for solo.
Puzzles aren't as tricky as they seem at first glance. Distracting and asisting at the beginning of the game, is fox's job and leading the way is Nuna's task.
Climbing the walls, distracting the bear or any other enemy, drifting the ropes down and detecting the spirit helpers are the things that fox has to take care of.
Sila is the weather and believed to posses a soul which is why the spirit helpers; particularly souls of animals that only fox can detect, appear to help when the girl and fox have none left to get help from or to move on.
Nuna is the one to deal with scavengers, to use a tool called Bola to break the icicles, catch spirit helpers and fragile wood.
Various "cultural insights" can be viewed and continued to be unlocked during the game showing how native people lived throughout years or maybe centuries on thundra how they ought to live just on snow, dwelling among the gusts of vicious blizzards, even high up on moutain's verge facing the unpredictable waves of the sea and keep out of the reach of the ursa that kept roaming on frozen arcs.
I quite enjoyed the game. It has not-so-difficult puzzles, we only ought to know few tricks and most importantly the direction of wind because that was, somehow, the forgetable part of the game for me specially when it comes to long jumps that could only be possible with deep blowing gusts of wind.

This software allows you to make dungeon maps (and even "overworld" maps too) that look very good, especially when you apply filters like shadows. Seriously: if you use good quality textures, the maps look like stuff you would find in D&D official adventures.
The interface is not perfect, and some features could be more user-friendly, which means it should take a few hours for you to really get the hang of how everything works. But once that happens, it becomes an excellent tool. So, if you buy it, don't give up on it after a couple of minutes.
Something that I thought annoying in the beginning, but now I find awesome, is how every texture, wall, and object are organized into layers, just like an image editing software. This allows you to move things around easily and, more importantly, toggle the visibility on or off in groups of objects. So, for example, in my maps I have a group of objects for secrets (things players will see only when they find it) and another one for DM reference (numbers of rooms, cues for encounters, etc.).
I highly recommend downloading extra texture/object packs from Steam Workshop. They're free and amazing. Another good aspect of this software is how easy it is to add your own textures and objects. There's a button for that, but the easiest way is to simply create folders in your PCs and add the PNG to it. You can also find the files of the textures that came with the software (or the extra packs) and edit them in another software. For example, I needed a green trap door. There was only a regular, wood color, one. So I opened the relevant file on GIMP, changed its color and created a new folder/file, which was then readily available in Dungeon Painter Studio.
TLDR: it takes some time to get used to, but it does exactly what you want, and the maps look amazing.

After hearing Rich Evans from Red Letter Media obsess over this, I was eager to try it for myself. I was extremely disappointed. While not horrible by any mean, it's my least favorite Platinum title so far. The problems are two-fold:
1. First, technical. I have a decent PC and I'm able to run some fairly demanding games, so I didn't think a port of a PS3 game from over 5 years ago would run poorly. I was wrong. Even with all the settings turned down, every time a swarm of enemies appeared or missiles starting exploding around me, the game slowed down to a near standstill (and no, sadly, it was not AR mode enngaging).
2. Even if I was able to play it at full power, the game is just not that interesting. The environments are bland, the dialogue and story are cheesy, and the cover based shooting starts feeling very repetitive, very fast. These types of third-person shooters are a dime a dozen; give me SOMETHING dramatically different to keep me interested. Bullet time and power sliding just does not cut it.
Rich Evans constantly lamented the fact that this game was underrated and forgotten. I think there may have been a reason for that.

The combat feels floaty and off, the minion AI is laughable, and the graphics have aged horribly. Worse still, it fails at it's most basic level, being neither funny, or letting the player be particularly evil. It's not a terrible game, but unless it's going for a couple quid and you really fancy a naffer version of pikmin, I'd give this one a miss.

Probably the best puzzle-platformer that I've ever played.
The PS3 has Journey and PC has Thomas Was Alone.
It's an enjoyable platformer in which you control and freely switch between a group of different characters, who each have invidual traits that suit them to different tasks. The puzzles vary from the simple "reach the end" type, to timed sections that often require one character to cary others and to even more creative puzzles that will challenge you to think laterally.
But what makes this game the real gem that it is, is it's story-telling. The main story is told through narration that also tells individual characters thoughts at the time. There is also a 'meta-story' that is told through short pieces of text at the end of each chapter.
All in all, an amazing game. Well worth every penny, even if you only play it once. I've played through it twice so far and I expect that I'll play it again, the next time I want a good story told to me,mixed in with solid platforming.

I'm a bit confused why the reviews are so fanatically positive, they refuse to address the elephant in the room. I know we all like Frictional and Amnesia, but people are really blowing smoke up their♥♥♥♥♥ So far this game has been extremely walking simulator-y. You run until you come across an enemy area, crouch through it, then go back to running around turning power on and unplugging stuff. Oh, and reading computer terminals and iPads for passwords or to know which power to turn on.  (BTW, they can build a geothermal power plant underwater and superintelligent AI but can't get their tablets thinner than 6 inches thick? Or put more than notes and pictures on them? WTF? The dumbed down interactions with any kind of computer or engineering equipment completely ruined any kind of immersion for me personally) That's seriously as much gameplay as there is.
The good parts, the Sci-Fi and plot is creative, the atmosphere and sound design is creepy, the lack of HUD is immersive and functional, the way you interact with the world is cool, and the philosophical questions raised are all well done. Overall it's enough to make my review about neutral. If it was a book or movie instead, I'd be all about it.
But again there just isn't much gameplay, the most you can do is pick up items to learn the story, occasionally unplug or power something, and interact with computer terminals. Literally. The enemies are infrequent, simplistic, and easy to run away or hide for a second from. The experience is light-puzzle, linear adventure game with ambient horror thrown in, but nothing is ever truly a threat or even difficult.
It's definitely becoming a chore to keep coming back to this game. Hopefully the gameplay progresses to something more compelling, or the conclusion is enough to justify all the slogging. I really feel like Soma would've been much better presented as a movie or short film instead of a video game.
edit : I finally finished..... the ending that was supposedly so mind blowing.... fell flat on its face. I was expecting something that would wrap up the entire story leading up to it, or some kind of deep philosophical insight would be enraptured to me... but it was exactly the ending that logically should happen. And even worse is the post-credit ending, which completely ruins any decency of the ending that they chose to go with.... I'm impressed at how such existential ideas were presented and made so popular among gamers but overall I felt let down by the pay off, especially the way people were hyping it. And also that none of your choices really matter in the end. I'll say it over and over again, I wish this was made into a movie instead of a game. The story and sci-fi is interesting but there just isn't enough gameplay to justify making it into a game. I think a lot more could've been done with it in the form a film.
This is the last time I play through a game just to get to the end. If you aren't enjoying Soma by hour 3 or 4 I don't think you'll like the rest of it. Go with your gut on this one. If you're into it you'll love it more as the story goes, if you don't you'll grow to despise it.

Rating: 8.5/10
NOTE: For some reason, a lot of my hours are not being logged in Steam for this game.
EXPERIENCE LEVEL:
BEGINNER/INTERMEDIATE
PROS:
1. Session mode:
This is hands-down the coolest tool I've ever seen to teach scales and jamming to musicians. You can customize your back-up band from a decent amount of options, and you can even choose the BPM. If you want to learn basics fast, this is the way to go.
2. Learn a song naturally progresses with how well you're doing. This might not seem amazing, but you'll feel awesome when you land that hard lick and the game rewards you by taking the difficulty up a notch during the next verse. Master mode (although I haven't seen it myself yet, aside from various youtube vids) is also really fun.
3. Riff Repeater & Other suggestions:
RS will automatically generate tasks to work on after you play a song. It might suggest using the riff repeater to cover a part of the song you struggled with, or it might suggest that you like at the chord book or play in the arcade. Ultimately, this is really helpful, as gamification makes it easier to keep working at the same song over and over until you nail it. Dedication is key when learning a new song, after all.
CONS:
1. Relatively small song list:
Sure, you can buy more, but each song is fairly expensive. Additionally, I'm just not a huge fan of the some of the available options. If I get bored, I might try out a Disturbed song, but I can't say I'll ever like that band (for instance). I know this probably isn't possible for the RS team yet, but I can't wait until we're able to play almost any song through audio recognition technology.
2. Random problems with hardware & tuning:
When I first booted the game, I couldn't get RS to recognize the Real Tone cord. Of course, the solution was as simple as unplugging the quick-snap adapter and plugging it back in quickly. However, I also ran into a few other small problems, including RS not recognizing that a string was tuned or that I was playing all strings at once (as opposed to fretting). In the end, nothing gamebreaking, and there are most likely kinks since this is a new type of genre (real musician music games? Haha.)
CONCLUSION:
Regardless of its flaws, this is probably the best thing I've spent money on in a longtime. Simply put, Rocksmith 2014 is amazing. I've messed with other guitar software in the past, but nothing like this. If you have a guitar, I strongly recommend picking up the needed Rocksmith cable from Amazon and a copy of the game. You won't be sorry.

Designing a good puzzle game is difficult. In too many entries in this genre, you will get either a very limited set of rule that does not allow for creative puzzles or so many new rules along the way that none feel properly explored in their puzzle design potential. You will often get totally trivial levels at first that rapidly evolve into extraordinarily difficult puzzles or extraordinarily tedious ones. The brilliance of Increpare's English Country Tune is that it finds almost the perfect balance and avoid all of these pitfalls to offer constant challenge and clever use of its mechanisms.
This is not the most welcoming game and some of the fundamental rules are a tad tricky to assimilate, but it is an extremely rewarding game packed full with superb level design.

If you pick up this game looking for an extensive or challenging platformer, you'll probably be disappointed. The game is relatively short, and the interesting mechanic of controlling two complementary characters who have to cooperate to pass some sections isn't really enough to make the the package stand on its own, even with the addition of the Fox Tales DLC.
For all that, I still recommend this game if you're into a story-telling experience from another culture. The game's basis in Inuit tradition immerses you in a gorgeously rendered environment, and in a kind of story that is unusual and interesting in a Hollywood-soaked world. Adding to the impressive atmosphere of the game environment is a series of mini documentaries on Inuit culture, history, tradition, and modern life, which are unlocked by finding (sometimes hidden) certain spots during gameplay.
Taken together,
combines a satisfactory (if not exceptional) platformer, a bridge into another culture, as well as a sense of the preservation of the memories a traditional way of life in a changing, digital age. Wrapped up with stunning visuals and atmospheric soundtrack, this game is worth your while, as long as you go into it expecting it to be just as much documentary as button pushing.
A good collection of block-movement puzzles of various kinds. The interface is generally poor, but the core game works and the puzzle design is consistently good, and that's what matters.

really interests me because it is about a story told by indigenous people. The game was first introduced to me by a professor, who asked us to write an essay about the game. It is claimed to be not a representation by other people about what the story is about, but a story to be truly told by the indigenous people themselves. And after all this time I finally got to play this game. And I can see the truth of the claim. It really felt like I was sitting around a camp fire, listening to some of my people telling their stories.
I did not particularly look for spectacular gameplay in this game. I want storytelling. And this game has done a great job. I love the way they include the videos interviewing the indigenous people about their culture.
, the gameplay is just too much of a downside, to an extent that even though the length of the game is not really that long (I took my time playing the game and watching the videos, and still finished the game in less than 3-hour time), it felt really stretched out and I could not say I enjoy every moment of it.
The gameplay started out fine. The game mechanics are simple but still interesting as far as platformer goes.  It does not feel repetitive as the total length of the game is not that long to begin with. But as the game goes on and more mechanics get introduced, such as to move spiritual objects using the fox or jumping as the protagonist in the same direction as the wind blows to climb onto a ladder, the controls seem weird. It is just hard to control in general. It became all the more frustrating in the final chasing scene as you have to use most of the game mechanics, and they are hard to control as hell. They are simple mechanics, but hard to control. Not to mention more and more bugs appeared as you went through the game. I got stuck jumping on a stick thrice in a row, and the protangonist got bugged out and die. Near the end, the ground would move such a large extent that the camera would zoom out and move so much that you would die standing still when the camera pans out all of a sudden (and it is not an intentional difficult part of the game either, it is just a bug).
Gameplay wise, the game could be so much more polished. I enjoy the storytelling, but I definitely would not play it again. If I would have known, I would just go watch a Youtube video of other people playing it. Playing the game by myself is just too frustrating in my opinion, and it is not atmospheric enough to make it a unique gaming experience; I cannot  get fully absorbed in the story anyway because of how bad and frustrating the controls are. Thus I would also suggest others to not bother trying out this game themselves. I also bought the Foxtales DLC, but I do not think I am going to play it. I would watch it on Youtube though.
One more thing. There are a total of 24 videos that you can unlock and watch in the original game. They are locked and needed you to unlock before you can access and watch them. The videos are what make this game special. However only most of them are available by playing and going through the game normally. I got 2 videos still locked after finishing the game. I have some videos unlocked by walking to a small area (with an owl) just adjacent to the normal route area, so I guess I missed 2 of them in the end... Since the videos are the core of this game (to convey culture), it should not be unlocked like Easter Eggs anyway. Or they could just be unlocked as you progress through the game, not by finding some random owls in the game, since the gameplay itself is already frustrating enough to deter you from playing.
Either that, or have some improvement in the programming of the game. I cannot stress enough how the gameplay completely ruins this game. The saddest part is that this "game" could be better off if it just aims to be a animated story or a documentary film because it completely fails to be a game. You can still buy this game just to support the spirit behind this game, but do
play it. Just watch it on Youtube.

Update 6:
The real review: the game is, as of patch 1.0d everything that has been promised.
The new research-system and exclusive tree is pretty amazing, makes you think what is best for your empire, but not just now, as well as in the future. Trade and negotiation becomes essential to acquire tech, especially espionnage =3 (all you diplomacy-enthusiasts)
Planet management is extremely nice, smooth and intuitive. It is some kind of known system, but it fits well in the game.
Troop management and equipment adds an individual aspect that I have never experienced in a 4x game before (I played most, beginning with Space Empires IV).
The turn system is pretty much the manual version, in my point of view, of the predecessors 5 sec turn instance system. With 8 AI enemies 5 turns, as for my machine, are 5 sec in sum. When needed, this system provides you with planning-possibilities you might and/or will need.
To criticise, in my experience, is the 8 ships only build list. You can edit it, ok, but I do not like to manually swap the updated designs for the older ones. Stardrive 1 had the better system with actual and obsolete designs, autoupdates and (for me) never ending design list to choose from.
Update: After long hours of intense gameplay, i came to a different understanding. Unique ships are worthy units. You bild them once, they remain in service till they are destroyed or dismissed. Mainline battleships are build often, destroyed often, and updated regularly. Even a humble frigate becomes the cornerstone of a fleet, advances through the system of achievements, collects experience and becomes even more valuable; even a carrier can have experienced fightersquads that are much more survivable and do a better job than freshly produced ones. This feature requires some micromanagement, but time is not a matter.
Now for the games key feature: Ship design
Everything matters now, not just the sum of components. You can armor them, outfit special characteristics.... Range, angles, everything matters now. Weight and other subsystem-characteristics are detailed and explained within the editor, so no more one-shot ships that need constant supply because their reactors are woefully underrated (engine rating should at least equal power consumption rate). Unfortunately, as of this build, the powergrid system (a rector only supplies power within a limited range) is lost.
Damage is applied to different sectors of the ship, is one gone the ship or station is as well.
I am continuing to play, have not encountered any bug within 8 hours of gaming.
Till the next update!
