I've purchased every release of The Jackbox Party Pack so far, and it's one of my favorite things to bring to any gathering of people. I only say this to help back up my opinion a little bit on this 4th installment.
To sum it up, I definitely think this installment is worthy of your money! I understand there are some criticisms of this game with it's content, and I don't necessarily disagree. In comparison to the other three installments, I'd say this one isn't quite as good as Party Pack 3, but easily on par or better than Party Pack 1 or 2. If you're simply looking for more Jackbox, and have already purchased at least one of the others, this is an easy pick.
Let me go ahead and give my quick opinion on all the pieces, since that seems to be a common trend, here.
Fibbage 3: Compared to the other Fibbages, this is my favorite! It helps shake up the usual formula with special one-off segments where they show you a picture or a celebrity tweet and base a fibbage off of that. They also included a new mode (Fibbage Enough About You) where you base fibbage questions off of you and your friend's response. Think of something similar to the game One Truth and a Lie. Not to mention this version has a beautiful 70s aesthetic that they really nailed, here!
Survive the Internet: Easily requires the most wit out of these games; if you get the right group of people together, this one is surprisingly great. Some of the topics within the game are worse than others, but overall this contains a fun range of topics and variety. A very welcome installment!
Monster Seeking Monster: This game may just be my favorite of the bunch! It really plays with the chatting formula in a way that no other Party Pack game has done, and it's a very novel concept to fake-flirt with all your friends. I think the special powers that the monsters have could have been more drastic and alter the game more, but they shake up the game enough to change the end result more than a couple of times.
Bracketeering: Out of all the games, this one is more bare bones than the rest. Basically, different responses to a theme compete against others until a winner is formed, somewhat like TEE-KO. The best moments are when the category switches on you mid game and makes your responses much more colorful in context. There's unfortunately not enough new events that happen to keep it interesting for long, since you'll be seeing the same answers for many minutes at a time. This particular game can surprisingly support 16 players which is nice, but compared to the others it's sort of a dud.
Civic Doodle: Watching one small drawing become an amalgamation of nonsense as more and more players add to it is very novel, and the last round, where everybody draws at the same time, is a highlight, but by the end it doesn't feel like much has been accomplished in the process. I'd rank this one a little highter than Bracketeering, and if you're looking for a better drawing game, Drawful is a better choice.
So overall, I'm really digging this installment! The small amount of missteps don't bring down the highly entertaining prospects of the others, and if you've been buying Party Packs before, you're probably used to having a few games that aren't your favorite to play. Based solely on Fibbage 3, Survive the Internet, and Monster Seeking Monster, this is worth it, so having the other two games in the mix is just icing on the cake. If you're on the fence, I don't think you should be worried, but I recommend you check out some gameplay if you're curious.

I highly recommend getting this game, *especially* if it's on sale. Just grab it, play it, and be blown away by how compelling such a simple game can be.

Thomas Was Alone is an abstract puzzle-based platformer.
The player guides a series of polygonal forms with distinct abilities through geometric landscapes.
Everything starts with the artificial intelligence Thomas. Thomas unexpectedly gains consciousness in a foreign land. Slowly, he becomes cognizant of his abilities. He can slide across the ground, fall dizzying heights without taking a scratch, and hop over moderate obstacles.
Thomas is quickly joined by other quadrilaterals of different shapes, sizes and abilities. A tall, skinny yellow one can jump amazing distances. A short, flat pink one can bounce others like a trampoline. A large, blue square can float in water.
Together, the group must traverse each level, clear its obstacles and reach the designated exit portals.
The level design, striking visuals and sumptuous audio are not its greatest assets. What sets it apart are the themes and the stories, all delivered in a well-written script which is brilliantly narrated.
Thomas Was Alone is a simple, straightforward, brilliant indie game and worth to be picked up.

Well I'm a bit more than 10 days of use time into this so I'm not exactly unbiased.  This software is very buggy, let's just start with that.  The more things you put into the map, the more tools start not working properly, and at times textures or effect filters just stop showing up.  I haven't lost anything important like that, and it will restore pretty close to before it crashes, but that is something you need to know.  A few of the controls are a bit hard to get used to such as scroll wheel sometimes not zooming out but flipping through object textures or grouping, but really I'd expect some amount of learning curve with any mapmaking program worthwhile.
I get putting a negative review to anything with this many bugs, but despite all that it's still the most powerful mapmaking tool I have.  I would rather save frequently and use this by such a wide margin and for one very simple reason - availibility of mapping packs.  There's a few megapacks that round this out nicely, and just creating my own packs is simple.  I've gone through 2 or 3 "free" tools that have some complicated packmaking process and that killed them for me.  This one is just making a couple folders and dumping in stuff.  No size restrictions, no fancy list files, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hoops.  There's a few other things in its favor like the effects filter for changing tint, putting on shadows, bevels, and probably other stuff I havent explored.  That's nice for creatively repurposing assets.  The texture rotation, x and y offset, and zoom are pretty nice as well, along with decent size and rotation for objects.  There's probably more I just haven't needed to dig into yet.  There hasn't yet been a thing I wanted to map out and not had a way to do it.
If you're a DM who's very picky about your maps, I'd say this is worth it in its current state.  You'll have to work around some frustrations, but I have not yet found a mapmaking tool that isn't drowning in frustrations.  Pyro, I like where this is going.  Please don't stop with the fixes.  Expand and polish this right and you could have the defining mapmaking tool.

First & foremost, I'd like to point out that "Platinum Games", the developers of Vanquish, Bayonetta and a multitude of other notable titles, are to be regarded as one of the best dev teams for game ports due to their impeccable performance, quality and refinements.

Vanquish is a hyper paced, high octaned 3rd person sci-fi action shooter.
It is a game title that adminsters a distinctively unique experience particularly revolving around its gameplay mechanics.
The game depicts a futuristic era of war where a group of Russians launch an assault on certain cities of the United States of America which consequently leads to a spacial conflict.
The gameplay is primarily known for its "Matrix" like slow-mo modes that can be triggered with certain maneuvers that comes at a cost of its exaustion if made use of overly. Regarded as one of the core mechanics, it plays a vital role at defeating many robotic adversaries making up for a andreline fueled action game experience.
One of the gripes that one could have with Vanquish is its short campaign that encompasses a total play-time of  6 hours.

I've always been a big fan of this game, hoping sometime there would be another sequel, but it seems the idea was dropped. To give you an idea of how much I adore this game, I've played through it about four times by this point.
There's always question about which Overlord you should pick up if any, the first or the second? Personally, I say both. Here I will just review the first one though.
A fantastic singleplayer RPG with clever humor, good boss fights, enticing story and an interesting combat system that I can't say I've seen in any other game.
You are the Overlord. Your job is to restore your tower to its former glory, convince the lowly townsfolk that you are indeed the Overlord and to wreak havoc with your minions (although sometimes you might decide to be nice to the citizens of your domain to make them praise you rather than fear you)
But what is an Overlord without his minions? There are four types of minions, which you unlock over time, but pretty early in the game you have all four. The first type is your default melee minions that just love to get in trouble and start fights, the second is a ranged type that are terrible in melee but can put out fires and throw fireballs, the third is a sneakier kind that can be used with clever positioning to take out key targets rapidly, but they suffer in direct confrontation, and the fourth is a healer that can resurrect your fallen minions for a while before their corpses decay (They can also swim, unlike all your other minions)
The overlord himself of course also has combat potential. He can hit people with his melee weapon of choice and cast spells that he has unlocked, there are plenty of spells ranging from direct damage (throwing fire at all your enemies and watching them burn to death while laughing horrifically) to buffing your minions (and watching them claw your enemies apart in a maddened frenzy before they start tearing each other apart)
There's also a crafting system that lets you craft weapons and armour with special stat bonuses given by letting your minions throw themselves into the flames to enhance your equipment.
This is definitely one of the most overlooked games that I know of, and that couldn't be a more undeserving title to have.

Anna is wonderful little atmospheric horror and puzzle game that keeps you thinking about its story well past its conclusion.
The puzzles gradually increase in difficulty, starting off relatively logical until the end where they become, at times, truly some of the most bizarre events of any game. Though they can all be completed using the increasingly vague hints given throughout the story in the form of old texts, many players will turn to a guide for at least some because some will truly leave you asking what the hell you actually just did.
However, do not let the puzzles stop you from experiencing the best part of the game: its story. Drawing on various folk legends and the Pagan religion, as well as having multiple endings, the story will have you thinking about it and drawing connections well past the end. It's very easy to miss parts and multiple play throughs are required to do everything, giving it great replay value.
Finally the graphics and audio are absolutely gorgeous and serve their purpose of creating an incredibly creepy , surreal atmosphere throughout the game. Although some audio and lightning glitches are present, they did not detract from the overall experience very much.
While it may not be worth the full $10 to some, it is certainly worth its sale prices and has become one of the most intriquing games I've played because of its elements. Certainly not for everyone, but well worth a try if you get the chance.

If you've played any of Platinum's games before you basically already know what to expect - terrible story, decent cutscenes, and over-the-top action gameplay.
Vanquish is a breath of fresh air in a shooter that doesn't restrain mobility - it's based around sliding around in and out of cover, using juuuust enough boost meter to shotgun blast an enemy, then rolling in between assault rifle bursts until your meter recharges. It's tough in the beginning when you're first getting used to it, but once you get a handle on how much boost-meter you have, how fast you can kill enemies, and whether you -really- need to use your slow-mo now or if you can wait, it takes on a new dimension as a stylish score attack where you're constantly improving. The excitement of when you boost-melee an enemy, then switch weapons and kill three others while in the air in slow-motion never really goes away. It controls great on M&KB and your speed is only restrained by your skill. The announcement trailer is honestly what you can expect from Vanquish once you get some practice in.
The game's a bit short - 7 hours on the first playthrough with cutscenes, but there's challenges/other difficulties and it's pretty replayable, whether it's just getting new high-scores or trying out guns you didn't pick up on the last playthrough.

This is not a hard game. The AI also DOES NOT CHEAT. It will unsettle most of your 4x game habits. You will not get 50-100 turns of peace to quietly build resources & infastructure and expand to your hearts content. You have to prepare for an attack immediately. The AI is AMAZING! Any game you have ever played where the AI decision making could be exploited and you thought to yourself, I shouldn't be able to do this. The AI is actually very cunning. I highly recommend this game. You will have to practice at it to get better. The in game tutorial is excellent. The tooltips are excellent. Do not give up on the game if you start losing. Start another game and instead of building that nice to have thing that gives +1 to whatever, build a ship. =)

text:
If you showed a historian footage of For Honor, a game in which samurai, vikings, and knights fight each other, they’d spit their tea out and politely ask you to leave. It makes no sense for these chronologically distinct factions to be fighting for control of the same continent, but it doesn’t really matter. They’re fighting because it’s cool, and there’s something endearing about the way the game takes a gleaming broadsword to historical accuracy to make it as enjoyable a celebration of medieval combat possible.
There’s not a trace of cynicism in For Honor. You can tell the developers earnestly believe that burly warriors decked out in ornate armour pummelling each other with deadly weapons is as good as it gets. There’s a lot going on, from a confusing faction war metagame that sees players working together to conquer territory, to modes like Dominion where you fight to capture and defend points on a map. But, really, it’s all just noise. A flashy distraction from the game’s true, beating, ironclad heart: the combat.
It’s when you’re locked in battle with a single adversary that For Honor’s blade is sharpest. Each fighter can attack and block in three directions: left, right, and high. If your opponent goes for a high attack, an arrow indicating its direction will flash on the screen just before it connects, giving you a brief window to block. Sounds simple enough, but the skill lies in second-guessing your foe and waiting for precisely the right moment to block, attack, or dodge. As you slowly circle your opponent, eyes fixed on their sword hand, wondering if they’ll make the first move, it’s genuinely tense. Especially if they're human.
Nothing beats the unpredictable thrill of facing another player online.
You can play For Honor against surprisingly competent and disarmingly ruthless AI bots, but nothing beats the unpredictable thrill of facing another player online. And doing so forces you to dive deeper into the combat system, which goes way beyond mere strikes and blocks. Advanced tactics include feints, which let you begin an attack, then suddenly cancel it. So your opponent will see the arrow indicating a left attack and go to block, but then you feint and quickly change to a right attack and catch them off guard. It takes some mastery, but fooling someone with this trick is enormously satisfying.
Then there’s parrying, stamina, throws, guard breaks, and class-specific special moves, which deepen the game further. Rickety bridges, cliff edges, and spike traps are particularly dangerous if you’re next to one and your opponent transitions from a guard break into a throw. Strike too often without pausing and your stamina will drain, making your attacks slow and laboured, which an aware opponent can exploit. There’s an impressive amount of depth and nuance to the fighting, which may be daunting for casual players. It demands time, dedication, and patience that some people just won’t have. And this may result in less committed players slowly drifting away, leaving a small, impenetrable community of hardcore players behind.
But before charging headlong into multiplayer, it’s worth playing story mode. These missions, flanked by largely forgettable cutscenes, teach you the basics of combat, as well as how to deal with certain classes when you finally go online. There are a few fun moments specific to the story, including a boss that fights alongside a pack of wolves and a cinematic battle on a frozen lake that’s being broken apart by catapult fire. But if you were thinking of buying For Honor just to play solo, don’t bother. The intricacies of the combat system only emerge when you’re fighting a living, thinking opponent.
In multiplayer there are 4v4 deathmatches, the aforementioned Dominion mode, and 2v2 brawls, but it’s the duels that kept me coming back. The purity of fighting one-on-one without any distractions—or other players stabbing you in the back—is where For Honor shines brightest. Duels are as much about waging psychological war on your opponent as besting them in combat. Lulling them into a false sense of security, wearing them down, taking advantage of their impatience. Every fight feels intimate and personal, which you don’t often experience in online multiplayer games. And it helps that the community the game has attracted is, by and large, well-mannered and respectful.
Outside of the fighting, however, For Honor is a needlessly bloated game. There’s a lot of tediously granular customisation, a tacky free-to-play-style storefront selling in-game currency for real-world money, and a tangle of ugly, confusing menus to wrestle through before you can get into a battle. And as time goes on, and those stalwart, hardcore players continue to hone their skills, it’ll be even more unwelcoming to newcomers. Stick with it, though, and you’ll find a rich, tactical fighting game with wonderfully weighty combat and hidden depths to uncover. But if you want something accessible you can easily dip in and out of, you may want to swear fealty to another lord.
FOR HONOR-A tense,tactical brawler that will reward anyone with the patience and will to master it. 74/100

Never Alone is an action-adventure puzzle platformer in 2.5D that will take you through a wonderful folk story told by the Iñupiat (Alaska Natives) through the ages. While I’m not familiar with the story itself, so I can’t speak for how close it is to the original or how well adapted it was, I can say it is (at least in so far as I played it) definitely a very beautiful story, with gorgeous graphics and sound effects/music to match.
Visually, the game is striking. Playing it… it leaves a lot to be desired.
In Never Alone you switch between two characters: a young girl named Nuna and an Arctic Fox, who go in search of the source of a neverending blizzard in order to stop it and save her people. The puzzles are fairly average, and the controls for the game aren’t what I would call the most comfortable ever but they are also not too bad (WASD, space, and a couple other keys)… when they work. For you see, as beautiful as the game is, the performance leaves a lot to be desired.
It took 4 levels of menu to reach the detailed video settings, and even at its lowest, it performed poorly on my computer. This is rather undesirable, particularly when your introduction to the game involves being chased by a polar bear who likes to glitch back and forth when performance falls, and having to jump lots. Failure to run from it or jump properly results in your death and having to begin from the last checkpoint. Or, you know, glitching the game and running as an invisible form until you reach the fox and then running on and on and having to restart yourself because that’s clearly getting you nowhere…
The game does have many glitches and annoyances. Walls are sometimes impossible to jump onto, the camera can become uncomfortable, the fox can become a little bit unhelpful, you may fall forever from the map, and you will die because of all of these… a lot. It’s one of those games that when it works, it’s a wonder to play for the story and visuals, but when it doesn’t you just want to flip a table and never touch it again.
If you manage to get through the entire eight chapters, you will be rewarded by unlocking the entirety of a documentary on the Iñupiat. What little I managed to unlock of it looked both interesting and very well done, but as beautiful as the game was, the annoyances were much greater than my desire to watch the documentary.
All in all, for the story, looks and sounds, and the documentary, as well as the obvious interest in making more people aware of the Iñupiat, I would like to rate this game highly; but the amount of times low performance and glitches caused my death ended up making me quite frustrated. If you have a low specs PC I would definitely not recommend you try it.
If you have a decent PC you may still get some glitches, but if you’re interested in the story, it might be worth seeing if it works, as it is quite a beautiful experience when it works.

If you are interested in a military 4X game with a heavy focus on extermination then Stardrive 2 is recommended.  However, if you want to play a more peaceful or diplomatic game then I would not recommend it as it’s really not possible to play that way at the moment.
There are various early game opponents and some events with nods to sci-fi fans.
The AI is strong early game and I had to reload during my first game a few times to improve my strategy before winning on Normal difficulty.
The technology tree really does feel like Master of Orion 2 and I enjoyed mulling over the options.
The Battle Arena has been good fun to test designs and weapons and the combat is generally a highlight.
I've encountered no major bugs and while there were some minor bugs, there was nothing gamebreaking.
In some ways it is an improved game over Stardrive 1 but there is plenty of room for improvement.
The technologies and weapons need to be better balanced.  Once you've tested them in the Battle Arena it becomes apparent some are worthless.
The late game is really tedious.  Colony governors are needed particularly for the mid to late game as it becomes micro intensive.  There are no defaults for troop loadouts so you have to do every one manually.  Late game AI ship designs are very weak so the battles become trivial and nowhere near as much fun as the early game.
The ground combat is weak.  Automatic resolution comes at a high price as it leads to excessive losses compared to manual combat even when you have a massive advantage, so it essentially forces the lame ground combat or bombardment to avoid it.
The AI’s are far too aggressive in responding to expansion.  The AI's are very similar and it's difficult to avoid anything other than Total War.  The tolerance mechanic used in diplomacy is good but needs to be increased as currently diplomacy is a bit of a side show.
Brutal difficulty is not hard enough once you get familiar.  In fact once you learn the mechanics this is the easiest 4X game I can remember.
I had a lot of fun with the early game and Battle Arena.  As a result of the time I've played the game, I'll stick with a recommend, but without more serious improvements I don't see myself wanting to load the game up again (and I tend to play genuinely good 4X games much longer than this).

Currently has a relatively flexible library of assets and tiles that are useful for general dungeon design. Could use a little more variety, but I'm assuming that more will come since this is still in early access. That being said, DPS does support custom artwork, so it's possible to just grab a token off of google if need be.
What really shines about DPS isn't the assets, but rather the series of tools used to place and manipulate various tiles. As someone who typically stays away from grid systems for my tabletop gaming, I've found the placement, rotation, and layering tools to be very succinct and easy to pick up. The lighting and effects tools are still very much a work in progress, though I'm frankly unsure how things like lighting dynamics would be integrated effectively in a system that exports battlemaps to image files.
It certainly still has areas that need development, but Dungeon Painter Studio is still a highly-accessible dungeon mapping system with lots of promsie.

IF you keep hearing comparisons to the Civ or Gal Civ series then ignore them, this is a very different kettle of fish.
What this game really should be compared to is the Space Empires series.
-Turn-based empire building
-Real-time space combat
-Directly controlable ground combat
-Fully customisable troops and ships
Stardrive two is basically an updated and much refined version of those games, and for that this game rocks.
Reasons to play
-The right things are automated.  You have full control, but a lot of tedius micro is done for you by the fraighter system.
-The research tree presents you with hard choices, but doesn't mean you can never have the things you don't research.
-The planets have several characteristics that make for more hard choices when colonising.  You might desperately need an outpost for your war, but all the planets in that system are small and toxic.  You'll hate it, but love it too.

Stories Untold storyline is a little predictable, but the in-game atmosphere is so cleverly crafted that there's an inescapable sense of dread that lasts the entire game. This stems partly from the game's wonderful aesthetic - a twisted 80s world whose underlying themes remind me more of Stephen King's
than Men at Work. It's about time a game did more than just parrot retro tropes.
The Unity Engine works wonders (mostly), with gorgeous textures and lighting. Even set within fairly small spaces, Stories Untold still persuades the player that what they see is only a small part of a larger world. Interaction with the world is limited, but fits well within the scope of the game itself.
The audio is fantastic: the voice actors believable, the click-clacking of keys sublime, and the music a darkened nostalgia. This is a game that deserves headphones and the volume turned up.
Gameplay wise, more polish is needed. The text parser used in some chapters rarely accepts synonyms or similar words, which can become frustrating. I also experienced large stuttering in the final chapter, regardless of quality settings, but this didn't make the game unplayable. The way the player switches between in-game interfaces is clunky; it becomes faster to write things down. Although I suppose in the 80s context of the game, this is certainly more realistic.
The game is episodic, the stories link chronologically. Give the demo a try if you're still unconvinced.

I love the game, and you've done a number of things that I've wanted to do to similar games over the years.  First, congrats on taking the MOO2 skeleton and fleshing it out.  Took some guts, and it could have easily been a very bad move.  Second, I really dig the storyline missions and the interactions that come with them.  Good job.  Third, ship building is wonderful, and pretty fast.  A boost to what I expected (I really just want one more feature, changing the arc of fire).  Next, I love the medals for units.  And good job with the revamped ground combat system.  Finally, the small specialty random events ("Your planet is becoming very skilled at building freighters...") is a brilliant stroke and really adds to the game (is there a way that these bonuses smack you in the face, to make it easier to see, and more difficult to lose a planet to an invasion?)
A couple of things:
Let us trade, steal, or develop new ship layouts!
More tech, racial tech trees, and storylines.  Yeah, I realize I'm asking for addtional content.  I'm happy to pay for good DLC.
Let us shift the firing arcs in our ships during the build.  Some arcs on the lateral build sectors should be able to reach fore and/or aft.
Better player-side AI management of resource management.  It seems that my planets are always producing food, no matter what.  Even a simple radio box "New population produces X by default" would do wonders for play flow.
I would love to see a "Civ-Style" unit advancement system upon experience boosts.  Let us choose if the unit gets an offense, defense, or other boost.  I love the system there, and I wish we had it here.  It gives units more personality, and attachment.
If you miss Masters of Orion 2, get this game.  If you looked at MOO2 and said "I just wish it had...", get this game.  If you want a game with decent detail, but no overwhelming micromanaging, get this game.

Now there is Forts, where you build and upgrade a tower using bridge constructor like physics and you arm it with mortars to shoot the enemy's fort to pieces, machine guns to defend against mortars (or to rain down lead onto them), snipers to ...well snipe..they also use laser designators to target missiles from silos into the enemy :)
Hits are satisfying as you watch where your mortar just hit engulfed in flames, support beams snapping, parts of the enemy tower falling under its own weight or that satisfying moment when you see a door open on the enemy tower, fire a sniper shot in and hear the scream of an enemy gunner.

First, let's talk about Steam release.
This compilation includes the original 2 games of the series. You may seen other games which have numbering from 3 to 7, but those were made by other publishers and aren't exactly official, from what I know. (Most of them are quite ugly and didn't bring any evolution/revolution to the formula of the first game)
This Steam release is a simple and flat "put game as is". This can be blamed on that new publishers have no access to the source port or other materials. Thus you will not find any trading cards, achievements, widescreen or any optimisation at all, not even Steam Overlay work in this one. On good side, the game should still work on modern computers.
Now the games themselves:
Neighbours From Hell 1 is point'n'click quest in which you control Woody as you make him sneak around the house, avoiding being seen by Mr. Rottweiler, and make traps, which usually involes first collecting an item in the house and then applying them to the object in house. Some traps may lead neighbour to another nasty trap. Oh, and tip-toeing around Neighbour's pets.
Beating the game by getting minium requeirement of traps is quite easy. Beating it by finding and applying every trap in every level is simple as well.
But what make the game the real crunchy puzzler is getting 100% rating on each level. To do this you are required not only to make use of every trap, but to make sure that Mr. Rottweiler get in as many of them in a row before he cools off from previous trap, resulting in him breaking down on each new one (with animation of him almost breaking his back). The timing, order of tricks and placement of traps which can be put in any room (items like marbles) to connect faraway traps is everything there, making you actually think and plan there.
The second game then takes place outside of house on various exotic locations. Sneaking is no more, gone are guardian pets. System of multiple lifes were added, so you aren't immeditly screwed when Neighbour sees you for the first time. And this time your life is made harder by a sudden appearance of mom of out bully, who keeps an eye and fists for you as well. Shame that she mostly spends her time either sleeping or shopping.
This time around getting the golden statue, which is equalient to what 100% rating was in the first game, is much easier, as Neighbour rage now stores on a meter that can stack "breakdowns" from other tricks and it cools down much slower. So it's a simply matter of making trap ahead of neighbour path non-stop, with no real thinking. Instead the game concentrates more on the figuring out tricks themselves and their activating, with some tricks working as part of "combo". Still, no real puzzle.
Now, the games are overall quite fun, with great music which fits to the game goodly and the joyful graphics that use prerendered 3D assets, which are greatly animated. It especially shows with a cartoony characters that the second game is full with. My only complaints would be same repeating breakdown animation for Mr. Rottwell in the first game, which was varied nicely in sequel, and how underplayed neighbour's mom is in Vacations, who could be less passive.
OH, and one of more important things: If you are fan of the slapstick humor (and slightly black one), then I am sure that you will be holding for your belly in this game from laughter.

Honestly, great software. It is almost like a faux photoshop to me. It has many similar mechanics and the like, but it's lack there of some key features honestly make me sad a little. Some pros and cons:
Pros:
-Relatively easy to use
-Pretty good assets to use from with access to the workshop to gather fan made assets gives this thing limitless potential
-Photoshop-esque control. Meaning, layers, lighting, outlines, effects, and the like.
Cons, in my opinion:
-No Eraser tool. There is a "brush texture" tool that can be used to simulate, but a simple eraser brush would go a long way into crafting those fine details that make a difference to me. Not to mention you can't just cut pieces of a texture. I made my map and used an object as a floor instead because I liked the edging. But, I can't cut the remaining aspect of the object so I am forced to paint and play over something in an attempt to hide it.
-Bad selector tool. There is a tool that allows you to select a couple layers you are working on. It isn't smart however. You have to select the ENTIRE box of that texture for it to pick it up and that can be annoying, or at least it was for me. Not to sound like a photoshop fantic but a lot of tooks from that software would work wonderfully here and take the selector tool from their would be a godsend.
-Assets, color. and textures are bound to the "object". That sounds probably confusing but let me try to explain. I use the PaperStyles mod from the work shop to build my maps. Great ♥♥♥♥ing mod, check them out, and I want to make a room with a broken floor, connecting to a pillar of rough stone where an Arcane Trickster is trying to resurrect a lich. Now this mod includes "rock formations" with the edges I wanted, so I scaled the up as large as the sofrware would permit me and it didn't fit the scale of my map as much as I wanted it too. Since I can't fit the clif to make one large piece, I just copy and past the object a few times. Now, seeing as I can't grab the specific color pallet for the "rock structure" I am forced to grab a "nearly close but not quite there" "floor tile" and play with the oppacity as much as I can to attempt to blend these colors.
TL;DR: Overall good program that makes me realize how much I miss photoshop. Maybe needs to borrow a few key tools, but nice all the same. If you want something that gives you a litte bit of control for your online D&D pals, this isn't a bad choice.

If you like third person shooters you owe it to yourself to play Vanquish. The combat is amazing, easily one of the combat systems of any TPS. It's fast, frantic, and makes you feel like a badass when you slide into a group of enemies, immediately enter ARS, and take them all out while in Bullet Time. It has a cover mechanic as well, and while you're not encouraged to use it, it is really nice to let your energy recharge or take out far away units from a safe position. The game is also pretty challenging, which makes it all the more satsifying once you beat a hard encounter.
Port wise, the port is excellent with a few issues. It's fairly well optimized, being able to run everything maxed out at 1080p and get a consistent 120 FPS on a GTX 970, i5-7600k, and 16 GB of RAM. The lowest it ever drops is to around 80-90, but even then it quickly recovers. The KB+M controls are also really good, and it's definitely the best way to play the game. And while there isn't an in game option to, SEGA has made ways to change Aspect Ratio and FOV with launch commands "-unlockaspectratio" and "-fov <40-120>". The only real issue so far is that enemies deal more damage to you  if you go above 60 FPS, which is an issue that can affect the game for some, but if that's the case just enable vsync or just force an FPS cap though something such as nVidia Inspector or whatever the AMD equivalent is.
As for the story, it's mostly forgettable with a few exceptions. The story is mainly just a way to get you from one encounter to the next which is perfectly fine imo, but I know some people are going to be disappointed at that. Act 5 however does have a pretty decent story to it, it's just a shame Act 5 is also the last and the shortest Act in the game. The voice acting is also pretty eh. Not everyone will like Sam's or Burns voice, which is fine. I didn't like them at first, but it grew on me the more I played the game.
Overall though, I give the game a solid 8/10. If you were expecting a good story there's probably other games to look at, but if you just want a game with fantastic gameplay and don't really care for the story I can't recommend this enough.  It's easily one of the best third person shooters out there from a gameplay perspective, and what it lacks in story it more than makes up for in just about everything else.

Другой, (менее важный) раздражавший в первую пару заходов в игру фактор, это некоторая сложность нахождения баланса между погружением в мир игры и успешным продвижением по сюжету. Многовато тупиков и фатальностей, приводящих или к периодическим просмотрам занудных неотключаемых ложных концовок или к перезагрузкам с сейвов.

Музыка, озвучка и сам смысл элементов сюжета, образно говоря, все того же цвета. Однако во все это вложено и немало мрачной красоты.

Похожа она в результате на одну более менее понятнуюю историю, к которой приделано несколько случайных элементов от пары других историй ради увеличения общего объема. Не уверен правда что имеющейся степени понятности для этого достаточно. Даже после ознакомления с тем что по этому поводу пишет википедия)).
Но в целом игра впечатлила и заинтересовала достаточно для того, чтобы хотелось ее допроходить до ачивки "вы завершили эту игру на 100%".
У меня в конце концов хватает игр с гораздо более очевидными сюжетами, где можно спасти миры, зачистить локации и надрать всевозможные вражеские задницы.

I need to start by saying that this is not my first time playing a musical instrument by any means.  However it is my first real attempt at learning to play guitar.  After 2 weeks of using Rocksmith 2014 I can say that I've seen a major improvement!
Rocksmith 2014 starts you out easy, playing maybe 1 out of 10 notes through easy passages, and maybe 1 out of 20 through the more challenging parts.  As you improve Rocksmith throws more at you, and if its too much at first it backs it down a notch.  After each time playing through a song the program will show you your longest streak and your accuracy, along with song mastery and a few exercises that Rocksmith 2014 believes will help you improve the next time.
Pros:
1) Simple, effective and user friendly set up (note highway, similar to Guitar Hero)
2) The riff repeater is very helpful allowing you to repeat a section over and over until you get it, and will let you increase or decrease difficulty (awesome for learning solos)

Without this game, I would not have known about this tribe and even thought about half of the things they talked about in the Cultural Insights. Another thing that people were complaining about was how annoying it was to watch two characters as one falls into a hole or gets stuck in a rock.  I never experienced anything like that. This game is awesome! If you're a fan of old school 16-bit graphics like from Link to the Past or Secret of Mana, you're going to fall in love with this game. If you like online co-op, a witty story, and action RPGs- pull the trigger and buy it.
Pros:
- Great for online co-op!!! Definitely the highlight of the game, I probably would have never played it otherwise. Playing with a friend made for a great experince.

Cons:
- The game is about ~75% complete. The fourth temple is not in the game yet, and there's also a few things you can't do yet.

- Low replay value because of the linear story. However, because of character customization and online co-op it could be fun to play with others again and try new builds.

Stunning puzzle game, best I've played by far - 10/10. Copied below is my review on metacritic:
Superb game, and near-perfect in it's execution and atmosphere, English Country Tune is a deep meditation on 3-dimensional space.
The game presents a series of puzzles in a rich and mysterious world that even in the beginning can be quite challenging. Through the rapid introduction of interacting variables in the puzzle space, the challenge reaches such a degree of difficulty that only sustained meditation and visualisation of possibilities will generate a solution.
This could have been a lot of un-fun work, but somehow the combination of atmospheric and uninterrupted music, colours and a space that is utterly joyous to navigate make this game one of the most incredible experiences of any I've played. I distinctly remember feeling moments where my neurons connected in ways I did not think possible, and the satisfaction of finding a solution was often overwhelmingly pleasurable.
Highly recommended, very original, and best played without a walkthough, and resetting puzzles instead of using the undo function.

This is a fantastic piece of software with an excellent price point (especially compared to other, similar tile based mapping programs of which I've seen go as high as over $100 for a license.) It is still in early access, thus, it does lack some functionality I would like to see in the future (such as a brushed eraser function, or layer organization.) However, any missing tools does not detract from your ability to make fully fleshed out maps for any grid based rpg encounters you are looking to run. I have encountered some odd bugs involving dissapearing objects and strange layer placement, but most of these issues can be resolved in seconds by consulting the list of layers.
I do enjoy making my own maps by hand, but this program saves me a lot of time. I balance it by making things like world maps by hand and using DP to make quick encounters and dungeons. This balance has worked well for me as I do think that DP is less useful for making atlases.
I'd also like to make a quick note that the company was very forthright with their EULA. Each section is spelled out in layman's terms, so that comprehension is quick and straightforward. They also allow any content conceivable to be imported and exported from the program.
Finally, and equally importantly, this product has fantastic (though small) community that has posted a number of high quality tile packs to be used by any user for free.
Highly Reccomended.

This keeps happening every year, but "Best One Yet!" This year feels especially applicable because there is no obvious "worst game" of the bunch.

- Monster Seeking Monster is a game where you text other players and try to get them to shag you. It's pretty fun, but depends on who you're playing with (probably shouldn't play with family at all lmao) and how creative they are with flirting.

Compete head-to-head with other players and vote on who provides the best addition to the work of art you all are collectively working on. This tool is well on its way to being a real boon for game masters and wordbuilders everywhere, however if you're hoping to using this tool right away, I'd reccommend holding off, as it is nowhere near complete and in its current state it is frankly frustrating to use.  Various functionality issues currently plague its early release, including:
* Objects randomly disappearing from the list, despite still being visible on the grid
* completely nonsensical object placement (sometimes objects, walls, and floors appear at the top of the layers list, sometimes at the bottom, sometimes in the middle with no regularity).
While designing a simple map, I had to quit and start over three times because the layers list kept glitching out.  On the fourth time, I finally started to make some progress, but that was hindered when objects began being placed below the floor on the visibility list, but because every. single. click. creates a new layer, I was unable to determine which of my objects or floors I needed to adjust to do this properly.  This is partially my own fault, as I should have been labeling and categorizing things as I went, but really, all I needed this tool to do was help me sketch up a dungeon I had already created and I honestly feel like I'll have it done quicker if I just re-sketch it on graph paper at this point.
I fully expect that when this product leaves early access, it will be one of the best tools out there, and I look forward to using it in its completed state, and will revise my review accordingly, but I think that it is only fair that I'm honest in reccommending not to use this software during this early access.

I played a lot of original stardrive and while it had it's flaws I enjoyed the game a lot.
StarDrive 2 however, I can't enjoy at all. No matter how hard I try. Game has numerous problems that really hurt the experience and generally it is quite unpolished.
Thing that ticks me off most are the ridiculous "random" event raids and attacks. Yeah, they aren't random at all and if you were planning to try pacifist playthrough I got some bad news for you. Every time you encounter your first race you soon get these warhawks with 2 options, either declare war on newfound race or get attacked by a considerably large fleet. So you either build war fleet or build war fleet, great and diverse options. Then there are these crystal things coming after your butt constantly, as well as remnant wormholes popping left and right. Wanna guess how well your diplomatic approach works on these buggers? Not very well. You can either have no random raids at all, ever. Or you can have them every single time in same order forcing you to have large fleets ready no matter what playstyle you would want to use. Would be nice to have some options to the mandatory fights.
Diplomacy is quite literally worthless for anything else than getting more tech, many of the races are hyper aggressive and will just demand tributes and send their fleets after you anyway. Tolerance is unpolished feature and will simply hinder any attempts to do meaningful trades. You can't ask other races for example to freaking bugger off from your space as they fly all the way over your area and colonise a planet right in the middle of your solar system when you have 5 battleships orbiting the damn thing waiting your own colony ship 1 turn away to get there.
So, what we have at this point is pretty much a turn based space combat game. Now you might wonder if that at least is amazing... well no, not at all. Battles are boring to play and watch, and auto battle doesn't know anything about how the battles would actually turn out making you lose about 4 times as much fleet. Modules are horribly balanced too, fighter bays seem to be the be-all-end-all module and bunch of carriers will just wreck the AI every single time (also wrecks your performance and freezes the game for a while after every battle). Ground combat isn't any better, it's just slow and boring and auto battle again will just lose you troops for no reason.
Tech tree is just plain bad and some of the choices make no sense at all to exclude another. Got fusion shields? Great. Now you might want fusion engines? Too bad.
UI is bad with many features needing unnecessary clicking and scrolling around with relevant information not being where it needs to be. Like the empire overview, why can't it have X/X population numbers?
Turns are annoyingly short and you will find yourself mashing spacebar more than your keyboard can handle.
I guess the ship building is cool though... that's about only nice thing I can think of, although UI makes even this much worse experience than what it needs to be.
I hope this game gets some serious patching, that might well be what makes this game worth your time.

People are complaining in reviews about how this pack is worse than its predicessors. And they're probably right. However, I still have enjoyed this pack so far with friends. Some of the games may be a little lackluster and there's several technical issues, but if you are playing with friends it is still very enjoyable. Fibbage: Enough about you

Civic Doodle:

Survive the Internet:

Bracketeering:

Simple rule: Don't play this with close family or a small group of friends you know too well. This game is a fun party-pleaser that is sure to generate laughs. While it doesn't stand quite as tall as the third party pack, it's a solid collection and definitely worth its price, at least during a sale.

So, I beat the game in 2.8 hours.  I do not believe this is a good game.  Here's why:
1. Text-based elements are underwhelming.  Sure it's interactive and there are loud noises and flashes at the right moments, based on your input, but you don't have to think about it.  It's very guided.  Efforts to type something different are rarely acknowledged, and you cannot fail.
2. The puzzles are dumbed-down.  Easy-peasy!  It's possibly to see how they can be a challenge for non-technical people, though.
3. Graphical issues are present.  I noticed some boxy shadows occasionally, and the mouse kept escaping from the game window.  Otherwise, the pre-rendered scenes are pretty good.
4. Storyline is pretentious as F.  The numerous disembodied voices reminded me of Dear Esther.  This game has more focus and a conclusion, but is very much more self-referential.
5. Horror aspect is good.  As said before, there are lots of flashing lights/images and loud noises at the right places (this doesn't spoil anything as there is a photosensitivity warning), but the weak storyline lets it down.

It's extremely close to Masters of Orion 2 and I believe it's far superior in many aspects. I've played MoO2 quite a lot and I've played tons of other 4X games and none were this close in design and yet still feel modern and well thought out.
the game's not perfect but it's definitely one of the best 4X games out there. with a bit more extra development, some DLC adding some more depth and some cool mods by the community and it probably will be the best out there.
best parts:
-ship design (lots of choice and flexibility without some of the hassle from SD1)
-combat (AI is pretty clever, including that of your own ships)
-research (MoO2 style, wish it was copied more)
-no unneeded micro-management (like freighters. thank god)
-easy to understand, hard to master economic system overal
-solid diplomacy system. (takes some getting used to but when you get it it works fine)
-bit of genre savvy humor on the sides, lest we take the game too seriously. (best to leave that to the expert, i.e. distant worlds)
-free range battle ground is an excellent way to test your designs. just wish there was a way to adjust the tech level of your modules. the various missions are way too difficult for my tastes, though >.>
haven't done any ground battles yet. can't comment on how good or bad those are, but I hear good things.
worst parts:
-I feel I have to scroll and drag the map around a -lot- to get a good view on what my planets are doing. I feel many other 4X games do this a little better. especially endless space. yes, this is a minor issue but gets more annoying the longer you play and you have a bigger empire to manage. it'd help if you don't have to zoom in as far to get planet details. I don't really feel the empire management screen is a proper replacement of an easy to use galaxy map, though it does what it should well.
-no multiplayer! no real dealbreaker as truthfully I hardly ever play online with or against other people, but considering this game's outstanding ship design feature it really would suit it particularly well.
-the game secretely hates your guts and will let you know about it any chance it gets. 20 turns in and get your first ♥♥♥♥♥♥ corvette out the door? congrats, let's celebrate with a remant fleet at your doorstep you wouldn't have a chance of defeating 200 turns in. do not overestimate your 4X skills and just start your first game on easy like a noob should!

Earlier review holds true:
Short review - A simplified rewrap of Stardrive 1 which pulls away innovative features and improves on nothing but graphics.
4/10 based upon how immersive the game felt measured against it's predecessor and the numerous disadvantages the second offers.
More detailed review:
First off, measuring it against it's predecessor, the starting menu itself is downgraded. No biggy, but made me raise an eyebrow seeing as how the first felt a lot more engaging.
The empire-building is/feels a lot more restricted, especially with the old "Masters of Orion favorite" 'creative' now being added - Trait balancing for min-maxing is currently required for a playable longterm game.
Entering the game itself, it is now fully turnbased - And nothing has been done to improve the UI. The tooltips are, in many cases, closer to 'flavor text' which is not useful.
Instead of having conflict and strategy on the same map, a simple round circle has been applied where your ships and the enemies will be enter and bash away until one of you run out of things to bash. There is one strategy - Get artillery on everything since it has the longest range and you'll usually be able to win. No random events, no area modifiers.
The ground combat follows the same route, though it has squares in a big square instead. Terrain is not included so just gear up with rifles, medikit and sidearm of choice and slaughter your enemies since they will just go for nearest enemy.
The artwork is mostly reused from Stardrive 1 with a few new additions.
The ship customization has been downsized as you can no longer turn mounts the way you desire or at least I've yet to find a way to do it - Do feel free to enlighten me if I'm wrong here, I'd love to find it.
I've found no way to adjust my fleets in deployment outside of individual click'n'drag - Quite a bother since entering space-fights is (at the very least, more if you play warmongerer) half of what you do in this game.
The UI is simplified beyond usability. Since both left and right buttons can be used for orders, you'll be giving contraorders repeatedly and watch action points waste away as troops run around when you tried to click the enemy to find out what gear he had - Or, perish the thought, deselect your current unit.
I don't know if anyone else bothered building construction ships since the stations seem pretty much a waste of production - But I'd love to know if there's a way to delete a station? Since they instant deployed rather than let you target, I ended up with one blocking my capitol and it was a real nuisance.
I've tried to remain objective here, but as I try and figure out anything positive about this game against others, I fail.
Everyone has the colonization section and I'd recommend Stardrive 1 since it has a lot more entertaining elements.
The one positive thing I can think of about this game is that the loading screen when starting the game looks really, really nice and is animated.

A puzzle platformer game that beautifully ties gameplay mechanics with narrative- incidentally, this happens to be a story with writing of a superb nature. The execution is almost entirely phenomenal bar some minor hiccups: collisions can get funky when you mistime a jump and hit a block horizontally, the control system to swap characters is a little clunky on keyboard/mouse but  functional, and lastly the game can randomly freeze temporarily during gameplay (around 10-15 seconds, maybe a little longer).
What was great? Pretty much everything else: soundtrack, narrator is delightful every time, the minimalist aesthetic design that managed to convey so much with so little, and the optional achievement pickups were actually really fun to get (they also often reference other games or pop culture). In addition, the length and pacing of the game is just right and doesn't overextend or wear out the strengths [I took around 3.5 hours to 100% this game]
The simplicity of the core concepts combined with varied and purposeful level design of this game really shines and open the game to all sorts of players. I could see people trying to speed run this game as well as casually having fun and discovering alternative solutions.
Summary: This is without a doubt an extremely enjoyable experience all around and deserves to be played by anyone considering it!

Ober-/Unterhitze: etwa 200°C
Heißluft: etwa 180°C
Knetteig:
Mehl mit Backin in einer Rührschüssel mischen. Übrige Zutaten hinzufügen und alles mit einem Mixer (Knethaken) zunächst auf niedrigster, dann auf höchster Stufe zu einem Teig verarbeiten. Gut die Hälfte des Teiges auf dem Springformboden ausrollen und den Springformrand darumlegen. Form auf dem Rost in den Backofen schieben.
Einschub: unteres Drittel
Backzeit: etwa 15 Min.
Vorgebackenen Boden auf einem Kuchenrost etwas abkühlen lassen. Übrigen Teig zu einer Rolle formen, als Rand an die Form drücken, so dass ein gut 4 cm hoher Rand entsteht.
Belag:
Sahne steif schlagen. Eier mit Zucker, Vanillin-Zucker und Finesse in einer Rührschüssel mit dem Mixer (Rührstäbe) kurz auf niedrigster, dann auf höchster Stufe etwa 2 Min. aufschlagen. Puddingpulver, saure Sahne, Quark und Schichtkäse unterrühren. Zum Schluss die Sahne unterheben. Die Quarkmasse gleichmäßig in die Form gießen und backen. Backtemperatur reduzieren!
Ober-/Unterhitze: etwa 180°C
Heißluft: etwa 160°C
Backzeit: etwa 75 Min.
Den Kuchen nach der Backzeit noch etwa 15 Min. im ausgeschalteten Ofen stehen lassen, dann in der Form auf einem Kuchenrost erkalten lassen.
Kuchen aus der Form lösen. Käsekuchen nach Belieben mit Puderzucker bestreut und geschlagener Sahne servieren.

Sure, the PC port has a minor thing here and there that could be better, but for a port of a cult hit game: this is what you want. This is the definitive version of the game: hitting 60+ FPS in a game that hit 30 on consoles, and it really does help in the action gameplay. You'll speed around killing everything you can, and while yes there's a bug that makes you easier to kill via the framerate, I actually think it semi balances out with the new aiming controls that you have via the mouse and keyboard.
As for the gameplay: this isn't necessarily the Plantium action formula that you know from games like Bayonetta and Transformers, but it doesn't me the design here is bad at all: quite the opposite. There's something about speeding around, shooting enemies left and right in the head, while getting rugburns on the ground metaphorically. It's cheesy and over the top in a bunch of good ways, and for the low price here: you are getting a game with a lot of replayability, at least in my mind. Good challenges to keep your interest. Sure, the campaign is rather short compared to most: but that doesn't really have a bad section to it either. It's a game that you'll love to perfect: try every weapon combination, see how powerful you can make a weapon, or just punch things in the face a bunch.
I want to thank Platinum and Sega for putting the effort into that port, because people really needed to see what this game was all about. It's a classic in my mind, and worth the price of admission at 60 dollars even today. And the fact that you get it for at least a third of that? Yeah, definitely a must buy.

People say that this game is Pay 2 Win. That is wrong. This game is Pay 2 Advance at a rate of 50% faster than others. Yes, you can buy weapon/gear packs in the store. NO, you can not immediately use them. You have to be at the rank of the gear in that faction. No, you can not buy faction rank. Yes, you will encounter players of a higher rank in matches who will slaughter you. Yes, you can kill them with level 1 weapons. It just takes more shots to get through the body armor.
The only difference between a stock gun and a gold gun besides the skin and name variation is that the gold guns have 3 random weapon adjustments on it. (dispersion, recoil, weight, etc). You can get all these adjustments and more via the in-game workshop. So, all you really get from a gold gun aside from a skin and name is a fully upgraded version of a stock weapon.
Put some hours into it, get a feel for the gameplay mechanics, ballistics, etc before you judge the game.

A profound story told by calmly explorable environments, great dialog and voice acting, as well as several action sequences all tightly bundled into an immersive experience that will keep you thinking and feeling long after you finish the game.
Where SOMA falters slightly is in balancing the gameplay elements. Most of the game is based on free-form exploration. There are no gameplay rewards (XP, loot, etc.) for this: all there is to gain is more insight into the story and its world. There are also some un-skippable puzzle mini-games of medium difficulty, which can be solved by anyone with enough patience. Finally, there are also numerous horror-stealth action sequences. While these fit very well with the story, I found them more frustrating than fun: the AIs are simplistic and seemingly random, while the environments do not provide enough complexity for true stealth tactics. If there were just one or two of these sequences it would not be worth mentioning, but there are a handful, which is too many.
But that's nitpicking: frustrations are overcome quite easily and SOMA will take you on an amazing journey that you won't soon forget.
Finally, thank you, developers, for supporting Linux!

This game offers a sense of nostalgia for STALKER players, however that's as far as it goes. The game has some good points, however they would be the same good points of any modern PvP shooter on the market: Use guns to kill bad guys. Check. Environments are attractive. Check. Environment layouts offer interesting tactical choices. Close enough. Game modes are intuitive and easy to jump in to. Check. IMO, listing the things this game gets right isn't too helpful since it covers the fundamentals.
I was able to experience the game early enough to see what it was like to play when everyone had standard weapons. With only a PvP mode, the gaming experience was middling. Besides the STALKER-esque visuals, Survarium is so far, just another team versus team shooter. The RPG type elements (leveling up, getting currency, adding skills modifiers, etc.) are solid in principal. They progress as fast as you would expect (though we players never seem to think we level fast enough it would seem). The whole experience is simply typical.
Anomalies add interesting looking but deadly environmental hazards into the mix. Other reviewers have said that this is an innovative addition, however the inclusion of these is no different than adding a fire hazard, or a bottomless pit into deathmatch maps. We've seen this bofore. Their implementation of anomalies does adds a sense of visual wonder, which while interesting, is a little out of place in a PvP game mode. Some anomalies however are invisible, such as radiation patches. It creates a rather poor gaming experience to be in a skirmish and run into an invsible anomaly that ends up killing you. For a game series like Fallout, an open world PvE sandbox, this works since the penalties are managable. In a deathmatch, not so much. The best maps in Survarium were the ones where you could focus on the objectives of the game mode at hand.
None of those negative points caused me to give up on the game however. What turned me away was the in game store and the pay to win model of the game. In the beginning, I was confident that everyone was scraping their way through the experience rat race the same as I was. I was content. But matches became dominated by players who bought their way to the best gear and skipped the RPG-like advancement. If a new player could reasonably compete in such a scenario, this might be forgivable, however the balance between the paid advancement and the natural advancement was non-existant. Paid for gear was far superior to the starting gear making the PvP competition, no contest. It's a pity too, the leveling system, which seemed promising, ended up being marginalized by the in game store permitting players to skip to the end.
Unfortunately, I doubt I will be giving this game a second look. For a good PvE experience of this flavor, I'll be happy to play STALKER again.

Bought two copies of it full price to play with my brother - best purchases of my life. This game is fantastic for a number of reasons. Great music (though it can get repetitive) immersive skills, and challenging (oh man challenging) combat and boss fights. Some other reviewers will abstain from recommending this game solely because the bosses are "too difficult". But you have infinite enemies to grind up  your loot and levels so this isn't a long-term issue. I mean the game has "grind" in the title.
It is early access and the Devs seem to be updating fairly consistently. But don't let the Alpha dissuade you, the game is fully functional and highly enjoyable in its current state. I have encountered little to no bugs, and the multiplayer plays flawlessly. Many games today are built for singleplayer with some lower quality multiplayer on the side - like a wilted salad or mushy microwaved fries. But this game, while still fantastic solo, takes co-op to the next level including relevant dialogue to having 2 persons and so much more. I can't recommend this game enough.
As a message to the Devs - if they ever read this - I would like to make a few suggestions as this is early access. Firstly, while the music that is present is pleasant, there is only one track per area. And since a large portion of what you're doing in this game is grinding, it can get a little repetitive.
Additionally, it would be nice to be able to re-fight bosses on the path of grinding for levels and loot. Not in arena or endless mode, but by going back to the place you originally fought them and using a summoning item or something if you want to limit it. This would open up the possibility for boss cards, which would be pretty swell.
Finally, age old complaint that I'm sure all developers get sick of. "We want moaar!" Honestly though it would be nice to have more melee combat options. Perhaps rather than having the bow as a side item with semi-limited arrows, have a ranger "class." Right now there are only 1h and 2h weapons. Maybe specify them further to include daggers, 1h swords, 1h clubs/hammers, 2h swords, 2h spears, 2h clubs/hammers, and some specialty mixes each with specific abilities/skill trees.
Honestly I love the game and want to help make it better from my limited perspective as a player.

1. Bosses are very difficult in this game. And not like dark souls where you learn the bosses patterns and slowly become better and better until you can kill the boss without even getting touched. Every boss fight is terribly unfun and annoying as ♥♥♥♥, extremely gimmicky and straight up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I have no idea how you could possibly defeat most of the bosses playing solo, a friend is almost required if you want to play this game on the lowest difficulty level. Don't even get me started on the hard mode.
2. Me and a friend defeated 4 bosses in our second session of play. All of these bosses stemmed from the same quest line. Not once did we recieve experience points or loot from ANY of these bosses. So we stayed the same level basically this entire questline as it become increasingly difficult to get enough xp to level from simple mobs. And the grand reward for this quest that took 4+ hours? About 1/3rd a bar of XP (at level 14) and a talent orb. Talent orbs are worthless and some of the bonuses you can unlock with them include 2% max health increase or 2% magic attack increase. This quest did not even give a skill point or a sword or staff or helmet or anything. There is no reward to playing this game: xp, new gear, and skills - arguably the most important part of an RPG - are scarcely given to you and I don't think I've ever felt more unrewarded for playing a game in my entire life.
3/10, kinda fun game and absolutely abysmal RPG.

I honestly want very much to be able to recommend For Honor. The core gameplay is absolutely unique, taking the spirit of the fighting genre and turning it into something new and exciting. It's smooth, intuitive, heart-pounding action with the depth to keep you constantly learning and improving and getting better. And when it all comes together, it feels amazing. Not to mention how astonishingly beautiful the animations are. We as gamers tend to gloss over games having unrealistic animations so it's truly mind-blowing when you sit there and realize just how incredibly realistic your characters move around in For Honor no matter what they're doing.
But the heart of this game is tainted. Tainted by greed. And it truly does ruin an otherwise fantastic game.
Now to start, For Honor has an in-game currency called "Steel". You get Steel by playing the campaign, or doing daily "orders", and you even get a little after every match. And this would be all well and good if Steel was just for buying cosmetics. It would be a nice progression system to keep you playing and drip feed you extras as a reward. But no, that's not where this story ends. Because this game also has another very important progression system: gear.
And gear is not just cosmetic. Gear has stats. And this gear can have a lot of stats. The difference between a fresh character (0) and a fully upgraded set of gear (108) is nothing short of downright unfair. When you first start out, you'll be playing against other players playing the same exact hero you are but hitting twice as hard, taking half damage, using almost no stamina, getting revenge four times as fast, or many other numerous advantages depending on what stats they invested in. You can win if you're the better player, sure, but you have to be a MUCH better player.
So this system in concept is not terrible. It allows you to choose strengths and weaknesses for your hero to fit your playstyle. That's great! But the problem is that getting maxed gear is a massive, massive grind. It took me roughly 70 hours of gameplay to finally fully outfit one single hero in 108 gear. Does that sound bad? Well that's still not it.
Gear is divided into 3 rarities: grey, blue, and purple. So if you want to accelerate your gear grind, you might figure that you'll just blow all your Steel on gear crates until you get a full purple set, and then start upgrading. Seems like a solid plan, right? But whoops, purple gear can't drop until you're Reputation level 3 or higher with your hero, and this information is NEVER PRESENTED IN GAME. So in effect, trying to buy gear crates before you're Reputation 3 with a hero is a complete and utter waste of Steel, and you have no way of knowing this unless you read guides or other community resources.
And here's the real kicker: the matchmaker literally doesn't consider your gearscore when making a match. Ubisoft fully intended for brand new players to be getting put up against maxed out players. So if you were thinking "well if I just get matched with people who have similar gearscore to me, this doesn't sound so bad", consider your totally reasonable dreams crushed.
Because if you haven't guessed by now, Steel can also be bought with real money. Ah, now see with that in mind, all this seemingly senseless game design suddenly starts making a very sinister kind of sense. Why con people out of Steel by intentionally providing only vague descriptions of how loot works? To get them to buy more! Why have a matchmaker that regularly puts together extremely imbalanced, one-sided matches? So that players get frustrated that they don't have good gear and potentially spend money on Steel to accelerate their gear grind! Why lock purple gear behind Reputation levels, anyway? To get people to spend money on Steel to spend on Champion Status so that they can grind Reputation levels faster!
And that's how they see For Honor. They see it as a way to milk money out of you. This is easily one of the most innovative and fresh competitive multiplayer games of recent years, but Ubisoft has mutilated and perverted it into the sick and twisted cash cow that now stands before you. I am truly heartbroken at what could have been, and I can only hope that with enough critical feedback, eventually Ubisoft will give For Honor the respect it deserves as a video game and not as a psychologically manipulative microtransaction machine.

I went into Never Alone with high expectations. I have Native American background myself, and the idea of finally being able to play a game that incorporates traditional stories and Native culture into its gameplay after years of playing games overflowing with influence from European mythos sounded wonderful. Kudos to the creators for authenticity: Never Alone is a beautifully genuine and earnest game, and at times I got chills because of how familiar the ideas depicted in the game are, especially those talked about in the cultural insights. I've seen Never Alone described as an interactive Ghibli movie; that's a fair description, because this game is both atmospheric and magical.
The praise ends there because Never Alone has major problems. The Ghibli comparison might be fair, but it's certainly not deserved. Never Alone plays like a SNES era 2D sidescrolling platformer (think Donkey Kong Country); 2D platformers aren't exactly known for their sense of adventure, exploration, or heck, even world building, but typically they aren't this monotone. The wintry, arctic atmosphere is utterly unrelenting and there's no variety. Every area is virtually indistinguishable with few, if any, unique traits to separate one wintry, arctic landscape from the other wintry, arctic landscapes. I understand the purpose is to create a cold, hopeless atmosphere, to make the players feel as if they are being assaulted by the blizzard themselves, but when the entire game is like this it just becomes dull.
The other tremendous problem is the controls. They're clunky, slow, and just difficult. The keyboard layout is a struggle to use efficiently and the controls can't be remapped to a custom configuration either; I tried using a controller but the bola, a key part of the gameplay, is essentially unusable on a controller so that's just not an option. Movement is slow, swimming is worse, and general maneuvering makes the actual platforming far more difficult than it should be if it the gameplay wasn't so clunky and sluggish.
Unfortunately, that describes the general gameplay as well. The blizzard mechanic is tiresome and frustrating. It probably would have been okay if it was implemented sparingly, but the frequency of its intrusion where you're blown around (often to your death) just because you didn't hit Ctrl soon enough or just slowed down for no reason whatsoever isn't fun, it's tiring. The platforming puzzles are fairly basic and also are often less fun than they are tedious, especially because of the sluggish and clunky controls. The final "level" culminates the frustration because there are death traps everywhere, yet they'd be pretty easily avoided if the controls were more fluid.
Honestly, this is another example of why Steam should have a neutral option for review feedback, because it's still worth trying despite the flaws. The cultural exposure and the way it is incorporated into the game is lovely, and that permeates the entire experience. It's just that the execution needed a lot more refinement. I was lucky enough to get this for essentially nothing via a Humble Bundle; at the current $15 price tag this absolutely isn't worth it unless you're one of those people obsessed with snow and winter like Jari Mäenpää, in which case go crazy I guess.
