I own all 4 Jackbox packs and this one is the second best, behind Jackbox 3. i will review each game on its own just like every other review.
Monster Seeking Monster (4/5):
The most devicive game they have ever made, and I think it is becuase it's the most complex. Everyone has to be locked into this game to have the maximum amount of fun. You also have to play with people who do not mind reciving really sexual messages from everyone else in the group, otherwise it will be super akward.
Basically you all become one of sixteen classes (which is actually quite a lot) and try to manipulate people into dating you (or others) and gain hearts for every time you successfully date another person. The crux is that you can only send 4 text messages between everyone per round, so you have to maximize your convincing. The game gets so complicated by the last round it turns into mayhem, and that was fun because everyone just guilts eachother into dating them or else you get a penalty from their powers.
Overall: This is the most complex and complete game Jackbox has ever made, and you have to change your play style depending on which monster you get.
Survive the Internet (4/5):
Basically internet edgelords the game. You each get a prompt from the game that you enter truthfully, and someone makes a headline (or attaches a hashtag / location marker) for another player's answer. It makes the group laugh the hardest if no one gets offended easily. It also has the best art style they have made, the winner even gets thrown into hell at the end of the game. The only reason this isn't a 5/5 is the last round (where you make captions for pictures) uses super basic stock pictures so everything you make up seems like a stretch.
Overall: Produces the most absurd answers of any Jackbox game. Only play if you are okay with being offensive. Sidenote, the scoring in this game is super feast-or-famine, win 2 rounds and you basically can't lose after that, but the scoring isn' that much of a focus for us.
Fibbage 3 (4/5):
Fibbage is where the game gives a prompt and everyone makes a plausible lie to trick other players into mis-guessing what the true answer is. It's the same as Fibbage 1 and 2 with different prompts. The art style is great.
The big difference is in the new game mode Enough About You where the prompts are about your friends. Everyone gets a prompt that they answer truthfully and one by one the game acts as regular Fibbage.
The only reason this game isn't 5/5 is becuase the last round of Enough About You is literally just entering a truth and a lie without a prompt, and people have a 50/50 chance of getting it right. This could be easily fixed by giving the user a basic prompt  like "How do you feel about dogs?" (that would be boring but you know what I mean).
Overall: Fibbage is great and Enough About You is a great addition. Always a crowd-pleaser.
Bracketeering (2/5):
Tournament Quiplash. The big crutch is that the prompts aren't that interesting, but I think that's by design because in later rounds the prompt changes and the answers stay the same. The person with the best answer doesn't get the most points, instead you get points for placing bets on which answer you think will win (sometimes you need to bet against / for your own answer). It creates a few laughs but since the answers remain for 2-4 rounds they lose their luster.
Overall: Fun art style (every game in this pack is lively and fun), initial rounds are funny because it is basically Quiplash, but they get boring and the game drags on for too long.
Civic Doodle (2/5):
Cumulative Drawful. The game starts where two people draw a picture that starts as a single line the game gives you, and the others vote using emoji. Then the winner's drawing gets passed to the next two players and they add on to that drawing, and another round of votes are done. I would reccommend never playing with extended timers on becuase teh drawings get way too cluttered even without them.
Round two is much better, all players draw at the same time and only draw what the game instructs in steps (ex: round 1 draw eyes, round 2 draw nose, etc.) and everyone votes for which is the best, and then everyone is given the winning drawing and add to it.
Overall:  The game gets way too cluttered in general. Jackbox has made two much better drawing games in the past (TeeKO and Drawful). Sidenote, I find the announcers annoying, they talk for way too long.
Overall I give it a (3.8/5).

There's a lot to like about this game.
The ship design is in depth and works pretty great. It's great fun to design ships with specific roles since every decision were you put which parts matters.
But there are also a lot of issues and some of them show that this is an indie developer and not someone very adept at game design.
1. The combat is just boring. It has a lot of good things about it. The graphics are pretty, the ships move in cool ways and it's pretty tactical. But it just moves soooo slow. There is no option to speed of the passage of time which kills the pacing in these battles. First you position your troops, then you wait half a minute were they crawl across the map until their actually in firing range and then you wait till the ships slowly widdle down each others help until you're done. It's just too damn slow. I once had to wait two minutes being bored because my big ships turned too slowly and always missed a fast small ship of the enemy. The last one. The ship was way too weak to even get through my ships shields, but i still had to wait two whole minutes until my ships finally hit that little bugger.
2. The ground combat is even worse. It's designed in an Xcom sort of way were you move your units around a grid to attack and finally kill the enemies. But it's just not fun. It takes way too long to finish any mission, because the enemies always have about 10 times your numbers and all you can do is crawl through the level.
Rule number one of game design: If you can't implement a feature properly don't implement it. These ground battles, which you can't auto resolve by the way, only add tedium to the game and are not fun to play.
3. This all would not have been terrible if the strategy part of the game would have been great, but it's not. The game crawls very slowly. Often you are just forced to end turn after turn without doing anything, because the pollution mechanics means your production is pretty much always♥♥♥♥♥♥and takes forever to finish anything. The research isn't all that interesting and worst of all it locks you out of technologies unless you make a creative race or use the horrible diplomacy to trade for the tech.
4. I heard from quite a few people that the AI cheats massively and stomps you with unkillable armies in the later game, but i didn't even get that far without growing bored.
Don't buy. It's not good.

I am a huge Jackbox fan and am continuously introducing the game to more and more people that also love the games. I like the direction the games are heading with more of a focus on having fun rather than winning. Jackbox 3 managed this very well even with a Trivia Game that is now the best trivia game I have ever played. For example, I was not much of a fan of Fibbage in previous games because in order to win you had to answer questions correctly or make up believable lies which cannot be at all outrageous or funny because then it would obviously be a lie. The added game mode for answering questions about yourself and friends brings the focus back to having fun over winning. Every game in this back is about being funny, creative, and clever rather than being right. Monster Seeking Monster is the one that stands out the most as unique (well, it is kind of like Cluster♥♥♥♥!) and garnered the most laughs from both experienced and new players.

I am basing my "Do Not Recommend" on the case that the average person doesn't have the other three games. If that is the case and you want more Jackbox then by all means buy it right away. I would also recommend trying out Brentalfloss' game of the same vein "Use Your Words".
If you have yet to play ANY Jackbox Party Pack then this is definitely one of the worst to jump into. It has one REALLY bad game, and a drawing game which is very jaded on if you'll like it, which is typical for the Party Packs, and when I say bad I mean play it once and never again bad. The other three games are pretty good but don't even come close to some of the content you will find in the previous three packs.
Fibbage 3 is more Fibbage: you come up with a lie that sounds convincing enough to be the truth and you get points if your friends pick your lie. The best part about this third edition of Fibbage is the fact that it brings a new game mode to the front titled "Fibbage Enough About You". In this mode you will be doing the normal Fibbage routine but the questions are entirely centered about yourself and your friends. These can lead to some great moments and can show just how much you really know your friends. I find it fairly similar to Fakin It from the Jackbox Party Pack 3 in that you need to have good knowledge of the people around you to effectively suss out the lie.
Monster Seeking Monster is a game in which you are a monster that is trying to date... a monster. You are given 4 messages per night which you can use to send any message of your choice to another player. You have to convince the other player to date you so you can get a point and move up in the rankings. Each character has a hidden identity or power that spices the game up such as the Blob that doubles all of his points ever time he dates three unique players. This game is a little like Town Of Salem where you are trying to lie about your role or create a friendship that will garner you a guaranteed point every night.
Survive The Internet: It is basically edgelord the game, and its hilarious. You are initially given a prompt to respond to such as "Describe Milk". You then respond to the prompt: "Its white, tastes great, and I love it in my cereal". A different player will then receive your response and try to put a twist on it to make you look like a bad person: "Describe Ejaculate"  "It's white, tastes great, and I love it in my cereal".  This game can obviously snow ball into a competition in who will go the farthest before going too far. And for that it is amazing, If you like Quiplash from the previous packs then this game is right up your ally.
And now for the duds:
Bracketeering: This game is just terrible Quiplash. Everybody is given the same prompt and at the end everyone votes on the best response. The only thing different from Quiplash is that you vote on which answer you think will win the popular vote and sometimes the prompt gets switched up mid bracket. It is really just a low tier Quiplash and probably the worst game in any Party Pack let alone this one.
Civic Doodle: The token drawing game of the pack. Two people duke it out in drawing a picture out of a line already on the canvas. The viewers vote on which picture is the funniest and that picture is then given to the next to players to try and improve on. The problem with thsi game is that drawing on a cell phone is absolutely horrible and there really isn't too much canvas space to work with. The game does get a little better the furhter you go on by giving you prompts but the games themselves last a solid 20 minutes which is very uncommon for a Jackbox Game where the main point is to be short and hilarious. Not long and boring.
These last two games really drag the entire experience down. When compared to the Jackbox Party Pack 3 this game doesn't even hold a candle to it. Three had STELLAR games like Trivia Murder Party and of course Quiplash. It also had my personal favorite Jackbox game Fakin It which is extremely fun when you know your friends well enough to suss out their lies.
If you haven't played Jackbox 2 or 3 yet then don't even think about buying this one instead. You will just be disappointed in what could've been.
When you compared it to the other three games it just falls completely flat and for that reason I can't recommend unless you have the other few and are craving for more. It defnitely has some good moments but for $25 its hard to justify the price when the other games are just so much better.

I currently have logged over 24 hours in game time and felt the need to express my opinion about Stardrive 2. My time with Stardrive 2 has been very up and very down.
Let's start with the up's. First the price of the game is competitive with other indi games. Second the races are fairly balanced. Third the tech tree that forces you to skip a particular tech but later aquire it through trade is a fantastic idea, forcing you to expand your playstyle into areas you might not have chosen with diplomacy mattering. Fourth is designing ships. Seeing a ship that you custom built wreck the universe is one of the best parts of the game. Last is having the ship battles being free moving and not on a grid. Gridded ship battles would have been so much easier to create but free moving ships that can dodge with a proper timed burst of speed or be swarmed with smaller ships is the best.
Now the worst. Bad starting systems can spell doom on turn one. Having a hero buff three even four planets can be such a huge boost to playability that getting stuck with only one hurts bad. Next is wormholes. Wormholes often give a direct perment route to your home solar system which spells doom for the player as the AI seems to cheat with ship building production. Also on the topic of wormholes a mysterious race will nonstop attack you with much more advanced ships when you least can afford to be attacked from special random wormholes. Most of my playtime was spent turtling due to wormholes. Kind of kills the explore part of 4X. Special research is avaliable but has to be turned on and off with a slider by the user and isn't explained very well. Hell sliders don't work well at all due to zero percise control of the numaric imput. Ships need a testing ground because important battles have been lost because a ship did not function as I believed it would. DO NOT USE MISSLES. Take my word for it. Last is the stability/loading issues. I did have a few nothing a autosave load didn't fix but after patch 1 I cannot load a campaign more than 33% rendering that mode useless. Deleted the game and redownloaded but same issue. I guess I will wait for patch 2.
At the moment I feel very torn about the game. It is very much a 4x game but with amazing RTS portions that make it very fun to play but the speed you make contact with hostile AI combined with often lack luster starts can force rerolls untill a viable start can be had. That paired with the INABILITY TO PLAY THE GAME makes it where I cannot recommend the game to anyone who is reading this. Maybe in a month when it has been properly patched but that is another review.

Gosh this game is brilliant! It's not a simple game by any means even though it looks that way maybe on first glance. Expect to have a learning curve of 1 - 2 hours until you can hold your ground in a multiplayer game.
There's a great campaign to guide you along the way which is quite fun to play but the meat of the game to me is in the Multiplayer. You can play up to 4v4 with shared or separate control (as in everyone controls one fort) and that's where the game really starts to shine as you have a couple different approaches to everything and counters to them as well. There's nothing more satisfying than taking down that pesky fort that you have hammered for quite some time now with a surprise attack the enemy didnt see coming. Coordinating your attacks and outplaying your oponents defenses is very very rewarding as you can't turtle forever, at some point you have to bring the fight to your oponents.
Top that off with a simple but great physics engine that limits you in the way you can build. You can slant armor so bullets just ricochet off but now you're giving a prime target for mortars, so what is it going to be commander ?
The game is not perfect yet however, some things especially in the multiplayer lobby need explaining (AI Settings, separate commanders for teammates, more info on maps), more varied Maps for 2v2 / 3v3 / 4v4. But as of now you can expect to have a blast regardless if you're not to serious. (There's no ranked system yet)
There are people who complain about the content, i feel thats not fair as the content comes mainly through what you do with the tools at your disposal, i'm not sure the game needs more weapons as you already have a ton of ways to use them in conjunction to how your build your base etc.
A specific feedback to the devs is also about the machineguns, give us an option to deactivate their automatic fire, but avoid introducing mechanics that one can only figure out when he researches them: that machineguns stop firing above a certain height is unintuitive and not good for whatever reason you implemented it.
Another thing is to take the "E" hotkey into the tutorial, it's the single most important thing in multiplayer as you can use your control groups without looking at them and aiming all over again. People who played the game certainly agree with me there.

DR;TL -- No save function combined with steep difficulty tarnish this otherwise beautiful game. If you are a die-hard of this genre, like a good horror story, or don't mind the lack of saves, then get it on discount.
This game is in 4 "episodes", if you play perfectly you could probably finish each in a half-hour. However the learning curve is steep. There is not much hand-holding in this game. Luckily there is a good Steam guide (had to consult at least once per chapter) and also some videos. There are a few hints offered when the game is paused or loading. Pay attention to these an it will save some frustration.
There are a combination of sound, text-parsing and equipment usage puzzles.  A little familiarity with text-parsing games (like Zork and other Infocom games) helps but is not necessary. Again, I had to consult the guide when I knew what to do but couldn't figure out *how* to do it. I enjoyed most of the puzzles, but again felt some were on the hard side. The screen aliasing makes some of the fine details hard to make out - I don't know if thus was deliberate or not to increase the difficulty of some puzzles.
And this is where the lack of save function comes up. The only way to "save" a game is to finish an episode. For most other games I'd just save and do something else when I get stuck. Can't do that here. You can always pause the game and mabe hibernate your computer, but then you can't go to a different Steam game. If the episodes were shorter or easier, I could overlook this. There are several places each episode that could logically be save points. But I think this is enough of an issue that most people should be aware before buying this one that I'm barely down-checking this one, If I could give a neutral recommendation I would,
It's really too bad, since the graphics and voice acting are great, and the story is excellent. It hits many of the classic horror tropes, and does it well. Very few games have this many twists and unexpected turns, and I was on the edge of my seat quite a bit. The game designers put alot of thought into this one. It took me 9 hours to complete (a bunch of it was doing something else while an episode was in progress) and I want to right away re-play the game.

Story:One-note characters talking about one-note♥♥♥♥♥♥ Nothing too special about the story, just gives you a reason to kill stuff. Though i will advise people to change the voice acting to japanese not because of weeb♥♥♥♥♥♥but because the english voices will make your ears bleed due to them being stupidly growly.
Graphics:Now the visuals are pretty impressive, i have to say. For a game that was released back in 2010, it looks really nice. The developers did a great job in terms of graphical fidelity and performance. Sure some textures look a bit questionable but that doesn't really hurt the game. The only negative thing i could say about the games look is that it could use a bit more color. It looks a bit sterile at times but who knows maybe that's what they were going for.
Music and sound: The sound design in regards to weapons, environmental stuff etc. is well done. However i will say that the soundtrack is pretty forgettable, just a bunch of techo-music blasting in the background.
Gameplay:Now this is where the main course begins. The gameplay basically consist of you running through everything from corridors to big open areas, blasting robots that get in your way. This tool gives you so much mobility and control on your character, which makes the fighting all the more enjoyable because you have to solely rely on your reactions. This game also uses a cover system which you would think be intrusive and break the pacing of the game but it doesn't. It's only used in very short bursts because hiding behind cover can get you killed due to enemies flanking you or throwing grenades, shooting missles etc. Constant movement is a must. This game also features a slow-down mechanic which adds even more to the games fun factor. As for the weapons they're all  pretty satisfying to use, they feel powerful and have a good sence of impact and your given a decent amount of them to keep things interesting. Got this game for 5$ on 360 years and years ago. Then several years later I got a PS3 copy for 5$. Fast forward a few years and I've given the same game another 20$ to play it on my PC. I own this game on every platform it's existed on.
That takes a certain level of quality, and Vanquish definitely meets that as one big diamond in the rough.
I say this as someone who failed to ever conciously recognize the game's existence- when Vanquish came out, it got universally panned because the advertisements focused on the plot, and yeah, that was a big mistake. So let me set the record straight.
PROS:
- The best cover based shooter you're ever gonna play because you're too busy scooting around to use it.
- Great sci-fi soundtrack. I've got the Bogey Battle theme on my Ipod.
- I think Vanquish set the bar for quality enemy design. Every enemy in Vanquish has multiple behaviors that can be influenced by the variety of ways you attack or otherwise dismember them, and they never stop being valid threats. The lowly Gorgi will still turn you inside out if you get meleed by him, or a wounded one goes suicide bomber on you. They all have unique roles in combat and demand a certain level of adaptability from the player to deal with them. Couple this with their unique appearences and personalities, I think these guys end up being just as, if not even more important than the game's rocket thrusters for game longetivity.
- A superb port job on this Platinum title sharply contrasts the shakey start the Nier Automata PC launch had. This game has a fully unlocked FPS and refresh rates. I've played this game many times on consoles, and this readily outshines their performance.
- They added new weapons to the game! Having played it many times before, this was a pleasant surprise and opened up some new options for combat styles. They're a little bit rarer drops than the other weapons however, so be sure to respect your ammo count.
- While they're not actually both voiced by Steve Blum, the two protagonists both sound like they're voiced by Steve Blum with slightly different gruff voices. It's adorable.
- It's fast, aggressive action that seldom ever stops.
CONS:
- As of May 26th, there is a very bizzare glitch where the increased framerate causes you to take a much higher amount of damage than normal. I honestly didn't notice for awhile, having previously played the game on harder difficulties, but even veterans are gonna start feeling this glitch in the last several acts, and it'll be far more punishing to new players. If you're a newbie to Vanquish, it might not hurt to wait until this gets patched before you buy.
-The Sniper Rifle is dumb and getting it in a weapons box always feels like a little kick to the♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm not sure what the hell a sniper rifle is doing in a game where you're perpetually rocketing around and doing wheelies on robot faces, but it's there. It's so lame that the devs felt the need to crowbar in a single sequence where you MUST use the sniper rifle in a wannabe stealth segment that slows down the whole pace of the game. It's kinda like when your mom invites that one mouthbreather over to your birthday party and makes you hang out with him for 5 minutes instead of your best friends so he doesn't feel left out.
- And of course, well, the big one. The story.
Space Putin blows up L.A with a space laser in a bizzarely disturbing sequence that might be the only reason the game is rated M, sans the occasional F bomb getting launched by Steve GrumpyPants Blum. President Not-Hillary-Clinton (topical, amirite?) launches the space soldiers into space to storm the death laser satellite that also doubles as a city for a bunch of space Russians that don't exist and you gotta stop Space Putin from blowing up New York. There's the entire plot, sans a very goofy plot twist that gets only funnier in light of recent events.
Ultimately the plot really doesn't matter as it's just an excuse for a variety of action set pieces, but at the time of the game's release, Vanquish was near universally panned because the advertisements focused on the story and everyone thought the game looked dumb as hell. They aren't entirely wrong in a sense- the Vanquish story is ripped right from that one notebook you had in middle school where you wrote stories for games/movies/comics you wanted to make, and you thought tossing in profanity and lots of wannabe tough guy quips after you watched a bunch of Schwarzenneger movies would make it super cool.
Don't get me wrong, I think it's actually pretty charming in a schlock B-movie sort of way, and the game lets you skip all cutscenes so you can skip them and get right to shooting if it irks you. But it's very much an objective flaw, as it initially sank the game's chances of making it's money back. But that's just dumb people's fault for thinking every game has to be Bioshock or the Last of Us.

Theres very few games i can honestly say i love, and get completely drawn into, i can probably count on one hand the few games i've become a nerdy addict too. One of those games is Fable, so i wanted something to fill that little humourous funny game void thingy left in my gaming heart after finishing those games. This is when i stumbled upon Overlord.
Overlord is the best game i've played on PC so far, and considering i've only been playing for a few weeks i suppose that isn't saying much. But this game has the fun of an action'y fight'y kind of game. plus it has all the benefits of something thats relaxing and humourous, this game has made me laugh a few times, which is sad really... but thats beside the point.
Basically you play as an Overlord (what a surprise) You have a selection of minions, and to clarify, no they're not yellow and they do not wear dungaree's and goggles! They are however, blue, red, brown or green, they each have their own special 'powers', which i think is in a way what gives this game a slight sense of strategy, in a weird deluded way.
You must pick the right minions for each quest, inevitably some minions will die, or you'll kill them, so you or your minions kill different bugs to get 'orbs' of minion life, these orbs get stored at little colour co-ordinated crators where you can summon them at selected points in the game, you can also convert your minions back into orbs, or trade your minions in for health,  thus killing them.
Once you've selected your minions you purse through quests, throwing them into battles with a range of different creatures, and occasionally lending them a hand yourself, although the overlords fighting isn't the most thrilling and he doesn't have a wide range of weapons to chose from, he does have the benefit of 4 spells that can be cast, using your 'mana health bar' that can add a bit of a punch to otherwise space bar bashing when the minions need a hand.
The quests follow a simple story line and you can pick up and drop them as you wish, which really adds a sense of Free roam to this game, you can simply teleport to most areas and view open quests in these areas from you're main tower which you can revert back to from the main menu or tower crator, this tower is also something you can upgrade through in game currency as you progress which is a nice little back feature, but not something i think the game necessarily needs and certainly isn't a big feature, just an added bonus.
So in summary, If you've played fable and enjoyed it, you're 99.9% likely to enjoy this game, (You can even kick your minions if you miss days of kicking chickens!) if you havne't played fable, what is wrong with you? But just buy it anyways. There is nothing to not love about this cute little devious game!

Anna - Extended Edition does psychological horror better than any title I have ever played.  The sound, music, narration, story, design - all these things are absolutely remarkable, and Anna should be played by anyone who wants to see how a game like this should be done.
Quite unfortunately, the entire game is left in ruins due to an insulting puzzle-solving mechanic.  If the other features build the perfect arc, all that's necessary is a keystone that'll just keep those things in place.  It doesn't exist, and worse, this was reportedly done on purpose.
You repeatedly pick up items that you'll never use.  Puzzles make no sense and worse, there's no effort for them to do so.  I tried my damndest to get through the game without a guide, but it's impossible.  Unless you plan to hammer away at this title for a solid month for hours on end each day, you will never figure out each puzzle.  Worse yet, there are multiple endings depending on how you play the game - and nothing is explained to you at any point.  There are useful guides online, but I'd imagine even THEY needed help before writing it, or they went into the game's code to make sense of it all.
The only way I can recommend Anna is with a guide.  There are some on Steam and you can find some on YouTube.  They are non-negotiable.  If you want to enjoy Anna, you have to abandon your sense of integrity when it comes to solving puzzles on your own and use a guide.  If you can accept this, Anna will give you a new understanding of how games should be made with regards to every other feature.
Specifically the horror.  This game, numerous times, sent chills down my entire body.  They started at my neck and spread throughout my body and to my arms and legs.  Yet, not once though was I afraid to continue.  I never thought I shouldn't do something because something's lurking around the corner.  This game does horror better than any other title.  It exists on a level above all others.  There are no jump-scares or smash cuts to scary images.  While I might react quickly to a zombie or monster in another game, in this there are no monsters.  The every-changing environment is enough to scare you.  One feature in particular is a visage of a woman made of wood that changes position and follows you.  It never attacks you, it's simply there.  Yet each time it appears in a place I don't expect, even if I was just looking there, it managed to get me almost every time.
For this reason alone, I recommend Anna.  Everything in the game is fantastic.  The one thing that is completely absent, and insultingly so by design, is sensible puzzle solving.  If you can stomach the fact that you'll need a guide from the onset, this title is thoroughly enjoyable.

Onto the actual review, it's a tactical shooter with two teams of five. Each team, the defenders and attackers, has its own selection of operators who each have a special gadget or gimmick of some kind. The match end when one team has all of its members elimated, the time runs out or the objective is secured.
Each operator has to be unlocked by playing the game, acquiring "renown," the sytem of currency then choosing one of your choice. In the standard version it won't be too difficult to get a good selection. The operators aren't specifically designed to counter specific enemy operators nor to complement an ally operator, but you'll notice that certain team compositions do have more synergy than others. It's unlike other class based shooters in that a team of any selection of characters has a fair chance at winning.
This game is more about tactics and attention to detail than just skill in aiming and reflex time. If you're smart then you can often kill an opponent before he even knows where you are, by a cleverly placed trap or by shot through a wall. It's very frustrating when you're at the receiving end of a smart maneuver, but you always feel as if you're learning a tactic every match and that you ca always try something new. If you want a first person shooter focusing on small team tactics that isn't Counter Strike or if you just need a break from Counter Strike, then I would strongly recommend this.

I really wish this game had a bigger fan base, because it's honestly a fantastic game! It's a great example of what a horror game should really be about. While it's not as scary as Amnesia or other games of its type and does not have the greatest gameplay, it does a very good job of immersing the player into its exceptionally freaky and creepy story. In this game, what scares you the most are not the monsters, but the idea that you are alone trying to fight your way through so many things to save whatever is left of humankind. While playing, this game will make you question: "What if this was different? What if that never happened? What if..." every time giving you a different outcome in each of your speculations about it. That's what makes this game great and, in my opinion, something that other horror games should really try to focus on.

This game super nostalgic, pure retro 90's NES goodness. It seems the developers where fond of this era of gameing and where trying to really encapsulate what made great games back in the day. You can tell they put a lot of love and effort into this game since almost everthing fits in that style like the gameplay, the music, the cheesy storyline and the colors in the 8-BIT Pellet.
You can tell that this isnt one of those games that tries to be retro for the sake of it, but out of true love for the era in which this games come from, which is something I have seen other developers try and fail, since some use it as an excuse, Oniken uses as a deliverate choice.
Tight and hard gameplay is what really sells this game as a cool retro throwback to the 90's as it feels like a later title in the NES lifespan, but still it doesnt fully goes dumb like some games do, it does it with clever enemy spawns and bosses, that while simple to understand the pattern of, can be frustrating to beat.
This game is trully a love letter to the NES classic action games of the era and I fully recomend it to anybody who likes that style game.

This atmospheric horror game gets so much mileage out of its simple mechanics, and in 3 short hours tells a story that is engrossing, disturbing, and eventually even moving. You really have to play it to believe it. The individual episodes give you elements of horror, sci-fi, and survival  genres, but ultimately this is a game of escalating psychological tension, in which you experience the protagonist's feelings of dread, anxiety, guilt, and powerlessness at the horrors unfolding in front you.
At least that's how it works when everything comes together. Stories Untold is presented as an anthology, and as is usually the case, not every entry in the anthology holds up equally well. The second and third episodes felt slow and sometimes frustrating as stand-alones; the second one compensates for this with a memorable scene and story, but the thid one is almost a total miss, combining the most tedious gameplay with the least suspenseful setting. It all pays off in the last episode though. I would have been satisfied if the game ended with a final stand-alone vignette, instead you get an astonishing final act that brings the seemingly unrelated episodes together and reveals the truth about the game's protagonist.
The music is sublime. The graphics, while rudimentary, still contain their fair share of haunting images. I imagine some players will find the game frustrating or dull, and if you like your horror games full of action and/or gore, this is probably not the game for you. But if you're looking for a smart, scary game that will stick with you after you're done, you should definitely give Stories Untold a try.

For those familiar with the game and Platinum and just want to know if the port's good, then yes it is. There are tons of gameplay, control, graphical, and audio options, the game runs beautifully, and feels even better with M+K controls. The only issue I've run into are some choppy cutscenes after extended play.
For those looking for more info on the game, Vanquish is a third person shooter that plays around with the mechanics of both cover-based shooters like Gears of War and faster-paced dodge-and-dash action games. The game doesn't pick a side between the two, instead opting to encourage the player into mixing up between dodging, taking cover, and sprinting. In typical Platinum Games fashion, they give you a set of mechanics to use while giving you lots of different challenges to use those mechanics. It just feels really good and challenging in a satisfying way. There's replay value in streamlining your runs and trying higher difficulties or using different weapons for each run.
The second biggest thing going for Vanquish is its spectacle. Battles are generally varied in style and are large and epic in scale. Cutscenes and dialogue like in Metal Gear Rising are well-localized and entertaining to watch in a cornball sort of way.
Any problems I have with the game are niggling and easily fixable or ignorable like the cutscene problem I mentioned in the first paragraph. I can definitely recommend this to anybody even slightly interested in buying it.

Overlord is certainly worth playing. It has good gamplay and a nice chunk of humour. Keep in mind though that there is no serious plot in it, as it relies on its humour.
In the game you control minions along with the main character, which is, the Overlord. The Overlord is fairly squishy alone, but is capable of doing decent damage. This is where the minions come handy. They can overwhelm opponents with their numbers, leaving the Overlord out of harms way.
There are four types of minions. Brown, Red, Green and Blue. Every type has their own special abilities and uses. Brown minions lack a special quality, but are the thoughest in a fight. Reds throw fireballs, are immune to fire and can extinguish fires blocking your way. Greens are immune to poison and can remove toxic fumes. Blues can go into water without drowning.
Then there is your tower. In the tower you can forge armor and weapons for the Overlord to use, customize its looks and you can even get a mistress there. Yay. There is also a teleporter, which you can use to get to places you have visited previously.
The music in this game fits it very well. The soundtrack is not awesome, but as stated, it fits the games setting and helps set up the atmosphere. Visuals are nice for such a old game. The animations looked a bit awkward in certain situations, but it kind of just adds to the humour. One might even think that they were made awkward on purpose. Heh.
Overall this game has a lot of good points and a very few bad ones. The controls for the gamepad did feel a bit "iffy", so I'd recommend using a keyboard and a mouse. If I had to name to biggest issue I have with the game, I'd have to say it's the fact that you can't save manually. Anywho, this game is definetly worth picking up if you're looking for a humorous and lighthearted RPG.

+ Overlord is a fun and wonderful game. If you have any liking whatsoever towards the Tolkien Universe and don't mind a game that actually succesfully makes fun of it I would recommend it. This is not just a uninspired shoddy attempt for a parody, the developers have taken their spoof seriously. The graphics are bright and detailed and the engine runs smooth. Character models and animation are great and I can't help but enjoy the sound of breaking pots and dishes. There are lots of mechanics to be explored as you progress in the game and you'll have a good sense of satisfaction once you're done.
- The world is not exactly an open one, but not entirely linear either. You can walk about and kill sheep or loot places at your own leisure, although that might get a bit boring if you choose to do so for a long time. Some parts of the game you can do in a different order, but you won't get further until you've reached certain goals in certain areas.
If you're not playing with a controller you'll experience some annoyance when trying to swipe your flock of gremlins to the back of the field, but it's far from gamebreaking and at least you don't need to do it all the time. However if you do use a controller there are far worse issues with camera angles and target selection, so I just really wouldn't recommend that (unless you actually manage to get used to it somehow).
I think the game is worth its full price including the raising hell expansion pack, but if you're not sure wait for the sales.

Oniken is a fun little platformer that pays hommage to NES titles such as Ninja Gaiden and Rygar; however, takes all the elements that makes those titles good and makes it it's own, even the difficulty. It has a lot of polish in all the right areas; however, it does have it's quirks. Here are all the noticable pros and cons I picked up while playing this wonderful, yet difficult game:
+ Has a fully animated opening cinematic shown before even seeing the main menu.
+ Super tight jump controls that feels just right.
+ Diverse repertoire of enemies offer a sense accomplishment when defeated.
+ Hidden breakable walls offer reward for exploration.
+ Level design polish in the form of animations on breakable things that normally wouldn’t be breakable, such as falling rocks. Some developers would simply program them fall vertically and damage the player accordingly; however, JoyMasher goes above and beyond, and as a testament to the quality of their game via polish, you can slash their rocks.
- Oniken launches in a windowed launcher that lets the player have access to features should have been handled in the main menu instead.
- Limited supply of powerups diminish the player experience, there are literally two: Sword Powerup and Grenades.
- Where Oniken did succeed in learning from it's predecessor's mistakes, it falls short with it's convoluted grenade throwing mechanic.
- Unbalanced gameplay difficulty makes for more of a three-yard hurdle by the second stage, forcing the player through three long unique sections of the game that feel like they should all three be their own stages.

I recommend this game if you like Ninja Gaiden, Shatterhand or other 8-bit games. Music rocks, controls are tight, cool bosses, there is everything you want.

So far, this is an excellent, robust training tool -- RS2014 provides a guided experience, but gives you tons of options to go your own way if you prefer. I'm very impressed.
I got Rock Band 3's Pro Guitar peripheral when that game came out, and the difference here is striking. Rock Band's Pro Mode was an impressive achievement, but the game was organized around casual group play. That was great for the "normal" Rock Band instruments, but extremely awkward for anyone playing Pro Guitar or Pro Bass -- learning new songs for those players was time consuming and would hold up the group, while everyone else could jump in or out and play things at a comfortable skill level, as the game intended.
RS2014, by contrast, would not be entertaining for a room full of people. And that's good. It assumes there's one person playing, and it watches them, and tries like hell to figure out how to help them learn. It's as fast or (more importantly) as slow as you need it to be, and it understands that learning an instrument is a marathon, not a sprint.
I haven't used Rocksmith long enough yet to know how good it is at conferring really advanced skills. But everything I've seen up to this point has been promising -- I'm having a ton of fun, and I know I'm learning. Definitely recommended.

Some people who are familiar with me might remember me talking on launch day about my excitement at finally getting to learn guitar and my plans to post all kinds of updates as I got better and stuff. Those same people might realise that I never did that. (Good old college finals wrecking everything...) So now that I'm finally on break, I decided to start putting some serious time into Rocksmith 2014 starting with the new year, and make learning a thing or two about guitar my new year's resolution, so to speak. Well I've managed to keep with that promise to myself fairly well, and have been playing quite a bit this year, making sure to spend time practicing and doing finger workouts (Yes! Finger workouts!) every sing day. From my time spent right after buying Rocksmith 2014, I'd learned a few things about playing, but hadn't put much serious work in till the start of this year, so in effect the 4 days of 2014 I've had prior to this post are the only real time I've spent actually trying to learn and improve and not just screw around.
(TL;DR I've been practicing for 4 days)
Now that we've got that little bit of exposition out of the way...
Wow.
Rocksmith works. It seriously works. It brings all the tools to the table for you to use, and then just simply shows and helps you use them to improve, and improve fast. After 4 days of Rocksmith and a few youtube videos, I'm comfortable enough with the fretboard to play through a handful of the lower difficulty songs with solid hit rates, able to figure out spots I'm having trouble with and practice them until I feel comfortable, and challenge myself to get better all while having fun and actually feeling like I'm making progress.
In fact, the feeling of making progress is my favorite part of this game/tool. Every single time I stand up to play it, I feel like I'm moving forward, becoming just a little bit quicker with my fingers, more consistent with my strumming, and more accurate with my timing. This software manages to perfectly blend combine a learning environment with the entertainment and approachabiality of a game in a way that's convinced me that I want to learn, I want to keep hammering away at Blitzkrieg Bop and Next Girl, that I want to struggle with the weird way Smoke on the Water is played, and that I want to spend time learning guitar rather than playing other games.
(TL;DR After 4 days I feel like I've made real progress, and I'm motivated to keep progressing)
The game won't teach you guitar yourself, you've got to bring your own motivation to the game to get anything out of it, but if you're willing to work, the game helps you in ways that make your work feel rewarding. I finally brought my motivation into Rocksmith, and I'm starting to get skills out of it that I find absolutely amazing, and I can't wait to see how much more progress I can make the next time I stand up and play.
(TL;DR If you're motivated, like I am now, this game will help you turn your motivation into real guitar playing skills.)
Absolutely reccomended.
Edit: Just as an FYI, I bought this with the Epiphone Les Paul Junior through Amazon for $200, and I'm extremely happy with guitar as well.

I just rage quit this game, and that is never a good state of mind to write a review. But I can't not recommend the game. The fact is that
; This is for people who wants a nostalgia fueled game that does not compromise its retroness. The single concession it seems to make is to let you choose the mission you want to start playing, if you beat the previous mission at least once. So thankfully, it seems to acknowledge that the lives/continue system so common back then was a pointless inheritance of the arcade. But this modern concept is definitely the exception in Oniken.
What I'm trying to say is that every poor design choice in the game seems intentional. The designers seem very aware of what they did. Even if I do not enjoy the game, their goal was to make a unapologetically nostalgic game and they did exactly that!  And it does a good job at it; If someone showed me footage of this game telling me it's an nes game I would believe it.
So if that is EXACTLY what you want get it now. Emphasis on "exactly" because if you just like retro graphics or chiptunes or just enjoy platformers, then skip it.
I got this with Odallus, by the same devs. If you want a simple platformer with pixel graphics but none of this ninja gaiden memorization-driven difficulty, Odallus is a... slightly safer bet.

The Darkness 2 is a First Person Shooter which is based on a comic book series with the similar name. In the story campaign you play as Jackie Estacado, an italian mob boss with supernatural power based on darkness. This game has a comic book feel and look to it in term of aesthetic. There are also a decent amount of weapons and abilities that you could use to mow your way through enemies. The combat feels really fun as you mix both gunplay and supernatural powers to slay your enemy, although your abilities would be disabled in the presence of light! Abilities can also be upgraded from a skill tree through points gained from killing enemies. there are also several collectables hidden in this game that you could find and they would provide some backstory to the game.
In Vendetta mode, which is basically the co-op component of the game you could play between 4 different characters which has their own unique personality, weapon and abilities. They have their own unique dialogue in each different mission and would have banter with other characters if they are there. They also have their own skill tree which you can upgrade through points gained from killing enemies.
However, this game does have a weird bug regarding V-Sync. Apparently if you were to turn off v-sync, you would be stuck in vents for some reason and this would prevent progression. Turning on v-sync would fix the issue.
Overall, this is a pretty decent game and still looks pretty good at the time of this review, however you would most likely be playing vendetta mode alone unless you got friends as there are almost nobody available in the matchmaking since this is a pretty old game. I would give this game a 7/10.

Basically, avoid this game like the plague right now. As an avid fan of the STALKER games it pains me to see a game that promises to carry on their legacy turn out to be something like this, but, save for a small handful of SMGs, sniper rifles and shotguns dominate entirely, no matter the map, and high-level people with the perk to take both on one loadout slot are impossible to kill if you don't get the drop on them with a shotgun or sniper rifle yourself. Assault rifles have so much recoil that you can't accurately hit someone, especially when they're moving, and their damage output is pitiful compared to that of any other gun (For example an AK-47 firing 7.62mm rifle rounds does one point of damage more than a PPSH SMG firing 9mm pistol rounds, and it has much higher recoil as well.), and there's a fine line between realistic damage that makes for a satisfying experience and damage so high that the only way for you to influence the fight to go in your favor is using the most absurd guns and getting the drop on someone, and this game blasts through that line and goes deep into the territory of the later catagory. On top of all that, shotguns and snipers don't suffer from any real sort of recoil, definitely nowhere near the recoil of the assault rifles, so even someone with almost no experience with FPS games would have no problem keeping one on target. The only real way to miss shots is to not have your crosshairs in the general area of your target. The devs don't seem to care about the blatant problems in the game, players in Russia will always have better ping than you, sometimes leading to killcams showing them shooting at a wall and the game telling the server that wall was your head, the community is absolutely full of a-holes, and development progress doesn't exist. In the year or two since my previous review, they've added one new game mode and that's about it. PVE is still not in the game, PVP maps and modes are boring and repetative, especially since a good 80% of the game's arsenal is useless. The game's only real good side is that it looks kinda pretty. If they ever add PVE, then the game might be worth a look, but until then, move on.

I never write reviews but what the hell...
So, I love the Stalker games, and the Metro games, and for me Survarium continues that tense atmosphere of post apocalyptic world full of deadly anomalies, radiation, and creepy abandoned locations. The one thing those games lacked however, was multiplayer. Survarium fills that space.
I'm going to pick out a few criticisms from other users and offer my opinion...
Matchmaking - People complain a lot about the wait time for a match. It's no CS:GO, that's for sure. It usually takes around 3 minutes to find a match on EU servers. Sometimes more, sometimes less. The player base is fairly small so it really depends on the time and day.
OP Weapons - There's few weapons that stand out as OP for sure, but the game is still in beta and weapon balance will certainly change.
Hackers - I've seen quite a few to be honest. Although this seems to be less of a problem now as Vostok Games have introduced BattlEye anti-cheat.
Pay to win - Not really. It's more like pay to level faster. You can unlock everything by grinding away for hours and hours if you choose. You can buy gold that can be used to buy a premium pass and level 50% faster if you want. If you do choose to spend money on 'premium' weapons, the game matches you with others based on the level of your gear.
Freeplay - I honestly don't care too much about that. I'd rather see Vostok Games use their time and resources to improve what they already have and make it as polished as possible. If you want a free-roam Stalker experience you should look into a mod called “Call of Chernobyl”.
The game has improved massively with the most recent updates, but it's definitely rough around the edges and theres a lot of lag. Having said that, it's not awful by any means, and doesn't deserve so many negative reviews. The graphics are pretty nice if you have a machine that can run them on full settings. Especially if you can increase the resolution scale slider too.
My advice is to give it a try if you are a fan of the Stalker and Metro games. It continues the post apocalypse setting and creepy atmosphere they captured so well, but brings a PvP multiplayer experience that they never did. Overall I'd give it a 6/10, and I'll continue to follow it's development.

Pretty awesome to hear this starship and empire building game was created solely or mainly by one person. The quality is AAA all the way from the excellent animated cut scenes and incredible still art to the intensely helpful professionally voiced tutorial to the gameplay mechanics everything radiates superb polish.
Ship building is very exciting as one tries to see what is the best design for the job you intend to do. It is a major high creating a ship and seeing its purpose fulfilled exceptionally whether its for combat or colonizing or to transport workers and troops to another planet. There are also supply lines one has to keep open by avoiding enemy blockades as you will need supply lines to keep your ships fueled for the long trek into enemy territory to destroy their main empire planet.
Combat is tense and alot of fun as i was maneuvering my ships to avoid enemy fire while getting in the best position to do the most damage while being able to pause at any time to revaluate the situation. Winning commendations after a battle also gave a added sense of satisfaction after a victory over raiders or another empire.
Races are varied and interesting from the honorable shogun like bear race to the violent pyschotic wolf race. There are also space pirates to contend with which will harass your territories until you deal with them.
There is a vast research tree which allows for the discovery of many new advances from ships to making life easier for your planetary populations such as increased population breeding and stronger lighter metals for ships along with better handling power plants to keep energy weapons going along with many other discoveries just waiting to be researched.
Music and sound effects  have a excellent science fiction vibe creating moments of peaceful stellar harmony as you view the vastness of the space map or watch the humorous galactic news feeds. Many a focused moment i have found myself suddenly in a relaxed mental state taking in all the audio goodness with hypnotic futuristic music by the legendary likes of Isao Tomita. This combined with the soothing visuals made me feel i was back playing MASTER OF ORION 2 but with modern enhancement making for a smooth user interface experiance with excellent tool tips popping up revealing information on every single big and little thing happening on the screen. I definitely appreciate this and it has made my enjoyment of StarDrive 2 a much more richer experiance.

I really wanted to hate this game. I'm a die-hard fan of StarDrive 1, even though it had its quirks and flaws.. I dumped more time than I care to admit into that game. I waited a day or two after release to see how the game fared, because I was a bit apprehensive of all the new changes. Mostly, I thought the transition to turn-based and instanced combat was neat and a cool way to go, but I felt the ship design was severely lacking in comparison to the first game.
It is certainly a little less complex than in StarDrive 1, but I couldn't bring myself to dislike it. The ship combat just works out to be so much more fun. The small simplification in ship design has actually served to enhance the whole experience, and makes designing ships take a little more nuanced approach. Ship combat now feels a lot more massive ("slow motion" is awesome and feels more like "cinematic speed", and gives you lots of time to issue commands. I can't even play it in normal speed anymore).
On top of this, due to the command point system you tend to value each individual ship far more, especially because they gain experience and can be given names. It certainly makes for a far more immersive experience, when you have a battlefleet of eight or ten heavy cruisers, and each one means something to you, which means battle losses actually make you feel kind of sad. I might have won a great victory over one of the enemy core worlds, but the valiant crews of the UFF Retribution and UFF Valiant, who were with the fleet and served with distinction since the start of the war, did not live to see it. Such is war!
There's a little bit for everyone in the game and in ship design/combat -- for the Honor Harrington nerds, ships at long/medium engagement distance loose enormous waves of missiles, which slowly get plinked away by point-defence, flares and jammers as they approach (and it's incredibly entertaining to watch).. for the Star Trek geeks, there's ships which can swing around at breakneck speeds and blast eachother with photon torpedos and phasers. For the Star Wars junkies, there's waves of fighters and big ships with batteries of laser cannons.
Ground combat right now is a little bare, but the designer will likely improve this as time goes on. The system itself is certainly a good foundation.
As much as I wanted/figured I would dislike this game, I can't help but really enjoy it. For a mostly one-man team, this is still likely the best 4x currently on the market -- or at least will be once some minor issues are fixed and things like ground combat are padded out a bit more.

Maps should be bigger, encountered a bug where I started a battle as the enemy, some ship modules look exactly the same as others and/or the image was stretched to be blurry, ground battles need more work, AI are a bit too aggressive (why do they always demand tribute?).
I found myself wishing I could:
- Get a notification when a colony is building nothing.
- View what strategic resources do while negotiating with AI.
- View the base food and production I can reap from a planet that already has farmers / workers.
- Heal ground units when they're on a planet I own, you shouldn't need to research hospitals....
- Control ships in battle easier. You can only use special abilities with 1 ship selected.
Also the "ammo used per second if all weapons fired at once" can be misleading. You could have a module that uses 100 ammo but only fires once every 10 seconds. It will show 10 ammo per second, but will never actually fire if you don't have at least 100 ammo capacity. You'll have to keep this in mind when building ships.
Despite all these things I found the game to be fun. Maybe it's not compared to other 4x games in it's genre but this is the only one I've played. Considering it was made by such a small team (only one person?) I can look past things. It can be hard and confusing at first, but once you understand it then it's easier. Building ships is one of my favorite parts. I look forward to this game being further updated (there was already one). At least it isn't a triple A game asking for 60-70 bucks while hardly being a game.
I would recommend to wait until it's on sale or improved upon.

The game is a good buy and enjoyable, overall worth the money. However, it is not yet a great game and will require patches and expansion packs to make it so. Detailed comments below.
+ Throughout the game there is the feeling of an arms race, constantly needing new technology and designs to stay ahead.
+ The diplomacy is quite good, albeit lacking alliances and a diplomatic victory. You also do get a few funny requests (such as one of my opponents declaring war on me for not giving them my homeworld).
+ Graphics are good (from my experience for the 4X genre).
+ AI and the game seems balanced but it does take c. 10 hours of trial and error as it is quite tough.
+ Race customisation options are good.
- The game does have a number of bugs e.g. for c. 25% of my first full game I would end up playing ground combat as the enemy. This is not game breaking as I could guarantee myself a win by therefore intentionally losing as the enemy but it is odd for such an obvious bug to be present at release.
- The UI is at times awkward, e.g. for some races Titan ships (the largest vessels) are too large on the strategic map and prevent the ability to select any other planets or fleets in the system. This again is not game breaking but is quite frustrating.
- As far as I can tell, elimination of all races is the only victory condition. This makes it very sad to have to turn on your closest friends to win the game.
- Ground combat is relatively poorly designed; a system such as MOO2 would have been fine or a later expansion pack.

Forts is a physics-based RTS/Base Building game revolving around a world running out of resources. Build and battle your way across every continent in your search for liquid gold - oil.
Forts is set in a 2D world inhabited by cartoon people across every continent on Earth. There are 3 differing factions in the world of Forts - The Eagle Army, The Dragon Army and the Iron Bear Alliance. Each faction has differing sprites and units unique to the aforementioned faction. Since you can travel across the world to pre-set destinations, each continent has it's own set of backgrounds art, all of which add a sense of progression as you venture forth across the Earth, destroying enemies in your wake and claiming oil as your rightful prize.
Forts has a very nice soundtrack composed by Jeff van Dyck who is known for his work in other games, including Submerged, Assault Android Cactus, and Hand of Fate - a game that I have reviewed in the past that had an impressive audio rating of 8.9. It comes to no surprise then that Forts has an excellent soundtrack, with music that resembles a techno-mix of soundtracks of action movie flicks from the 1990s. I quite like the music from Forts as it really sets the pace for the game - all of the music is fast paced, which is a nice fit when there are explosions, bullets, and lazers flying across your screen from one fort to the other.
You can buy the complete soundtrack for a cool 7 dollars on Bandcamp if you wish to support the composer Jeff van Dyck if you find his music to be of your taste.
Forts is, as I previously mentioned, a physics-based RTS/Base building game, and it does an excellent job at being exactly that. Although I haven't yet played the online mode of the game (which there is, and sounds like a great deal of enjoyment), I have played through a significant portion of the game's campaign, and I have to say I'm quite impressed by what I've seen so far. I'm not usually into RTS games like the sorts of Forts, and the only other game that I have really played like Forts would be Angry Birds, and I didn't really enjoy that game in it's own right, however, I did find a decent share of fun playing the game. Although it did take me a few tries to get a hang of the game, I found myself getting better and better and setting up defences against the enemy.
My only recommendation for the gameplay aspect of the game would have to be making aiming easier during combat. You can aim to an extent with units, but Forts doesn't do a whole lot in letting you know where your shots are going to land, which is especially irritating when using slow-shooting units such as a mortar or a sniper, but I can see why the developers made it that way.
Forts is set in a cartoon world with a storyline similar to that of the Fallout series (which I adore, by the way). The world is running out of oil, a precious commodity that powers the world. In the campaign (as far as I can see), you play as the Eagle Army  (the equivalent of our world's America) in a conquest for oil against the two other world powers; the Dragon Army (the equivalent of China) and the Iron Bear Alliance (the equivalent of Russia). So, like every sane person would, the three large super powers of the world began constructing flying fortresses that are capable of landing and constructing the Forts you see in game. Instead of landing troops on the ground, why not land a whole base instead?
Overall, Forts is a pretty good deal of fun. You can easily play a few levels of the campaign in a couple minutes if youre strapped for time, but there are also online capabilities if youre interested in playing with friends or battling agaisnt strangers across the world. Enjoy an intereting game with decent cartoon graphics and a modest storyline that is a bit over cooked.

Wow. This one really took me by surprise. I had never even heard of this game until I got it in last month’s Humble Monthly Bundle. It didn’t really look like my type of thing so I didn’t check it out until a few days ago but I have to say it far exceeded my expectations.
Stories Untold is a compilation of four short games - or “episodes” as the game calls them. The game takes on the aesthetic of an ‘80s anthology show with each “episode” beginning with an opening title and ending with a credit roll. Initially only first episode is available and completing an episode unlocks the next one. The four episodes are apparently unrelated except that they all follow the basic premise of a character sitting and interacting with a computer screen, this mainly means typing commands or clicking on things.
The gameplay is really nothing special, but the gameplay is not the focus here, the story is. Unfortunately, I can’t really say much about the story without spoiling it. If this looks like something you would enjoy, then don’t read any more reviews, just buy the game. This really is the sort of game where the less you know going in the better.
Now, this game isn’t for everybody. I think it’s the sort of thing you either love or hate. While I highly recommend it to fans of interactive fiction, if you are looking for innovative or challenging gameplay, look elsewhere.
There are also a few things I didn’t like about it. First, at points it has the classic text-based game problem of “guess what word the developer was thinking of”. This is generally not a major problem but at one point I did have to consult a walkthrough because I knew what to do but wasn’t quite sure what to type to make it happen. The other annoyance is that there is no saving. If you quit the game, you will have to restart the current episode from the beginning. This is not a huge deal because each episode is fairly short - just over half an hour each - but it is something to be aware of.

I'll make that absolutely clear, right from the beginning. This is not a Gears of War clone. It may have an atmosphere vaguely similar to Gears, but it is not Gears, does not play like Gears, and playing like Gears should not be attempted. Cover is for making sure your head is on straight before you jump back into the action.
The game is a fast-paced bullet hell mania, like somebody crossed Sonic the Hedgehog and Touhou with our beloved Gears of War. If you play it like Gears of War, you're gonna have a bad time.
The gameplay is amazing. You get a rocket slide that really makes you feel like you have rockets strapped to you. You get a slow-mo mode that you can trigger whenever you want (provided it's not on cooldown). Everything is glitzy and cheesy, and completely over-the-top. It's action. It's eyecandy. It's not supposed to be anything else, and it's all the more glorious for it. Like DOOM 2016, this is a game that knows what it wants to be and is unapologetically confident about it. The dialogue and story are just as over-the-top and cheesy as the action. The game knows it. It wants to be over-the-top, and by god, it manages it.
If you're not a fan of moving around a lot while you shoot, this isn't your game. If you prefer shooters where you can play the sniper, this isn't your game. If you like using cover, or dislike twitch shooters, go somewhere else. This isn't your game. However...... If you like getting up in the face of an enemy at speeds that make you feel like the mother♥♥♥♥ing flash, rocketboot flip-kicking them in the chest, and following that up with a shotgun blast to the face while you're still in midair (and then a grenade like the cherry on top) - this game is absolutely, one hundred percent for you.
The gameplay is hard. There's no question about that. This game isn't forgiving and it'll make you work for the wins you get, but as you play, you'll get very noticeably better. And the better you get, the cooler it will feel.
Cons:
- Yes, this game is short. There's a lot of replay value, though, especially if you're the type that likes speedrunning or perfecting your playstyle. The skill ceiling is VERY high in this game.
- There's currently a bug that makes you take damage a lot faster at high framerates. If this discourages you, sit it out until it's fixed.
- The story is terrible. It's a good kind of terrible, though - the kind where it doesn't really matter how bad the story or acting is - it doesn't matter that the actors sound like they're constipated after swallowing a cup of gravel. The gameplay is fun enough that you likely won't even care.

Thank you SEGA, Thank you PlatinumGames.

Back in 2008, PlatinumGames announced their first major partnership in a four-game publishing deal with Sega: two of which being Madworld, directed by Shigenori Nishikawa, one of the lead designers for RE4, Infinite Space, directed by Hifumi Kono, former higher-up with Human Entertainment, best known for the Fire Pro Wrestling and Clock Tower games.  However, the big two that had people interested were Bayonetta, a 3D beat-em-up spiritual successor to Devil May Cry called Bayonetta, directed by DMC creator and Resident Evil 2 mainstay Hideki Kamiya, and a 'mystery shooter' from the godfather of modern survival horror himself and Kamiya's predecessor, Shinji Mikami.
His first game since the cult hit God Hand back in 2006, the four-year span between God Hand and Vanquish after Clover's closing was the longest hiatus Mikami had spent between games, but it doesn't show here: Vanquish is easily as polished as Kamiya's Bayonetta, if still not as commercially successful.  Where Bayonetta takes the 'style-em-up' approach of DMC and pushes it over the limit with slick action, Vanquish - like God Hand - fully embraces the arcade high-score gluttony of old-school beat-em-ups, only with a third-person shooter.  The game does have cover mechanics for those who would prefer it, but it also is based around a streamlined control system with unique movement controls and melee attacks dependent on weapon loadouts to justify switching weapons on-the-fly for variation, with the chest-high walls as fallback for those who may need it.  WIth these systems in place, as well as four largely varying difficulty levels, it makes Vanquish an accessible shooter that, while not as pretty as a game like Bayonetta, rewards replayability.
Which brings us to the bad news: if you're not a fan of high score gameplay, then outside of the extra challenges, there is very little content to the main game itself.  If one playthrough is more than enough for you, it's going to be a very short game.  Luckily, the $20 price tag is a reasonable price for such a game.
As for the PC port itself, it's definitely a step up from the original console versions.  Originally developed for both 360 and PS3, but developed primarily for the PS3 in an attempt to avoid 'shoddy PS3 ports', this game has uncapped frame rate and resolution settings, multiple language settings, and numerous other technical settings.  On the other hand, most of the cutscenes are prerendered, and will usually cap at 30 fps, and sometimes even stutter on more low-end rigs, and if that's something that bothers you, it might not be the game for you.  In terms of controls, I've tried this on both mouse & keyboard and an XBox 360 controller, and the controls are extremely intuitive for either control scheme.  I've had the game crash on me only once, but a few others have stated issues with crashing, so it's also something to keep in mind.
