Much like a fairly good portion and generally a good consensus of the internet, I was rather disappointing overall with the lastest pack from Jackbox Games. I decided to buy the thing at launch, play it with some friends, one of whom, the person hosting it, also bought the game and liked it very much, and at the end of the night I decided to refund it myself. Nothing really stood out in this year's releases, where as with Jackbox Party Pack 3, games like Tee K.O. (when it doesn't bug out or lock up), Guesspionage and the fan favourite Trivia Murder Party really showed that Jackbox Games still had that spark of innovation and creativity to them, and that they weren't running out of ideas any time soon. Alas, let's review Jackbox Party Pack 4.
There are 2 things going in Jackbox Games's favor here with this year's releases. The first is there are 6 games this time around and not just 5, well sorta. More is always better, to some people. The second is none of this year's releases are strictly meant for local-play, every game you can play online with other people because let's face it, this is Steam and Steam is for online gamers. Not everyone is able to play locally, though with the consoles releases, I can see why Jackbox Games would include one or two local-play games in each iteration of their previous packs. In this year's releases however, none of these games are strictly local-play, but there is maybe one that would be a more enjoyable experience if it were to be played local and I'll get into that in a bit. Now it's time to review the games themselves:
1. Fibbage 3: If you were expecting anything different to come out of the third game in the Fibbage series... yeah. It's just a re-hash of the Fibbage series with different prompts. Fibbage 3 is Fibbage, moving on.
2. Fibbage Enough About You: Probably my favourite addition to this year's Party Pack, and it isn't even a game in the main menu, it's a side mode to Fibbage 3. Good job Jackbox! Nonetheless, Fibbage Enough About You is, well, basically Fibbage, but the prompts are about the person answering them, and everyone else reads the prompts and has to figure out which one is the player's truth, while the player's answering also submits lies to the player's truth. Basically, the player with the prompt writes the truth about them and everyone else writes lies while trying to figure out the truth to the player. I found this mode to be alot of fun, but I highly recommend playing this with people you are friends with locally or online and not with randos, I recommend that with all of these games, but especially with this one.
3. Survive The Internet: The overly enjoyment and hilarity that can ensue from Survive The Internet seems to be heavily reliant on not just the prompts provided, but rather the catagory that is present. Survive The Internet has multiple different catragories to it, all relating to the internet obviously. Catagories like videos, news and photosharing are some of the more wittier ones, and prompts like shopping and fundraising are more weaker and yield worse results. Basically, you take what someone else said and try to turn what they said as a response to something ridiculous or negative. In practice, sounds like alot of fun and it is, but sometimes it is hard to work with what other people give you and what you can type as a "burn" with the specific catagory you currently have. Still though, alot of fun and definitely one of the better games in the pack.
4. Monster Seeking Monster: I hate this game with a burning passion! Let's me explain. There are 7 players and the objective is to have the most hearts by having the most dates at the end of 6 nights. This seems like a game that would work way better with friends locally rather than online. Futhermore, for like an entire game of it, I had no idea what to do or how to win or how dating being successful or anything really. Basically, each player is something different and their win condition varies. I had the Werewolf and it sucked because I had to ensure getting dates and turning them into werewolves or basically just losing a bunch of hearts, in a game where I didn't understand what was going on. It's kinda like a strategy game more than anything else, where you get 4 messages that you can sent to any of the participants, trying to convince them to either date you or not date someone if you have let's say the Mother role for example, for each time their child doesn't get a date, they get a heart. It's awful and was the biggest reason I decided to refund the whole pack. This one sucked, the music was awesome, but the game was boring and I was angry pretty much the whole time playing it. Avoid it like the plague!
5. Bracketeering: Not alot to say about this one. It's kinda like Quiplash, just really dumbed down, faster-paced and is 16 players, but with like a betting mechanic to it where each round, certain players get to bet on which prompt will win the vote for extra coins and the player with the most coins at the end is the winner. Seeing I played this one just after Monster Seeking Monster, I wasn't in a very good mood going into it, so obviously my first time playing it wasn't a very good experience. It seems like the kind of thing that would work best with alot of people, and that is a problem seeing it is hard to get 16 friends together for a game that lasts like 10 minutes at most. Overall, pretty mediocre, nothing special.
6. Civic Doodle: Gotta have a drawing game somewhere in a Jackbox Party Pack and this is maybe the worst drawing game Jackbox has ever released, and yes, I am aware of Bidiots's existence. It's a shame too, because as a amateur graphic artist and illustrator, I always find the drawing games to be the most enjoyable things in the Party Packs, but this one really sucks, mostly because there isn't alot of drawing to it, minus the final round. You get a piece of paper with something on it and you have like 30 seconds to add onto it, but the problem is you go in turns of 2. So two people draw a thing, the rest of us vote on which drawing is better and then two more people add on to that drawing that won the vote, which adding onto someone else's drawing I really don't like from an artistic standpoint, I rather the whole game just be what the last round is where we are told to draw something, then vote on who has the best drawing. The whole thing that Civil Doodle does where you draw and someone else draws, then 2 other people add onto the more popular of the previous drawings really shoots Civic Doodle in the foot and takes away alot of player creativity. It also has this stupid emoji thing to it where you can spam an emoji for a certain drawing and the mayor randomly chooses which emoji wins, giving that player additional points. One of the worst games in the pack, but at least the mayor is funny.
Overall... well I requested a refund for the game and got it, so you know my opinion of it. One of the weakest packs in the series with some of the worst games to boot. If you are a die hard Jackbox player with tons of friends, pick it up, but otherwise, get 3, the far superior pack instead. It isn't the worst of the Jackbox Packs, but there really isn't alot of competition for the best either.

Aside from some very quick timers, Twitch extended ones too, in Fibbage 3 and Civic Doodle (which kinda makes sense in C.D.), and one time Monster Seeking Monster caused BSoD, it's so far been an absolute blast.
My only question, why did they get rid of the leaderboard that was in Party Pack 3? I loved that. Being able to see who is doing what and where and being able to switch to a Twitch leaderboard to boot.
But those are not reasons to avoid the game at all. This game is extremely fun and I, my friends, and my Twitch viewers all look forward to playing this game even more.
Now how about giving us a "Hub" app that shows all of our purchased titles in one place instead of having to switch games with awkward pauses in between? Why not just have a "hub" like program that just detects what you own and can exit one title and go into another without too much hassle. I know I'm not the only one who has wanted such a feature and it would be easy to update say when Tee Ko 2 or Jackbox Party Pack 5 comes out. Pretty please? Pretty please with a cherry on top?
Would I recommend? YES, YES, a million times YES.

Anna - Extended Edition is a unique and extremely creepy adventure game.  In fact, I thought that the audio and visuals were even more disturbing that the arguable more famous Amnesia.  The story is interesting and unfolds gradually as the player interacts with different puzzles and objects in an abandonded house, piecing together the mystery of what happened there.  There is no dialogue interactions in the game but the storytelling is well done without them.  The steam overlay, widescreen resolutions and steam achievements are supported but unfortunately the controller is not.  Anna's strength is also it's weakness, it is maddeningly difficult to figure out how to solve the puzzles.  In fact, this is a game that is nearly impossible to complete without the assistance of a walkthrough video.  However, the several possible endings based on the choices you make bring some replayability to the game that is often missing from adventure titles.  In all, Anna is a succesful but flawed entry into the genre and should be considered by anyone who enjoys a difficult adventure game.

It's possible to save at almost any point in the game. So this can be something that you play for 10 minutes, take a break, then come back to later.
The only caveat in this game is it doesn't have controller support. It's very much made only to be played on a PC.  There's also the annoying login/registration screen that you need to deal with before starting the game. What gives? I already bought the game!
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a scare.

I really want to recommend this one, and in the '80s I would have.  The thing is we've come a ways since then.  A contemporary game that mimics games like Ninja Gaiden, Shatterhand, etc. should have everything those games did well and more.  Oniken doesn't unfortunately.  It's not a terrible game by any means.  The graphics, sound, control, levels, and themes would be right at home on an NES cart.  Again, that's the problem though.  The game could look and sound exactly like this and the gameplay could be twice as good as it stands here.  If you're desperate for something that nails the NES look and feel, go for it.  Otherwise there are better games out there even at this price.

Oniken is basically a cross between several 8 bit era games.  It has the feel of a Contra game with it's strange robot alien monsters, the physics of Ninja Gaiden with wall jumping and sword slashing, along with a touch of battle toads with its variable stages.  It is difficult, it will punish you, but in true classic style its about replaying the game to develop skill.  The cutscenes are like something out of anime.  The artwork is absolutely beautiful and the music fits the game itself.
If you want to feel like an 80s kid sitting down after school playing your NES, this is it right here.  Oniken has a number of secrets as well.  It honestly is a fun game but challenging and at times will make you feel like throwing your controller.

I'll give some examples of glitches that artificially inflate the difficulty of Oniken.
1: Stored jumps, for lack of a better term this is what we'll call it. This doesn't happen very often outside of the vehicle sections but goddamn does it happen in EVERY. SINGLE. VEHICLE. SECTION. Your character will jump randomly, even if you aren't touching the controller which more often than not, will lead to your death.
2: The powerup sword which can be activated to give you invulnerability will randomly activate itself, 5 or 6 times I've picked up this sword, going to carry it to the boss (as I assume the developers intended) and halfway there the sword will activate, this one won't make you die like the vehicle jump glitch but it is still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that it happens in the first place.
3: Boss of the forest level (4?) has a ludicrously bad hitbox, so much so that this is the point where I just stopped.
Some other gripes that don't involve difficulty include:
-Cutscene framerates are hilariously bad, I don't know if this is intentional or a glitch or what the deal is, but when text pops up on the screen it takes a solid 5 seconds per word, no NES game would behave like this.
-Game takes far longer to boot than it should.
-External launcher (did this game REALLY need a ♥♥♥♥ing launcher?)
-Many animations are lackluster, some sprites don't even HAVE animations

All in all the game isn't the WORST thing in the world, but it was pretty disappointing to me. I'm a huge fan of Castlevania, Ninja Gaiden, Shovel Knight and the lesser known Bad Dudes and Bionic Commando; so you'd think I would really like Oniken but this was not the case.

Very nice game with active and dedicated developers. If u are into the STALKER and apocalyptic scenery, this is the game for you. Alto the game is still in BETA version, it shows great promise and bright future. So since the game is still BETA, you should expect to find bugs and some balance or other issues. But overall the game is quite good and playable. I have logged both closed beta and open beta time for a few hours...
But here some pros/cons:
Pros:
*Many different maps to play and different modes (Team Deathmatch, Research - kinda like capture and hold flags, Batteries - You need to search batteries on map and bring em to your base and Artifact hunt where you have to retrieve the artifact spawning somewhere on the map).
*A lot of different weapons from Pistols to MG's and powerful Sniper Rifles, and even more to come from STALKER series (Some people whine about the game is P2W but not really, all weapons can be countered)
*Great graphics and ambience
*Great sounds for both weapons and overall environment
*Attatchments for the weapons and ability to upgrade the equipment (more armor, damage, resistance etc.)
*Maps have different cycles (For example, sunset, evening, dark sky, storm with rain etc.)
*Overall gameplay is good
*Updates are coming quite often
*League system giving a chance of getting equipment and weapons, and end of the match drops make getting things easier and faster.
*Giveaways on different game communities (MMOHUT etc.) for premium account and cash etc.
Cons:
*Sometimes long wate for matches since the servers can be sometimes messy and not many people around sometimes (due the difference in time zones)
*Some minor bugs like batteries falling through floor when killed sometimes or grenades falling through map
*Some minor weapon balance issues (Shotguns shoot better than snipers sometimes etc.)
*Sometimes when you want to get attatchments then it will make you grind hard (sometimes 1000+ kills for attatchment)
Overall if u want a decent shooter, this is one of them. Altho it is still in beta, the work is quite good and will keep you busy for a while :) So ignore the naysayers. just get  into the game and try to enjoy, it is not that hard and it will be quite fun :)

I see quite a few negative reviews on here talking about the difficulty of the game, so I'll share my point of view on that. So far I've played a number of games over 11 hours (normal) and have lost every single one. You know what though? I get a little bit better every time, and I know I'm getting close to winning. The first time I conquer the galaxy I will feel like I earned it. The AI doesn't cheat, it's not entirely ruthless towards you as long as you dont take the repulsive trait because you want the easy 4 points.
It's a game that takes practice, turn it on to easy if you are struggling and make sure you understand the mechanics of the game.  There is a tutorial which lots of people ignore and several help sections in the game. Some mechanics are a little obscure, for example how your empire generates galactic credits beyond population is not explained very well.  However, there is an insane amount of tooltips explaining anything you mouse over which makes it really easy to find information.
Combat is really fun, though the fact that the default ships are designed incredibly efficiently probably contributes to the difficulty new players are having.  However you can easily see the default layouts (which again are quite good) and can work on designing your ship from there. There are a few performance issues with large scale battles, but I hope to see them ironed out in the future. There are a large variety of weapons and options for those weapons, as well as support systems so you can design ships any way you like them. It also looks pretty damn good too. I hope to see more activatable abilities in the future, but right now space combat is a solid tactical experience.
The economy is good. It's really irritating that people are complaining about the map size, because I can't imagine playing on something like a 150 system map. There would be too much to do. I think a few people loaded the game and said "what, 70 stars default?" without understanding the depth of the economy. You'll be really busy managing your empire with even a few systems. You can specialize your planets and they also develop over time, gaining unique traits depending on what you do with them. High research planets attract universities, big farming planets will eventually attract a farmers market, etc.
There is more I could go on about but overall I'm happy with my purchase. I'm excited to see a few balance passes over the next few weaks, but other then that it is already a solid experience.

I found myself playing StarDrive 1 again after a while playing StarDrive 2!
I need atmosphere, so I expect that your star empire evolves from Earth, as it is in the real universe.
This is at least true for the Humans of Sol, where Earth is. And in StarDrive 1 you get a pretty good image of Sol - just like it is.
(Yes, I'm probably a Human fanboy!) :)
The only problem is that in StarDrive 1 the planets circumnavigate the central sun (Sol) in the wrong direction.
But it looks good to see it in real time, for they are all there: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and so on.
In StarDrive 2 you have the same situation like you had in MoO2, but the battles are in real time and there is no multiplayer!
Anyway, the game feels like MoO2, regarding a lot of aspects. Your home system always consists of 1 to 5 planets in random order. You'll face up to 8 different opponents and a lot of rouges! Battles take place in space, on planets and even on ships, with your away team entering! You start with a colony ship and a recon vessel. And you have to deal with research, money and ship design.
I'm loving it!

Where to start.....I'll say this. I re-installed SD1. I played enough to say that although the graphics are a step in the right direction, everything else is not. The artwork is recycled, the UI is clunky and limited, the functionality is limited and almost rectricted. Why can't I hit "E" on my explorer frigates and have them run all over the galaxy????
So I'll break it down like this: I'll base my grades off of two criteria. The first criteria is "was this a step in the right direction from the original SD" The second criteria is based off of other games in this genre, I'll give a letter grade for this. Let's begin:
GRAPHICS: SD1<SD2 This was a step in the right direction. Overall grade compared to other 4X Space games: B-
ARTWORK: SD1=SD2. The art is recycled. Overall grade compared to other 4X Space games: C-
FUNCTIONALITY: SD1>SD2. Definately a step back. Overall grade: D+
UI: SD1<SD2. This is almost a push..just needs to be patched. Overall Grade: C+
AI: SD1<SD2. So far the other factions haven't banned together to form one giant super federation.(My biggest complaint from SD1) Overall Grade: A
Tactics: SD1>SD2. The turn based system does not work, unless you're GalCiv or MoO.
I'm actually fed up from writing this review....$30 not worth spending. If you don't own it already buy SD1 instead. Wait for this to get patched or scrapped all together.

Okay so I'm not going to delete my previous post, but I will say this. There have been at least 5 patches since my review and becasue of that I give this game overall a passing grade. The short version: this is an insane game for insane people, and I loved nearly every moment of it.
The long version: this starts as, basically, Sokoban, but quickly reveals itself as much more than that: the spheres (or "larvae") you push "simulate gravity as camouflage" i.e. fall in the direction dependant on how they wre pushed. The difficulty past the first five or six levels skyrockets, and the game keeps piling up new mechanics on you until almost the very end. It requires excellent spatial awareness, but the feeling of satisfaction after cracking a particularly fiendish puzzle is unparalleled. The levels are ordered in semi-nonlinear fashion, but there are several "chokepoints" that may block you from further progress for hours as you despair for a solution.
The presentation is very simplistic (as you van see from the screenshots), but clear and legible. The sound and music are, fittingly, ascetic, with ambient humming and chanting.
You will get stuck. More than once. And you'll love it.

This is a game of patience. Upgrading the components to your base will take months, and meanwhile there are rare items and blueprints to gather from NPC fleets and special events. You need all of it, so keep your progress even. There are plenty of events for low level players every month, but some are only meaningful for higher levels.
You can spend money, or not. If you choose to spend money, paying to win is very expensive. There are players who have been playing the game for years and are in so deep they spend a few hundred dollars every month.
The big downsides are that while there are rules against scripts/bot farming and multiple accounts, the rules are not enforced. Also, sector chat is often filled with foul-mouthed children. Despite that, the game is pretty fun and new content is added regularly.

This title has a long way to go before it's worth the price. The concept is there but it needs more improvements before it can be considered a worthwhile purchase:
More stable connections in multiplayer.
More diversity in commanders.
Multiplayer ranks to judge skill level.
Progression systems be it levels or rankings.
Since the multiplayer is what the game is made for and the single player is a campaign that boils down to a tutorial for the multiplayer, enhancing the multiplayer is a necessity. There is no incentive to play beyond the first few moments as every commander and weapon is already unlocked and once you play a few moments, you've played everything.
EDIT: 6 months later and the game still feels like a shell, now with embellishment. Sure, they added new guns, balances, and tricks but the core problems listed above are still prevelant. When you can see everything the game has to offer in a single match of skirmish, there is a problem.

If I had to sum up what I thought about this PP compared to the others, I'd probably say: "More Polish, More Consitency, Less Oomf." I know that seems vague, and I'll preface this by saying that I liked this and the recommendation is true, but let me try to explain.
Overall, the presentation this time around is superb. Each game has a distinct style that sets it apart from the other games in the pack, even if not from the other games in JB history. (I feel like I've seen the Bracketeering colour scheme and design style somewhere before...) The sound is top-notch too, with the usual narrator banter that helps gives the games their iconic wittiness, and with decent music as always. I will say that I found that the themes weren't all to my taste (Fibbage 3's 70s TV vibe wasn't exactly appealing to me), but I can't deny that it's not bad; If you can get into the theme of the game, you'll love the details, and if you don't, it's not hateable.
Now for individual game reviews:
Fibbage is the only returning game from previous packs, and Fibbage 2 is one of my favourites from PP2. But here, it's a middle of the road version at best. Design and theme aside, it just feels like a seemingly more tired version of 2. The prompts on the device screen almost always ended up sounding more interesting than the actual question, and the answers for the questions me and my group got were almost always boring.
But that's just 3. If you want Fibbage, stick with 2.
Enough About You, however, is the better half of this game. The personalized nature of it obviously draws you in and engages you better, especially in a small, local group. It also helps that you aren't hindered by answers that the Jackbox team finds funny. You and your friends can go wild with whatever personal facts you have. Enough About You wouldn't be fun at all for streams, I can imagine, but for the night me and my friends tried it out? It was one of the few we came back to.
Overall: If you play with friends, play Enough About You. If you stream it, avoid Fibbage 3 altogether.
A clear winner in the pack, for one simple reason, and not one the creators probably intented.
If you play it "straight", and follow all of the prompts, it's still clearly one of this pack's better games. The overall theme of a 90's desktop, complete with scam pop-ups and a clippy rip-off is the most dedicated of them all, and it pays off with some great side jokes. That, and the prompts aren't half bad either.
But the thing is, there's nothing mechanically, in-game, that forces you to play by those rules, or follow those prompts. So if you dare, and if your group is snarky enough, you can basically modify StI to become a fully personalized version of Quiplash. That, I am happy to report, is as profane, gut-busting, and twistedly awesome as it sounds.
You won't just survive the internet. You'll be coming back every time.
Middle of the road. I barely remember it. I can see why a lot of people are made uncomfortable by the game's central conceit, but if you and your fellow players take the joking date-app texts so far as to "cross the line twice", it's good for an occasional break-up of the monotony of just playing StI and CD.
But ultimately, MsM's greatest sin is not standing out: I remember being somewhat amused and intrigued by the monsters and their abilities, and enjoying the quaint "dollar-store disco" music, but I can't remember that much else about it.
I don't like using this kind of sentence when reviewing or talking about a game, but this time I will say it in earnest: Bracketeering wastes a spot in this PP that could have been given to a classic, or to a new game that wasn't based around a concept for mouth-breathers.
The idea is simple: Quiplash, but the same joke over and over again. And not just people using the same quip round in and round out, as is common in QL, but literally just the same prompt and joke over. And Over. And Over.
My friends didn't seem to mind it, but honestly, I was insulted that the JB crew thought that anyone would find this funny or enjoyable. The ONLY, and I MEAN ONLY, pro I can think of is that the prompts aren't terrible, but that's not even that great a compliment when you'll be seeing them repeatedly enough to hate them.
I'm going to say it. F**k Bracketeering. And if this becomes a stream favourite somehow, I'm going to lose faith in the JB community.
A mediocre game saved, and ultimately made replayable and enjoyable, by 3 things: the best drawing mechanics in any Jackbox game, a pair of truely humourous and likeable narrators, and a sense of involvement from the non-active players.
The drawings are at their best, with *gasp* a near full palette of colours and an undo option? What is this sorcery? Joking aside, it's never been more fun to draw ridiculous scribbles between friends. On top of that, even the players that aren't drawing can interact through the use of emoji-like reactions, which are meant to be used less like individual reactions, and more spammed like on a stream, for maximum effect. Finally, the bumbling, somewhat dim Mayor made this game for me. Even when drawing crude sexual pictograms and spamming the puke emoji got old, I could get into this rambling old man's delusions easily. One of my favourite JB characters to date.
But overall, I have one point that I've noticed, that makes me wonder if this is perhaps the least of the packs: I don't really have any strong desire to play it again. I'm sure I will, when the others get stale, but I'm not sure if this pack will ever see any playtime from me again otherwise. It has its standouts, for sure, so when I do turn to it, I know exactly what I'll want to play. But I can't see myself looking up streams of this pack to play along like I do for 2 and 3.
FINAL THOUGHTS: Not a waste of 25$, and even a worthwhile purchase, I'd say. The only one I really dislike is Bracketeering, and the others are at very least charming enough to enjoy. But I do recommend that this not be your first JackBox. Get 2 or 3 first, and then consider getting this if those start to get old.
Final Score, if you care: 7/10

Jackbox Party Pack 4 is a welcoming addition to the continuation of the Jackbox Series. As usual, there are 1 or 2 weaker games in the pack, but Jackbox Party Pack 4 does its best to keep this to a minimum. While previous had games that
be played with 3-4 people, this party pack definitely requires more people and rewards more excitement than the previous packs. So without ado, a quick review on each game
Fibbage 3 is another expansion of the Fibbage game. As other users have mentioned, the audio quality for Fibbage 3 has significantly improved and of course, new prompts/questions have been added. Their biggest and newest side-addition is the introduction of Enough About You. With prompts/questions directed to the players, this game really tests how well you know or you think you know your friends. The biggest downfall to Enough About You is the final round. With every final round being open to 1 truth and 1 lie,
One workaround is to play the game up until the final round and leave from there, but the hassle of remaking the lobby is present.
Survive The Internet is an extremely interesting game where you twist the words of your friends into funny/dark situations. The game has high potential in providing different scenarios but also plateaus when reaching the final round with PhotoSharing. This game is highly independent on the players to provide witty scenarios/situations or else the game will fall short. Having creative/quick-thinking people will definitely make-or-break the game.
This game is a game of psychological warfare that is amazing among close friends. As I mentioned in the beginning, this party pack requires more people to play to keep the game interesting. Monster Seeking Monster definitely falls into this role since the players' powers are revealed over 5 nights (dating takes 6 nights). When I played with 4 other players, all of our powers were revealed to each other. However, if more players had joined, not every players' powers would've been revealed. This game is extremely fun and relies heavily on strategy to beat the other players.
EDIT: I've noticed comments about groups being too awkward to play or the game being too predictable. One great suggestion I've seen is for everyone to enter a gibberish name so no one knows which is player is which.
Bracketeering is definitely the weakest of the bunch. Although it can support up to 16 players, it feels like it needs 16 players to play. Playing with a small group means you enter prompts twice and this can get repetitive as the brackets are constantly pit against each other. Playing with an even number also subjects you to ties, which drag out in terms of who can mash the vote button the most. Perhaps the only saving grace is the blind bracket, where you enter your answer before you get the prompt, but this heavily relies on having a fun or interesting prompt for the players to enjoy. Prediction betting throws the game heavily onto 1 vote or another and can be difficult to maintain interest without a good number of people.
Civic Doodle has finally been subjected to a huge improvement that past drawing games have suffered from. Jackbox has included the option of
This huge overhaul in the drawing UI has truly been a blessing in terms of playing these drawing games. Civic Doodle plays off of drawings made by previous players with other players voting to continue these drawings. Important things to note is that players should be wary of the canvas space being used. A drawing made by another player can be funny, but if there is no room for any addition when you draw on it, you probably shouldn't vote for it. Civic Doodle has greatly improved the overall drawing experience and combines the typical voting concept to create a great game.
To conclude, these games are a fantastic addition to the Jackbox series, but definitely
More people means: more prompts on Enough About You, more monsters in Monster Seeking Monster, more brackets for Bracketeering etc. Games like Murder Trivia, Bidiots, Drawful or Quiplash didn't always require to have a large group to enjoy the games.
With 7+ people: 9.5/10
With smaller groups from 3-6: 8.5/10

---SPOILER FREE!-----
This is a game you do NOT want to spoil, so pick through the reviews carefully.
The narrative of this game was excellent and it comes together brilliantly in the end.  It is tantalizing and mysterious, and it never lost my attention.  There is no tutorial, so you might get stuck at bit while learning the commands and inner workings of the game play.  If you get too lost, there are some excellent guides to turn to, so don't get discouraged.  I cannot say more about the actual game without ruining it for you, but know that this is an experience worth having.
There is one con to mention.  The game is separated into parts and once a part is started, you have to finish playing through the whole thing or start it over again.  There is no save function during gameplay.  This factor was really annoying to me, but since the parts are roughly an hour long each, it's forgivable.  Do not let this con turn you off from Stories Untold, just make sure you play the game when you have ample time to complete each section.
Now buy it and enjoy the hell out of it.

Stories Untold was a psychological horror story experience at A+ level. You honestly should go in as blind as you could, and especially don't give up when reaching episode 3 and you'll see why I rate this game so well. Yes, it's worth your money and little time. You don't need to know more, but if you do:
+ Stranger Things type setting/atmosphere (80's sci-fi ish) which works really well
+ Not at all what you expect (good job done on steam description)
+ Final episode blew me away
+ Experimental game done so cleverly
+ Great story
+ Great audio (voice acting and soundtrack)
- It's so -loud-!
- Don't play this if you're susceptible to seizures or have issues with flashing lights and loud sounds,
- You can't skip texts you might have to re-read and it slows you down
- Commands for the text adventure don't always work the way you want them
- Short, but worth the money vs. experience

This is not Dead Space. Nor is it Silent Hill or Amnesia. This is a game about being spooky and creeped out. And in my book, it succeeded wonderfully. So many times during my playthroughs I found myself with a severe case of the goosebumps. Be warned though: while this is certanly an entertaining title, it is quite short. My first playthrough took about 5 hours. If you are a skeptical person, this is not a game for you. If you have a hard time allowing yourself to be immeresed into the world and atmosphere of a game, again shy away. This is a game that requires effort from the player in order to enjoy it fully. It doesn't give you hand outs or force feed you intentions, and so the player must make inferences. You may dislike the story at face level, but it's something that made me think. Many claim "lack of immersion" when they realize that the monsters/disturbences can't "really hurt you," thus removing the fear of a horror game. This game IS NOT A HORROR GAME, but a creepy game with great atmoshpere. The puzzles are often much simpler than you think, and many times you simply glance over what you need to progress, reminiscent of the MYST style of puzzles. So my final word is this:
Good puzzles as long as you don't mind thoroughly searching the enviroment, and rememberto combine items in your inventory
GREAT atmoshpere. Creepy and spooky. Goosebumps, NOT wet underwear or screams.
Thought provoking story with multiple endings, some of which can keep you thinking for weeks after the game interpreting.
NOT an instant gratification game, requires player commitment, thought, and willingness to accept the game world without trying to pick it apart at every seam.
This is by far the best suspense game I have played in a while. The atmosphere is like no other horror game I have come across so far.  This is a must play if you love horro/suspense games!

I'm only going to mention the original StarDrive once because it would be unfair to base this game solely on its predecessor. I loved StarDrive and had a ton of fun with it, I practically threw my wallet at my monitor when I found out StarDrive 2 existed and had already been released.
The graphical and sound options aren’t abundant but the consistent and unchangeable graphics are part of what’s unique about this game. It has a cool look to it which is appealing. The best planets in your empire come to life as they grow, space stations can be seen orbiting them and large cities lights can be seen from space.
Real time battles look nice and it is exciting to watch your ship designs stomp the enemy. On the contrary it’s also fun to watch your ships get smashed because you never took that class on the importance of point defense. The trial and error required to design a potent military add an exciting element to the game. I have never been engaged in a large battle however, every battle I have fought has consisted of mostly between 10-30 ships.
Diplomacy doesn’t seem to do much at the moment. Each faction will contact you (probably once every 10 turns so get ready for the spam depending on how many AI you have encountered) and offer trade agreements or technology swaps (or to demand tribute if they're a more aggressive AI). The AI honor their treaties as far as I am aware (haven’t had any issues myself but others might have). By treaties I mean trade agreements or non-aggression pacts and nothing else. The game has a weird way of negotiating using some sort of tolerance system which I haven’t figured out yet.
Spies allow you to perform multiple functions. Defensively they protect you from enemy spies. Offensively they can steal technology (in the form of moles which are currently unstoppable to my knowledge), reveal enemy fleets and movements and two other functions I cannot recall. Essentially you can just spam build spies because they can be produced quickly and have no cost or maintenance. Once you have an armada of spies you can plant an infinite number of moles to steal all the technology you need (the AI will do it to you so I hope you don’t enjoy your privacy).
Technology works in (nine?) different tech trees. When you research anything in one of the tech trees that tech tree advances. You have to choose what is important for now and trade or steal (probably steal) the rest. The tech you unlock includes everything from ship parts, new space stations, upgrades or buildings for your empire.
Gameplay wise imagine that someone told you civilization five was similar to a real time strategy game. All you have to do is hold down the end turn button. The problem is that it doesn’t work. It isn’t entertaining and StarDrive 2 ends up feeling painfully slow at times. The larger your empire gets the more it needs to be micromanaged (which is to be expected but ends up being oddly complicated).
As the game slows down you’ll find yourself dealing with countless nuisances. Neutral AI entities will spawn at a constant rate to attack your undefended systems. Wormholes will open up faster than a hookers legs. I have not had a single game where a wormholes have not opened up in the heart of my empire to allow free reign to anyone who wanted to ravage my sweet virgin body.
Countering the pirate/neutral AI threat would be fairly easy except that there are unreasonable soft population caps which punish you for having a fleet capable of defending yourself. I have not figured out a way around this aside from raising taxes to obscene levels during incursions or just having a huge surplus of space cash. Couple this with the fact that finding habitable worlds is like trying to find a straight guy in a gay bar. Your empire will end up being large and spread out but still only containing 4-5 good planets (meaning your limited size fleets had better be well managed)
In conclusion StarDrive 2 is not a bad a game but at this time there are too many small annoyances that keep me from enjoying what might be a great game. It feels like I spend most of my time fighting everything but other empires. Its problems leave it average and unenjoyable. In time this game will probably become great through its mod support and continued developer input (the dev has been working non-stop to fix issues). <3 you Zero.

This review is only about the campaign - as many of the issues are not present in multiplayer.
Forts is at first quite fun but it quickly turns to frustration purely due to restrictions placed on the player.
Besides the campaign feeling like a tutorial for the first few levels until you unlock all the weapons, the difficulty ramps up and you have missions where suddenly you need to skill shot through indestructible terrain, yet things like auto fire, or keeping aim true are intentionally gone, it really is disappointing and frustrating at times.
Disappointing because I want to auto fire my machine guns, I want to auto fire my mortars, I want to group more than just 3 measly weapons together.
Frustrating because weapons lose their aim, their reticles wonder.
Reading other dev reviews you will see they say that auto fire makes the game less fun.  But then designed into the levels are areas in which it is PAINFUL to constantly click group 1, all fire, group 2, all fire, group 3, all fire, 6 keys to fire.. etc
I feel artificial difficulty has been added and in the worst way possible, where I could be having fun I am putting attention into just firing weapons.  Furthermore double-clicking a control group(because you can't autofire and if you want to laydown fire you'll be mashing keys) brings your focus to them, which in this game is pointless.
The only suggestions I have to offer is add an a option to auto-fire or group more than 3 for single player only.
Pros:
Nice graphics, cool world, cool idea, a community involved dev
Cons:
No autofire, max of 3 weapons in a group, artificial difficulty with micromanagement.
I would give this game 8/10 but I don’t recommend (I really want too but it is too frustrating).

MAKE SURE TO TURN OFF FULL SCREEN IN IN-GAME SETTINGS

This is almost worth buying for the first chapter alone. Almost.
The team that made this clearly has the talent to create something amazing, and there are hints throughout at the potential that Stories Untold has, but it fails to achieve it at almost every juncture.
The House Abandon is excellent. While sometimes a little restrictive on commands and interactions, and it could certainly use a wider vocabulary, it is engaging, immersive, atmospheric, and full of delightfully morbid surprises. I was hooked, and eager for more. More never came.
The remaining 3 chapters have some interesting elements, but essentially remove any element of interaction, replacing it with commands that must be performed. This isnt so bad or noticable in chapter 2, since they are relatively simple, and the atmosphere draws you in.
Chapter 3 is a mess. The gameplay is cross referencing, syntax checking and data entry. There's enough going on seperate to that to at least keep me interested, or at least willing to put up with the tedium to see what was next. What was next was (spoiler alert) it was all a dream, along with a bog standard, unity default first person section with appaling FOV, and some really poorly sculpted terrain. The interface was not updated here, leaving me with a mouse cursor
Chapter 4 is like a compilation of the worst parts of all of the previous episodes. You're essentially told the ending immediately, and the rest is just going through the motions. The worst offender is the revisit of the text adventure from chapter 1, where in most situations there is only one, very specific command you can type at each step, made more difficult to decipher due to the fact that no consistant commands have been established. Your presense is a formality, and stumbling to the conclusion is a very tedious exercise, killing what little tension and atmosphere there was to an increasing cliche story.
Despite the amazing potential, I simply cannot reccomend it.

A wonderful calling card for the people who made it.
[No Spoilers]
Let me start off by stating that I've completed 3 out of 4 episodes.
Each episode takes roughly 20 mins-half an hour. Yes you are looking at under two hours play time for the entire 'game'. This one of those purchases that it is difficult to give a definite 'thumbs up' or 'thumbs down' for, as what it does, it does really well, but it would hard pressed to call this a 'game'.
Each episode is very different in flavour, but with the same core mechanic: that is you primarilary interact with the story by typing commands into a terminal, flavoured visually in some way with some 80's tech styling, and in later chapters you interact in more creative ways with this old technology. This is where they have done a great job: the attention to detail, visually and audibly, everything looks, feels and sounds, at least like a nostalgic and simplified, analogue reproduction of an era gone past. Here, however is where it differs from the 80's text based adventures it is based on - whereas a 'Level 9' text adventure might keep you entertained for weeks, Each Episode here will keep you entertained while your dinner is in the oven. They have a couple of gimmicks that might make you feel like you've experienced something unique, I won't spoil what they are, but suffice it to say, the terminal in which you type is in it's own 3D world itself, and each episode kind of explores the possibilities of where that could lead.
And here is the problem of this game: it feels like a 'please hire us' concept demo. It's the kind of thing that you might see at a trade show or a 10 minute 'immersive experience' you might see at a science museum. There is no doubting that a huge amount of detail has been lavished on to these 10 minutes per chapter, from the graphics to the voice acting to the sound design, but really when the self-aggrandising, overly drawn out credits roll down after each frisson, you can't help wondering if the entire thing has just been a cyncial attempt to land them all a job in designing, you know, an actual game.
There will be doubtless many other hyperbolic reviews extolling how life changing this game is - it's not, but it does have a very impressive, but brief, perspective shifting gimmick - reviews I feel are more a product of our collaborative yearning for the computer game to come in to it's own as a medium, say compared to the film, the play or the novel; a cause I am rooting for as much as the next man, but come on, I demand more playtime for my money at this price (any price for sub 2 hours gameplay for that matter), clever gimmick or not, and hey, every other medium has been experimenting with these sorts of narrative shifts for years.
And putting the same name, several times in the same credits is plain old narcissistic.

I was raised on puzzle games, growing up with Myst, Adventure Co., and Lovecraft, so I was hopeful about this game. But I must say that it was wholly disappointing and I really had to force myself to finish it. Everything that I will briefly mention is negative, unfortunately.
It was not as beautiful as I had hoped, and I found the levels to be mostly dark and ugly. The music was pleasant enough, but often seemed to clash with what was actually occurring. The story itself was very ugly. Be prepared to not only read about but also participate in pagan rituals (and not really have a clear idea of why you’re having to do them). I felt very, very uncomfortable doing these. Finding out who the characters are is the main goal of the game, but there really isn’t any personal connection to the characters, and no real motivation to want to know them. They are just a mystery. The puzzles are ambiguous and I found that it often became an inventory click-fest. The inventory I found to be one of the biggest irritants. There were about three pages of inventory items, half of them red-herrings and dead ends, and I was constantly scrolling back and forth, equipping and unequipping items, and waiting for the game to load while doing so. That became quite tedious, as did having to read and reread the slow-loading item descriptions that may or may not change the second and third time you click on an item. The text itself I found to be the most irritating part of all. Generally I love to go around collecting books and letters. In this game, I cringed every time I found a book, knowing I would have to read it. The books were generally a mash of useless, repetitive, uninteresting words that you nevertheless had to read through to find a recipe for some puzzle. Not only are they in a rather difficult font to read, the attempts at sounding archaic—filtered through a poor translation—were extremely distracting and unpleasant.
The one thing I appreciated was the idea of mouse movement being a sort of feedback for the reactions of the player. However, all that means is that looking around when events are happening will get you killed. In other words, whenever something interesting happens, you are supposed to freeze and look at a wall (I guess). That really isn’t fun. Since a sanity meter was never mentioned, to me this just did not make any sense in the context it was used, and I would have appreciated being told why I was dying.

So when I laid down $15 for this software I kind of expected a typical budget tool that would be fine making the very specific types of maps you see in the video on Steam, but wouldn't be useful for much else.  Well...I was wrong.  I've just been fiddling with this tool for a day, but I must say, I'm ridiculously impressed.
First, the drawing interface of the tool itself is both powerful and user friendly.  It provides some really simple things like drawing floors as squares on a grid, but it also provides more advanced functionality like drawing floors with n-sides polygons, and a terrain brush that is more like a paintbrush.  It has a special wall tool that makes it really simple to put walls down as well.
Second, this tool heavily utilizes layers, which is great.  It gives you the power to put as many objects on top of something as you want, and in whatever order of occlusion you want.  It also allows you to add effects like shadows and such to layers, it even allows you to create your own custom effects!  Finally, it had some nice functionality with layer grouping so that you can easily group a bunch of layers and then do things like mass replace the floor texture with something else.
Third, and here's where it starts to get really good, is the community content.  Sooo when I checked out the workshop, I thought I would see maybe a few intrepid users that made like 3 or 4 floor tiles or something.  Nope...there are GIGS of community content on there.  Basically, people used to post huge collections of dungeon mapping content on sharing sites, and some users have taken this content and provided it on the workshop.  I don't think I'll ever see every image I downloaded yet alone use all of them lol.
Also, it allows you to use the Random Dungeon Generator from the donjon website and import that dungeon right into DPS for editing!  This is a pretty awesome feature, especially since you can easily mass select all the floors and just replace them with whatever texture you want.
Fourth, and I think this is the best point, is the dev Pyromancer.  While I was playing around with this tool, at several points I wouldn't be able to find some feature I thought the tool should have so I would google it.  In most occasions I would find a thread where some user asks for a feature, and a few posts down Pyromancer says that he added it.  This is pretty amazing customer support.  Pyromancer seems really dedicated to making this app a winner, and I think he's on the right track.
So finally, the downsides of the product.  I've noticed that it freezes sometimes, which is annoying.  Hopefully these crashes will get worked out soon.  Also, you can't resize the "panes" in the DPS window.  Like, you can't make the tile/object selection window larger.  This makes it a little difficult to pick a tile when you have one of those massive packs from the workshop.  Hopefully this will get added later.
In conclusion, I highly recommend this tool.  For $15, it offers amazing functionality, and I don't see how it can be beat for the price.

This is potentially the greatest story rich game ever. A truly spectacular narrative with an even balance of horror, tragedy, ethical dilemmas and philosophical conundrums. The game even forces the player to make impossible choices that don't necessarily effect the story in any drastic way, but leave the player with a sense of unease and dispute about what exactly counts as 'human' and the value of being alive. Whilst the monsters that chase you about the abondoned underwater labs of Pathos II are somewhat alarming, the real horror stems from the psychological torture that the remants of mankind are forced to endure at the hands of their own desire to preserve the ghost of humanity. I think the reason this narrative works so well as a game and not a film is the function of perspective. It's important that the story is percived subjectively to provide context to the plot points and inspire motivation for your decisions. Decent, well fleshed out characters that provoke empathy, even if there are only a few with limited interaction time. And of course the visuals are quite nice as well. Cannot recommend this game enough.

Alright y'all, I've been seein' a whole bunch of negative reviews on this game that I dont personally think it deserves. So Im gonna give it to you straight and narrow. I've put around 300+ hours into this game and I still enjoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it. So here are some pros and cons for you silly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Pros:
-Fun af, revolutionary combat system thats easy to learn, hard to master.
-Absolutely incredible graphics and animations, the executions are so grisly it makes you feel like you're actually beheading someone.
-Great gamemodes, except for one (Im looking at you skirmish...) that really provide a great level of fun.

-So far Ubisoft is doing an okay job by listening to the community, so far anyway...

Cons:
-Uplay. Uplay is a hot pile of garbage, and makes playing with friends a real pain
-Pier to Pier servers. Hopefully they'll get dedicated servers in the future, but for now we're stuck with P2P...
-Unbalanced characters. For the most part, some characters are pretty well balanced, then you have some that are just ridiculously over powered (I'm looking at you warlord...), but Ubisoft has been doing theyre best to bring some balance into the game, so hopefully they'll get it all balanced.

-$60. Pretty pricey...

Overall, I am very happy with this game, yes its not perfect by any means, but from what I can tell, Ubisoft is taking steps (as small as they might be...) in the right direction with balancing and making this a better game. Where it stands right now it still needs some work, but as long as you dont take it too seriously, its a whole lot of fun. The best NES game that was never released on the NES! Oniken achieves so purely what it tries to achieve, and that makes it feel crazy authentic. It doesn't emulate a NES title, it is a NES title, through and through. The game plays like yesterday, feels like yesterday, and sounds like yesterday. But you should play it today!
In all honesty, Oniken so closely recreates a NES action title that some questionable aspects are included as well. We have lives, no checkpoints in individual levels, no upgrades at all through the whole game. I do not personally consider these aspects negative but I could understand those that do. All these aspects only adds to the authenticity. In the end, Oniken won't blow your mind, it doesn't introduce crazy new platformer concepts and it doesn't have a super memorable story or crazy boss fights. However, it does what it sets out to do, and for that I can only give it the highest of recommendations for those seeking this kind of experience.

Evil cyborgs, ronin, and wacky 80s NES style all come together to form Oniken, the first offering from Joymasher. The plot is pretty straightforward: you, a big strong guy, must go slice up all the bad robot guys and save the world somehow.
Playing this game reminds me a lot of the Contra series on NES/SNES. You definitely need to memorize every part of each stage along with every enemy and boss attack pattern as just relying on your reflexes will lead to an early death. The game is equally unforgiving, putting you back on the very first level in a chapter after losing your last life (though you do get infinite continues, thankfully). This can seem tedious at first but it also serves to give you time to reflect on why exactly you lost and how to improve your chances on the next attempt.
Oniken combines just the right amount of difficulty and gameplay to give an experience that is akin to retro titles while stopping just short of breaking your will to continue. Consider grabbing it if you’re a fan of older Contra-style games.

4x =  "eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate"
This game is
combat focused. The only way to win is to eXterminate. From the very beginning, you are met with hyper aggressive ai pirates and crystals entities who invade your space.
The design philosophy here is that you MUST be combat-centric in order to survive and succeed. You MUST focus on military and defenses. This is not a matter of subjective, personal opinion, even the dev has stated this is necessary.
And that is why it deviates from the traditional, popular, successful 4x genre that most 4x fans enjoy.  This game is a 0x, 0x, 0x, 1x game.
...this is not an empire building game. It's not an exploration game. It's not a "focus on advancement game". It's not a diplomacy game. It's purely a "do specific actions so you are as efficient as possible." Why? Because the AI is incredibly efficient and does not play as a human being would (flawed) or simulated race would, it plays as a computer trying to be as efficient as possible and does so with no setbacks.
I yearn for the days of MOO and MOO2, even Gal Civ series. These were 4x games that did it right. They allowed
in how the player would mold their empire and interact with the universe. You have no such freedom here.
A 4x game (whether it is set in space or otherwise, typically gives the player the opportunity to focus on non-military philosophies. You can't do that with SD2, it's all about military power and having it as early as possible, and having as much of it as possible.
A 4x game typically allows you the freedom to focus on being the most advanced race. You can't with SD2, it's all about military power and having it as early as possible, and having as much of it as possible.
I, like many playhers, enjoy turtle races, taking the higher road, the more benevolent path. Focus on maximizing colonies to their fullest potential, maximizing diplomacy, maximizing technology, and having a big stick (advanced military) that is capable or sufficient, but isn't needed for rapid expansion or constant defenses due to hyper-aggressive ai. You can't do that with SD2, it's all about military power and having it as early as possible, and having as much of it as possible.
Cool mechanics, good graphics...all goofed up because of silly design choices that require the player to focus on military might or else.
SD2 does do some things right, but when it comes to allowing the player to play a variety of strategies and roles...it fails miserably IMO.
A recent patch was implemented to make it "easier" for those who felt the ai was too aggressive. What this did was made it so you had a slightly better chance at combat in the beginning. You still have to focus on establishing a strong military however.
In other words, the patch address the concerns of those who wish to focus on combat and aggressive play by making it easier for them to do so...but it does absolutely nothing for the fans of the 4x genre who actually enjoy different strategies other than combat.  You are still requierd to quickly build up a solid defense and military so you can succeed.
For those who are wanting a traditional 4x space game like the classic such as Masters of Orion or Galactic Civilization, you will not find it here. You will be heavily disappointed.
For those who prefer to play with a very aggressive military, focus on combat and a large or advanced military (as it is required), you will probably enjoy the game.
As others have said in the forums, the inspiration for this game does not appear to be the traditional 4x space game, but rather rts games (SC2 for example). The game probably would have been better received if it were an RTS actually as that is the crowd that seems to enjoy it the most.
"Combat! Combat! Combat!"  If that isn't your "rallying cry" for what you want in a game...then Star Drive 2 probably isn't going to appeal to you as that is all it is, a space combat sim...and one that you really need to be efficient in as the AI does not make mistakes or cut corners when it comes to building fleets or engaging yours.

While this game is short even when compared to other Platinum games such as Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising, let alone Nier Automata, this is probably Platinum's best shot at transferring their iconic combat style to a shooter. The dodge and slow-mo can still be performed, and it is just as stylish as any other games from Platinum (maybe except those avatar and transformer games...). The weapons can be upgraded as you go through tons of robot enemies as well, though up to this point I still don't see any obtainable power upgrades for the Exo-suit, or the ARS, Sam is wearing throughout the game.
Combat is really fun. In addition to a combat system that works well with both controller and tradional keyboard-and-mouse setup (I personally use a Dualshock 4, it works great btw), and I would say the mechanics that allow the player to shoot someone while gliding with style with a heavy machine gun feels very intuitive. If only more games could do that, gliding with a leg booster is cool af.
As a previous-gen game being remastered, Vanquish has phenomenal performance and graphics. I'm running this game at 4K constant 60fps on my GTX1080 and no hiccups whatsoever, so one could tell this not only is another great port from Platinum, but also a great remastered version of the game.
Then again, the game is really short, I launched the game after I've had lunch, and I finished it before dinner. However it is well balanced and fun on normal difficulty, and it would provide anyone who loves a challenge with its various difficulty settings. It is well worth its low price tag and definitely worth giving it a go.

Stardrive 2 have been a highly anticipated game for me personally this year so i eagerly sat down and started playing it the 10th.
First of all it was completely different from SD1 and so there was alot more to learn, but if you know the basics of x4 games this wont be too difficult as you need to follow the basic "explore, expand, exploit and exterminate". Thus you will do this and the AI will do this during the whole course of the game through a wide variety of strategies with invasions and diplomacy.
What i really like is that the tech tree has been improved, now i am still a little uncertain if it is for the better og worse as you only get to choose a handfull of technologies (in a normal game), but this will push you towards "roleplaying" or acting more with your races' traits, if you choose the trait "creative" however you will be able to get all the technologies except racial/experimental tech from the other races. I was a big fan of SD1 not exactly being turn based so everything happened in real time like space battles and exploration, but to compensate for that the developer gave us BATTLE ARENAS! which i for one enjoy very much and it makes for a more interesting experience though i hate that i always manage to get destroyed.
What i dont like that much is mostly a few smaller problems like when i try to box-select my ships in a battle arena the mouse cursor may touch the minimap and then my view gets teleported to the other side of the arena which is annoying. I am very unsure about the ground combat, but that is my personal preference, it does however feel a little quick made in many ways; firstly it looks bad but i can always get over that fact, Secondly the player is too prone to missclick and give orders by accident, there should be some way to give the soldiers orders in a proper way (example: i tend to click and check what soldiers are equipped with so i can send my short ranged soldiers to the front, but it is too easy to give them orders so they will either shoot or walk somewhere by accident).
These are tiny problems of course and i will enjoy the game to the fullest no matter, but it would be nice to see some sort of fix for this.
Now i havent even touched the surface for how good this game can be, i mean the best part about it is to construct your own ships and send them into combat to see how long they survive, but it seems to me that the remnant invasion, angry crystal ships, pirates and the other empires loves to harrass the player alot. (i was so lucky to get the "Zapp Brannigan" leader on my first run and didnt understand why i was attacked so much). Maybe i am just a complete idiot and embarrasingly bad at constructing ships too, but i spent most of my time researching tech and turtling while being blokaded by remnant ships and pirates until the empires around me sandwitched me to kingdom come.
So all in all if you are still reading, this game is very good! it is easy to understand and get into, the AI will destroy you on Normal and you must learn that Patience is a virtue, i recommend this highly, especially in the future when there probably will be alot of exciting mods to come from a great modding community.

So yeah, if you think this looks cool and tactical, then I recommend it, if you to micro manage everything, if you think it has potential as a strategy game, then its not recommended.

Every Jackbox Party Pack so far has had one game that stuck out, one that was just
, and the rest were somewhere in between. The first had Drawful, but it also had Word Spud. The second had Fibbage 2, but it also had the quickly obsolete Quiplash XL. The third has Fakin' It, but it also has Guesspionage. But this one, this one here is great, all of them (Except for MSM). Let's talk about the games.
This is the highest quality Fibbage based on the fact that the audio wasn't recorded on a laptop microphone. Fibbage 2 suffered potato quality audio the worst, but this was finally recorded properly. But it also has some other features that makes this one better than the previous Fibbages. The art style is fantastic, the audio finally isn't crap, the facts are updated (but this is always one of the reasons).
Fibbage 3 comes with a new game mode titled Enough About You. Surprisingly a letdown for our group. The questions did not always apply to certain people, and the final question is always “Tell a truth and a lie”, which is too open-ended, it's extremely difficult to come up with answers without any direction.
I enjoyed the fact that this Fibbage included a lot more questions that I could remember reading about, there's always something great about remembering something, even when it's minor. The “Lie for me” allows you to come up with a lie, without coming up with a lie, which due to my
I have difficulty coming up with a lie.
Fibbage has always been a favorite in our group, and with the improved design, it's a favorite-er game of ours! The best part about Fibbage is that the old games never become obsolete. Because of the minimal changes to gameplay, sequels just add more questions to the game, similar to You Don't Know Jack.. Which we haven't gotten in two years.. Jackbox.
While people are answering prompts, little popups will show up on the screen that make fun of the little things that annoy us. While you probably won't burst out laughing from these, they really add something to the game and deserve it's own section in this review.
The last round, every. single. time. I'm not the only one that has this complaint, I've seen others talking about it too. Photosharing is the most unique round in the game.. It's also the worst. I've played this game numerous times, and every single time,
. The images are very generic, and there just aren't enough of them.
The concept is great, my group enjoyed this one, and our unfunny selves somehow got some laughs (out loud!) every round. It's a funny game, and isn't MSM. It has both of those going for it. Of course, the photosharing round could use improvement, but it won't keep us from playing it. The good thing about Survive The Internet is how no matter how much you play it, it shouldn't ever end up repeating itself.
Survive The Internet gives people prompts to answer, but nobody ever sees those prompts but the person answering it, and the answers can usually end up being pretty generic anyway. Even if you get the same prompt again, the other people are going to have a different answer, because we're (totally) not robots. You're not going to end up saying “oh, we've had this before”, because what hardcoded strings are in the game don't matter.
, Photosharing does repeat, and goddamn it, it repeats too much. One game mode kept this from being the perfect game. Regardless of that, Survive The Internet is probably the best introductory game to this Party Pack.
Much like how Photosharing keeps STI from being the perfect game, Monster Seeking Monster is the game that keeps the pack from being the perfect pack.

===
Forts is a real-time single and multi-player artillery shooter with greatly emphasized building elements. In this game, you will act as one of the many available commanders and take on players online in a variety of maps and modes, or partake in a single-player campaign against the AI. This game heavily draws inspiration from the all-time classic Worms, but adds base building to the gameplay formula, in addition to real-time which makes matches a bit more fast-paced.
===
Basically in forts you have always two main objectives: building your base and destroy the enemy one: to do so, you'll have to destroy the enemy base core, as the enemy will try to do so aswell. To protect it, there is a plethora of defensive constructs ranging from simple wooden platforms to high-tech energy shields, with which you'll have to build a true fortress, but mind taking into account the laws of physics, as unstable structures will quickly fall apart.
The building system is simple and immediate, drag and release whole base segments or just single ones, have your base up in no time, then place some of the many weapons available, which will fire automatically for defense but it will come down to you to control them for attacking, deciding direction, force (if applicable) and trajectory of the projectiles.
To do all of this you'll also need to manage Energy and Metal, derived from Mines and Turbines, so some planning ahead is required in order to build a functional fortress to accomodate all this machinery. Being real-time and not turn based as most games of this kind, all these things unfold rather quickly, and you'll often have to multitask repairs, new structures, attack and production together.
Overall, the proposed gameplay formula works smoothly, is not too long thanks to the RTS approach, but still involves a lot of tactics and planning especially in 2v2 and above matches, where multiple adversaries make strategic options very varied.
All combat happens in real time. There are basically two types of armaments, which are direct fire, like machineguns, or indirect fire, like mortars. Each weapon has its own strenghts and weaknesses, as does each construction part, some must be unlocked by building specific Upgrade structures in the base before being able to build them. Knowing what weapons work best against a given enemy base layout is fundamental in being victorious, as is balancing attack and defense.
Environmental hazards like expanding fire upon wood and also gravity are to be taken into account, damage to your base may get it to fall apart because of structural strain, while fire might just consume it all in the blink of an eye. Structures often have good bonuses but also set off huge explosions and damage if destroyed, so you really need to think where to put them.
On top of all this, there are very powerful commander abilities, each commander got his own, usable once in a while during a match, which can turn the tide of a battle if used correctly.
The centerpiece of content in Forts is without a doubt Multiplayer which can potentially offer endless entertainment if you get hooked to this game. The single player campaign has limited duration and serves mostly as a tutorial. If you like the game, being mostly multiplayer-oriented, you can get a lot of content for your money.
Overall there are no major balance issues, apart from maybe Sniper Turrets being a bit overpowered, being able to mostly 1-shot any enemy turret at any distance, can be a very powerful weapon in the hands of accurate players.
This game involves a good degree of multi-tasking and planning abilities, the strategic possibilities are many and the more players you add the more things you have to consider. We rated the Challenge factor taking into account the learning curve of the game mechanics and how it applies to multiplayer gameplay. Definitely, a High challenge rating is to be assigned.
===
Graphics are 2D and realized in a simple, cartoonish fashion which is decently appropriate for the general ambience the game gives out. Do not expect to find elaborate, last-gen graphics in this title, because you won't. The art style is appreciable, there aren't inconsistencies with the overall quality.
Basic effects and sountracks, nothing out of the ordinary, no either bad or good mentions to make.
No particular issues were found, this game should run well even on dated systems.
No issues were found.
Enemy AI during the campaign or skirmish modes will follow a pre-determinated building pattern with their base, if a segment is destroyed the AI will rebuild it again, do not expect good adaptability from AI because it serves mainly as tutorial against the players. Sufficent, but nothing more.
Controls and UI are appreciable, nothing bad to report.
No severe ones to report, found a few, minor ones who do not compromise gameplay in any way.
===
A fresh take on a classic type of game which rocked back in the early times of PC gaming, deep strategy involved, decently developed overall, won't disappoint the RTS enthusiasts who want to try something different.

Three to four or so years ago, this now washed up game I play called Vega Conflict started out with a promising future. Gamers of all budgets could pick up this free-to-play game without much fear of being beaten into the ground with a wallet warrior willing to shell out hundreds of dollars a week (The low end for some players.) It was generally understood at the time why microtransactions were so prevalant, as the game was free-to-play, and SOMEONE has to pay for the resources that go into development. No big deal at the time, as no matter how much money you put into this game then, you would not have a significant advantage over someone who spent less. As the years and months have come to pass, Kixeye has been overly aggressive with throwing offers for their in-game currency coins, while implementing their inherently broken ship "mark" upgrade system, giving players who purchase said offers horrifically large advantages over players who don't purchase them. To make matters worse, for a large period of time after these offers come out, the content enabling low budget players to grind their way up to the content the "coiners" were able to purchase is willfully held back from release by Kixeye for weeks and sometimes well over a month, in order to convince the player base over time that purchasing these offers is a MUST if you want to get anywhere in the game.
The purpose of a game review in reality is to inform any potential gamers who are on the fence about whether they should pick Vega Conflict up or not. At the time of this writing, Kixeye does nothing to develop content to bridge low-medium tier players up to the high tier. The only content that is developed appeals to players who A) Have already been playing for years and are very seasoned, and B) Players who fork over a fortune to bridge the infinitely widening gap to the "end" tier. What I am trying to say is, if you start this game now, and don't intend to put (seriously!) thousands of dollars into the in-game currency offers, you will never get far.
Being a player who has been around for since 2013 when Vega Conflict was still in it's beta phase, I can confidently tell you that this game is most likely NOT for you if you are just starting.
Good luck.
