This game gets an A for good intentions...
...and stinking, sad F for execution. I would really like to give this game more mercy points, but honestly I can't. This is, without a doubt, one of the worst programmed and most boring platformers I ever played.
You clearly made a bad game, when at least once player reminds himself of infamous Sonic 2006 when playing it. Controls are that bad! They are completely unresponsive, sluggish and unreliable, leading you into pits of death and frustration constantly. Game isn't challenging in any shape or form, so my fight with those controls became the one of the only sources of any kind of emotions from playing it. Levels are extremely linear, flat and they don't provide any interesting mechanics and clever platforming. Bugs are everywhere. You can see yourself unnaturally teleporting, tripping, slowing down, merging with level's geometry, blocking progress for the next level section. No game is bug free, but there is a limit and Never Alone clearly surpasses it with flying colors!
While playing you are constantly peppered with "Cultural Insings" - micro-documentaries about people and life at frozen Alaskan tundra. You aren't forced to watch them, but at least they are a bit interesting and they give some salvation from the horrible gameplay. That said, those aren't game's saving graces. It's pretty staggering how gameplay seems to be an afterthought to the initial idea and not a core focus of the game. There are many titles that mix interesing cultural knowledge with top-notch gameplay and they are better for it. Year Walk for example, where connections are subtile and gameplay is polished. Never Alone unfortunately doesn't do that. It plays it safe and does it poorly.
I would also like to notice that in my opinion this game DOES NOT deserve any accolades and awards that you can see on the store page. Great, award-worthy games need to play well or be very engaging. I'm sadly shocked that interesting, but ultimately fatally executed subject matter is enough for many judges, while other games that are in real, pushing the medium forward with clever designs and ideas go unrecognized.
That 15 dollars price tag only adds insult to injury... and I didn't even managed to get all the Steam cards while completing the main game and it's DLC to 100%! Developers completely wasted their potential and created a game what it not worth your time, money and makes a great disservice for the interesting topics it tries to preset.

My friends and I are big fans of the Jackbox Party Pack series, so it was a given that we would try out the latest addition to the series and see if it measures up. In short, it does! We had an absolute blast playing the variety of games included in this pack, sometimes laughing so hard we could hardly breath.
-
. Fibbage 3 is an alright addition, but the other Fibbage game mode, titled “Fibbage: Enough About You” turned out to be my favorite in this pack. This new mode takes what made Fibbage fun and makes it personal. My friends and I had a lot of fun entering the most bizarre truths and lies about ourselves and trying to pick out the truth among them. The game was equally fun when played with family. It really tests how well you know those playing with you (and how good a liar you can be).
-
. The game where witty responses win all. Given another player’s response to a random question, what kind of headline (or product, location, whatever the category may be) would make that response look the most absurd. Another great addition to the pack, and with my favorite visuals across all games in the pack. The game plays through the Internet browser of what looks to be a Windows 98 knockoff. On top of the fantastic visuals, Survive the Internet rewards players for making his/her friends look bad, something my friends and I are already good at. As such, we felt right at home with this game and plenty of laughs ensued.
-
. Civic Doodle is easily the most laughter-inducing game included in this iteration of the Party Pack. The concept is brilliant: given a canvas with some line or shape on it, who can come up with a better addition given this base? We had an absolute blast making the stupidest of additions to each other’s drawings. We somehow turned a small squiggle of a line into a stick figure wearing a goat head, with both the stick figure and goat head wearing eye patches over each eye, for a total of four eye patches (along with an eggplant off in the corner for whatever reason). Several artistic masterpieces were born while playing this one.
-
. I found this game to be weaker compared to the others, but it was still fun to play. It requires a certain degree of strategy, at least more than any of the other games in the pack. The player basically has to score dates with other players and play around his/her special monster power. To do so the player must exchange flirtatious texts with the other players, keeping in mind his/her own monster power. The game then shows the messages exchanged and whether or not the players hooked up or if one was rejected. One aspect that I disliked about this was the fact that the game does not show all of the texts exchanged after each round in certain cases. If a player hooks up with another player, any other player that attempted to hook up with either of the two that scored a date will not have his/her messages displayed. Instead the game just shows that they were rejected. Plenty of missed laughs with some of the messages my friends and I were throwing around.
-
. I found Bracketeering to be the weakest of the games. Sure it can be enjoyable at times, but it simply does not compare to the rest of the games in the pack. It is also the only game that supports more than eight players (up to 16!), so maybe I just did not play it with a proper amount of players, as our largest play session was only six strong. It is basically a game about voting in a bracket, although with a twist. In one round, we were given the question “what is a turn-on for you?”. We had the usual responses, such as “long hair” and “nice abs”, then we had my super witty response: “pressing the power button”. Well, after we put in our answers for the bracket, the question changed to “what is a great skill to include on a resume” and then the voting commenced until a winner was found (and what a great skill “pressing the power button” turned out to be!). Then after moving onto the last round, the questions started changing after every round of voting. It can get quite bizarre, but this ended up being our least played game in the pack.
Overall, Party Pack 4 is a solid entry to the series. There may be a couple weaker games included, but the majority are a blast to play. I have played it with both friends and family and will definitely keep coming back to it in the future. As for how I rank each game included in this party pack, I would rank them as such:  Fibbage: Enough About You > Civic Doodle > Survive the Internet > Fibbage 3 > Monster Seeking Monster > Bracketeering.

In this review I'll cover some common aspects like the story, gameplay, graphics and other noteworthy things about this game. This is all from my personal point of view and experience.
SOMA is a first-person horror game set in the underwater research facility Pathos-II. After taking an experimental brain scan in a medical institute in his hometown, protagonist Simon Jarett blacks out and wakes up in the facility, nearly a hundred years later with no memories of how he got there or what happened after the scan. Simon soon learns that a meteor has destroyed life on earth as we know it and that the scan he took saved a conscious copy of him that lives on. Many others have taken the same sort of scan and are stored in a data bank somewhere in the facility. It's up to Simon to save this data from extinction. But he is not alone on the sea floor...
While the story itself doesn't go very deep (it's best described as all the events during and prior to the emergency state of the facility), it's both relatively easy to follow and its eeriness keeps you tuned, that's what I like about it. The notes and terminal data files are of good length: not too shallow as to function simply as memos and not too long as to result in saying "whatever" and not bothering with them. I found myself looking in every room and at every terminal for datalogs, notes, audio files and more.
The ending is also really memorable and bitter-sweet and left me with the feels and thoughts. I won't spoil anything of it, you have to experience it whole yourself.
Regarding the gameplay, it's a lot like the Amnesia series: you go through doors and ladders, flip some switches, access computers, run and hide from monsters, etc. You have no means of attacking. Despite tab being mapped for "Inventory", there's no real tangible inventory and partially because of that, the puzzles aren't very challenging. On one side, that is a good thing as some people get frustrated by complex tasks/puzzles in games but on the other hand keeps the gameplay somewhat simple. Despite that, some puzzles were pretty creative.
It's fairly possible to complete this game within 10 hours, making the price of 28$ a little steep. In my personal opinion it's worth it but it might be worth waiting for a sale, too.
SOMA being a product of Frictional Games, developers of the Penumbra and Amnesia series, this game is bound to give some good frights. This game mostly relies on building up anxiety in the form of the presence of (atmospheric) sounds and monsters rather than relying solely on jumpscares.
This game also really does a good job at making the player feel hopelessly lost (in a good way) on the sea floor. Nothing is certain and anything can happen. Every corner, every exit and every tunnel can lead to a victory or another obstacle, or worse....
While there is a variety of enemies and enough sightings to keep you on the tip of your chair, I must admit there could've been a little bit more of them.
It's a pretty new game, even when we're speaking of 2015. Most medium-grade PCs can run it just fine, albeit it on a bit lowered settings. It seems the framerate is locked but can be unlocked, just Google around.
This is where the game really shines. The sounds of the facility, machinery, underwater world and so on are absolutely spot-on, not a bad word about it. Even the sounds of different locations where a character is in is taken care of. The music, being somewhat minimalistic at some points, also really fits in the game.
An excellent game from Frictional Games and I truly despair having finished it as I really wanted it to go on. I even restarted up to some point to find out any notes and other data I might've missed as well as spending some time on the Wiki to know more about everything inside this awesome game.
P.S. upon completing this game, it's guaranteed you have all achievements.

Traveling through the depths of the ocean, you try to save the remnants of humanity while tackling monsters created by a cancerous growth-like AI, and find conflict within yourself, and your character.
The thoughts of "what makes a human, human" and "if you were copied into another body, would you still be you", are deep thoughts that aren't commonly thought about in daily life. SOMA is a truly horrifying, thoughtful experience.
10/10, would recommend to anyone and everyone.

Oniken is an NES-style action game with a lot of spirit, but it’s ultimately not very fun and I can’t quite recommend it. Now don’t get me wrong, there’s some good stuff to talk about here. When the game’s action works, it works very well: I definitely had several nice moments where I was really in the zone, wasting enemies, lobbing grenades, and managing to survive on just a sliver of health. If you’ve ever found yourself pining for the days of deadly, challenging, two-button NES action, Oniken is specifically designed to scratch that itch. The 8-bit graphics are really well-done, the music is pretty good, and there are plenty of cool (if strangely wordy) Ninja Gaiden-like cut scenes.
Unfortuntaely, these strengths can’t make up for the game’s weaknesses. Oniken is an extremely difficult game, but its difficulty doesn’t always feel compelling or well-earned. There are tons of cheap deaths and lame obstacles that seem more interested in punishing you than giving you an interesting and fun challenge. The platforming sections are terrible; whenever you have to jump around and hang from something, the game becomes especially annoying. The levels are also way too long, which can’t be said of most of the NES games that Oniken wants to emulate; those old games are tough but they usually dole out the action in bite-sized pieces. Oniken, on the other hand, just feels like a slog. When I beat a mission in Oniken, I thought “ugh, I’m glad that’s finally over” and not “that was a fun and worthwhile way to spend my time.”
I love tough NES action games like Shatterhand, Ninja Gaiden, Shadow of the Ninja, etc., so I was very prepared to enjoy this. However, I think that Oniken only takes certain things from those games (difficulty, art style) but leaves out the stuff that actually made them great (fun, creating a compelling experience for the player). If you're a real old school NES head, I can definitely see how this game would interest you, but it's just not very good. If you're extremely curious and you really want to play it, the game goes on sale a lot and shows up in bundles, so wait until you can get it on the cheap.

If you're into the classic 8-bit action platformers of old like Ninja Gaiden, Shatterhand, Batman: The Video Game, and Castlevania then you should give Oniken a look. One of the most faithful love letters to that genre of classic games I have ever played. Arguably comparable to the work put into the famed indie darling Shovel Knight. It's graphics and audio really do capture that 80s Japanese cyberpunk aesthetic really well. Joymasher really knew what they were doing when they made this game.
Oniken is not for the faint of heart, though. It demands a level of skill that veterans of those aforementioned old-school platformers may appreciate but may turn off players not used to the game's difficult fast-paced platforming and demanding boss battles. For those who want a bigger challenge, the game's unlockable boss rush and hardcore mode will push you to learn every facet of the game.
The new Unstoppable Edition update added some major improvements to parts of the game's visual department and some more fleshed out boss battles. The QoL fixes are that make the game a much more enjoyable experience, like the more fair random boss patterns and the ability to auto-fire your shots on the jetbike sections.
The few points I would mark the game against is its short length and its buggy launcher. The former can be consoled by the fact that it is very cheap to purchase even when it's not on sale but the launcher not being able to remove V-sync or the TV mode filter is pretty fusterating. I believe this bug came about with the new update so I hope the developers fixes it soon. Those who might want to play Oniken on a couch and TV set-up might get fustrated with it popping up instead of the game as well. I generally don't like game launchers and much prefer these Steam games to give the option to choose between the launcher and running the .exe directly but that's just me.
Anyway, give this game a shot. Even if it kicks you♥♥♥♥♥at least it won't burn a hole in your wallet. And if you come back wanting more than you might just get your money's worth in the end.

The game is definitely addictive for a while. But I have to say, that the game is not that well balanced. Playing on hard was one of the hardest experiences of my life, way worse than games like Meatboy where its actually supposed to be insanely hard. Dark Souls 2 and 3 are a breeze compared to this.
There are many instances in the game where you feel you literally have no chance, and most of the spells or abilities you have access to won't help you at all in those situations, meaning you have to rely purely on luck and hope the enemy AI doesn't cast spells in a particular order or with a particular frequency. Example: Fighting the two fairies (fall and summer) in the winter palace. And this is, apparently only *3 out of 5 star* difficulty level, according to the author of the game.
What the heck is five star difficulty? I probably don't want to know, it would be inhumanly difficult.
Its definitely an interesting juxtaposition, to be playing a game that looks like its for kids, yet (on hard difficulty) is actually the most painful experience you will ever have.
Anyway that's the main thing I wanted to get across. Besides that, I don't remember there being any music or noticeably good sound effects. The textures are decent. Every character is super-attractive (even the guards) which is kind of funny. Beyond that I liked the sense of humor. The fairies are kind of like cute babies, so I think this game will appeal to girls :P. And me apparently.
There is decent player progression overall, but a lot of the skills are unfinished, and they have been unfinished for years now as far as I can tell. I seriously doubt that this game will ever be finished. I think the developer left to start a different project, because no progress has really been made and its been about 5 years since I played this game last. I doubt any games takes that long to make, unless its Star Citizen in which case you will get to play it when you turn 80.
That's about it for this review. Hopefully I helped!!!

If there is one big flaw with this game, it is the total lack of Multiplayer. There are not even space or ground skirmishes against other players (at least as of 1.0c). This is a pure Singleplayer vs AI game. If you want Multiplayer strategy, that princess is in another castle.
For the rest, it takes some of the best concepts of other (indy) games. The game plays on 3 areas: Galactic, Space Combat, Ground Combat
Galactic:
Is turn based on a 2D map.
The colonisation and colony building closest resembles Civilisation for me. Other liken it to Master of Orion, but I have not playe that series. It focuses more on few, well developed colonies with the right buildings.
It borrows planetary effects and random events/miniquests from Galactic Civilsiations.
You can freely pick you fleets destiantion (no squars/hexes), but fuel greatly limits range outside of your territory.
Diplomacy has two unique turns:
1. The evaluation mechanic is open, with the game actually telling you leader personalities and the weighted values of diplomacy items.
2. The tollerancy mechanic means you cannot simply ignore negative relation modifiers or past deeds of the AI. Your people are a factor too and just won't allow certan deals to happen.
Research:
You can only research one tech per "Tier" giving you some hard choices and you have to aquire the others via espionage or diplomacy.
Space combat:
Is realtime on a 2D map. It closest resembles space empires for me.
It seems to focus more on decisive, large scale battles rather then skirmishes.
Ship design is also seems heavily borrowed from SE, but simplified. Facings matter. There is few geartypes/hulls and almost no levels, but there are lots of modifiers (1-4) you can apply to nearly every item.
Upgrading and retrofitting is seamless.
Ground:
Turn based on a isometic, square based map.
Battles are fought by small elite teams or "boarding parties" rather then large armies.
Troops can have up to 3 abilities (active and passive, with cooldown or without) and based on technology and events you can almost freely choose thier gear while at a planet.
There is no boarding outside of events.
Documentation:
There a lots of tooltips and spoken/interactive toutorials.
Tech descriptions for new ship modules are often quite vague wich can result in picking the wrong tech.

---------------------------------------------------
Mayan Death Robots takes the Artillery genre of video games and gives it some much appreciated innovation.  Like other artillery games, the basic structure of Mayan Death Robots centers around a turn of selecting a weapon, and then aiming it, relying on the players sense of trajectory to land hits on the opponent's side to accomplish a goal.
Worms is perhaps the series best known for popularizing the artillery genre, but Mayan Death Robots is a distinctly different kind of game from Worms, and it's important to know that in advance.  I'll briefly explain the differences, and why they're important.
---------------------------------------------------
Action Artillery Games vs Strategic Artillery Games
In worms and other artillery games, combat is far more Strategic rather than Action based.  In those games, turns last longer, involve a combination of moving, weapon selection, and shooting.  Players take alternating turns, and a game might last upwards of half-an-hour or more.
Mayan Death Robots is more of an Action Artillery game instead of a Strategic Artillery game.  The goal isn't to blow up the opponent, but rather the opponent's core.  Losing your robot essentially equates to a one turn penalty.  This prevents games from being too short, and is more forgiving to players whom make mistakes when learning their robot.
In MDR, players take their turns at the same time, and turns are fast.  Players get six seconds to make their weapon (or jump, or blocks) selection, and then six seconds to aim it.  Weapons fire automatically at the end of those six seconds.  The fast pace of turns can be slightly daunting to new players at first, but it's easy to adjust to because Weapon selection is very streamlined.
Although there are a lot of weapons in the game, each robot is essentially limited to two signature attacks, so you're rarely pressed to make a tough decision during those first six seconds.  That design decision means that the individual matches can be fast but not stressful.  A match usually only lasts between five and ten minutes, so it's really easy for casual players to get in to, yet rewarding for more hardcore players whom want to practice and master each robot's unique combat style.
---------------------------------------------------
Multiplayer Friendly
The single biggest issue facing MDR has to do with the lack of online multiplayer.  One has to keep in mind that Sileni Studios is a tiny team, and simply put it'd be grossly unfair to hold them to the same standards as Team 17 which has a ton of corporate backing to fund a plethora of features.  But still, it is an issue because obviously if you buy a game like this, you're going to want to play it with friends.
That being said, the game has robust support for local Multiplayer, allowing for two players to use the same keyboard, a keyboard and gamepad, or two gamepads.
And it's seriously fun.
Seriously.
This would hands down be a terrific College Dorm game for whenever friends are hanging out.  The fast pace of the game makes it easy for two players to play a match, and then have the loser hand the controller or keyboard off to the next person waiting in line.  And the sheer hilarity of the visuals and action in game make it ridiculously fun for spectators to watch.
For the last few weeks I've played this game with my friends and their kids, switching out the players every match, and it felt like the beautiful nostalgia of video gaming from back when I was in college, passing a controller around whenever typical two-player games were played with an audience of three or more.
---------------------------------------------------
Single Player Friendly
In addition, the solo player campaign is bonkers cool.  There's a great over-the-top storyline about the Death Robots galactic TV show, and all the insanity that ensues.  There are soooo many different scenarios in the game to be unlocked, from maps where Conquistadors constantly attempt to steal your cores, to Elder Gods that dramatically reshape the map, to man-eating plants.  Combined with the ten different playstyles of the robots, the game packs a ton of replayability.
---------------------------------------------------
In Closing
Hands down, for the price, there is a ton of entertainment one can get out of this game.  It's my hope that online multiplayer will be added in the future, but in the meantime there's no real reason to short change yourself by passing over such a well-developed and designed game.

I didn't expect to like this game as much as I did. When you join a game, you are randomly selected as either a camp counselor or as Jason. As a camp counselor, you need to escape using various randomly placed items or survive for 20 minutes, which is a tall order considering you are being hunted by Jason. There are many tools to assist your escape, including calling in Jason's arch-nemesis. Tommy Jarvice, who is the only one that can actually kill Jason (and even this is extremely difficult).
Additionally, you earn CP, which gives you the ability to "roll" for perks that will either enhance your chosen counselor's strengths or make up for the weaknesses (each counselor has stats like strength, speed, luck, etc). You can also grab additional methods of execution for Jason.
If you are randomly chosen to play Jason, your goal is to hunt down and kill all the counselors using the special powers: You can teleport to any location on the map, sense counselors that are nearby, shift to the counselor's location, or stalk the counselors. Also at your disposal are traps and throwing knives. Once you catch a counselor, there are many creative ways to slaughter your prey, and each "kill" has a gory animation. There are also "environmental kills" at specific areas of each map.
There are several choices for Jason, each one corresponding to specific movie versions of him. As with the counselors, each Jason has strengths and weaknesses (ie: for one, the "Sense" power may last longer than the others, but his teleport may take longer to recharge). Every version of Jason, however, can hear his mother's voice telling him to kill them or encouraging him when he is stunned.
This game should have a disclaimer that states: "The developers are not responsible for intense addictions to this game."

The potential functionality is fantastic, and it does certainly do the job right now, but it's got some pretty glaring alpha-version-type problems. The layout is not at all intuitive, the keyboard shortcuts are very poorly thought out (ctrl+A to use the line tool? Esc to use the move tool? Really?), the UI elements aren't scaleable, the menus are about as barebones as possible (the Save function is actually Save As, there's no File/Edit menus). The way the layers work is weird too - they're not at all like layers in Photoshop/GIMP/etc.; rather, every single object you place is a separate "layer" that you can then organize in folders (again, with an unintuitive process). It's also been crashing periodically, but it seems to make backups often enough that I've never actually lost anything, so points for the solid failsafe!
Those gripes aside, I'm still willing to recommend this software overall; if you don't mind working around some weirdness, the results you end up with can be excellent, and the tilesets in the Workshop are well worth your time. Even the stock tilesets have a good breadth of options and are internally consistent, artistically speaking, so if that's your aesthetic, you're good to go. If they make the UI more intuitive and easy to use (if the devs are reading this: why not model it after existing software, like Photoshop? No reason to reinvent the wheel) and do some general polishing, it'd be a solid 10/10.

* Tired of games that hold you hand?
* Want a game that focuses on story?
* Wish you could play System Shock 3?
* Need a cure for constipation?
Well then SOMA is the game for you.
SOMA is the real spiritual successor to System Shock 1 & 2.
Bioshock claimed to be the spiritual successor when it came out, but, having played it, it was only a spiritual successor in regards to game mechanics... shoot stuff, upgrade things, research stuff, rpg elements, etc.
SOMA goes a different direction .. strip out all that game mechanic kludge, and focus purely on story and horror. So, without bulky game mechanics to hide behind, they have to really make the story and horror stand out.
And they do. It is amped up to 11.
They way they do it is by focusing completely on immersion...
No weapons
No health bars
No HUD (no compass, no map)
No objective lists
No arrows guiding you
The game is about as immersive as you can get, and since there's nothing holding your hand, and no way to defend yourself, you have to pay more attention to details.
Like...
* when someone tells you to go do something, you need to actually listen to them to understand what you have to do.
* when you notice some clues, you need to actually pay attention to them and possibly memorize or write things down.
* when you're exploring an area, you need to actually memorize where you're going and what you're doing .. b/c you may need to beat a hasty retreat when things go south.
There is nothing holding your hand here, so you invest yourself more mentally, which heightens your senses to pay attention... and then they spring some scary stuff on you to take advantage of it.
You are completely immersed in the game .. and at their mercy.
It's pure giddy horror / terror / thrill.
I have never cussed so much at a video game for scaring the ever-loving crap out of me in my life, but while I was cussing I was also excited and having a blast.
I'm getting old, and have a hard time staying focused on games, b/c I just get bored with the usual "fetch me a rock, deliver this toothpick" BS that games rehash all the time.
This game had me bolted to my sit and playing near-non-stop.
However, I almost didn't complete it.
I laugh at the paltry attempts at "shock horror" in most games, like Bioshock having scenes of a crazy doctor, or splicers or other junk. Or Quake games having butchered cyborgs and meat factories. *yawn*
But this game... this m***** f****** game ...
I almost had to turn it off at a certain point when I was staring out into darkness going "am I supposed to go that way?" Because the position they put you in is very compromising and vulnerable... and dark.. and stuff lurking in that darkness. And when I googled up a guide that said "yup, ... you gotta go that way." ... I was freaking out.
Some places in the game take place underwater, where you move slow. While you are walking, it can still bring on feelings of Thalassophobia .. fear of open water. (Fear of lack of movement, speed, coordination, being out of your element (ie: on land), and that you are vulnerable to attack from all angles by faster things adapted to the environment while you're too slow to stop them).
Most people get Thalassophobia while treading water ... fear of open water... fear of a shark coming up from under them, or not knowing what's down in the murky darkness below their feet while in open water.
When I was staring out into pitch black underwater, and the game expected me to just start walking ... I had a sort of reverse Thalassophobia ... now, I've had Thalassophobia on other games like Subnautica and SHARK: Hunting the Great White... but those were where you were diving and worried about something below you coming at you.
But, here ... I got this panic attack staring out into that darkeness not knowing what was going to come after me. And I knew something was going to be out there.
I almost didn't make... as in, I almost turned the game off for good and gave up, b/c I got this overwhelming sense of wanting to throw up. The game was making me physically ill, I was panicing so bad.
But, I ran like a little girl so fast... when I heard noises or saw distractions, I didn't even stop to look.. I just kept running. And you know how you get that feeling on the back of your neck when you walk down the hall.. like you feel something is coming up behind you so it makes you feel like you need to run all of a sudden..
Good lord... I had that the whole time I was running through that part.
This game is just panic-inducing at times. There are a few jump scares, but everything else is just real terror... it puts you into situations where you are uncomfortable, then you have to over come that in order to keep from getting killed (eg: when monsters come near, you often have to look away from them and sit still to keep from dying... while they're standing right next to you breathing down your back.)
They put you into uncomfortable situations then ask you to act unnaturally to handle them (stop and don't look at monsters, run right out into the middle of pitch black to progress, etc)... every ounce of your being is telling you to act a certain way (like "run, fool! He's about to kill you!" or "don't go out there, stupid!"). But the game expects you to act opposite.
This makes it double terrifying. (Face horrible situation, then go against your instincts to survive it).
And the lack of HUD means you're completely immersed in it all, so your senses are firing on all cylinders, and you're completely in the moment.... as the game pretty much has it's way with you.
I can't recommend this game highly enough. Even calling it a "game" seems insulting, b/c this is an FPS interactive fiction novel / simulation / philisophy lesson that really makes you think about greater things while also scaring the crap out of you. It's simply amazing. The story is amazing, the fear is amazing, just everything.
And the creatures and stuff all make sense based on the story. Some games populate "scary" enemies just for shock value, but there's no valid reason or they make little sense (thus there's no reason to take them seriously). But, the story in SOMA makes everything in the game plausible, which just adds to the immersion.
If you ever wished they made a System Shock 3, get SOMA and see what it could have been.

You can upload your own objects and textures and the inclusion of Steam Workshop support is a godsend if you are using this in a non-professional capacity. There are mods which add literally THOUSANDS of new objects/textures to the program (though the user should be careful to ensure they have the correct license if intending to use for professional purposes).
When saving or exporting maps options are provided for the main VTT software options in the market or as a simple graphic file if you prefer.
Whilst still in early access I recommend this program.

This game's problem is...it 'tries too hard to be MOO2 without understanding what made MOO2 fun and balanced'. Having played through and done some reading I will point out some glaring flaws.
AI is hyper-aggressive stupid expansionist. It will gobble up as much as it can as fast as it can and use that to produce as many junk ships as it can to throw at you the instant it detects weakness. That's ALL it will do - the ships it uses are pre-designed and total junk. It makes no attempt at clever diplomacy or alliances. It doesn't use starbases. No hiding in the trees to do a devastating flank attack here - no sir it will conga line straight into your wall-o-doom in the puddle size combat arenas.
Constant escalating attacks by 'NPC factions' - remnants and pirates and space crystals that don't attack the AI, so you have to dedicate a fleet to defending against them while the AI out-expands you then sends a fleet of doom at you.
Diplomacy is a joke. Half the races Want To Eat Your Granny and will declare war right away if they have more ships. Every other species is going to demand/threaten right off the bat, sometimes your homeworld, and if you don't give it to them they'll declare war if they have more ships. If you do they'll declare war anyway a few turns later if they have more ships. More ships >>> diplomacy.
Balance is...nonexistant. Tech 0 lasers and tech 2 mass drivers are all you ever need, maybe gauss later. They aren't the best weapons in the game because you can use them to flank or do ninja flips and death from above the command center, they are the best weapons in the game because their stats are better than anything else you can research. Some traits are grossly overpowered - subterranean + more money per pop. The optiris have ships that are TWICE as large for the same CP cost as the vulfar.
Ground invasions are 3rd wheel. What is a stripped down Xcom doing in my 4x? Ugly, simple, beyond mindless, pointless, click-fests that can be avoided at no cost by having one ship filled with nukes. Seriously, you'll need a ship with nukes and one trooper per fleet and that third of the game can be safely ignored.
The bugs! Oh God the bugs! And I don't mean the hivers. Ranging from game-breaking (autoresolve with many losses) to devastating (can not scroll systems in leader-assign screen) to merely annoying (deployment area does not auto-size for fleet).
Do Not Buy. Will update in 6 months if they fix stuff, it's gonna need at least that long. Unless the dev abandons it like he did his first game.

As the name suggests, Secrets of Grindea has a LOT to grind. Being purely luck based, the game could have you playing for hours on end without getting what you want, or simply getting it too quickly. Secrets of Grindea, if I had to explain it in the shortest way possible, I'd say this: Completionist's Wet Dream. Why do I say that? Well, continue reading and you'll see why.
The reason I'm giving Early Access a 10/10, is because the developer has and continues to update the game, and allows us to see the process in which he is doing it, shows us what he is doing and tells us what he has planned for the future. He promised a housing system when I first got the game, one of the lastest patches gave us that housing system, with enough furniture for me to be pleased. This is what Early Access games should be like.
Fighting is 90% of what you will be doing in the game. Although there are different things such as Fishing and Housing System, the game is centered around its fighting. It starts off simple, the game gives you your first weapons, a one-handed sword, a two-handed club and a shield. Now, different to the fighting system in most games, you get to use the shield for both. The Two-Handed weapons, and the One-Handed weapons contain different abilities you can learn through the game, 5 abilities for each, allowing you to polish your fighting style. In the future, you may also specialize in magic, having to choose from four different elements: Fire, Ice, Earth and Air.
Personally, I was a bit sad there were no classes in the game, but at the same time you may build your character however you want without any sort of limitation. I loved the fighting, nonetheless. I'll say it's one of the funnest fighting systems. More in-depth explanation in "Talent System"
The Talent System is very easy to use. One-Handed and Two-Handed get a certain amount of abilities, which you will be upgrading as you level up. So the Talent System has multiple points you can utilize, one you can use on your abilities, in a basic matter (1-5) and from there you use another point, called the Golden point (5-10) which enhances your ability. I personally felt the two-handed and one-handed played very differently.
The last point, the third one is used on your passives. This is where you decide whether your character is tanky, by giving it +%HP or building your character crit damage, even Magic Attack. If you end up regreting your decision, you can click the ability and refund, which will cost you a bit of gold. You will be getting a lot of gold if you stick around to grind for everything.
With that being said, let's move onto the grinding. The grinding in this game, is fantastic. Giving you multiple things to finish, farm, and complete. This is why I said, a completionist will love this game. Every zone has 5 fish which you can catch, it is very fun and fish are good for use in the future.
Aside from the fishing in every zone, every monster in the game has a very low drop rate to their "card" .. These cards, give you permanent boosts, some to your magic attack, some to simple things like extra discount on items you buy. The most common card being a 0.3% droprate. If you dedicate yourself to getting all of these cards, it will increase your gametime exponentially.
The controls in this game are very simple. You move with the arrow keys, attack with Z and block with X. Your abilities also being close to the Z and X for easier reaction time (C, A, S, D, V, F, Q, W, E, R) All the keys being modifiable, and controller support making it great.
The Mechanics are very interesting. When you pick up an item of interest (Armor or Weapon) it will appear on the top right, comparing it to the item you have equipped. If you wish to equip your picked up item, you press Tab and ta-da! Your item has been equipped.
As for the menu, while you'll be going there a lot to check your talents, and there is no specific button to open it, it's extremely easy to navigate. Separated into 8 categories (Character, Equipment, Inventory, Crafting, Skills, Journal, World Map, System.) the game is easy to work around. Realistically speaking, you'll be using a maximum of 4 of those 8, but it's still nice to be able to see your character's stats.
Everything you equip in the game can be changed into an item you own. If you have a two-handed weapon you like the way it looks, but it's weaker, you can equip it as "Style" and it will replace your current weapon. It's the same with your Hat, Facegear and Shield. And if you are not the type of person to care for it, you may always hide it by right-clicking on the original item.
The Housing System is great, but I will warn you now, it takes a lot of money. It's great because you may make it as big as you want (As far as I've seen, I haven't tested the limit but I have spent over 50k gold on it) with upcoming furniture and a very intuitive system to change the house around, allowing you to change even the lighting on different rooms, to how you want your house's structure to be. Keep in mind, the game is still beta and housing is still not perfect, missing some furniture to fill your house perfectly, you will get more furniture as you complete more dungeons.
Co-op in the game works beautifully, with a very easy to set-up server for newbies, it's just a point and click with multiple options, You may set the loot to Round-Robin or Every man for himself, where you just run to get the items, first come, first serve. With an Arcade Mode that I haven't truly gotten around to trying and an arena zone, where you can play Player vs. Player, or unite all to try and kill waves of monsters, getting graded by your time and damage you took, making it interesting to have everyone screaming at each other because a person got tickled by a monster and now you can't get that perfect S.
The difficulty is flexible and can be changed inside the game, even during a fight. I wasn't much of a fan on the hard aspect of the game, because I never truly liked bullet hells, and it definitely turns the boss fights into just that. But if it gets too difficult, you can always go back to normal difficulty.
And last, but not least, the story in this game is pretty basic. Without getting too much into detail, you can play with your friends through it all, it adds no change, apart from the fact that you need to farm for more cards per player. I couldn't get into the story, some very funny characters I enjoyed interacting with, some I couldn't wait to get off my back. I laughed a lot in the dialogue, that I won't lie about. The con of the game, for me, was the storyline. But it did not make the gameplay through the story unenjoyable, I just prefered the aspects of farming in the game.

The original Stardrive was a fun little game, and I probably spent over a hundred hours on it. But it had quite a few problems too, so I was a bit skeptical in how the sequel would be.
I was however positively surprised! This game addresses nearly all my issues I had with the first title. The presentation, and game flow feels far better this time around.
It does however still have a few random bugs every now and then, even if none of them game breaking it can be slightly annoying. Besides that, the game itself runs smooth, and the turn changes are near instant. The prequel had a tendency to become near unplayable at higher difficulties due to performance drops, as the enemies would clog the galaxy with endless fleet battles. I think the new instanced battle system is an improvement from the old one in that regard ( no late game lag anymore ).
As for the people complaining about the AI “cheating” in some reviews – I see no proof of this, and I have no trouble personally keeping up with the AI at medium and hard difficulties ( currently halfway into a game on hard as Vulfen, with me owning 1/4th of the galaxy ) . The game however does have bit of a learning curve, and the AI is quite aggressive for some races. Expect to die a few times before you learn the ropes.  ( when to expand, what to research first, figuring out what ship designs to make etc )
I for one like the AI this time around, it feels more clever than before. Although I’d guess a “Beginner” difficulty setting wouldn’t be a bad thing though, to let new players get to learn the game at a slower pace. (I might write a beginner guide sometime )
I don’t really have a lot more to say. The gameplay is fun, the races varied, and the artwork is neat. If you like x4 games, and don’t mind a challenge. This is a solid indie buy and I would recommend it to my friends.

Also, due to the way the characters 'snap' to edges of platforms, this can make things a bit tricky to navigate.
The art in the game part of this is good though, with character models that were much more detailed than I had initially anticipated. The accompanying music is also very nice.
There are hidden collectible documentary videos throughout. These are short pieces that describe the various arctic animals, and history of people who live there. These are interesting enough, my only gripe being that they have to be played in the game. You can't use your own media player to view them.
Basically, this may not be the best platformer around, but the documentary side of it is very good, and you should get it if you're interested in that kind of thing.

As someone who enjoyed playing StarDrive, I'd like to share my experience of playing Stardrive 2. So far (14.6h) I've been playing as Humans (with my own custom civ traits of course - they make a MAJOR difference in your gameplay experience) on Normal difficulty, huge system with 9 other civs, and I'm currently faced with enemies on both my northern and southern space borders. I'm also becoming quite chummy with some samurai space bears.
Now I've seen some complaints about Stardrive 2, and I have to admit my first few hours had a couple of complaints - mainly research and... well, I'll tell you what else when I get to it. Further into the game I found out how they downgraded the spy system, but let's get back to research. I was annoyed at how you could not research all the tech on the same tier, and then I encountered my first race. (I'd like to mention that I don't go exploring the entire galaxy, so I don't encounter multiple races before I'm ready to deal with them. That'd just be STUPID... Hmm was that too rude of me?) When I entered diplomacy with them, I was happily surprised to find out that you could trade the tech they had researched for whatever you feel like giving them. After encountering a few more civs, and by the time I met up with my favorite bear shogunate, I realized that unless you take diplomatic action towards these aliens, they're gonna wonder why they should keep the stupid foriegners around rather than kill and conquer them.
I should probably mention that being able to customize your ships relatively freely is a big plus for me. They made it a touch simpler than the original StarDrive, but while it was disappointing at first - I realized it cut down the time I spent designing my failures and designing new ships to replace the failures (since they sucked in combat) or redesigning my redundant ships (due to new tech). For example, in SD1 you could face all your weapon firing arcs forward. In SD2, the location of your weapon decides where it aims (except cannons/mass drivers - they always aim forward) The way around this though is to select the *arc extend* feature on the turrets you mount so they cover a 180* angle - aka they can fire forward.
I'll be updating this review in a few days once I'm back home and play a bit more, so I'll leave you with this: if you like customization and you find that you can understand a game's mechanics fairly quickly, then you'll enjoy this game.
A very tough puzzle game that feels strangely akin to going about writing mathematical proofs. A clean, stylish aesthetic to boot.

First of all, this is not puzzle game, but low budget first person point&click adventure (a very typical one), with clunky controls. The main problem is that this adventure takes every textbook design aspect, even the bad ones and just applies them with very little thought. By the first 15minutes of the game you will be in your inventory combining stuff with a stuff, running around the house to figure out what to click next, because you just missed something. Point&click adventures without logic behind their actions usually end up as a very frustrating experience and so does this game. I could possibly forgive this problem (because I do like adventures), but as you progress in the game it gets more and more tedious. Inventory gets bigger, more rooms to visit... so many illogical possibilities open up.
The game also wants to be horror experience and so is trying to be like (for example) Amnesia with its "sanity meter", but in the end it forces you to miss a lot of the cool and "scary" stuff around you, because the game is built upon events that will spring around you and so when you stop and look at some of it, you will lose a portion of sanity. Sometime you will even lose sanity seemingly by itself... making you to even more to focus on the running around blind to the scenes around you. Do you hear a scary sound? Quickly
walk away, it might be something cool for a change.
On the other hand, the story seems to be interesting even if the delivery is bit of a mess. Level design is very fine, with bits and pieces done wrong. Music is very good, and as voice acting goes, it will not offend you even though script is totally forgettable.
Simply put, the game is not well designed. It has very pesky and completely unnecessary DRM. Technical aspects of the game have their share of problems (I guess Unity engine implementation done wrong) and to this day my Linux version still does not work properly, for some reason I could only walk around in the garden.

Star Drive 2 takes allot of what made the original star drive fun. Improves on it, then changes the game into more of  a traditional 4X experience, with turn based game play.
The Good:
Ship design - This is very deep with a level of subtlety and customization which no other game seems to have, at least in terms of whats on your ships and how they behave in combat.
Personallity - The races all have distinct ship models and very distinct personallities. There is a bit of cheesy humour in the game and allot of pop culture referencing which is worth a laugh. *spoiler* I got to weld guns to a t-rex's head and then use it to eat people!!!*
AI - After about 8 hours I have come to appreciate the difficulty of the AI, they wait till your fleets are out of position and attack core worlds, will try and undermine you diplomatically and have varied personallities ranging from homicidal to just the nicest little plant people ever. They also seem to adapt to your ship building strategies and it seems very difficult to cheese the AI in this game.
Empire Management - This is HARD and requires allot of thought. Managing some worlds to be food producing worlds and others to be ship producers or science worlds is an interesting balance and sometimes having more population on your homeworld is not the best choice. This means that a variety of adaptive stratagies are required, absed on your surroundings. This adds allot of replayabillity as games can vary wildly.
Fleet Combat - very pretty, plenty of strategy and a bit of point and click. Not one of those games where i want to autoresolve every battle.
The Bad
Ground combat - Can still be fun but is not quite up to the standard or polish that the rest of the game seems to have. There is however a suprising degree of strategy in what looks at first to be a very simple minigame. Especially when you take the variability of some of the races into account. I freaked out when i realized the squid men could squirt ink into peoples eyes......
Some balance on certain weapons - Overall ship modules are well balanced with few weapons ever truly becoming obsolete which is AWESOME. However there are some modules (Im looking at you plasma cannons) which could really use a buff.
The Ugly:
Haters - There are ALLOT of haters after some of the issues with SD1. Personally I can see where they are coming from but i easily got my 30 bucks worth outa the game. BUT i swear i am sick to death of the illiterate streams of untruthfull vitriol that get posted about this series. This is the onlly reason i wrote this review. I am a busy person, but i got so sick of all the polarized BS i felt i had to write something.
To Sum-up: Stardrive 2 is a difficult game with a steep learining curve that has deep and rewarding systems. Its not for the feebleminded. Some of the production values in certain areas of the game are a little low but otherwise it feels like a AAA game. I would heartily reccomend this game to any lover of 4x or grand strategy games and to anyone as obsessive as i am about building the deadliest ship ever.

Anyone who's ever played a worms game would know the basic concept. You play as a worm, your job? To kill the opposing worms. Obviously, the main  components in this game is multiplayer, but there's a few other modes for people who can't use multiplayer.... for particular reasons.
Let's get right into the multiplayer! The multiplayer works just like every other worms game in the series, turn based. One player goes first, attacks... or not, depends, and then after they have either attacked or ran out of time, the next player goes. Before you start a match though, there's a slot machine, that can be used to randomly select 3 twists to add to your game, your you can choose them yourself! These twists are really interesting, and make every game different from the last. Some of them are; not being able to use anything but ranged weapons, you can only move using the grappling hook,or only being able to use weapons from crates! The online mode is basically the same thing, but no slot machine, and so is single player battles, except you play against a computer.
The campaign is by far my favourite part of the game. At the start of each level, you are given an objective, e.g. destroy the building, kill the enemies, climb the tower, all that kind of stuff you would expect. The variety of different levels really keep things fresh, from a dinosaur attack, to the old western, nothing ever seems dull. At the end of each level though, you get coins, which can be used to buy things for your worms in the shop.
The shop is where you can buy more things to customize your worms. You see, before you start the actual game, you should make yourself a team. You can name your team members, dress them up, and even choose a speech bank to make them sound like English Bobby,  or even a robot! Not only can you buy things to customize your worm with in the store, but you can also buy new premade levels based on the single player missions to use in multiplayer, or even new game modes! There is also a whole load of items you can only unlock if you own other games on your steam account though.
In the end, worms ultimate mayhem is tons of fun with friends, also a whole load of fun in single player,  and with the immense variety of levels and customization options, you will not get bored soon.
My final rating is... 8.5/10

Basically you have this adventure game with a pretty intriguing story and a very cool atmosphere.  Sounds like it has a lot of potential right?
But let's talk about the controls.  There's idiotic things like not letting you escape out of your inventory by hitting ESC.  You have to hit "I" again.  And then there's the inventory itself.  It's very awkward where you have to scroll through a bunch of stuff you have.  The interface could use a lot of work.
And now let's talk about "pixel hunting".   You know what's frustrating?  Going into a dark room with a bunch of items scattered about the room.  The thing you want isn't an more noticeable and hidden a certain area and it looks just like all the other stuff you can't click on.  So the only way to find it is to move your mouse over every possible item on the screen.  Ugh.  I combed rooms and missed things before and I had to use a walk through a few times to find things.
And now let's talk about the worst part of the game.  The puzzles.  Some make sense, many do not.   There's a very thin section of wall you need to break through.  Maybe use a stone or something?  Nope.  You have this metal gear piece.  Maybe you can use that to break through?  It's metal and looks fairly heavy, should bust through.  Nope.  I have a full canteen, that should be kinda heavy...  Nope.   Solution?  You gotta use a tree branch to break through.  A tree branch!  To break through a wall.
Yes, that makes sense, right?  The whole game is full of puzzles that barely make sense.   The other use for a tree branch?  There's a knife lodged in a wooden table.  You want that knife.  Your possible tools to get this knife blade out?  Your hands.  Nope, you''ll cut yourself, that makes sense.  An axe!  Let's just chop it out.  Nope.  A shovel?  Maybe you can whack it out or pry it?  Nope.  Ah ha!  I found a woodworking tool!  That's gotta be it.  I mean how else do you get a knife out of a WOODEN table!  HAHA YEAH RIGHT.  Obviously you would use a tree branch to get a knife out of a wooden table.
Good puzzle games, when you figure them out, you go "AHHHHH!  That makes sense!  Why didn't I think of that?"  Anna, you can actually play with a walk through and be like "uhhhh, ok, I don't get it but sure whatever.  I guess it might make sense maybe?"  That's what made the Lucas Arts games so much fun.  You might have NO idea how to pass a certain part of the game but if someone tells you the answer or you brute force the answer you think "Oh my god, that makes sense!" I loved this program when it was web-based and free. It was easy to use and I could gen up a map for Roll20 in a jiffy (once I got used to the mechanics). I love DPS and everything that Pyromancer has added and very excited that I can look forward to many updates in the future. I still have a lot to learn, but here are my additional thoughts after 12 hours and five detailed maps.
Some of my favorite features:
- The creator is very responsive to inquiries
- The export options which include  a Roll20 image export
- The art is varied and high quality, plus interchangable
- Easy to use, change and edit.
- I haven't used it yet, but like the idea of Workshop content.
Some areas for improvement:
- The options for Objects is great, but still a bit limited. For example, there are no images of a statue, secret door, pits, etc. I get around this  by using the old school D&D symbols, which are included.
- I can't figure out how to change the scale of the art tiles. You can easily change the scale of objects, which is awesome, but sometimes the terrain looks out of scale when making large maps.
- Sometimes it is hard to find layers. It would be nice if I could doubleclick on a layer and it would snap right to it in the layer list.
Anyway, love this product and can't wait to see what else Pyromancer has in store for us!

Soma was a roller coaster of a game for me.
I was not sure if i would recommend it or not, but i decided its flaws arent big enough to dissuade me from recommending it.
First off, its a type of game i seldomly enjoy and often stop quickly, at the first obstacle, puzzle or out of boredom.
Soma does one thing really well..well a few things, to me those were the characters, the story, the setting. As you start to unveil the world by progressing, you are treated to a mystery and a story worth the steps you took to get there.
I will say a few things, but ill keep it short, most of what i could say good about the game is spoiler territory, and the game is much better without them.
The game atmosphere, sense of loss, dicovery, curiosity, is well tied in by the characters and the graphics. Nothing feels out of character, something that is normal for someone, and is not for someone else, is carried out properly. The game offer a lot of small details and choices that feel meaningful, if only for your own roleplay. You will feel sad, scared, you will also get rushes of adrenaline and sense of wonder/amazement. The game will not take you in every directions you expect, but you will enjoy the journey there.
The game feels genuine, until the very end, and thats rare these days.
I cannot really say anything more about it, its worth seeing yourself.
Now for what it does that annoyed me... its how things are all tied together.
I am not a fan of stealth segments that are all about .. wait a while for monster to pass... do something.. wait again.. do something else or leave.
I am not a fan of 'i need x items segments' especially when you dont have any clues how to get to them or where they are, so you end up exploring every nook and cranny, then eventually figure out you did not mouse over a smecific small thing.
I am not a fan of games creating a world and then adding obstacles that make no sense for the world. If i was playign a game that happen in our world in 2017, seeing teleporting people or flying humans would be weird?.. for instance you'd question why youre fighting microwave men in our world in 2017.
And.. i am not a fan of one last thing in soma.. everything that is not in a 'you need to go there place' is.. pointless. there is nothing much to see, no collectible, etc. After a few games have spoiled me for exploring (witcher 3 for instance), i find it hard to accept 'walking simulator' games that offer nothing much for exploring beyond the main path. Dont get me wrong, its not barren, some sections reward exploration with extra story elements, but this usually happen during times where you need to explore for items/objectives.
All in all, im glad i finished it! and it took a fair bit longer than i expect for a game like this.

Oniken is a solid throwback to NES games.  It's simple to play but provides a challenge without being artificially difficult.
Gameplay is pretty basic.  Move, jump, swing your sword, and throw grenades, that's it.  There are crates scattered throughout levels which randomly provide grenades, health, or a sword power up that extends the range of your sword attack but goes away after you get hit several times.  You have plenty of life, often enough to take at least 10 hits before you die.  There are 6 levels in the game plus a bonus level.  Each level has three stages.  You are given 3 lives to complete each level, plus each level has a hidden extra life in it which are usually very easy to find, so really 4 lives per level.  If you die during a level, you'll start back at the beginning of whichever stage you're on.  If you run out of lives and have to continue, you will restart the level.  This isn't that big of a deal.  Stages can often be completed in under 3 minutes and every level can be completed in 5-10 minutes, so at worst, you lose a couple minutes of progress, and should get further with each attempt.  Once you complete a level, you never have to go back to it again.
Most of the negative complaints seem to be about the how difficult and unfair this game is.  On my only playthrough, I beat the entire first level without dying and didn't need to use a continue until the fourth level.  I beat the game plus the bonus level in 2 to 2 ½ hours, I would hardly call that overly difficult or unfair.  I'd imagine most of these complaints are from gamers who haven't played a game that challenges them.  The game is challenging and you will have to get better to progress, but it is nowhere as hard as some old school NES games, and I rarely felt as though I died due to something cheap or artificially difficult.  The only thing I felt was slightly unfair was the final boss at the end of level 6, but once I figured out a good strategy, I was able to take him down.  Enemies, traps, and bosses are fair and attack in noticeable patterns that you can learn and exploit.  You have plenty of life so messing up and getting hit often isn't a big issue.  The game restores your health at the beginning of each stage during a level plus you'll likely find a health kit at some point in a stage.
My only real complaints are that sometimes the game wouldn't recognize when I was trying to throw a grenade, but that was probably more of an issue of me using the control stick instead of the pad.  I would've also liked the game to be longer, but still enjoyed what I got.
Not much else to say.  Story is there to give you an excuse to play levels, characters don't have much depth, music is ok.  The game is all about challenging fun gameplay and it delivers.  Do you have what it takes to become the true Oniken?

I didn't have much patience for this game the first time I played it.
Like many others I treated it as some crappy $1 indie game with pixel graphics that I bought on sale.
Coming back to it though, I can see why others liked it and am actually starting to enjoy It myself.
I didn't play the types of NES and SNES games that this game tries to emulate as I was far too young and only enjoyed first party nintendo games.
I have been playing a lot of NES/SNES inspired games on steam in my adult years though and I can definitely see the influence in the game from games like strider and anime such as fist of the north star and possibly berserk.
It is clear to me from seeing this game and their other game which is a faithful homage to castlevania that these people thoroughly revere and love the classic nintendo games.
Others may complain of unfair difficulty and cheap hits (staples of early arcade and console games) and I'll admit those annoyed me at first too.
And then I came back and finally started beating levels and It occurred to me what type of game I was playing.  The levels are short, and you have checkpoints and extra lives at your disposal.
The game expects that you will die and next time through remember enemy placements and effective attack patterns.  You were never meant to breeze through this game in one try.
Controls are simple, enemy attacks can be dodged if you learn placements and timing and you're given a fairly large health pool and plentiful resource drops (considering what type of game this is).
Much as I hate that everything gets compared to dark souls, It's the same concept here: be patient, look out for patterns, expect to die a few times until you learn and git gud.

I pick this up after I read an article that placed it in the best 50 FPS ever made. And DAMN if they weren't right.
The first thing I noticed upon starting the game is that I was missing a LOT of backstory. I managed to piece most of it together before the end, but I'm still not clear on some things. So, you're Jackie Estacado, some sort of Mafia Don. You're well-loved by the people in your organization, even they're very much aware that you've made some sort of deal with a demonic entity that causes you to sprout eel-like growths from your back that you can cut people in half with (Which I find weird, considering that most popular media portrays most of the Italian mob as at least moderately Catholic, but whatever).
The game is starting to show it's age, but when it came out, it would have been looking pretty good. It's still an attractive game, and the various little visual effects are pretty sweet for when it came out. The art style is very dark, which fits the story to a "T." The various NPCs you interact with are all interesting, if 2-dimensional. Maybe if I'd played the first one, I'd be more invested in them.
The learning curve is pretty much ideal. The tutorial is a mite frustrating, considering that you don't have any agency over what you can do when, but that's just me. Otherwise, the skills take long enough to grab that you become practiced at using each of them before you grab a new one.
The enemy's AI is pretty damn solid, I gotta say. Good use of cover, suppressing fire, and even flanking actions. It surprised me quite a few times.
The gameplay is where this game REALLY shines. Right in the first 10 minutes of the game, you're using your two tentacle beasts to wreak havoc and MAN it's fun. The right tentacle beast looks like it's kinda more fragile, and has massive friggin' fangs. Accordingly, this is the one you use to slash people up and whip 'em to death. This simple tentacle whip remains a valid strategy right up until the very last fight. The left tentacle is more muscle-y, and is definitely my favorite of the two. With it, you can grab various bits of scenery and chuck 'em around at high speed, with a generous auto-target. And not just blunt trauma. You can cut blokes in half with car doors and fans, impale them with bits of pipe, or even bludgeon them with bits and pieces of their dead buddies. Loads of fun. The game affords you a generous armament, but you really don't want to use them for kills, as a bullet kill nets you a lousy 10 essence.
I haven't even gotten to the skill tree yet! Each kill you get and action you take gives you "essence" which basically functions as xp. 20 essence for impaling a guy, 30 for ripping him in half lengthwise, 30 for ripping out his intestines through his♥♥♥♥♥♥ etc. The fights are frantic enough, and your body count high enough, that you can amass massive amounts of essence relatively quickly.  The skills themselves are high in cost, especially the top-tier ones, but some of them are absolutely absurd. I picked up one near the end that let me harvest miniature black holes from dead bodies and throw them. How awesome is that?
The music was good. No complaints there. There were some bits in cutscenes that gave me the friggin' heebie-jeebies, all because of the music.
So, all told, I'd definitely recommend this. Even if you're not super invested in the plot, it's fun as hell.

I've see Mayan Death Robots on several events and it was always a crowd pleaser. It does several cool things to shake up the artillery game formula (ie.Worms) quite a bit!
For one, the pace is way faster than Worms', with all players playing at the same time so if both players know the game, matches move on forward very pleasantly.
Adding characters with specific skills does a lot to increase variety and the boss fights help in changing the pace quite dramatically (ad they're very well put together).
The character skills have a lot of variety and there are some nice touches like the Tetris-inspired wall-building and the "skill-roulette" that manage to shake things up a bit by granting a random super skill to players.
Of course everything is not perfect and the game can feel a bit overwhelming at first due to the quick pace and busy screen. The campaign does a good job of teaching you the basics though so I recommend starting from there to explore the main features one by one.
It's also cool that you can tackle the campaign alone or with people, which is a great way to learn the specifics of the game together (that's how we played it with a friend).
Highly recommended if you're looking for an intense couch multiplayer game!

Being a fan of the Worms franchise I was excited to try out Mayan Death Robots and I have to say that I wasn't disappointed.
The game plays a lot like Worms with the two main differences being that you are trying to kill the other player's power core instead of their robot and Mayan Death Robots is more streamlined than Worms.
For the most part I liked the streamlining done in Mayan Death Robots. The game moves really quickly. Since both players move at the same time there is no need to sit around waiting for the other player to make their move. Turns move so quickly that you will always be thinking about what you are going to do next and lining up your next shot. The only problem with the streamlining process is that each robot doesn't have as many weapon choices as you had in Worms.
Each robot only has two different weapons with the occasional chance to use a third weapon. The only significant complaint I have with the game is that I wish each robot had a few more attacks which would have given you some more variety in how you could attack your opponent. The good news is that the robots do play differently as each robot's attacks are different enough to give each robot different strategies.
While the game is probably going to be more fun against another player I have to give the game a lot of credit for creating a very capable AI computer to play against. At times it is a little too easy and sometimes a little too hard but the AI does a great job adjusting to your skill level in order to give you a challenge without feeling frustrating.
If you like games like Worms I think you will really enjoy Mayan Death Robots.
Note: I received a review copy from the developer.
