As a recently-retired VC player of 18 months, I figured I’d weigh in and give an honest review, using some of the app notes as a guide. Pour yourself a cup of space tea, because this is going to be lengthy.
“Stake your claim, command your fleets, and wage epic war in space. Band together with other players in a bloody rebellion to take back the galaxy from the evil VEGA Federation.”
This much at least is true: VEGA Conflict is a cross-platform MMORTS published by Kixeye. You build up a space base, construct fleets of ships from 5 different factions over weeks and months, and fight against either one of the VEGA Federation’s many branches and groups in PvE or against other players in PvP.
Here’s the first major sticking point though: for all its marketing as a PvP-based game, the game mechanics themselves provide no incentive or benefit to attacking other player fleets. Sure, you can go and smash up your neighbour’s fleets and feel good about yourself… but why should you bother? A player doesn’t get any reward or in-game progress by doing this, only a large repair bill, which we’ll discuss later.
Players can also attack each other’s in-game bases to win resources and Medals, which act as the game’s only ranking system to measure players against each other. And as any player worth their Bomber Squadrons will tell you, these medals are completely worthless, also providing no tangible in-game buffs or benefits, partly because such a system would immediately be exploited by players with multiple accounts. (We’ll also discuss this later.)
“REAL-TIME PvP: Real war doesn’t wait its turn - attack enemies at will in real-time.”
Sticking point #2: Real war doesn’t wait its turn… but you have to. As alluded to previously, if your ships/base are damaged or destroyed in combat, they must be fixed in real-time before you can use them again. This might only be a few minutes for new players, but an end-gamer at war can easily rack up a week’s worth of repair in 30 minutes play. And when one considers the rock-paper-scissors mechanic employed by the different ship classes, as well as the sheer firepower they can dish out, you might not even need 30 minutes!
Of course, one could spend $30 USD in Coins (the game’s premium currency) to fix the damage instantly and get back out there, but if not… better sit back and get fixing. Good luck, Rebels!
“GAME EVENTS: Battle in weekly events for top prizes.”
This is a big one, so bear with me. Progression in VEGA revolves around the player acquiring Blueprints, for bigger ships, shootier guns and other bits of space kit, in order to move up the proverbial ladder. These events take several forms:
1)	Riots – these are intended for low-level players to catch up and gain existing items to help them progress. But if you want these items as a newbie, you’d better be prepared to sit and grind out Loot points for the 4 days the event runs for. And this mechanic is considered to be reasonably good…
2)	Feature Events – these are the big ones. Running once a month, each one has a suitably impressive name, and contains a new hull and a slew of new shiny technologies, which you can win… provided you can beat the special AI targets. As Kixeye’s business wisdom apparently does not extend to play-testing their events in advance, these targets can be anywhere on the spectrum of laughably easy (the first two hours of Scorched Earth) to monstrously powerful (Warfront) or simply mind-numbingly dull (Zero Hour). If you can’t beat them? Git gud, scrublord.
But let’s say you power through and win the shiny new things. Alright! What happens now? Well first off, there’s no guarantee your shiny new toys are actually any good, or that they won’t either be buffed into the stratosphere or nerfed into oblivion somewhere down the line. If you don’t believe me on this point, go onto the Kixeye forum and ask someone about the Brimstone Torpedo. Or the Rapture Cruiser. Or the Skirmish Armour. Or the Unstable Reactor. I could go on.
In the meantime, you’ll have to allocate Ship Factory time to actually build the shiny new things, or refit them to your existing ships. And with build times being the way there are currently, it could be a while before this happens. I have event prizes I won last year which I’ve never had the chance to build, and now never will. So long, Vigilante Battleship, I hardly knew ye.
3)	Civil War – this is supposed to be a flagship PvP event, where one can earn points by fighting other players. In reality, these are only won by those with the biggest wallets, or those with the best auto-scripts and most alternate accounts to kill the same fleets over and over again. (Here’s looking at you, [ELU]!) Kixeye have attempted to rectify this by changing the point curve, but all this has accomplished is the punishment of skilful piloting and the encouragement of suicide tactics. The fact that this is beneficial for their bottom line is surely a coincidence.
4)	Alien Mobilization – space bugs are attacking! This event really is only for the chosen few, but those who can defeat the menace can win exclusive tech, which is either mostly useless or game-breakingly strong (at the time of writing). You want to believe things will get better? Sorry Mulder, you’re wasting your time.
“ALLIANCES: Create or join an alliance and crush your enemies.”
While you can join your alliances and fly with your buddies, this too remains an incomplete feature; coalitions and alliance wars have yet to be formalised, while the prospect of alliance flagships seems largely forgotten.
“CRAFTING: Craft powerful ship upgrades to help you defeat the VEGA Federation.”
A lot of players cite the introduction of the crafting system in Oct/Nov 2015 as the point where VEGA Conflict started to fall apart. On paper, it sounds like a good idea; upgrade your ships to get an edge over your enemies/a killer paint job, and the devs get to boost the longevity of their existing content. Everybody wins!
Well… not so much. For a start, this system makes late-game hulls very powerful, leaving older tech obsolete, and disproportionately favours certain hull types such as cutters. The crafting materials themselves take a long time to acquire, turning the PvP dream into a PvE black pit. But you need all those bits, because if you don’t get them, you’ll be left behind and at the mercy of the big spenders, who can simply cough up £200 a month and get all the latest gubbinz without lifting a finger. That’s the price you pay to stay competitive.
But do you know what the worst bit is? The company knows about all these problems, and simply doesn’t care. People have requested, pleaded and raged about many aspects and features for as long as I can remember; long repair times, a coin confirmation button (the last guy to try and make this happen got fired for his trouble), a refit bay to let players actually test and use their new tech, rampant Civil War scripting, server instability (particularly in crowded sectors), speed normalisation in the Great Grand Rebalance, buffs and nerfs to people’s favourite tech seemingly without rhyme or reason, the time sink of marking up fleets, seemingly unstoppable power creep and the simple fact that this is a very, very expensive game to play. And none of it looks likely to get any better any time soon.
So, have I gotten enjoyment out of VEGA over 18 months? Yes. Would I recommend it to you? Not in a million years.
Love from [KOS],

This is an amazingly fun game. The graphics are beautiful for its time and it reminds one of Fable when playing. (Though I'm not 100% sure, I believe some of the same voice actors are present in this game)
Basically, you are awakened as the new Overlord and your first priority is to retrieve the 3 lost Minion clans which each have special powers of their own. Browns (Your starters) have all the power. Greens (Your assassins) are a lethal group, though they can't take the hits as much as the browns. Reds ( Can dish out the long distant damage and are great for area advantages such as ledges and whatnot) One hit and they are goners. Lastly, the Blues (Revivers) that's pretty much all they can, oh and they're the only ones who can defeat magical creatures.
6 hours in and there is already a mass amount of content. For starters, you can customize your very own tower. Everything from banner colors to so much more. Then there is the arena, in which you and your minion horde takes on foes in which you've already defeated. There is the smelter, in which you make new armour/weapons and upgrade your current armour/weapons as well as your minions attack and defense as well. And also..well so far..that's I'll I've gotten.
It's exciting viewing the beautiful scenery as well as the hearing the crude humor which this game offers. It's a great laugh. Though there doesn't seem to be a whole lot of story present, that's not a problem. You are mostly doing random quests and deciding whether or not to grow your corruption level. Killing equals more corruption. Not killing..is pretty much being good.
There is quite a bit of strategy involved which is nice. Example, certain trolls will wave their arms before hurdling themselves in the air and doing body slams. Your job is to notice this signal, call your minions back (sparing them such a horrible fate) an finally throwing them back in their after it's landed. Figuring these things out is exciting on it's own.
Overall, the Fable nostalgic feel I get from the graphics and certain characters in this game make it a pretty great game, for me at least. Also, the gameplay as well. I start feeling connected to my little guys and though it's not necessary, I always tend to see myself in the mix of battle. The content which you get for the price in fantastic, but if you want more, it's worth the cash to get Raising Hell instead, simply because it's an expansion to this game.
The only cons for this game involve the random minion glitches. Occasionally, the minions will be carrying items and simply stop. Even if nothing is blocking their paths. Also, minions themselves tend to get stuck in or under objects as well, but not too often. This usually occurs when some of your other minions are carrying items and they just happen to get in the way. Overall, They do a phenomenal job following your orders, only 1 time have I had a minion lost and I've had to backtrack it.

Do not underestimate this software: For its price, you can do most of the stuff of other (in my opinion) overpriced mapping software. What makes this software unique in my opinion is the Steam Workshop: You can import (and export) a multitude of libraries, each containing a lot of essential stuff for mapping, thanks to the effort of dedicated users. This is kind of the weakness of the software, too; at its "vanilla" state, it does not offer much. Even so, it has very useful tools to create maps, giving a sort of Photoshop vibe to all of it (layers and effects). So far, this has been the most easy-to-use and efficient mapping tool I have encountered, not to mention the most inexpensive one. Still, there are some things missing that I REALLY would love to be added (see below).
Let's make a quick summary:
PROS:
-Very unexpensive, compared to other mapping tools
-Open to modding (additional content, Steam Workshop)
-Easy to use
-Easy import and export of maps (to PDF, PNG extensions, the import accepts a lot of formats)
CONS:
-The unmodded program lacks content
-Could use some more sofisticated effects
-It lacks some tools (undo button, tint bucket to fill an an area)
-Could use better features to make large area maps, such as atlases (current tools are very supperficial)
FINAL VERDICT:
Dungeon Painter Studio is the choice to go if you are looking for an easy to use and cheap software to make dungeon maps (it is also good to make overland maps, but not ideal). If you want to do more sofisticated and detalied stuff, envolving pretty effects, I recommend you try another software.
TO THE DEV:
Dev, I'd love to have a way of apllying a brightness effect to my floors, it's a pain in the *** to do that manually (by creating multiple layers with different colors varying in brightness). I miss a way of apllying lighntning effects to my floors and making more beautiful scenarios :(
All in all, keep up the good work and thank you for this amazing software!

The Ubisoft guys did a nice job on this version.  I previously had the Xbox version, and I hated playing on my console through a TV.  The HDMI lag was not great.  With Rocksmith 2014, I bought the Steam version, installed in on the Mac i use for music work, and have it running through my studio setup.  Makes all the difference in the world.  Zero lag, great sound.
Improvements this version include a session mode, where you pick a key and some band members, and they just sort of follow along with you.  While they arent the best backing band, it does give you an opportunity to practice scales and riffs with a rythm section behind you.  Another improvement is that it seems to more accurately catch what you are playing, shift difficulty at more appropriate times and the riff repeater is superb for really learning a part.  You get a ton of control over when it ups the difficulty (or whether it does) and speed.
I've been playing guitar, rythm, lead and bass, for over 30 years now, and I can honestly say that while I thought this was going to be a toy, ala rockband, I have definitely increased my skill by playing it.  At first I dismissed the guitarcade as a gimmick, but it definitely has made my scales faster, and my accuracy and fretboard position awareness significantly better.
The only complaints I have are:
1. I wish riff repeater was slightly more controllable as to when it starts and stop instead of being such large sections.  There have been a couple times where I was trying to learn a tough little flourish that occurs at the end of an easy section, and had to play the easy section over and over to get to the short riff because i couldnt shorten the RR selection enough.  That said, I got really good at it :)
2. The instructions for getting the Rocksmith 1 content should have been clearer.  I did finally get it to work, but I shouldn't have had to go to the forums for answers, that should have been a simple step by step process with rock solid documentation.
Overall I give it a 9/10.  Great tool for learning, and even for those of us with lots of experience there is a lot of learning to do.  It still amazes me when you spend 10 minutes on it, and suddenly pick up a tricky section as they throw it at you seemingly out of the blue at times.

Soma was a roller coaster of a game for me.
I was not sure if i would recommend it or not, but i decided its flaws arent big enough to dissuade me from recommending it.
First off, its a type of game i seldomly enjoy and often stop quickly, at the first obstacle, puzzle or out of boredom.
Soma does one thing really well..well a few things, to me those were the characters, the story, the setting. As you start to unveil the world by progressing, you are treated to a mystery and a story worth the steps you took to get there.
I will say a few things, but ill keep it short, most of what i could say good about the game is spoiler territory, and the game is much better without them.
The game atmosphere, sense of loss, dicovery, curiosity, is well tied in by the characters and the graphics. Nothing feels out of character, something that is normal for someone, and is not for someone else, is carried out properly. The game offer a lot of small details and choices that feel meaningful, if only for your own roleplay. You will feel sad, scared, you will also get rushes of adrenaline and sense of wonder/amazement. The game will not take you in every directions you expect, but you will enjoy the journey there.
The game feels genuine, until the very end, and thats rare these days.
I cannot really say anything more about it, its worth seeing yourself.
Now for what it does that annoyed me... its how things are all tied together.
I am not a fan of stealth segments that are all about .. wait a while for monster to pass... do something.. wait again.. do something else or leave.
I am not a fan of 'i need x items segments' especially when you dont have any clues how to get to them or where they are, so you end up exploring every nook and cranny, then eventually figure out you did not mouse over a smecific small thing.
I am not a fan of games creating a world and then adding obstacles that make no sense for the world. If i was playign a game that happen in our world in 2017, seeing teleporting people or flying humans would be weird?.. for instance you'd question why youre fighting microwave men in our world in 2017.
And.. i am not a fan of one last thing in soma.. everything that is not in a 'you need to go there place' is.. pointless. there is nothing much to see, no collectible, etc. After a few games have spoiled me for exploring (witcher 3 for instance), i find it hard to accept 'walking simulator' games that offer nothing much for exploring beyond the main path. Dont get me wrong, its not barren, some sections reward exploration with extra story elements, but this usually happen during times where you need to explore for items/objectives.
All in all, im glad i finished it! and it took a fair bit longer than i expect for a game like this.

This is the Steam debut of the
Dungeon Painter, a popular introductory mapping tool for use in fantasy tabletop gaming.  Dungeon Painter breathes new life into a stale genre still dominated by decades-old software such as AutoREALM and Dundjinni.   It focuses on small-scale maps as opposed to the world-scale maps generated by Inkarnate or Campaign Cartographer.
Dungeon Painter is accessible to new mappers, allowing them to quickly develop relatively polished maps without much time in the tool.   It has an array of common textures and objects that can be added to provide detail.  Once satisfied, the map maker can quickly export to a variety of sizes, either with or without grid.  The desktop version adds a number of presets suitable for Roll20 or Fantasy Grounds.
Downsides include a relatively rough interface, particularly for power users.  Functions such as "Undo" simply don't exist.  What is termed "layering" is actually just object ordering rather than the layering of Photoshop or GIMP.   Inexplicably, files saved by the
Dungeon Painter are not compatible with Dungeon Painter Studio.  A conversion tool for users of the site switching to DPS would be useful.
Overall, Dungeon Painter Studio is still able to quickly generate usable maps in spite of its downsides.

Stories Untold was recommended to me by a fellow lover of Indie 'experiential' games.   It didn't take me long to play through it. maybe 4h or 5h, including going back to get some extra achievements I'd missed... All in all, I'd say it was excellently executed!
So, the game plays like a four-part miniseries.  Each 'episode' starts with a wonderfully professional intro, and is self-contained, although the later episodes do refer back in certain ways. The episodes feel like a 1970s / 1980s B-rated horror series that you'd find on a lesser-watched channel at 1am on a thursday night...
Each of the episodes involves interacting with a screen, to solve problems, perform actions and so on.  It has a similar feel in some ways to "Please don't touch" or "Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes"...  A series of buttons, knobs, wires and so forth that you have to manipulate in a certain order...    However, unlike those two other games, this one has some fascinating effects and a bizarre storyline which comes together at the end.
I don't want to talk about the specific contents of each episode, because each one is wonderful, and a brilliant surprise each time.  They're all subtly different but like "KTaNE", the things you have to do build up as the game plays, so you start off typing on a computer, and the last episode has a mix of FPS, some typing and some button-pressing.
The voice overs, sounds, and visuals are all superb!  The atmosphere projected in the first few episodes had my heart racing.   The third and fourth episodes are just wonderful, with brilliant production values.  Switching between gzmeplay modes is really well done, and the FPS sections are wonderfully balanced against the point-and-click sections.
The game holds together briliantly, and really works for an alternative 'experience' game.      It does require you to use your brain, and there are one or two bits where you have to really puzzle out what you have to do next.  Unfortuntely there are a few little niggles whereby you need to figure out how the game works, before you can figure out what you have to do... And it's easy to miss a small button, or a blurry object, or not know you have to type a certain thing at a certain time.    By and large, though, it's relatively straightforward.
A brilliant game, I really enjoyed every minute of it.  Well worth the money.

TL:DR The game is great if you want something with depth of learning and great PVP battles, but be aware of the servers.
For all the faults that this game has, outside of chivalry in its prime you will never have a better real time medieval combat experience in a video game.
The three factions all have enjoyable classes for your individual playstyle, however you will definitely learn to hate certain people for playing certain playstyles if you have a slow enough computer like mine. The story for this game at best falls completely flat on it's face in terms of reasoning for the factions fighting, however to contrast that, the fights on realistic are hard and gripping as you get a true rush of joy when you finally beat those final bosses and throw your controller accross the room in euphoria.
If you buy this game you are buying it to play the multiplayer though, and for all the complaints about p2p honestly i bought this game to 1v1 my friends on, so for me this game has rarely shown me it's ugly side (which i can assure you when you are reconnecting mid swing is a pain in your behind). The combat is fluid and works off or reactionary or proactive play based on how you enjoy playing, although you are rewarded more for baiting mistakes out from your opponent  which can honestly lower the enjoyment of out playing them in a flurry of differently timed attacks mixed with feints and guard breaks.
In summary for all the hate this game gets for the lack of developer communication and terrible p2p servers, I believe if you can enter the game with a couple mates just to play between yourselves or on your own just to tackle the story on realistic, it is worth your time and satisfaction.

This is an excellent puzzle game.  It's very challenging at times but it's also very well paced.  In the 17 worlds (with plenty of levels in each) a new mechanic is introduced, or a few of the older ones are combined so it's tough to get tired of the same old puzzles, because there's always something new to try.  The soft, colorful visuals and the ambient music make it pretty relaxing too, if you just want to fiddle around a bit.
I've honestly never fallen in love with a game quite so quickly, especially having never heard anything about it before it was gifted to me one year.  As a player, you're afforded so many opportunities for those wonderful "aha!" moments.  So many chances to think hard inside (and outside) the game and its logic to figure out the best way to use the varied mechanics in solving puzzles in occasionally surprising ways.  The level of ingenuity and creativity offered here instantly skyrocketed this unknown, oddly titled gem, to my number one favorite game of all time.

Well I've had a blast playing oniken, awesome game. Not only feels like a retro old school platformer, but plays like an old game. Even with those small things that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥us off back on the NES times: throwback when hit, specially near cliffs, back to beginning of the level after losing all lives, instant death things on the environment, cheap bosses and such.
But after all those frustrating features, the game have much better controls than the old games. It's very fluid and precise. I played with a X One controller and the character 'weight' seemed very nice. The key to beat this game is to have patience and learn every single step you'll need to take, the accurate precision of the control is more than necessary to master the levels. When you do, it's so rewarding. Its just like in the past, when you beat a tough level and feel like mastering the game indeed.
The graphics and sounds are not memorable comparing to other indie retro games around. They're nice though. Oniken for me seems like one of that obscure little gems that almost no one knew and few talked about, until a friend got it and all kids on the neighbourhood went to that friend's house to see the game.
Overall I'd recommend this one to big retro platformer fans, who likes difficult games and could spend 1 hour trying to beat one single level. If you don't like those kind of games and are willing to play more casual or not so difficult games, you probably be frustrated with oniken. You probably should look for similar titles like Shovel Knight and such.
But I'd kindly insist that casual players should take a look at it and have a little extra patience to play Oniken. It'll totally worth it.

Mayan Death Robots is a worms-esque game where each character has unique abilities
The main objective is to destroy your opponent's core. You can completely destroy the level and are forced to overcome obstacles on your way while simultaneously protecting your core in some way.
Each round has a short timer in which both players select their moves at the same time. When the timer runs out your action is carried out. All Death Robots can rebuild the terrain by placing Tetris-shaped blocks to either barricade their core off or create a platform. All the Robots can also use a jump action and fly across the map.
Where the characters differ is their weaponry. Some weapons will stick to a surface and climb around, others will drill through, while others can release cluster grenades from the air. The aiming system takes gravity into account, which is why I compared the game to Worms' similar artillery type of aiming (as well as the destructible terrain).
As you progress through levels randomizers are added to keep the game interesting. You are given random weapons, or sometimes little Mayan people attempt to defend your core and attack your opponent if they stand next to your followers. You even get a few bonuses like larger explosion radius if you destroy more things in the environment.
However, the best event of all has to be the gigantic bosses that appear in levels occasionally. Halfway through your battle, the boss will wreak havoc and level the entire stage. You and your opponent have to work together to kill the boss, since your cores are teleported out of the battlefield. After the boss is killed, the cores are brought back and you get to fight in a basically brand new level.
The art style and character designs are really cool-looking in my opinion.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun. The objective-based combat makes the game exciting, and the randomizers like Mayan followers keep the levels from getting stale. (And oh man, the bosses are just so badass)

The Ubisoft guys did a nice job on this version.  I previously had the Xbox version, and I hated playing on my console through a TV.  The HDMI lag was not great.  With Rocksmith 2014, I bought the Steam version, installed in on the Mac i use for music work, and have it running through my studio setup.  Makes all the difference in the world.  Zero lag, great sound.
Improvements this version include a session mode, where you pick a key and some band members, and they just sort of follow along with you.  While they arent the best backing band, it does give you an opportunity to practice scales and riffs with a rythm section behind you.  Another improvement is that it seems to more accurately catch what you are playing, shift difficulty at more appropriate times and the riff repeater is superb for really learning a part.  You get a ton of control over when it ups the difficulty (or whether it does) and speed.
I've been playing guitar, rythm, lead and bass, for over 30 years now, and I can honestly say that while I thought this was going to be a toy, ala rockband, I have definitely increased my skill by playing it.  At first I dismissed the guitarcade as a gimmick, but it definitely has made my scales faster, and my accuracy and fretboard position awareness significantly better.
The only complaints I have are:
1. I wish riff repeater was slightly more controllable as to when it starts and stop instead of being such large sections.  There have been a couple times where I was trying to learn a tough little flourish that occurs at the end of an easy section, and had to play the easy section over and over to get to the short riff because i couldnt shorten the RR selection enough.  That said, I got really good at it :)
2. The instructions for getting the Rocksmith 1 content should have been clearer.  I did finally get it to work, but I shouldn't have had to go to the forums for answers, that should have been a simple step by step process with rock solid documentation.
Overall I give it a 9/10.  Great tool for learning, and even for those of us with lots of experience there is a lot of learning to do.  It still amazes me when you spend 10 minutes on it, and suddenly pick up a tricky section as they throw it at you seemingly out of the blue at times.

Stardrive 2 is the game for you if:
1.You like a 'fast' turn based feel, don't expect to wait for minutes while ai's take their turns!
2.A true Master of Orion 2 successor, which you notice very well as you play the game. Lots of ideas taken from there, so you can adapt very quickly to the game. So if you like MOO2 you will like this game.
3. A nice ship combat system, really nice to watch, and you can actually apply tactics--especially if you design your fleets well. You won't just sit there and watch the battle happen. Unless you have a titan packed with mass drivers, defense guns,and a tough armor or shield.
4. Focus on planets has improved drastically, especially how population and building special buildings has a huge impact. Colonists can either be taking care of the food business, the production business, or be Einstein-tier researchers.
5. Customize ships. Shipyard is back, and while it isn't as free as Stardrive 1 the limitations are there because it makes the ship combat more realistic. Far more choice too with every component, want it to be armored-its going to be heavier,cost more, and take longer to build. Lots of different weapon options as well.
6. Lore, lots and lots of it. Also add to that the funny jokes and items you come across taken from many different sci-fi series
7. Enjoy mods, because this game is build to support plenty and plenty of mods. Star Trek mods are already on their way. Also, with the current game engine choice it's bound to look  good.
-----------------------------------
Stardrive 2 has innovated upon
1. Concept of freighter fleets is high in this game, don't remember if MOO2 has it though. So protecting freighter fleets is very important unless you want your empire to stagnate and crumble.
2. Simultaneous turns system,it's turn based with a realtime feel.I might be the only one that really likes this system though. Turns happen instantly,not many(or any) 4x games have such a quick turn system.Also, every empire makes the turn at the 'same' time more or less.
3. 3D ground combat, you rarely if never see that in a 4x game, while it is at the moment simple it has great potential.

COLLECTIBLES!
AWESOME BUTTON MASH CUTSCENES! PUNCH THE GIANT ROBOTS HEAD!

The Cons:
Your AI friendlies are dumb as a bean bag with a brain.

More than a game this is a tool that makes guitar learning fun. This edition offers a simpler and better interface, with a much more streamlined experienced when compared to the original Rocksmith. You no longer have to go through 10 menus to play a song and back through the loop to play it again. Career and free play modes have been condensed into learn a song, which brings you right to track list which you can sort in a number of ways including difficulty or recommended, which replaces the old career stages, meaning you no longer have to go through that particular song you don't like and don't want to play in order to progress.
Experienced players should enjoy the option to set the difficulty right to master mode from the start and use the game as colourful moving tabs, also the new session mode which lets you form and ajust your own band to play along your jam sessions. The continuous play mode is neat as well, you can set the time and remove songs you don't want to play and just go along with what gets thrown at you.
For begginers you get a nice set of lessons and practice minigames that help grasp or refresh the basic techniques. These aren't compreehensive and don't replace more thorough resources but serve well in providing you with the fundamentals to jump on to the stage and massacre a classic or modern rock song you know and (used to) love. It's a blast when you hit that 1 note that nearly made the song sound alright, much better than painfully repeating tedious lessons with no sense of progression.
The track list is considerable, including DLC and the option to import all the content from the original Rocksmith, you are going to be doing a lot of scrolling. So far I haven't found any major flaws with this edition, however there are some mildly annoying details (grab your seat!), the new achivements are crap, you will get 10 for visiting the uplay store (whatever that is) and none for reaching master mode in a song for the first time, which brings me to my major complaint thus far: half the time you will try to log in with your uplay account and you will get a "server is not available try again later", which is harmless until you want to play that new song you just bought and can't because you need to be connected to uplay and activate it in the ingame store after buying it on steam (thanks jewbisoft). Curiously the first Rocksmith had none of this uplay mischief, and so the DLC you get from the original gets imported automatically without the need for uplay consent.

So, over two months out and I am now writing a review for this game. I cannot, in my good will, recommend this game in its current state. I'll gladly go over a few reasons why as well.
1. This game has absolutely terrible matchmaking. The p2p system(while actually being ok for 1v1) sucks for every other gamemode, especially if you have a not so good internet connection. If you aren't the one seeing lag, you very well may be lagging and not even feeling it. It ruins the experience for you and the person against you. Not to mention p2p is an absolute dream for cheaters.
2. Balance. I will say it, and I will take the hate that comes with it. This game has bad balance. Some characters are way too good for how easy they are. For example the Peacekeeper(I have legit stuff here, don't pitchfork me yet). She has fast light attacks, which in itself is not a bad thing, but add in the latency from the p2p and then you have a disaster coming fast. Not to mention her Zone Attack. The thing has an UNGODLY flicker bug which makes it non-reactable unless you preimptively guard your left(and even then you have to be reactionary with PK). As a note though, there is a patch that supposedly fixed the Zone Attack flicker bug for every character, but I can't confirm on that. Other characters are insanely weak. Berzerker has no way to open people up, and against good turtles it is a nightmare to play him. And then you have the characters that are just, meh. Conqueror went from an absolute god to terrible in ONE patch. Warlord is still a near unstoppable killing machine. Raider and Kensei are alright, and then you turn around and the Warden, the first Vanguard hero(Raider and Kensei being the second and third respectively) is near unstoppable if played even at an average level. When you have Tournament level players like TrueTalent guessing, that is a bit absurd. Not to mention this unbalance led to a character actually being banned from Console Tournaments, and not some side tournament, actual MLG events. Terrible balance isn't a good start, but oh boy are we just getting started.
3. Playstyle. This game panders to turtles. Getting a parry is WAY to rewarding, especially with how easy it is to land them on most attacks. Playing as Warlord or Conqueror(pre-nerf) was almost a sure fire win. And the problem is many characters are built around parries. Lawbringer(pre-buff), Raider, and Zerker just to name a few. They had to get parries to do any sort of damage against a good turtle, which leads to slow and boring feint spam contests until one person makes a mistake.
4. The Microtransactions in this game are absolutely awful. You're telling me in a game that I payed full triple A price for, that I can't customize the characters immediatly? I have to pay my ingame currency to change the color of their armor? That isn't even the worst part. You can pay to unlock all of the feats in the game from start. It's a terrible deal but some poor saps probably did it without realizing that Steel gain is slow. If you want any of the Mythic outfits, but don't want to pay money, good luck. It will take days, maybe weeks of playing to get enough Steel for ONE of them. Or you could just go buy Steel in the store. They have already buffed Steel gain once, and they need to do it again, and much more of a buff this time. It needs to take me maybe 1-2 days to unlock an outfit, not 1-2 WEEKS. What happened to challenges in games for skins and cosmetics? Not to mention that there is over $700 worth of purchases in the game. If you bought everything with Steel that you only purchased with real world cash, you would be set back SEVEN HUNDRED DOLLARS. That is absurd. And it is a shame cause there is some really cool looking stuff there. But sadly, it's nowhere near worth it with the lousy Steel gain. And did I mention Champion status? This little gem here costs two thousand Steel, or at least, the three day duration one does. You can purchase Champion status for three days, all the way up to one year. "And what does Champion status do?" I hear you all asking. It's simple, it boosts your Steel and EXP gain while active. So, not only is my Steel gain rate lousy, but then I have to buy a three day status just to earn more of it? And you have to keep repurchasing it, over and over.
5. Developer to Community interaction. This is one of the saddest interactions I have seen between devs and their community in a long time. They avoided talking about netcode for weeks, and then when they finally talked about it all they did was discuss NAT. How about you stop pushing new outfits and focus on connectivity issues so people can get your outfits. The Raider buff has been "In the works" for weeks now, and last I checked we got no news on it(May have news on it soon. If so that point is moot.) Not to mention we didn't have two maps that were supposed to launch WITH the game for over a month because of "Technical issues." That is something you are supposed to fix BEFORE your game launches, not after.
6. This point is for the people who like to rate communities based on how toxic and aggressive they are. For Honor has a decent community, but you will find a lot, and I mean A LOT of toxic players inside matchmaking assuming you can find a match. People calling characters spamming, cursing each other out, not to mention lagswitchers sometimes(Had a run in with one or two of those). All in all, decent community, but has a near 50/50 ratio of nice people to rude players.
So, on the whole, I will say this about For Honor. It has potential, and a lot of it. The fighting system is in depth, characters feel different and strong in their respective fields. The game looks gorgeous, and other than a very bad memory leak problem which has since been sorted, it runs well too. I don't hate this game, I wouldn't have been able to put nearly 200 hours into it if I did. But I cannot recommend this to anyone after the poor launch, and support it has been given. This game would be amazing if it was in the hands of a more capable studio, but Ubisoft once again underdelivers on a game that had so much promise. That hurts me to say, really. But, I have to say it, so the people who haven't decided yet can steer clear of this game.

Some people say that games can never be art. Well, here we have one of the examples that video games can in fact be art.
Thomas was Alone is a puzzle platformer in which you play as a bunch of rectangles. But not just any rectangles! These rectangles has been given personalities and have more character than many characters build out of thousands of polygons. In fact, the game's biggest focus is on it's story, which is told by an amazing narrator. Throughout the story you'll learn about the chracters, their interactions with each other and more.
Except for the wonderful narration, the game is also accompanied by an amazing soundtrack by David Housden. It's perfect to listen to even outside of the game and it just adds more feelings to the game. Graphically, Thomas was Alone is minimalistic with simple but good-looking graphics with some very nice looking background elements and "lighting". The level design often leads to some nice-looking visuals too.
The gameplay is quite simple. Every character has their own unique abilities which the player needs to take advantage of in order to get to the goal portals. Thomas and his friends will have to cooperate quite a lot in order to get through all the obstacles. The game isn't too hard, but you'll get to think more in some places
The game isn't very long, but this is one of those game that are good experiences and do not need to be longer. I enjoyed every single moment of it, from Thomas' first though to the ending that is open for interpretation. If you still haven't played this game, you should.

Survarium is a first person shooter based in a post-apocalyptic landscape. It involves lots of complicated but easy to learn gameplay mechanics along with a vast range of gameplay styles and routes for the players to choose from. Broad character customisations means that every player can really get involved into the game and enjoy themselves thoroughly.

To start off, Survarium contains four different factions for the players to choose from: Black Market, Fringe Settlers, Renaissance Army and the Scavengers. Each faction has a slightly different style of gameplay that really starts to take an effect later on in the game and every player has the option to choose from either of these four. The biggest effect that these factions have on gameplay entails the use of different equipment and weapons, which doesn’t have a profound effect on making a certain faction unbalanced; it allows players to choose a race suited to them and therefore immerses them into the game even more as the character they really want to be.

Within all the factions there are ten tiers to unlock, each with new and better equipment. Starting off in tier one, players have the initial weapons and equipment of each faction and it seems to mimic World War One and Two weaponry and as you go up the tiers, better, more advanced arsenal is unlocked. Players are normally matched to other players or in the same tier as them, but due to the limited playerbase, it’s common to be placed in games with players of one tier higher or lower than you. Very rarely are you placed with people from two to three tiers higher than you. This can cause for a frustrating fifteen minutes to say the least.

Survarium contains four basic game modes in your standard matchmaking. A game can consist of 5-8 players on both sides. If a player doesn’t like a specific game mode, they can decide to uncheck a box and simply not play it.

The four game modes are:

Battery Retrieval: Teams have to find the battery, capture it and take it back to their battery pack. First team to reach the maximum amount of batteries or those have the most when the time is up (normally around 10-15 minutes), wins the game. The batteries normally have 1-3 set spawn points, or spawn randomly.
Research: Teams have to take control of the 3 capture points. When a point is captured the percentage towards finishing the research into anomalous activity. The first team to reach 100 percent or to have the most when the time runs out, wins.
Team Deathmatch: A simple team deathmatch game where both teams fight with no objectives other than to kill each other. First team to deplete the other team’s reinforcements to 0 and wipe them off the map or the team with the most reinforcements at the end of time win.
Artefact Hunt: Basically a one flag ‘capture the flag’ gamemode where the beginning of the round plays out like a normal deathmatch, and then an artefact spawns randomly in the map. When the artefact is captures, the round restarts. First to five or most when the time runs out.

Although the game modes are just simple recreations of some of the classic ones, I believe that they’ve executed it really well and the games are really enjoyable. My only problem with these game modes is that some random elements pertain to the map layout and objective placement which can lead to unfair games. Although the unfairness is only slightly noticeable in some maps, I believe most to all maps aren’t completely balanced, but no maps really are. Competitive games such as ‘Counterstrike: Global Offensive’ fix this by giving each team an opportunity to play both sides.

There is also a wide range of maps to play (9) which keeps gameplay interesting, but I definitely think more can be added overtime to captivate some of the older audiences.

Every player also has a profile level that earns Skill Points to put into your Skill Trees. Your skill tree has a slight effect on your stats and you can enhance your ‘Physical’, ‘Firearms’ and ‘Knowledge of the Forest (‘Survival and ‘Technical’ currently under development). This is very similar to the League of Legends’ ‘Mastery system’.

What I find extremely annoying about this game is spawn-camping. The fact that there is no way that the game prevents to stop spawn camping and it most maps it’s not only possible, but extremely easy to do. Although most of the time it doesn’t work out for the attacking team, there have been several instances, especially at lower tiers, where we have sat in their base and killed them over and over again. In most maps where spawn camping is possible, there are many spawn points around the building that you spawn in to help prevent this. Otherwise I think the game should do more to try and discourage it.

The game is a Free-to-Play with a micro transactions model. Although the game isn’t strictly pay to win, I fear that there are elements of pay to win that if tampered with, can completely ruin the game. Premium members receive one extra loadout slot along with experience bonuses, silver bonuses and other perks. Also, items in the tiers above you can be brought for real life currency which I believe is pushing the game into a pay to win direction. I really don’t like the fact that players can do that, it can really take away the competitiveness of the game and making it less about the skills of the individuals but rather how much people are willing to spend. Although there’s not a lot that can be brought for real life currency, it’s still an unfair advantage that I think shouldn’t be there.

Because the game is free-to-play it does come with the mandatory hackers. Despite saying this, the community is efficient at seeking these hackers out and hundreds of bans happen every couple of days. The anti-cheat must be really good as I’m yet to see someone blatantly hacking.

In my opinion, Survarium is a really exciting to play first person shooter. I absolutely love the customisation and how I can choose how I want to dress my character and what guns I want to use. I do find the game frustrating at times, especially when I’m placed with and against players in tiers above me. The queuing times aren’t too bad and the game seems well optimized and runs easily on my computer.

An NES-inspired action-platformer that nails the visual aesthetic but has flaws.
Oniken is a game in which you play as a ridiculously powerful mercenary named [s]Kenshiro[/s] Zaku and beat up bad guys.  It's essentially a "neo-NES" game that goes far to capture the look and feel of games from that era, using lots of black filler space skillfully like later NES games tended to do to maximize color usag eand depth, and even including Ninja Gaiden-esque cutscenes with some well-done pixel art for the characters.  Graphically, the game has succeeded nobly in what it set out to do, though sadly the audio doesn't quite match up; the sound effects are fine, but the music is quite drab (some of it's alright, but most is really almost surprisingly bad) and sounds a bit more like something like GXSCC that tries to emulate this kind of sound rather than something from the system itself (should've used Famitracker probably).
As far as gameplay goes, it's pretty damn solid.  The "weight" of your character takes some getting used to, as he feels fairly heavy, but not in a way that's very uncomfortable after a few minutes of play.  In essence it fits in fairly well with any given action-platformer of the NES's later lifespan, like your Power Blade or Shatterhand type games, although a bit simpler -- the ONLY powerups you'll find (besides the rare health pack or 1-up) are grenades, your one and only (but quite effective) sub-weapon, and a sword icon that doubles the length of your blade until you take damage - or you can press the 'berserk' button to sacrifice it early in favor of a brief attack buff.  Despite the game's look and feel definitely trying to evoke classic Nintendo, the swordplay decidedly feels like Sega's
.
It's not a terribly long or difficult game, surprising considering the era and style it's trying to emulate; the game automatically adds each stage to a 'natural stage select' on the main menu as you pass them, there are plenty of powerups and you have a huge life bar that's slow to deplete with relatively few platforming challenges.  The real difficulty comes from the bonus content that comes after you finish the game, including a lengthy, challenging, but unique new stage and two extremely taxing new modes that definitely make the game "Nintendo-hard", so keep that in mind if the game feels a bit flimsy to you, oh classic game master.
It's not perfect.. aside from the music, the story's pretty pathetic (though so fitting for the time period it's forgivable) and there's just no depth or innovation here at all.  But if you're looking for a totally decent NES love-letter that does the job better than a good chunk of the modern retro-indie drivel you see out there, give Oniken a go.

While I enjoyed StarDrive 1, it was never finished. This game looked, at first glance, to be an attempt to create the game SD 1 was supposed to be. A lot of the changes are good (turn based but still quick gameplay), tech tree in which every choice feels like it makes a difference (but also extremely remniscient of MoO2) and hints of a story you might learn if you spend enough time with the game.
Ship building is basically similar to the first game, but streamlined, which I highly approve of.
The bad (and/or not yet done features) are too many to give this game a pass. If anything, this most certainly belongs in early access. If the designer disagrees, he ought to stop making games.
A few specifics:
-The tech tree is basically a mash-up of SD 1 and MoO2. But with sparsely any game effects visible (except for buildings, which are all well detailed, which makes the difference all the more obvious). The description certainly doesn't convey how utterly useless researching Plasma cannons was (in every way a worse choice than the weapons you start with, since they just almost never seem to hit) nor that researching and equipping rail guns to my troops would be a worse choice than sticking to the laser rifles you start with.
-Ground combat. Wow. Are you serious? You release a game with this "feature"?
Graphics are acceptable, if barely, but there's neither good advancement nor is there ever a point to this. The enemy advances in a direct line at you and will select it's targets and use it's abilities in the same exact manner every time.
There is no way to define a standard equipment for your troops, you have to adjust every planet on it's own (not like there's really a point, your starting equipment is what you'll switch back to, once you realize how superior it is to later research, unless you go really far in the tech tree).
-Diplomacy: The basic system is alright, but it sadly needs work.
-The space combat is nice, but very one-sided, with some weapons being utterly superior to others. But there is great potential here. But there really needs to be a way to speed up combat. There's nothing more annoying than waiting forever for a fight that's been decided minutes ago to end and it taking forever because there's one last annoying small ship or fighter still alive and dodging like an ace.
-The game's seriousness or lack thereof. It's not that there's humor in here. It's that the game seems like it's trying too hard, while also insecure about how funny or serious it should be. I wouldn't mind either way. Even a slight shift in either direction might be enough, but as is, it's in a weird place. Whenever I start taking the events in the game seriously, something reminds me I ought not to.
I could go on, but while I don't want people to waste their money on this, I also don't want to make the wrong impression: There is real potential here. I had fun with this game, but I can't see myself playing it in this state.
Currently, it feels less finished than most early access games I have.
The bad, sadly, vastly outweigh the good. At this moment, I strongly suggest watching this game from a safe distance and waiting for it to either evolve into what it might be or to stagnate as the first one did.

I love the concept, but the game is not very forgiving to new players.  The tutorial seems very helpful, but that's somewhat deceptive.  It doesn't tell you how to make money, for instance, and it merely touches on most of the game's concepts.  Sensing that the game had multiple layers of complexity, I started on easy to familiarize myself with the game's mechanics.  My starting position was horrible.  I was placed on a nice, resource rich planet, but was producing negative food.  Before I could stabilize that situation, I had lost two citizens to starvation.  Perhaps even worse, the tutorial forced me to colonize the nearest planet before I was even able to stabilize my home world.  The tutorial actually said, "You have no choice" and made me colonize.  The trouble is, the nearest planet was incapable of growing any food whatsoever, which meant simply that it starved out in four or five turns, wasting a colony ship.  The tutorial did say, however, "here's how to fix the lack of food - import food from  your other planet."  Very helpful advice, and I'm sure I could have managed it if, perhaps, my home world was even capable of sustaining itself at that point.
In terms of finances, I was constantly running a negative of at least -2 BC (billions of credits), usually -5.  At one point I went from -30 BC in the bank to a surplus of over 300, with no explanation at all.  Then my surplus slowly dwindled.  Or quickly, because in the first part of the game, you're really just hitting "end turn" as fast as you can because there's nothing really to do.  There's no concept of time, or how long things should take to build and some of the items seem prohibitively lengthy to construct.  Even with my citizens focused on production, the most basic of star ships took 15-20 turns to produce.
Of course that's to say you have an idea of the relative power of the ships to begin with.  You don't, at least not initially.  You don't know what ships are good, and certainly not compared to the AI's ships.  You don't know how big you should create your fleet.  With the construction times, it turns out that if I were to produce a fleet that was big enough to defend against the armada the AI brought to the final battle, I woulnd't have produced anything else in my home world, and I even then it would have been big enough.  If you don't have a big enough fleet, well, by the time you realize it it's too late.  It's hard to add two ships to your fleet in hopes of staving off the enemy that just appeared in your system when the smallest ship takes a half dozen turns.
Undoubtedly this can all be chalked up to my unfamiliarity with the game.  I was unable to colonize any planets effectively (I finally retook that first colony, only to have it destroyed from orbit a few turns later), whereas my neighbors had six, seven, or eight planets all, ostensibly, churning out ships.  I hope that I'll get better at it, though at this point it feels like several hours of my life were wasted.  Coupled with the utter hopelessness of seeing a big fleet appear when you thought you were content with four or five small ships...  Hard to want to keep playing.  Plus the AI is quite deceptive; the first engagements were very easy to win.  You're lulled into a false sense of security with a modest fleet, focus on building up your population and home world, and then the AI hits you hard.  Game. Over.
Speaking of the AI: It's pretty aggressive.  My first encounters with it were positive.  Let's trade?  Okay?  Good.  You want to trade tech?  Sure.  Then it demanded tech, for nothing.  Then, all the sudden, it tells me, "I told you I claimed that world, now I'm going to take it!" and declares war.  He never mentioned that at all, first of all, and second of all, it was my home world...
Technology is a bit awkward.  As I understand it, you can only research one tech in a given part of the tree.  After you get the one, that's it for that part (unless you trade tech) and the tree moves on to a different part.  Sort of interesting, I suppose, but you feel pretty locked in, and if you make a mistake and research something that doesn't fit with your eventual style, tough.  And I think that even the first techs took at least seven turns to research.  The third or fourth tier jumps to over 60.
Shipbuilding and fleet management is also a bit awkward.  I can't see any way of retrofitting new tech like armor to existing ships.  You can change the ship's template, I think.  But even that's klunky.  I didn't see any way to strip a template to start from scratch, so you have to manually remove everything.  There's probably a way, but I didn't see one.  I don't see any way to remove designs from the list of designs either.  The concept of this is fantastic, and it looks great.  But there could be some refinements.  For example, there's a button that allows you to replace all the steel armor in a design with a newer form (plasteel).  However, when you click that button it only replaced half the armor and removed the rest, leaving huge blank spaces.  I'm sure there was a reason, but the game offered none.  So by clicking that button you made your ship invalid (because every design must have 75% of its space filled with components).  It isn't as simple as replacing armor, now you have to add other stuff.  The second time I tried it, a few turns later, it replaced all the armor properly.  Again, no explaination for what went wrong or anything.
All in all, I think the game has a lot of potential.   I love the idea of being able to customize your ships.  But the game is not very forgiving.  The tutorial is somewhat lacking.  And you don't know if you're doing anything right at all.  Would I recommend it?  Yes, probably.  Just be aware that the learning curve might be a bit steeper than you anticipate.

The original Rocksmith was the first of its kind -- a music game built from the ground up around learning to actually play songs on a real guitar. What made it great was unfortunately muffled by a poor interface but the core gameplay worked fantastically. Rocksmith 2014 took everything that was wrong with the first game and fixed it. The interface is much more intuitive, it no longer is trying to be a game first and is instead a fun tool for learning to play guitar.
It is a bit too forgiving in some cases for things like chords but the riff repeater is greatly improved allowing you to play as many sections as you'd like in a row where the original Rocksmith only let you practice one riff at a time. The new interface also lets you 'favorite' certain songs and sort the songlist to put those at the top. Another MAJOR improvement is that you no longer need to tune your guitar before every song, every minigame, etc... You check the tuning once at the start and that's it. If you want you can pull up the tuner any time.
All around it is just a better game than the original Rocksmith. And with the Disc Import Tool, you can have all your old Rocksmith songs and DLC in Rocksmith 2014. The bottom line is that if you have a guitar or bass and/or played the first Rocksmith, then this sequel is in every possible way a better product. Easily worth $30 and depending on your budget and interest, probably worth full price.

As a veteran of Imperium galactic series, Galactic Civ, and SD1 as well as a few others I have to say StarDrive 2 holds its head up high among its piers.
the gameplay is fresh yet familiar. I have to admit I was leery of the new turn based system but in the scheme of things it makes sense and it's a welcomed addition.
Currently I've restarted the campaign 3 times as I wrap my head around some of the new mechanics and because my poor human civilization was blasted to death by alien scum - which means either I'm terrible at this game or it's hard, which is awesome!.
The graphics are beautiful, especially the way space combat looks, the planets are all awesome looking as well, the new hex system and fresh.
The mechanics of researching and building your fleet is pretty much the same as SD1, which is a good thing.
Space combat is enjoyable and satisfying, nice big explosions and a slow motion mode too! One gripe I have in space combat is that weapons don't lead targets, they aim at where the target was, not at its expected position. Missiles don't turn to intercept targets instead they make weird turns trying to catch up to it... it all feels very unnatural and I hope it's addressed in a patch.
When it comes to planet colonization, the variety of planets is massive making the whole experience of picking and choosing where you want to focus the new seeds of your civilization as engaging as it is important.
I like the way they've handled the freighters. Moving food and colonists around really saves us from a lot of the needless planetary micro from SD1. However freighters are not controllable, combine that with the smaller fleet caps and it makes it difficult to protect freighters when your main fleet is off attacking or exploring, they will literally fly directly at an enemy and suicide themselves. We should be able to control freighters, either directly or give us the ability to force them to dock at the nearest planet until the enemy fleet is taken care of.
Fleet Caps: I really don't see the point of fleet caps. Since each ship has an upkeep cost which in itself is the fleet cap, to compound that with an additional cap to me seems redundant. I like the idea of the fleet cap but instead of having it give you a monetary penalty, it might be more interesting if it gave you a penalty to ships rearm and repair rate, maybe even a damage dealing reduction to ships. Reasoning being they just aren't receiving the maintenance they should.
Ground combat. The research and upgrades aspect of it is well thought out and implemented however the actual ground combat is meek, it needs a re-tune. If it would have followed in the footsteps of Fallout 2 or X-COM it would have been amazing! But currently, weapons have a hard limit of minimum and maximum ranges,
Covert Ops: Works similar to the first one, but different enough to be fresh, that being said I think it needs a re-tune. I have 5 spy's doing counter espionage which is the max and I'm still getting tech stolen from me every few turns, which is really quite frustrating. Perhaps remove the spy caps for home defense?
Spatial anomalies, these are quite fun and new, really enjoying them so far and is a very welcomed addition.
Interface: interface is well designed, lots of tooltips and the information is easy to understand and readily available in most circumstances. A few gripes I have, on the planetary screen, when cycling from planet to planet via the arrows - every time you click to go to a different planet, the arrows location move to a slightly different spot, making cycling planets in this way annoying, and dizzying. If a fleet is hovering over a planet, the planet under the fleet becomes un clickable, there's also a few other minor annoyances that needs that little bit extra polish.
Overall, StarDrive2 is an engaging experience and I will surely play many more hours of it as I attempt to conquer the universe however as much as I like it, it's not quite there yet. everything seems 70-80%. It just needs one more good thick coat of polish to make this game really shine

There's a pretty big dichotomy in the way this game looks and the way it plays. It's a beautiful game, using a rarely invoked environment and culture (the Inuit) for its story and style, and the characters are very cute in their presentation, for the most part.  But the gameplay belies the idea that this is a kid's game. It got frustrating on many occasions, not because the game's puzzles and platforming are particularly challenging (although riding the variable wind for jumps was often annoying), but because the controls are too stiff and imprecise. The worst example of this is that you cannot jump backwards.  And the game is designed for Co-Op, so playing it Single Player, while definitely possible, makes it more complicated and less pleasant.
Still, the sight of a non-traditional hero in an unfamiliar story/legend just about outweighs the frustrations that come from the controls. And the FoxTales DLC is a very different experience from the main game, focused almost entirely on swimming and rowing, neither of which are in the main game. If you play the game, make sure to play the DLC; it's a more pleasant overall experience, even though control issues mar it as well. So if you prefer story and ambiance to gameplay, this is definitely worth your time.

Anna Extended Edition- Explore The Darker Side Of Human Psyche.
Hey there! Thanks for reading my #2 Review, on Anna Extended Edition. I kind of liked Anna despite the fact that it received Mixed reviews, I honestly feel this game is a gem, and a must-grab during sales and of course, a must-play in your library.
What is Anna?
Anna is a first person immersive puzzle horror that revolves around an unnamed protagonist who finds himself in front of an abandoned house because he saw that house in his dreams. That's stupidity at it's finest, but I would personally go there if it's a woman calling, and same stuff happened here, he heard Anna, calling him. This protagonist enters the house and roams around, doing stuff, and discovers what really happened, and to be honest, the ending wasn't what I expected, but it was sad. It was not predictable.
Descriptive Analysis!
Anna Extended Edition is developed by Dreampainters. The developers are Italian-based. The company is totally indie, by totally I mean, TOTALLY, T-O-T-A-L-L-Y. This game fits in the definition of Indie. So, I was browsing their site, here you go,
and saw,
"To design and develop the best narrative games with the highest possible quality.”
And they did, Anna is a hidden gem. The company seems to be composed of fairly young people with minimal experience, and Anna being their first game, and to be honest, they did exceptionally good for their first game. The game is minimalistic. No HUD, Good sound effects, a nice BGM and good visuals. A good combination, something like I want from games.
This game is extremely narrative and hence you should not buy it if you don't like slow narration.
As you know, I'm a soundtrack-♥♥♥♥♥ and hence I would just play this game to hear the beautiful soundtrack.
So, let's start now.
Gameplay-
The game is a typical FPS. This is the first game I've played in narrative category, and the second one being Dear Esther(I didn't like Dear Esther). I guess I haven't played enough games to set standard for grading, but still, it's good. Unlike Dear Esther, you solve actual puzzles. You click stuff, you examine stuff, like a Point 'n' Click with FPS. There is an inventory system, and a journal system where the protagonist's darker side is hidden. They're really long, really, but to understand the storyline, I recommend you do that, and complete the game at your own pace.
Typical WASD controls.
Mechanics and Features-
The game is psychological horror so don't expect jump scares. The game gets predictable sometimes but you would still pee in your pants, that's because it's happening exactly the way you don't want. The game won't throw stuff at you directly, but in a random pattern, same places, same stuff, but random moments, when you won't be expecting them. I literally put down my headphones because one such encounter scared me, not 'to death' but still very much.
The game has good collision data, and physics, although, physics don't matter much, but still you would notice some bugged out places in the game. Like a floating chair(NOT PART OF THE GAMEPLAY, ACTUAL BUG BUT STILL SCARY).
Another feature I liked is the 'Truth' feature. You have to examine stuff to remind the protagonist what really happened. This makes you think what is worth examining, although you could examine everything.
There's another minute feature that still adds some fun, exiting the house.
Instead of an average horror movie where the door gets locked, you actually have a choice to exit the house, but the game would end and give you an ending depending upon which moment you ran out of the house. There are achievements for rational thinking like this too!
The Plot-
The plot is boring at first, until you enter the house. Nice BGM with bright colours, my ideal holiday spot, but once you enter, the colours fade, you enter darkness, you'll poop your pants.
The storyline is intriguing, but not at a level you'd want it to be. It's narrative, slow and easy to understand. The storyline has a few plot twists, the ending itself is one.
There are multiple choices, depending upon how you play the game, which alters the final ending. But let me tell you, you won't feel happy. None of the endings is like how you would expect. I kinda expected Anna Ressure..*oops* No Spoilers.
Difficulty Level-
A bit difficult since you don't know what to do unless and until you read the journal, carefully hear the narrations and use common sense.
OVERALL!
Graphics-
Good. Not bad. It's an indie, I don't care about graphics but it deserves an 8/10.
Gameplay+Mechanics-
Narrative, Slow, Multiple choices, random encounters. Deserves 7/10
Price-
I don't have a problem buying it at 10$ but you should wait for sales.
Soundtrack-
Pls, the one aspect I loved the most <3. Buy the soundtrack.
Worth the money?
Yes, kind of. IF you're a Dear Esther fan or into atmospheric, narrative, horror, psychological, you should get this. Assuming you're new to narrative ones, I'd like you to give this one a try. I don't think you would regret it.

In the levels, one may find owls. Each owl found unlocks a short video clip, where Iñupiat people talks about aspecs of their culture and how they relate to the world. While it takes you out of the gameplay, they do provide background inforamtion about the story and does in my opinion enrich the experience.
Graphically, it is not the prettiest game out there, but the different styles used in cutscenes and the gameplay complement each other. The game is surprisingly colorful for taking place in a snowstorm, on an iceberg in a snowstorm and in a forest in a snowstorm. The levels are well designed and contain different gimmics, making each area feel unique. The music is feels well adapted to the levels and is well made, but does not stick out for either good or bad.
The gameplay is the one thing that really brings down the experience. The controls feel slow and unresponsive at times and the AI controlling the movement of the other character could be improved, especailly in the areas where tey might end up standing on collapsing platforms or in the way of insta-death creatures.
Also, the length of the game may be worthwile to take into consideration. 5-8 hours, depending on your level of skill and need to 100% complete it, is not that much.
All in all, it's not great, but I would call it a good game for what it is.

Review #2:
My first review hit on the fact that the developer "released" the game while it looked and felt like a tech demo and further development on the game ceased.  A lot of folks were spurned by the fact that they pledged money on kickstarter hoping they would get a highly modifiable Jagged Alliance like game in a newer engine, only to see the game largely unfinished, and unpolished.  I too felt swindled when I bought in during the alpha phase, and saw the announcement that the game was done shortly afterwards.  I wrote it off as a loss, but the developers have seemed to be apologetic of some sort, as more development has continued, albeit not for quite some time now.
So what's the status now that some time has passed?  Well, the game runs stable, though I can see my primary squad's character names appearing through the ground in the center of the screen, even when I am in another squad on another map cell.  However, the game is much improved compared to when it launched.  A lot more cover and objects have been added into the game.  There are also more quests, and the story actually progresses, although it's boring.  Overall, Flashback is still not a fun tactical game.  The simplistic square tile and XCom Enemy Unknown cover system rip off just doesn't work for me.  It would have been better if there was raised terrain, additional floors, cliffs, etc.  The battles are largely based on your ability to setup an ambush from cover and lure the enemies into a firefight from your fighting positions.  There isn't much of a point to sneaking, the enemy seems to always detect you no matter what.  So take cover and hold on to your hats.
So I will now break the game down into the good and bad:
The Good:
- You can buy mercs.
- It has IMP, so you can create yourself.  This was updated as well, so there are more customization options than what I played with a long time ago.
-You can find mercs in towns and special locations and hire them later, I thought that was kind of a cool dynamic.  That you aren't limited to online mercenaries, but could call locals.
-Militia is working
-Economy
-Lots of gun choices
-Snipers working in tandem with scouts are quite useful
-Graphics aren't bad
-AI reads and reacts, sort of.  They sometimes flank you, though I don't know if that was the random positioned enemy responding to noise or a real flanking manuever.  Noise draws them in, though this is also a flaw in tactics.
-Dialogue tree
-mods
The Bad:
-No Bobby Rays.  I'm sorry, but you fail at JA if you don't have Bobby Ray's
-Only some of the Mercenaries from the original game are in this.  In fact, if it wasn't for the fact you can find mercs in town, I would argue that there just aren't enough mercenaries online to pick from.  They also randomly go out on missions, so you aren't always gauranteed to get the guy you want.
-Square tile combat is an XCom Enemy Unknown ripoff, and it sucks.
-Movement feels very restricted, and moving units around feels clunky because of the restrictive square tile system.
-Cannot interact with doors
-No height elevations, everything is on the ground floor
-Enemies always seem to detect your most skilled ninjas after you hang around them for a while, IE: I had an 85 sneak character hiding behind a tree trunk about 15 tiles BEHIND the enemy soldier.  After about 10 seconds, he automatically started combat with me and started shooting, even though I was prone, hiding, not making noise, had high sneak, and he wasn't looking at me.  Quite frankly, I was never able to successfully sneak up on anyone and engage in melee.  It's useless.
-Story is not that interesting, in fact, it makes no sense.  You are a CIA agent sent on a rescue / recovery operation that got botched, and now you have to assassinate a dictator because some foreign lady on the radio said so.
-Though the game has a dialogue tree, most of the NPC's feel like you respond with "OK" and "Whatever".
-There aren't really any mods that scream Jagged Alliance 2 version 1.13.
-A lot of the tiles and objects feel cookie cutter.  The fact that everything is squeezed into entire blocks, all the same size, makes the game feel like a math puzzle, unnatural.
-No obstacle interaction, climbing, jumping, etc.  It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you get flanked or have to move.  Everything is measured in equal sized blocks, so you have to walk all the way around an obstacle to get cover from a flanker.
Summary: If you love Jagged Alliance and think you want this game, don't.  I really think the developer just wanted to make a quick buck, but found it wasn't such a great idea.  This turd is likely a black mark on their resume.
