SOMA was hard for me to review. I personally love this title, but I wasn't 100% sure at first if I'd recommend it to others, mostly because of its nearly-complete lack of gameplay. In fact, I'd go as far to say that SOMA feels less like a game and more like an interactive experience.
This isn't necessarily a bad thing: the world created by SOMA's rich, dense backstory is both very lovingly detailed and vividly realized, and this is combined with how beatifully the world is graphically rendered. The sound effects and music are also well designed, and there some moments where the voice acting is just spot-on and performed so convincingly well.
However, there are many points where the voice acting is much less than spot-on, the enemies that you face mostly feel oppressive but not necessarily dangerous or scary, and, as mentioned earlier, the game's biggest "turn-off" for many players is that there's very little actual gameplay. Most of what you'll be doing in SOMA is exploring its vast world and occasionally trying to escape from some aggressive monstrosities. However, these monster encounters really aren't that good or fun for the most part. This isn't helped by the fact that certain creatures (one in particular, named the Proxy) are said to follow a certain pattern (like relying on its sense of hearing because it's supposedly blind), but when you encounter that creature, it doesn't always obey those rules. (The aforementioned Proxy, for example, won't hear when I open and close a loud-as-hell door, but it seems to instantly see me if I'm a few yards away but not moving.)
So the question that I've been wrestling with is this: despite these negatives, would I still recommend this game? The answer is easily "yes", but at least be aware of what experience you'll be getting out of SOMA before you purchase it. This is not Amnesia or Outlast. This is an interactive journey that's full of tension, but not necessarily horror. Even so, the game's setting and story of the decrepit PATHOS-II are so well conceived and near-perfectly rendered that it's hard not to recommend diving into the universe of SOMA at least once.

To start, if you're looking for more horror than thriller, you're in the wrong boat, jump ship.
This is most accurately defined as a semi-text based thriller adventure in 4 parts.
This game has amazing gameplay and interaction, with each of the episodes setting a different kind of unease into you. Unfortunately the payoff for this unease is very weak. It doesn't ever reach full fear, which is why I am very reluctant to recommend this as a horror title, even as it is one of the best games, mechanically, that I've seen in the Text-Based genre.
I find the story to be lack luster in its conclusion, and each of the episodes to also suffer that fate. In each of them, they had the chance to make it end in some way that had more punch, and yet they didn't. Yet, even this didn't distract from the amazing way this game was put together. If there were more games like this one, I would play them. No Code perfectly integrated Text-Based games into an interactive adventure, and for that, they get a big thumbs up from me.

Great price for a decent tool!
I accidentally stumbled upon this tool looking through Steam sections and had no idea this software was being made. Here it was for a meager 14.99$ and I thought to myself "That's not too expensive to try out."
While it is still Early Access, it offers quite a bit of functionality that is point and click simple to use. I come from creating maps in Photoshop using a tablet, or in the ever expensive Pro Fantasy Campaign Cartographer and this tool was a refreshing change in a lot of ways.
Firstly how easy layers and objects are to manage was wonderful. There is also a lot of objects and textures to start with which are actually very well drawn for creating the look and feel of dungeons. A feature I -truly- enjoy about it is when exporting to an image you pick the actual pixel per squares you want to export the image as. If anyone has used something like CC3 you know how annoying it can get to truly be exact with that option for importing into your virtual table top, that is not a problem in this tool.
It really gives you that speed for quickly putting a dungeon together that you might need on short notice and for me that is a giant plus because I play RPGs quite often and have to stay ahead of the content my players are getting through week to week in multiple games.
One major problem that made my face wrinkle was the terrain brush too. While this tool is a must have for smooth blending of terrain, the tool itself is not smooth with it's drawing. The drawing lags heavily behind the mouse and doesn't use pathing for the drawing. This means if you move your mouse faster than a few pixels per second you create dotted lines instead of a constant stream like you'd expect. It also is click on and click off instead of click and hold with release. Maybe this was intentional and preferred for some people but I would like to see that as a toggled option. I can handle the click on and click off, but the sluggish painting and the way it moves is simply horrendous.
However, it's early access so this might improve!

The absolute best "retro" style game on Steam. I have a lot more than the apparent 3 hours put into it, but on Offline Mode. This game genuinely looks and sounds like an 8-bit game and plays like a NES game. On first play through of each level, it feels difficult but never frustrating. Once you've died a couple of times though, you should be able to play back to that point without dying once; it's incredibly fair. Due to being able to choose your level once you've reached it, the difficulty on normal mode isn't quite NES levels but it makes up for this by having 3 or 4 sections to each level that could be considered individual levels (often with a boss in each section). Controls, particularly with a gamepad (though keyboard is fine for this game), are great altogether. Some levels feel like Ninja Gaiden or Vice: Project Doom, while there are segments that feel more like Shinobi III (the jet ski sections specifically) but with 8-bit graphics. Really an incredible job done on it. Recommended at any price.

If you liked StarDrive but found that there were flaws in the game, you'll highly enjoy SD2.
The combat and ship building system is made much clearer and honestly, this is the game that SD1 should have been - while there are some new things in this game that makes it interesting (new races, ship systems, research system), there does seem similar to the previous game and diplomacy with different races are similiary unfair due to racial traits.
That's not to say that there isn't problems with the game - diplomacy is actually pretty weak in that it's mainly trading, and anything the AI does with you takes up part of the guage the system uses to limit broken diplomacy. However, it also does not allow stronger diplomatic actions like asking the AI to help you in wars, or declare war with others, etc.
The ground combat UI can also use a lot of work. It uses a rather clunky "click on this weapon to use, click again to cancel" system, and there's a hero that joins on a pretty high chance that will wreck any ground force simply because airdrops deals a lot on a large area.
Overall, I say if you're looking at Stardrive, get this instead. If you're looking for a casual space 4x, this is a good choice. There are better ones, but this is one that you can play without worrying too much about winning or losing simply because it'll absorb your attention for quite some time. But I do recommend that you get this on a sale, and not the $30+ price.
Edit April 13 2015
Having played till the end, I can no longer recommend this game.
One of the weakest points of the Stardrive has always been its endgame. Now in Stardrive 2, there's a rather interesting research system that... actually penalizes players for expanding. That means, if you want to make it to late game you must limit your expansion because otherwise the AI will out-research you.
So, what does this mean? This means that if you play on a large map, you'll be forced to invade every planet that you let go and that could get boring fast because there still isn't any alternate end conditions.
Oh, and if you're wondering how big of difference having a small emprie vs a large one makes? On average, I'm one ship size higher than the AI which focused on expanding and killing neighbours. Which also means that my ships, at minimum, kill 5 of theirs due to advantages from weapon, shields, and other military advantages.

First of all, this is an early access game and should be undstood as such; however the beta was pushed out in 2013 according to their dev blog.  With that said, below is a review based on my time playing the game and my concerns regarding its future development.
*Note: This review does not include the multiplayer or arcade aspects and this should be taken into consideration when reading this review.
1.) Visuals: 3/5
- Reminiscent of Super Nintendo games such as The Legend of Zelda, Star Dew Valley and Secret of Mana but nothing new or exciting to the visual experience.
- Animations are very basic but do not add to the genre.
2.) Mechanics: 3/5
- Follows the same templates as older SNES adventure/RPG titles and adds a little bit of depth to the real-time combat with the talent trees and progression systems but doesn't do much to seperate itself from other finished titles.
3.) Sound: 3/5
- Music is well done and helps to serve the landscape equally as well.
- Sound Effects are basic and satisfy the requirements.
4.) Story: 1/5
- It's basic at best and unfinished at worst.
5.) Overall: 3/5
- The game isn't good but isn't bad and doesn't add to the genre.  It feels more like a rebuild of older SNES games with features picked from each to replicate what Nintendo has done to it's fans for decades (ie: selling nostalgia.)  From the visuals to the sound, the game offers little to be excited about since the story is unfinished (ie: restrictions from proceeding forward to the end of the game's story.)  If you're seeking a game that takes you back to the early 90s then this may be the game for you but expect to only get a few hours out of it before you get bored and move on.
Concerns:
- The dev team seems to be all over the place with no real plan for completing the game.  I say this because the game is full of features... and that's pretty much it since no single element feels complete.
- Development started in 2011, Beta released in 2013, Early Accessed in 2015, Release date Still TBD... I don't attribute this to laziness but instead is a byproduct of likely poor understanding of tools, workflows and project management overall.
- The dev team wants to polish the game as they go.  This means that they will have an extremely slow release cycle of impactful content since they keep revisiting and re-polishing the game over and over and over again.

Pretty much every 4X game that has come out since the genre has started gets asked one question. How does it compare to the styles of Master of Orion 2 or Civilization. A lot of them fall short because they are missing key features or ideas from one of those two iconic games.
Stardrive 2 is a game that manages to remake the classic feeling of those games while also adding to the formula. In a nutshell and remake of the legendary MOO2. You only need to glance at it to see the similarities. This is both good and bad. If you are a diehard Civilization fan, you will immediately notice the game focuses less on empire simulation and more on conflict and exploration. That may leave you a bit disappointed. On the other hand though, if you like MOO you will love this game for those exact reasons.
Each game has a lot of customization options, though I wish there were a few more galaxy option types. Still there are a lot to fool around with and you can customize a lot of the details of each opponent race. Once a game is started there is a lot to explore and do. Things start out slow for your planets, but you will eventually unlock a ton of tech to build each planet or asteroid. I find myself satisfied with these options and can churn out planets exactly how I like. So for empire building it is a thumbs up.
A little while into the game you will see that it is very combat focused. And the game is difficult on normal setting. The AI is aggressive and challenging. You can’t sit on your laurels waiting for things to happen. You have to be constantly building and expanding to stay competitive. To make matters worse for any fledgling Emperors, your empire will also face random scenarios from time to time that usually involve someone attacking or pillaging your empire. The AI doesn’t have to deal with this events and if you are not careful, you can find yourself surrounded by other empires as well as random event attacks. On the plus side, the scenarios usually grant your rewards for their completion.
Combat and ship design are definitely SD2’s strong point there are a lot of options to make some truly unique ships that fight how you want. It is very rewarding to watch your designs bring your victory. In actual combat, the game looks and plays great. Tactics are key and the right or wrong moves can turn a lopsided battle into a victory or defeat. The AI employs some solid designs and tactics, however he should be a little quicker to adapt to my designs. Ground combat is okay. It is nice to see something attempted and I am having fun with it, but it could definitely be more fleshed out. This maybe because the maps feel a little empty.
SD2’s biggest weakness right now is diplomacy. It has the standard options, but uses a system called Tolerance to represent a race’s familiarity to limit the amount of options you can conduct in a session to keep you from just spamming options. The system is great on paper and was super cool early in the game, however the AI’s aggressiveness will soon override your options. Too many things can effect a races opinion of you negatively. If the AI wants to trade for a tech even when he has nothing worthwhile if I turn him down our relationship suffers. If I say yes our tolerance gets used up so I can’t ask for things I want later. If I don’t pay them money for their threats they get angry. If I expand too much they get angry. It is hard to keep them happy without simply giving into all their requests. Conversely, they seem to not care at all about my happiness. Worse I have no option to complain about their spying or attempts to colonize planets in my systems. The concept is sound, but the balance needs to be reworked. Right now it is a little more frustrating than rewarding.
Overall, the game really is a great accomplishment. It just does so many things I have always wanted in a 4X right. There are plenty of nitpicks here and there, but the amount of fun I am having with it far outweighs those issues. The game only retails for 30 USD. As of this review I have 16 hours logged in so for me it was well worth the price. There are a lot of options and plenty of ways to get in all 4 of the Xs. And it certainly has the “Just one more turn feel”

It's a neat idea, and I was excited to give it a shot, but it's poorly executed. The controls are super clunky,and most of the 'difficulty' with the game is in getting your guys to do what you want and build where you want withing the restrictions of the controls. You have to click on each gun and fire each time. No way to give orders to continue firing, and very little in the way of automated defense. Your guys are super dumb and need extreeme micromanaging, basically.
Example: You can protect your guys with gun behind doors, so you put your sniper behind a door. You want to fire a mortar to draw the fire of the enemy machine guns, okay, you click on the mortar, and click in the super tiny and difficult to use reticle for firing it (it's a nice size when zoomed in, but you have to zoom out to use the mortar, and the interface for the mortar doesn't get any bigger, which is awful). Anyway: That's on it's way, so your enemy opens their doors to fire at the mortar round, so now it's time to snipe, execpt when you clicked away from the sniper, his door closed, so you have to zoom all the way in to click on the door, and click the open door button, so now the door is openeing, and the enemy doors are already closing, and now you can line up your shot, but the doors are closed now so too late.
Example: I want to build a bridge from one part of my base to another, so I start adding some beams and making some trianges for stability, but when I do, the tower makes a lurching motion with each one I place, and the wole base sways because of it, a 'feature?' that only exists to make building harder and more likely to result in failure.
This game had a lot of potential to be the next Worms, and I wanted it to be, but it gets in it's own way too many differnt little ways.
--
Response to dev comments:
I'm glad you're continuing to work on your game and taking feedback. As a more detailed feedback: I got that you could extrude, and that does make building faster, but I didn't want faster, I wanted 'not contantly wobbling'.I think it was an intentional design decision for your team, but I didn't like that it was there just to make building harder.
Doors auto open when you click the fire button in the arc, BUT this also changes your 'last fire' icon, so, if, from a zoomed out mode, I want to get that door open, I just click on the unit, then click in their fire arc, I loose my 'last shot' mark, which may be very important for the next shot I have planned. Making me click twice within my last shot (coupled with forcing my mouse cursor to jump away every time I fire) was annoying, not challenging. and with the little fire arc things getting so small when you zoom out, it just made it more likely thatmy shot would not go where I want. (Check out Worms, where the firing interface remains the same size no matter what zoom level you're at. That may make some shots easier based on zoom, but that's okay, it easier to control and more fun.) Perhaps this would work better if the gun fired as soon as the door was open enough to make the shot that the player clicked to make instead of making them click again?
Auto-defenses were the only thing that made the game even playable with mortars in, but more needs to be automated. Not every person is an RTS super-click-master. I don't play RTSs anymore because they make me click too many things too often without purpose. At the very least, all guns should have an auto-fire mode that simply takes the same shot over and over as soon as they reload (make it another option at set-up even). That change alone would turn it from a slog into a joy.
I think maybe you have a focus I don't agree with? I mean, that's fine, you can't please everyone, right? But I feel like this game has a lot of potential to be a fun "I want to have a laugh with my friends" type of game, like Worms, Chicken Horse, or Mount Your Friends. That's what I was hopping it would be when I saw the videos and purchased the title. I was fully planning to give it a try so I could tell my friends all to buy it, and we could add it to our rotation of games we play when we want a laugh at each other's expense. The graphics and the style all made it feel like that was what you were going for, but the gameplay does not feel like that was what you were going for. The gameplay feels like you want "serious" RTS players to pick it up, people who are proud of their clicks-per-second or whatever. IF you want to draw in the party-game audience, it needs a mode that is much more focused on fun, and less on tactics and fairness and clicking. :D

I don't have time to go read the forum for every game in order to figure out how to play. Once I'm in and I like the game already and I want to know more, maybe, but I'm not going to go read the forum as a way to see if I can find a way to like it. That's silly.
and Second: It's basically an admission that your game is incomplete as it stands.
Like: Imagine a novelist or a movie producer told fans that in order to get the most from their book or movie you had to go read the forum. That would be awful, and games are no differnt. It's good that there is a forum or whatever, but don't tell people they need to go there to understand the game. :/

Decisions decisions!  I also really like the ship building.  Here again, many decisions to be made yet the construction interface is easy to use and makes sense.  More decisions when it comes to expansion and building.  I found that the normal 4x land grab rush may not work as well here due to various encounters and mechanics.  It can be pretty dangerous right out of the shoot even close to your home planet.  A more planned and thoughtful build/expansion strategy is required.
At the end of the day, I find the games mechanics to present many more meaningful decisions than some of the other 4x space genre fare out there.  Kudo's to the SD2 team!  Looks like you might have a winner!

I've invested a little less than half an hour into this game after it became abundantly clear that this is not something I can enjoy. I love a good adventure game and after playing Amnesia, I've bought this game -thankfully on a sale- to satisfy my urge for more scary, adventure-y goodness.  Unfortunately I was disappointed.
The game starts with asking you to create a Kalypso user account (which is essentially an extra layer of unneccesary DRM); something we don't need nor will probably ever use. It is noted on the Store page for the title however, so buyers beware.
In the game, your character moves in a fashion that I could only call unnatural. I don't know if it is due to the FOV or something else, but I felt literally nauseated after playing for 15 minutes. I normally don't get motion sickness from first-person games, especially ones with a relatively slower movement speed, like this one. But since I've spent very little time with the title I can't tell if its a fluke or not.
The user interface is horrible. It simply is badly designed, so much so that I had to check if it was a console port or something(It isn't). It is completely counter-intuitive, hard to navigate and use. In an adventure game, this is unacceptable. The options menu is very barebones, it feels like the developers made it as an afterthought, quite reminiscent of a bad port instead of the PC exclusive title that we have.
The puzzles are very contrived and illogical(unlike say, Monkey Island, it really doesn't have any redeeming qualities, such as being humorous). By the time I managed to go into the house(you start outside at the beggining) I've already lost my interest in the game.  I don't care  if the game opens up or gets very scary afterwards, I simply didn't see any reason to stick with it any longer.
The game looks pretty and it ran on my machine smoothly without any problems. I haven't encountered any bugs. The sound assets used were quite good.
All in all, the game might get better later on, for all I know. But I didn't want to struggle with the bad UI and the uninspired puzzles to get to the meat. I uninstalled the title immediately after exiting it. I would recommend the prospective buyer to watch a gameplay video so that they can decide if the problems I report are relevant to them.
If you're a fan of the genre, you might want to pick it up at a sale. But I can not, in good conscience, recommend this game.

- Their website keeps track of the number of the amount of time you've put into playing and your progress.
- The lessons auto scale to your ability by slowing down the riffs and removing chords/frets.  As you progress, it slowly adds them in.
- The Guitarcade offers a bunch of games to help build upon your abilities learned within the lessons.
- 50 songs are included and you can learn them once you develop your skill (I'm very far from that right now).
- They have over 200 more songs that you can download and learn.  One offs cost the same as what you would purchase on iTunes.  You can also buy band packs that range from a few bucks up to $12.
Cons:
- I quickly realized that I need to develop finger strength and dexterity to hit the frets via the four finger method.  The software doesn't cover how to improve these through exercises, but I found a few video's on Youtube to cover this minor shortcoming.
That's pretty much it.  All of the reviews online give this 4.5 to 5/5 stars.  I have to agree and if you have interest in learning guitar, then you should pick this up.

As a person who has always been afraid of horror games, this game was quite the catch I needed to help me overcome that fear. There are no monsters like Amnesia or other horror games. The scenery is beautiful, the music is wonderful as well, though at times it seems like it does not fit the atmosphere of the game. Now, a couple of things I did not really like about this game. It felt WAY too short... Maybe even a little rushed at some parts. I feel there could be so much more done to this to help aid the story along and to add more to it. I also hated some of the puzzles. I had no idea what to do for some of them, and eventually had to give in and look up a guide. There are a couple of puzzles that give hints, but other than that, nothing. The controls are rather easy to remember. The inventory is another issue that I had. There were some items that were SO pointless to have that the end of the game, and even throughout the game.
Aside from the few cons and issues I had with this game, it definitely terrified me to play the first couple of times. There were some things that could be improved, but overall I think it was a very interesting, very plot-twisting game.

Overlord is one of those games where you are evil and it is actually very exciting and funny to be evil! Its hilarious approach is similar to that of Dungeon Keeper. The Overlord you control has the ability to control dozens of so-called minions - creatures that do the fighting and looting on behalf of you. This is a must as the Overlord cannot kill a handful of enemies single-handedly.
There are 4 types of minions each with unique abilities so the game requires you to carefully think about which race you want to send into battle against what kind of an enemy. The blue ones can cross water while the green ones are good against giant ogre-like creatures as they can jump on their back to swiftly eliminate them. Reds prefer ranged attacks while the browns are best at melee - and if all else fails the blue ones can revive your fallen soldiers.
Your minions are hilarious along with some of the sidequests you need to complete. The main quest is basically a quest for revenge - your predecessor was killed by heroes and you need to take revenge for what they have done. It is a nice touch that the developers included a so-called corruption level: you can eliminate innocent townsfolk that will only make you more corrupt. This will eventually change the way you look like and the behaviour from these people around you.
You can retreat to your own tower occasionally where you can carry out some upgrades depending on the looted items you have found throughout the game. There are also visual upgrades such as changing banners or statues. Single-player campaign offers a long and funny story and the game is getting gradually more challenging along the way.
Overlord is a funny game! Other than Dungeon Keeper I cannot recall anything with a similar approach towards being evil which can only be fun in such games. It's worth picking up its bundle version which includes an expansion pack as well as the sequel to Overlord.

Cons:

TL DR: The game has a few technical issues right now, but nothing critical. It's still one of the best games I've played in the last years (30 hours in 3 days tells something about being hooked). I would expect a game of such gameplay quality from Blizzard, not from Ubisoft.
PROS
- Easy to get into, hard to master (particularly on some characters)
- Dark Souls-like combat, MK-like combinations and cancels, Chivalry-like setting (what can be better?)
- Deep metagame (numerous ways to surprise your opponent, victory heavily depends on being able to adapt to your opponent playstyle and counter it)
- Almost endless customization (don't even get me started here)
- Enough characters with different playstyles to fit any kind of player
- Great and extensive progression that will take a couple hundred hours at least to fully beat
- Kills are extremely satisfying, deaths are infurating as hell (the game is really good at provoking true, primal emotions in you)
- Bots in this game decimate and BM you (I swear it's hilarious)
- Beautiful, seamless and fluid animations (on par with Witcher 3)
- Atmospheric and well-designed maps (except for a few oversights here and there)
- Amazing visuals
CONS
- Random disconnects. Sometimes the game will drop you from battles and kick you from matchmaking queue. You can simply requeue though, so nothing too bad here. Doesn't happen too often to be very noticeable and is probably going to be addressed soon.
- Language lock. Some regions are language-locked (including mine). However, you don't really see any text in this game and all the audio is English, so not a big deal unlike singleplayer titles.
SUBJECTIVE
- Connection type. A lot of people claim it's P2P while it's not, however the only fact that it doesn't have dedicated servers is enough to turn many away from this game. Firstly, the game is P2M (peer-to-master) which means it chooses the best machine (best connection, best hardware) to host a game on and validate player actions with additional cheater protection unlike peer-to-peer when everyone is connected to everyone else. Secondly, if you have a good connection and just ignore the p2p cancer for a moment to actually try this game, you'll probably find it's absolutely fine. I haven't had a single lag or ping issue with it. The game attempts to recognize your NAT type and assigns a color to you — if it's green, you're golden. If it's not green, you can try different tweaks that are usually done in your router settings or with the help of your ISP (UPNP, port forwarding, static IP) and get it to be recognized as open (green).
- Microtransactions. Yes, there are microtransactions in the game, and yes, some of them even directly influence your effective power in battles (I say effective because it's only up to you if you can benefit from it). However, since players are matched by their relative skill and performance, it doesn't really matter. If you spend a lot on buying equipment but you're not a top player, you will still have a lot of fun because the game will match you against an opponent with similar performance, not simply by gear. Besides, there's no content hidden behind paywalls - you can achieve anything simply by playing. And there are separate modes in the game where gear is disabled (like duel and brawl). All in all, I haven't noticed microtransactions being an issue in the game.
- No harsh leaver penalty. Actually, if you leave you don't get anything for the battle which already is a penalty since people mostly play for XP/steel and victories. Besides, you probably get an automatic defeat which screws your winrate. How is that not a penalty? A leaver instantly gets replaced by a bot player, and trust me - bots in this game are brutal, level 3 bots are better than 90% of players.

3rd person, action, adventure, hack and slash RPG. In this game you play as Overlord, and command different kind of imps in battles.
Four kinds of imps, with their own strengths and weaknesses. You are very vulnerable without your army of imps, though you can do decent amount of damage. Game has plenty rich and colorful environments, with many missions available. Story is basic and linear with good/bad choices you can make on the way, that will shape your Overlord to look more badasss if you go evil.
You have your own Tower "base", which you can pimp out, by buying statues, banners, room accessories, etc. At some point in game you'll even get your very own Mistress, with some more darker and voluptuous surprise ahead.
Game has decent visuals and good texture quality for 2007. Voice acting is good, animations are basic, unit control can sometimes be wonky. Game has some funny moments and humor here and there, and generally is great and fun experience.
It's taken a long time, but it is still impressive they're fixing and improving 2 years after launch. Good content comes out often, and the payment model is fair. Fun game.

I use this to make
battle maps so I my review of DPS is weighted towards that end.  Having said that, I'd give it 4-out-of-5 stars.
The only other map-making software I own is Campaign Cartographer 3 (CC3+).  Compared to that,  DPS is far, far,  better suited to making quick battle maps, and about 1000 times less complex to use.    The ease of use for making quality battle maps is the best I've seen in any app or on-line solution to date.  And the export function is super-simple to use to create correctly-scaled maps you can directly upload to
.
As a first release, I'm very impressed with the overall quality and stability of the program as well as the quality and amount of art work that is included with the package, especially for this low price-point (CC3+, while it is a true CAD program, is $40 for just the basic dungeon designer module).
Other than a few UI suggestions (such as being able to zoom in/out with CTRL+mousewheel, or having the [Esc] key exit any mode you're in) I have no complaints on the program operation.  As for the included art work, it is very nice and there is a fair amount of it.  I do wish there were a few more "standard" interior objects included (e.g. fireplaces, interior stairways, more house-type furniture, etc.)
Overall, this program is well-worth the price and very well suited for making role-playing battle maps that don't look like something your two-year-old drew.

As a reto-styled indie game, Oniken is hardly unique in premise. However; most retro-styled indie games are only "retro" in terms of visuals/sound and do not capture the enticing gameplay aspects of retro gaming. Retro games were about introducing new challenges to the player and making the most out of the limited hardware available at the time. Since graphical fidelity has progressed well past 8-bit sprites no indie game can capture the latter aspect, but Oniken certainly feels authentically retro because of its focus on platforming-action mechanics, challenging level design and simple but addictive weapons. This puts it well ahead of the curve as most other "retro" indie games have no depth to their game design and feel like performing a series of menial tasks.
Oniken borrows a lot of design cues from some of the best action platformers available on the NES such as ninja gaiden, pitting the player against a variety of different bosses, enemies and level hazards which encourage the player to memorise the levels and come up with their own solutions. It further mixes things up with auto-scrolling levels which take the form of either platforming challenges or run-n'-gun style vehicle levels where the player will have to time their shots and jumps right to proceed.
The quality of the movement system and the simple, responsive controls prevent all of this challenge from feeling tedious/frustrating, along with this the sword and grenade weapons although lacking in variety, feel versatile enough to reliably deal with everything the game throws at you if you are willing to think about how to get past new obstacles.
The most important part of all of this is that it does feel rewarding to progress, as the cutscenes are a great throwback to the 80's, with badass gruff characters, cheesy-but-likeable villains, insane campy stunts and true-to-NES seizure effects. Although Oniken could not get away with all the gore and swearing that it has if it was to be published on the NES in the 80's, it still feels like a love letter to the action heroes of the era. What feels even more rewarding is completing each level without dying, and then progressing through the levels quickly enough to get the steam achievements. It gives Oniken a lot of replay value and is a case of game achievements actually being done right (as in, it actually feels like you've achieved something in a sense).
Overall, Oniken stands up there with games like Shovel Knight, Satazius, and Cave Story as "retro-styled" indie games that are actually retro in terms of design and comes with all of the glorious challenge and fun that comes with this style of game design actually being executed correctly. One of the best things about retro action games was that you could actually become as badass as the protagonist by playing well, and Oniken captures this aspect perfectly.

The long and short of it is that this is the Space 4x we've been waiting for for 20 years. Were you disappointed in games like Endless Space, Horizon or Galactic Civilizations, games that ALMOST delivered what they promised but fell short in key areas? This game is for you. Taking cues from Master of Orion, and building on the first installment, this game feels like it hit a nearly perfect storm.
The planet management is deep, but not overly complex, the tech trees are interesting, exploration system is finely tuned, and the combat is a blast. Space combat is visceral and fun. Ground combat is a little bare bones, but deeper than it appears on the surface, and very difficult and satisfying.
There are many approaches to situations, and the dynamics between you and the rest of the galaxy is interesting and fun.
It isn't the perfect Space 4X, but that game hasn't been made yet. This is the best one made in modern times. Pick it up if you are a fan of the genre or have been sitting around since Master of Orion 2 wondering why someone couldn't do better in 20 damned years. Is it better than MOO2? I don't know, but it's a damned fine game.
Highly recommended, this game is a blast and a half.

The game isn't particularly taxing, but it effectively conveys its message through the narrator as well as the tone of the story, which is perfectly captured by the minimalist environments and the procedurally generated audio which mixes the soundtrack into an audio experience that exceeds the original tracks.
In all, I'd recommend this game - but try to get your hands on a steam key from the Humble Bundle since it's been part of a bundle before!

Early Access disclaimer: When I buy an EA-Title, I buy what is there. Not nececarily what is to come. Also, as EA-Customer I view myself, and all other buyers, as Quality Management. We get something that is still not finished. Which means we have the possibility of giving input and also we work as quality control. It is to be expected that game crashing bugs arise. It is to be expected, that balancing will be off at some points. It has to be clear, that it is not a finished product. Which means I disregard issues of this kind, as something normal. Not something to ♥♥♥♥♥ about, as long as the issues are dealt with.
I used to work for a software company, so I do have a bit of insight on how the business works and more importantly, how long it can take to get stuff done. The devs here do have a nice level of communication with the community and most importantly: The SoG Devs are honest with what to expect from them. It's a team of 3 people and the level of care for each new implementation is big. I play Frontline, which means I expect crashes, broken Savestates etc. in exchange I get to play new content sooner. Still, I had yesterday my first crash with the game and never did I have a broken Savestate. I have seen "finished" games that did not perform as well as SoG. That level of care takes time. Which means. If you expect big updates on a regular basis, then you should not buy this game yet.
When I've first seen this game, it instantly reminded me of a mashup of Legend of Zelda and Secret of Mana. Which is and was exactly what I am looking for, since SoM is one of my all time favourites. So, after a few hours of reading through forums and the devblog I decided to buy the game. And I don't regret it. The game I have right now has given me plenty of fun time, enough to say this: I wouldn't be mad if they leave the project. I still have a game that is fun to play as is. But I am excited about every new content in Story Mode.
Bad things first. As of this moment there is only one thing I really dislike about Secrets of Grindea: No local Co-op and no direct plans for implementing one. I really hoped it would have a SoM like local co-op implementation and still hope it will get one. This is a game for the couch with friends. Period. I've found a dev comment within the forums that this topic is not entirely off the table, but also it's not sure to come. So that is the one big minus from me for the following reason:
When this game will be finished, I will probably have already played it through 10+ times (I have finished my 4th playthrough already.) since I replay the whole game with every new major update (i. e. when there's a new region to explore.) to systematically look for bugs. As said I view myself as QC.
Starting the game for the first time, the game didn't feel like an alpha or early access in general. The parts done seem to be done. The graphics are nice and feel exactly right. With little use of placeholders. If placeholders are used, they too fit well enough to be regarded as satisfactory. Which gets me to the second "bad thing" - which I personally do not regard as bad, but others do, soooo... the time between major updates is rather long which makes the game progress rather slow.
Personally I think this is a good thing. If you watch the Devblog, you'll get information on what work they do right now and how they progress. It's in not on hiatus, but the devs take the time they need to finish the game as they want it to be. I'd hate a rushed process, just because of *bleep* ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that have nothing else to do as to ♥♥♥♥♥ around. Those kind of people will be the first to ♥♥♥♥♥ if the game is rushed and not polished enough. So yeah, I don't care how much time it takes, as long as I see that there's work done and progress made.
As we start the game we have the possibility of character customization. Meaning that we can choose our name, sex, hairdo, hair color and the color of our clothing. In general, we have a solid, not too fancy character customization.
You can equip different types of armarment for Stat purposes. In addition you can also choose a weapon, shield, hat or facegear for decoration, which will be seen ingame, if you fancy the look of a different weapon instead of the one you're currently wielding. That's an elegant solution to the age old problem of "Oh, this new weapon is badass! *equip* that's bloody ugly". I cherish that.
Also you have 12 commandslots at hand, which you can fill with items, weapons or spells. Makes for comfortable controls.
The game contains 24 skills at the time. 7 passive skills are still not implemented. The skills you get to choose from are either Melee-, Magic- or Support-Types. Each skill has 10 Levels of it's own. You pay for a level with Skillpoints. Skillpoints come in two types.
Blue ones, which pay for level 1 to 5.
Golden ones, which pay for level 6 to 10.
The game also contains a Talenttree with 30 Talents in total. Talents can have level up to 3 or 5 with Talentpoints.
Obviously you get those points through leveling up.
Your aim is to collect cards and do quests. While you do that you get around the World. Which has 7 differently themed areas for now.
There's a card for every Monstertype except Bosses. Cards give passive boosts and are somewhat rare drops. You get them through Mobgrinding. The enemies respawn continously within the area, which allows for easy grinding.
You can get different pets, which give you stat-boosts as you train (feed) them. You choose one which walks around you. You can also change their skins/color.
Also you can craft a lot of different items. Which is rather simple. Just navigate through the receipe list and if you have enough materials, you can craft the item, wherever you are, at whatever time. As long as you can get into the menu, you can do that.
You have also the option to buy a house and decorate it. Since this is from the latest update I can't tell that much about it. Haven't used this function enough.
If you like Pixelart, you will like this game's look. The artdesign is nice and with high level of detail. It feels just right.

So, 9/10 from me.

I realize I'm going to be bashed in the comments by a bunch of fan boys and that's fine because personally after painfully trying to play this game for as long as I did and that I struggled to attempt to enjoy it I don't mind people insulting me, at least I didn't waste perfectly good drinking money on them.
Let me start off with saying I loved StarDrive, it still remains one of my favorite games I've played. The dev had quite the gem with it and because of StarDrive, I had no hesitation whatsoever to purchase StarDrive 2, especially after the wonderful discovery of ground combat being added, even bought the digital deluxe one just to show support. I also tried so very hard to enjoy this game, I really did.
This game is a sham and a huge letdown, I haven't been this disappointed in a game since Unity came out after Black Flag, and CA tried to pass off Rome 2 as a playable game on launch.
Pros
-Customizable ships (Although was far superior in StarDrive 1 as well)
-Ground combat (Or well, the idea of it anyways.)
-4x space game worth playing (When talking about StarDrive 1)
Cons
-Ground combat (As it's far too easy and seems to be more of an aesthetic feature than anything serious)
-Space Combat (StarDrive 1 was far superior to this drivel of a combat simulator, again this is far too easy. Also to mention that in StarDrive 1 you were able to move your ships into systems and they would automatically battle to the death with aliens, not some little battle screen that takes away the fun of the old combat system)
-Tech Tree (Now I understand the thrill of being able to only choose one tech from a branch at a time and having to plan it out ahead of time but it gets way too old, far too fast. Being able to build onto previous techs is far more realistic than saying "Oh hey, should we focus on a rover bay or xeno mine?" Then you choose one, then suddenly "Well that's that, why should we bother with the other?" Now I didn't get too far in detail in the tech tree and if you are capable of going back to research the ones you didn't pick please leave an insulting comment down below although according to the tutorial you had to pick the other ones up through espionage or diplomacy which is fine if you want to get them that way but let us build on as in the first StarDrive)
-Turn based (Now the beauty of StarDrive 1 was that it was automatic turns that happened every 4 seconds if I recall correctly (Please leave an insulting comment down below if I'm wrong) having to manually click to the next turn gets irritating because it allows you to ensure everything is done before you want to move on. In my opinion this makes the game far too easy because you never get caught out of sync and have to deal with a random invasion out of the blue, and holding the space button is just demented, they should have added a feature in the menu that lets you select continuous play or turn based. That feature actually set StarDrive 1 apart from Gal Civ for me and pushed it to my favorite.)
-Customizable Ships (It feels like the ship design has been modified to make it "Easier" but far less creative and worthwhile)
-Feels like a dummed down version of the original StarDrive with some aesthetic looks to make it smell less foul.
I really am disappointed in Zero and sad to say he's been added to the list of terrible devs. If you have any soul or self respect left, please refund my money. I realize you won't, but you can't blame a guy for trying although I just want the money back for the principal. You may try and pretend that this is "an exciting and evolutionary step forward for the StarDrive franchise." But, in actuality it's a sad step backwards. Let's not try to take crap and call it gold, let's just call it for what it is. Even if you won't refund my money, please take this atrocity down from steam and give us an actual enjoyable experience that I came to expect from you. And as stated above, if any fan boys want to insult me, I welcome your comments. Make sure they're extra spicy as well please.

This review is based upon Never Alone & Foxtales DLC.
The game is a puzzle-platformer heavily influenced by Alaskan culture, told by the Iñupiat people. It follows Nuna and Fox as the two main protagonists. This game came out and I had an absolute blast playing it.  In terms of enjoyment, this game (initially) gave me more enjoyment than most games i've played in my entire life.  The intensity was great at times, and the game was so funny at others.  Discovering the game and slowly peeling it's layers with the people who played at the time was just a thrill.  If I never play this game again, I will say it was worth what I paid just for those first couple months.  Met cool people, didn't have to work for two weeks when this was released so I played it ridiculous, and to my amazement I was one of the higher level players (at the time) and when I pulled out my final Jason (Level 32 I think) I regularly heard others gasp in awe because they hand't seen him yet.  That's how new and fresh and exciting this whole thing was.
But then... they had some double xp weekend and released a new patch with nintendo jason skin... but a bug stopped me from being able to play and nobody else seemed to have the issues at the time so everybody pretty much wrote it off.  I will admit this left a bitter taste in my mouth and caused me to stop playing for awhile.
Fast forward a few weeks ago, picked it up again and the game seems to have regressed a lot... I'm somewhat in awe.  The maps have shrunk. DLC is being added.  The single player story mode is not here (seems to be retconned too).  Still a glitchy mess (Initially didn't bother me as I overlooked it for just launching), and servers are still randomized in ridiculous ways. And the one that really got me in the past, allowing 3rd party programs to run while this game is being played.  You kill somebody, they look at campground cams and stuff only to say on skype or discord "hey jasons here" and crap like that... that is infuriating in this kind of game.  Especially when they have chat set a certain way for a certain reason.
The major reason I can no longer recommend this game however... is this.
Jason sometimes gets surrounded and fought (which is completely fair) in these hilarious and amazing fights that are generally centered around a car escape etc.  That was the intensity in this game and the core of it.  Jason has somebody in a grip, "TOMMY SHOOT HIM SAVE ME!" Tommy panics and fires... wounding jason but killing the player. This upset a lot of people over time. Sometimes they would insist they shot Jason from such a way they couldn't have hit the player, othertimes you would be dead on and the shotgun did absolutely nothing... but regardless if they are a bad shot, a troll, just panicked etc...   Rather than fix the poor hit detection (this is what was REALLY making people mad) Or fixing Jasons grip to simply have a player (push E to save them) Or adding a lock on ability while in combat mode... Rather than fix the long♥♥♥♥♥kill animations to be interupted under certain circumstances...
They said, hey screw it take out team damage because it's making people mad and a few people kill other players.  But the truth is... the streamers were getting trolled.  It all came down to the streamers.  Which is really upsetting because now trolls can just grab keys and run off and hide.  That battery sitting by the car, no not there anymore because Chad grabbed it and is running to hide it somewhere... oh if only he could be killed because he's trolling the hell out of us and now jason just lets him go past.
The core of the game itself is damaged.  Now, the few people who got trolled a few games out of 20-30 (it was over exaggerated) removed the mechanic that made the game what it was by keeping everybody in check. It made you tense, people would fight over boats and cars (and guess what, they would in real life too) sometimes... and others somebody would make the choice to stay (this is most often what happened)  but the uncertainty and ability to try to survive and screw people over is what made this realistic.  Now... instead you have forcibly changed peoples styles of play and it hurts the game as a whole.  It doesn't feel fun anymore like it did.
Final Note - I will keep revisiting this game periodically and will change my review as updates continue.

TLDR
The game looks great and it offers a very well-made documentary about the Alaskan natives but unlocking the documentary requires playing a boring and tedious platformer that fails to offer any real enjoyment or creative level design.
This game has a lot of problems.  For one, it's a documentary pretending to be a video game, leaving most of the game aspects subpar at best.  Controls are sluggish and glitchy, often resulting in the main character getting stuck midair or falling to her death after sliding off of a cliff due to the delay between commanding her to jump and her actually jumping.  Other issues include poor camera management that occasionally leaves one character off screen and inconsistent mechanics that allow water to kill you in most levels except one.  Lastly, controlling the Bola is a huge pain and pretty much impossible to use with any real accuracy.
Most of the puzzles consist merely of jumping from one ledge to another.  I'd say there are less than 5 actual puzzles (consisting of more than just platforming) in the entire game, summing to less than 30 minutes of play time.  These puzzles were enjoyable, but you do spend an awful lot of time simply walking and jumping from left to right.
The culture insights to the Alaskan natives are very well presented and you're pretty much guaranteed to unlock all 24 of them as you play through the game.  I think only 2 of them are missable.  Watching these videos as they unlock is necessary in order to understand the content of each level (such as why the northern lights want to hug you to death or why midget natives live underground), yet some of the videos also spoil upcoming game content in the levels.  So you lose out on the gaming aspects if you watch the videos but you lose out on understanding the setting if you don't.  This makes for a lose-lose situation either way.
The game itself directly follows a story of the Alaskan natives, and I'd say each level fits very well with the narration.  The story isn't spectacular, but at least it adds some meaning to your otherwise suicidal wandering through the blizzard.  There's only one thing about the story I didn't understand: how does chipping an axe have anything to do with caribou feet?  This is a rather strange ending to an otherwise interesting fable about the cause of a blizzard.

What can I say about Rocksmith that hasn't already been said... In short, this software is absolutely amazing.
I have a hard time calling Rocksmith 2014 a "game". It's more of an absolutely massive software package featuring many of both learning tools and games in a beautifully intertwined and perfectly balanced format. Everything within this software is meant to help you both learn and improve your skills on guitar and bass, and have fun doing it.
Let's say you're a complete novice. You've picked up a guitar once or twice in your life, strummed some strings, and probably thought maybe this is too hard, as all the neighborhood household pets scream in terror/anguish and attack you on sight. But fret not my poor mangled friend, for Rocksmith 2014 will pick you up off the ground, show you how to hold the instrument upside right, and guide your dainty fingers heavenly across the strings and make you feel like you're a rock god(dess).
I say dainty, because as a warning, if you don't play guitar or practice any other highly strenuous fingering activity (okay, calm down kiddos) you will be fighting both your learning mentally, and physically as your fingers will need to bulk up quite a bit to get these skills under your belt. So don't feel discouraged if the skills feel impossible or out of your grasp. Keep practicing, and keep playing mini games (especially with chords). You'll get there :) Oh, and that stinging/burning/flamesfromhell feeling you are having on your finger tips, that goes away after about a week. As with all feeling at all, so enjoy that.
Anyways, back on track. Rocksmith does this by first asking you how skilled you feel you are with guitar. It'll then ask you a few more questions to get an idea of what kind of guitar player you are. If you go with novice, it'll show you everything from how to attach your guitar strap, hold your guitar/pick, etc to how to actually pluck strings and play notes. (You can obviously skip the super basic stuff by picking one of the 3 higher experience levels)
It then throws you into a song at a super basic level, and from that point on (through almost everything you do) it guides you through everything you need to know/do/practice to get better at guitar. It adapts itself and the difficulty of the songs you play so it's constantly pushing you to do better. It provides you with a lot of things to help you along the way as well. 2 primary things:
1) The Lessons portion of the software actually teaches you, in a very interactive manner, things you need to know to play guitar, as well as own them and take care of them. Want to know how to string a guitar? It has you covered. Want to learn how to play scales, chords, notes, slides, bends, harmonics, and much much more? It'll teach you what you need to know, and coach you through it with advice such as "It sounds like you have a finger touching the G string..." (again, kiddos, lets keep it PG, eh?) "... try it again, being sure your second finger is only touching the string(s) it should be."
2) The Guitarcade. This section of the software is a whole suite full of very well made arcade style mini games that allow you to practice almost everything learned in the Lessons section of the software in a fun, score centric environment. There are arcade games that allow you to shoot a target by picking the designated string at the fret shown on screen, games that give you a chord that you must form and strum to shoot down an enemy space ship, "String Skip" which is pretty self explanatory, and lots lots more.
All along the way, Rocksmith is going to be giving you multiple suggestions for what you should do next so you don't get lost, however you still remain free to do as you please. Between the lessons and mini games, and the actual main portion of the software which is the Guitar Hero meets Guitar style gameplay (which is of course very fun and productive) you're going to learn and/or improve your guitar and bass playing abilities.
One last thing. The Session Mode. It's hard for me to put my excitement concerning this feature into words, so I'll keep this short. Try it out, you'll absolutely love it and will spend a lot of time there as you grow your articulation skills. It shows you a scale based on your settings (of which there are many) and allows you to play along a fully dynamic band that plays to your music. The band is entirely customizable, or you can pick from dozens of preset bands that include drums, bass, rhythm guitar, lead guitar, and piano/other instruments. If you stick to the scale, it'll sound really good to you, pretty much regardless of your skill which encourages you to really work at it and keep coming back for a couple hours a day. This is a great learning tool for scales, and also wonderful for your motivation. I recommend playing 30 minutes at least of Session Mode at the end of every time you play.
TL;DR: Buy this. You'll love it. It's going to blow your expectations away. This is an incredibly valuable tool for any present/future guitarist.

-The servers, which aren't a big problem for me, but is for a lot of people. Such as having a group of friends, with 2 of them lagging out, which ruins the fun.
-Pay to Play. It's not as major as in most games, but if you pay for steel (Or that EXP pass thingy), you level up much faster, with higher tier gear being available sooner. This gives the terrible result of a prestige 25 guy being up against a prestige 108 and getting shredded since the matchmaking puts highly skilled players against decent or just starting players.
Those are my opinions on For Honor. In the end I enjoy this game, but it's not for everyone.

Alright, so Ive played Secrets of Grindea for nearly 100 hours, here's what I have to say about the game so far.
First of all, I'd like to say that Secrets of Grindea can easily be seen as repetitive to those who don't manage to see the beauty of this game beyond just the "grinding". When this game first came out, I was the same way. But now that the developers have worked on this game and polished it up more and more, I've begun to enjoy it more as well.
So, the plot of the story is pretty good! I actually felt compelled to "end" of the story (at the time of writing this the game is not yet entirely done) and see what lies ahead. The characters are actually very memorable! And the names, dont even get me started, are pretty funny if you can catch afew puns here and there in them.
The mechanics are pretty explanitory in the name of the game itself. There is a chance you'll have to do A LOT of grinding if you're new to this kind of game or just want to kinda play it as it was designed to be played. The grinding is actually not boring, since you are actually doing it not just for money, or EXP, but for the rare cards that give you permanant bonuses that will help you out in the long run.
Since there are an abundance of items in this game, you can experiment with different setups. Whether it be 1 Handed, 2 Handed, or Magic, there is plenty for you to play for 15$. Though, at the moment, for me what seems to be the most powerful is Magic (Flamethrower and Cloud are OP in hard mode) and 1H (Shadow Clone is really good).
Now let me just explain a few negatives of this game.
The game can be kind of short depending on how fast you play and what you decide to do along your journey. Even though I took 100 hours, that doesnt quite mean that the game is extremely long, it just means I took my time to go through this game (obviously).
I would like to ask the developers to possibly add a warning regarding taking your character to frontline mode. I recently put my character into the frontline beta mode and now I cannot take my character out of frontline. Please add a better warning so other people dont have to spend 40+ hours trying to get a new character up to speed with their original.
Last Id like to say that sometimes the artstyle sort of changes on the characters picture (the one that pops up when you engage in a convo with them) that can kind of feel slightly out of place. Im not saying it ruins the game drastically but perhaps the devs could look at it if they could and fix that XD
Thanks for making a good game on steam! Im so glad I invested 15$ for some good quality 18 bit awesomeness ^__^

You know, I've never really liked those old NES games, the super difficult ones. They don't really hold up today that well imo. Same goes for all these retro NES inspired games, it always striked me as lazy when devs rely on nostalgia and outdated game mechanics. However, Oniken is a game that made me question this bias of mine. I was originally drawn to it by the cool 1980's sci fi aesthetic, with references to old movies like Terminator and Aliens. When I started it, I was treated to an awesome cinematic of a postapocalytic world ruled by Cyborges, and a fantastic soundtrack that really got me in the mood. Upon playing it, I died frequently and got frustrated, but I kept coming back for more. That's the power of this game, it get's its claws into you and wont let go. You know, I think the challange is one of the things that keeps the game interesting. Game devs nowadays don't understand that an overly easy game just becomes boring and repetetive after a while. Human beings want to overcome obsticles, it gives them a sense of accomplishment. How can you get that when your game is simple childs play?
Anyways, if there is one gripe I have towards this game............ Actually naw, there's nothing wrong with it that I can think of. Just a really fun and addictive game, with a badass soundtrack and 1980's look and feel. Highly reccomend it!

So, I have never played The Darkness series, but I was told to play the first one, since steam didn't have the first darkness game, I played this one instead. The story is mediocre, and has moments that make you think, then it's explained near the end. The conclusions aren't the best, and the endings aren't bad, but they didn't have much emphasis or build up. But don't let that discourage you, I love amazing stories, but even with a somewhat mediocre campaign, the gameplay is sure as all fun. I played on the hardest difficulty and the abilites, few weapons, and things you can do is fun. It's a hassle to play on a keyboard a bit, so I recomend a controller. If you haven't played the first Darkness game, then you might be a bit lost on some characters. There is a scene you can play to know what happened in the first game, and the characters you pick up who they are even if you are new to the series, but the characters that have things happen to them don't have much feeling or build up for what happens, you don't feel remorse unless you played the first. It does have a multiplayer mode, but it is mostly Jackie's abilities split between the characters. It is a seperate campaign with more lore, but isn't needed. It can be fun but can get boring quickly. Here's a quick list of the goods and bads
GOOD
-Fun gameplay
-Fun abilities
-Unique locations
BAD
-Somewhat required to play the first Darkness game
-Keyboard users may have a bit of difficulty
-Bosses aren't diffuclt even on the hardest difficulty
Overall, The Darkness II isn't bad, but it isn't that good, I would recommend getting the game when it is ever on sale. It's absolutely fun and the game is interesting, so I'l give the game a rating of 7/10.

What an experience! A unqiue, original game. It's a horror game with puzzle elements essentially, and I loved it. So the theme is very similar to that of Amnesia's and was made by the same team (I believe.) The game's premese is testing facilities, underwater with killer robots, and abominations running rampid. As soon as I got control of the character I knew it had very similar mechanics to Amnesia's, the physics, throwing abjects to produce noise, and so on. The game is linear, I'll say that off the bat, there is quite a bit of exploration to be had however, not multiple routes, but rooms where you can gain information about what's going on. The puzzles can be a bit confusing, I only got stuck on one of them, so I imagine they could be frustrating for people who dislike puzzles or are bad at them. I spent quite a bit of time getting lost/confused because I miss obvious things very easily :P. The game's story is fantastic, and is very enjoyable to unravel the mystery, and what needs to be done. That's all I can say really, a really great horror game with puzzle mechanics. I'd say avoid if you're really bad at puzzles, otherwise, I recommend it, great game, maybe wait for it to go on sale, because 30 euro is a bit pricy for a few hours, but it was a fun game. There's also workshop support for the game, need to go have a look, which may extend the gameplay time!

(Sorry for my english) For the moments, I have only play 2 hours on this game, so here my impression of the game.
First a little explanation of the game, we player, have to manage a forts and we have to defend the core, in that case we need to builds and reinforces the forts, makes ressources with mines and energies with the winds turbines, and we need to defend it with machine guns but we also need to attack with motars, missiles or big artillery. In a game who remind me some of the games I give below.
His gameplay;
The gameplay is a mix of Worms (for the destructions and weapons, and the characters designs in the games remind me the worms), Polybridge (for the construction and architectures of your base/forts) and World of Goo (for the physics of the contruction of your base).  The system of construction is very simple at the beggining but become more harder with times or maps (exemple : The forts hangs on the mountains), the system of weapon is also simple but if you didn't managed to builds your forts correctly your weapons can becomes totaly useless or a target to aim...
The sounds;
The sounds of the game (not the music) is pretty useful for trying to guess what is the aim of the enemy (because the sound of the constructions and weapons is listenable from the players).
And the music, for the moment I did'nt have a music I love to listening to...
Graphics;
I like the drawing-like graphics they are soft and easy to load for a potato computer like mine, and it's rare for a new game to be playable on my computer ^^
Story / Skirmish / Sandbox / Multiplayer/ Map Creator;
The campaign is a hidden tutorial with a context for the characters desgins and why we fights in this game.
Skirmish and Multiplayer, the pure game, but I hear there problems of disconnection in multiplayers (when I write).
Sandbox, the place where you train yourself to aims or builds.
Map Creator, the map creator seem to be very difficult to used...
Pros
The game as a good frame rate for potato computer with good looking graphics.
It's fun to kill slowy your enemy and let him thinks he as a chance to win but you kill him with a plasma/laser shot directly in the core.
Cons
There only a few weapons for the moments (only Machine Gun, Sniper, Mortar, Missile Base, Big Artillery and Laser Artillery with their upgrades), I thinks it will be great to add more weapons like flamethrower, light artillery, aa guns or a possibility to do Airstrike. Or even to make a ground/air army (like a casern/airport you put it in the forts).
The Map Creator is very difficult to use for me (it's for that I said "seem"), I think if it was way easier I will pass hours to create maps ^^
To conclude, I recommend the game if you love a RTS and Construction game.

I tried out this game recently after a friend said I would love this game,and MAN was he right :).
The plot is about an unnamed man(the character you play as),who has recurring nightmares about a sawmill and a woman named Anna. As you investigate the sawmill,finding various items and intuitions(basically little bits and pieces of your character's memories),you begin to find out the whole story of just what happened in the sawmill,who Anna is,and just what our character did to Anna,witnessing several horrifying events as you piece together the truth.
The characters are pretty good,especially that wood mannequin that looks like a woman(I can't reveal who the mannequin is because of spoilers),which creeped me out/scared me several times in my 10 hour playthrough. xD
The music is really good,especially the music that plays during when you're outside the sawmill,and the credits themes.
The atmosphere in this game is amazing,where one moment you have that music from outside the sawmill playing,making you feel all safe,and then the next there's some creepy music with that mannequin woman right in your face.
The gameplay is pretty great,which involves solving dif puzzles to progress,and after Stage 2,a sanity meter is added,which lowers the longer you look at a"creepy event"(an example would be looking at the woman mannequin for too long).
The puzzles are kinda challenging your first time through,and the difficulty of the puzzles really depends on if you know what you're doing,and have the items you need(which sometimes your first time through you can miss,believe me I missed about 4 items in Living Quarters,and had to go back there 4 times xD)
Overall,this is a VERY good horror game that I recommend to everyone,even those that haven't played horror puzzle games like this.
9.5/10 from me :)

-The servers, which aren't a big problem for me, but is for a lot of people. Such as having a group of friends, with 2 of them lagging out, which ruins the fun.
-Pay to Play. It's not as major as in most games, but if you pay for steel (Or that EXP pass thingy), you level up much faster, with higher tier gear being available sooner. First, let me say that half the reason I'm typing this out is to take inventory of my thoughts on it. This is an outstanding game, and loads of fun. Let me say that you DO NOT want to buy it at full price, at least not in its current state. I've played since the open beta, and even with the complaints I have, I'll continue to do so. The combat system is technical yet fluid, has several distinct tiers of player skill, and is surprisingly addictive. Now, who's ready for the string of giant BUTS that follow?
1) The netcode is a CRIME AGAINST GOD AND MAN. Famously so. This game uses a 'novel new peer-to-peer layout system' or some such that... actually worked great for a lot of people for the first couple weeks of release. Many of us it never worked for, some of us still have it working fine, and some of us had it crap out a couple weeks in thanks to an alleged 'fix' that they made. Somehow, I don't know how, the first patch to improve network functionality did the precise opposite for more than a couple players, myself included, and made us experience the same connectivity problems as the players who'd been having them from day one. On to the problems you get when it's not working great.
Let's tackle the elephant in the room here first: the random disconnects. Sometimes you can fail matchmaking ten times in a row, only to be abruptly kicked within two minutes when you finally get into a match, or you can get up to the last few moments of a match and then be suddenly disconnected, making the fifteen minutes you just spent fighting moot. There are NO warning signs as to when this could happen, and you start living in paranoia. Next, there is a constant level of lag for everyone that isn't the host,
. Lastly, and this one hits everybody, the matchmaking is prone to crashing out of the lobby and/or hanging, and for some reason it'll sometimes try for ten minutes to connect to a full lobby. They could try to patch up their P2P networking into something usable, or they could just set up a goddamned server, it's not that hard. I'll personally be fine with either.
2) Not the game itself, per se, but the community is cancerous. I don't just mean that people get salty when they lose. No. It's a blight. So much so as to be off-putting. This community is worse than
, which, for those of you unfamiliar, is already quite atrocious, and one-upping it is a goddamn accomplishment. This game needs chemo. Swastika and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥player emblems
(good luck playing an hour without seeing at least one, unless you keep disconnecting like in #1), people have complete double standards about play, cheap move combos that are counterable unless you're under any amount of lag (which you nigh on literally always are, see #1) get spammed right and left, people killsteal and run around hampering you with friendly fire that staggers but doesn't meaningfully damage... yeah. It's a real ♥♥♥♥♥how. Not recommended for those with thin skin or with no patience or sense of humour.
3) Where the DLC at? The season pass is an exorbitant FORTY dollars, and now, several months after launch, we've not even seen a release about what's supposed to be coming.
4) What the actual ♥♥♥♥ happened with the GUI? It looks beautiful! Most of it's laid out very logically! Unfortunately, the part where you actually INTERFACE with your gorgeous interface is all kinds of wonky, and seldom do you use the command you'd think you would to accomplish something in a menu. Furthermore, anything you're not intended to constantly use (like the report button) tends to wind up in some or other arcane and forgettable place, leaving you scrambling for the report button when you see your third swastika of the day cussing out everyone in the match over nothing, and find yourself tired of dealing with it.
5) Gaining ingame currency is... odd. A lot of people here are saying that it's a painfully slow process. Well, they're right. They're also wrong. See, in terms of actual
, it can be anywhere from glacial to lightning quick, as the best way of gaining currency is to either pay for it in the shop (see #6), or to do your daily assignments. Currency gain per completed match or story mission is negligible, which is problematic and actively discourages the longer play sessions pretty much everyone is inclined towards.
6) There are microtransactions in a paid game. That's kinda messed up, I think we can all agree on that much. Now, the nature of the transactions is a lot like in Warframe, where it's not so much 'pay to win' as 'pay to not have to farm like mad.' I personally don't mind that, but I know more than a few of you do, so I'm including it here.
Basically, if the gameplay wasn't so engaging, I'd think this was a mobile game. At the end of the day I'd recommend it, I guess. If Ubisoft can get their act together and give it some DLC, usable networking, and good, proper patches, it'll be one for the ages. Mileage may vary as to whether you think they will.
