Don't let this game fool you. While it may appear to be a run-of-the-mill indie minimilast platformer, Thomas Was Alone is actually full of unique beauty and depth. It is a minimalist platformer with minor puzzle elements centered around the journey of several differently colored squares. Each square surprisingly has a name and its own unique ability that helps itslef and others navigate the platformer world. There are 100 different stages divided into 10 chapters. The goal of each stage is to navigate your jumping square characters to their respective portals.
The brilliance and beauty of this game lies not in the gameplay itself (which was consistently fun throughout all 100 levels), but in the narrative. An amusing and insightful narrator presents the thoughts of the square characters throughout each level. These narratives actually flech out character for the 2D squares in better ways than I have seen in some A-list blockbuster htis.
The only gripe I have with this game is the ending. The narrative starts to get confusing towards the end and the final moments are more ambiguous than I hoped for in a game that made me care about the characters. Regardless, I have no qualms with calling Thomas Was Alone a beautiful game and an exemplar of why video games can indeed be considered art.

Frictional Games went in a slightly different direction this time, having the focus be more on story than scares. That's not to say it's not scary, it's still a horror game with a creepy atmosphere and monsters that you have to run or hide from, but I found it to not be as terrifying as their previous games. This is fine though, because the overall experience and the way the narrative is presented is excellent. I would consider SOMA to be more of a spooky adventure game as such.
Gameplay is nothing special. Progression is linear and the little puzzles and tasks are very simple, again because the focus is on story. I would prefer more puzzles but it's such a good story that I don't really mind. The main plot is easy enough to understand and there's a backstory to piece together for those interested. I like how much detail they put into the world of SOMA as well, and I think it's a step up from Amnesia and Penumbra in that regard. There's more voice acting than I expected but it's done very well and really adds to the experience.
About the story itself, I don't want to spoil anything so I'll just say that it kept me engaged and wanting to keep going all the way to the end. This game made me come away thinking a lot about it, and it has emotional impact for sure. Overall I really enjoyed playing SOMA and recommend it to anyone interested in existential sci-fi/horror.

This game is really quite enchanting. At least… for me it is.
Sounds a little weird, but it really is a wonderful little indie game. Getting to know the characters and watch how things progress was a great experience. Especially seeing as the characters are common shapes. They aren’t exactly things you would usually try to make an emotional connection with.
In fact, the whole thing kind of reminds me of an experience I had when I gave gel pens personality’s and made up a story about them in my head whilst on MDMA once. The shapes in this game being the gel pens and the guy narrating being me. Weird, I know. But this game reminds me of that bazaar experience. You grow to like the characters and there little ponderings about who or what they are.
It has beautiful music to go along side it, and even though the graphics may be simple, they more than definitely do the trick at setting the scene. It’s simplistic but in a good way. I guess it makes it so you don’t get all that distracted from the story or the characters. Them being the main focus I would say.
The narration of the story was done well, a “quirky” Brit doing the voice was quite nice. I got the “Wheatley from portal 2” vibe off of it, but that may just be because they sound similar. I’ve noticed a few games that use the British narrator in a similar fashion.
It would be lie to say I followed the storyline 100% the whole way through, I’m even a little confused even after finishing it, but in a good way. A kind of curiosity which made me want to read up about it. Which I guess is always good, it shows that I found it intriguing.
The game is easily played through in one sitting (at least that was the case for me) but I quite liked the length of it, it wasn’t too long and it was quite easy to complete, achievements and all.
It feels good to have another 100% game and it was quite an easy one to get.
All in all I really liked this game, and would highly recommend it. If you love indie games this is definitely one to have. The whole thing with the characters being common shapes was a real plus for me, it makes the game more unique.
TL;DR : Intriguing story, likeable narrator, good characters, nice graphics, beautiful music and more. Definitely give it a go.

Many side-scrollers and platformers claim to play and / or feel like they're out of the 80's. Like they are from the (S)NES era.
Some of them really do look like NES games. Some of them look like HD NES games. Some of them claim to play like NES games while looking totally "new-age?". None of them really plays nor feels like old-school retro side-scrollers tho.
I'm not saying they're bad games. They mostly aren't. But they don't feel nor play like (S)NES games.
I was sure that Oniken is another one of those pixelated games that is super hard, claims to be "old-school" but doesn't feel or play like an NES classic and once again poor old Mets would be dissapointed.
I still gave it a shot and WOW! Just WOW!
Unlike any other false "old-school" games on Steam, Oniken keeps it simple: You have 2 different attacks (one of them being a pick-up), you can jump...and move back and forth. The game is hard tho. Not Ninja Gaiden hard, but hard. Challenging is the key word here.
The combat is smooth - Your main weapon is a sword (that looks like a katana) and you can throw grenades as a secondary weapon. Grenades are pick-ups tho and you can run out of them. You can also find secret 1-UPs and some sword power-ups if you get lucky.

I managed to finish the entire game in 6h...it's possible to speedrun through the game in 15-30 minutes tho. Just like with classic NES games. Their true lengths were about 15-40 minutes but they took hundreds, if not thousands, of tries to finish.
There are 6 stages and each stage takes you about 2-5 minutes...That is if you know what to expect and you're familiar with the level layout. The first playthrough will take some time. I especially hate level 4 which took me the longest amount of time to beat.

Combining high-speed/risk-reward gameplay evocative of RE6/Devil May Cry, and Michael Bay action/explosions Vanquish is an interesting blend of a bullet hell game mixed with stylish action. Getting up in the faces of enemies and learning their weaknesses to take them down efficiently combines with Max Payne-like bullet time to compensate for the sheer amount of enemy and enemy projectiles onscreen while making the player feel like a badass when they pull off multiple kills.
The most interesting aspect of putting pressure on the player is that aside from your ammo stores, your A.R.S meter is also linked to your reserves for sliding about and maintaining your mobility. The A.R.S meter drains whenever you use it to slow time down. In otherwords: Abusing and mismanaging bullet time is penalized heavily if you accidentally drain your bar fully, at which point you will be unable to slide and the I-frames and speed of your dodges are severely reduced. If you do not learn to maintain a balance and synergy in your tactics you will eventually get yourself killed. The bar will also rapidly drain if you take far too much damage, this again emphasizes the need to understand how enemies attack and how to quickly dismantle them if you want to get out unscathed. It feels great once you get the hang of it all and there are a few hidden mechanics to learn (deploying grenades while sliding and the "Smoke break." tricks.)
Each weapon has a unique functionality to varying levels of usefulness depending on how one plays. And certain enemies have specific behaviors that can be used against them (Romanovs). Flamethrower Romanovs can be killed instantly by shooting their fuel tanks enough, and the missile variant will somethimes fire a large warhead that can be shot as it is launched for an instant kill.
My biggest gripe with the game would be with God Hard difficulty, where the A.R.S bar depletes twice as fast in bullet time. The game starts to fall apart mechanically and rewards the player more for cheesing/abusing cover instead of getting into the fight, as A.R.S is much less useful, I concede that even in the "regular" difficulties the A.R.S bar should recharge a bit faster and have its duration reduced a bit to incentivize the player into using cover as little as possible if they're playing well. On God Hard, the game starts to become way too cover-centric and more of a frustrating ordeal.
As a PC port I'm extremely impressed, pretty well-optimized, SSAO support very straight-forward and functional keyboard/mouse support as well as the standard 360 controller. It's one of the few console TPSes I've ever played that felt just as much at home on mouse and keyboard as on its native controller.
The game is short and the story isn't really all that interesting, the learning curve is also a bit too oriented towards simply having good reflexes than I'd like, but it's definitely an experience I'd recommend.

Great game for passing time, and really good fun. I have made friends playing it. Would recomend.
Pros:
-Good Community, for the most part anyway. Some rude guys, but you always find them in every game.
-Challenging Level Curve, which means the game does not get borning. This is also under Cons, for reason listed there.
-Weekly Events, which offer a way to get to later game by farming enemies.
-Equal PvP in Early Game, meaning a new player isn't going to get attacked by veterans. You can only be attacked by players who are +/- 7 levels(I believe... not 100% sure on the max level difference)
-Good Alliance's, which is how you can advance faster as well as make friends.
Cons:
-Challenging Level Curve, which means that it can be hard to advance, as well as requiring some luck to get stuff done.
-Disappointing Updates, where the developer, Kixeye, releases "improvements" to the game that are not very good.
-Hard PvP at Late Game, since the moment you hit level 35, you can be attacked by anyone over level 35.
Overall:
I enjoy this game and, as I said, it is good for passing time. It is enjoyable as long as you do not get exteremly upset at how things go. Enjoy the fight, Rebel.
Updated Review:
Kixeye has continued to "update" the game, and it seems they are now trying to push away players who either cannot invest large amounts of money or time into the game. There is almost no early game support, with all events being targeted at end game players. It is very frustrating that, after all the time I have spent playing the game casually, it seems there is no longer a place for me in this game. Great job Kixeye... you ruined one of my favorite games.
Final Update:
Throughout the last few updates to the game, Kixeye has re-added some early game support, with easier events that allow early game players to advance easier. However, these events are not meant to push the player forward in little steps, but bring them straight into middle-late game, with some of the best stuff. While I am not necessarily upset by this, it is also frustrating that I put a bunch of time into the game, then had it mean nothing by just skipping ahead. This is probably the last time I am going to change this review, unless some major happens. Is the game perfect? No. Is it fixed? Not entirely. Is it getting better? Yes.

Don't come into it expecting this to be a new caveman Rimworld, or a Dwarf Fortress. While it has some similarities, that's not what this game tries to be, and it would be unfair to suggest otherwise.
The basics of the game revolve around you trying to lead your tribe of cavemen to greatness. This isn't done by advancing through ages and research or anything like that, but instead by building up your little settlement. More houses, monuments, vast storage areas filled with goodies, well equipped tribesmen; all are hallmarks of a successful tribe. The more prosperous your tribe, the more people will want to be a part of it, etc.
The game as it is is fun. If you like management games, you'll be at least somewhat familiar with this, though there's a lot of focus on having a dynamic environment; more so than most anything else out there. Rivers and ground can freeze over in winter, making it not only cold, but harder to get water. Spring rains can flood areas of the map, etc. This affects your settlement in more than just the obvious ways too. If water builds up in your storage areas, things can go bad quickly. Same goes with storing food out in the heat, and so on. While it's not overbearingly harsh, it might may you take a second longer to consider how you'll plan things out.
Not everything is rosy though. The game is certainly lackluster when it comes to graphics, and the user interface is pretty clunky. Those are honestly the biggest complaints I have for it though, other than no multiplayer. :p
The price point seems pretty fair as well. It's a game you could easily sink a few hours into, possibly on a few occasions, but it's not going to consume your life for weeks on end.
Tribe of Pok is what it is, and it's a pretty decent game if that's what you're expecting out of it.

This is my first review on steam, because most games that I find noteworthy either flounder without comment or get a trove of people giving feedback within a few days.
Tribe of Pok is a simulation game about controlling a primitive tribe, and whatever that means to you. They can starve or prosper at your whim, or by your ignorance. That being said, like many modern simulation games it is made in a popular niche of the genre. The most similar, currently popular, game in my opinion that is in this same niche is Rimworld.
That being said, there are several more established games that it bears similarities to, such as Dwarf Fortress, that I won't put in the same bag because they have been around for a long time and have a huge establishment of fans and supporters who help update it and make it accessible to new players.
So, going back to Rimworld as the most apt comparison ;
Rimworld had a
pre-beta/pre-alpha (Not really because then it would typically be unplayable but that's the common marketing language for "not finished") phase before it came onto steam, which immediately marks it as unfair competition. It was shown to the public before widespread release, and got feedback before hitting major sellers. So, on the developmental scale it is not a fair comparison. The popular Rimworld that most people know is far past Tribe of Pok, and was by the time most people got it.
An apt anology would be if someone showed you two tapes of basketball players, but one was from the NBA and the other was from their nephew's middle school. Yes, they're both basketball players. Yes you got them presented to you in similar time. But they were not given to you at the same time in the player's progression, you know that the NBA player had to have had middle school experience, but you didn't see it and you didn't look for it beforehand.
So now that the development and gameplay comparison is out of the way, compare the graphics between Tribe of Pok and Rimworld ;
or at least not
. Games are a largely artistic medium, granted they're an interactive one but they're one regardless. As such you can't hold them in the same standard based on your views. I can't say that red is a bad color because my favorite color is green. The two games did
try to have similar graphics, and so they can't be compared. You might like one, you might hate the other, oh well that's subjective. I personally find both charming for different reasons, Rimworld is more sleek, but Tribe of Pok feels more cutesy in its simplicity. This, in my mind, makes me expect more from my colonists in Rimworld and berate them when they fail, but I end up cheering for the tribespeople because they feel simpler. Most people get a feel for the world by the graphics, and if the world looks sophisticated I want sophisticated behavior from the people.
I have approximately 4 hours in Tribe of Pok at the time of writing. I didn't delay on the menu or pad my time artificially, this was all in play time. That being said I only JUST finished the base tutorial, I'm right at the diplomacy unlocked point. I could've beelined the tutorial but I spent a lot of time not making shirts and instead building up a larder and digging trenches to collect rain water.
In these four hours I have not noticed any issues, everything I tried to do I could do without an issue on the game's part. What Tribe of Pok tries to do, in my opinion, it does well. It doesn't try to make you build a giant fort with the expectation that you are willing to lose a hundred times just for the one time you survive your first month in game. It doesn't expect you to build a giant wall and cower inside of it until your stomach growls. It expects you to want to guide a tribe of neolithic people, and be almost directly responsible for the story that unfolds. On that part, it succeeds.
Tribe of Pok is not like similar games in the genre when compared in context. It simulates a lot of things in a very narrow scope, instead of few things on grand scale. This narrow scope means that the developers have no choice but to notice any glaring bugs and stomp them out before an update, and fine tune minor features later.
What it does, it does well in my opinion.

Fair disclosure, I'm a alpha/beta tester of this game. Sunk a good 200 hours of time into this game throughout it's development cycle.
This game styles itself as a kind of spiritual successor to MoO2. It's a mix of turn based strategy with real time tactical combat. Because the game instances the fights, similar to Total War (But in space), the game is able to support hundreds of fleets, and thousands of ships in the same galaxy.
The main feature of this game is that, like in SD1, you design the ships you take into combat. There's a few pictures on the store page that depict it. You can design your ships to do whatever you want them to do in combat. You can load them down with fighter bays and kill your enemies with bug bites, artillery ships that stay far back and lob Gauss cannon rounds and torpedoes, short range anti-fighter ships with beam and flak weaponry, or ships that combine multiple features. By far, this is one of my favorite features of the game. There's nothing like designing your own fleets to send against your enemies.
The replayability is also great because of the customization options for your species, and because each species gets their own unique technologies. Both ground combat and space combat can be autoresolved based upon the relative strength of your forces VS the enemy's forces. This is helpful in the late game, when there are a lot of small skirmishes (Which I usually autoresolve) and a few huge battles (Which I command myself).
All in all, I think this is a wonderful 4x game. I'd suggest it to anyone who enjoys strategy/4x games, and for sure anyone who played and enjoyed MoO2.

I can't really recommend this game.
I admit, I haven't played it for the 15 hours or whatever is the accepted standard around here for a review to be credible, but it is my opinion that first impressions are everything.  And my first impression with this game is not good.
You control a tribe of stone-age villagers and take care of them, building shelter, collecting resources like wood, furs, and food, have them make tools and weapons to defend themselves from neighboring tribes and make their lives easier, etc.
The premise is good, where it falls apart is the execution.  I'll confess, the whole time I've been playing the game, I was thinking to myself "This is essentially Dwarf Fortress or RimWorld, but with far less variety in things to do."  And that's what this game is to me, more simplistic Dwarf Fortress, or Gnomoria, or Towns, or Stonehearth, or whatever village-simulator game you play.
The graphics for this game are, to put it simply, terrible.  2d sprites that bounce around the screen and bounce off each other to simulate fighting.  And yes, I play Dwarf Fortress, which has NO graphics to speak of, but in my opinion that allows one's imagination to fill in the gaps, whereas this half-hearted attempt at graphics is depressing, everything is either a dull shade of green, or blue for water.
The UI is a lot like Gnomoria or Towns, which aren't very good as far as user interfaces go anyway, not much to say there except theres a lot of digging through menus to get to the thing you want to do.
The pace of the game is very slow, and villagers never seem to get around to doing something that you want done quickly.  There doesn't seem to be a "priority" system in place, and your food will sit on the ground rotting whilst your villagers shamble over and collect that 500th piece of long grass that just HAS to get collected now.
Combat in the game is very simple, make sure your villagers have stone spears (more menu digging to make sure of that!) and then enter combat mode, right click on target, and they go and kill it.  Your villagers don't typically lose to animals, especially if they team up on them, but the animals seem wildly aggressive, how often do you think a giant sloth goes sprinting into your camp attempting to murder everyone?  Yes, giant sloth, sprinting, you read that correctly.
The TL;DR version: save your money.  Dwarf Fortress is way more in-depth, has graphics packs that look way better than this game, and is completely free.  This is a knock-off that dares to charge 9 dollars for the "privelege."

This is the first Jagged Alliance game I've played that I wanted to be over. At one point, I was only playing just for the tactical combat, which is a sad thing because as any JA fan knows, the game was about much, much more.
Where the original franchise shone (JA, JA2, Deadly Games) was the attention to detail, the amazing voice acting and characterizations, the humor, strategic depth, the fact that all the mercs and NPCs felt "alive". It felt like you were in an interactive movie, not playing the game.
I logged hundreds of hours playing the original JA series, and I didn't want it to end! Sadly, I couldn't wait to finish this one...
(updated 25 June: since i realized some readers may want to know why)
Pros:
Not many. Tactical combat is acceptable. Weapons appear to be realistic and follow physics models when deciding outcomes. The battles made the game bearable.
Cons:
Voice acting nowhere close to the original JA series. Characters feel empty and 2-dimensional. NPCs could be developed more.
Storyline was blah. I guess they did the best they could with a couple of twists here and there. Anyone remember a company called Sir-Tech and how they developed stories??
Neutral on graphics, etc. They don't impress me that much for this type of game anyway, which is driven by other things.
Lacking overall strategic depth. Apart from the tactical battles, the strategic management aspect of the game is pretty mild to non-existent. In the original JA, you could commandeer vehicles, travel by chopper, meet strange NPCs at random, etc. On this strategic map you can... train guards... oh wait...we do that already...
Verdict:
If you're REALLY REALLY curious and the game is on sale, pick it up and give it a test drive, otherwise don't bother. Hopefully some other devs can pick up the JA franchise and give it the attention that it (and the fans) deserve.

First, you probably want to know my sales pitch as to why I would recommend this game when I have yet to even complete it.  Until June the 30th, you can get this game for 1.99 at least (although there's always a chance it will be added to a flash or community choice that takes off even more of the amount - if not already.)
I love horror genre in most all entertainment departments, so unfortunately I don't scare extremely easy.  So far, which after completing the game I might update the review, I have been pretty impressed.  I haven't slept now for going on a couple of days and I have not spent most of my time playing any games, but since the very first time I turned this game on - I just did not want to stop.  I am just as lost as the character I am playing.  I love how the journal is writing as I go along.  I'll admit I have to focus a little here and there because I'm trying to see the big picture before the small ones.  It's definitely got some creepy and supernatural going on here and I'm trying hard to take it all in and keep up.
I actually feel as though I am living through this person and I am trying to put the pieces together at the same time.  I have just picked out a new book and my senses are being stimulated through more than just in my head and with my eyes.  I have now became this character.  I'm not sure exactly where I am going or what I am doing, but I'm desperate to figure it out!  And honestly, as a single player, I feel much more connected to the game than if I was playing it with someone else at this point.  I have stepped inside a book that is slowly unraveling itself to me, but I have to figure it out as I go along.
I already know that I will replay this game over again.  I love that if you read in the information about the game - there are 8 possible endings!  I LOVE alternate endings based on my choices - even if I might mess up and it's game over, please try again.  I don't know the difference between the regular or extended version, and if I had a choice I would have still chosen the extended (I want it all - I want more!)  I am even really digging the soundtrack (which may be more girly?) but I really like it!  So, I am starting to babble on, and once I finish the game if I need to redo my review then I totally will (and btw, I feel so upset with myself when I take a peek at a hint or guidebook, but I'm going to admit that I totally did with one eye shut!)  I still am not sure what some of the things that come up in the game are for or how I use them.  I decided just to go with it and try to figure it out as I go along.  It took me a few minutes to realize that I could toss things and open and move them with my hands.  I keep forgetting it's not a point and clicker.  And I will be paying more attention to look out for Dreampainters, and I am one of those people who needs a sequel quite often.
So, this is my review so far, since I thought this was an amazing price for this game.  I've paid more for games and I haven't felt as excited to see what's going to happen next.  I could go on comparing 2 dollar items vs. the game but I will just end here until I have completed the game, for the first time around, and then, I will read what I wrote to see how I feel about it after that.

This game is absolutely amazing.  If you have any interestin learning guitar I can't recommend it enough.  I have played guitar (mostly self-taught) on and off for about 10 years but I have barely touched it in the last 5.  I kept hitting plateaus and getting frustrated with the feeling that I couldn't improve as much as I wanted so pretty much left my guitar to collect dust.  Then this game came along and I basically can't put my guitar down and am not touching any other the other 10 games I have bought off steam in the last few months.  My guitar playing far surpassed the level I was playing at years ago when I was pretty active.  I think there is a great variety of songs to play with a great range of difficulties.  Plus, session mode is really quite impressive and I didn't realize I could have so much fun practicing scales when there was a band playing in the background to make it fun.  For beginners there are a ton of lessons that are really quite solid and would help you learn all the basics if you had never played a guitar before.  My single complaint about the game is the cost of the DLC.  Three dollars for a song seems pretty steep to me, but I guess it takes a bit of effort to map out all the notes and get the licensing rights.  On the other hand, the game is so good (though I hesitate to call it a game, it is so much more than that... it is more of a personal guitar instructor), I want the developer to really succeed so they can be rewarded for their work so I guess the DLC cost could be justified.
In short, this program is going to revoltionize the way people learn to play guitar.  Get it.

DRM aside, this is a great game. It manages to be thought-provoking without sacrificing the fun or becoming pretentious. (*cough* Gone Home *cough*) It's not just about pagan folklore, but also the effect it has on sexual archetypes. I like the ending in particular.  Goddess VS woman. Male obsession. Makes you think about how harmful 'benevolent' sexism really is to those who don't fit the bill. And it stays nicely creepy all the while.
Gameplay-wise, the puzzles are a bit too complicated. And I personally find the flashing screens annoying. (It probably should come with an epilepsy warning!) That said, the game has such a unique atmosphere I was ready to overlook all that and just immerse myself in it. The story is also about a classic mix of desire and fear. A delicious mix I would say.
P.S. It says I only played for 2 hours. Actually, I've played it before on a friend's account. It took about 5-6 hours to finish, with guide.

Lots, lots of potential. Beautiful art-style; it's rare to see such a breathtaking view when playing games with this sort of art-style but it really works here. The music is also serene and arcade-y. Will bring mad nostalgia to 80s and 90s kids, and is an exemplary game for younger audience who want to understand the value of classic games when it's executed well.
It is however in early access and is still unfinished, albeit well polished. I do believe it sill has a long way to go, as it's not just missing a few items, but missing whole skill trees. There's also not much NPC interaction, and the combat can get stale if you're grinding.
As you can see, I don't have that many hours in this game so I don't blame you if you don't believe me. I do think it's a good game, but it needs to really pick up and hook the audience if it expects a complete playthrough. The combat in itself is not varied and interesting enough to be the main reason to play this game. Even the art-style, arguably the game's strongest point, is the kind of art-style that will illicit "wow"s and "woo"s and "cool"s and "nice"s, but it's not going to keep gamers coming back. The devs need to work on the longevity of the game, but it has undoubtedly a very strong first impression.
I'm always very cautious when reviewing early access games as I'm not sure whether to review the current build or the final product (which one can only guess).
Current build: 72.5/100
If they manage to deliver everything as promised: 75/100
If they deliver everything as promised and fine tune the combat, add more loot and interactable NPCS: 80/100

Hardest roguelike I've ever played, with no reward loop.  Doesn't matter what I do, I lose, then I get fired, then I get to do it again with the same broken tools.  I think the franchise has forgotten that it's a 'game', because it quickly stops being fun (unless you like rolling dice with the numbers rubbed off).
EDIT:
After my frustrated rant above, I started using 'Instant Result' and a light dawned.  The Match Plan feature makes a lot of sense when trying to understand what to do during matches.  It also helps explain a little better  why the 'Mentality' tactical options should be used, and how.
Problem is, the ability to use a Match Plan is linked only to Instrant Result, and isn't something you can apply pre-game to a match you are about to manage yourself.  Having the Assistant tell you what changes you should make based on your chosen match plan would definately help the more caual player (like me!) get to grips with the mechanics, and even if you said 'yes' to everything, that would basically be the same as pressing Instant Result (with the added immersion you get from watchuing the match engine live).
I will stand by my 'broken tools' comment, because there is a big gap between what your Assistant Manager can do with a Match Plan and Instant Result, and what feedback the Assistant currently gives you when you are watching it unfold live.
EDIT 2:
Good news:
Found the Math Plan thing in the match engine!  It was in one of the top dropdowns all along, so that's good, I can now watch the match while my assistant does the donkey work.
Bad news:
The new tooltip which appears on the Match Plan wizard tells you it is for Instant Result matches and when you don't want to attend the game, so that's what has mislead me, hope they update it soon!
Using Match Plans reveals new confusions, as it asks you to pick a starting strategy (I picked Contain/highly structured) which appears loud and proud at the top of your Match Plan summary, as if it's the foundation of your approach.  Problem is, I'd also picked 'play to win' as the template of the Match Plan, so every scenario (from kick-off) used something other than the contain/highly structured stuff I'd picked... so I'm not sure how all that's all working together.
Also I've seen screenshots of the full game Tactics screen and it includes a Familiarity bar which tells you how competent your team are with your chosen tactic - a simple and useful piece of indormation that isn't on Touch! You get that info in a monthly email from your AM, but as a streamlined piece of info I'd say that's the sort of thing that Touch needs.. You can change tactics then go back to the email and the bar will have changed (along with the breakdown when you hover over it) but that's more a glitch than a feature.
The Familiarity thing also got me thinking about how the Tactics and Match Plans tie together... the game asks you to train with one chosen mentality/team shape, but then rewards you for changing them up during matches, which is counter-intuitive - it's basically saying you will play better by picking unfamiliar mentalities during games, which makes the whole thing harder to fathom.  Seems to me that the whole training/familiarity thing should be around Match Plans, and not one particular tactic within a match plan.
Only those who can't resist themself to click "FINISH NOW" would need coin.

Full disclosure: I am a Stardrive 2 closed beta tester, but I have not received any compensation for my testing or for this review. I'm really just a 4x gaming fan at heart who was lucky enough to be given access to Stardrive 2 during its development :)
I highly recommend this game for anyone looking for a galactic empire building game featuring that "just one more turn" itch that some of the great 4x games of the past have offered. This is definitely a game that can keep you up late at night, constantly clicking end turn just to see what lies ahead in the development and struggles of the star nation you've spent hours carefully building.
Right from the start, you'll be faced with interesting events, encounters, and anomalies that will drive you to spread your chosen species farther out amongst the stars. You'll research interesting technologies, some of them unique to your species and others totally random in nature. You'll find valuable resources to claim through colonization and exploration. You'll design and build your own starships to conquer your enemies and protect all you've gained. You'll engage in diplomacy and espionage with/against a variety of interesting and unique alien species all with their own agendas. You'll meet minor species to either befriend, enslave, or exterminate.
The combination of turn-based empire management with real-time space combat helps to break up the pace of the game into enjoyable yet distinct pieces. Being able to see a newly researched weapon help your ships blaze a path of destruction across an enemy fleet in real-time combat helps to tie the entire game together and makes it feel like every decision you've made matters. The ship designing and customization are definitely high points of Stardrive 2. The space combat is visually impressive and always fun to play. The ground combat is turn-based, with an X-Com Enemy Unknown feel to it, which I've come to really enjoy as an entirely separate mini-game within Stardrive 2.
In short, if you're looking to escape from reality for hours at a time by putting on the hat of a space emperor and building your very own interstellar civilization this is the game for you!

Never Alone is a game whose charm you will desperately want to love, and on the surface there is enough elegance to be intrigued. Unfortunately the Never Alone doesn't do very much as a game. However, as an overall experience, the game still has quite a lot to offer. It is a game I can recommend, just with some caveats, as I do not feel it deserves a thumbs down.
While Never Alone was for the most part somewhat enjoyable, I simply could not shake the feeling of mediocrity that I was left with at the end of the experience. Looking back, this game doesn't bring anything revolutionary to the 2D platforming genre, however, I don't think anybody expected that much. But ultimately, it ends up taking a few steps backwards.
Gameplay and Design:
For the first 90 minutes the platforming felt alright, but about halfway through the fourth chapter things began to fall apart. The true nature of the controls were starting to become more and more apparent. Controlling the characters felt clunkier, attaching to ledges properly sometimes took several tries. The bola stood out as being particularly awkward and could have controlled better to say the least. In a game that seemed to be aiming for simplicity, some of these factors definitely detracted from the experience as a whole.
The level design felt a bit redundant after a while as well, a lot of the levels or particular aspects of them began to feel the same or just too gimmicky, and for a game that can easily be completed in just over three hours this type of design isn't particularly welcome.
Extra Content:
The cultural insights (documentary type clips) were the true star of the show and largely responsible for keeping me interested in the game all the way through. However, first and foremost, the game should be critiqued for how it performs as an actual game. The cultural insights and story are very nice touches but that alone cannot shape the entire experience. In this case however, the cultural insights are the glue that holds everything together.
All in all, Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) has enough charm on its surface to make for a really enjoyable and educational journey. However, a lot of that enjoyment is lost in the boring level design and sometimes mildly frustrating controls that make for a mediocre 2D plaforming experience.
While it is a game I recommend based on its cultural value. If you're looking JUST for a good game think twice before playing.

Finally got this thing working... stupid senseless UPlay.
Install Uplay, log in to Uplay. Register game ON STEAM FIRST, then copy steam code to copy into Uplay registration INGAME and log in to Uplay IN GAME. It's a convoluted contrived pain in the butt.
Thankfully, and while it can be a royal pain for many, increasing your TONE and db in options can help you overcome a lot of these pains with "You're too low". When you get that notice you have to CALIBRATE, some people are lucky and it works the first or second time. Took me aboput 7 since my guitar is a bit old, I'll have to get new strings for the bottom two but thankfully I'm not at the level where I require them yet.
PROTIP: When calibrating, just strum all the strings as loud and fast as you can, they LITERALLY want you to make some noise! Use your whole closed palm and press down immediately on all the strings when they tell you too.
You think go into tuning your strings after that if needed, if still low, again adjust your TONE nobs on guitar and the Boost ingame and your audio settings. That last one only if the others don't help.
A few other things like a simple test of your ability to follow and hit notes and then use them in session will tell the game where it thinks you need to be. Nothing is mandatory, you can make it stop auto-adjusting for you, though I find it most helpful being in the novice/beginner range.
The lessons range from the simplest of basics of setting up your strap and playing with your fingers all the way to mastering your first song. I'm currently taking them up on their 60 day challenge and will be commiting that hour a day or more. I'll say this, I went from a total hack to at least being able to play my first song with accuracy of 100% and technique of 84%.
Pros
+Tutorials: Repetition helps. But the amount of training options and Master mode, you certainly don't have to pace yourself if you just want to rush in and test your limits!
+Band Session: When you feel a bit burnt out, go on and have a go at Sessions, the play with a 'Live Band' is most fun. You can even take what you learned and adjust everything in the band to your liking.
Cons
-UPlay. It just is. And the horrible fact that if you use your Steam registration code by mistake on UPlay and not teh one Steam makes for you on its launcher window/CD Key, you risk being banned mercilessly and stripped of ALL your UPLAY titles on UPlay. BE CAREFUL!
-Repetitive voices that won't shutup when you aren't even hitting other cords. Mainly during tuning, but fixed with enough calibrating and making sure your Guitar's Tone's are at least a good level over 5 (anything below and it can't seem to hear my guitar no matter how much I calibrate) so bear with it.
Final Thoughts: In the end, if you can stomach a few tweaking of options, both ingame and PC advanced audio settings, this is a most enjoyable experience, my first good one after the hours of UPlay lockout issues I had to fight through, and I have no regrets buying this WITH cord on Amazon for fifty bucks.
As for whether its worth 110 bucks when not on sale, assuming you have no Real Tone Cable? Well, I'll have to say it depends how serious you are. I'm just a hobbist who can't afford the time or the money to travel to take lessons to play my guitar, this has been best alternative and thankfully it was JUST the right amount to make the leap.
Yes. This really does work. It IS a lot of fun. And despite my seething hatred for UPlay, I must say I love music and this title, while I'd say it should be labeled SOFTWARE and not GAME, it has such a lovely mix of both, and while I won't get into here, there are modders who can help you get even more enjoyment out of this if your taste in music is more advanced or want to add in your own personal created songs and want to feel what you would be like in your very own band if you're looking to bring in any band members of your own down the road.
This has massive potential. Ubisoft will not fully explore its potential but the community very well is. Such a shame, a SteamWorkshop to share and even play with other people, even practice with others would be most amazing.

You get to play as two roles in F13, counselor and Jason. As a counselor your job is to escape and not get killed by Jason. Your objectives include fixing a car, boat, and phone box in order to escape. Which need certain parts that are randomly spawned on the map. So everything is random and you'll most likely never find the same part in the same place. You can also just wait out the match and even kill Jason. I do want to warn you that your probably going to die. A lot. You might get a second chance if someone calls Tommy Jarvis but that's really it. I should also mention that each counselor has it's specific strengths/weaknesses. Some counselors are best suited to defend people and fight Jason. Others are great at repair and stealth. Then there's the counselors that are best for distracting Jason. So I highly suggest playing around and see what best suits your play style. You can also roll perks that can help aid you in the game with a small downside.
When playing Jason, your job is to kill all the counselors and make sure no one escapes. Just like the counselors, each Jason has a set of strengths/weaknesses. Some are great in the water, has good teleport, etc. When you start out as Jason, you always have a set number of traps and throwing knives to start out with. The traps can be use to trap certain objectives and will alert you if some one steps in them. The throwing knives are used to throw at people to hurt them. You can pick up more throwing knives but you can't pick up more traps. So use your traps wisely. Jason also has four abilities and a passive as well. He can teleport anywhere on the map and use a shift ability to quickly catch speed to a counselor. He can also use a sense ability to help find counselors and a stalk ability that can be used to catch unexpecting couselors off guard. You also have a variety of unique grab kills to use and you can do enviromental kills as well. However most of the grab kills need to be bought. You can be stunned if a counselor hits you with a weapon like a baseball, step in a counselor trap, get shot, step in firecrackers, or stabbed with a pocket knife. You can even be killed as well but it's very uncommon.
What I like the most about the game is that not every game is the same, for the most part. Your never really sure where everything is, even after playing it for a while. Your not always sure where the phone box is going to spawn or where certain parts are. Sometimes you find everything for the car and escape in the first five minutes. Other times you die right away or can't find the one part you need for the boat. Sometimes you get a two car map, sometimes you get a boat/car map. Maybe you even get to come back as Tommy Jarvis if you die or already escaped. I like that every game isn't really the same or not knowing what could happen. It's also great to play with friends, which probably isn't too surprising. It may take a while to get use too but it becomes fun once you figure stuff out.
However this game isn't without it's flaws. From it's disastrous first week to all the glitches. Features that were promised missing from the game entirely and the lack of a kick/report function. Also doesn't help with the drama the devs tend to get itself into as well. Like with most fanbases/communities for anything ever, the game's community can be pretty toxic as well. You will have your fair share of games where you have toxic teammates or someone glitches onto the roof to avoid getting killed by Jason. The matchmaking can be pretty terrible at times and you can get terrible ping because of it.   You will also run into people helping Jason, which oh by the way. You can't kick them from the game or report them at all currently. Then there's the drama with this game and the issues with consoles that I could go on about if this review wasn't already getting too long.
Overall, fun game but it has it's problems. Hopefully in the future some things will change and it'll get better. So some of the stuff I stated above might have changed. As of writing this review, I suggest getting this game at a sale or hope someone gives it to you.

Underrated "point and click" horror.  Anna is pretty entertaining.  There is multiple endings and quite a bit to collect.  It has some replayablility to it.  The story is also interesting and one should try to complete all endings inorder to piece together their own interpretation of the story.
As your sanity gets lower you do experience quite a few jump scares.  Apparently the game engine watches your movements and predicts your vulnerability to try to scare you when you least expect it.  I play horror games all the time and I don't generally get scared easily, but there were a few points in this game that made me jump.  And I appreciate that.
This is a "point and click" style game in which you examine items and craft things to solve the puzzles.  The puzzles can be irritating at times though, and not much help is given to the player apart from journal entries and books.  The soundtrack is repetitive but it is nice.
Though some other reviewers and websites tend to view this game negatively, I think it's wonderful.
It's not too often we have a horror puzzle game that is actually creepy.  Though the scares are supernatural in nature and some tend to be a bit on the cheezy side, I guarantee you will be surprised when it gets silent and you turn around to find the creepiest wooden mannequins ever, which always appear in different spots.   Or if you see a shadow in the corner of the room, only to turn around to see 8 more inches from your face.  Sounds lame: I know.  But trust me, it's really great.
For what it is, I think Anna is a wonderful game and has a lot of interesting features.  From what I heard, Dreampainters is making a "spiritual sequel" to this game, and if they improve on it, it might be something to watch out for.
Would recommend.

Every level ist cut up into three segments, and finishing a segment completely refills your health. Oh, and speaking of Pixels, the Art and the Music are glorious, especially the Cut-Scenes are a lot of fun. Absolutely recommended if you're into old-school action.

Relive the nostalgic era of text-based adventures with an interesting first person twist in Stories Untold, a point, click, and type adventure.  Divided into 4 episodes, your adventure takes place across a series of seemingly unrelated environments that all eventually tie together in the finale.
Similar to Zork or early Sierra adventure games, Stories Untold requires a familiarity with classic text parser style input. Rather than moving from room to room or clicking on objects, you sit stationary in front of a screen and type in commands such as “look around” or “use key in door”. Later episodes combine various puzzles with manual text input and some of them can be quite challenging.
I’d have a lot to write on the story (which in my opinion was very well done) but it’s hard to talk about it without spoiling the whole thing. I will point out though that a full playthrough of this game is likely to run you 2-3 hours at the very most so budget accordingly for your time.

This game is essentially a RTS hybrid of Worm + Polybridge.
In terms of Gameplay, you have to plan/build your fort, manage your resource/tech, and destroy opposing fort while keep yours standing. You have to accomplish all that in real time, and it can feel a bit overwhelming at first. However, once you overcome the learning curve, the game is without a doubt fun and addictive.
There is a single player campaign/ skirmish, but the selling point of the game is the multiplayer aspect. There are map scenarios where a team of players control a fort, which involved great deal of communication and teamwork. Alternatively, there are also maps where individual player control their own fort for less "chaotic" teamplay.
Pros:
-High replayability potential- Each match feels very different, simply because the style and design of forts you see from other players are highly divese and creative. There is already a map editor build in the game, so expected new map creation in the future.
-Easy to play, difficult to master- To build a decent fort, you need good physics building. To manage your fort efficiently, you need good multitasking skill. To kill enemy fort, you need good aiming/ geometry, as well as good awareness to keep track of what enemy fort is planning. This makes the gameplay feels rich and satisfying.
Cons:
-Atrocious multiplayer lobby ui- The game lacks match filter. Currently, you will see a list of match, but you will not know whether that game is in progress or waiting for players to join. Finding a match is extremely tedious, with lots of joining/leaving.
-Network/ Technical issues- Although the game is playable, ping issues and random disconnect do occur. Hopefully this issue is addressed in later patches.
-Questionable campaign dialogue- If your sense of humor is not tolerable, the references may rub certain people off in a wrong way. Though this is more of a nickpicking critique.
Verdict:
Should you get the game? Absolutly.
The gameplay is both rich and satisfying. It is like playing polybridge with guns, except you get to smash other's bridge/fort.
There are some technical and ui issues, but that's expected in any titles at launch.

To start, I do recommend this game, however it's not without its qualities that I absolutely dislike.
That's not to say they're faults of the game, just that they make
angry enough to need a break.
There are so many things about this game done right, the artwork is well done, the sound and music is pretty spot on, and the story is decent so far.
I enjoy the combat and the leveling+skill system all feels pretty good, despite there still being some unfinished skills.
I also really like the items and collecting in the game, what with unique drops, elite monsters, etc.
About the only thing that turns me off about the game is that some of the boss battles and puzzles can drag the experience on, artificially inflating actual play time.
I fought the first real boss, a giant robot, and kept dying, trying to take it down in its last stage. What I didn't know, without checking the guide,
I'm not a fan of having to look at a guide online, just because the game doesn't indicate its mechanics clearly enough.
A character could easily say something like "It's imploding on itself, just stay out of its way, and we're almost there!" or something. There was no indication of what I should do, and this, frankly, is what happens quite a bit in the game. You're supposed to just "know" something completely random in order to progress.
Another gripe I have is that the difficulty spikes a lot, in various different places. You'll be feeling pretty proud of yourself for beating a boss, or grinding up a dozen levels. You'll be killing everything without issue, feeling like a bad@$$, and then suddenly your face gets smashed in by a boss that seems to be dozens of levels too high for you.
This will happen a lot, which left me feeling like "am I going to have a good time, or am I suddenly going to face a challenge that frustrates me for two hours?"
Also on my list of annoyances are the puzzles. I spent two hours trying to solve a single puzzle last night. In the end, I caved and looked at a guide. The solution rather♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, because it was the ONLY solution involving moving around 12 pieces. So, a puzzle that involves 12 pieces on a grid of let's say 40X80, to find the exact right way to place each piece, this wasn't fun. The room design for that puzzle also wasn't at all suggestive of a solution, which is something most good games with puzzles do, suggest a solution through the level design.
You'd think with all my complaining, I'd not recommend this game, and in fact you'd be wrong.
Regardless of its downfalls, things that I personally don't like, it's a really good game. As I mentioned above, the leveling is good (super grindy, but what did you expect from Secrets of Grindea), the skill system, the art style, the music, the item collection, crafting, story...
All of it is done quite well.
If you're into retro-styled RPGs, with very definite nods to the past, you'll probably like this one, even if it does make you feel stupid, from time to time.

Where to begin with SOMA? In minutes, I was enthralled. The story is good. The ambience, great. It’s more thrilling – or perhaps chilling, than horror. As other reviews have stated there’s no cheap jump scares. It makes you value companionship, even if that companion is just a voice, because when you don’t have it… you are alone and the game makes sure you feel it! It makes you care about the characters. The entire thing is very thought provoking and there are difficult choices that you must make. Some of the game is quite easy, some can be challenging but there is little that is frustrating.
The game is very linear, but this really only occurred to me as I write this review. While playing, you won’t care. The ending left me feeling like I just experienced something important – something that will stick with me.
Pros and Cons:
+ Graphics
+ Story
+ Sound/ambience
+ General gameplay
+ Seems decently well optimized
+ All achievements trigger properly – No need for a guide, you’ll get them all if you finish the game.
+ The game works well at wide resolutions. I played using AMD’s Eyefinity with 16:3 ratio.
- I felt the Bloom was overdone. I played the game with it off as the glows it created were distracting and unrealistic
- The AI for some monsters wasn’t all that amazing
- Too much blur used to convey the feeling of pressure of extreme water depth was a bit annoying in a couple of instances
The last of the two negatives are nitpicking, really. In my experience, the game was bug free. Others have reported invisible walls or bad frame speeds. I suffered from none of these things. Perhaps the game was patched, or I was lucky, but it performed flawlessly with all settings maxed (except Bloom) at 5760x1080 res on an AMD R9 290X.
Shun the darkness, love the light!
Important!! Stick around through the credits at the end.

This is a Tower Defense where enemies are coming in a straight line to attack your towers. The most basic enemy takes half the hp of your most basic tower. And once you put your towers in the upper half of the screen, the enemies are almost always offscreen.
You spend more time repairing your tower that anything else.
One of the common strategy to play seems to lure the enemies in empty columns, then suddenly build a tower in front of them. This way, you can have enemies onscreen getting hit by more towers.
Let's add that on the same screen, there are crystal deposits where you build stuff to get ressources, and you have special powers (depending from your character). Also, it's really strange that the devs choose to make a vertical layer, where an horizontal one would have given them far more space.
Aside the battle screen, there is a galaxy map allowing you to choose a level, and you have a small upgrade panel.
This is a barebone Tower Defense where the main gameplay is not really interesting.

When it comes to TEN TIULENYA team’s debut game on Steam I am going to ask you for a simple favor. Don’t write this game off before you’ve given it an opportunity. That’s the easiest thing to do when looking at the game’s screenshots and the trailer video. The game doesn’t look like much from some simple sampling. But there’s been an unbelievable amount of work go into the artistry and the development of the game and honestly it’s well worth your while to give it a play. The reason why I say this is because I almost laughed the game off without giving it an opportunity myself. The game play initially reminded me of the type of first year game developers classes that various universities are offering around the world. It reminded me of my first year IT programming unit. But I’m glad that I sat back and asked if I was giving the game the chance that it deserved to which I very quickly realized that I wasn’t so I engaged myself with the content and found that I was having more fun than I thought that was possible.
In One Man is Not No Man you control the combatant of your choice against hordes of enemies who are trying to dethrone the king. It’s a pretty simple concept that is well executed and well designed. Each of the four characters that you can play are significantly different from the other with each having their own special abilities and powers. You control your hero with the WASD keys and attack using the left and right mouse buttons. These mechanics are easy to play yet the game becomes difficult to absolutely master the further into the game you play.
What makes the game stand out is that each and every character in the game is made out of modelling clay. This provides the characters a distinct and unique look when compared to similar games. This would have taken such an insane amount of time considering the detail that they are given. It somewhat reminded me of
As always I would love for all developers of Steam games to incorporate achievements and trading cards into their games. They’ve both become very important marketing aspects of the product that they’re pushing to the consumer and without them they’re losing some of their potential purchasers to other games that have incorporated them into their games. That’s truly the biggest flaw with the game in my opinion. The game can become a little bit repetitive but given that there are four characters that you can choose to play as this is somewhat minimized.
So please give One Man is Not No Man an opportunity. I believe that you will be pleasantly surprised that you did.

Thomas Was Alone probably sets the record for "lowest-budget to biggest-heart" ratio in a game. And if not, it's pretty high up there. Now, don't get me wrong, when I say "low budget", I don't mean it's half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in any way. It's actually really well made - rather, the look of it is purposely lo-fi. You play as a red rectangle named Thomas whose goal is to make it through a series of 2D puzzle-platforming levels. Along the way you'll also meet other colored rectangles, each with their own unique abilities and personality. And that's all I'll really say about the plot. Suffice it to say that you will be amazed at how much you'll actually care about a bunch of little rectangles. That is due in equal parts to the writing and the well-done narration that accompanies it. As for the actual gameplay, it's good, but very easy. The levels involve puzzle-solving and platforming, but neither aspect is even remotely difficult, except perhaps in a couple of spots here and there (which I would classify more as tedious than hard). So this is not a game you should buy looking for a challenge. You should buy it if you are into indie games with unique looks, story and ideas. It's a great experience, all around - a perfect casual game to while away an afternoon. The game will take around 3-4 hours total, including all secrets, so it's not very long, but it also doesn't overstay its welcome. Definitely check it out if you like these types of games.

When you break horror games down, they tend to fit into a few convenient categories. Sometimes there are real monsters to fear, sometimes you end up in their domain, sometimes you're struggling to stop them from running amok, and sometimes they're all in your head. I'm not going to spoil Stories Untold by indicating which road it travels, but I have to be honest that it's my least favorite one. And if it didn't do everything else so very, very well that might be a dealbreaker for me. Luckily, it still manages to be exceptional in every way except its story. Ironic, isn't it?
Stories Untold is a collection of four horror-themed vignettes built around interacting with old 1980s-era technology. The first, The House Abandon, is an old 80s-style text adventure played on an ancient, boxy computer. The second is set in a science lab with plenty of clicky, chunky audio/visual equipment to play with. The third is at a polar listening station where you must transmit coded radio messages. And the fourth vignette ties it all together very effectively. Each one works a creeping unease into your activities in different and clever ways, often by toying with your perspective as you mess with antiquated interfaces.
The real hook of Stories Untold is how you play it. Not content to simply give everything a thick 80s sheen of fake wood paneling and cathode ray tubes, your primary means of interacting with the game is via text parser. Not only that, but the computers you enter your text commands on are distinct entities within the game world. In The House Abandon, for example, you're playing through a text adventure on an old Commodore-style terminal. Instead of just showing the screen, the monitor, keyboard, desk, and seemingly extraneous details like pictures and clocks are all modeled around it.
These elements are not actually extraneous, of course, because the way this game gets you is in how your text parsing adventures affect everything around them. Your commands are obviously going to have different effects between a text adventure, scientific equipment, and code transmitters, but the story also unfolds around you as you go through the motions of your tasks. There are further forms of interaction as well which are used to great effect, and can inspire surprising amounts of dread in how they diverge from your safe typing up to that point.
As effective as the moments are in Stories Unknown, I would be remiss not to clarify that they are inconsistent in their pacing and effectiveness. The House Abandon is an incredibly strong starter and sets the tone for the game perfectly, but the scares trail off a bit from there. The second chapter lost steam for me pretty quickly, and while the third has an excellent buildup, the payoff was weaker than I expected. This is less a function of how the scares are planned and executed and more how they tie into the overall story, which for me detracted from everything that was going on.
Mechanically the game is perfectly sound, and for a text parser I found the term recognition mostly adequate. You're not going to have a ton of options at any point, so the game is mostly figuring out what command you need to enter to proceed. The third chapter in particular has you following a lot of coding instructions that feel like a play on how linear the actual gameplay is. Still, it forms a natural puzzle system where you can divine the next line to enter based on a little experimentation and observation. I only got stuck on one line at the very end of the game, only because the parser wanted me to specify the contents of a bottle instead of the bottle itself. Overly picky, but certainly not a dealbreaker.
The only potential dealbreaker is the story, and I wish I could expand on it for your benefit but it really is best experienced for yourself. That's really where I'd put Stories Untold, as a game that's worth experiencing so long as you're prepared for what may or may not come in the end. As much as I dislike the story I adored the retro aesthetic and the tactile pleasure of hearing keys clicking as I typed into the terminals. Obviously if the story lands in the right spot for you this is an excellent buy, but even if it doesn't this is a fine take on a dormant genre that proves text parsing can still carry a game.

I will never, ever a huge fan first-person games. They give me headaches, I find it ridiculously hard to keep the controls still and focused. I just really dislike them. However, Anna managed it masterfully and I actually found it beneficial for once.
Now I will agreee with some of the others that the puzzles in this game can be kind of ridiculous. THey can be pretty hard and you're not really given much to guide you in solving them. There was one point in the game where you have to start putting certain information that you collected together and I honestly only found out through glancing at a guide. I either missed it being hinted at in the game or it really wasn't there.
There's also a fair amount of backtracking that got annoying sometimes though it was understandable giving how self-contained the playing field was. But towards the end there was one point when I had to keep going up to the attic and down and into this room and out of this room. And sometimes it's hard to interact with the objects or tell if you grabbed something.
But I still worked my way through it because it was intriguing and I wanted to know the rest of the story. I found myself getting pretty immersed in it from the beginning. I found myself wanting to explore everything in the house and actually taking my time to read everything that I had picked up. I do wish the beginning part when you're outside the cabin was a little bit longer because it's such a big contrast to the dark, dreary, and sometimes bloody inside of the cabin but I don't think the game suffered from the that.
And the scares! The scares were just awesome. They were very rarely in your face scares and it was the subtle nature of them that made it frightened. You'd see things going on at the edge of your screen and you'd turn around and notice something weird happening or that something in the scene had changed. It was never extremely frightening but always really creepy which is why I really enjoyed playing this game.

To start, I do recommend this game, however it's not without its qualities that I absolutely dislike.
That's not to say they're faults of the game, just that they make
angry enough to need a break.
There are so many things about this game done right, the artwork is well done, the sound and music is pretty spot on, and the story is decent so far.
I enjoy the combat and the leveling+skill system all feels pretty good, despite there still being some unfinished skills.
I also really like the items and collecting in the game, what with unique drops, elite monsters, etc.
About the only thing that turns me off about the game is that some of the boss battles and puzzles can drag the experience on, artificially inflating actual play time.
I fought the first real boss, a giant robot, and kept dying, trying to take it down in its last stage. What I didn't know, without checking the guide,
I'm not a fan of having to look at a guide online, just because the game doesn't indicate its mechanics clearly enough.
A character could easily say something like "It's imploding on itself, just stay out of its way, and we're almost there!" or something. There was no indication of what I should do, and this, frankly, is what happens quite a bit in the game. You're supposed to just "know" something completely random in order to progress.
Another gripe I have is that the difficulty spikes a lot, in various different places. You'll be feeling pretty proud of yourself for beating a boss, or grinding up a dozen levels. You'll be killing everything without issue, feeling like a bad@$$, and then suddenly your face gets smashed in by a boss that seems to be dozens of levels too high for you.
This will happen a lot, which left me feeling like "am I going to have a good time, or am I suddenly going to face a challenge that frustrates me for two hours?"
Also on my list of annoyances are the puzzles. I spent two hours trying to solve a single puzzle last night. In the end, I caved and looked at a guide. The solution rather♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, because it was the ONLY solution involving moving around 12 pieces. So, a puzzle that involves 12 pieces on a grid of let's say 40X80, to find the exact right way to place each piece, this wasn't fun. The room design for that puzzle also wasn't at all suggestive of a solution, which is something most good games with puzzles do, suggest a solution through the level design.
You'd think with all my complaining, I'd not recommend this game, and in fact you'd be wrong.
Regardless of its downfalls, things that I personally don't like, it's a really good game. As I mentioned above, the leveling is good (super grindy, but what did you expect from Secrets of Grindea), the skill system, the art style, the music, the item collection, crafting, story...
All of it is done quite well.
If you're into retro-styled RPGs, with very definite nods to the past, you'll probably like this one, even if it does make you feel stupid, from time to time.

Where to begin with SOMA? In minutes, I was enthralled. The story is good. The ambience, great. It’s more thrilling – or perhaps chilling, than horror. As other reviews have stated there’s no cheap jump scares. It makes you value companionship, even if that companion is just a voice, because when you don’t have it… you are alone and the game makes sure you feel it! It makes you care about the characters. The entire thing is very thought provoking and there are difficult choices that you must make. Some of the game is quite easy, some can be challenging but there is little that is frustrating.
The game is very linear, but this really only occurred to me as I write this review. While playing, you won’t care. The ending left me feeling like I just experienced something important – something that will stick with me.
Pros and Cons:
+ Graphics
+ Story
+ Sound/ambience
+ General gameplay
+ Seems decently well optimized
+ All achievements trigger properly – No need for a guide, you’ll get them all if you finish the game.
+ The game works well at wide resolutions. I played using AMD’s Eyefinity with 16:3 ratio.
- I felt the Bloom was overdone. I played the game with it off as the glows it created were distracting and unrealistic
- The AI for some monsters wasn’t all that amazing
- Too much blur used to convey the feeling of pressure of extreme water depth was a bit annoying in a couple of instances
The last of the two negatives are nitpicking, really. In my experience, the game was bug free. Others have reported invisible walls or bad frame speeds. I suffered from none of these things. Perhaps the game was patched, or I was lucky, but it performed flawlessly with all settings maxed (except Bloom) at 5760x1080 res on an AMD R9 290X.
Shun the darkness, love the light!
Important!! Stick around through the credits at the end.

A fantastic ode to 8-bit action games (even if the visuals are a bit more colorful than 8-bit really could have supported), this game does neo-retro right. Great controls, a game that is long enough to be fulfilling but doesn't wear thin, interesting levels, and a level of difficulty that is challenging but not unfair, it's an easy recommendation.

This cute, grind-y RPG has great pixel graphics and a pleasing soundtrack, and the characters have a lot of personality. The puzzles are satisfying, and the ability to tame different pets has a unique mechanic. The bosses and their accompanying temples are fun and challenging, requiring you to utilize new skills you pick up along the way. There's a great story to follow, and I look forward to each installment as the areas are added.
I don't regret purchasing this title in its Early Access phase because, although the content is slowly added, I am able to watch everything develop. Usually I only see the finished product, but it's a neat experience to see everything come together. I will say that the controls are a little awkward, but I've managed to come up with a workable system with a fourteen-button gamer mouse. That's my only complaint, and it doesn't detract from my gameplay enough to push me away.
I was hesitant at first to purchase it when some of the reviews accused this game of being impossibly slow to update. There's always that fear with Early Access games that the developer will decide to abandon it in its unfinished state and leave you wanting more. However, the developers do post pretty regularly, and they have an outside blog that is very thorough about their progress and future plans. (I'm eager for the next update, which will apparently include player housing! Sounds exciting.)
All in all, I recommend this game for a lot of different reasons, although I wish I could get some of my friends to play it. I'm sure it would be a lot of fun to try in multiplayer. I think once it's finally finished and polished up I will have more luck. Keep up the great work, devs!

Well, I FINALLY finished it. Think a good mix of Lost Planet 2 and Gears of War, using the MDK coil suit after rocket boosters are strapped to the back of it, plus Steve Blum and Leon's QTE-suplexing power, taped to Warframe's Nezha for maximum drift.  Did you understand any of that?  No?  Don't try to.  Just FEEL it.
It's a Platinum game, so expect to get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you on a silver platter by the first boss (and the first level in general)... by the time you beat that boss, you'll be ready to fly through pretty much everything, as the boss makes you really get the hang of the controls before letting you go on.  Tough, but not unfair is the Platinum rule, and Vanquish [thankfully] is no exception... that is, until you reach Act 5.  HOLY CRAP.  37 deaths on the last stage alone...
... oh right, the PC version.  So yeah, it works.  AMD FX 8300, R7 360, nothing particularly special specswise.  It runs at a solid 50 FPS most of the time at 1440p (granted, I'm using the an Xbox One GPU equivalent overclocked), but this is a Platinum game, so expect lots of framerate-destroying explosions... and expect to like every single one of them.  The framerate at 1080p is of course much more solid, frequently staying around 80 FPS.
The actual visuals are awesome, the texturework is generally fine and completely clean (but nothing noteworthy by today's standards, as if that actually changed anything), and SSAO/other-stuff has been added to make the game look a bit nicer.  There's also quite a few jaggies with the default Medium settings, nothing that can't be fixed with a higher resolution.
I have three main complaints:
This is some bottom-of-the-barrel nitpicking and Vanquish PC is an absolute must for anyone.  I haven't tried the KB/M controls so I can't really say how good they are, but playing on mostly-60-except-when-it's-11 FPS with a controller feels absolutely great.  (Update: I was playing at 1440p on a crap GPU.  1080p is fine!)
Oh, and it's got Mikami on board, the Resident Evil 4 director, so expect perfect pacing and some absolutely absurd gravity-defying BS in the quicktime events.  Other than the usual Platinum problems (the initial git-gud shock, the hard-as-f@#% first half of the final boss before it gets fun, and so on), Platinum has only minor issues setting it apart from the best in the genre, and as long as you stay out of hardlocked cover, you'll be doing crazy s@#% within the first three hours.
I really can't recommend it enough.  It's rare that I preorder something, and even rarer that I don't feel like an idiot for doing so, but Vanquish was worth every penny and was exactly what I was hoping for waiting in hopes that it would be ported.  There are a few complaints about game length, but if you look at my own hour count... that's not bad for a $20 game.  I can say without a doubt that Vanquish is incredibly well paced, and doesn't overstay its welcome whatsoever.
