The objective is to destroy the enemy fort. The game features a campaign mode that serves as a tutorial and contains somewhat scripted scenarios, a skirmish mode that lacks random maps, a more freeform sandbox mode, and online multplayer. Once the enemy reactor is destroyed, you win. Each structure may be made out of wood or armor, with doors and ropes offering other options. Metal (collected from mines) and energy (collected from wind turbines) are used to build everything in the game, including defensive shields and sandbags. The workshop, factory, and upgrade center unlock new weapons. Those weapons include machine guns (primarily used for defense), mortars, snipers, missiles, cannons, and lasers. Since machine guns automatically fire at incoming projectiles, getting past the line of defense is tough (snipers are intended to take out machine gun emplacements). Offensive weapons must be manually fired in real time, which takes away from base building too much; you also cannot set a weapon to continually fire at a specific power and trajectory, increasing the micromanagement. Any damage can be repaired by simply holding down the “R” key and moving the mouse around; this process is too quick and results in rapid recovery before a fatal blow can be levelled. Thus, most games drag out far too long. The physics are plausible and the AI is generally a skilled opponent. Forts is a fine concept, but a number of shortcomings in gameplay (defensive advantages, repetitive aiming, fast repair) hold back ultimate enjoyment.

This game was initially released in June of 2007. Although dated, Overlord provides an alternative take on the fantasy genre. Instead of being a hero out to save the world, you start out as an evil lord who needs to rebuild his tower that was previously ransacked by heroes in the past. Throughout the course of the game, you are provided a handful of moral choices that will either raise or lower your evilness also known as "corruption". The higher your corruption, the more evil you will look. Don't take the game too seriously though as it has a quirky, satirical humor to it.
The gameplay is very basic. Controlling the Overlord is as simple as moving and pressing the attack button repeatedly. The complexity is in controlling your minions. There are four types of minions based on color that you recruit into your army: fighters, mages, assassins, and healers. As long as you're willing to collect enough life-force, your minions will have an infinite number of lives and you can spam them carelessly against each enemy to beat the game. To add a little more difficulty, you can employ tactics to beat the game with the least number of minion casualties. This will help reduce the grind for life-force, which is also used in upgrading your equipment so using tactics will help you become stronger much faster.
Once you have fully upgraded your weapons and armor with Arcanium and their life-force upgrades, the difficulty of the game becomes laughably easy. You can literally kill everything in your path without even using your minions at all.
The game does have a couple of issues. The audio and voice-acting is fairly bad. There are some characters that you will come across that will make you want to turn off your speakers when they talk. Not a huge deal if you play with subtitles. Gameplay can get very repetitive about halfway through the game. Controlling the minions can also become frustrating, especially when navigating complex routes. Sometimes they just don't go where you want them to or they just do what they want to do. It definitely fits the description of a "chaotic" army.
The most glaring issue is the lack of any kind of map. You will need to either memorize your way around, which isn't too difficult, or wander aimlessly until you find what you are looking for.
Overlord has a Steam sale just about every other month. This is an unbeatable value for only a couple of dollars.

Drawn from a traditional story shared by the Iñupiat, an Alaskan Native people,
is a puzzle platformer about a young girl named Nuna who sets out on a journey to save her village from an eternal blizzard.  In her search for the source of the blizzard, she is joined by Fox, a white fox/animal spirit who aids Nuna in her quest.
++ Fascinating Story
++ Beautiful Artwork/Graphics
+ Fun Puzzles
+ Bonus Documentary Videos
- Short Game
- Meant for Co-Op and felt in Solo Play
= No brainer here.  It's a little short, so you might want to catch it at a lower price, but definitely play this at least once!
-- This game was made with lot of love for the culture and inspired by stories that have been passed down for generations.  I was mesmerized by the narrator's voice as he told this story, and enjoyed it so much that I played the game straight through, including the DLC, without stopping.  Not a major feat, considering its length, but still pretty amazing for me.
What added to it even more was the beautiful artwork and graphics.  It looked somewhat simple at first, but quickly I because to have a much greater respect for the style and detail that was put into it.  There's a lot going on here graphically and it did an incredible job of drawing me into the story even more.
As for the gameplay, the puzzles were fun and interesting, and the mechanics were rather cool.  And it was interesting how well the puzzles and tricky landscape fit so well within the story.  It certainly wasn't super easy all the way through, which is a good thing, but it did get frustrating in parts.  This was more my fault that anything, however, so I don't hold it against the game.  I admit, I did underestimate the difficulty a little bit and it responded by putting me in my place lol.  Once I focused a little more though it wasn't so bad.
Above I called the documentary videos a "bonus", but the more I think about it, I'd say they are just as much as part of the game as anything else.  They are completely optional, of course, but I feel you'd be missing out by skipping them.  I would suggest you take the time to watch them as go for even more insight, understanding and appreciation of the game you're playing.
-- Not much to add here, honestly.  The game was rather short, which I found mildly disappointing only because I was enjoying it so much.  Also, the gameplay mechanics seemed a bit off and a little tricky at times.  I think
was meant more for Co-Op, because switching between Nuna and Fox is most of the trouble, especially when it has to be done quickly.  It's quite playable solo, don't get me wrong, but I warn ya, it can get a little frustrating in spots.
--  If you've read this far, then it's probably no surprise that I highly recommend you play this at least once.  Wait for a sale if you want to, because it IS short, but definitely play it.

With the risk of becoming a target of the “Hey! This is not Jagged Alliance 2!” lynching mob I’ll say: I like this game.
There are many people around the forums accusing this game and the developers as a “cash grab” or similar terms, usually based on nostalgia reasons. As a Jagged Alliance fan of the very first hour myself, I can partly see where they are coming from. Compared to JA2, this game has much less content, the game world isn’t as vibrant and full of surprises and the voice acting that made the characters of JA2 so memorable has taken a step or two into the wrong direction.
However, this game does have its merits and I dare even say some improvements over its “older brother”. These things can be a matter of opinion of course but I like: team inventory, weather influence (clearly shown on the tactical screen), number of enemies visible on the mercs icon, half/full cover visibility, much more clear how/when interrupts are occurring, panic mode, visible which enemies are/aren’t targetable from a new location etcetera. Also, I think the music is spot on.
I have two major gripes with the game: One is the emphasis on loot, combined with the awkward way to obtain that loot. Pixel hunting is no fun at all, instead containers should have some visible clue when a merc is standing close. Second gripe is the lack of challenge: some enemies must of course come running towards you, but not all of them - especially not when they’ve seen all the others that went running before them die so easily. Some of the enemies should camp (easy fix, I would say?) or even try to flank you. Also, money never felt like a real problem because once you liberated the first mine you can just sit on it and watch your bank account grow. A “hard” or “iron man” mode would certainly help.
All things considered, I think my 7 euros (I bought it during a sale, mostly because of the bad reviews) were well spent. Just don’t expect the richness of JA2, and for those people that are still waiting for that worthy successor: please stop making claims like “even the graphics were better in JA2” and stop your “piece of crap not worthy of the name” rants without even a single reason why or any constructive criticism. You are not helping. Instead, you might even scare future developers away from this already niche genre.

Just like Jagged Alliance: Back in Action before it, and the recent XCOM game this games doesn't deserve a lot of the negative reviews it gets.
So, it's not Jagged Alliance 2.  That doesn't mean it is a bad game.  A brand like "Jagged Alliance" is a double edged sword.  On one hand, there is a lot of name recognition; on the other, damned if you do, damend if you don't.
Had they just re-released JA2 with better graphics people would have whined "it's just the same game again".  They took a different route and made some design changes and people are whining "it's not the same game".
It's a seperate game and deserves to be treated and rated as a seperate game, not as a comparison to some ideal fantasy memory you had playing a game from your youth.
Does it have problems?  Why, yes it does!  Camera angles are frequently awful.  You have a choice of 4 diagnals to view the field from.  Frequently, none of them are useful.  Thankfully, there are already mods to fix that.
The UI can be a little awkward at time (but the UI is bloody awkward in JA2 by today's standards too!)
I can't count on one hand the number of times I've tried to shoot a bad guy and instead my stupid merc has gone running to him instead.
All that said, it's a fun game.  It takes getting used to.  It took an hour or two of play before I really started enjoying myself- but now I really am.  Unlike other similar games- you don't hunt down the enemy... once you encounter one- they all hear the gunfire and come to you.
There are pros and cons to this... on the con side- you can just park in convenient spots and let them run to you.  On the pro side, no annoying searching around for that last soldier when you could have sworn you've checked everywhere already.
There are some other weird quirks... it's flat... no roofs or height advantages and doors stay either permanently open or closed- you can't open/close them.  There are no combustible map tiles- and some things are out of proportion.  Pigs look the size of rhinoceroses next to the mercs.
Combat is clear and straightforwards though.. it is mostly intuitive.  The game has lots of tools to show you what is considered cover and not- how likely you are to make a shot, etc.
Overall the game is fun, definitely worthwhile when on sale.  It has an unpolished feel- but there is HUGE potential in this game- especially since the developers look devoted to improving the game with patches long after the main sales have been made.
If you enjoyed this game, I would encourage you to leave positive reviews to help keep the franchise alive.  I think a lot of the poor sales have been down to unfair negative reviews from people expecting a games that this was never going to be.

The least worst JA title in 15 years?
Where to start...
It was an amateur Kickstarter that spent only a year in development.  Unfortunately, that shows just about everywhere.  The game opens with you as an the sole survivor of a covert CIA mission to assassinate a drug kingpin on his island.  A servicable plot, but rather than use a cut scene or even a slideshow, this is presented in a popup.  *All* of the non-essential NPCs were given away as Kickstarter rewards, so towns are populated by internet usernames spouting insufferable in-jokes.  The game engine is obviously some kind of game-maker-like product that feels very cheap.  The maps are genuinely gorgeous, but lack interaction: doors don't exist (no really, they're all open), I didn't see any kind of lootable objects, rooftops don't exist (JA without rooftop snipers?!?), livestock is immobile and immortal cover (seriously, goats count as heavy cover).  Whereas JA2 had a notoriously catchy soundtrack that cued the action perfectly, I heard no music whatsoever in this game.
Ultimately, it's an okay game, arguably better than JA: BiA.  Still, if you came to this expecting JA3, you're going to be disappointed.

Okay, so you’ve without a doubt seen the reviews blasting the game’s matchmaking, Peer to Peer, gear that over powers opponents, and so forth. These things are god awful and are well worth noting before you decide to make a purchase on this game. But, I still love this game despite Ubisoft’s unforgivable handling of it.
For Honor has an amazing combat system. Duels are intense and feel very skill based (unless the mother ♥♥♥♥er you’re fighting has better gear than you). There is a large learning curve here, and the combat is deep. I realized this when my friend made a ♥♥♥♥ing flow chart of proper actions to take based on enemy movements.
I did enjoy the campaign. You get to select from a series of pre-made custom characters’ male or female and play through fairly well made levels. Some are very open and a blast to play through. The Samurai and Knight sections of the campaign were fantastic. There is a cool world here too and learning about it was fun. The villain is comedically edgy, so if goofy things like that ruin games for ya don’t bother. I myself had too much fun with it. The campaign is two player co-op as well.
This is going to sound pathetic but my favorite thing to do in this game is load up custom games and play against bots or friends (I immediately turn off gear buffs because ♥♥♥♥ gear buffs and the autist who suggested them.) This is when For Honor’s duels shine. No gear buffs, you fighting your buddies or some high-level bots. I’m only level 9 as of the time of writing this review. So, I ain’t got♥♥♥♥♥♥in terms of gear. I’m practically cannon fodder in multiplayer matches.

Like I said earlier the multiplayer is ♥♥♥♥ed. Matchmaking, stability, and gear buffs completely kill it. The community is salty but I don’t really care. It adds some humor for me personally. And I will admit beating players who have better gear than you is akin to having your♥♥♥♥♥♥sucked (I’d imagine).
So, why do I ultimately recommend this game despite those glairing problems?
Because it’s fun. Even when I get heated playing I don’t stop. Cause I love the combat system and the universe created here. This game fully deserves the♥♥♥♥♥♥people are giving it. Ubisoft should’ve placed in dedicated servers, and a better matchmaking system. And the dev team should’ve gotten rid of gear buffs. (But hey, microtransactions) If you and a group of friends are interested pick this one up. I’d say on sale. Because even if you hate matchmaking you can still play custom games with your pals and enjoy a pretty fun campaign.

Two months on store shelves and all this whining? It's like this review section wants the game to die before it can flourish.
I bought this game on trailer alone. Not the smartest choice in the world, but something about this game grabbed me. Maybe it was the unique way it uses its characters. Maybe it was the technique of implimenting your surrounding in your strategies. Maybe I just wanted to use a katana to slit the throats of every "deus vult" player I come across. In any case, this game has had great respect from me, and I hope more people will give it a chance.
Ignoring the issues with connectivity, the multiplayer experience is really solid. The combat system was a huge success imo, using the player's defense as their offense, all on a light, easy to understand UI. Every character plays in a very unique style, using the "easy to use, hard to master" learning curve very well. (Props to Ubi for finding an easy and creative way to let every hero stand a chance in combat) Every battle has a high risk, high reward payoff for learning the specials, and for two months in, the balancing is pretty solid (save a few oddly spammed chain attacks). Of course, PvP is not the only way. Ubi finally listened, and PvE fights are a thing, allowing players to level up and learn without being constantly flipped off a cliff by a higher level player. Not only that, but Ubisoft has been surprisingly ready to listen to player feedback on any unfair glitches and bugs that crop up. Look at the more recent updates to see just how well they care for and work with the community to bring the most fun experience possible.
The campaign was a great tool that the devs use to introduce the players to the arena. The first thing everyone should do is play the story, as it helps teach the basics for fighting and even learning a hero's weakpoints and strengths. Plus, certain maps in the multiplayer are used by the singleplayer, meaning that you can learn how certain maps play before even starting the multiplayer. I played through on three different occasions just so I discover more about how each hero and map plays. Not a lot of games can say that. I've been turned off from games for having their campaigns be the main focus and the multiplayer be basically a "and now with other players!" extension (looking at you, CoD).
Overall, this game has blown me away. I can't believe how underappreciated this title is, and I've played Mighty No. 9! For as many "issues" as players find, the positives cannot be outweighed. The entire concept is breathtaking, and I would love to find more people on here in the following months, because this game as yet to come to fruition. Consider buying it, and I'm sure you'll enjoy it too.

Survarium is a multiplayer shooter in a post-apocalyptic setting by Vostok Games. Several members of this team formerly were part of GSC Game World who created the awesome S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games – if you take a look at screenshots from the game you’ll probably immediately see similarities.
On a couple of medium-sized maps Survarium offers 3 different game modes: capturing and holding research stations, finding and retrieving batteries and the classic Team Deathmatch which means a nice mix of modes with different dynamics. The maps usually are well-designed and vary from big and fairly open country-side maps to tighter ones fighting in cities or over factories, offering opportunities for all weapon classes. On several of those maps you will also encounter large anomalies like a huge mutated tree, a distortion field or giant fire-pits.
Roaming through abandoned farms, rusty factories and collapsing research stations you may encounter smaller anomalies, called artefacts, which not only disturb your vision but also damage you if you get too close. It’s possible to remove them or – if you have the right equipment – even use the anomalies for you own gains which gives you boosts to your stats during the match.
The art-style is quite distinctive, grim and dirty fitting to the setting and rather different from most other shooters, here too following the path of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series. Overall it looks really nice and very atmospheric, especially on higher settings with all effects enabled.
Vostok Games decided to implement a faction system, each having its own selection of armour-items and weapons fitting to their respective profile: from the rather lightly armoured snipers from the Scavenger faction to the heavy armoured Renaissance Army with access to light machine guns later on. By playing for a faction you level up your relation with them, gaining access to better equipment over time– you can switch between all 4 factions and unlock the items of all of them if you want. This almost becomes a necessity when aiming at a flexible weapon loadout, since only like this you’ll get access to a balanced mix of long, medium and short-range weapons to be equipped for every situation.
Equipment items give you certain bonuses, from armour over health to protection from anomalies or extra bags for medicine and can be further improved with 3 additional attributes. Those 3 possible upgrades have to paid with silver (or the premium currency gold) and spare parts which you can get as a random drop after each match. In addition, weapons can be customized by adding attachments like scopes or different muzzles after getting a certain numbers of kills with the gun. This can be annoying in some cases, having to play a couple of matches to finally be able to put a scope on your sniper rifle.
Survarium also features a skill system which gives you bonuses on your stats like weapon switching and zooming or reduces the damage taken by anomalies. Some skills also unlock abilities, like for example being able to use certain artefacts as grenades.
The real-money shop offers, aside from the premium currency Gold, a couple of “starter and equipment packs” which help at the beginning as well as some random weapon crates. Otherwise there isn’t really much. The prices are okay for a F2P game; a starter pack definitely speeds up your progress at the beginning and gives you a slight edge, the premium system helps in the same way, giving you a boost to XP, reputation and money as well as an additional weapon loadout slot, which is especially nice at the start. Otherwise there isn’t much to spend your money on – which maybe is a good thing cause this way the game fortunately stays away from P2W.
The faction system – while being similarly motivating to the leveling-up-system in an MMO with the “getting stronger and looking cooler”-mechanic– for me seems to be slightly problematic since it divides the playerbase: Due to the higher-tier equipment getting stronger and stronger, players are divided by the stats of their items for matchmaking, instead of skill only like in other pvp shooters. This means less players per level-margin which is potentially problematic for a game in EA which doesn’t have that many players to begin with. The waiting times to get into a match can sometimes be quite long, from 30seconds to 2 minutes or more everything is possible.
The development progress seems to be not that fast lately, even though the game’s in early access/beta for already quite some time. However in its current state it’s very well playable and immediately creates the atmosphere of the old S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games; as a veteran you may wish for slightly larger maps though. The current amount of content is fine but could definitely be improved, especially in regards to map variety. The progress system is, due to the division on several factions, not very fast, making you level up several factions to get the right equipment which is a little bit grindy. However, if you’re currently looking for a grimmer, darker multiplayer shooter you should definitely give this game a shot.

The objective is to destroy the enemy fort. The game features a campaign mode that serves as a tutorial and contains somewhat scripted scenarios, a skirmish mode that lacks random maps, a more freeform sandbox mode, and online multplayer. Once the enemy reactor is destroyed, you win. Each structure may be made out of wood or armor, with doors and ropes offering other options. Metal (collected from mines) and energy (collected from wind turbines) are used to build everything in the game, including defensive shields and sandbags. The workshop, factory, and upgrade center unlock new weapons. Those weapons include machine guns (primarily used for defense), mortars, snipers, missiles, cannons, and lasers. Since machine guns automatically fire at incoming projectiles, getting past the line of defense is tough (snipers are intended to take out machine gun emplacements). Offensive weapons must be manually fired in real time, which takes away from base building too much; you also cannot set a weapon to continually fire at a specific power and trajectory, increasing the micromanagement. Any damage can be repaired by simply holding down the “R” key and moving the mouse around; this process is too quick and results in rapid recovery before a fatal blow can be levelled. Thus, most games drag out far too long. The physics are plausible and the AI is generally a skilled opponent. Forts is a fine concept, but a number of shortcomings in gameplay (defensive advantages, repetitive aiming, fast repair) hold back ultimate enjoyment.

Nobody appreciates more than me a developer that tries to revive the old ways of video games. However, games today have to have mechanics that can hold your attention. NES sidescrollers are a dime a dozen, so it's no wonder that only a handful of them became popular with gamers. Oniken compares more to those random obscure sidescrollers when it should be more comparable to the memorable ones like Ninja Gaiden.
In honor of this game's admirable attempt to revive the NES era, I will review it as any magazine from the old days would.
---
Controls - 3/5 - Movement in Oniken is extremely fast which often leaves you little time to react to an enemy. Pressing up and attack uses a grenade, but pressing up while in the air halts your forward movement which can lead to accidental deaths when you push up.
Graphics - 4/5 - The cutscenes are decent, but the sprite animations are boring. The main character's run cycle is only about 3 or 4 frames. Backgrounds really capture the spirit of NES era graphics and are well made.
Sound - 2/5 - Music is acceptable, but has no melody to it and is easily forgettable. The sound effect you'll be hearing the most is the sword swing. Strangely, most of the other sound effects are barely audible.
Replayability - 2/5 - The game is extremely linear and doesn't offer any deviation from the main path. The only benefit of replaying the game is having an easier time due to prior knowledge of enemy placement and mechanics. Some secrets can be found in destructible walls.
---
I enjoyed the novelty of playing something that felt like an NES game on Steam, but that's about the extent of my enjoyment. Getting it cheap in a bundle is the only way I could recommend it. Paying full price is highly discouraged.

Ok I don't write reviews very often....I'd rather be working on my overflowing game backlog.  But this one deserves some love since it seems to be getting a ton of hate.
I've been a HUGE JA fan ever since I found a boxed copy of JA2 in a clearance bin over 12 years ago.  I was really looking forward to this game but then was turned off by the horrid reviews that it received upon release.  I decided to just wait for a Steam sale and pick it up cheap.  I picked it up a few days ago and I'm actually pretty happy that I decided to give it a chance.  Is it as good as JA2?  No....that game is pretty tough to beat even after all these years.  This game doesn't have the amount of cool features that JA2 had and is not as immersive.  I miss the website/email UI and the merc interactions.  There are a few things that I wish were done better in this game and there are a few small bugs that weren't hammered out.
But having said that...this game is actually pretty good.  The combat is fun and the graphics are impressive once you get into the game.  Even though it misses a few things from the original games it still manages to capture the essence of what I enjoy about the JA franchise.  I can create my own merc, load him up with guns and gear (that actually are shown on the character model) and send him out to wage war.  There are a few great mods on the Workshop that really help improve the games camera and gun info.  ALL in all I would recommend this game to JA fans and newcomers to the series.  I hope that modders (or fingers crossed) the devs revisit this game and add more content and squash the remaining bugs.  It is soooo close to being a great JA game.  But even in it's current state it is FAR better than what some of the reviews are saying.  Give this one a shot folks...it's worth the time.

What happened to Jagged Alliance: Flashback? What happened was that it didn't have a chance.
Two things were working against this game: The sub-standard budget ($360,000 Kickstarter budget + however many sales this game got on Early Access at $30 minus royalties) and Full Control's developers, who have in the past turned the board game Space Hulk into Space Suck through a ham-handed understanding of the mechanics and lack of polish.
The former is unfortunate - because of this, features had to be cut. Features like character animations, a bunch of the mechanics from Jagged Alliance 2 (which is telling, because Flashback was supposed to be a lot like Jagged Alliance 2 with v1.13 patch features), running and managing your own base of operations, and skill trees. The developers didn't have enough funds or manpower to implement everything, which is a major disappointment.
The latter is also unfortunate, because this game has one of the worst looking user interfaces I've ever seen. There's only one font for this game and it's an obnoxious '90's looking Geocities font that slides off the eyeballs. Thankfully, there isn't anything worth reading here, because the character bios and flavor text that help make Jagged Alliance's storytelling have been neutered by word limits and bland writing. The enemy AI is poor, the kind of poor intelligence that makes enemies stop when they see you and open fire, like dumb turrets asking for a bullet in the face. There's all sorts of minor yet annoying bugs that coalesce into one huge Megazord of♥♥♥♥♥♥ There is voice acting from every one of the mercs, but a lot of them re-use lines from Jagged Alliance 2 except in a worse manner OH♥♥♥♥♥♥HERE I AM COMPARING THIS GAME TO JAGGED ALLIANCE 2 AGAIN.
All of this is a huge leap backwards, turning this Jagged Alliance game into something functional yet generic. I did have a little fun (I ran out of bullets for my squad thanks to terrible loot distribution, but had three or four flashbang grenades. So I had my gunner flashbang all the mercs while my melee-only character runs up and delivers fists of death into faces), but I'm not interested in seeing where this game goes because it's too much of a mess to play.
I will say that the soundtrack is good and is successful at capturing the spirit of the old Jagged Alliance games. And I admire Full Control's persistence in trying to fix all of this with post-launch support and soldiering on when things look seemingly impossible. But I haven't seen anything in the past 16 years that would be a true successor to the franchise, and how Flashback turned out I don't think I'm ever going to at this point.
Rest in peace, Jagged Alliance.

Unlike most of the previous 2D Worms games, Worms Ultimate Mayhem features a 3D, turn-based artillery strategy that allows player to move freely rather from left and right. In the game lobby, players are able to choose from a wide variety of different weapons and use them when the game starts. At the start of the game each player is able to control four worms, due to the game turned-base nature, each player control one worm at a time with a set time limit; when the time limit expires or when the worm fires a weapon, the player's turn will end and the opponent will start his turn. The objective of the game is to eliminate all of the enemy team worms. There are two ways that a worm can be eliminated. The simplest way is to deplete the worm of its health, that can be done by choosing a weapon, aiming it at the enemy worm, and firing at the opposing team worm. The second way is to knock the worm out of the platform; some weapons provide the ability to push or knock back the opposing worm. Once a worm is eliminated, it cannot be brought back to life and once all four of a player's worms are eliminated the game will end. The team with worms left standing is the winner.

Two months on store shelves and all this whining? It's like this review section wants the game to die before it can flourish.
I bought this game on trailer alone. Not the smartest choice in the world, but something about this game grabbed me. Maybe it was the unique way it uses its characters. Maybe it was the technique of implimenting your surrounding in your strategies. Maybe I just wanted to use a katana to slit the throats of every "deus vult" player I come across. In any case, this game has had great respect from me, and I hope more people will give it a chance.
Ignoring the issues with connectivity, the multiplayer experience is really solid. The combat system was a huge success imo, using the player's defense as their offense, all on a light, easy to understand UI. Every character plays in a very unique style, using the "easy to use, hard to master" learning curve very well. (Props to Ubi for finding an easy and creative way to let every hero stand a chance in combat) Every battle has a high risk, high reward payoff for learning the specials, and for two months in, the balancing is pretty solid (save a few oddly spammed chain attacks). Of course, PvP is not the only way. Ubi finally listened, and PvE fights are a thing, allowing players to level up and learn without being constantly flipped off a cliff by a higher level player. Not only that, but Ubisoft has been surprisingly ready to listen to player feedback on any unfair glitches and bugs that crop up. Look at the more recent updates to see just how well they care for and work with the community to bring the most fun experience possible.
The campaign was a great tool that the devs use to introduce the players to the arena. The first thing everyone should do is play the story, as it helps teach the basics for fighting and even learning a hero's weakpoints and strengths. Plus, certain maps in the multiplayer are used by the singleplayer, meaning that you can learn how certain maps play before even starting the multiplayer. I played through on three different occasions just so I discover more about how each hero and map plays. Not a lot of games can say that. I've been turned off from games for having their campaigns be the main focus and the multiplayer be basically a "and now with other players!" extension (looking at you, CoD).
Overall, this game has blown me away. I can't believe how underappreciated this title is, and I've played Mighty No. 9! For as many "issues" as players find, the positives cannot be outweighed. The entire concept is breathtaking, and I would love to find more people on here in the following months, because this game as yet to come to fruition. Consider buying it, and I'm sure you'll enjoy it too.

I don't understand the massive hate this game is getting. Off course there are some issues but in my opinion the good far outweighs the bad.
Positive things:
* This game has lots of unique characters that individually have various possible play styles and a lot of costumization options. The endless moaning about some classes being OP is something that's present in pretty much any game imo.
* Beautifull maps with environmental risks (yes I love traps because it keeps you on your toes (always mind your surroundings)).
* Fun and fast gameplay
* Definitly fewer hackers than for example dark souls PVP
* If you don't like PVP you can now just PVE and still complete all the objectives and progress your character
* The campaign is pretty short but has a great story imo. This game is primarily focussed on the PVP part so it shouldn't be that much of a surprise that it doesn't have a massive campaign.
* You can obtain everything by just playing the game (I know spending 45k steel on some outfits is only done by ppl who buy steel). Yes there are micro transactions but it's not like if you're reputation 0 or 1 you can get a gear score of 108 straight away. You still need to play the game. A badly equiped, skilled player can still beat a better geared opponent that has no skill.
* Various matching types. You can basically play any game style that you like. 1v1 or 2v2 enables you to fight without gear score or feats so it all comes down to skill. The only thing I'd like is maybe bigger maps (e.g. 8v8 but I only see that happening with dedicated servers)
Negative things:
* Internet connection is required. Not like it's the only game that requires it but it does suck.
* P2P connection. Although so far this hasn't been a big issue for me at all so far. I now have about 60 hours into this game and I hardly ever get disconnected from a game. When the host leaves there is some lag for a bit untill the connection re-establishes itself but I hardly ever get DC'd from a game.
* Unbalanced matchmaking. This is only an issue in games where gear stats are enabled where high gear scores clearly have an advantage. To be fair though, this is only a minor issue since it doesn't guarentee victory either. I've had lots of dominion games where we were outclassed but still won. Yes you often encounter more experienced players that'll wipe the floor with you but you can only get stronger by playing a stronger opponent. Learn from them and if you can't stand getting your ask kicked, don't play pvp games.
*€ 60 is a steep price for this game (not including the season pass which I also hate).

Anna - Extended edition is a horror/adventure game without deaths and chasing monsters. Instead it pressures a player with a ghastly, dark athmosphere where paranormal things happen and twisted hallucinations appear.
The story begins at a courtyard of a homely cottage surrounded with beautiful peaceful landscapes. At the first moments the game explains a bit about a male protogonist's background with few sentences, which reveal that man suffers amnesia and has somekind of overwhelming obsession on the cottage.
After the short perioid of relaxing puzzle solving strange supernatural things begin to happen: these events will not leave in dropping food cans nor mysterious voices, but instead take increasingly scaier features which I won't list here to avoid spoilers. I'll just say that this is about a very terrifying game where it is really hard to make yourself confortable.
The gameplay in "Anna" is excelent and offers various interesting puzzles, whereas some of them honestly were a little dumb and far fetched. Luckily though player is provided with customizable hint system which can be turned on/off whenever player wants. As in many other adventure games during quest the inventory is filled with many items, which can be examined and attached together. As a new innovation player also gathers some thoughts and conclusions that can be blended together to see some details about the story.
Anna - Extended edition surprised me as a game and especially as a horror game, which storyline eventually sorted out to be sad, but also inspiring. I hope that the develeopers carry on with the same genre.

This game gets a lot of hate, not all without good reason. This review will go over BOTH sides of the For Honor coin; the things that make it one of the most unique fighting games I've ever had the good fortune of playing, and the things that need to be changed in order for this game to become truly successful one day.
The Good:
-Truly Unique Combat System: I've never played a game like this. The depth of swordplay in this game is the closest thing I've found to real life swordfighting in any video game I've ever played, and I've played many.
-Setting: Alright, who the hell HASN'T pretended to be a Knight or a Viking or a Samurai at some point in their lives? This game allows you to play any one of those badasses and it feels amazing.
-Visuals: Visually the game is downright stunning. 60FPS makes combat look/feel smooth and the devs put a MASSIVE amount of detail into all of the environments. You look out into the distance on any map and you can feel this sense of scale to the world they built.
-Executions: C'mon, who doesn't love impaling someone on a halberd, or lopping off a head with a katana? Executions are brutal and satisfying.
The Bad:
-P2P Connection: Currently, this game has no real servers. It relies entirely on Player to Player connection, which in 1v1 or 2v2 is alright. It eliminates the usual lag games get from PING. However, this becomes a serious hinderance when you play any of the 4v4 modes. One person can ragequit, and sometimes everyone in the game is booted to the main menu for it, leaving you with no experience or steel and wasted time.
-Balance: Admittedly, the game is new and this is something the devs ARE working on but it needs to be said anyway. Some of the characters in the game are downright unbalanced. If you aren't playing one of the top 5 characters, odds are good that you're losing quite a bit. The devs have released several updates at this point however so I'm hopeful that the game will be balanced properly one day.
-Microtransactions: All microtransactions are purely cosmetic, and can all be purchased with in-game currency. However the rate at which you attain this currency (Steel) is pretty slow, so of course Ubisoft lets you buy Steel with real money. But in order to purchase ALL of the current cosmetics would cost close to 700 US Dollars and that is completely ridiculous.
End note: I fully support this game and I truly hope that Ubisoft gets their sh*t together so they can turn all of the negativity surrounding this game around. I've never played a game that's more satisfying or more frustrating, and that's coming from someone with over 200 hours played in League of Legends.
TL;DR - For Honor is basically 3D Mortal Kombat with Knights/Vikings/Samurai. Its a great game, but it has some serious flaws that need to be worked out. I'd say it's worth $40 in its current state, but I do not regret my purchase at all.

Well, as it finally turns out, this game has been abandoned in a very buggy state for quite a long while after failing to meet various promises which I'm sure plenty of other reviews will have covered, be it promises of an anticheat that was never released, promises of no paid DLC being present or even the non-verbal promises of the store page screenshots being different from the actual game's aesthetics.
I must say, my attitude with the few early-access games I've regrettably bought has mostly been "regret until further notice", but after giving this one plenty of time, hoping that the less-than-desirable developers would take some extra time to develop it as opposed to abandoning it entirely, I can see that it's not getting anywhere. I'm glad that I've been all the wiser since then.
Even if it did get better, it's not necessarily deserving of the money to put every community member through those kinds of hurdles before ever seeing a complete game. It then goes from "meh" to "oh hell no" when a long wait now turns out to have no end in sight at all.
I mean, I'd quite like a refund, but I kind of don't expect that. All I can do at this point (and encourage people to do) is to report the game as broken (flag button) and discourage people from buying this. The market won't exactly function too well if this is the kind of effort, or lack thereof, that gets rewarded.

To clarify, I got access to the private Beta back in September for free. I'm going to buy this now as the key for it was removed from my account but I can say the content I experienced back then has made me want to try more.
So where to begin with Forts? I'd say it strikes me as a cross between bridge building simulators, Worms, and... it's own unique thing. That holds up only if your bridge building simulator has someone firing a laser at your design while your building it and you play worms by sitting still against someone who also sits still...
So to clarify, it strikes me as "Worm-like" with its projectile system, 2D plane map, it's aesthetic and range of weapons which all feel pretty much unique. The bridge simulator part comes in with the the whole "build your own fort" as there is stresses involved and the thing can swing ever so precariously. To the point that sticking heavy armour onto the top of your fort can seem like a good idea to stop mortar blasts but with caveat that if anything blasts the lower part of your base you're going over.
The combat is fun, as your doing it around building your own base, and the early dash to see how much early damage you can do to the enemy fort is brilliant, as every little piece destroyed feels like a minor victory. Later on playing defence against incoming mortars and missiles can get dull, as your playing "point defence simulator" which sounds dull, but again, it leads into the fast combat that Forts is inevitably about. This all pays off when you get to the late stages of a match where it comes down to "who got the mega weapon first". Not so much fun being on the losing side, but I hope that's been changed since beta so there's a little counter play. But it sure is hell fun to hit the enemy base with a cannon and see their laser go up in smoke... better luck next time developers. (Though I did set them back by sniping theirs off... should mention that. Still teaches them to not not use armoured doors to save costs.)
And the tension as to who can get their top tier weapon built first generally carries the whole experience as there is always the chance that the enemy miss their shots and you can pull it back...
All in all, Forts is a brilliant game to play and have fun with. The campaign was meh when I tried it (it may have changed since September/October), but the multiplayer is where it's at.

I played the whole game until the end of the "current beta" (Spoilers)
While the game is rich there are a lot of things that really made this game a bad experience:
Combat seems to offer a lot at first sight but after playing it has a lot of flaws. I did not suck at combat, i think i did pretty well, i also farmed nearly all cards, but during combat a always felt annoyed, they are a chore:
- The deeper into the game the more unbearable the combat system becomes. At first everything is fine and plays decent, enemies have some advertised charge abilities and some require you to block or dodge.
- Then suddenly the enemies start to kite like hell and abuse your 4 directional attack restrictions of your abilities by dodging diagonally all the time (Skycastle). Next you have the Snowball jugging guys in the snow-areas which throw nearly invisible projectiles at you.
- The gift-box enemies just throw an infinite amount of bombs at you to create random area-denial which taunts you to respec your combat style to spells but this costs much gold
- The season temple was ok, except for the hydra fight which shows what is the biggest problem for the remaining game: The game sets up a framework for combat, and then completely cripples this framework by denying you in all sorts of ways in order to create artificial difficulty.
The hydra either does Area denial in a much too small arena, makes you blind (what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ design choice) or removes your ability to move responsively (ice-floor, even when you have the spiky boots) in a battle that requires evasion of charges, so you are fully dependend on your dodge ability, which makes the fight pretty easy again, as if the developer wants you to do things a certain way, like Apple. The fight vs the Winter-dude sucks because it has so much randomness and badly advertised attacks. I decide therefore to just gimp him by blocking the storm that was supposed to lure me the the opposite site of his long vincibility frame with the mushroom shield. This creates a blind-patch that boosted my crit by 25. That and a dmg-potion and he can be killed after two of his "i just wait 30s until you pass through my ice-maze that totally abuses the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ movement to damage you"-phases. Did i mention that diagonal movment isnt normalized? so you move Root of 2 faster when moving diagonally.
The game has its zenit in the Crystal-cave- zone where every enemy and NPC is just designed to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off until you just skip them.
There are Worms that create Area Denial patches everywhere that must be outwaited in order to take no dmg. Mushrooms create blinding fields if you vanquish them. Shell Monsters do a random charge-bounce thing that is so fast that it WILL hit you randomly... All this artificial crippling is shoved into your face one last time with the fight vs the Power-Flower in order to remind you why you hate this games combat.
After that you are having the most annoying npc interaction of the game so far with a caveling that is scamming you obviously, but you have to follow through and at the end you are completely mocked, 2 minutes later the game ends.
Other:
- You cannot really try every skill without grinding loads of gold because there is a somewhat hefty fee required everytime you want to respec your points. There is no way of trying abilities without spending your sparse points into it, maybe save game manipulation, the descriptions are detailed though
- The bag (your travaling companion) constantly patronizes you and is in general a scum-bag (pun anyone?). It comments on your inferiorness every time you die, which really feels discouraging because some battles are really badly implemented and always regards you as an incapable kid through the course of the game. I would throw this thing away immidiately if i was given the option.
- While the Pixelart-Animation is wonderful and very fluid, the Background Artwork lacks some texturing at the snow and grass areas which make them feel like MS-Paint-Jobs. The Woods and Caves are gorgeous. The dialog-box-faces look strangely out of place and i wonder if they where made by a different artist

Try to imagine Fist of the North Star, Berserker, Strider, Contra and Ninja Gaiden having a NES/Famicom baby during the early '90s - the outcome would basically be
.
As sword-wielding Zaku it's up to you to slice up enemies through 6 pretty challenging stages and to save the world from an evil overlord and his menacing cyborg army. Especially the later sections in the game are quite tough but still manageable if you memorize the boss patterns and make use of some simple methods.
Even though many players may not be impressed by the pseudo 8-Bit graphics, I still must stress out the smooth pixel artwork. The devs sure have a good taste of gory Anime shows and rock hard sidescrollers from the golden past. Music, sound effects and even controls all feel like a legit NES game and do their job perfectly. Sweet.
The only letdown is that it's not really a long game at the end of the day. Sure, the later stages indeed consume a lot of time until you beat them, but theoretically it's possible to see the ending after half an hour if you're really good.
Ultimately I can say that Oniken represents a solid Strider/Ninja Gaiden clone with some really nice moments and awesome boss fights. Preferably get it during sales when it's almost free. And beat the game in Hardcore Mode if you've got balls of steel.

Clash of clans in space. That pretty much sums up the core mechanic of VEGA Conflict.
You own a space base, and you manufacture fleets of ships to destroy other players space bases, and farm NPC ships for loot and building materials. Additionally, ships aren't lost when they are used, unlike clash of clans, and you can directly give orders to your ships, which actually makes for a rather strategic combat system.
Unfortunately, while the game's concept may be sound, the game is ultimately ruined by the corrupting evil known as KIXEYE, the game's developer. As you will notice after playing for about a day, build times in this game are staggeringly long. High level ships can take literally weeks to build, and can take days to repair once they are destroyed.
Of course, if you do not want to wait, you can spend real money to speed up the repair.
KIXEYE capitalizes on this shamelessly, as the repair time of your ships depends on their HP. The higher the HP, the higher the repair time, which is effectively a way to shackle any players unwilling to spend coins. (Coins are the premium currency.) Whales that spend mass amounts of cash can effectively use their ships as much as they want, even if they are destroyed, and can use them to freely destroy the ships of players that cannot afford to spend the money to get instant repairs.
Those who cannot afford to be whales must either settle for weaker ships with shorter repair times, or must accept the fact that their play session will be over the moment a whale sets their beady gaze upon their fleets.
We're talking 8 hour repair times at high level play, people.
What's worse, KIXEYE has a penchant for releasing powerful blueprints in events; these allow you to build ships with new and overpowered weapons. Of course, to win these events, you need to have powerful ships.
You have two choices when these events arrive; farm for literally 4 hours a day for 3 days....or spend cash.
See the pattern? But wait! If you're not a whale, and you can't get the special gear from the events, that means the whales get access to something you can't have. So the whales get stronger, beat your fleets/base to a pulp, and the whole cycle continues.
And if say, you don't mind spending a little bit of money in a F2P game, good luck!
Since most of the players that remain are new and naive, achievement hunters (such as myself), or whales that drop thousands of dollars a month on the game, KIXEYE has placed the highest possible prices in place that it knows the whales will be willing to pay. Skipping a 5 hour repair will cost you 500-1000 "coins"; that's 5 to 10 dollars! PER SHIP!
To insta-repair an entire end-game fleet will cost you 30-60 dollars! That's right, for the price of Fallout 4, you can skip the repair cost on your fleet of ships. SUCH WORTH.
To add insult to injury, KIXEYE feels they can do no wrong, and holds nothing but resentment and disgust for their player base. They refuse to change, and they won't add anything to the game, unless they think it will get people to spend coins. They won't tolerate criticism, even when warrented, and they take offense every time the playerbase DARES to tell KIXEYE what they want (and don't want) from the game. (Take a look at their recent idea for a "high counsel.")
Unless you yourself are prepared to spend thousands of dollars on this glorified, misplaced mobile game, or are as insane as I am, and simple must have the achievements, stay far away from this game, and the foul developers responsible for it.

First I'll say I never had the chance to try out the original Rocksmith, but as for Rocksmith 2014, it definitely has merit. There are of course good and bad aspects.
After only putting a few hours of time in on Rocksmith 2014 I had already gone leagues beyond what I had learned spending countless hours over weeks practicing with video tutorials and other generic instructional information. So the software does have potential to help those who have never played guitar, or are wanting to get back into it and increase their skill/knowledge.
I've encountered a few drawbacks, though these are just my personal gripes. At times the scaling difficulty in rocksmith 2014 can take a decent leap in the earlier stages. Now while stepping out of your comfort zone to learn new things can be helpful sometimes. I at times found rocksmith throwing too much at me that I haven't tried before, and can cause a sense of failure and desire to put the guitar down.
Add to that the 60 day challenge idea behind rocksmith. They want people to play for an hour a day for 60 days. Sounds good on paper, but if you haven't been playing a instrument like a guitar in the past, your fingers need time to adjust to holding down the strings. I myself have often needed to take breaks going on several days just to give my fingers a break from the punishment.
That being said, don't pick it up and expect to play the guitar for an hour a day everyday if you are a beginner. Just move at your own pace, odds are that rockmith will definitely help you improve your skill/knowledge of a guitar. And if you already are familiar with a guitar, it is a good method for learning new songs.

***Revision to review (bottom) added 11/7/2017, original review (top) made 06/21/2016.***
I am a casual gamer, so i don't invest a whole lot of resources in the games i play.  I take my time in the games i play and enjoy myself, i already have a full-time job, i'm not looking for another.
I reiterate what i said before in my review.  Researching, repairing, and constructing things takes time, the higher level, the more time it takes, the more damage to repair, the more time it takes.  You can only repair one fleet at a time (they should make it where you can repair more than one fleet at a time, or research or build more than one thing at a time, if you pay real money for it, beings it's a Free To Play game.)  Honestly, the only things that don't take allot of time (for the most part) are the battles.
A great way to compare this game is if EVE Online was a base building RTS with "small scale" fleets (each fleet being no more than 6ish ships for players.)  For combat, everything is open world.  Meaning you seek out (or get sought out) opponents, npc or player alike, in an open universe.  The actual "combat" takes place in instances that are made on the spot to keep other players/npc's from jumping in and ganking you during combat.
The nice thing about this game is that you can spend as much or as little time at any given time as you want.  Play casually and have one or two fleets and kill as many npc's or players as you like, send ships home to repair, maybe research/upgrade your base (or ships before you send them out) and go play something else.  Or play more hardcore and have allot of fleets and do allot of combat at any given time.
There is a little risk of higher lvl players harassing lower level players, but there is a restriction.  A lvl 40 player fleet can't attack a lvl 20 player fleet  (but there is no lvl restriction on a player attacking an npc fleet, just warnings not to attack too high lvl npc's.)  I'm not 100% positive on the rules of pvp, seeing as i don't do pvp.  Only very specific npc's will attack your fleets or bases.
But i think the thing i love about this game the most, is that it reminds me of one of my all-time favorite games, Robot Rising.  Where you have to split your time/resources between your fleets (or robot in Robot Rising) and your base.  The only difference between Vega Conflict and Robot Rising in that regard is that in Vega Conflict, the enemy can attack your base, which i think is an excellent concept.  It makes the player more invested in their base, as opposed to not caring about it as much and focusing on their charcter/fleet.  I would love to see a return of Robot Rising, but until then, Vega Conflict will hold me over.
Despite all the bad reviews, Vega Conflict thankfully doesn't seem to be going anywhere anytime soon.  In regards to the "microtransaction" claims, i have only spent $10 on this game.  Enough to get the Commerce Module so i can generate coins for free (coins are used to purchase special items at certain times as opposed to grinding for them, or accelerate repairs/research/building.)  I may spend more in the future to help the developers, but until then, it is only necessary to spend money if you want to save time.
Between YouTube videos, the community, and the corperation i'm in, i've had all of my questions answered and help received.  The community does make for a fun game, and there is still more than enough players playing to find friends and opponents.  ::)

Overlord is a woefully average adventure game. It revolves around being an evil hero who quests through the lands slaughtering innocents and using your minions to do your bidding.
It's strange since Overlord isn't just a hack and slash, which it is. It's also an action RTS, which comes into play while ordering your minions into combat. This is a fairly intuiative feature on the gamepad but not so much with mouse/keyboard. If you're at all interested in this game I recommend using a gamepad due to this.
However that's where all my favorite bits end, as it stands Overlord is linear and fairly simple. It lacks RPG elements and any complex RTS/Sim elements. It has a minimal, black and white, hand-drawn art style, which suits the concept well and proved to be quite striking. The UI, in general, was quite basic, but more than sufficient. The in-game text was also less visually appealing and was difficult to read at times, especially being white with a black outline on a white background! The soundtrack is quite pretty, sticking to the minimalist feel, but with distinct tracks for different areas.
I imagine there were many time and/or budget constraints, among others, and the developers have worked well with these limitations, even using them to an advantage, creating a game that is consistent in both concept and tone.
As the protagonist, you find yourself in an unknown place which you traverse in an attempt to find reason and purpose and eventually escape. You'll need to complete the small (and simple) puzzles that are dotted between vaguely philosophical musings questioning fate, autonomy, meaning and existence in general.
I completed Sisyphus Reborn, with all achievements in just under 1 hour, including time spent making a cup of coffee. Overall, I enjoyed the game and would recommend it to anyone wanting a short, contemplative experience.

Okay, so. This review USED to be negative. It was filled with the complaints that everyone was raving about. While problems still do persist, Ubisoft stepped up their game with Season 2 and the release of Centurion and Shinobi. So to keep this brief, I shall list gripes I have, old and new, and go on to actually praise this game.
Negatives
-Spammable combos that leave no room for counters
-Subpar balancing
-Iffy connections (not as bad as launch, but can still be a pest. Not overly annoying.)
-Community is maturing, but there is still cancer that CS:GO could dream of having.
-New Gear Scores are overpowered
-P2P still a thing.
And now, onto the positives.
One of the main complaints in Season 1 was the broken matchmaking. Connecting to people in the "Strict (Roughly Same Level)" and Extended (Larger Level Range)" was rare and "All Skill Levels" would be common. It got frustrating being paired up with Prestiege 11 people when you may or may not have prestieged once. Season 2 tweaked it so connecting in the Strict and Extended phases are infinitely more common. These were much needed changes for the game's longevity.
Stats for Gear Scores also have had changes. Stat alignment has changed for the better, showing exact percentages for certain stats and changing stats affected by the items, leaving making character builds both easier and more balanced. The Gear Score may also be linked to matchmaking, as when I've played, the Gear Score among all participating players was pretty much the same.
The introduction of Centurion is a godsend. Centurion's moveset is very much based on quick, unblockable attacks that stun or knock over foes. Centurion is, without a doubt, a counter to the shielded and larger characters. He's versatile in any situation and arguably one of the best classes. I can't wait to play him next week (from writing this, of course), as he is currently only available via the Season Pass' early access along with Shinobi. Speaking of...
Shinobi is an interesting concept. They are For Honor's first ranged class. Their HP compensates for this advantage, but their damage does not. It's apparent that Shinobi is the game's glass cannon, but even most glass cannons don't hurt this bad. They can endlessly combo you for most, if not all, of your health, leaving you eating dirt real quick. A small damage nerf is all they need really, and did they REALLY need bleed? That's 3 out of the 5 Samurai that have bleed procs, including Orochi's feats. Oh well. All in all, creative and good class, just need to keep an eye on their reception among players.
For all its problems, and for all the things Ubisoft stood up and fixed, my score for this game is 6.5/10, which fundamentally is a pass. Still not great, still overpriced, but it's on its way. Its combat is still addicting and fun, albeit exploitable. Just need to find the counters to all the cheese. Pick it up when it goes on sale and join the crusade/raid/anime club!

I'd totally recommend getting Kisima Ingitchuna on special with the DLC.

This game is quite disturbing, that's the first thing I will say. Anna - Extended Edition is a challenging point and click type of game that nudges the survival horror genre a little. I mention survival horror mainly because it seems quite inspired by Amnesia - The Dark Descent, however it does not require you to run away and hide from monsters once in a while. The game does have a sanity meter, though, but other than that it continues down the puzzle road, mainly.
You start outside, in the yard of a house - a sawmill, and you suffer from amnesia. What's with all of the amnesia themed horror games these days? Putting that question aside, your first challenge begins. The house is locked, how do you get in? Ah, our first puzzle! The first of gazillions, crazy, disturbing and somewhat illogical puzzles! Although, I have to admit that the original game was worse in the 'illogical' part.
Once you get inside the horror starts. This game will mess with your mind. I found myself disturbed many times as I progressed through the game. There are several events that triggers randomly, different intuitions to unlock and combine, a lot of books to read and on top of that Anna has eight different endings! This of course boosts the replayability a lot, if you can stomach going through the game several times.
Visually, it's decent. It's not the prettiest one in the bunch, but it has the atmosphere nailed. Graphics are not important when it comes to psychological mind*bleep* games, in my opinion. The sound quality is somewhat lacking at times and there are occasional frame rate issues, sadly. It's not a flawless game but if you can close your eyes to various bugs then you won't have a problem playing the it, despite its somewhat awkward controls.
All in all, I was pleasantly surprised by the game but then again I knew nothing about it so I had no expectations when I first started playing it. I will admit that it's not for 'everyone' and it's definitely not a game for the youngest gamers out there. If you'd like to experience a twisted story then look no further - Anna is quite effed up in terms of story. It's a bit like The Cat Lady - you really have no damn clue about what's going on, which will generate a numerous of "WTF?!"s as you continue deeper into the secrets of that abandoned house.

Try to imagine Fist of the North Star, Berserker, Strider, Contra and Ninja Gaiden having a NES/Famicom baby during the early '90s - the outcome would basically be
.
As sword-wielding Zaku it's up to you to slice up enemies through 6 pretty challenging stages and to save the world from an evil overlord and his menacing cyborg army. Especially the later sections in the game are quite tough but still manageable if you memorize the boss patterns and make use of some simple methods.
Even though many players may not be impressed by the pseudo 8-Bit graphics, I still must stress out the smooth pixel artwork. The devs sure have a good taste of gory Anime shows and rock hard sidescrollers from the golden past. Music, sound effects and even controls all feel like a legit NES game and do their job perfectly. Sweet.
The only letdown is that it's not really a long game at the end of the day. Sure, the later stages indeed consume a lot of time until you beat them, but theoretically it's possible to see the ending after half an hour if you're really good.
Ultimately I can say that Oniken represents a solid Strider/Ninja Gaiden clone with some really nice moments and awesome boss fights. Preferably get it during sales when it's almost free. And beat the game in Hardcore Mode if you've got balls of steel.

The Darkness is one of my favorite games. It really aged well, even after 9 years, as of writing this review. It's one of those games that is so well put together that you enjoy even just roaming around. The music is so adding to it. But enough walking around it. I strongly recommend playing The Darkness I before The Darkness II. The Darkness II is fun, but it misses that realistic atmosphere. On the other hand they traded that in for comic book visuals, which I guess is being true to the origins of The Darkness as a comic book. The game is fun though. There's a wide palette of content. From interesting story, to interesting locations. Of course the thing about both games is The Darkness itself. It's a power that lets you wield 2 demon arms, in addition to ordinary weapons. You can impale/slice people up or create a black hole to suck them in. There's more to that, but I don't want to spoil too much. I hope you pick both of these games up.

To clarify, I got access to the private Beta back in September for free. I'm going to buy this now as the key for it was removed from my account but I can say the content I experienced back then has made me want to try more.
So where to begin with Forts? I'd say it strikes me as a cross between bridge building simulators, Worms, and... it's own unique thing. That holds up only if your bridge building simulator has someone firing a laser at your design while your building it and you play worms by sitting still against someone who also sits still...
So to clarify, it strikes me as "Worm-like" with its projectile system, 2D plane map, it's aesthetic and range of weapons which all feel pretty much unique. The bridge simulator part comes in with the the whole "build your own fort" as there is stresses involved and the thing can swing ever so precariously. To the point that sticking heavy armour onto the top of your fort can seem like a good idea to stop mortar blasts but with caveat that if anything blasts the lower part of your base you're going over.
The combat is fun, as your doing it around building your own base, and the early dash to see how much early damage you can do to the enemy fort is brilliant, as every little piece destroyed feels like a minor victory. Later on playing defence against incoming mortars and missiles can get dull, as your playing "point defence simulator" which sounds dull, but again, it leads into the fast combat that Forts is inevitably about. This all pays off when you get to the late stages of a match where it comes down to "who got the mega weapon first". Not so much fun being on the losing side, but I hope that's been changed since beta so there's a little counter play. But it sure is hell fun to hit the enemy base with a cannon and see their laser go up in smoke... better luck next time developers. (Though I did set them back by sniping theirs off... should mention that. Still teaches them to not not use armoured doors to save costs.)
And the tension as to who can get their top tier weapon built first generally carries the whole experience as there is always the chance that the enemy miss their shots and you can pull it back...
All in all, Forts is a brilliant game to play and have fun with. The campaign was meh when I tried it (it may have changed since September/October), but the multiplayer is where it's at.

There's not too much to say about it, it's a straight forward shooter with good gunplay and very satisfying "Darkness powers" in the form of 2 demon arms, which can lift and throw as well as slice enemies in half. The 2 arms can be controlled independently of each other and your fire arms. You can probably beat the game without ever firing a shot. Vice versa the darkness powers are not necessary to kill enemies, they just vary up the gameplay and make it more interesting. Plus they look awesome.
Apart from that you will wield an assortment of handguns, shotguns, machine guns and assault rifles. Nothing out of the ordinary here, but as I said the gunplay is great and the brutal feedback (this game is very gory) makes it so much more satisfying. Beware: Don't let kids near this game imho.
Enemy variety is ok. You get more advanced enemies as the game goes on, but pretty much all of them just want to shoot you...
The story is actually quite good for an FPS and on your way you can collect various relics, which even get voiceover once you aquire a certain individual. These as well as kills and eating the hearts of your enemies reward you with essence with which you can upgrade your darkness powers. These range from different executions for various benefits like ammunition or health to more powerful guns and some fun little gimmicks like Black Holes! Those are really fun.
There's also a coop mode named Vendetta (can be played solo), which runs parallel to the main campaign. I did not bother playing it, because I was just doing it for the story, and there's apparently not much of that there...and it doesn't really matter after you've beaten the game. You can choose between 4 assassins with their own unique weapons and darkness powers. If you need some more Darkness II gunplay, go for it.
There's also a New Game+ in which you keep your already earned powers and upgrades, but to be honest, you can pretty much max out most of it during your first playthrough, so not sure what the point of it is. There doesn't seem to be any kind of secret ending. Although there IS a "secret" ending right before the actual ending, but you can't miss it. Just stay there.
Four potentially major problems with this game though: Number 1, played on Windows 10, there was a nasty glare effect that sometimes happened for no reason at all. Usually when you go into the light, your powers will vanish for the time being and you get blinded, but this was just a haze laid over the normal game and was clearly a graphics bug...very annoying. Sometimes it helped to just change something in the graphics settings (some decals or such) and hit apply, but not always. Very annoying, since it just looks like you're drunk.
Number 2: The game's graphics in general are sort of cell shaded. You either like it...or you don't. Personally I think it doesn't fit at all. First game's graphics were more subdued, more realistic. This one is too bright and colourful imho, plus it actually causes some shadow issues, at least on Win 10. Nothing severe. Just though you should know.
Number 3: The "alternate loony bin" areas. You'll see, but these are essentially non-combat cinematic experiences. They are relatively boring and take away from the actual meat of the game.
Number 4: This game is short. We're talking about 5, possibly 6 hours for the main campaign. The problem is that since the missions are all pretty much the same and the gameplay does not change or evolve apart from a few different and rare parts. Even with the loony bin...and all the cutscenes, so actual gameplay is maybe an hour less or so. So if it were longer, say 10 hours or so, you would probably get sick of it by then. Get it during a discount and watch the recap in the game or better still, watch the "movie" on YouTube to get an idea of what the ♥♥♥♥ is even going on.

Overview: Keep in mind that this is an indie game, so it's not quite designed to bring you the same experience as AAA titles. What I like about indie games in general is that they usually require a small sense of imagination, something that games lack in this era, but that they didn't 10 years ago...
Story: 8/10
The story is what drives this game. The nearer I was toward the end, the more I could feel that sweet Just-One-More-Level Syndrome, just because of how the story is paced. It is also quite ambiguous and philosophical, so I can't be one to judge how well written it is, simply because it should be open for everyone to decide on their own. You play as Thomas and his friends, computer programs that started to pose the most basic questions anyone would ask themselves: "Why are we here?". You join in them in their pursuit of knowledge of their surroundings, with a new character appearing every act or so. They each have different personalities and across the levels, they're split up in almost every single combination imaginable between levels. The glue that holds everything together is the narrator, who is expertly voiced in my opinion, simultaneously the only voice heard during the game.
Graphics: 7/10
This is an indie game, it's not supposed to be flashy. Still, while all the water and steam effects are well handled, the game is simple, just as it should be. Still, i think this game could use some more edge curving in the graphics options. Maybe a few more different particle effects.... But, since this is a very artistic game, the one to judge should be the player.
Sound: 8/10
None of the music felt redundant. None at all. For that, the game earns major respect. I can see how much time went into the pacing of this game. The sound effects though are a different matter, I must admit that I was starting to dislike the jump sound for the characters near the end of the game, especially since this is, after all, a platformer, which brings me to the final and most important part of a game:
Gameplay: 7/10
I am a fan of platformers, so I'm not easily tired by them. So as a veteran of the genre, I got to say that this is an extremely easy addition to it. The penalty for dying as any character in a level is simply going back to the last checkpoint, but the game only managed to kill me off in, at most, around 15 levels, levels usually designed from a "learn from your mistakes" basis. Still, it's also kind of what makes the experience enjoyable, since it's practically a breeze. It lets you focus on the story thanks to that. I guess it just isn't supposed to be a challenging game, like platformers such as Super Meat Boy or Rayman.
Conclusion 7/10
Very enjoyable. If you got this off a Humble Bundle, it is worth the whole bundle. Still, to be completely honest, I think 8 euros on the steam store is just too much. That is my opinion, and it is final because I've finished the game. Still, I've enjoyed every minute in this game (except maybe that one level with those small platforms overthe water), and i recommend it to anyone, since it is unique and doesnt require pro gaming skills.
