It seems that a lot of the top reviews have forgotten something important from the devs:
So, before you read any reviews,
read that EA description.
Back? Alright.
The main concerns I’ve seen from top commenters are amount of content and update frequency. Interestingly enough, the devs address both. First, content. Many complaints tend to stem from the fact that, if you skip cutscenes and side missions, there’s about four hours of content, and their disappointment at its limited playtime, etc. However, the developers noted this in the EA info: “it takes about 4 hours to complete if you skip most of the side content. If you want to do everything currently in Story Mode, expect to invest at least 10 hours.” Does this mean you should buy the game immediately? No. It just makes those complaints about content seem a little less grounded when they were given warning. Next, update frequency. This seems to be the major complaint with most Not Recommended reviews. Surprise surprise, the devs were prepared again.
Again, those complaints lose a little luster once it’s clear that there was a warning. With a large development team, big and detailed games can take years. This game is being made by three people. It’s going to take a long time. However, as of today on day of writing, March 27, 2017, the devs posted an update that ends the area that will be the largest until the game’s very end, which means the update frequency should increase. (Sidenote: I don’t blame reviewers for not knowing that. I only learned it existed twenty minutes ago. But, it is important to note.) In any case, the update frequency is pretty good for three people on this intensive of a game. With that out of the way, let’s move to:
This is the star of the game. The swing arcs are clearly defined for each weapon, the animations are smooth, it feels good to hit enemies, with enemy recoil and appropriate sound effects, and a wide variety of character expansion options. In Grindea, there is no class system. When you level up, you receive points that you can put into skills, spells, and stat bonuses of your choice. Want to be a brutal tank who crushes their enemies? Do it. Want to be a deadly mage who roasts and electrocutes their opponents from afar? Do it. Want to be a glass cannon who can crit 25% of the time for 165% of their damage? Do it. That’s where the replayability comes from: a wide variety of combat options and stat choices. I personally have all nine character slots filled with hard-hitting tanks and long-range mages and spellswords and summoners and so on. There are even a couple support spells, with more planned for implementation. You can also get a pet by taming some of the common enemies in the game. You can feed them, and they’ll give you stat bonuses if you put enough into one stat.  Grindea is also very playable with a controller, and I recommend it. While keyboard is good, a controller hearkens back to SNES-era RPG’s and feels great. This game also doesn’t want you to grind. Yes, it’s in the name. That’s the joke. The more you try to farm in this game, the more enemies that appear. You can get overwhelmed if you aren’t careful.
I honestly love this game’s story. While the core plot is pretty simple, get some things so the world doesn’t explode, it’s really the characters that make Grindea feel alive. Every character’s text box portraits are detailed and have multiple expressions. Their in-game sprites look good and have smooth animation. These animations give personality to the characters and distinguish them from “blue-haired dude” and “is that Cloud?” There’s growth and blooming relationships between characters. Even with the protagonist, I was pleasantly surprised. Rather than being The Great Hero of the Ancient Prophecy, you’re just a kid doing their job as a Collector, like a lot of other people. You fall into having to save the world rather than being born as the Savior of the Earth or Whatever. You end up “borrowing” some Really Old Super Dangerous and Powerful Artifacts not because a legend told you to, nor because you woke up and decided to, nor because your dead parent spoke to you in a dream or whatever. You just end up having to save the world. There’s charm, wit, humor, and no end of pun names.
There are arguments for both sides of this. While singleplayer is viable and the same experience, you’re just not as strong as with others. Some bosses are very tough without help.
With friends that also enjoy this genre, Grindea is excellent. As long as everyone has a half-decent router and a computer that meets the minimum on the store page, you probably won’t have issues. While large areas do take a while to load on less superb computers, it’s nothing unbearable. Unless
ping is 30,000. So, if you’re playing this alone, it’s still fun, but you’re going to have to work harder and longer than with others simply because more people make the game easier.
If you want a finished game, don’t buy this. If you want a perfectly polished game, don’t buy this. If you want a game that absolutely positively has no bugs, don’t buy this. If what I and the store page have told you has you itching to buy this, buy it. It’s a lot of fun and a good game. If you’re on the fence, pick up the demo. It’ll give you a better sense of gameplay than words ever could. I came into this Early Access game expecting just that. I was pleasantly surprised.  I recommend this game for stellar characters, graphics, animations, music, and mechanics. It’s not finished, certainly. It takes time to make a game, certainly. There are issues, certainly. But what’s there is good. Just because it’s slow doesn’t make it bad.

First I'll say I never had the chance to try out the original Rocksmith, but as for Rocksmith 2014, it definitely has merit. There are of course good and bad aspects.
After only putting a few hours of time in on Rocksmith 2014 I had already gone leagues beyond what I had learned spending countless hours over weeks practicing with video tutorials and other generic instructional information. So the software does have potential to help those who have never played guitar, or are wanting to get back into it and increase their skill/knowledge.
I've encountered a few drawbacks, though these are just my personal gripes. At times the scaling difficulty in rocksmith 2014 can take a decent leap in the earlier stages. Now while stepping out of your comfort zone to learn new things can be helpful sometimes. I at times found rocksmith throwing too much at me that I haven't tried before, and can cause a sense of failure and desire to put the guitar down.
Add to that the 60 day challenge idea behind rocksmith. They want people to play for an hour a day for 60 days. Sounds good on paper, but if you haven't been playing a instrument like a guitar in the past, your fingers need time to adjust to holding down the strings. I myself have often needed to take breaks going on several days just to give my fingers a break from the punishment.
That being said, don't pick it up and expect to play the guitar for an hour a day everyday if you are a beginner. Just move at your own pace, odds are that rockmith will definitely help you improve your skill/knowledge of a guitar. And if you already are familiar with a guitar, it is a good method for learning new songs.

I played the first SteamWorld Dig a day or two before this one and thought it could have been really good if it was just a little bit... more. As it was, I found it so tedious I could be barely be bothered to continue. I didn't give it the in-depth review it probably deserved at the time, but once you saw the store page video you've basically seen the game.
Enter SteamWorld Dig 2. The game starts up with a flying start with an almost-immediate boss fight. Sweet! The enemies in general mean business and have new abilities that make them more challenging and fun to fight, which is good because now you gain experience and occasionally gems for killing them. Great! The levels are busier and more interesting, the cave trials are legitimate challenges that are almost never unfair, the new abilities are fun to use... basically, it's SteamWorld Dig but more, which is basically all I wanted from it! The progression feels significantly faster than the original as well, and because the upgrades are all different you won't feel like you're playing a simple upgrade.
More isn't always better; you are saddled with an obnoxious support character early on, and I really don't think the increased prominence of the dialogue suits the game. It is not bad, but I ended up ignoring a majority of the NPCs in this game that do not help feed the ever-upgrading dig engine.
Speaking of the story, I have a serious complaint. Without spoilers: the game has a serious downer ending. This was foreshadowed adequately such that it doesn't come as a surprise when it happens (at least if you're paying attention), but I cannot help but feel that it could have been prevented. You visit an important site from the previous game and some very strange stuff happens that is never explained. I legitimately have no idea why we went there or, more importantly, how our character escaped certain death. From what I can tell, the trip is entirely optional and yet this is one of the most difficult parts in the game. The trip felt like it should have been a step in the True Ending, but there is no alternate ending.
*sigh*
In any event, this game is very much worth your time. Contrary to what some of the other reviews here say, I do not believe the original game is necessary to enjoy this one. Play this, and give the prequel a miss.

Even if you don't know it by name, I think just about everyone has heard, to some extent, the story of Sisyphus, the crafty king in Greek mythology sentenced by the gods to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity only for it to always roll back down again. In more "recent" years, Albert Camus wrote The Myth of Sisyphus exploring the notion of the absurdity of life and living; to actively maintain participation in an act known to be futile given its lack of ultimate consequence, but to contently "revolt" by continuing to do so whilst also wilfully rejecting concepts of hope or faith. This game touches upon many of those same themes.
In this particular allegory, our Sisyphus is a stranger who awakens without any memories in a bizarre, unfamiliar land, inhabited by people who perform actions without any justifiable reason, or even clearly defined knowledge for why they really do so. What follows is a character's journey to try and understand what's going on around him, and also find his own justifications for his own actions. In case it wasn't already abundantly clear... this is a very intellectually deep, contemplative game.
Gameplay-wise, this all takes the form of a very basic, 2D, point-and-click, side-scrolling game using simplistic art and minimal animation. On a technical level, this isn't especially impressive, but that's really not where the main crux of the substance lies, as much of your time will be spent reading lots of text and delving into some complex issues of a philosophical and existential nature.
Like most good philosophy, this doesn't offer any answers, but instead raises questions whilst offering forth suggestions or positing possibilities from its own individual perspective and beliefs or opinions. As in all such cases, the recipient's millage may vary depending on how they choose to read into it.
While I'm still not actually sure how I really feel about the game on several levels, I did at the very least really enjoy the change of pace in experiencing a game which delved into a subject matter so directly where others would normally never even dream of going anywhere near. As such, I could very easily see why this wouldn't be for everyone, but am also really glad that I took the time to explore this one and could recommend that others do so, too.

Pros:

Jagged Alliance Flashback is a Kickstarted game that aims to recapture the greatness that was Jagged Alliance and Jagged Alliance 2.  Did it succeed?  Not completely.  First off, if you're expecting Jagged Alliance 2, you'll be a bit disappointed.  Flashback is closer to JA1 than JA2, in my opinion.  That's not necessarily a terrible thing, though, as JA1 was a great game in its own right.
So let's dive into the details.  Like the games it is attempting to emulate, Jagged Alliance Flashback is a turn-based, tactical, squad strategy game with some RPG-lite elements.  You control squads of up to 6 mercenaries (you get to make one of your own then hire the rest), as many squads as you'd like, provided you can afford to hire them.  You get dropped off on a tropical island and are tasked with overthrowing a warlord.  The way you do this is by systematically taking over sectors to gain control of the island and capture areas that will generate revenue for you, allowing you to hire more mercs.  You can train militia in controlled sectors that will defend the area from enemy attacks.
Mercs, including the one you create, have stats and skills.  Stats go up when you level up while skills go up as you use them.  It's a very simple RPG-lite system where you have fairly little control of how your squad mates will evolve.  Beyond a short backstory, a different look, starting stats and skills, and different (often hilarious) barks, the hirable mercs are completely interchangeable and have no real personalities.  In fact, no one in the game has much personality beyond extremely simple motivations in the game, which is one of its biggest weaknesses.  The story is quite straightforaward and frankly pretty dull too.
Combat is the meat of the game and is thankfully quite good.  It's obvious this is where most of the resources of development went into, and rightly so.  The combat is turn-based and really well executed, in my opinion.  I'd say that it's better in many respects than XCOM.  While your characters lack special abilities, the combat mechanics themselves are quite well implemented.  As you might expect, combat revolves around positioning, cover, and AP (action point) management.  Every action, whether a movement or firing a gun, requires a certain amount of AP.  If you don't have enough AP then you can't perform that action, simple as.  You can stand, crouch, or lie prone anywhere on the battlefield (it costs AP to change stances) and can move in each stance (run, sneak while crouched, and crawl).  Crawling costs more AP per distance than sneaking, snaking costs more than running).  Crouching and lying prone also gives both offensive and defensive bonuses and can make you or your target impossible to hit, due to cover.  There is an overwatch-like interrupt system too where you can save AP unused during your turn and an interrupt will trigger if an enemy walks into your cone of vision and you can spend AP to do whatever (fire, run, crouch, etc).  Line of sight is implemented quite well, and lighting, time of day, and weather both significantly impact gameplay as they play into line of sight and the fairly simple but well implemented stealth system.  Stealth uses line of sight, visibility, and noise (crawling makes less noise than running, firing a weapon without a silencer gives your relative direction away, etc).  It all works really well and makes for a satisfying turn-based tactical experience.
Visually, while the game won't win any awards for graphical fidelity, I found the look of the game to be quite nice.  It uses a somewhat simplistic art style that purposely omits small details in favor of more solid shapes.  The highly saturated color palette works great with the tropical setting too.
The audio is pretty good too.  There is not much in the way of voice acting, besides some pretty funny barks, and there isn't a whole lot of music, so you'll be hearing the same combat music a lot.  The weapon sounds however are very punchy and satisfying, which adds a lot to the game.
The game is somewhat buggy.  Nothing game breaking, mostly little annoyances that can be put up with or worked around.  It's a somewhat rough around the edges budget title, but there's nothing I encountered that ruined my day.
If you like turn-based squad strategy then I would recommend this game, particularly if you're a fan of the old Jagged Alliance games.  just know that it;s closer to JA1 than JA2.  The game is far from perfect and has its share of shortcomings, but overall I thought the quality combat mechanics carried it and made it a satisfying experience.  I'd love to see Full Control make another JA game now that they have a framework and solid mechanics in place and could concentrate more on writing a better story with characters I might care about.

is a short, absurd reference to the work of author/philosopher Albert Camus -
-  rather than being a game. Being the sole project of Myshkin Entertaintment so far, it is a journey worthy of taking note if you do enjoy philosophical displays even the slightest. I, as a long standing lover of philosophy, especially existentialism, must say that this short little adventure manages to grasp the full content of Camus' work, and even challenges his theme of hope/hopelessness.
Well, to be able to understand the proper theme of the game, one has to be familiar with the story of Sisyphus first. According to the Greek myth, Sisyphus was the cunning and deceitful King of Corinth who managed to trick Thanatos - the Death itself - and chain him so no one in the world would die for some time, causing the old and the sick to suffer. As punishment, he was doomed to roll a huge boulder up a steep hill, yet every time that he would be about to accomplish the task, the boulder would roll down and he'd have to start all over again. He is the embodiment of a meaningless labor, doomed to take place for eternity without any conclusion.
In his essay, Camus describes the existence of man a paradox in this world. The world being devoid of any meaning - scientific or religious - mankind's constant pursuit for meaning would be equally devoid of meaning, even absurd. So, with the realization of this absurdity, would suicide be the only way out? Such is the philosophical issue that Camus thoroughly discusses in his work. According to Camus' conclusion though, the realization of the absurd asks for revolt. Yet, it is not the kind of revolt one would think of. One has to acknowledge the existence of the absurdity, yet keep challenging it by contended acceptance, thus the work itself becomes our own meaning. Such acceptance of futility would be the only freedom the absurd man can hope for.
Grim, huh? It surely is, considering existentialism and absurdity are philosophies born just after the WWII. Let's take a look back at the game though. This short little adventure world portraits the vision of Camus explicitly, yet bears a completely different approach for its conclusion - a bit close to Sartre rather than Camus. The futility dominates all conditions within, yet bearing the minimum of choices, if one manages to choose even a slightly different path dominated by his own rule... - you have to dig, yet no one describes where to dig - there is still hope. The work itself, the experience it presents us becomes our hope and our choice, breaking the seemingly omnipotent paradox.
It would take 15 minutes or so for you to experience all this short little display can present you, and excluding its additional content - it is free. If you enjoy the experience though, I strongly recommend purchasing additional content, even to only support the developer. It is simplicity done right with a great atmosphere and fitting narrative. It is a bold little experience, created by an educated mind. I think we need more of its examples here around. Its sole existence, being wholly symbolic, provokes you to think. Please enjoy!

Anna is a game that scared me like no other. Having played plenty before from Amnesia to Haunting Ground and not being overly blown away, Anna has the one special brand of horror which I can only accurately describe as 'haunting'.
While some people aren't quite effected by it, Anna posesses a subtle type of horror, relying less on combat encounters or fleeing from peril and more on simply noticing strange occurances around you, playing heavily on your perception of the area. Many paranormal events are far from obvious and what few you may witness range from unnerving to deeply unsettling but will almost often leave you second guessing your senses. I can't tell you the number of times I asked myself, "Am I seeing things?" or "Was that there before?". It's the type of horror I personally feel should be present in more games of the genre, and Anna does it exceedingly well.
Gameplay-wise however, Anna is securely medicore. The interface with your inventory and the world feels dated and clunky, and you can almost see the code chugging away during some of the puzzles. The puzzles themselves, however, are challenging and require a pretty heavy degree of thinking, more often then not in a good way. My only problem is several times over I found myself knowing the answer to the puzzle but not knowing how to execute it due to the shoddy interface.
The narrative is also very mediocre with few twists and turns away from what one would expect from a horror story. I won't go into details to avoid spoilers, but it's definitely not something to write home about.
The sound design on the other hand is nothing short of excellent and definitely builds on Anna's already chilling atmosphere. The soundtrack consists of gorgeously somber and quiet string/choir melodies, which in any other situation would seem graceful or even serene, but only build the haunting atmosphere of the environment. Audio cues being a key indicator that something around you is amiss are also executed with the perfect desgree of subtlety, though too many times I was on edge due to my own footsteps.
Overall Anna is a unique horror experience that may appeal to anyone who has struggled to find their niche in horror games to date. It's a wonderfully creepy and haunting experience only held back by it's awkward design and clunky interface.

Ok. I want to start this review by saying that there are a lot of people ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over this game really hard and that just really pisses me off, because the people behind worked very hard in it and it really shows. Now, without further adieu let's delve into this game.
First of all, it is necessary to say that Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is not just a game, is a statement, a cultural overview about the Iñupiaq community and its lore and more important, an experience. At times I found myself more fascinated with the compelling story or even the cultural insights than the game itself, which in my opinion is not a bad thing, it is just different. When you start playing Never Alone there is something that inmediately stands out from other games of the same genre, and that is the atmosphere. In the majority of today's platformers there is a consistency where every single game looks and "feels" exactly the same as the next one in line, however, Never Alone stands alone and shines because of the atmosphere it achieves to portray. Every character, every background and every level works towards the goal of setting a tone of deprivation, sadness, spirituality and hope that adjust very well to the concept of the whole project.
Also, the story of Nuna and the fox is really sad and beautiful, and one the best stories I came across in a platformer. And since this is the heart of the project, in this aspect, the developers nailed it. Not only is compelling but also a celebration of squimal culture and all the lore that brings along with it. The people and the animals merge together into an awesome mix of spirituality and guidance. Everything in the story starts to make sense once you start to find out more about the Iñupiaq community.
However, despite all of the excellent artwork and storytelling put into it, there are some major flaws in Never Alone.
The most obvious miss of the game is the abundance of various glitches that can make the gameplay very frustrating. Everytime you jump or climb up a ladder, you basically are praying to the spirits of the North for being able to make it to the goal without falling off the map or not being able to hold on to the edges. Another important flaw is the complicated scheme of controls. They might seem easy to handle in the first levels but as you progress through the game, their complexity increases as well, having to keep pressed certain keys to maximize the movement. It would a nice touch to hint at those control tactics at the beggining of the game. And regarding the gameplay itself, it needs to be polished. I got stuck many times because I wasn't able to make some jumps or follow the right sequences, which got me a little frustrated at times.
Nevertheless, Never Alone is an amazing experience that needs to be shared with the world and enjoyed at its fullest. And, on a final note, I think white foxes have escalated in my scale of cute things to the cutest things I have ever seen.

Recently I sat down and decided to search the Humble Bundle page for some potentially cheap and cheerful games. My brother has always recommended this site and well, I finally decided to give it a go. He said 'there are some right diamonds among the rough' a lot of the time, especially when it came to the Indie game scene.
His recommendation finally resulted with me purchasing the Indie Bundle 16, which of course included this game Never Alone.
To state that this is a game would not do justice to the research, history, cultural background and work behind it. To me, Never Alone is best describe as a piece of art, carefully woven together by an intriguing and engaging story-line.
You play as an Iñupiaq (a group of people native to Alaska) girl named Nuna. One day her village suffers from a constant and never ending blizzard. Being the inquisitive and humble girl that she is, Nuna decides to find the source of the storm and try her up most to stop it in the interests of saving her family. Along the way she befriends an Arctic fox and encounters ferocious winds and a few enemies that stop at nothing to cease her progress, eat her or simply want her goods.
For me, the game wasn't particular challenging. It's described as a 2D atmospheric-puzzle platformer (which, it is) but there weren't enough 'puzzles' for me to feel any real challenge. I was able to completely carve through it with little to no resist. It is incredibly short. So short in fact that it had been shorter that the most quickest of play throughs I have ever done - which was Zone Of The Enders, a game notoriously know for being short. There are pick-ups and additional downloadable content available that extend the game's life, but I have already got at least 90% of these pick-ups without even really searching for them, so replay ability is going to be minimal. I also feel like I missed out on one of the bigger game's mechcanics - it's co-operative play. Playing alone, I found myself constantly taking longer to undertake tasks rather than relying on my regular co-op partner, my brother, to help with these. The game isn't long, but doing all these tasks alone can become a bit of a bore as you find yourself taking twice as long than what you usually could achieve the desire outcome in. Having said that however, I don't feel like I am the game's target audience, nor do I believe that the point of Never Alone was to create an experience solely placed around game-play.
Never Alone's 'point' is make us aware of the strengths of nature and the cultural story-telling of the Iñupiaq people. Even though I didn't feel like the game pushed to break the boundaries of in-play styling, it's story-line induced me to push further into the game to follow Nuna's story and her struggle against the elements of Northern Alaska. I found myself actually wanting Nuna to succeed and as I followed her story, almost becoming emotionally bonded to not only herself but also with the narrator. Without the narration (which is done in the tradition Iñupiaq tongue with subtitles), I feel the real strength, the games story, would had been dramatically reduced in terms of appeal... so kudos for the game developers for not by-passing for an easier alternative of simply just putting it all in English.
All in all, Never Alone is a wonderful, all most fairy tale like story that is beautifully presented and expertly delivered. It's art style is reminiscent of a Dreamwork's Studio animation film and it's story line would be a charming children's film. As a game, I struggled to enjoy it as much as I did the behind the scenes footage (which is a collectible within the game) which told the background of the game and it's story so eloquently and with sentiment. But I am almost thirty... and Never Alone is best suited for children under thirteen.
Strongly recommended for child and players who share their gaming with their families.

The Darkness II continues the tale of Jacky Estecado from the first game (which was never released for PC). There's not too much to say about it, it's a straight forward shooter with good gunplay and very satisfying "Darkness powers" in the form of 2 demon arms, which can lift and throw as well as slice enemies in half. The 2 arms can be controlled independently of each other and your fire arms. You can probably beat the game without ever firing a shot. Vice versa the darkness powers are not necessary to kill enemies, they just vary up the gameplay and make it more interesting. Plus they look awesome.
Apart from that you will wield an assortment of handguns, shotguns, machine guns and assault rifles. Nothing out of the ordinary here, but as I said the gunplay is great and the brutal feedback (this game is very gory) makes it so much more satisfying. Beware: Don't let kids near this game imho.
Enemy variety is ok. You get more advanced enemies as the game goes on, but pretty much all of them just want to shoot you...
The story is actually quite good for an FPS and on your way you can collect various relics, which even get voiceover once you aquire a certain individual. These as well as kills and eating the hearts of your enemies reward you with essence with which you can upgrade your darkness powers. These range from different executions for various benefits like ammunition or health to more powerful guns and some fun little gimmicks like Black Holes! Those are really fun.
There's also a coop mode named Vendetta (can be played solo), which runs parallel to the main campaign. I did not bother playing it, because I was just doing it for the story, and there's apparently not much of that there...and it doesn't really matter after you've beaten the game. You can choose between 4 assassins with their own unique weapons and darkness powers. If you need some more Darkness II gunplay, go for it.
There's also a New Game+ in which you keep your already earned powers and upgrades, but to be honest, you can pretty much max out most of it during your first playthrough, so not sure what the point of it is. There doesn't seem to be any kind of secret ending. Although there IS a "secret" ending right before the actual ending, but you can't miss it. Just stay there.
Four potentially major problems with this game though: Number 1, played on Windows 10, there was a nasty glare effect that sometimes happened for no reason at all. Usually when you go into the light, your powers will vanish for the time being and you get blinded, but this was just a haze laid over the normal game and was clearly a graphics bug...very annoying. Sometimes it helped to just change something in the graphics settings (some decals or such) and hit apply, but not always. Very annoying, since it just looks like you're drunk.
Number 2: The game's graphics in general are sort of cell shaded. You either like it...or you don't. Personally I think it doesn't fit at all. First game's graphics were more subdued, more realistic. This one is too bright and colourful imho, plus it actually causes some shadow issues, at least on Win 10. Nothing severe. Just though you should know.
Number 3: The "alternate loony bin" areas. You'll see, but these are essentially non-combat cinematic experiences. They are relatively boring and take away from the actual meat of the game.
Number 4: This game is short. We're talking about 5, possibly 6 hours for the main campaign. The problem is that since the missions are all pretty much the same and the gameplay does not change or evolve apart from a few different and rare parts. Even with the loony bin...and all the cutscenes, so actual gameplay is maybe an hour less or so. So if it were longer, say 10 hours or so, you would probably get sick of it by then. Get it during a discount and watch the recap in the game or better still, watch the "movie" on YouTube to get an idea of what the ♥♥♥♥ is even going on.

I have mixed feelings about retro style games that are mere copycats from the golden age of video games. I get the nostalgia aspect, but the odd reality is that I cherish the memory of playing those old school games more than I actually enjoy playing them today. When I do play them, it's an immediate reminder of where games are today and how far along games have come and why products have advanced the way they have. While old school games were considered technically superior in their time, they are considered technically inferior today. In fact, most games of yesteryear made the most of the technology available to them. So designing a technically inferior product today, on purpose, is not that impressive to me.
Many great old school games are classified as abandonware and the ROMs and emulation software can be easily found to play them for whatever gaming system you cherished the most. Find them, play them, and try to enjoy them the same way you did 30 years ago. I've tried, but it's not the same. Reflecting on the memories of playing them gives me more pleasure.
Oniken is a good copycat from an era gone by, nothing more, nothing less.

I've seen people constantly complain on how it's such a P2W game. While I agree, I don't think the game is bad. Yes, people are cheap and better than others in this game, BUT THAT'S HOW MOST ONLINE GAMES ARE! TF2, LoL, WoW, etc. are just like this, except people don't complain about those games. I've played this game for a long time, and it's the type of game where you can get research going while doing something else. It has its flaws, and trust me, those flaws get annoying, but otherwise, its a good play that you can enjoy, F2P or P2W. I haven't spent a single cent, and I've enjoyed it.
Gameplay - 7.5/10
The gameplay is stable for the most part. Players have to navigate their ships against other ships and maneuver them in a way that ensures victory, or must use strategical movements against a bases defenses. There are three major problems however. First, the game may sometimes lose connection, so if you were doing manual movements on your ships, they're bound to be destroyed. Second, the repair time becomes repulsive and exasperating. A 5 minute battle could easily cost 4+ hours of repair, depending on the fleet you're using. Finally, it becomes VERY unbalanced once anything of yours hits Level 35. If a fleet reaches this acme, Level 55 fleets can attack you, and it is awful when this happens. When your base reaches Level 35, you are made an absolute target by higher-leveled players, especially if you have multiple medals.
Plot - 4.5/10
You're a rebel fighting against an evil organization in space searching for some object(s). Where have I heard this before?
Audio - 5/10
What do you expect? It's extraterrestrial weaponry being fired. That's most of the sound you'll hear.
Characters - 2/10
By far the most forgettable. They barely appear, and when they do, it's for an event. Bishop is the main antagonist, and even he is very forgettable. Larus is a defected VSec officer, and when he appears, it takes you a minute to remember who he is!
In total, I rate this game a 6.5/10. If you have other things you can do, this game is passable. During a school year, it is most passable. However, if you want to play only one game at a time, then DO NOT even think about getting it.

Basic concepts :
1 - You have a base, you build attachments and upgrade them, you build ship and upgrade them, you make research to unlock upgrades for ships and base.
2 - You have fleets that are used to attack and salvage neutral frets so you have resources to pay for your researches/builds/upgrades.
3 - You can join an alliance that help speed up builds/researches as well as being useful for dissuading others players to attack you (though being attacked and defeated only have minor consequences).
4 - You can attack other players for medals (I haven't understood this concept yet).
I mean, the game is good and reproduce the concept of many mobile games of this genre.  Its not a 4X game so if that's what you're looking for you should look elsewhere.  In fact, the game need more time investment when you start rather than later.  The more you progress, the more time you require to build/repair/research things (this can go up to DAYS and probably WEEKS even further).  This exponential time needed to build/repair/research things reduce the progression to a crawl after a few weeks unless you pay real money.
Does it worth it to pay??  I'm not sure.  I haven't and still play it around 20 minutes day in order to keep my base, my ships, my economy and my researches growing (slowly).  If you wanna go F2P and you can live with that you will appreciate the game. However, if you wanna reach leader boards and be competitive, be prepared to invest a ton a cash.
Recommended as a casual ''hobby'' to waste time.  If you really want to play a game in which things matter and you actually feels like achieving something, go for something else.

From Myshkin Entertainment comes Sisyphus Reborn, a simple point and click adventure game.
Sisyphus Reborn is a short game that is heavy on atmosphere, but relatively light on puzzles; this game explores philosophical ideas in a short form. Waking up in a world where everyone merely digs forever, and no one dies, how do you find meaning in a meaningless world?
It took me a long time to figure out how to review this game. It gave me a lot to think about, and it made me question a lot of things in my life. For such a short game, it really left me stunned when the credits rolled. At first, I really didn’t think it could ever have such a massive effect on my life, but it really left me floored.
This is incredibly simple, first and foremost. The artwork isn’t amazing, but the audio tracks are absolutely stunning, and really help create the atmosphere around you as you play through the game. With a few light puzzles that aren’t that hard to crack (and there’s a walk through, if they do seem to be too hard), this is a pretty easy to complete game.
Enjoyable and short, with some achievements that are easy to collect, Sisyphus Reborn is a game I would personally say everyone should play and experience. Never before have I been so moved by a game, let alone a game that took under an hour to complete. This is a work of art, and I believe it should definitely be appreciated a lot more.

Greetings fellow spaceship warfare enthusiast!
Starhammer: TVP as i will shorthand it, is a well designed space naval combat game.
I say naval because you do fight on a 2D plane with 3 "layers" pretending at "height" and "depth".
Your ships can move up and down but it does matter very little in th end as far as combat tactics go, its more useful to avoid colissions (oh yes, you can ram and be rammed). A clever tactician might abuse this by flying low or high all the time and using the dorsal or ventral shielding arcs as cheap shield batteries,. but you do not have that nugget from me, no sir you do not.
Combat itself plays out turn based, insofar you give your ships movement and firing orders and rebaance power levels to match the game situation then hit "play" and the "turn" will proceed in quite adorably cinematic manner, you can watch the shooting and enjoy, you will not be faced with twitch reaction requirements.
The combat does move in rahter similar routes once you have eased into  "your" set of combat maneuvers and got comfortable with your tactics, and som consider it stale. I consider it the mark of a good tactician if the fight goes "uneventful" XD.
The story features likable characters (i will not spoil this for you) and a good, branching campaign that offers replayability.
Its got  humor, action, spaceships and a good plot.
Graphics:
The graphics are good looking and will not crush a low end pc. Effects are well done and the sound design is very good: a big spaceship laser or gun SOUNDS as impressive as you would want to have it.
No pling pling here, no sir.
The game gets 4 stars out of 5, its a fun romp that does nothing wrong. While one might argue they could have done "more", it would be good to remembr that this game is well rounded and "works" as opposed to ambitioned projects that just turn into roadkill.

Stories Untold is a rather short game of four seemingly independent short stories. There are multiple different gameplay mechanics, that range from text adventure to point & click and to number puzzling. The whole game sets the player into a 80's atmosphere.
What I really liked about the game was at first the atmosphere and thrilling feeling it gave you. I have to admit I am not a fan of text adventures, I find it tiring and rather boring. And when the game started with exactly this mechanic, I was not very enthusiastic. But to my surprise it was actually really entertaining and also surprisingly creepy. The text adventures parts have been cut to just the right length, and were implemented very well to the modern gaming feeling. Also I liked that the game uses multiple different gameplay mechanics, that may be all rather simple, but the change of mechanics causes the game to not become boring so fast due to simple gameplay.
The story (stories?) are all really exciting, they can put you in place of the protagonist immediately, and most of the time you have no clue about what is actually going on until you almost completed the short story. I enjoyed this mysteriousness quite a lot.
Lastly, I feared already when playing the game for a few minutes, that the ending would be open for interpretation, so I tried to gather every little piece of information and turn it around three times to just find a connection that could become relevant in the end. But I have to confess that I was relieved that the game ends with a linear ending, which I think fits better to the game and was the right decision.
Although there are multiple different gameplay mechanics, some of them felt tiring nonetheless. It was not the text adventure, just to make this clear, it was really awesome. But the number puzzling was dragging a bit because it was so long, just as well as the point and click part, because you did not have to think almost anything and it did't push the story very much. Additionally, the game is no technical highlight. Graphics look fine on Steam screenshots, but in truth they are very washed, not optimized and very edgy. I think there is some potential for improvement. Other than that, the only thing I can point out as a Con is the playing time. I did not check the clock, but I cannot have been playing much longer than 2 hours. I really enjoyed these 2 hours, but I also wished the game would have lasted for a bit longer, left me a bit longer in the dark and tell me another mysterious story. A fifth episode somewhere in the middle would be a big improvement imho.
An atmospheric and gripping game with refreshing gameplay elements and an exciting story. It drags behind technically, and can become boring at some points, but for a short ride with this one you cannot make much of a mistake. I would give Stories Untold

So, After about 170 hours put into For Honor, I think it's finally time i put my two sense in...
So, Let's start with the pro's of For Honor, Shall we?

Pros
Combat: Like im sure it's been said before, For Honor's combat does not disappoint in my eyes. A 3 way attack and defensive mechanism that works almost perfectly for the third person fighting game, It's one of those ''Easy to pick up, Hard to master sort of game''
Graphics: I run this game on the highest of settings at 1080p, While not the most impressive looking feat of any game nowadays, For Honor doesn't come up short in the aesthetic or beauty of it's design. The armor detail of each fraction is impressive beyond belief, Ubisoft did one thing perfectly, And that was the armor detail.
Story: Now, Before you get all picky and critical about this part. I add the story to the pro's because as much of a cheesy and short story, Was still entertaining to me. While i don't recommend you pick this up for just the story, It's good for what it is in a obvious Mulitplayer focused game.
Now for the biggest section, The Cons.
P2P: As if the review already didn't sum this horrid section apart, I won't add much to this as it is heavily discussed everywhere. Why Ubisoft thought P2P would work better then dedicated servers, Is beyond me. It cleary plays a big reason this game is under 50% in reviews.
Community: The community has gotten to the point where it's best you just advert your attention from the chat section at all times. I have never seen more toxicity in a game since LoL or CS;GO. From salty 12 year old children who constantly type insults for beating them, Or being called horrid or a no life for beating them. By far a big thumbs down.
The Classes themselves: To me, A big gripe i have is the classes being extremely cheesy and broken, I will list 3 good examples. Warden, Peacekeeper, And Warlord. (Excluding Shugoki because ♥♥♥♥ him) Each class here to me is the cheesiest classes you could play, With the wardens vortex being able to cancel into GB, it's almost impossible to dodge or counter, Dodging could lead you into being GB while not dodging at all will leave you to a shoulder bash and 2 hit light combo.. PROS:
+ Interesting premise. Which I won't reveal!
+ Story kept me hooked until I finished all four episodes.
CONS:
- Repetitive puzzles. In the third episode, you basically complete the same puzzle four times in a row. And it wasn't even challenging the first time...
- Often frustrating to figure out exactly what the text-based sections want you to type. I spent close to five minutes trying to figure out one entry, and ended up going online to get past.
- Too short. I finished the game in a few hours. I really wish there was a little more story.
- Not horror? I was excited to see how scary this game would actually turn out to be. And I was disappointed. The first episode was fairly creepy, the second and third weren't scary at all, and the fourth was iffy. I saw the ending coming from about a mile away, so it wasn't satisfying in the least.
- No music. The first episode has SFX only, no music. So I put on some spooky music on YouTube as I was playing. Helped a lot.
CONCLUSION:
This is a great idea for a game, but doesn't pull it off. To be a really good game, it needs more content, more build-up, more tension, better interface, and music. If you want a couple of hours of light spookery, go ahead and try it, but you can probably find something better.
FINAL RATING: 3/7

A thoroughly enjoyable game that is in equal parts entertaining and educational - 5/5
The game uses a series of short documentary clips (roughly 30 mins in total) to explain aspects of history and folklore as you progress throught the game, which can be freely re-watched from the main menu once unlocked. Highly recommended for those interested in learning about Inuit culture.
I disagree however with the negative reviews regarding frustration with the platform elements of the game. Not sure whether it's because I'm a latecomer to this gem of a game, and the issues reported are long since fixed, or whether I had a better time by using a controller, but I didn't have any issues with gameplay. Some of the tutorials introducing new mechanics can however be a little bit vague (took me a few minutes to figure out the bola using a controller), but aside from that no complaints.
Play time for myself was around 3 hours at a decent pace, but for casual players, children or those playing local co-op this is likely to be longer. Controller(s) recommend (Played with Xbox controller myself).
Though it does at first seem a little pricey for the overall playtime (£11.99 at the time of writing), I'd still recommend at full price, but it would be a worthwhile addition to any collection if picked up on sale. Definately a game you'll want to replay at some point too.
The musical score is also a particular highlight (it's available as DLC), and perfectly compliments the unique visual styles of the game.

Perfect port of one of Platinum's, and Shinji Mikami's, weaker titles. I had really high hopes for this game, and it sort of met them, but also sort of didn't, but that's not to call it a bad game. It's absolutely a really good fast-paced third-person shooter that finds fun ways to infuse the genre with over-the-top platinum flair, and mastering the game's mechanics is great fun, but the one big sticking point is that the usual platinum flair is... kind of muted?
The characters are fun, the gameplay is fun, but there's somewhere in the game's presentation where it kind of critically fails to come together in a satisfying way. It doesn't ruin the game at all, but coming in expecting the same kind of excitement you'll get from Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising, or even Resident Evil 4 or God Hand, is a bit of a mistake. It's worth playing, especially with keyboard and mouse making it a lot easier to get the hang of moving and shooting accurately at once, but don't expect a particularly memorable rival character to butt heads with, or an ending that'll make your head spin and then continue to spin it all the way through the credits.

It starts off pretty well and looks like a good spin off of the original series... but a few things ruin the fun totally:
1) enemy turns take ages. After a few days (sectors taken), you need to wait several minutes, until all enemy turns are done.. you can imagine, how long it takes, when you need to fight 12 enemies...
2) you can only use one squad in a fight, even when multiple squads are in the sector. This means, you are unable to attack from several sides at once (e.g. 2 from south, 4 from west).
3) enemy AI is stupid. Once the game starts, enemies run blindly into your direction, so it's very easy to get them out of cover
4) when you hire a merc, he appears _instantly_ in the sector. No need to plan ahead, no need to get them from an airport to the sector you need him.
5) the whole economy is unbalanced and partly stupid: you hire a soldier with all his gear, once the contract ends, he leaves all his gear in your team. Next time you hire him, he brings the same stuff (every time for very little money).
I can continue with these kind of things... so it looks very close to the original and very promising, but it get's totally boring way too fast, while the originals (and even Back in action) is fun to play even after years again and again.

I'm a huge fan of the entire JA franchise and have been with it since the days of Metavira.
At first, I was very skeptical when yet another new company wanted to try their hand on a new iteration of the game, Full Control calling it a "reset" or "prequel".
I backed the Kickstarter campaign and went all the way in for Alpha access, which I didn't regret. As an IT professional myself, I appreciate the way Full Control managed the Kickstarter campaign and despite the ups and downs they seemed to make good progress.
When the first playable alpha version was released, I was impressed. However, the progress didn't go as fast as I had hoped towards a beta version. That being said however, I do appreciate the openness with which FC communicated to their backers what the progress was and whether they ran into obstacles. I cannot give them enough credit for incorporating feedback from backers during the early development stages - a thing that seems to be unheard of when compared to other EarlyAccess titles and Kickstarter game projects of the recent past (Spintires...)
Bottom line is: JA Flashback is a great little game with rough edges. I would recommend this game to true fans of the genre. Certainly, it broke with some of the JA "traditions", but hey, they never said they would do a remake with HD textures! So all you "hardcore" JA fans of the first hour: quit being grumpy old farts and try something new! :-)

Initially I wanted to recommend this game, but it's just not even remotly worth the asking price and there is no long-term factor that makes the game any fun.
The premise is that your federation or whatever is attacked by aliens. So far so standard. You're sent into battle with a few of your starting ships. In the upper left corner someone is talking (writing, since there is no VO in the game. At all. Not even in combat.), but you really couldn't care any less. The characters lack depth, the story is as standard and full of holes as it gets. I rarely even checked which one of my crew mates suddenly had something to say. But let's not focus on the story, since this game is about gameplay.
Sadly it's lacking in this department as well. You're playing this game mission by mission, but you can choose several routes at times. I have no idea what these are doing though. Perhaps you get more story exposition and XP to follow "optional" routes. In any case, combat, the meat of the game:
Before combat starts you can "arrange" your ships in a "tactical position". Why the quotes? Because it really doesn't matter. You don't even know where on the map you will spawn. After that it's simply giving move commands to your individual ships and letting them fire upon the enemy. You can focus fire on some enemies, but that doesn't always work that well and is clunky (you have to select each ship manually, then change the fire mode to targeted fire and then find the target you want to attack, since the game switches to an exclusive targeting mode in which you have to tab through enemy ships, unless the ship is visible on the screen...then you can even click it). Enemy and friendly ships all have different shield bars, but for some reason a ship taking damage on it's right side somehow lost shields for its left side...yeah). After each turn you can redistribute shield power to certain sides (though I have no idea how top and bottom could even be effectively attacked, since you CAN switch planes). You will also periodically have to redistribute system power between weapons, shields and engines to either regen shields quicker, have a higher movement allowance or do more damage). You can also change engagement ranges for each weapon subsystem, though no idea why you would bother with that.
Technically it's not a bad idea, just the execution is mediocre at best. You don't know where enemy ships will go of course and more often then not they're just trying to ram you. Using special abilities apart from rockets is also not very clear. Firing lines are a nice idea but every battle pretty much plays out the same with you trying to keep your fleet together while not crashing. I've lost ships with full health to something I don't even know. That was a destroyer even.
After battle you get XP and some sort of "morale" stuff that determines if you've been aggressive or defensive. No idea how that works, since I always get aggressive. I mean, we're fighting after all...I guess it's the crew members you can equip that offer various agg and def bonuses that can be toggled. Apparently they also form some sort of relationship with one another. It's even an achievement...hm, speaking of which, many of them just don't seem to trigger. Ive' definitely killed more than 25 "squids" and I've also recruited a few people that should have given an achieve...oh well.
In any case, levelling them and your ships up doesn't really DO anything. Your crew mates get passive % bonuses. Yay. And your ships get automatically stronger the more enemies they have destroyed, which means your strongest ships will level up quicker since they often get the kill shot due to superior weaponry. And that's the problem: It gets boring after only  a few hours. I'm currently sitting at 1 battle cruiser, 2 destroyers and 1 frigate (there is a ship points limit), but there are no upgrades, no customization, no layout changes, no variants. A destroyer will always just do what a destroyer does, can't change weaponry, focus on shields or engines. There are also no carriers as far as I can tell. And there is apparently only 1 more ship class (your flag ship gets upgraded automatically). Also, if you want to repurpose a ship or replace one you have to do that in an actual mission, which takes quite a long time, so you're starting a mission weaker then necessary.
Graphics and sound are not terrible, but also nothing great, especially sounds are boring.
Overall it's not a terrible game, mediocre maybe, but definitely overpriced and it lacks longevity. After 16 missions I just can't bring myself to play any more of it, since every mission is essentially the same: kill all enemies. The UI isn't really PC optimized either. Maybe a 6/10 for effort. Might benefit from a MP mode. I think you need to add
a) an interesting and well voiced plot
b) a clear progression system
c) more user friendly controls
d) more customization options
e) better sound and visual design

Good game! one major pro for me personally is, that Flashback is the first game of all the attempts of keeping JA alive which shows the same level of visual charm like the old JA and JA2 had, but in a new, up to date, way. I of course was eager to try it as soon as I heard there would be another JA. After the release I first got sceptical because of the reviews but what JA veteran would not check out every piece of work with something like JA in it's title?!! As I said the visuals had me right away and I really enjoyed playing it. However I of course also was disappointed with the missing content and depth of gameplay, and even more with missing obvious must have features, be it gameplay or technical issues. BUT I sense much potential in Flashback. It is called Flashback and not JA3, that was crucial for me to realize. It is obviously meant as interim solution from JA veterans for other JA fans in order to keep the title alive. It is a technical and visual overhaul of the basic JA functionalities without reinventing the wheel like BIA tried to. It supplies the JA modding community with very good core functionalities and visuals, and pretty high capabilities for modding - you just can't emphasize this enough. Obviously FC did miss to do the correct marketing
So I put all my faith in the proven, very capable modding community of JA vets. It is no finished game, it is no sequel to JA2, but it gives the community the possibility to fill the hole of a missing successor with very enjoyable content and charming content. I am excited what the community will come up with.
A kickstarter would have never been able to cope with the expectations of a JA2 sequel, nowadays a major is needed which is able to come up with the time, meaning money, to continue the series with a game full of new functionalities and the depth the community is expecting at the same time.
So would I recommend the game ?
to JA veterans or even new players who understand that this might be a very good filler and are aware of what great games the JA mod community can come up with: oh yes!!
to JA veterans or new players who expect this to be some full-fledged game/successor with hours of content and the revelation of true TBS: nope - because I fear you screw it's steam rating even more and thus prevent the desperately needed money to continue the work on it

However what makes this game great is just that everything works. The developers clearly put a lot of effort in both the gameplay as the campaign and the main characters and interactions are very well portrayed and don't seem as cliché as one might expect from a game at this price.

At its most fundamental level, a game is only a series of questions that the player must answer with an action. Sisyphus Reborn manages to use this core nature to walk players through a complicated thought process. This may sound like a description of edutainment titles in general, but where this game succeeds and so many others fail is in its subtly. I wasn't aware I was learning until I read about Camus' Myth of Sisyphus in the discussion boards after playing. What motivated me to continue wasn't the need to complete an assignment but the need to discover more about the world constructed around his essay.
The landscapes themselves are left uncluttered, almost blank. Instead of flashy colors or movements, Sisyphus Reborn maintains visual interest with small tricks like distorting lines to mimic heat's effect on the horizon and stick figures that skip animated legs for wraith-like tails. Along with a soundtrack that focuses on note repetition and hints of religious music, the aesthetic builds a climate of sullen dread, one that implies you might be trapped in a sort of purgatory. It was that sense of disquiet that brought me back to learn more in a second playthrough.
The only complaint I'll level against Sisyphus Reborn is that your choices are laid out a little too neatly, as games are wont to do. There does seem to be a single correct choice in the end. All other alternatives are beset by hints towards that 'correct answer' and prompts to quit. But the player is free to ignore the developer's – and the philosopher's – answer in favor of their own and isn't that what philosophy is all about?

Read danny_maland's review (most helpful) to contrast with this. Similar points, he barely gave a thumbs down, I barely give a thumbs up.
TL;DR: Spacy. Combines elements for a story above its price. Gameplay gets more challenging and more complex as the game progresses. About 20 total ship types in game between two factions. Many bugs. No voiceovers. If they had more time or budget, this could have rivalled Homeworld.
Longer version, but I'll try to keep points short.
Story guy did his/her job (too lazy to look up credits). People have personalities. The world has politics. Everybody has a motive for their actions. Story in a game is important to me; this one shows a world.
Graphics did their job. Limited number of ships, but they look nice. Weapons are visible and are indicated when changing firing behavior. Worked well with story team: one station looks like a giant ship, fleet admiralty intended it that way.
Combat designers did their job. We-go/turned based system that plays out in real-time where you can review the previous turn with no loading delays. Movement indicators similar to recent XCOM games, they look nice. Turret firing arc indicators optional. Most turrets have the same range; damage and accuracy determine target priorities. Multi-mission chapters (can repair ships between missions, can only rearm ammo between chapters) is a sweet-sweet idea implemented well. Ships have a limited veterancy system, which benefits keeping ships alive. Requested reinforcements can show up mid-battle if they're small ships, which is nice to see happen. Qualms: can't target sentient mines (bigger than the smallest ship and very slow); no ship has overlapping turret arcs; targeted firing mode causes all turrets to hold fire unless firing on the target (contrast: autofire ships can hit as many targets as the ship has guns); sprayer acid clouds are numerous enough to blanket large amounts of the battlefield in late game missions; some missions give an escort objective, then order you to kill everything anyway (making it easier to ignore escort objectives); war score might be based mostly on ship energy distribution, making defensive scores a chore to obtain; enemies can sit still, while player ships cannot; nautalid(enemy) corpses can be so numerous that maneuver becomes unnecessarily difficult toward the end-game. Small points, but numerous. Would have preferred a few missions fighting alongside allies. That's personal preference though. Interface is a bit clunky/complex for some; I found it okay.
QA did not do their job. There are many bugs that are the make-or-break issues for many players. Final mission attempt 2 of 3: enemy monarch corpse drifted out of battlefield, enemies rallied at the corpse and made the fight very long, then 2 enemies left, killed one, the turn never ended, I had to restart. Clicking on crew skills button while a mission briefing is open will cause mission selection icons to disappear (solution: exit to main menu and resume, no loading time so it's superfast). Achievements are bugged; gone through the game twice and haven't gotten basic achievements for getting crew members. Ships will (as best I can tell) spontaneously hold fire, meaning they won't fire on enemies until you notice and change their fire orders. Acid spray area of effect may be much larger than the graphic; noticed ships with substantial space between them and the nearest stream still suffered ill effects.
The game's design allows for a lot of meta-game. You can dismiss corvettes with empty missile racks and request another corvette as reinforcement, and the corvette will show up mid-battle with full ammo. Reinforcements can also be used to go over the ship limit; dismiss the reinforcements before the next battle and request new ones to go over the limit in the next fight. Well-timed countermeasure launches can destroy up to 4 missiles, instead of just 1 (though this might be intentional); if well-placed, the countermeasures can also cause missile AOE to damage enemies. While a challenge, sprayer streams (temporarily degrade shields) and missiles can be baited and tricked with good raider maneuvers. Allied missiles can unfortunately hit allies; enemy missiles can be tricked into enemies. There are probably a lot of options I'm missing.
Personal idea: would have been nice for some mercenary work. Corporations pay for responding to distress beacons, personal rewards for securing a certain number of transports, recovering a certain amount of information, holding off an enemy for a certain amount of time, or destroying a certain number of enemies. Use that money to purchase a capital ship and pay for upgrades: armor, power core, engine and weapon tuning, more missile space, more powerful missiles, etc. The in-game greed factor would have helped longevity.
Unfortunately, the game's kind of dead. Steamspy says there is an average of 1 player at any given time. The last forum post was 6 weeks ago. Doubt there'd be any improvement, since there'd be almost no money to be made. [Edit: two weeks later and 0 ratings on the review. Sad because it's a game that at least deserves the attention.]
Despite the issues, the gameplay and story get the game a thumbs up.

The story is still on the weak side, but honestly you don't play games like this for the story. You play it for compelling turn based gun and melee combat. While the game in its current state is missing the ability to climb on roofs or get any sort of height advantage (or disadvantage)  it still has fun and solid mechanics.
Modding. The game has great mod support and I fully expect to see some quality mods start to come out in the coming months. There are already several mods available that make some nice "common sense" improvements to the item descriptions and sector maps.
tl;dr: Good game. Will get even better in time. Good developer worthy of support. Modding support. Fun turn based action.

Titled as the manuscript made by Albert Camus, father of the Absurd movement, this adventure game neatly deals with concepts of an individual having no purpose or meaning in the realm devoid of God or any other construct of Order, and how one might find happiness in only one way: accept the meaningless of life and enjoy in its mundanity, all thru endless work.
You are Sisyphus, man who has lived for unknown period of lives in a cave alone, and now you are scratching and fighting to reach the outside world so that you could make a decision: is life worth living or not? Made in AGS engine, graphics are simplistic 2D fare, but it is the artistic touch of the game's creator that give it an ethereal and mesmerizing quality, and the same goes for music.
You'll need a very short time to reach through all Sisyphus Reborn endings, but in return it will leave you pondering on the meaning of life. A noble success, I'd say.

Anna is a first person adventure game involving the supernatural and psychological horrors held within an old mountain sawmill/home that has fallen into disrepair.  You play as an, apparently un-named, history professor who has been mysteriously drawn the sawmill by a strong feeling of deja vu when he finds pictures of the place in his closet, despite having no memory of the place.
When I watched the trailer on Steam I noticed that most of the objects in the game aren't even animated, and almost passed by this game because of it.  While it is true that there is almost no animation outside of physics objects, the mood and setup was all that's needed to emerse me into the game.  Also, because many of the objects are stationary, it led me to question whether the house is in fact haunted or if the man I was playing as was going insane.  It's obvious that this was an intentional choice as the game uses clever placement to ensure that you're not looking when certain objects move or materialize, which to be honest did make me jump a few times.
The story of what happened at the sawmill and the ways in which I was required to reveal it are also better than I expected.  The things I was required to do to find out the truth made me question the sanity of the man I played as, and the truth itself is something that would probably cause the average person to go insane.  None of that "Timmy fell down a well and died and now he's a ghost that feels betrayed" crap.
What little music is in the game is very good and, along with the sounds, enhances the experience of the game.
My only negative criticism is that some of the puzzles require ridiculous logic to try to solve on your own and there are usually clues for each one they are either hard to find or not nearly enough to get you close to a solution.
Recommended for anyone who likes adventure puzzles, solve it yourself stories, and psychological horror.

Stories Untold is a delightful little suspense game. Very retro in design and execution, it evokes an ’80s aesthetic in everything from the audio and visual design to using a text parser for some of the gameplay. The individual stories are interesting and varied, and are at times really clever. They build on each other, employing things you learn in the first story in the second, and so on. While the first story starts out with an initially intimidating text parser, it was easy and simple to play through, and later stories use more mouse-based interaction.
I enjoyed playing through the individual stories, but it’s the fourth story that really made me think, “Wow, this game is great!” It’s really clever and smartly done, and was an excellent conclusion that elevated the entire game.
I would characterize Stories Untold more as suspense rather than horror, because it builds and instills a feeling of dread throughout rather than utilizing jump scares, or body horror, or being chased by a monster. As someone who doesn’t like horror games (or movies) because they’re too scary, I had no problems playing Stories Untold.

Full disclaimer: I did not finish this game. I really really really wanted to like this game. Really truly. However it has some really serious flaws that made me want to stop playing. So I did.
First off, the atmosphere and ambiance in this game are phenomenal. It is very immersive and beautiful to look at. The sound design is smart, the visuals are stunning. The way in which the story is told is very nice, very intriguing, and really weaves an interesting world for the player. The horror is excellent. Very few games have made me jump and just physically react like some of the scares in this game have.
However, despite all it has in it's favor, it has some serious issues that make actually playing the game exceptionally frustrating. Perhaps the biggest offender, and probably what gets harped on the most, is how completely obtuse and irrationally difficult many of the puzzles are. You will carry items around with you for most of the game without ever having a use for them. Your inventory will be so waterlogged with pointless items that you'll find yourself trying every possible combination of items on a puzzle, no matter how illogical, and when you finally think you've got a solution that makes sense, the game says no, that's not the right answer, continue scavenging every square inch of the house for that one item you missed in a dark corner. Additionally, death is very unforgiving. Granted I got through half the game without dying, but when you do, you get the bad ending, and if you want to continue have to go back to your last (manual) save. You do not make a game with perma-death and no checkpoints, this is not 1995, I don't want to sound entitled but I really do feel like that is just basic game design common sense. And on the topic of death, every time you see a scary event, you lose health. This might be okay if there were more ways to restore your health, but there are not. And in a horror game, you kind of want to check out all the scary things. I mean, they're some of the strongest design points of the game, I'd be loathe to run away from any of them. But no, they damage you, and lead to death, so you should avoid these smart well-made scenes that really make the game experience.
This game had so much potential. I am very disappointed that it didn't live up to it.
4/10

My problem with this game is that it doesn't inspire me to continue.  Like other modern throwback platformers (Meatboy, I Wanna Be The Guy, WHATEVER) Oniken sets out to make you die and try again until you get it right, but unlike those games you aren't dying due to a brilliantly crafted trap or deviously challenging stage design but instead due to an unclear boss attack pattern.  Oniken never makes me say, "Oh ho, I see what I did wrong and I can't wait to try again!" it just makes me say, "ugh." And then I run out of lives and have to continue from the start of the stage before reaching the boss again, and, well, that's not something anyone missed from old NES games.
The graphical style is great, a really nice emulation of games like Ninja Gaiden or Vice: Project Doom, and the music is catchy, but I just don't think it's much fun to play.

Before i even start. This is such a cool beta game. Not only does it combine the call of duty feel with a post apocalyptic world, but it is also similar to another game that i liked called Stalker. Even though this game is in beta, i find this game to be almost as addictive as crack. I have only had and played the game for 2 days and already have 25 hours on it. I also like the fact that the game looks freaking amazing, but yet my media pc can still run it on the high end pc setting. A couple of problems and my solutions to these problems (I will start with the minor problem and then work my way up). The first thing is that the scope menu is in the way of the actual scope. Once again, its a beta, so this will probably get fixed in the future. Now on to the things that bug me. First of all, i feel like they could add in the leaning feature, like whats in dayz, unturned and call of duty for example. Now dont get me wrong, this game is a complete master of immersion, with there being many buildings, cracks and crevices to hide in, but i feel like if the game developers were to add in this feature, it would make the game just that more awesome. My other problem is with the hackers. I know that the devs have fixed this problem and banned some 200 users in 2015, but for some reason they started to pop back up again. However, as i said about 3 times now, the game is a beta, so it will probably get fixed. My last problem is with the actual pairing up system for the games. It seemed like when i first started off in the game, i was getting matched up to level 4 scavengers and level 3 black markets. It just makes the game hard for all of the newcomers to try and get off of there feet in the first few games because they are constantly getting killed by these higher tiered players. In my mind, however, all of these cons are extremely outwieghed by the pros, which i have kind of already expressed earlier. All in all, is this game perfect; no, it could use some work. Would i recomend this game to someone; hell yes! And if i had to give this game a rating, i would honestly give this game 4.5/5 stars. So if you made it this far, thank you for reading my review that possibly has misspelling mistakes riddled through it. Lets hope the devs see our reviews and works on some of these problems. By the way, Devs, your doing a great job on this game so far. Keep it up guys.

Having not grown up with this sort of game, i did not feel any nostalgia while playing it. However, that didnt stop me from really enjoying it.
Its still in beta, but the story still gave me about 10 hours of gameplay, and it also has an arcade mode which is based on the fighting parts of the story. As of writing this review, i have spent 2 hours in the arcade mode, and I doubt i will be stopping there.
Dont let the fact that it's still in beta stop you from at least thinking about this game, as its already really good. Parts of the world map aren't free for players to explore as of now, and im sure they will take very long to make as the game looks astoundingly beautiful, but what there is currently is great. The main quest is also still not finished, it just abruptly stopped, though there is still alot of it. As i said, the game gave me 10 hours of gameplay, which i find is a very suitable amount of time for a game.
The story consists of puzzles, bullet hell styled boss fights, combat, side quests and obiously the story itself. Some of the puzzles were actually quite hard, to the point where i had to look up gameplay videos find out the solution, while others were a decent head scratcher that wouldn't last too long, or too short. The boss fights all take a couple tries to beat, but never enrage you like other games (namely shovel knight).
I recommend this game to everyone, though especially to people who like The legend of Zelda, and other RPGs like it.
