Realy fun. The controls feel really fluid and using two guns and two porn tentacles is awesome. You've got your shotguns, Assault rifles, fast pistol and slow pistols, and smg. Not bad, but they feel bland compared to your powers. The gameplay shines in the supernatural powers, with your wide range of different brutal takedowns. Your left tentacle is for grabbing and throwing, and your right tentacle is for melee and mutilation. Melee feels powerful all the way through the game and thrown objects auto target on enemies.
Supernatural powers are satisfying, for a better word. There's are simple skill trees to unlock, and a few cool and not so cool abilities. You don't really need to prioritize your build since the game is so short. You get two activated skills, swarm and gun channeling. If you playe Bioshock and enjoyed bees/murder of crows, it's basically the same thing, but with cooldown. You blast out "dark essense" which distracts enemies. The upgrades simply decrease charge time and increases stun time. Gun channeling gives you unlimited ammo and increased gun damage for a short time. This becomes absolutely broken when you upgrade it to A) autoaim onto close enemies when using dual weilding and B) also allows you to see and SHOOT through walls. Yeah, this game makes you feel badass.
The story didn't make me want to roll my eyes, so that's a plus. All the characters were really fun to listen to, the story is coherent enough to make sense, and while the main character is portrayed as a dark, anti-hero mobster, he's not an edgelord.  As you go through the game, you can find collectables called relics. Each one has an indepth description narrated by Johny Powell, your friend neighborhood looney. The descriptions are so full of his personality and hearing him read is a nice comedic break. Characters keep dialogue light and upbeat and get serious when♥♥♥♥♥♥goes down.
Sadly, the game feels short, and I beat it in about 5 and a half hours. Second time took 4 hours. But I guess it's better to have something great for a short time than have something crappy stretched out. I recommend to surburban moms and young children.

This review is a tough one, because I wanted to like this game - a lot.
The concept is a really nifty thing: Deliver tactical-pause mechanics to the same genre occupied by, say, "Homeworld." In a trailer it looks VERY cool. Guide the trajectories of fighters, use 3D space to your advantage, set up some killer pincer movements, and just generally have some real control.
That's the promise. The reality is slow, clunky, and - strategically - just like everything else. Mass your firepower, and just hammer the problem until it goes away.
The 3D nature of the game IS important. You should organize your fleet such that your ships are unlikely to bump into each other. Past that, though, maneuvering for the optimal shot is a giant pain, and a waste of time. WIth any decently mobile enemy, chasing them down and specifying them as a designated target is an exercise in near futility. You'll end up just going around in circles or "S" curves, all the while being chewed up by whatever is not the designated target. The "turn-rhythm" of the game is such that it tends to produce stalemate, with designated enemies in and out of firing arcs long before your ships decide to actually shoot at anything.
You're far better off just allowing your fleet to fire at anything they think they can hit, while keeping your ships able to support each other. This means that all the fancy maneuver mechanics can be reduced to a few variations: Everybody turns in a clockwise circle, everybody turns in a counterclockwise circle, or some ships turn one way and the other ships go the opposite way. (The "movement limits" represenation was actually done really well, by the way, even if it could be hard to click on the ship you actually wanted if a big crowd had formed.)
A major contributor to the "clunk" factor is that all non-movement commands go through the HUD interface, with basically zero provision for "context." For instance, designating an enemy to chase down and fire upon should be a matter of right-clicking the enemy and selecting something from a short menu. Instead, it's a chore involving finding the enemy you want, finding the designated fire button, clicking on it, and not really getting much helpful feedback as to what's going on. Shortcut keys do help a bit, but the whole thing realy ought to have been more direct. Missile fire is even worse, with a target designation system which zooms into an enemy (completely breaking your contextual sene of the battle). While you can click directly on a foe to designate them, the "enemy to shoot at picker" is designed around two buttons: Previous and Next. That's fine when there are a few enemies on the map...and horrific when there are tens of them.
And, of course, the auto zoom from the target picker often means that finding the target you want becomes a ponderous, multi-step process instead of a snappy one.
Another thing that drove me pretty crazy was that every mission required the manual rebalancing of energy systems for each ship. Since shields don't regenerate by default, avoiding the loss of a fleet member pretty much demands that you rebalance your power use towards shields. Doing that for each ship, over and over again, was a bit of tedium that could have been done without.
The metagame also has problems. "Star Hammer" doesn't allow saves during a mission, which creates an all-or-nothing type of scenario that punishes mistakes, bad luck, and the sometimes vague win-conditions far too harshly. It also makes glitches very, very frustrating, especially when a long mission has been going on. More than once, I ran into a situation where the game never fully exited the realtime portion of a turn, and my only option was to restart. What finally soured me completely on the experience was almost finishing a long, difficult engagement...only to have my fleet suddenly refuse to fire at anything.
"Star Hammer" actually does a decent job with its setting, with your bridge being inhabited by real, identifiable characters who converse through text boxes. The humanization of the game is good in that sense, but the wider context tends to get lost. The "world" is actually a spiderweb of various organizations and people - and that's a cool idea - but the way it all comes across is as a confusing mash of names that don't end up meaning much.
I feel like "Star Hammer" might contain the seed of something that's really first-rate. It didn't clear the bar of recommendation for me, but doing so doesn't seem like it would be out of reach for the developers. The way the experience works as a whole needs quite a bit of polishing-up, though, before I would want to try it again.

I really, really wanted to like this game. I'd say it was my first kickstarter disappointment. Part of the problem may have been that I finished Shadowrun Returns and Wasteland 2 first, so my expectations going into JA:F were very high. Right from character creation, JA:F was confusing and frustating. I had to look up a guide to get the perks I wanted for my custom character, and I'm still not sure how some attributes and skills are connected. The benefits of training militia are unclear. I never was able to win a fight with militia, and militia can't join you even if you're in the same sector when attacked. Combat and the overall campaign felt futile. For every sector I'd take over, I'd lose another on the other side of the island. So it became a constant retreadding over the same territory. I wouldn't mind if ammo was scarce, but enemy weapons often just disappear. Stealth proved inconsistently effective as well. Perhaps the most frustrating part was the lack of clear mission markers and clunky UI. I would often have to return to a sector to hunt down the person who gave me a mission without remembering where they were. The locations all look extremely similar, so memorizing an NPC location is extremely difficult. I've covered this review without mentioning graphics, because for me, mediocre graphics are much less important than good gameplay. I stuck it out through countless reloads before finally ragequitting and uninstalling. I'll give the developers credit: They delivered the game the promised; it's just not particularly fun to play.

Summary: A short game about what it means to make choices in life and whether those choices are truly your own. And even if they are completely yours - do they truly mean anything? What's more worthy: to be complacent and achieve nothing yet lose nothing, surrounded by likeminded people; or live a much harder life by yourself, to one day break out of a stagnant, colorless world into regrowth and beauty? Is there truly only working, being nothing, and being alone? Are these choices made before we're ever aware of them, and if they are, does it matter? Does
matter?
Now to the the game itself: the art is what you see in the images, and the soundtrack is good. The writing is impactful, but short and direct. The controls are very simple but work for what's needed. I personally didn't have that life changing moment that some people did, but I did enjoy playing through it in half an hour, and I could see playing through it again every once in a while as a reminder to myself.
Overall - if you like short games that have a different pace and make you think a little bit, I fully recommend this game. And heck, it's free. If you easily spiral into exisistential crises (and don't enjoy it), don't play this. Otherwise? Check it out!

When i first heard about Never Alone, i feared that it would be a mediocre game, an excuse to talk about Iñupiaq culture. Luckily, that's not the case.
Right at the start, i was taking in by the animation. The girl and the fox are well animated, it's such a joy to watch them run or jump, and it's even more fun to actually be in control of them.
The game is then a mix of light platforming and light puzzling and progressing through the games will unlock interesting short videos about the Iñupiaq and their culture.
However, the game isn't perfect. After a while, and despite the short length overall, boredom and tediouness creeps in. There is too many similar elements to what you've been doing before, and not enough rewards to get them. The platforming bits become repetitive and meanwhile, the reward, the documentary tidbits, tend to become shorter, and reuse previously seen images.
I think a bit more challenge or at least optional hidden stuff to unlock would have carried the game farther. That's something that Marvin's Mittens, another super cute game, did admirably well with optional stars to collect, for experienced gamers wanting more from the game.
To be fair, i've only played solo, and I'm sure playing coop would alleviate some of this trouble. First, it's always more fun to play with a friend. More importantly, you would only need to control one character, so you would have less tasks to accomplish by yourself, which mean less opportunities for annoying mistakes while switching characters. However, I have not played coop, so this is only guesswork on my part.
So, on the whole, Never Alone only gets a soft recommendation from me. It's cute, it has great animation, but the last 2 hours aren't as enjoyable as the first one.
PS: A note to people wanting to play with children: though the game has a low difficulty that might be suitable for children (especially in coop), there are still some "scary" moments and characters, so play it alone beforehand to make sure it's gonna be ok with your child.

Wow, you think, one positive review - well this review is written on my experiences on the game
The matchmaking is not TERRIBLE - it just is'nt perfect - and of course if your buying this late on into the release, most people are going to be better than you anyways. In games your mostly put in with a wide variety of players - and that is to be expected
The P2P servers are a bit annoying - but they were hardly problomatic for me - the game might pause for connection every 10 games or so, and even then not for a long time at all
But yes, i can definitely say, this game has NO HONOR - and there are quite a few scrubs in for honor and it can be quite annoying sometimes - but so are all games sometimes right?
The gameplay however is fantastic
It is a massive learning curve, finding your favourite hero (mines in my profile picture ;-)) learning his/her moveset, learning what to do in certain situations and learning the maps - and all very stress free and actually very addicting. You will allways be finding yourself to wanting to get better and better, and thats the real fun of For Honor. For Honor requires a lot of concentration - to be able to pary an attack just in time or to know when to acvtivate your unblockable on your enemy. And it is so rewarding when you get your first execution - the feeling of knowing you've truly outsmarted your oponent. And all the customisation...
You can customise your character to be a breal badass if you have the steel (the in game currency) and it can be quite fun getting your favourite character top look this way. This game is extremely customisable! You can change things about your hero him/herself by changing his'her's gender and selecting tattoos all while buying cool ornaments for them and buying crates to get different types of cosmetics which can give you the upper hand or the disadvantage in a fight.
The campaign?
Well its just a bit of fun really, not really anything to buy the game for at all, but it might give you a laugh or two. The campaign is what you'd think it is - factions fighting against factions - execrpt the campaign gives you a bigger look at the factions and how they live and their towns and villages and their social system. It also teaches you a bit about the games itself
There are many really well done things in For Honor - things that make the game totally worth to buy and really quite enjoyable. The main thing is to ignore the occasional bad things and concentrate on the many good things

Oniken is a 2D run and sword action game. The controls are simple, attack, jump, duck, berserk and up + attack to throw a grenade. It is all so nice. The attack distance is good and can be boosted with power ups you find. You can hang from things. This game really goes the extra mile to make you think you're playing something for the original Nintendo, while most other games going for the nostalgia feel don't have actual 8 bit graphics and music. I feel such a buzz playing this game unlike other 'retro-ish' games that miss the mark with modernized graphics and sound.
The cut scenes are nice to look at, but the real fun of the game is the game play and the enemy variety. You'll see a lot of enemies and tackle them in different ways. For modern gamers the game might be seen as difficult due to the fact if you die, you restart the section of the level. Die at a boss, restart that entire section. You'll get better! Lose all of your lives and you'll have to restart the level.  Each level mainly consists of 3 sections, each with a mini boss of some sort. Since the save file allows you to just jump to a level, if I die on the first section of a level, I just go back to the menu and warp to the level I was on. Kinda makes lives on the first section of each level pointless. You have a hefty health bar like Mega Man, so the game is pretty forgiving. Pits are of course instant death.
The level variety is a mixed bag. Some levels are just bluntly walk to the right, others make you scale to the top and still others put you in a jet ski with a scrolling screen. There are a few sections that feel open where you're free to make your own path, which feels good. Some levels are needlessly difficult with a lot of action happening, but if your a veteran of old Nintendo games, you should be used to it. If not, then make an angry video about it.
There isn't that much replayability for the game, there are a few hidden items, one per level, and there are achievements for beating a level without dying. The game saves your high score for each level, but really, once you've beaten the game, there's no reason to come back to it.
Again, this is an awesome game well worth $10, it is so awesome that I'd buy any other game this studio comes out with. They hit the nail on the head. If you aren't into old school Nintendo games, avoid it.

A very atmospheric first-person horror adventure that emphasizes story over pacing with a lot of reading involved when you want to get invested in its narrative. Most of the puzzles are rather hard to solve without either the ingame help feature or external walkthroughs. Yet all the necessary information is in the game, be it in the collectible books, notes or visual environmental hints. Just don't expect your run of the mill puzzle solutions like in most of todays adventures.
Completionists be warned, this game is a nightmare to complete 100%.
Overall you can expect a lot of replayability  with several unique endings and the option to find out more about the ingame history. If you are willing to invest that time then the atmosphere will consume you and present you a horror experience of a kind you do not see very often.
If you are into this subtle kind of horror this game is worth the time and money.

Short version:  Simple fun.
==================
Long version:
----------
The good:
- The controls are responsive.  The character is fun to control.
- Very little is just handed to you.  Your upgrades feel like you have earned them, which is satisfying.
- The upgrades feel impactful as soon as you get them.  Progress feels good.
- The colors and areas are vibrant except for Vectron, the machine place (Fair warning: that place can be a tad scary).  Areas stretch on for a bit, but they've put in good effort to vary up the locales.
- The map is simple but is easy to use.
Mixed:
- Not exactly difficult.  Most of the fun comes from exploration and remembering places that you can access with later upgrades.
- While there is a bonus for finding all of the collectables, there is only one ending.
The bad:
- I mentioned that some of the areas stretch on for a bit.  I got slightly lost a few times just from the sheer expanse of the tunnels.
- The plot is probably the weakest point.  You start off with a simple yet adequate story of "Find your friend.  He was last seen at this place."  Nothing wrong with that, but the culmination to the ending lacks any real sense of "OH SNAP.  S*** IS GETTING REAL." except for a single prompt before the final boss that says you won't be able to go back.
In summary:
Though the abrupt ending will probably leave you wanting more, you want more for a reason.  The gameplay feels good all around.

For the record my favorite Worms game of all time is Worms Armageddon. The art style, the game play, weapons, level editor, and game layout (options, theme, layout of menus) were all done right. This is when games were made to be bought once, and to be bought as a whole.
I saw Worms Ultimate Mayhem as a recommended game instead of Armageddon. The first thing that caught my eye was that this game was the 3D version of what I loved so much. I figured for the on sale price, I'll give it a shot. I can tell you that I am not at all disappointed with my purchase (except that Worms is still a turn based game! I wish they would make a real time one - how? Well I'm not getting paid to make or suggest games). Seeing worms in 3D is phenomenal, and the art and them style they chose to go along with the game just fits it perfectly. The
is just as good as ever, however will take some time to adjust and get used to the new range/power system. I didn't know a worm could throw a grenade three football fields away from the map. Lesson learned.
Game play itself can be seen from first person or third person worm view. Weapons are varied as usual and are cool to use and shoot. The explosive or corrosive materials found around the map can also be used to eliminate your opponent. Does the 3D land disappear after you blow it up? Damn right it does. How are the camera angles? Actually quite consistent when using weapons, can be a bit confusing or frustrating when simply observing the map. I find that even with unchecking the inverse box for camera angles sometimes it turns itself back on. This is usually fixed by simply squaring the screen with the worm again. That's essentially the only complaint I have is the camera controls.
This game does have CONTROLLER SUPPORT - which is greatly appreciated.
This deserves an 8.1/10 as worms in 3D with the game play and art style they chose, I'd have to give it a .1 over than my solid 8 average. It is a fun game - and can keep you busy for a while with the story, challenges, or just a quick match.
For future Mayhem games (or 3D worm games), maybe try getting rid of the turn based system, or play around with allowing more first person type of play. Do something XCOM : enemy unknown would do (wait, take cover and fire at the enemy when in range) with worms the player isn't using. Also, please try to improve the camera controls!
(I did get this game on sale :)

Wow. This 25-minute indie game is entirely a metaphor for finding your place in life. You start off within yourself and have to break out into the arid, outside world to find meaning to your existence. A majority of the people you meet along the way cannot help you, content to have their meaning defined by digging holes and filling them in again for eternity. Then you meet someone like you, a mentor who shows you the reality of the world: you can either work as a digger living a meaningless existence, or give up entirely and become nothing.
Finding your place in life isn't always easy, but every moment leading up to that self-discovery will have been worth it once you do.
(Sisyphus was a king condemned to roll a boulder up and down a hill for eternity)

Fulfilling my bucket list by learning to play guitar. Rocksmith, while not focusing upon notation, is still a fantastic resource for learning to play. Not only are there songs to learn (a la Rock Band or Guitar Hero), but the lessons/tutorials are top-notch and the Guitarcade (mini-games) are so well-designed, you can easily understand which skills are being developed while playing ... it's playing with a purpose. While playing anywhere in the game (including tutorials) the game will self-correct your level of difficulty downward if it detects you having some difficulty.
The only drawback to the game is that "unclean" notes (strumming multiple strings or multiple frets simultaneously) is usually detected as a "hit" on the correct note. Wanting to sound crisp and precise in real life, I feel like I'm cheating when it registers. Oh, well ... guess I just need to practice with an amp from time to time.
Fantastic game/utility!

What a lovely game! It's a story told by drawn shadow figures, spoken parts, small video clips and a side scrolling 3D adventure. You start being a girl in the cold winter landscape of Alaska and being very curious. Soon you are chased by a polar bear and a snow fox appeasrs to help you and stay with you as a helping companion. You can switch between both charatcers and each has its own abilities, so you can't play through just by playing one of them. You control with ASWD, SHIFT, CTRL, SPACE and the mouse. Changing character is done with the right mouse button and in the last quarter of the game, you're glad to have it there. The visuals are stunning, the animations very smooth. Sometimes, a messages pops up that the system performance is low and offers to change them in the settings. Unfortunately, it showed this every now and then, no matter how smooth the game played or what I disabled. Playing the game is a joy and our children like it very much. At the end, it's quite a bit challanging, so you might need several attempts to solve a scene. It's also a bit short as I played it through in 2 evenings. But it's really worth it. So, I now will play the second part (Foxtales DLC) and I'm looking forward to it! :-)

It also straddles a few game genres - part text adventure, part walking simulator, part instruction-puzzle - and technically it does none of them terribly well.
Where this game shines is blending everything together. The different game genres are mixed within each episode, and the finale brings together the various story elements in a fitting way.

Never Alone (or Kisima Inŋitchuŋa in the native Alaskan tongue) puts you in a control of a young Iñupiaq girl, a hunter, named Nuna and her fox companion. The games story is based upon an amalgamation of several Alaskan indigenous folk tales with the narrator telling the story in his traditional tongue. Much like traditional folklore the stories are told to transfer wisdom to a younger generation and hence, is not as complex and convoluted as many games today.
Ultimately Never Alone is one of those games where it’s not so much a game, as a story masquerading as a game. The base game sees a young warrior child set out to find the cause of a constant blizzard bombarding her village. With the help of her fox companion who can see the spirits of the land, they ultimately save her village from starving. The dlc “Foxtales” sees a young hunter along with another fox set out to save a small mouse which was accidently set adrift to sea.
The gameplay is nothing to rave about, but it is passable. Just like most 2D platformers there’s a lot of running right, and then towards the end, a lot of running left with some jumping in between. You switch between two characters (think Trine) to solve puzzles, with each character having specific abilities. Whilst the puzzles are quite simple and very rarely require too much, if any, thought they were still enjoyable. The controls themselves can be rather clumsy at times. Nuna had the ability to use a Bola (see: slingshot) which would be required to clear pathways, destroy ice, etcetera, however, the lack of precision was quite irritating. Using a controller you have to pullback and then flick forward, whilst it might not sound too bad in theory, there was no indication of which orientation the projectile was going. I often found myself performing the motion several times with a trial and error style tactic. The AI could really use some work, I often had to a restart a section because the character I wasn’t controlling would fall to their death, or wouldn’t travel fast enough to escape an enemy chasing us.
The dlc, “Foxtales”, had a noticeably improved AI. The AI controlled character actually knew how to navigate several platforms to keep up with me. The puzzles themselves were slightly more complex requiring real time thinking as opposed to setting up the puzzle then watching the animation. A few new elements (such as rocks getting blown by spirits to clear pathways) were added which personally, made the experience more enjoyable and rewarding. The biggest difference between the dlc and the base game however would be the removal of the Bola. This was replaced with a rowing mechanic, which would randomly change direction and much like the Bola, got very irritating at times. Whilst the controls weren’t the most polished I’ve ever seen they were very tolerable.
Combining the base game and dlc total playtime would be close to three and half hours. The game can be replayed to collect owls which unlock live action documentary-esque excerpts detailing the life and culture of the native Alaskans. Whilst I didn’t pay too much attention to this aspect it would most certainly be compelling for some. The general consensus is these documentaries are short and sweet but have a compelling insight into the Alaskan culture and way of life.
The graphics and animations is where the game really stands out. The world is beautifully created and you can tell it was developed with a lot of love. The backgrounds are static, however, the detail within them create a sense of immersion. The character models and animations were very fluid, when Nuna pushes a box the model actually looks like she’s straining. She begins pushing it much like any other game, but after a small distance she groans, turns around and then uses her back. Granted a very small thing but it really added to the overall immersion. The cinematics between chapters were very reminiscent of cave paintings. This art direction matched the atmosphere of the game perfectly and felt as if you were one of the younger generation getting told the story by one of the tribes’ elders.
Granted Never Alone had its problems but the story and the beautifully detailed world more than makes up for it. If you’re looking for a complex 2D side scrolling platformer I’d recommend looking at Limbo or the Trine series as this game is not for you. If you’re looking for a simple story and a few hours of entertainment then I’d recommend this. It is quite short and the price tag of $15 (at the time of writing) in my opinion is a little steep, but I’d definitely pick it up on sale.

Its most like one of those DOS text adventure or later on when point and click type of adventure games came on. But unfortunately like some of them this game can be very confusing. At points some elements were really interesting in the puzzles, but more often than not it just made no sense or was illogical and confusing.  The books do help some but they only give you an inkling and the tips system if your stuck but have an idea of what you have to do is next to useless.
The seemingly random events such as stuff popping up or happening was interesting. And for the most part good. Look at something only to look away and back and its moved or gone. Gives a very creepy feeling that you are not safe and the world around you is alive. Which alot of games falter at and end up with a static feeling enviroment. The only problem is that puzzles are just anti-intuitive at times and just to much and thats pretty much all the gameplay. Just walking around and interacting with things that are apart of puzzles.
The story is spooky ghost sprittual stuff from what I can tell. But I didn't really get it.
If you want a confusing puzzle game where you pretty much have to google atleast some part of the puzzles or waste hours trying to figure them out then I suppose this maybe for you. Sure the game could possibly draw you in, but once your there your stuck at a puzzle while you want to adventure in a world unlike one your used to.
Something I think this game could have been really great with is some top notch narration for books, and other parts where there is onscreen text your intended to read. Oniken is an enjoyable pastiche in the style of NES action platformers, particularly those from the second half of the system's career. Its lineage is comprised of titles like Shatterhand, Ninja Gaiden and Contra and it mostly successfully emulates the structure and difficulty of those games. The graphics and music are excellent in their 8-Bit style and there are short cut-scenes between levels featuring an art style reminiscent of animes like Fist of the North Star and Berserk. It's quite difficult but not overly and can easily be devoured and conquered by an NES veteran in a couple of sessions. The gameplay, level design and boss battles are unique enough to overcome the limitations of being so derivitive of other games and if you're a member of the choir your soul will burn again.

Thomas Was Alone is a really fun and innovative platformer that's definitely not trying to be more than what it is. Aesthetically this game employs a nice desaturated but diverse color palette that I like. The use of lights, shadows, and other visual subtleties  are cool too. TWA is a very minimalistic approach to platforming where you traverse the stages by controlling up to 5 different characters each with unique abilities. There's actually a compelling storyline delivered by a witty third person narrator who tells a rather convoluted, yet highly entertaining, story of the humble group of quadrilaterals. Since it's a casual game, the storytelling really helps carry the game along pretty well, It's not too heavy just refreshing to hear in between the stages and queue you to your progression in the game. I rarely felt stuck on any particular task for too long, the game keeps things fresh by briskly moving back and forth though wide variety of skill sets. Its a surprisingly intriguing game for just controlling a bunch of different squares. 8.5 out of 10

Mining games are usually about making successive trips into the underground. Haul back a few loads of ore, and get equipment that allows you to dig deeper, haul back even more, stay down longer, etc. In Steamworld Dig 2, the mining is almost superficial. This is because the game layers one mechanic on top of another in steady beats, always opening up new options. Digging for gems is sort of a side-show that allows you to keep on upgrading all this gear you unlock.
The story is neat and ties into the whole Steamworld universe, but is self contained enough to allow you to play it without having played its predecessor or other Steamworld games. Each objective sends you deeper into one of its shafts, which you were inclined to do anyway for the precious gems. But each area is hand-crafted and designed to challenge you with the different tools you get.
Can you use the water bombs to their fullest potential to reach secrets? What options does the grappling hook open up? In true metroidvania style, you will pass areas that need a tool you don't have yet. But the vast majority of secrets are able to be discovered without needless backtracking. Which is great because once the loot is gone, it's gone. Handy fast travel points minimise the amount of time you need to be travelling to and from each area.
In all, it's a wonderfully crafted adventure. So much more than just a mining game.

I came into this as someone who enjoyed Steamworld Dig and thought it a fun little game with a fun twist on the genre. This is a more expansive title with greater emphasis on character building and hand crafted puzzle rooms. I found the experience a little too easy for my liking, but I was never lost interest in exploring the map. I think all of the mainpath upgrades are worthwhile and introduce new gameplay mechanics to keep the experience fresh for its entire duration. I'm a bit bummed that the vertical space isn't used very much. I still think combat is pretty weak, not sure why you can't use your melee weapon while jumping. Once I acquired the jetpack I went out to the open areas and explored to find a whole lotta nothing (save the endgame bonus room). All in all, I dug this title. It's a solid 12 hours if you explore thoroughly.
Strengths
Character Progression - there's a far greater empahsis on upgrades and perks with which you can tool out your character for a given area/challenge
Exploration - handcrafted puzzle rooms are littered throughout the game world that, while on the easy side, make good use of your upgrades
Upgrades - new gameplay mechanics are introduced that open new avenues of exploration and keep the game feeling fresh throughout
Weakness
combat - while ranged combat feels solid, melee combat feels clunky and I don't know why you're not able to attack while jumping.
veritcal space - severely underutilized. once I acquired the jetpack I was disappointed to learn that there were very few reasons to explore the vertical space in the outer areas
selling goods - having to come back and forht into town was grating in the early game. it reminded me of Torchlight and how that game allowed you to send a pet to sell your junk for you while you kept exploring. thankfully this became less of an issue once I was able to purchase the
skill caps - I'm not sure locking certain perks behind levels/blueprints was a good idea, I would have much prefereed being able to select from all of the perks, that way I could save my points for something I really wanted
invisible walls - this is mostly personal taste, but I'm not a fan of hiding secrets behind regular looking walls. anything that encoruages pixel hunting is a negative in my book. Thankfully, not all secrets are done in this manner

I have been a fan of the various Jagged Alliance games since JA2. However, I am not a hardcore fundamentalist fan. What I like about the game is that, when you have properly tweaked it, you can usually play through whatever storyline has been made available fairly easily - that is, that the game is fun and satisfying. This means that I enjoyed Jagged Alliance: Back In Action quite a lot, which apparently many did not. It also means that I put some money into the Jagged Alliance: Flashback Kickstarter expecting pretty much the game that has emerged.
Jagged Alliance: Flashback is intended as a base upon which modders will create wonders. That is important, because it promises a lot of fun in the future. But the base itself is pleasant to play and, like other versions of the game, it tends to reward gamers in proportion to what they put into it. Saying that in another way, I like it better and better the more I play it. I think that most negative comments on this game (and JA: BIA) are from gamers who want a simple update of JA2 and have not played these later games on their own terms. Jagged Alliance: Flashback is already better than a good game, and there is every chance that modders will make it even better than that.

The good:
- Simultaneous turn-based space combat! Was looking for this for a long time.
- Decent AI, with some tough scenarios (played on hard).
- Shield management is actually fun.
The bad:
- The ship variety is limited.
- Fourteen hours in and I never had the chance to customize my fleet. Every mission I have to use exactly what they give me. I never got any points to buy new ships.
- War Scale mechanics is opaque and seems pointless.
- Ammunition is unpredictable from mission to mission. Will I have 12 or 2 missiles this mission? Who knows!
- Crew RPG mechanics seems broken. Couldn't remove crew. Was given crew members I couldn't assign because there were no free slots. Because you can "respec" crew trees at any time, there is no sense of important decisions being made.
- Human ships are interesting, but I found the aliens to be boring (for whatever reason). Just not my thing, and they make up a majority of the battles.
- Screen gets really messy when the spitters start covering everything in their trails.
- No sense of drama during rescue/escort missions. Outcome is pre-determined, and no penalty for failing (you'll see).
- Dialog is boring. No voiceover.
Overall:
- Not recommended.

Overall a beautiful game, and naturally fantastic storytelling, but it suffers from unintuitive controls and is roughly 20 years behind in platforming mechanics.
If you plan on buying this game with the intent of absorbing amazing landscapes set in a myth from what's frankly an alien culture, this game is for you. Everything about this game plays straight into that idea and doesn't let go.
Unfortunately, everything else about it sucks. The controls often leave you fumbling around even when you know what to do because of how slowly your characters react. Even when they do, you don't get to do what you meant because of the sheer disconnect with what your hands did and what happens onscreen. Climbing cliffs as Fox or aiming your bola as Nuna is just as much a measure of luck as it is anything else.
If that weren't enough, everything you're actually expected to do has been done a million times, and far better. Push box, jump on platform, run from (not so scary) threat, rinse, repeat. For all the amazing story and art do, the design is lackluster and detracts from the game.
Oh yeah, and then the bad mechanics and design work together against you! Quite often I found myself having to redo entire puzzles because characters move when ou get to far away. Which puzzles then ask you to do, so Nuna will go back to the where fox is making you take control of her again, etc, etc until you finally time it right.
When those things aren't making the game hell, it becomes absurdly easy. I would breeze through levels until I got to THAT ONE PUZZLE of the level that makes you want to strangle whoever designed the control scheme. I got to admire the scenery, but it just wasn't enough to make up for the rote problem solving interspersed with control-tossing frustration.
Don't buy this game, it's just not worth it.

I didn't get very far with Guitar.
When Rocksmith (original) came out I was excited to pick it up and give it a shot, but had many issues with the game:  Input Lag, Audio feedback, and just wasn't really into the method.
Then comes Rocksmith 2014!  So far I've put about 45 hours into 2014, and I'm still having a blast.  All of the issues I experienced on Win32/x360 versions of Rocksmith 1 have been resolved.  And now there is a recommendation system that suggests things for you to do.

Unfortunately, I can't recommend this game, even though I would like to. This game has a great concept (a mostly text based horror game), which initially I enjoyed, as it was a nice change from the horror game norm. This lost its luster for me about 20 minutes into the game however, as typing the same sentence over and over again just to realise I had to word it differently became extremely irritating. This was, like I said, irritating, but manageable.
This brings me to my next point, which ultimately ruined the game for me: strobes, SUPER high pitch noises intended to
subconsiously instill fear in the player, and jump scares (this one is less present than the other two but still a pain). These three elements are present in almost all games in the horror genre, and in my opinion these are a cheap way to make your game scarier. Again, these three things, when used in small amounts, are manageable, but in this game, which is supposed to be a mostly text-based game, they are cranked up to 11. This gets really bad during one point in the second episode. I'll try not to spoil anything, but towards the end there is a puzzle that requires you to stare into a light while also typing something on your console. If you are like me, and didn't get it right away, this can turn into a solid 20 mins of staring into a strobing light while barely audible infrasouds scream at you. Long story short, by the end of this puzzle, you WILL have a migraine, and black spots in your vision (that is, only if you don't get a seizure).
This leaves you with the option of course to turn your sound off on your computer (which I did). Doing this however, leaves you without any audio cues, and honestly makes the game kind of boring, as it leaves you with a story you can play very slowly (eliminating all "spookiness"), and strobe lights.
All in all, this is a very short semi text-based horror game that relies too much on horror game clichés, and is literally a physical pain to play. I would love to play this game more, but only if I knew I would be able to finish it without deafaning/blinding myself. If this game were changed only slightly to tweak these issues I really think it could be great.

Rynn's Adventure: Trouble in the Enchanted Forest does not appeal to me, but may appeal to others who are fans of challenging platformers.
Rynn’s Adventure: Trouble in the Enchanted Forest is an unforgiving platformer, and not for someone looking for a casual game.
You start each level with 3 total lives, and a full health and mana bar,
You lose health if take any damage, and when you die, you lose a chunk of your health, but if your health bar can’t go lower then it refreshes both health and mana bars, and consumes 1 life. Killing creatures will sometimes cause health or mana bubbles to drop, but it seems random, and they don’t give a whole lot anyway. When you run out of lives and health, you lose the level and have to completely restart it.
You can kill most monsters, and avoid taking damage if you spin while jumping. If you hit something while spinning, you will keep the spin bounce going. You can also dive on top of monsters, and you will bounce higher than you are normally capable of.
The monsters in the game respawn VERY quickly, and there are some annoying mobs that you can’t kill at all. In the levels you collect gems and keys, and when you beat that level’s boss you unlock a special power up outfit that has it’s own unique ability, and your health and mana pool will also increase slightly based on what items you collected.
Each level has a boss fight at the end with different boss mechanics, but the bosses are a complete joke compared to the rest of the levels. You can use this spin jump to cheese many of the boss fights by just bouncing on their heads the entire time. I would have preferred less difficulty during the levels, but more on the boss fights, so it would be more balanced.
There isn’t much to say about the story, since it is very straightforward, and you’re trying to save your parents and the Enchanted Forest from the wizard and his minions.
The whole game took me 9 hours, but it took a few hours to beat the first level. Once I finally did, and I got the first power up, the game got easier, until the final level at least. I wanted to rage quit many times, so I have absolutely no desire to replay the game, but there are achievements for collecting everything if you’re into that sort of thing.
What drew me to the game were the 'casual' and 'adventure' labels, which were very misleading. I had expected more of a story driven platformer with some challenges, but not anything too difficult. This game is NOT casual whatsoever. I know I’m not amazing at platformers by any means, but I’m not that horrible at them either. I found the game very stressful and frustrating.
This game is absolutely NOT for someone looking for a casual adventure.

Thomas Was Alone does two things extremely well (aside from being a cromulent and quite fun platform-puzzle game).
It demonstrates the power of personification, though what’s being personified are mere quadrilaterals. Through simple narration and by linking characters’ interactions with their in-game jumping abilities, a sense of personality is achieved.
It also demonstrates, perhaps almost as well as Journey, the power of video games to amplify the emotion instilled on a player controlling a character as opposed to someone simply watching the character in another art form. The fact is that this is a game with jumping quadrilaterals and narration, and it shouldn’t convey the emotions that it does. But it works, because you’re controlling these characters, you’re leading them to their goals, and thus you end up caring about them, though some proper credit must go to the absolutely fantastic music for helping this as well.
Plus, the narrator is the snarky British fellow from the  Assassin’s Creed series, Danny Wallace, so you can’t go wrong there.
If you own Humble Indie Bundle 8, you already have this, and if not, one of your friends probably does. Or go buy it, because it’s worth it.

So, I know this game got some pretty bad reviews by big critics. I'm going to have to stop you there.
At first glance, this game appears to be an incredibly confusing and non-intuitive system. Sure, you've got the basic menu, click and point and click item use mechanic, you can walk and look just like normal. Crouching, but no jumping. And then you look around and realize you have no idea what you're supposed to do. Or that you do, but you can't. Perform the ritual? Ok, sure... how do I do that? What am I missing?
Well, yes, yor objectives can be pretty obscure. More importantly, it can be easy to miss crucial items you might need, depending upon the path you choose. But, if you're careful, check everything twice, and read everything at least once (journals, books, letters, etc), the answers are all there. Experiment with things, and eventually, with the knowledge you gain from the protagonist's intuitions and documents scattered about, you will find the way.
Keep in mind that in the original game there were only three endings, with one "true" ending. The extended edition has eight, giving moer variance than "leave now, leave then, or win the game." You can reach the end in the extended edition and STILL BE WRONG. It means you missed something along the way. But maybe you like that ending better. While there is a eries of events that must be performed to progress at all, the steps you take in between can matter greatly.
Will you scour the depths of hell to find Anna? Or will you leave with your sanity and your life? Or perhaps you will follow in the footsteps of the Sabot Maker? I don't know, but if you don't choose carefully, you'll find your carelessness chooses for you.
3.5/5, for obscurity but ingenuity.

The only con is the story is rather weak; there's a lot of text dialogue but very little of it is interesting or plot-related. I don't think it detracts from the experience at all though. One minor nitpick is that (like many games) the game ends quite soon after you get all of the awesome abilities; I would have appreciated a bit more game play being an ALL POWERFUL MINER.
This is "overwhelmingly positive" for a reason. Top notch, highly recommended.

text:
Avete presente i sogni che fate quando siete avvolti da un febbrone a 40?
Magic Wand (TM) riesce a replicare e sintetizzare la stessa sensazione di delirio allucinetico in 60 minuti di gameplay.
Si, la parola "allucinetico" non esiste, ma se siete interessati all'acquisto di Magic Wand (TM), è meglio che vi abituate a questo tipo di puttanate: infatti, i magnifici personaggi all'interno di questo action RPG si inventeranno più parole di Joyce in Ulisse e voi con lo sguardo sia allucinato (e incazzato) starete lì a strascicare ad alta voce stronzate come "rubberballe", "bigcitie" oppure termini arcaici come "ys" (is) e "thou", coniugazioni grammaticali dell'inglese antico ("-keth", per esempio) tutte sballate e cose varie.
In più, le conversazioni non seguono un filo: vi ritroverete spesso a discutere con pinguini che si lamentano del fatto che gli state calpestando il mantello, forbici che vi caricheranno urlando "CUT CUT CUT" e via dicendo.
In parte, è sicuramente parte del suo stile artistico: infatti 'ste cazzate si trovavano anche in Goblet Grotto e Space Funeral, altre sue creazioni più famose..in parte è anche la droga.
Il tuo obiettivo in questo gioco è quello di trovare la Magic Wand (non fate come me che cercate su google sennò escono i peggio pornazzi) e poi dicono qualcosa del regno lunare e blah blah poi prendi una airship e voli e poi fah fah fah ed in fine boh.
Ma andiamo al succo: il gameplay in se è..eh, niente, vai in giro ed ogni tanto prendi a sprangate su i denti i malcalpitati, parli con la gente ed entri dentro cose.
Non è il suo punto forte, ma non mi aspettavo una roba tipo FFV da (1) un gioco da 2 euro e (2) un prodotto di thecatamites.
Però ammetto che mi piacerebbe avere più gameplay in un prossimo gioco.
Se cercate un gioco con cui divertirvi, cercate altrove.
Se invece volete ketaminarvi dal mondo per 60 minuti e nel processo ridere come dei caproni hippie strafumati, avete trovato il gioco giusto.
Infatti, sia l'art style e sia la colonna sonora di questo gioco sono cose di un altro mondo: richiamano spudaratamente il retro, ma c'è quello strato di surrealismo ed impressionismo che gli danno un tocco unico e fanno in modo che appena lo vedi dici "cazzo ma io questa roba l'ho già giocata".
Ma quando?
Ma dove?
Questo è Magic Wand (TM).

Ok, So before I start there is one thing you should know.
This game is pretty much everything I've wanted from a space game for ages.
Ok, so now that you know that I drool over this game like an idiot just based on its mechanics alone... I do have a few complaints.
1. The RPG mechanics should be deeper.
The game makes a triffling effort at having RPG esk progression buts its very shallow and doesnt really appeal to me as a long time veteran of RPGs. Perhaps something more like a skilll point system where you can allocate and spec, your captain and crew to your OCD wracked, heart's desire?
2. No customization on a ship by ship level.
This game has a great system for customizing what ships are in a fleet, what position those ships start in, ect. But they still dont feel like MY ships. They are cardboard cutouts of what they should be. Ever play Nexus: The Jupiter Incident? The customization of that game, while linear and limited, still managed to make me feel like I was resposible for those few ships. They were very much MINE and loosing one was unacceptable.
3. The story, is somewhat lackluster.
Ive only played the first few missions of the game so far. But the rocky start is really not saying good things about the rest of them. Whats my problem? Well to put it bluntly, the MC is an over agressive idiot, The Military is fine with you not following orders to go do whatever, the antagonists are yawn inducing (not in their battle mechanics but their concept.)
This game could really shine if the writing was kicked up a couple of notches. Give us a real space opera, thats what the system feels like it was built for.
4.The art
Ok, the ships are wonderful, (if a bit on the low end for this day and age) but your 2D art? (which I dont have a problem with you using) Is just kind of lazy looking, its muddy and the characters look more like impressionist art than people. This was one issue I really agonised over wheter to put down or not. Im sorry for insulting someone's art like that but, it really should be top notch if your going to use it in a game.
So there you gave it all of my compaints.
If you think it doesnt paint a very nice picture of this game... well your right. This game feels like it was created by a very small group with highly limited resources. I STILL RECOMEND picking this up however. Lets get these guys some money so they can either patch up this game with the five star content it needs, or deliver to us a great title in the same vein in a few years.

Reminded me of a broken punk Fez RPG or a panoramic western Jumping Flash.
A game with its own coherence, set in a bewildering and innovative world between 2D and 3D, between fixed and mutable perspective. And a toy, where nostalgia has been updated - it gives you your nostalgia in a way that even the originals cannot provide because upon return, there is something lost. The 8-bit 3D and the papershredded plot allow the feeling.  I actually wanted to see what all the strange NPCs had to say, not necessarily in order to crack the puzzle of the plot or the setting, but to enjoy the blissful irreverence of it all. The game is brimming with ideas and a lot of its wonder is a swarm of "what if"s - which is becoming more enjoyable to me these days than fully hashed out systems. Also the sound effects were pretty lush, although the music was hit or miss for me. I wholeheartedly recommend this game, its a charming and heartfelt little piece. I just wish it were fullscreen (in the small window it can be like the computer equivalent of carsickness), controller functional (controlling perspective with a right analog stick would have been a lot more enjoyable), and perhaps longer.  I feel like this atmosphere, this experience, could be elongated in such a way that it could, much like a seer or psychadelic experience leave available lasting augmentations to the player.
+ blissful irreverence
+ palpable nostalgia
+ mutable perspective
+ interesting NPCs
+ bask in "what if"s
+ the adventure is your experience of the game rather than the protagonist's
- no fullscreen
- no controller support
- brief and fleeting though this might be appropriate for the expression

The game "Dungeon Keeper" by Bullfrog Productions changed dungeon crawling into dungeon creating whereby the player was the evil at the heart of the dungeon and the goal was to stop the heroes. "Overlord" is another variation of taking the player out of the role of being the hero and into the shoes of the bad guy.
The game parodies the typical heroic RPG and the goal is to conquer the lands surrounding your great evil tower, which you can upgrade using the treasures you collect. Also, there are decorative options to get your tower looking good as well.
You can control vast armies of goblins to terrorize the people, collect treasures, and burn villages but to what degree is up to you. The goblins will often make silly comments or jesters while adventuring or pillaging which will make you laugh and chuckle to the very end.
There are various options for upgrading your equipment using the forge in the tower while the goblins automatically equip gear found during raids on the villages or you can direct the horde with a mouse click to a stash of gear to which they plunder and equip if possible—I saw one goblin put a pumpkin on its head for a helmet.
The controls for the horde of goblins are very simple and easy to navigate. You even have the option of splitting the horde into smaller groups and covering more area. Several puzzles will make for a challenge and require you to adjust the type of goblin in your group like melee, range, or magic in order to move forward.
While the main goal is to conquer the lands through ruthlessness or mercy, you also have achievements you can collect and a statistics which shows the amount of total devastation you brought upon the people, which encourages replay.
I recommend the game if you want an action-adventure and RPG game that is hilariously witty but challenging. I also recommend purchasing the expansion which adds even more entertainment and fun.

I wanted to like this game, but there's certain things missing from it which I can't forgive in a game like this.
All the weapons fire look the same, just with different colours. It can't be difficult to design a different shape salvo for different weapons. As it stands most battles look like a few ships with a rainbow crying in the middle of them.
There's a crap load of salvage missions, mostly escorting some frigate to a wreck through a series of waypoints that are entirely irrelevant because everything on the map moves to attack you from the very start, and when they're all dead the mission is complete, making them waypointless. However, you don't actually hear about anything that's been salvaged. You get no equipment or new tech or anything from it.
There's a variety of different hardpoints on ships with different weapons on them. Good. However, there's no upgrades or chance of anything new or different. What's on them is what's on them until the end. Providing variety for this is an obvious way to increase the tactical challenge (and fun) of the game.
Big capital ships have the same range as a half decent staple gun (basically the same as everything else).
The ships are not what I would call well designed. There's nothing distinctive about them. Stick a couple of engines on a rhombus and you'd have a better looking ship than half the fleet.
The story is too fragmented for most people to follow. I mean, you have to *really try* to immerse yourself in it; it doesn't entrap you in the world. Homeworld pulled you in within three missions; you watched your home be destroyed, and from that point you were onboard for wherever it'd take you. In this, a guy, who it's been made clear doesn't like you that much, dies, and you get to salvage his ship (well, sort of, see above). Oh and your father is someone high ranking. Not exactly mind blowing.

If you don't care about graphical quality and are looking for a small fun space fleet combat game, then you will have a great time with this game.  While feeling graphically incomplete and unpolished there is a solid core game that is fun to play through multiple times.
Pros:
* This space combat portion of the game is great.
* The combat controls give you a sense of the characteristics of each ship, and the ships don't all feel the same.
* The methods used to control your ship are straightforward and easy to use.
* There are some solid RPG elements such as building your fleet over time, and mission decision making over the course of the campaign.
* The player's playstyle assessment assisting in the mission type availability is something I found rewarding and made me want to play through again but play the missions differently.
Cons:
* Graphically the game feels very prototype and unpolished even for the price point.
* The UI is definitely the most unpolished portion of the game.
* UI Layout for the ship is scattered all over the place.
* Menus overlap everywhere and the iconography is horrible, all the buttons are hard to read.
* The story dialog is very poorly written. Even though the storytelling format is solid.
* The campaign menu is poorly implemented graphically.

If you've played the old school Worms games, such as the all time classic Worms 2, you'll have a bit of a rough start. The learning curve isn't exactly forgiving, as now you play in a kind of "First Person" view mixed with 3rd person for movement, which is totally alien to regular Worms gameplay.
Don't rule the game out just yet, though. It's quite fun, as pretty much all worms games have been, and it's a good refresh to the series, also.
There are cutscenes (although of quite poor quality) with humorous remarks about your next mission and so on. The 3D is OK and just because you expect it to be cartoonish, the lack of complexity is barely noticeable.
The campaign is fun and tries to make sense and create a purpose for you to just keep playing level after level, sometimes just to see what the Worm General has at bay, hidden in his invisible sleeves.
I'd give this game a 7.5/10. It's a good time waster, both for casual and more hardcore players. Oh, and the hotseat mode makes it a good game to have when your friends come along and you run out of options on what to do!

This is a short and satisfying game experience that doubles up as a documentary about the indigenous people of Alaska.
The graphics and sound are beautiful, and the documentary is fascinating; however the game itself is a little clunky. The platforming can be a bit unresponsive at times so, whilst not difficult, getting through levels can be frustrating.
It's the first time I've experience this combination of documentary and game, and I found that it  worked well. "Earning" sections of the documenary is an interesting mechanic and a far more substantial achievement that a simple acknowledgement, unfortunately the clunkiness of the game means it's unlikely I will return to collect the parts I missed.
On the plus side the narrator's voice is very evocative and really gives the game a wonderful authentic tone. I was looking forward to each time I'd hear him speak in his native language.
You'll get around 4 - 5 hrs of entertainment and education out of this, including the DLC.  Given my issues with the game mechanics that was about right for me: the game did not outstay its welcome.
Worth a play.

Never Alone is truly beautiful, in two senses. The 3D art is gorgeous (though I'm not a fan of the 2D style) as is the story of the Alaskan people told through mini documentary videos.
What isn't beatiful is the gameplay. Very basic platforming with increasingly more insta-kill sections as you progress, as well as terrible AI that has been responsible for at least 75% of all my deaths (if the AI misses a jump, stands in the wrong place on a crushing platform or lags just a tad too far behind you and gets grabbed by moving enemies it counts as a death and you go back to the last checkpoint). The game may very well be better played co-op, but that's not an option for me, and the AI consistently lets me down. It's not just bad; it actively takes leaps of faith and fails, killing you without any input on your part, forcing you to repeat a section up to 10 times (in my experiance).
I want to like this game, I really do. I beleive it IS a great game for the first two reasons, and the platforming has a couple of good moments, but overall it's a frustrating game that gives no guidance and often requires you to die to know what you have to do during action sequences. I've even died during cutscenes. It's a nice idea poorly implimented. So with a heavy heart, as a videogame I can't recommend this, but if you want some great environment art and cultural interest, then I do.
[Edit] The final sequence is the worst gameplay I've experienced from any game for a very long time. I would not be surprised if most players gave up trying at this point. The AI doesn't follow, which kills you; the AI doesn't avoid enemies, which kills you; you have to wait for timed gusts of wind, if if you miss more than one, all you can do is wait for death. It's unbeleivable they thought such punishing, unenjoyable, unfair gameplay was good enough to ship. I can't un-recommend the gameplay enough.

TL:DR: Great story, poor mechanics.
This game is a seriously amazing work of art. Both telling stories and educating the player on real life culture. The game centers on a young female protagonist and an artic fox that helps her. You can play with two people, each controlling one of the characters, or by  yourself and switch between the two. You unlock short videos about the culture of a tribe of native people in the arctic as you go along by finding owls. Some are easily found through regular play, others are hidden down alternate paths. All-in-all, it's a great story
All that is great, but the game loses points for the sloppy platforming, confusing mechanics, and unintuitive design. For example, if you miss a jump, you will frequently glitch and hover in the air before finally falling to your doom. Later in the game, your fox friend can get trapped behind barriers, even when those barriers seem to lift out of his way. Throughout both stories, but particularly the second one, it's unclear when you can drown and when swimming is planned. Sometimes the game seems to demand 2 players with puzzles that require precise timing. I'm also not a fan of the pacing of the game. Through both stories, almost all the story is done slowly at the player's pace. In the last chapter of both, however, the game suddenly thinks it has to be fast and you go on rapid chase scenes. I get that it's supposed to be where players show off all the mechanics they mastered in the game in a thrilling climax, but it just feels out of place in a game where you aren't asked to have lightning fast reaction times 90% of the time, the sudden jolt of needing to do it SUPER FAST LOOK OUT THERE'S A THING CHASING YOU is a huge tonal shift that they repeat in both stories.
Verdict: Get this game on a sale of 50% or greater

This is a pretty decent horror and puzzle game, but I bought it for the story which ultimatly did not impress me and that is one of the reasons I cannot recommend it. Additionally I bought it during the summer sale, for a whole 70% off (which honestly I applaud frictional games for, they probably could have gotten away with doing 50% off and seeing better profit margins)
For many story driven games (or games which I am only interested in for the story) I usually just watch a playthrough online to experience the story but I decided the actually buy this game and experience it for myself for a couple of reasons
Now I'm going to break this review into 3 categories, horror, puzzle, and story and explain my feelings on each of them as to how they relate to the ultimate experience
If there is one thing I want to give this game, it sure gets your blood pumping, every time you see or are near a monster you are given certain audio and visual queues which you will quickly associate with danger, it makes you feel that fight or flight response in real life and that did make the horror sections very fun. But the problem was that despite each monster being slightly different and your objective changing from section to section, each monster segment felt very much the same, you just bait the monster away from where you need to go, then go there, maybe once or twice getting into a chase type sequence. Also I cant remember exactly but all and all I think there were only something like 5 monster areas, and while they were stressful, I would have appreciated more of them.
If I am completely honest with myself, the puzzles were probably not as hard as I made them out to be but I did spend a lot of time aimlessly wondering around, trying to figure out what to do, many times I found two terminals I needed to use together in the wrong order and never made the connection I needed to, only to go through a process of going back through every option I have available again. It could just be me, but really the puzzle sections made a majority of the game boring a frustrating for me, the game really could have done with fewer puzzles, and more just exploration or horror sequences.
Keeping in mind that I bought this game primarily as a story driven experience, I have to say that ultimately I am underwhelmed. All of the problems I've mentioned before I could have lived with if not for how basic and predicatble the story felt (I just finished the game before writing this review, and was not intending on reviewing the game until I saw the ending which left me so unfulfilled I felt I had to say something about it). Before I go into details let me say this: with the given basic plot and concept, I actually think it would have been impossible to make a good story out of this games. I'm sure anyone paying even a moderate amount of attention to the story could predict the ending pretty simply.
But you wanna know what the nail in the coffin was for me? The entire story is based around this concept of duplicated conciousness, which is very intriguing but, anyone who has seen the Black Mirror episode "White Christmas" (My personal favorite Black Mirror episode, please go watch it) has already been exposed to this concept and has likely already played around with the idea in their head a bit. In the end, the main selling point of this game for me was that it would be "thought provoking" but in reality it literally has not provoked any thought I have not already had.
This is a good game, and chances are it is worth buying (maybe not a whole $30 but on sale for sure) if you are a horror fan you will like it and many people will find the story interesting, but in the end for me personally, even with the 70% discount, I don't think it was worth the time and the money I put into it.

A great game by Frictional, the creators of the Penumbra and Amnesia series. SOMA is most similar to Amnesia, in that the playable character has limited means of self-defense beyond hiding from enemies, and the game is designed to be a horror experience. Compared to the industrial historical settings of Dark Descent and A Machine for Pigs, SOMA's environment is far more effective and interesting--especially for those who are afraid of the deep sea. The story is more complex, the characters have more depth, and the environments are chilling and unique. Best of all, there is a greater variety of enemy encounters--a total of 11 compared to the 3 or 4 which appeared in the Amnesia series, but no harm done to the length or quality of the "puzzles." Buckle up for a terrifying, severely interesting, and often-times heartbreaking sci-fi story.

It's a pretty alright game. Wish the devs hadn't abandoned it. For $10, not bad. That's $10 less than most other games of this sort. $10 less because we're not paying a dev team, or customer service team, or any team at all for that matter, it seems. I say give it a go. Now, all the negative reviews are true. Load screens are horrible the first couple logons, and without some manual graphic optimizations, it runs poorly. (And yes, if you neglect to read the bit where it says "REQUIRES A 64 BIT OPERATING SYSTEM," it will not get past the launcher for you. PvP is horrendous, but fortunately the devs DID make a PvE server branch. (rather than banning hackers, cause that takes consistancy.) If the game developers were to become more active, I'd gladly pay $20 (regarding roughly that as average price for your average survival game.) Now, the cash shop option is not nearly as bad as people make it seem. 9/10 items you can buy with real money, you can find in the world, or buy with in-game money. Now, character skins is where the real money comes in.... There are a lot of (rather lackluster) skins for your character, and all fairly cheap. BUT, the only way to get more than the standard 3 skins (two male, one female.(all bald...)) is to spend real money. However, given this game has no 3rd person camera, the only options you really need are provided; male, female, skin color, and the color of your clothes so you can choose to blend in to different environments more.
All in all, look at it this way. Average game price as stated at $20, this game is half the price, for half a game. Take it with a grain of salt.
And again, as a footnote... DO NOT BUY THIS GAME IF YOUR COMPUTER IS 32bit. That being said, if you have 64bit with low system specs, there are plenty of forums for optimizing it to run on the crappiest computers. (like mine.)

I read somewhere that SteamWorld Dig 2 was sort of, just a little bit, like Spelunky. Heck yes, I love me some Spelunky, so gimme!
Suffice to say: the comparison is apt. In SW Dig 2 you run and jump around a world mostly constructed of blocks. You can mine some of the blocks, gather ores, then sell those for profit, which in turn can be used to purchase upgrades to help you get deeper into the game world. Over time you will uncover secrets, puzzle rooms and, obviously, the story of the game, along with several boss fights.
SteamWorld Dig 2 has a visual style of its own, a curious hand-drawn look, but as I played the game I began to feel that this type of visual style and the intense labour required to create content with it might have limited the game somewhat. Enemy types are sparse, animations simple and none of the enemies in the game, save for the last boss, offer any significant challenge combat-wise. Somehow I feel that these matters are linked to one another...
As for audio, the game sits steadily in the "functional, fine, but not really memorable" -category. The music lacks memorable melodies, but serves its purpose as a fine ambient accompaniment to the more laid back moments of adventure, or strolling around the small town, talking to the handful of NPC's. Voice acting, if you can call it that, harkens back to the good ole' Nintendo 64 -days, where characters talk in unique little squeaks, beeps, boops and such.
So what do they talk about then? What's the story? Well, you play as a blue robot called Dorothy, adventuring out to find your lost friend Rusty. Alas, Rusty has gone missing deep in the mines and so you are sent deep down to find him. Oh, and to bring back a bunch of valuables. Gotta earn your keep, eh? What follows is an occasionally comedic romp through mines, caverns, temples and other, more otherworldly, locales, as you follow one clue after another and, as is the case with these things, try to stop the world from ending as your side job. Easy-peasy!
While I can't say I played the game anywhere near to a 100% completion, let alone go for the more challenging modes on offer later in the game, I feel that I have to go back to the Spelunky comparison for a moment: SteamWorld Dig 2 is a more streamlined, designed, hand-crafted adventure. It has a clear beginning, middle and an end, and it relies fairly heavily on its story. As such, there is very limited replayability, and I doubt anyone, apart from the hardcore speedrunning crowd, will find more than maybe 10-12 hours of gameplay here. Nowhere near the hundred hours one can sink into something randomly generated like Spelunky.
Is that a good thing or a bad thing? That depends heavily on the player, really. Spelunky gives more bang for your buck, when it comes to raw hours of gameplay, and while it is a simpler game at its core, it gives the player more of a sensation of discovering things. SteamWorld Dig 2 on the other hand has more potential to give its player a few nice evenings of adventuring, digging and exploring, followed by a satisfying ending and a feeling of accomplishment one might not find in Spelunky even after months of playing.
If you ask me: Both are good games and well worth your time!

I do kind of recommend this game, but it teeters on a knife's edge. I've switched between the 'Yes' and 'No' button several times, but ultimately the price is too high for the length and the potential of the game is wasted.
I played SteamWorld Dig on the 3DS and SteamWorld Heist on the PC, the latter of which is a far stronger game than this title in almost every way.
The game is roughly 9 hours long if you spend at least some time looking for secrets.
For 20€ that's way too short a game and it could've been made longer simply by adding more spaces to dig through, especially early on when you have to think over how to go about getting ore without any mistakes. There should've been more room to 'overfarm' ore and get all the upgrades and cogs to max out your character.
The pacing is kind of bad and the story is worse than in the first game and has a rushed conclusion. Fans of the first game probably remember Vectron fondly, but while it was featured nicely in Dig 2 the visit was all too brief.
Mechanically the game is fairly strong, the upgrades are interesting and while some of it is a repeat of the first Dig, most would accept that digging is the core part of these titles. Mechanically, my worst complaint is that the character floats too much in the air, which can be very frustrating in some areas.
For 10€ you could get Hollow Knight with its DLC's (which is an absolute steal!), or if you like alternative Metroidvania's then Song of the Deep is 15€ and nearly half again as long.
While Dig is a relaxing platformer/metroidvania, the lack of challenge is sorely felt. Whether it detracts from the game is up to the player, it might simply be how the developers want it to be.
When I finished this title, it reminded me of when I played Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow, if you didn't have the correct item to pass the first 'ending'. Sadly, while in C:DoS you'd realize there was much more, Dig 2 ends somewhat abruptly and you wish you'd saved your money.
Despite the negatives, Dig 2 isn't a bad game, I just wish there was a lot more of it.
