First a quick note: I did back this on Kickstarter and I'll be honest I completely forgot about it.
I played the beta maybe once for a few minutes but it didn't hold my attention against Wasteland 2 at the time; no fault of this game just Wasteland 2 is also awesome.
Anyways after putting a bit of time into this now complete game I gotta say I quite enjoy it. I have played the original JA games so I do have something to compare this to and I have also played Kalypso's very disappointing JA BiA.
Jagged Alliance Flashback is very well designed and I absolutely love the game engine. It's stylish yet simple with an almost pastel colour palette that really aces the presentation. Sound is also excellent and the music does not overpower the experience. The turn based combat is well built and flows very naturally, although I'm not a fan of the To-Hit system but it's less random than X-Com so that's something.
The random characters with the wacky names and inane dialogue kind of struck me as odd but I suppose they were probably part of a backer reward far above my teir. Wish they'd done something a little less in-your-face with them but it's easy enough to ignore. Speaking of characters the stable of AIM mercs is well fleshed out and the dialogue with NPCs is decently written; the story is standard JA fare and works well as do the excellent (so far) level designs.
I definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys a good turn based tactical RPG-lite shooter whether you're an original Jagged Alliance fan or not this has a lot to offer. It's an excellent spiritual continuation of the series and I'm not sure what all the negative fuss was about. From what I remember of the original pitch it was never touted as JA3 and I for one never expected the amount of polish that has been put into this game considering the rather meager budget Full Control worked with. Well done guys!
Side Note: JAF also gets HUGE bonus points from me for having a good solid version of the IMP which was my favorite part of JA2 and was MISSING from BiA. Bad Kalypso. No trophy for you.

I really liked this game, but I did have a few irritations, so I'll get those out of the way first...
I think the visual presentation is overly glossy, and doesn't really do justice to the *actual visual design* underlying it, which by contrast I quite liked (example: how much nicer does the title screen look than how things are rendered in-game?). and there are a few aspects of the controls which I suspect aren't as easy to use as they were meant to be, not to mention a puzzle area or two apparently designed by actual sadists, which force you to wallow in the mediocrity of specific aspects of the controls ("floor is lava" puzzle, looking at you. twice), rather than enjoying the parts of them which actually work well. as such, IMO this game could easily be doing a better job of playing to its strengths in these regards.
but those are basically my only real complaints, about a game which I'm otherwise finding to be very entertaining, engaging, rewarding, and also well-written, which is a rare bonus among games these days and one I really appreciate. and hey, it's always nice to see a female protagonist who doesn't appear to be any flavour of walking cliche, something which we still seem to struggle with producing.
the gameplay itself is a clever and (at least imo) somewhat innovative take on contemporary metroidvania-like games on the one hand, and contemporary boulderdash-like games such as spelunky et co on the other. there isn't a huge amount to add except simply that it's a well-designed and well-polished rendition of those basic concepts, along with a gear upgrades system and a reassignable customization interface which allow the player a large degree of agency over how they approach any particular area, even though which items you do or do not have depend on your progress through the game's plot.
between the clear thought and polish that have gone into mechanical gameplay concerns, the creative environment and character design, and the story and dialogue which have _clearly been written by actual writers_, this title is a clear standout against the flood of samey, uninspired drek which we on Steam are drowning in at present. and it does so in spite of being, mechanically speaking, a merger of two very well defined existing formats; this isn't hard to do when you have a world and a thematic concept which are original and which also map well to existing well-defined formats.
excellent work, from a studio I'll definitely be watching from now on. you folks are what keeps this industry, and this market, alive.

I own my fair share of Slitherine games, and I always approach them with a bit of caution - I'm still feeling a bit burned by Sovereignty, for example. Pike & Shot has scratched my historical wargaming itch, but it doesn't feel particularly polished. But like every other Slitherine game I've purchased, Star Hammer drew me in with it's concept. While their games are sometimes a bit rough (Sovereignty, I'm looking at you), Slitherine tackles concepts and mechanics very few other companies will - so I took the plunge.
It was worth it.
I'm only a few hours into the game so far, but I'm enjoying it. The controls are intuitive, The game is gorgeous, with ships moving in appropriately ship-like ways, shootng beams and railguns and missiles (oh, such satisfying missiles!) and dying in interesting ways - full on explosions, drifting hulks rocked by secondaries, the works. The campaign has been fun too - if you've read any Honor Harrington or Jack Geary you're not going to be _too_ surprised by anything you run into in the plot, but it's presented serviceably and the characters are likeable. There's a neat mechanic where you build bridge crews to give your ships passive buffs and the relationships between officers matter - pair folks up who hate each other and that buff suddenly doesn't look so great. Notably, the game presents pretty much all of the story in text and (wonder of wonders) that text is virtually typo free and decently written - and even a bit clever in places.
The missions so far haven't had a ton of variety - mostly they've boiled down to "kill all the baddies" sometimes with "and make sure this one thing doesn't die, either". Refreshingly, failing the second objective (protecting salvage crews, etc) doesn't always cause mission failures - though I presume there will be reprecussions later in the campaign. Combat feels right for the genre - closing with an enemy fleet is a fencing match of outgoing missiles and countermeasures before broadsides and spinal mounts start blazing.
So it's totally worth a buy if you want to reenact some David Weber novels or if you're having a hankering for some turn-based strategy goodness - but what are the downsides?
>The music is pretty generic. I turned it off within the first few minutes and put on something else. It's not bad, just bland.
>The character portraits are a bit "old school" in their design - they remind me of Wing Commander in a good way. However, when they're displayed in-mission they're blurred or low resolution or something, which doesn't look the best.
>Mopping up the last elements of an enemy fleet - particularly it's smaller/faster ships - can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ It boils down to a lot of circle strafing and predicting where that last enemy corvette is steering.
>The game is relatively unforgiving. Crews gain XP from missions, but if they die, they're gone forever. The game rewards patience and planning - be careless in moving your ships and they'll collide, inflicting massive damage to one another and stunning them. While you can save freely between missions, I didn't notice an option to save in-mission, which may lead to frustration.
I've noticed no glitches, freezes, or other hiccups. If none of the above turns you off, the game is absolutely worth a shot - you'll probably have a lot of fun.

First impressions:
Oniken plays much like a classic NES-era platformer. It's got the retro graphics and chiptune soundtrack to prove it.
Not only does it have retro graphics and music, but its also got that insane difficulty popular during the era. It takes quite some time to complete a level if you don't know what your'e doing (like me!). The game's controls are smooth and responsive, allowing for maximum carnage. You also have the choice of using the d-pad or the analog stick, a nice addition.
The gameplay makes use of some sword and grenade-throwing action, among other goodies, like power-ups. The platforming is alright, but I wouldn't have deemed that the focus of the game anyways, which is clearly the game's action, not its platforming. There were some parts, however, where I died due to the platforming (usually falling into a death trap of some sort). A lot of the game's enemies were really hard, especially the ones with a ranged attack. It was very difficult to get these guys because I had to be right next to them in order to kill.
I haven't played a game like Oniken in a long time. I think the last I played somewhat similar to it would be the original Metroid. It's nice to see such a game on Steam, and I hope to see more like it in the future!

Ok, going to preface this that the 'Yes' is under conditions. Now then..
This game has a very unique and enjoyable art style. The story is rather interesting to play through (and the extra details are going to be an interesting read; the historian in me is intrigued). The antagonist, despite being kinda monotone, does prove to be brutal and doesn't fluff about like most typical villains (a plus in my book). And the linux version, despite what I've seen read earlier, is fairly bug free and plays smooth.
Default controls could use a little work, but I think I saw options to modify them if you struggle with what they provide.
I also found that adding the mouse towards the middle as part of the controls can throw some off, especially since you spend the entire game to that point using the keyboard exclusively. (A swap key being mapped to a button on the mouse has also proven to make some of the later parts rather frustrating, but not unmanageable.)
The only major complaint is how painfully short the game is. Even with fumbling around and having to stop and pick the game back up after a few minutes because of issues unrelated to the game, I finished it within approximately 2 hours of playtime. For a $15 game, that's not a lot of value there. There's a lot of nice stuff in the game sure, but a $15 price tag hardly seems worth it.
So, do I recommend the game? Yes. At the $15 price point? No. Get it on a sale. At the writing of this review, Humble Bundle has it in their current Indie Bundle and you can pick it up on the cheap with a bunch of other games. Obviously, this is not going to last forever, so if you would like to experience the game, that's a good way to do it.

I've only dinked around with a few guitars over the years. I ultimately have very little idea what I'm actually doing with the guitar (save a few chords and memorized riffs here and there). Pure noob.
When I first heard about the concept of Rocksmith years ago I was very interested in the idea of a Guitar Hero or Rock Band type game that you actually played a real guitar. (I was a huge fan of those games.) The problem...I didn't know how to actually play a real guitar. Could it be possible that a game like Rocksmith could teach me to really play? The verdict went out, most reviews and videos I watched came back ecstatic about Rocksmith being not only a game, but a fantasic teaching tool as well. The only downsides I caught wind of were a horribly designed interface, some sound interface and gain issues. Alas I decided to hold off and moved on never purchasing the 'original Rocksmith' game.
Then came Rocksmith 2014. The same excitement bubbled up within me about a life long desire to teach myself guitar and play some of my favorite rock songs I've been listening to over the years. But would the game have fixed it minor short comings from the prior release? The reviews came in ....fantastic, 10/10, 5 stars, 9.5/10 etc.etc. Wow. They got it right and what's more they seemed to have greatly improved not only the interface, but the whole game experience itself. From the in game arcade where you can hone your guitar techniques that many guitar instructors teach in their lessons. To a great lesson section in which all the techniques and terminologies are carefully and skillfully delivered to those who need them, along with a practice session that increases the difficulty as you perform the lesson better. Then (of coarse) the actual learning of a song. Wow. Super fun. The problem with the real guitar lessons that my friends and other took is that they plateaued and grew bored with their slow progress and lame nursery songs for beginners. Rocksmith masterfully throws that old paradigm out the window and allows the player to learn their favorite songs, but at the level it detects the user can handle. Then it slowly increases the skill level as you master more perfectly the notes/chords that are launched your way. It is fun, motivational, and very progressive. Your skill will increase in just the first few weeks alone.
The game also includes and virtual band called Session Mode where you can play with your own band that you define and calibrate then play with. They adjust to your key/chord progession, tempo, style...etc.  Just another of many wows within the game. This game is a gem and has found it's place in my heart.
Ubisoft it seems has fully embraced the notion that a game like Rocksmith is equally used as a learning tool to learn from scratch how to play the electric/rythem/bass guitars, or the hone your skills even if your a guitar shredding vet. Both types seem to be happy with what Ubisoft has delivered this run.
Their are of coarse a good selection of tracks included with the game itself. Or they are always adding to the growing library of DLC songs or song packs to more greatly expand your library of favorite guitar songs/licks/riffs etc.
I haven't played a game where I was actually learning something that truly had a place and meaning outside of the gaming world. What a breathe of fresh air. They are trailblazing a new type of genre in effect. Not just the guitar playing genre, but the learning a real skill game genre. (lame name, but you get it.  :P  )

Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna) is a beautifully presented, tastefully told tale, based on a traditional folk story from the Iñupiat people - an Alaskan native tribe. I love the artistic style and was immediately drawn to the story of Nuna, a young girl whose life is saved by an Arctic Fox. Together with the fox who can speak to the arctic spirits, they set out to find out why the blizzards are so severe, which is causing her village to starve. I'm not going to go into the story in much detail because of spoilers, but it is well written, and very atmospheric, being voiced in the native language with subtitles. It is a unique and interesting way of telling a folk tale that very few people would otherwise get to hear.
Through playing the story you unlock informational panels which make up a video documentary taken to explain the life of the Iñupiat people. As the game tells us, this is a "living people, a living culture" - this is not ancient history, these are the people that still live in Northern Alaska today. This is their way of life. I found this extremely interesting and learned a lot about a cultural heritage I would not have explored otherwise. The mesh between game and documentary is a superb way to promote education in different cultures, tradition and language. I really hope that we get more games that can do this so well.
Never Alone is a linear, story driven game with basic puzzle and platform elements. You can switch between controlling the Nuna or Fox, and a co-op partner can take the form of Fox in local co-op only, making it a relaxing couch co-op game. I could see this being a fantastic game to play along with a child. Unfortunately, the platforming can be frustrating, as the controls are somewhat clunky and the animations slow and at times awkward. In a platformer, the last thing you want is to feel like your character is dying because of a lack of responsiveness, and this is sometimes the case with this game. The puzzles and interactions and actual mechanics are very simple, but I found them fun and engaging, but the platforming is mediocre at best. The game was also let down a little by some bugs and glitches; I had to restart a few times to get past places where my character had glitched.
The Foxtales DLC adds a separate short story and takes around 1 hour to complete, as well as unlocking five more videos. It adds a few minor mechanics, and has quite a different setting to the original game as it's mostly underwater. I enjoyed it just as much as the original. You will need to complete the DLC in addition to the main story if you would like to get 100% achievements, which can be obtained on one playthrough by simply completing the game, the DLC and unlocking all the Cultural Insights.

Overall I've enjoyed what I've played of the game. The more I've played it the more its grown on me. At this point I'd give it an 8/10. I doesn't come across as anything revolutionary but its a pretty solid game. It mixes neat elements like ships only being able to fire in a limited number of directions with turn based gameplay. So its kind of like naval combat in some of the Total War games (and probably other games) I guess in that sense. Combat also reminds me of the combat in Space Rangers 2 mixed in with the graphics and feel of Star Wolves 3.
I've only played the first five missions but so far story wise they seemed alright. Just alright though. I'm hoping at this point it evolves into something a bit more substancial because its coming across as being pretty generic.
Ultimately, its a turn based game. So if you aren't into that kind of thing you probably shouldn't buy it.
Most of the negatives I have about the game are more nitpicking on my part on ways it could be improved. I'd still overall recommend the game.
Positives:
- Combat is reasonably smooth and the game is pretty enjoyable as far as I'm concerned.

- I experienced no major bugs
- The background art between missions looks really nice. Obviously the game graphics themselves are not 2015 level graphics, but they are reasonable I think given the price.
- Seems like the game has a lot of potential.
Negatives/suggestions
- It would be nice if there was a waypoint option. Something like Space Rangers 2 where if you've selected a location on the map to travel to (that is outside of your ability to travel to in one turn) you don't have to manually say to go to the next turn in cases where you aren't being fired at.
- The commander/captain of any vessel probably could be shown in a larger text size.
- The first mission dumps a lot of info on you before you probably really need it. Info about the UI could probably be spread out more.
- Some kind of indicator that projects an enemies movement limitations. Particularly if I'm supposed to be (according to the story) familiar with a ship design.
- It would be good if you had an option to turn off automatic dialogue. Sometimes the pacing of the dialogue is a bit off and it takes forever for your wingman to say what they were going to say.
- Very limited ship customization options from what I've seen so far.
- To me it doesn't make much sense that given the 3D nature of space that a ship would only exclusively be able to fire forward or behind it (or exclusively to the sides). Outside of smaller craft like fighters ships should have some ability to shoot targets on their weaker sides, even if that ability is considerably weaker than their ability to shoot on their stronger sides. The only exception to that might be a ship that is exclusively designed to fire a big gun in one direction (like an Ion Frigate in the Homeworld series).
- More significance for the Z axis. If this has some significance then that isn't made clear. It doesn't seem like it has any combat significance.
- The movement of ships can be pretty finicky. You'll click on a ship's shadow and it won't register that you clicked on it. This could be improved I think.

Obviously there are some good parts to this game and it's got a lot of fans see reviews below. I however am not one of them and wanted to offer a balanced opinion for those on the fence about this purchase.
What is it?:
I would say it's a metroidvania, casual, cartoony, open-world, mining, platformer with a focus on puzzle solving, exploration, and simplfied combat.
What isn't it?:
Challenging, Original (in direct contrast to a certain popular websites reviewers stated opinion), Mechanically Sound, Long, or particularly deep.
The GOOD:
Constant Feel of Progression (Triple Star Here As I Believe This May be Why Many Love This Game and Overlook other Aspects)
Good-Balance (Helps and goes hand in hand with the first one) at least until you unlock a certain item and it seems to instantly break the game (which isn't necessairly a bad thing).
Bright and colorful world (the art does seem to be original and well done)
Exploration is consistently rewarding (prizes and unlockables galore)
If your looking for a true Casual Game it's probably going to be a winner
Easy Backtracking and frequent warp points (well pipes in game) make a difficult obstacle for this genre to overcome essentially null and void.
AC/DC:
Sound - Not my cup of tea but did not enchance or degrade the game for me
Length - If your not into exploring and just want to beat the pavement I think you could probably finish it in under 5 hours, however if you're going to explore you can probably squeeze 12 hours or so out of a single playthrough.
Plot - If your here for that it's probably best you go elsewhere...
The BAD:
Control - This is a platformer with stiff controls and awkward physics a cardinal sin in my gaming bible
Combat - It's repetitive which is okay except it's not challenging which makes it a bore. The exception here is for the challenge you will unnecessarily have controlling your character. It's an easy enough game that it won't jump out as being as unfair as other harder games that suffer from this issue but it's an annoyance some (obviously me) just won't be able to live with.
One path progression-Limited amount of customization, They try hard but honestly many of the upgrades are worthless and hurt this aspect of the game. It's also strange in that the World is pretty Open but your path through it seems extremely defined by the lackluster plot.
Challenge - Other than the standard setup of Metroidavnia roadblocks and finding a way around them I found the challenge here to be very lacking. It's a fine line to draw but I don't think I spent more than a minute or two on any one puzzle and they came off as uninteresting to me.
Plot - I mean it's there...If you really like cutesy cartoony characters perhaps the ones here and their limited amount of character traits will be of interest but there's nothing special about it. The best thing I can say is that most of the dialouge interactions are short.
Content to Cash Ratio - $20 dollars US when off sale seems a bit steep for this game. As a rule of thumb $1 for one hour played is what I'm expecting. Although with good polish and production values this game does lower the ratio I would need to feel content with my purchase.
Overall Rating 4.5/10

Well, Oniken certainly feels like an 8-bit era game... but not necessarily in a good way.
The game is full of cheap deaths, enemies tend to pop out of nowhere, levels rely on memorization through repetition, powerup content is luck-based, and the checkpoints are scarce and unforgiving. Died during a boss fight? Well, enjoy replaying a substantial portion of the level again until you're sick of it.
I get it that most of this is done on purpose. And some people will be fine with it. Some will call it a challenge and a throwback to the past. The thing is, it's not the 80s anymore and we're not forced to play this one single random game we've managed to get ourselves this month, which lasting appeal relies solely on the fact that it's unfairly difficult.
As a throwback to the past it's certainly good, in a bad way. If old-school action-platforming repetition and memorization is your thing then I guess you'll have fun with it. I surely didn't.

If you want to play yourself a hella-NES game, then I'd highly recommend grabbing yourself a copy of JoyMasher's Oniken, because believe me, it's a hella-NES game.
Oniken's reproduction of a retro style goes far beyond its pixelated visuals or its rockin' chiptune soundtrack. It mines the depths of those special things that made games like Contra, Power Blade, and Ninja Gaiden so good. Oniken doesn't just LOOK like the era it's trying to recreate, it feels like it too. Maddening difficulty set on top of a set of simple mechanics and insidious level layouts that will take you more than just a few tries to slash your way through. On top of that, the game packs in lots of fantastic bosses, hugely varied stages, and some very clever throwbacks to the game that inspired it.
While Oniken is definitely a fantastic retro-styled game, it manages to go beyond that by being a pretty damn great action game on top of that.

Overall - Very fun Ninja Gaiden-esque side scroller.  A little less limber, a little more walking apocalypse.  Not as difficult as the old nail biters for us who love them... but also not easy enough to get bored.
I love speedrunning games.  My main game was always Demon's Crest and Gargoyle's Quest 2, both of which I've spent thousands of hours on perfecting in order to get the times I've gotten.  I feel the same pace of action in these games even if its more sword less shooty.  The controls are tight and feel right.  Attacking has some really cool little gimmicks behind it.  Most of you from Symphony of the Night / other Metroidvanias will fondly recall the Jump slash land slash combo.  But more than that, you can cancel your slashes by crouching, so that you can Slash crouch slash slash crouch slash over and over for a really cool trick.  Things like this make games replayable, little skillsets that you can improve at and get better with.
That said, this game is not flawless.  This game has major issues with difficulty.  Now, most of you might wonder why.  Enemy placement / attacks are good and difficult to get around.  The problem comes from this -
1) Your health - You have too much health.  By simply brute forcing your way through levels and bosses you generally have enough HP to get to the next section.  Enemy attacks are not very damaging in general.  If you just keep moving forward and jumping, you'll likely make it to the next section with 2 bits of HP left only to be fully healed on the next section.  Combine this with the fact that you're likely to find 1 or even 2 health ups per section and you're blazing by pretty healthy.
2) Grenades - Strong enough to kill many problematic enemies in one HP as well as abundant enough to never worry about them.  Some minibosses can be killed by simply spamming your grenades a few times.  I like that they are not easy to land and thus grant a bit of a bonus for your effort, though I would have been more appreciative of a slightly less damaging item.
I realize as someone who's played the unholy hell out of Demon's Crest / Gargoyle's Quest II I am probably biased toward more difficult games.  And don't get me wrong, this game isn't 'Easy'.  If the developers wanted a 'Medium' for difficulty, they're certainly not far from it.
I'll be honest - I expected another 'Retro' game that misses the point of going back to the old days.  You guys did not miss that point.  You captured what was fun in these games by meticulously getting the controls and fighting right.  And for that you do deserve praise.  Keep up the good work and Odallus will be just as good, if not better.

Stories Untold is a rather odd game from Devolver Digital, which seems to sort of be their thing. At first, it appears to be some sort of weird text adventure thing, though in a “game within a game” sort of environment, as you are playing the game on a computer on a desk inside your computer.
The game has a very 1980s vibe to it, which isn’t surprising, because it is set in 1986. It reminds me somewhat of the 1980s Twilight Zone, or similar shows; the first story immediately makes you realize that the game is going to be rather meta, but the game has a number of additional twists in store as you go through its four episodes.
That being said, I use the term “game” somewhat loosely here; this is a strictly linear storytelling experience, and is almost entirely concerned with following directions rather than solving puzzles or interacting with the environment in any sort of meaningful way. Rather, this is more like an interactive made-for-TV movie, or perhaps miniseries – and it is about as long as one, too, clocking in at about 2 hours and 15 minutes to complete.
While this seems to be a horror game at first, it is not the “random monster jumps out and scares you” kind of horror, and while the first episode does a reasonable job of messing with you, the later ones become much less creepy, though all of them have at least somewhat worrisome aesthetics to them.
As the game goes on, increasingly more gameplay mechanics are added, and while the game never becomes complex, and you never really do much more than follow directions, the extremely limited adventure game text interface is actually limited to only a couple portions of the game.
All that being said, this is a very, very simple game. While this is not a walking simulator, this is still a very narrative-focused game with very little actual gameplay, perhaps more like a visual novel than anything else, though its interface is, if anything, most reminiscent of Don’t Touch Anything in terms of being in a very narrowly confined space most of the time, with just one or two screens of actual “content” per episode (though the finale is more complicated).
Sadly, said interface is also clunky at times; the text adventure sections are particularly frustrating at times due to the fact that the interface is not always very smart about what you’re telling it to do, and there were a couple points where I struggled to do what I was trying to do due to needing to find the “magic words” so to speak.
The only other major problem with the game is the fact that, in the end, the story as it ultimately pans out isn’t really nearly as twisty as you would have hoped based on all the other twists in the game. In fact, I was rather disappointed with the ending, as I was hoping that there was going to be one more twist, or rather, that what you were being pushed towards was not what had really happened, but was yet another lie. Alas, it was missing that extra layer, which I think might have added something more to the experience.
All in all, I feel like this was one of those things that tried, but didn't quite get there. If you’re looking for gameplay, this is probably not the place to go looking. And if you aren’t super enamored with dark stories with dark twist endings, this isn’t likely to be up your alley either. If you like a 1980s vibe, though, and a darker sort of vibe, this might be something you’d be interested in. It is certainly a different sort of game.

As a long time gamer and fan of the work of Frictional Games I decided to get their latest game "SOMA". I thought it would maybe go on to be as good as Frictionals other works "Amnesia the dark descent" and the Penumbra trilogy. How wrong I was. It is THE BEST game I have ever played in my entire life. Even if the gameplay doens't quite convince me for a 2015 release the story fully made up for that. Now 2 years later I still think of the story and the questions it asks like "What defines consciousness?" or "How could humanity live on after an apocolype?". I don't want to spoil anything of the story so everyone who reads this still has the opportunity to get it. At the time of writing this review the game is only 8,39€ which is the best deal of the entire summer sale. If anyone is not familiar with the works of Fricional Games I can tell you they make the best horror games there are on the market. No jumpscares or disturbing scenes are guaranteed. They rather make it horror in your mind even going as far as opening doors offscreen or just closing them off completely. It just makes everything much more terrifing. The real horror elements in this game are "monsters" who you have to avoid and solve riddles while they chase you. Speaking of it the puzzels in the game are sometimes easy but also sometimes extremely hard if you are not familiar with computer programming. As I already said the best part of the entire game is the story. I would be lying if I said I have ever seen a better story in a computer game. I would not recommend another game more than this one. If you have some spare bucks lying around get it!

First of all this is not Jagged Alliance 3, nor is it a 2014 version of Jagged Alliance 2. It is a prequel to Jagged Alliance (1).
The main focus of the developer seems to have been the tactical combat (and allowing for modding - see below), and the tactical part is pretty solid - I absolutely love the fact that rifles and sniper rifles are less accurate at short range, thereby leaving a niche for handguns and submachineguns in the later game.
The game has a decent selection of weapons, from the lowly .38 revolver to awe inspiring sniper rifles and lmgs. Also a solid attachments system has been added, allowing you to attach scopes, expanded magazines, bipods, duckbills and other stuff to your weapon of choice.
While the graphics are not revolutionary they do look very crisp and show solid craftmanship.
The music is quite catchy and very late 1980s ad while the gunshots are a bit flat, I think that the voice acting is very good and close to the spirit of the two former games.
There is a wide selection of mercenaries to choose from (both new and younger versions of merc from JA and JA2), and I've come accross many personal favorites such as Ice, Ivan, Lynx, Magic, Buzz and even Mike. Also IMP is in so you may design your own custom mercenary.
The game shows amazing modding potential and depending on your ambitions posibilities range from very simple (editing JSON files) to very complex (using Unity3d).
I find myself spending more and more time with Jagged Alliance Flashback, and while it is not perfect and certainly no updated version of JA2, it is a solid game and one of my favorites right now.
I rate i 8/10.

I want to start off by saying that you cannot find a more dedicated Jagged Alliance fan than I. Sure,  there will be those that have played every game for 500+ hours or created massive mods, but I truly adore the series, even the weird but fun Back In Action.
Now, I won't say the game doesn't have its issues; as a game built on less than 500k, it has faults that a much larger budget would have obviously helped fix, but the core that is there is very solid and addictive. It felt Jagged Alliance-y from the very start, with the classic island-nation motif and cadre
of insane mercs for hire. While the mercs are not as talkative as I would like, what they do say gets
their personalities across perfectly.
If asked should you get the game, I would say ABSOLUTELY!, and that is because you must be a strategy fan if you're checking the reviews to help make up your mind. A big reason to buy it is that
it will help ensure that the game does get patched and get even more content and features as more
cash comes in. See, with enough money, any feature that people miss would get added, so ragging
on the game does the exact opposite. Heck, even if you don't play it now, by buying the game you
help get more content made so that when you're ready, you'll have a much better game.
So, in summarization, while certain features need work (AI, party chatter etc) any and all of these
issues are due to a cash shotage not a vision or idea shortage, so buy the game already and help
make it even better! Trust me, these guys don't quit till they make a much better game (and the base
is very fun as it is)!

Anna, at least I found, is a pretty confusing mess of a game that doesn’t really know what it is trying to do. At first, it seems like a very cut-and-dry Unity based adventure game (think Gone Home, or Slenderman for its control scheme/layout/control feel). As supposed to those games, however, there is a much lighter tone (at least at first), but once you pass the first true puzzle of the game, the whole mood changes. Gone is the bright, beautiful scenery, replaced with a drab, plain shack essentially. Once in the new setting, more horror based elements start to present them. These aren’t necessarily fear-inducing (which is what I believe this style of game is commonly used for), instead it just has an overall creepy vibe. The creepy vibe is sometimes subdued by the absurdity of the scares at some points (“walk into a room, ooooh there’s blood on the wall! Isn’t that scary?!”). Sometimes, they do have a really effective moment (there is one puzzle I can recall upon completion, a floating mask will follow you around, with the sounds of muffled breathing coming from behind you until you turn around), but these moments are far and few between, and not enough to set the mood.
Although these horror elements are going on, there is very soft and relaxing guitar music playing, which partially breaks the immersion with the game. There is also never really any sense of danger (for one, you can’t die, but this is common in these sorts of games). I found there was always just a one off scare, then more relaxing music and adventure-esque puzzles (The first puzzle involves putting two pieces of a mirror shard in an eye hole in the wall, using a pine cone to make an iris, burning said pinecone to “burn the left side of the door to reveal a keyhole (I never gathered this occurred when playing)”, then putting out the eye with a filled canteen).
In terms of the story, it follows a person being drawn to the cabin by a mysterious voice to be revealed as “Anna.” Exploring through the game shows that she was an ancient goddess that would lure men into worshiping her, then killing for her pleasure (very similar in narrative to the ancient cult of Diana of Italian mythos). In terms of the endings, they tend to go against the norm that each ending gets progressively worse and worse for the main character as it goes on (the happier ending is the easiest).
In conclusion, the game seems to be slightly confused in terms of what it is trying to do. The story was very horror-esque, but at no point did it really feel like it was truly immersive into this role. The music (although nice) didn’t really fit into this game, as well as the different scare tatics implemented.  Overall, I cannot recommend this game for many. If you are a fan of much slower horror games, maybe give this a play (it’s not very long either, clocking in at about 3-4 hours), but as a general note, I cannot recommend the game.

Okay, first of all, I have been playing Vega Conflict for nearly 3 years now. 4 years, if you count the other games made by the same devs. I have never spent a dime on in-game assets; I learned, survived, and thrived. Even with that, it's still difficult to be competative in such a PVP orianted game without dumping some serious money into in-game assets. Here are my 2 cents on this review.
I really love this game. Seriously. It's quite an exciting game. Simple at a glance, but underneath, it's actally very deep in terms of ships, tactics, and even politics. But can I recommend this game? No. Not anymore at least.
Why? Because of three major reasons that the developers never seem to learn from.
Pay to win
It does not matter if you're an absolute newbie that just got the game when it came out on steam, or an elite pilot who has been playing since the beta days 3-4 years ago, if you don't spend real life money on in-game assets (coins!), you're not going to have a great time, nor be very competative in PVP. Period. And I am not talking about casuals who invest 20-50 dollars a month. I am talking about investing around 100-1000 dollars. Need a ship or base module build or refitted now? Pay up. Don't have the coins? Too bad. Wait 2-16 days. Your fleet is down? Pay up now, and get back in the fight (and/or spam that same fleet, rinse and repeat until the enemy is down.). Or wait until that fleet is done repairing.
Incompetent Devs
This is the biggest red flag in my opinion. Kixeye, the developers of Vega and other games, have quite a reputation (at least within their community) to make the same game killing actions on each and every one of their products. Especially over the course of the last 6 months, they have broken their promises again and again. Without shame. One such example is the black market. They explicitly stated that coins will not be involved in the black market. It will only involve a form of currency called Blood Amver, which is something that can only be earned by completeing daily missions. You actually got to play the game to earn Blood Amber, and buy cool tech. What happened? Well, around the start of November, Kixeye had the nerve to break their promise, and introduce coins into the black market. Want a good, effective item on the black market? Pay up 20 blood amber and you can only get one. OR you can buy 6-18 of that item for 200 coins each. On another note, good luck getting an actual response from support, because Kixeye support is pretty bad. The "responses" are moreorless copy/paste from the F&Q. So if you want to get that fleet that died thanks to a lag spike or a server outage on kixeye's end, chances are that you will not be riembursed.
New players are going to have a bad time at the current state of the game
I have seen many newbros get their fleets slaughtered thanks to the difference in technology between newbros, "semi-vets" and veterans. Each month, Kixieye launches events that often offers a unique ship hull that will probably never be offered until a year or two later. The ship hulls, weapons, and defenses that are researched are stepping stones at beast, and just plain garbage at worst. The problem? They had not been rebalanced since the game came out of beta (with the exception of a few). Back then, they dominated the game, in terms of PVE and PVP. Now? They are stupidly easy to destroy, if you have the most recent and state-of-the-art technology. So newbros are basically stuck with thise outdated technology. The only way to get better tech is to grind. Grind cargo fleets and hope to get some blueprint pieces that offer viable technology, or grind event fleets, which appeal to veterans rather than anything below. So unless you have a friend who is also a veteran at this game, you're going to have a real hard time aquiring the technology we veterans already have.
I really do enjoy this game, but I can't recommend it to others, for the reasons stated above. Now I cannot stop you from spending money on this game, but please, consider it deeply before doing so.
As for newbros, feel free to contact me. I want to help newbros as much as I can, and adapt them to this rather.... hostile enviornment.
There. /endrant

This game is a major pain to eyes. Most of the time you'll spend looking at white colors which then get covered by blood. Your blood. More accurately, your blood coming out of your eyes. After you finally spoon your eyes out just to end the pain, your ears are going to start bleeding. Why? Well the soundtrack is nice and all, but it's being disrupted by the narrator. And of course, there isn't a soothing voice of Kevan Brighting that would make your day much better. Instead, you'll have to listen to a (probably) toothless eskimo speaking in his folk language, explaining what is happening on the screen (not like you can't figure out yourself or anything).
After your eyes and ears are gone, you'll hit an another problem. Glitches and AI. Sometimes my fox friend spent more time checking out how it feels like to be a popscicle inside a wall, than help me solve a puzzle. Alternatively, during a jump rush sequence he's just going to hop right into some hostile's arms or simply go sing "Free falling" while faceplanting a bunch of spikes in a gloryhole.
<<<SPOILERS>>>
Finally let's move on to the storyline itself. Well let's see here: A young eskimo girl goes for an adventure to figure out what's causing a heavy wind. On her journey she encounters a hungry polar bear that proceeds to chase her right afterwards. The girl falls by some snowy cliff waiting to get consumed by the almighty bear when suddenly a snow fox saves the day, by jumping over the bear and baiting him into a trap. So far so good, seems like a promising game. After a while you realise the fox does most of the job during puzzles in first two chapters. Lovely, ain't it? The girl menages to get back to her village, just to see it being burnt down by the only fire on the entire iceberg. After that she travels to... Where exactly? Well, that's a good question, because she didn't really want to avenge her people since she was just running away (again) from the "evil person" and she just goes with her fox friend in a straight line to nowhere. Once again, this game shows it's quality.
<<<END OF SPOILERS>>>

This game has everything we have come to expect of a sci-fi, psychological horror game: existential questions, moral dilemmas, underwater basketweaving in the Marianas Trench, juking bitc* as* monsters for days. You know, the finer things in life.

Is it a direct successor to JA2? No. But they never promised it would be.
The game may not be quite as deep or as polished as JA2 was for its time but I feel FC have done a beautiful job of instilling the core essence of JA into their game. Throughout the entire dev process they have been open and honest about what they were promising, and after a slightly rocky release and some hard work on major patches I'm happy to say they've delivered pretty much everything I was expecting and hoping for.
There are a few mechanics I sorely miss from the franchise, a few minor bugs and die hard fans will probably say its a waste of money. But I've enjoyed the time I've spent on it so far and in the end isn't that how we should measure the quality of a game?

Disclaimer: Kickstarter backer here, which means I have been following this project since its first public appearance, and also that I was hyped enough to give money before it was even made (something I do not regret).
I honestly like this game, even though its far from perfect, its not one of those niche obscure games "only true [insert tag here] will appreciate". It is a tactical game with enjoyable battles which follows the footsteps of the original Silent Storm maybe more closely than those of Jagged Alliance, but if you have played the SS saga you might agree with me in that this is not bad at all. It also has some timely influences from modern genre hits (XCOM, Shadowrun), such as the way cover works, and it brings back most of the classic JA mercenaries we know and love, with an art direction and management possibilities more consistent that those in the BitComposer JA remakes.
As of weak points, it also has some, so do not expect a great story like Shadowrun Dragonfall or the carefully tailored scenarios of JA2, as battles here are quicker and need less thought. Also each sector map is smaller, which takes out most of the joy of trying wild or careful approaches (you´ll find that simple flanking is often the greatest trick you can play).  Having said that, at the time of writing this review I have not finished the main mission, so if my impression changes in the endgame I´ll correct this. Finally, regarding bugs and problematic designs, all my complains at release have been taken care of in the latest patches, which also included new scenarios and items.
In a nutshell: If you are a hardcore tactical fan this is will be probably too simple for you. I had my hopes high for a JA3, and this is not one. However, I also find a lot of fun in more lighthearted experiences such as Shadowrun Returns, and I find this very close to it and accept it as so. Some months from now you´ll probably not remember your grand campaign to kill the Prince of San Hermanos, but you´ll have spent some very enjoyable hours kicking his...

SteamWorld Dig 2
by Image & Form
Genre: Metroidvania
Release: September 8, 2017
-----
I REALLY love Metroidvania games! Those awesome exploration fests that require additional abilities to go back and unlock new areas or get awesome new abilities are some of my favorite games ever. So, when I saw (belatedly, I’m sorry to say) that Swedish developer Image & Form had released a sequel to their amazing game which I also loved, SteamWorld Dig, I jumped on it as soon as possible!
Rusty, the protagonist of the first game, is missing! So, the merchant from that game, Dorothy, sets off in search of him. She ends up in El Machino, a town buffeted by earthquakes from deep beneath Archaea, the planetwide mine which was also a setting of the first game! The town’s mayor beckons you to go underground and see what the problem is, mainly so the economy can keep rolling rather than for any safety concerns (such a politician, heh). Dorothy obliges him, and so sets off on her quest…
She has a little spark friend, who provides her with a constantly-updating map of the surroundings, and this time, once it’s in place, it’s locked – there’s no procedural generation here, which means there is more potential for great puzzle action! And that potential is fulfilled, in spades! Quite a few dozen caves have many secrets waiting for you to discover them, but to get far in the world, you will of course have to collect new items…
and that’s where the Metroidvania comes in! From the start you’ll be able to wall-climb, but it becomes clear very soon that you’ll need more advanced equipment! So, you get equipped with pressure bombs for precision detonation of pesky, out-of-reach blocks; a jackhammer to smash through brick; a hookshot to speed through the treacherous caverns with ease; and much, much more! Also, you can collect cogs throughout the mines and other locales! These can be installed on your equipment using the workbench up in town, and provide all kinds of interesting and useful effects!
Keep your lantern full of fuel at all times or you could be stranded in the dark! Keep that water tank as full as you can to fling those bombs and work your jackhammer! And watch out below; a long fall can really, really hurt, in more ways than one; when you’re scrapped, you give a share of your gathered valuable resources, mined from the very rock itself, to the powers that be that you may return to life.
I would most definitely recommend this to Metroidvania fans like me, and those who are enthralled by the SteamWorld; for more from this awesome franchise, also check out Heist, a tactical turn-based action game!

A very polished little ARPG, especially for Early Access. This is probably the closest I've felt to playing Four Swords Adventures or Crystal Chronicles with friends in years.
Pros:
- Fun Secret of Mana-style combat that rewards smart positioning and timing.
- Totally customizable skills and passive talents (no classes, get any ability you want) that let you really play any way.
- Perfectly functional online co-op that works over Steam or direct IP.
- Character-based saves: Play in single-player, then take your character online to do stuff with friends!
- Neat little sidequests for exploring or doing puzzles, and an arena with its own rewards.
- Lots of items to craft and buy for different play types.
- Boss fights with unique mechanics that'll kill you over and over until you get gud.
- Cute music that gets stuck in your head.
- Nice sprite art that doesn't feel like a cheap way to make graphics. Animations look real good.
- Light tongue-in-cheek story and dialogue that isn't blunt enough to be annoying or cringey.
- Arcade "roguelike" mode for when you just wanna chill and fight stuff with friends.
Cons:
- Facing in one direction is sometimes finicky; I've gotten hit often because my shield was up in the wrong place.
- No local co-op, only online. Online is awesome, but there's something special about local that it can't do.
- The game art is good, but character portraits look like Babby's First deviantART Submission.
- Slow and somewhat confusing menus: It takes more time and more button presses than I'd like in order to change equipment or use skill points. There are quick-swap and quick-level features to help, but they're only for when you get a new item or when you've just leveled up, and they don't help when you wanna switch to equipment you already have or level something new.
- Not all skills are in the game yet: There's a good range of one-handed, two-handed, and magical skills, but only two for support so far.
- Unfinished areas and features: Trying to go in certain directions or use certain options gives you a text box that says that that thing isn't in the game yet. This is only a chunk of the final game's world.
- Very rare crashes: I've encountered one crash so far. It was in a cut-scene where I was supposed to get a unique item, and since the host got the item fine, I had to go back and play the section in single-player to get it for my character. It really wasn't a big deal, but there might be more crashes that I'm not aware of.
Basically, the worst thing about this game is that they're still making more of it.

How to cook a very nice meal Spaghetti Carbonara "For Honor" edition:
1) Choose any multiplayer game mode and press "play"
2) Go to the kitchen, grap a bowl and mix four eggs, parmasan cheese and some cream to a nice mix.
3) Go back to your computer, press "Continue" on the pop up saying "Unable to connect. Error 0004502040"
4) Choose any multiplayer game mode and press "play"
5) Go back to the kitchen and start preparing the spaghetti. Take a pan and start boiling water. Meanwhile open up a bag of bacon and (optional) any desired vegetables.
6) Go back to your computer, press "Continue" on the pop up saying "Unable to join the match. Error 0043560000"
7) Choose any multiplayer game mode and press "play"
8) Go back to the kitchen and begin preparing the bacon. Make it semi crispy and add the optional vegetables. Stir it a few times.
9) Go back to your computer and now, choose your hero and press ready. Meanwhile the match is loading you can prepare your plate, salt and pepper + fork and knife in the kitchen.
10) Game is starting. Weee! Now press the pop up saying "Session lost. Returning to menu. Error 000403000050"
11) Choose any multiplayer game mode and press "play"
12) Go back to the kitchen, finish the boiling pasta- and begin mixing pasta, bacon and the mixture of egg and cheese your made in step two- into a pan and make it nice and juicy. Stir it on low heat.
13) Go back to your computer, press "Continue" on the pop up saying "Unable to join the match. Error 0043560000"
14) Go back to your kitchen and serve your nicely made Spaghetti Carbonara "For Honor" edition.
15) Sit by your computer and repeat step 1,3,4,6,7,9,10,11,13.
Enjoy your meal.

Let me tell you a little story.
Once there was a land called Steam. Steam had many kingdoms on it. Some were large and very rich. Others were small, and trying to obtain their wealth. In an decently-well established kingdom known as "Ubisoft" the king was very greedy. One day a peasant made a discovery. He had spied an island off the coast which looked to be filled with gold. Enough gold for everyone in the kingdom one might even say. So the king gave everyone in his holdings a crate of wood with which to build a boat in order to retrieve their gold. His only wish was for a small 60$ tribute from each person as payment for the wood he had supplied. Before the people set sail they each gave this greedy king his tribute. They then set a course for the island now known as "For Honor". Everything looked great as people were pushing off from "Beta" pier, where each person's boat was kept. Then as they neared the island things started to go wrong. Some boats sprung leaks and began to sink. Some boats fell apart, leaving their passengers treading water. some boats simply dissapeared as if they had suddenly "disconnected" from the universe. In the end most people made it to the island. "Most" people. Some people recieved wood full of termites and could never build a boat to begin with. Either way most had made it to the island, but without a boat they had no hope of retrieving any of the gold plentifully piled around the island. But as they were grieving the king mysteriously appeared on the island declaring "Do not grieve my humble subjects! For a mere 40$ I will give you a 'Season Pass' which grants access to my royal treasure fleet which will happily stow your riches for you. What do you say?" But the people knew better now. They stored whatever they could in their pockets and swam back to Ubisoft kingdom where they then bought passage to various other kingdoms, never to come back again. Until next year's Assassin's Creed that is.
Hopefully you enjoyed that very accurate representation of what For Honor is. It is a pile of gold on an island that we can see but can't actually obtain. Great graphics, great combat, great game-feel, everything was a ton of fun in the free beta, and it easily secured my purchase. After 3 or so weeks, I lost interest and stopped playing entirely.
So what went wrong?
Ubisoft. That's what went wrong.
Reasons you should not purchase this game:
- No dedicated servers, its on a Peer-to-Peer connection system. Constant connection errors and being booted back to the main menu, some of the worst matchmaking i've seen in a long time.
- Awful game balance, gear in general was an awful idea and they should've just left it at cosmetics. Instead, you'll often be pitted against rep 28 players while your not even Rep 1, all of which have maxed out lvl 108 gear which gives them insane advantages over you unless you're playing specific game modes.
- Gear, and cosmetics are all insanely expensive, unless your willing to do hundreds of hours of grinding (which most sane people aren't willing to put up with). Microtransactions abound in a game thats already 60 freaking dollars. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
- Story mode is linear and cheesy, though I personally enjoyed it, most people will find it lacking.
- Glitches. Again, i've been more lucky on this than most people, but this game can be a seriously buggy mess at times, even for me. Bugs range anywhere from annoying to completely game breaking, which is unaccetable in a AAA 60 dollar game.
I'd give this game a 6 out of 10, but that's only because of the immense enjoyment I had playing this game for the first few weeks. After awhile, my interest faded, and so did its playerbase. I wouldn't even recommend getting this on sale at the moment, considering the only people left playing are all probably overleveled try hards and people with too much time on their hands. If you're deadset on getting this, however, wait for it to go on sale, 15 dollars minimum, i'm not kidding, I really don't think the game is worth your time in its current state. Screw you Ubisoft.

This is certainly quite a unique experience for me in terms of storytelling.
The stories are linked together being played in sequence, each introducing some difference in terms of how you interact with the story. The story does tell of a lesson that would have been best learnt without experiencing in the real world.
Some of the aspects of the game that I feel could use some work are:
1. The text based reponse prominent in the first story is somewhat hard to get around. There is no indication on how we could interact and move within the story and it mostly came down to trial and error to get the neccessary responses.
2. The puzzles that are introduced are managable but does lack some explaination and clarifications. Some puzzle involves sounds and images that are hard to hear or look at and did prove some challenge for me in understanding and decifering.
3. I did feel that the pace of the game was somewhat broken whenever we were given the apportunity to move. In my opinion it would have been better if there was no movement required from me as a player.
The game does feel more like experiments looking into different combinations that would provide a good storytelling experience, rather than a full game. All in all the experience from this game was interesting but considering how short the game is I would only recommend buying on a discount.

So about 4 months ago, during the whole ban controversy, I posted my review and said to wait a while before buying it. So how is the game now?
Well, it's...more of the same. More maps, (one) more counselor, more bugs (though they currently aren't super game breaking and/or unavoidable). It certainly has gotten better though. They really needed to go with a different business model for purchasing the game--$40 is a lot to fork over for a multiplayer-only PC game, and I can see why so many are turned away by that price tag. Dead by Daylight at release did this perfectly, with a $20 game and more characters down the line so you only pay what you want. If F13 had followed a similar business model I think the playerbase would be much larger than it currently is (1000-2000 players daily). I have certainly gotten my $40's worth out of the game, but that's quite an initial investment that you may or may not enjoy.
Final verdict, again? It is fun, especially with a lot of friends. But wait for a sale--hopefully at the Steam Autumn Sale in about 2 weeks from now (10/18/17).
On top of the controversy about the devs' permabans (no temp-ban system?! Seriously?!) and the fact that they're a little too trigger-happy with them when personal relations come into play, this game is simply too buggy and unpolished to be worth $40. If it ever goes on sale for $20, it's totally worth it, but I doubt they will do so for a long time unless the game loses a huge chunk of its playerbase.
Final verdict? Give it a few months and see where it is.

If you play one player you constantly get stuck in sections where the AI keeps dying and forcing you to restart and if you are playing two player one player gets gyped because for the first level the fox has all the "puzzle solving" abilities and from then on out the human does everything and the fox is kind of there.
The platforming is WAY to slow, but the game insists on having chase sequences that seem to be based entirely on trial and error. Plus every level has many leaps of faith, or seaming leaps of faith that are actualy easily missable event triggers, or things that are supposed to be leaps of faith but the parter AI was slightly too far back to trigger the next platform. You are supposed to brace for harsh winds or get pushed back, but there doesn't seem to be a warning for when those happen and the whole duck animation is annoyingly long. I've died many times to random gaps where they wanted me to duck first before I could cross but I didn't find out till I was half way across.
Really, this would be a nice short film, but as a game it's just not working out. You like overly artsy indie games that don't have a lot of gameplay (and I know some people that do) than this game is really atmospheric and pretty (when the models aren't overlapping like crazy), but if you are looking for a fun gameplay experiance, I'd go looking somewhere else.

Never Alone is pretty enjoyable puzzle-platformer with gorgeous graphics, co-op and very interesting folk-tale setting. You play as Nuna, a girl with trusty animal companion, who embarks on a journey to find the source of blizzard that endangers her village. You will traverse various landscapes, endure some tense chase sequences and solve various environmental puzzles' which almost always require cooperation between both playable characters. Sadly I found that to be the weakest part of the game. Poor controls, unintuitive puzzles and various glitches really discouraged me at first. What kept me going however was the story and unique art style especially wonderfully drawn nature spirits. Along the way you unlock various "lore" movie segments about the culture of Inupiaq people. I found them very interesting and actually wanted to know more about customs and lifestyle or people living in subarctic climate.
Average game, but great educational experience. Pick it up when it is discounted.

Graphics:
The graphic style fits. It's a simple handdrawn style, all done in black and white.

text:
I was a member of the [made up statistic] of people who have a guitar just lying around, abandoned, perhaps adorning the wall or huddled in a dark corner, gently weeping. We people love listening to music, and we love it so much that we want to make music ourselves. However, many of us perhaps couldn't find the time, or couldn't afford lessons, so our picks were lost under the furniture somewhere, our amps relegated to the top shelf, and our guitars left to deteriorate in the great river of time. Metal, right?
Tis a sad fate, that of the wannabe musician. The pain never left me over the years, and every once in a while I tried to follow a Youtube video or a book to get into the groove. I wanted to play Blues. I wanted to play Funk. I wanted to Rock like Page and Hendrix, and to Roll like Clapton and Gilmour.
As it turned out, Rocksmith 2014 was pretty much what I was looking for.
It's pretty comprehensive- it has a host of techniques that you learn by watching a video and then playing along on a practice track. The practice tracks introduce the basic concept, and get harder as you get better, until you "master" the technique. You can then move on to the next technique, and eventually you'll get to more advanced versions of the first ones. It also allows you to go back and lower the difficulty and speed, making it just as versatile as a sheet of note paper in front of you.
My favorite section is the songs. The base game comes with a bunch of really good stuff, including some Boston, Stones, Rush, Petty, etc. and a lot of newer songs I don't know anything about. The songs work the same as the practice tracks, they get harder as you do better and you can repeat sections for "mastery." The only thing about this section is that I'm not sure how useful this is in real life applications, as reading sheet music is different than the Guitar Hero style here. However, the complete songs are there and on the highest difficulty level, you really are playing the real complete song.
Lastly there is an entire arcade section that I haven't gotten much into yet. What I have done is pretty great: there are essentially basic arcade games that are reminiscent of those old typing tutor video games. Instead of hitting a certain key, you play a certain chord, or strum a certain way, etc. My favorite so far is a space shooter similar to the classic TIE Fighter, in which you play chords to shoot asteroids/enemies. It helps you rapidly learn the names of chords because you get more points for play faster, and it shows you the name before it shows you the notes.
Anyway, so far this game has proved to be immensely useful, I can already play Blitzkrieg Bop at almost the highest difficulty level, and my poor guitar is finally getting the attention it deserves. I'm getting a bass guitar for Christmas, so I will be trying out that whole half of the game soon. Highly reccommended for those without much time/money/both who want to learn guitar techniques.

Anna is a first-person adventure/horror game. What I liked most is the suspenseful atmosphere and the story. Game's setting changes drastically over a few stages: first you find yourself outside a wooden sawmill, observing as the sun glistens from a calmly running stream. You feel intrigued to get inside the house and learn of it's secrets. Once you're inside - it gets pretty spooky. You solve puzzles and trigger scripted and random events to progress in the story. The puzzles are satisfying but usualy don't make much sense and are not really intuitive. I had to look up a few playthroughs to solve some puzzles - couldn't come up with solutions myself. Once you reach a certain point in the story, the setting becomes really grim. With an unholy presence in the sawmill and ambient sounds that chill down your spine - the experience is quite satisfying even for a horror junkie. The game has multiple endings which adds some replay value. All in all, Anna is a decent game with some flaws regarding puzzles, but if you're up for the challenge and have plenty of spare time to come up somewhat ridiculous solutions to solve puzzles - get this game. 7/10

Word to the wise. If you put time into this, you will probably put more money into this than a season pass game. This game does not forgive mistakes, and it's sole goal is the long haul. It has a community of those who care far too much for the game, as demonstrated by the sudden increase of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. But enough of that, here are the facts.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
--It's going to take about a year to get up to end gamer level at the most basic level.
--Most tech is based on weekly to bi weekly events, you won't be touching those for a while.
--You need to make allies, or learn how to play quickly if you want to catch up within a reasonable period of time.
--Building fleets and bases are an art unto itself. It takes time, the further you progress this turns from days to weeks.
--All progress moves forward unless the player itself deletes it.
--There are protections for new players, but also disadvanages.
--If you play this game, after a certain point, your weekends may be forfit until you invest in higher end equipment.
--You will have a significant learning curve and disadvantage until you recieve event tech.
--The game core dynamics have recently changed, you will have an edge if you can find a way to adapt.
--The community can be toxic as all hell, but they love the game.
--Like fight club there are 2 rules. The first is that there are no rules, and second is that you do not ask about the rules.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
In short it's a fun game I've sunk plenty of time into, but it is going to be difficult for a newcomer to put their time into. It's not to say that there is a significant learning curve, but it is stacked against you in comparision to much easier MMOs.
Regardless, best of luck in the void rebels.

The review blurbs don't lie: This game absolutely feels like it came right out of the late 80's NES but with fine tuned controls. Everything about it screams classic from the NES style color palette that neatly separates foreground from background and makes sure enemies stand out clearly  to the hard as balls platforming and combat, to the sparse checkpoints and lives and unforgiving boss battles that can crush you in an instant if you don't learn their patterns.
Gameplay feels like a mix of Strider and Shatterhand with swords and grenades as your primary weapons. A power-up item lets you cast a crescent shaped beam half the length of the screen with your primary attack but fails after you've been hit twice, requiring you to not only master the new attack range to keep enemies at bay but also hone your platforming and dodging skills to maintain your elevated attack power for harder enemies later in the stage.
The Terminator meets Vexille meets any kind of robo apocalypse storyline is pure '80's cheese and it's glorious, especially when a dude called Rico calls you on what looks like an '80's portable TV while you're riding a bright green rocket powered jetski. There's even a villain that feels like a pure throwback to the infamous Cats from Zero Wing.
Despite all the homage to action games of the late '80's, Oniken manages to be its own beast. It doesn't feel especially unique but it doesn't have to as it's a masterfully crafted experience that's equal parts nostalgia trip and exciting. Even with the harsh difficulty I find myself wanting to see what the next screen will be, what the next villain will be, what's the next enemy the game will throw at me and what will it do.
The audio feels ripped right from the era too, a masterfully crafted score of synthetic sounding music that perfectly fits the tone and transports you back to a childhood full of bleeps and bloops and incredible ear-pleasure that you're sure your audio chip is having an ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to produce.
Controls are tight, responsive and the ability to use the dpad or analogue stick makes everything a bit easier (or more authentic depending on how you look at it). Restricting controls to two buttons (attack and jump, with grenade being up+attack) feels like an unnecessary nod to the NES but it's not restricting or annoying. Neither is the game in general - when you die it's almost always your own fault, you own mistake or lack of attention that causes you to fail. That said, enemies are fast and unpredictable (at least the first time you meet them) and you'll get caught off guard by a rushing machine or chucked grenade more than once.
So do I recommend the game? Absolutely. No other game even comes close to the level of authenticity that Oniken achieves and it's obviously a labour of love from the developers who are very talented. The game isn't perfect though, for all the praise I have to give it the flashing backgrounds in some cutscenes are an epileptics worst nightmare that can't be disabled (except by skipping the whole cutscene).

I am torn with this game. I suppose I just couldn't get into it, but I will give this game credit where it is due : it is very creative and this ''Extented Edition'' is a vast upgrade over the original. It is also gorgeous and is a real work of art, so I REALLY recommend this game for anyone (like me) that believes games can be art. It is a very mature game, not for the faint of heart, and not for the easily bored.
It was also VERY freaky, and it just got freakier and freakier, to the point that I started to feel just as insane as the character I was playing. Yeah, you're not supposed to look directly at the freaky♥♥♥♥♥♥that pops up to scare you. You have a kind of insanity meter, and its game over if it runs out. You then get the bad ending, which was my ending. Couldn't finish the game you see, but that wasn't really the reason.
The reason I don't REALLY want to recommend this game, but I will anyway due to the aforementioned points, is the puzzles. They make little to no sense. The whole game is heavily cryptic, to the point of insanity... and I guess its kinda the point, but I couldn't even get passed the first area without a walkthrough, and I don't think that's a point in its favor. Yes, you'll sometimes find a few clues in the form of books as to what to do next, but they are vague at best, or seem to have no connection with anything at worst. I just went in circles, revisiting room after room after room (once I finally unlocked them), not understanding what to do until I finally saw too many hallucinations and it was over. I guess there's two words to describe this : beautiful... but weird. VERY WEIRD.
So, I am tempted to continue this game, but it is as a big freaky impassable wall of nonsensical puzzles, which only the metaphorical industrial drill of a walkthrough can penetrate, which kinda destroys the immersion it tries to create. And if you do get through, blood will spill out and you'll go insane, then its game over. That pretty much sums up my experience.
THUMBS UP FOR ARTSYNESS THOUGH. I will not replay this though. Give it a try... if you dare...

I haven't played much of this game so far, but I'm definitely interested in it! The landscape is beautiful, CryEngine definitely does this world justice. I like that the world isn't overpopulated with Dinosaurs. The first time I actually encountered a Rex was terrifying, and it pushed me to hide immediately even though I had the proper weapons to fight it. It's not a perfect world, though. I do have some small issues so far, but knowing that this game is still in early access, I imagine these will be smoothed out.
- Make items stackable. As of the time I'm playing it right now, there aren't many things I can do with the resources I have, but I find stuff all over the ground that I want to keep. I don't have the capacity to carry every little thing I find, though. It would be nice if at least smaller items could be stacked up to a certain capacity, such as the energy cells and stimpaks.
- Add more recipes. This will be expanded on, I imagine.
- Vsync. As I was playing, I noticed in some areas that my game would start having screen tearing issues. If Vsync could be added, that would definitely help.
- Waypoints. We have a map in game, so having waypoints or markers that we can add to help find new areas, or relocate previous ones would be useful.
I'm sure I could say a lot more, but these are just some examples. Do I recommend the game though? Absolutely. Even if there isn't much to the game currently, it's the base of something that could be phenomenal. I just ask that the developers keep the survival ideas. Don't hold the players hand. Let them find things for themselves, let them be in a state of uncertainty. That's what I really liked about this game. I knew there were Dinosaurs, I knew there were droids. But stepping out of that pod into a quiet, open world was a very haunting experience.

I purchased Collision Course because I have been searching (for years) for a dinosaur survival game that would accurately simulate being trapped in the prehistoric. This is by far the closest any game has come to meeting that personal wish. The reason this game is different from the likes of Ark, Saurian, The Isle, and any other dino game currently on the market, is because it pits you, as a human, up against beasts that you stand no real chance of defeating. There is no playing as the dinosaur, there is no riding or taming the dinosaurs. This is where the game shines. These beasts remain vicious and terrifying predators and on the off chance you happen to encounter one, you'll find yourself actually
of them. As far as I'm aware, this is the only game to do this, and even though it is in its infancy it is already doing right what so many others have done wrong.
I really feel for these devs, from the splitting of their team to work on Saurian, to their failed Indiegogo campaign. I really hope they are able to add more content to the game and will continue to support their efforts. Overall, I feel that this is the closest a game has come to satisfying my desire for a true dinosaur survival experience. It is definitely worth the $10 in my opinion even though it is substantially lacking in content. In it's current state and for what it is I would give this game an,
mostly because it is daring to be different from what the majority of people seem to want in dinosaur games. And that is a good thing in my eyes.

The story is quite linear, not that it's a bad thing. You are often free to complete Task B before doing Task A, but the game plays out in sections (a.k.a. maps or levels) and these are completed in a set sequence. An open world RPG it is not. Most of the time it's clear what you need to do, or how to get to your next objective, even though there's no mini-map or quest markers.
