SOMA is a game that I thought looked neat but wasn't really sold on enough to actually spend money on it. When it got announced as the early unlock game in September's Humble Monthly Bundle, I figured I'd give it a go seeing as how I've heard some good things about it. Those things were absolutely correct, and I am not disappointed.
SOMA is a horror game that feels very much like the love child of Bioshock and Alien: Isolation. It has the isolated "everything's going to kill me" feeling while being completely alone like Alien: Isolation, and it has the oceanic seafloor setting of Bioshock (except less Randian dystopia and more it-hit-the-fan research center). You play as a Canadian guy named Simon who goes in for an experimental brain scan and wakes up in a strange place that - tragically - has neither maple syrup nor professional ice hockey anywhere to be found.
I won't go into much detail because the plot is REALLY fantastic, and I don't want to spoil it for anyone who hasn't played the game yet, but you spend the next nine hours or so going from section to section in this research complex trying to figure out what happened to you, how you got there, and what the heck is going on. For 99% of the game, you have no weapon (you get one weapon in the middle of the game, and it breaks as soon as you kill the enemy you have to loot something from), so you spend the game sneaking around (or, in my case, running around like a ♥♥♥♥♥ screaming bloody murder) trying to remain undetected by the enemies. With my propensity for stealth, I was sorely tempted to pull up the Benny Hill theme on my phone and just let it play on repeat while I played the game.
Without spoiling anything, the game's strongest point - even with its incredible atmosphere, well designed setting, and interesting plot - are the existential philosophical questions it poses to you throughout the story. What is it to be alive? What is it merely to exist? Was Descartes right when he said "I think, therefore I am," or is there more to "life" than that? Where is the boundary between man and machine? Does the soul exist, and if it does, what is a soul?  I cannot recommend this game highly enough. It's an extremely tense horror romp and an exceptionally cerebral experience.

Never Alone is a game that attempts to tell some folklore stories of the Inupiat, and Alaskan Native tribe. We follow the story through the eyes of a young Inupiat girl named Nuna and her Fox companion. For all intents and purposes, this is a pretty cool concept for a game. Rarely do games choose to adapt stories like this, often sticking to much more well known mythologies (Greek, Roman, etc). And immediately on startup we're treated to some rather unique artwork and decent visuals. The entire experience takes a very large trip south as soon as you start "playing" however.
This game is not fun. It doesn't feel good. It doesn't work right most of the time. It's rarely clear what you're ever supposed to be doing. I'm not sure at what point I actually hated playing it, but this game will soon wear on you with it's incredibly poor craftsmenship. You'll fall into pits you shouldn't have, you'll clip through walls, you'll get stuck in midair a lot, and you'll die when you're AI controlled companion can't navigate correctly. It's really hard to recommend this game on ANY level. If you really want to learn about the stories in this game, just go read them. It is not worth putting up with two hours of slow, irritating gameplay just to say you learned something new. Maybe the devs will learn from this and craft something a bit more playable next time.

This game is art over substance in a nutshell. It has a very interesting story and setting. But that's about it. I couldn't even get myself to finish it, but let me tell you why.
- Terrible AI that consistantly dies on it's own causing you to go back to the previous checkpoint.
- Awful sluggish movement and platforming. Which is a problem because this game is a platformer at heart. Its just not fun to play.
- Glitches and bugs. Had myself fall through the floor in a boss fight. Polar bear got stuck. AI walking off random edges to its death.
- As much as it is story focused, it completely lost my interest. This is probably more because of the gameplay making me frustrated and ruining the story.
- The narration sometimes cut's off if you go too far ahead. Meaning you miss some of the story.
- Repetative.
- This game is meant to be played Co-op. Controlling two characters on your own is a chore and you have to fight to get them to do what you want.
- Bland graphics and art style. Sure the designs of the spirits are interesting but everything else seems...meh.
- Not once did i stop and just look at the world they created. In a game like this, where it is more about the world and story/ Puzzle solving, there should be some 'wow' moments. Not once. There are much better games similar to this one which do have those (Braid, Limbo, Ori, Contrast, Trine etc).
- Forgettable soundtrack.
- It can't make up it's mind if water kills you or not. Freezing water kills you. 30 mins later you can swim in the freezing water (You can't even drown). Then only five minuites after a section where you can swim water kills you again. It makes no sense.
In conclusion, i feel that Never Alone is a great premise which fell short due to clunky controls, design and execution. It's just not fun to play. It's a game that isn't fun to play. Disappointing.

I wanted to love this game. I loved the old text based adventure games and was surprised to see a new one, especially in my favorite genre: horror. The interface was perfect for the atmosphere and I was settled in ready to enjoy being creeped out. Then I played it. Ugh. In classic text based adventures, they had to make it understand a wide variety of commands and give responses to them. If you found a lock and typed "Smash lock" it might tell you the lock wouldn't break or you bashed and couldn't dent it. Something to make you feel like you were really there, even if you didn't put in the choice they wanted. And in a psychological horror game, that immersion is vital. Instead, I recieved a steady stream of "I don't understand"s. And when the tension is highest is when the game gives the least leeway in your commands. The story might tell you an object is in another room, but ignores your attmpts to enter the room and instead expects you to know you can interact with the object. With how far technology has come, I thought we might be at a place where text based adventures would be more immesive, not less. Sadly, I must give the thumbs down to a game i wanted so badly to be my new favorite game to talk about....

This game has a lot of bad reviews for being a completely unplayable port. For some reason I didn't have any of these problems, that doesn't mean that they're not there, I was just fortunate enough to not have them. All I needed for this game to run properly was the 60fps patch, the wet clothes fix and forcing V-Sync on with the NVIDIA control panel. This game is a lot shorter than the first one and it is also a lot easier, thankfully turning the difficulty up fixed that problem and it seems that upping up the difficulty even increases the enemy amount, which is alwassw nice. This game also has some pacing issues and only really starts after you've escaped the second planet, after that it's plays pretty much like the first one. Lightsaber combat feels a lot better and the fact that you can cut off peoples limbs is a great addition, the graphics hold up surprising well even though it's 5 years old at this point and has some fantastic lighting effects, they made the combo system a lot simpler and also made the upgrade tree a lot simpler but the upgrades still affect your abilities pretty heavily. The force grip controls feel A LOT better know and I never had any problems with them, unlike in the first game where the inverted controls made some sections a lot harder than they should've been. The Euphoria engine once again does a fantastic job at simulating body physics and using forces powers feels just as good as in the first game. This game ends with a bang and actually has a proper conclusion this time, if you pick the light side that is. Sam Witwer again does a fantastic job as Starkiller and puts every else to shame, I would almost say that he distracts from the rest of the game because no one else comes even close to him and so you have all these okay voice actors and then this fantastic top tier voice actor who could be very well be a known actor. I would not pay full price for this as it is just too short to justify the price of 20 bucks but I paid 7 bucks of it and it was well worth my money. If you're willing to risk a refund because the port's just too bad, I recommend this to everyone who liked the first game.

I feel bad rating down an indie game, but I think it's appropriate in this case.
I suppose the best way to describe it is to simply treat it like a sandbox horror and not a puzzle game.
Firstly I would like to establish that this game DOES have some VERY good moments (creepy poltergeist moments when you run affoul some of the 'spooks' like the wooden mannequins). But overall the game isn't actually remotely scary at all.
That aside, the gameplay is awful. The interface is very clumsty and requires a ridiculous amount of precision. It is supposed to be a 'puzzle' game, but the puzzles are completely nonsensical. There are little to no clues for solving most of them, you just spam trial-and-error with every silly combination of materials until something happens, and then you must repeat it a number of times just to get one puzzle done (and believe me, a lot of the combinations are the most inane and arbitrary you could imagine- like sticking a pinecone into a mirror and lighting it on fire to open a nearby door- and that's the easiest one). Basically, you don't "Solve" anything, you're just supposed to "know the answer".
Furthermore, after playing through the game, you just get the 'bad' ending, because you didn't solve the 'other puzzle'. After watching the solution played on youtube (the guy spent over an hour randomly punching in combinations until they fit together), I decided it wasn't remotely worth it and uninstalled it.

TLDR AT THE BOTTOM.
Star wars the force unleashed 2 was released in the 4th quarter of 2010. Players play a clone of starkiller, the secret apprentice of darth vader. The clone sets out to find his love interest Juno eclipse and find himself. More so to save her.(captain save a hoe). Along the way you meet general rahm kota, who tried to convince you to leave this woman alone and aid in the war between the rebels and empire.
Gameplay-
Gameplay was fun at first. I saved up enough force points to upgrade my saber to level 3 in 30 mins of the game maybe even less than that, so I never really saw the progression of the combos and strength of the lightsaber combat.  Other moves like the force lightning and force push were amazing to see develop into strong and devastating abilities. However, mind trick and force repel weren't really needed in my play through. Force grip was cool but it's main purpose was to solve easy and somewhat insulting puzzles and take shields from maybe two different enemies. You get about 12-15 different types of enemies ranging from the classic storm troopers, to big clunky machine driod thingys.
The gameplay starts off fun but repetitive after 2 hours or so.  The user interface is pretty simple and easy to use.
Sound-
Classic starwars sound effects. My favourite thing was the Intense boom coming form the force push when leveled up.  The voice acting was amazing definitely better than some games today. Cough cough fallout 4 cough.
Graphics- of course if you have top of the line gear youll play this on high but the game looks amazing.  The weather effects are so good and animations are realistic.
Final say-
The game is super short and repetitive after a while so it really doesn't have much replay value.  However, there are challenges and different light saber crystal combinations that try to get you to mix things up but it falls short of being a game that I'd say buy. The Darth vader fight was a complete let down and the platforming was so irritating toward the end of the game I almost raged quit. The game is worth a sales purchase because there won't be a star wars game like this again for quite some time, but if you aren't a fan, rent for a weekend if you can and keep it pushing. I bought for 7 bucks on steam and thought it was worth the investment.
Overall,  5/10.
TLDR -
The game isn't worth a full price purchase, 5 hour story line, repetitive combat, great graphics for its time and great voice acting. 5/10.

It's a good game, but I honestly feel that it's extremely overhyped for what it offers--which isn't much.
I wouldn't really play the game for its story, as it seems pretty basic and I didn't find there to be much character depth.  It does try and it does give you some background to the characters and features a nice "cinematic" of the player's mom (which is actually really awesome because they made it so that her hair+skin color is the same as whatever you chose for yourself).  But that's more of a game feature than something specifically story related--the story itself, like I said is pretty stereotypical.  Some people might like it, but after playing so many games, it just feels repetitive--if this was an mmo, you wouldn't even bother reading it.
The combat has some nice elements (though I do remember being a bit frustrated with a few things--sorry, it's been over a year since I played this, so I can't remember the details very much) and the art is cute enough that I would like to continue playing it, but since the game is unfinished at the moment, my only options are to play Arcade Mode or to grind for cards.  I don't really want to grind for cards when their website's forum FAQ states there may be a potential wipe when the game is finished.  Maybe this has changed, but even so it feels odd to grind for something you may never use.
The problem isn't that the game is unfinished--we knew that going into EA, but what we didn't know until after we had completed all there is to do was that it's been in development since 2011 and is still only about 30% to completion.  The description on Steam with the link to the devblog in bold paints the picture that development is constant and EA will soon be over, but this doesn't seem to hold true.
Many of the areas in the game that you try to go to will give you a little notification that it's not yet implemented.  (Also on this, if you try to go to another map and you're cooping, you will be denied access unless all party members are at standing on top of you--just a heads up for those who might be bothered by this.)  As is, I think there are about 10 or so hours of content in storymode.

On top of this, if you notice the Discussion Page on Steam features a locked sticky entitled, "Haven't played in over a year..." where in the last post, the developer states, "New threads will be locked, and if the same user keeps creating new ones we're going to assume they're just rabble rousing and we'll use the dusty ol' ban hammer that's mostly sitting in the corner."
Which boils down to: You are not allowed to mention the slow development.  Ever.
I don't know... I just don't think that kind of censorship is exactly right.
Additionally, the website's FAQ states that they are not looking for additional people to help with the project and all positions are filled, so while they say things are slow because they only have three people to work on the game, they're not actively trying to remedy that, despite people offering to help.
I checked out the latest post on the devblog again, and one of the things that was written, "Definitely looking forward to another year of fun gamedev, and I hope you’ll all stay with us through our journey!" doesn't sound too hopeful that the game will be finished next year, either.
Again, though, I'm not trying to say the game itself is bad; it's just that... there's not much there.  I'm really sad to leave this with a negative review, but I just cannot comprehend how these issues seem to be so overwhelmingly glossed over.
We bought this game over a year ago and keep checking back only to feel really discouraged; fifteen dollars is a lot for someone to spend on something that doesn't seem to have a lot of hope at the moment and I just don't want anyone to be put in a situation where they end up disappointed.
If the game is ever completed, I would probably change my recommendation, but at the moment, I don't think I can recommend it, sorry.

Never Alone deserves a straight A for its stunning visuals; it's one of the prettiest games I've played. Gameplay-wise, it's a disaster. Average on a good day, barely playable at a not-so-good day. Sometimes, the physics will work just fine, while other times, you feel like walking on the moon. Then the game glitches out, or your AI partner makes an unexplicable jump to their death, or gets stuck somewhere, and you have to start over. If there wasn't a checkpoint around every corner, this would be ragequit inducing.
The puzzles are hardly worth talking about; most of the time you have to find a hidden thing, use the same simple mechanic over and over, or time your jumps correctly. Sometimes I would run into a new area and die a couple of times before realizing what the game wants me to do. Then I do just that and move on. Nothing to it; it's not a challenging game.
The story is okay, but nothing special either. It's a children's fairy tale told by an Alaskan Native. No character development, just a basic there-and-back-again set in the harsh snowy desert, with some magic thrown in.
So while I appreciate the beautiful visuals, as well as the spotlight on Alaska Native folklore, this game just isn't good enough. I finished it in about 3 hours and did not have a good time. The broken gameplay was frustrating, the puzzles not challenging, and the story just okay. The presentation is this game's saving grace, and it could probably be enjoyed together with a friend in local co-op, but if you plan on playing this one alone, skip it.

Stories Untold is exceptionally original in its take on a text-based horror game. Split up into 4 episodes, each episode is about 30-45 minutes long. However, the quality and direction of the different episodes changes drastically. The first episode is an absolute blast to play, and sets extremely high expectations for the rest of the game.
Unfortunately, the other episodes don't quite measure up. The 2nd episode is tolerable, but the 3rd episode is a slog fest that will have you shift-tabbing into a walkthrough just to get through it faster. The 4th episode is a revisit of the previous three, with a big reveal that ultimately seems underwhelming for what you were put through to get there. That being said, the finale is disturbing and keeps you on the edge of your seat for a fair portion of it.
Gameplay aside, this game does have a few technical and mechanical issues. The screen real estate is realistic but impractical. The terminals in the game only take up maybe a third of the screen, and there are often bright lights in the other sections. On smaller screen (such as laptops) this can be frustrating as the text is hard to read.
Ultimately, the game as a whole is only slightly above average. However, the novelty and the sheer intensity of the first and last episodes make me remember it fondly.

The start up audio is extremely loud despite any sound settings. The game gave me an annoying blur effect glitch throughout the entire experience which made it much more difficult and unpleasant than it had to be since enemies will use light and flashbangs to put blur effects on your screen already. Expect plenty of blurring in the second half of the game. The kill animations are repetitive which is fine except when some of them take much longer than the others to finish (Anaconda vs Head Whip) and become very annoying. The game also really wanted me to use my controller since it didn't respond too well with mouse and keyboard. I didn't know the Darkness being bad news was referring to the port quality. Ohoho.
Despite all of that, I finished the game. It's extremely gory, has combat I haven't experienced before (big reason I finished), has a short to medium length, and ends on a huge cliffhanger that left me wanting more, but I don't think there will be a third one (sadness).
The combat has you wielding three different guns that you harvest off the dead or find and utilizing the Darkness as you see fit. The general weapon categories are pistols, smgs, rifles, and shotguns. I was a big fan of dual-wielding Desert Eagles. The Darkness on the other hand can pick up and throw various objects and people. You can also grab shields with it, throw your Darkling buddy, perform executions for health, ammo, reduced powers cooldown, summon swarms, enhance your bullets, and much more depending on what you decide to purchase on the four skill trees. You also have your dependable tentacle melee attacks that will slice people in half horizontally and vertically. Making your tentacles, guns, and powers all work together kept me interested in the game along with the revenge style story.
Unfortunately, the game has many problems. My problems weren't restricted to my experience either going off of what I read in the hub and in reviews. That's enough to not recommend this title, although, if you're curious, maybe pick it up on sale or if it ever pops up in a bundle again. From the bang for buck perspective, $30 is a very tall order for this title.

Note: this is written by a fanboi of the originals JA series. To the uninitiated it's a fair game that resembles the original series. Not sure whether it's worth the price tag, but it's a fun game, though clearly needs some polish. I give it thumbs up because it's a nice game to play, even if it's a long stretch from the original series.
For the fanboi-ish review: meh. This review won't be very positive. So this is supposed to be a fanbased remake of the original. Clearly it resembles the original in some ways. But it's actually the little and subtle things that make this game far from "like" the original. On top of that it feels unfinished, content seems missing, hints seem missing, achievements somewhat broken, but mainly it feels as if the story line was rushed in.
Note that in all this, I played on the default level, which feels very much like "easy", and I played in a save-game mode. For my playthrough that came down to a sector reload whenever I lost a soldier. Other damage is pretty irrelevant, at least in this game mode. Played on windows on a high end machine.
Some details.
The UI feels clunky. The game itself runs very smooth. This is a high end pc so I expect nothing less. However, the menu items, the quest list, the interaction all feels very laggy. Dragging items often need to be done twice. Feedback on actions, like reloading a merc from the map sometimes gives you immediate feedback, sometimes requires you to swap a gun around or something. Pressing forward or fast forward will start with an initial lag, really annoying. So generally, all the interface and interaction feels pretty bad, pretty unpolished.
Then there's interaction things that are weird, or maybe just different from the original series. It's not possible to select your entire squad with keys, only by mouse. The interface lag sometimes causes you to move your merc when you intended to attack an enemy, causing you to run straight toward your enemy with your sniper rifle. I'm sure it still hurts, but... Also, the old game had good inventory maintenance things, specifically view a sector inventory. Instead all loot (and dead bodies) disappear after you exit a sector. But it's also not possible to sort items in your inventory, only filter them by very high level categories. And whenever you move anything around from the fifth page of inventory, it refreshes the inventory and bumps you back to the first page. Combined with double dragging and general lag, makes that a bad experience. There seems to be a lot of low hanging fruit here and I keep wondering why it hasn't been picked up.
Game mechanics. One of the first things that annoyed me is how unfriendly the friendly fire system is. Because seriously, if you are standing behind some guy, certainly you won't shoot him while aiming for somebody way further away? Even worse, if you're aiming for some guy and there are one or two friendly mercs in between the target and you in a straight line, you're nearly guaranteed to hit them both. And if you were aiming for the head/legs, you'll hit your mercs there too, regardless of your stance. Ok your stance matters in that a standing merc will not hit a lower stanced merc. But if you're all proned, this still works. However, this works for the enemy as well. My best laugh was an enemy that was nearly dead, fired its last bullet, killed one of his friends trying to hit me, then kicked the bucket due to bleeding. Heh.
Bleeding is bugged. It makes sense to bleed every turn, but if you have an interupt, you'll also get a bleed tick. Get 4 interupts? Then also 4 bleed ticks.
I played most of the game with just four mercs with 90+ aim. Other characters were just mules and militia trainers. Aim and dex seem the only interesting properties for the four mercs. The rest is kinda irrelevant. More than four mercs just becomes a hassle in fights, managing them all. Especially with the aforementioned friendly fire, it's a pita. Four mercs can group together or ambush enemies.
The AI is terrible. Oh and bugged. It's terrible because as soon as you shoot a single bullet they'll come swarming for you. Nearly all enemies do this and near the end I just dropped down in a line of four, shot a single bullet at an enemy, and picked up anything that came towards me. Especially that elephant gun with head shots is godlike. The enemies should try to circle around a bit, flank you from different sides, remain stationary in their hideouts, stay hidden until they had a fair chance of hitting me, something like that you know? The AI is also bugged in that it sometimes doesn't seem to compute AP properly. So you'll get a system message that you can't do this action because there aren't enough hitpoints left (often right after an enemy changed stance). It's funny because at least it shows that the engine isn't cheating; same rules apply :) But really, the user shouldn't see these messages at all.
Being attacked in a sector is another thing. It's very unfair. You sometimes get like 10 seconds to round up your men and dig in before an enemy spots you. Without the ability to select all mercs in one key stroke, that gets a bit frantic. Especially since the game will reposition your men somewhere in the centre, randomly, so you can't really "prepare" for the "ambush" either. In that sense it's really an ambush, but in my opininon it's not the fair kind of ambush.
The militia is... different from the original series. So on the one hand you no longer see your friendly militia walk around. In fact, you won't see them at all. You won't fight with them (they get their own, text only, phase) and you can only train them in a linear time. This is weird because no matter how many mercs, or their experience in antyhing, you'll get your militia in a linear time. And once a sector has a certain number of militia, it's pretty much safe from hostiles. You can only lose militia by being attacked, and once you have the max (15?) you won't lose any militia during an attack. They'll become elite and that's it. The biggest danger is taking over a city on the front line and having to build up a buffer of militia before the enemy attacks again. It also means that having 5 militia means nothing as they'll not even put up a fight against 9 enemies. They'll die and you'll face 9 fully healthy enemies after they do.
So health. You don't actually see enemy health. Kind of annoying at times, but kind of realistic in a way so not a problem per se. You do get to see them bleed, but that's kind of irrelevant. You get a tip of how strong the enemy is, but very very poor tip (soldier, militia, elite). Your own health is irrelevant as long as you're not dead. The enemy AI does seem to pick on one target at a time. That can be annoying, but it's a good tactic and they should do this as it's the most efficient way to eliminate a squad fast. Once you conquer a sector you can usually take your time to heal up though. You don't need to patch up mercs before "resting". You can assign a doctor to speed things up, but your merc won't bleed to death if you don't apply a bandage, like it would in the originals. Eventually, your merc heals up and you can continue with the next. I felt little pressure, especially after settling in the beginning.
Another thing you can do is repair your stuff. However, you won't find (m)any repair kits until much later in the game. This is annoying since your stuff is going to wear down and you'll have _no_ way of repairing it until you acquire a new repair kit. There's no way to guide the repair merc on which items to repair first. Worn down guns never choke, they'll only perform worse or stop working entirely. So either your gun is gonna fire or it won't, there's no risk at all. Broken guns won't get fixed.
There's more. Morale is useless, no arbitrary shooting, no time lapse in free mode, no teachers. But Steam limits these reviews, so:

I believe I'm a less common player on Steam, I buy games for several different reasons, some I buy for myself and also for other people, some games I prefer to watch and comment on instead of play. I collect games for their beauty, for their art design, for their challenge or if they convince me they have a good story. This "game" is, above all, a philosophical reading, you basically need to follow the only way of doing the things.
Inspired by the Albert Camus' essay in which he introduces his philosophy of the absurd: that of the man in search of meaning, unity and clarity in the face of an unintelligible world devoid of God and eternity. Does the realization of the absurd demand suicide? Camus replies: "No. It demands revolt." He then describes various approaches to the absurd in life. The last chapter compares the absurdity of man's life with the situation of Sisyphus, a personage of Greek mythology, condemned to always repeat the same task of pushing a rock to the top of a mountain, and every time he was almost at the top, the stone rolled down the mountain again to the point of departure by an irresistible force, completely invalidating the hard effort expended. You can and, sometimes, you have to do your own way, and even your closer beloved ones will be against you, because people are doctrinated to live an absurd life with no purpose other than gather properties. I call it contemporary (and cheap) slavery, the utilitarian and materialist world we live to serve purposes and reach goals that are not the ours.
I recommend the game for people who, like me, are not always in search of a game that fits the most common patterns (or that have the main) purpose of entertaining, Sisyphus Reborn is a good opportunity to reflect and entertain yourself with the very consciousness.

Following on from the first game, The Force Unleashed II improves on its predecessor in some aspects, but also manages to go backwards in others.
The story is a direct continuation of the first game - once again, you play as Starkiller; but are you really Starkiller, or are you merely a clone? This is the great question of the campaign, once which keeps you guessing right to the very end. In terms of storyline and general gameplay, the sequel is a fair improvement on its predecessor: gone are the dodgy camera angles, wonky controls, poor optimisation, etc. Instead, we have a fairly polished package, with most of the major gripes from the original resolved - the combat in particular is far more fluid this time around.
That being said, there are still some glaring issues. The framerate is STILL capped to 30 (see the fix below), the campaign is far shorter than the previous entry in the series, and I encountered a couple of bugs during my playthrough, each of which resulted in me restarting the level just to get past it. It baffles me how these issues can remain unpatched after release; naturally, expecting a fix so long after the release date is futile.
To fix the 30FPS cap, I suggest using the below guide - yes, it is for the original game, but the archive contains files for this game as well. All credit for the guide goes to the OP:
I suggest using the 60FPS file, as playing with the unlimited option breaks certain aspects of the physics engine, and introduces other bugs into the gameplay.
Recommended to anyone who enjoyed the first game, and to Star Wars fans.

It's like Pikmin for the PC. It's great ! And it's a Dutch product, which instantly makes it about 5x better ! For those who don't know what the idea behind Pikmin (and therefore Overlord) is (shame on you !); you control a character who's being followed by 4 different kinds of creatures. In the case of Overlord you have blue ones (for water traveling), red ones (for fire traveling), green ones (for sneak attacks) and brown ones (for basic fighting really). You can send them all to the same location, or you can send only a specific group of minions to do something for you. You start with the brown ones by the way, and you'll have to unlock the rest during your playthrough. Anyway, you use them to kill enemies (the boss fights are excellent and very fun !), collect items and solve puzzles. The controls are frustrating when using the keyboard and mouse so I recommend using a controller, to those who have one. So, buy Overlord AND a controller. Trust me, you'll love it !

Anna - Extended Edition review:
Anna is a spooky as hell game, it's not much more than a point-and-click adventure game, yet it is so much more than a point-and-click adventure game. You play an 'amnesiac' who is drawn to an old abandoned sawmill, where some really disturbing events happened and you need to discover who you are and why this 'Anna' calls to you. The main gameplay mechanism is - pick up items and combine/use items on things in the environment to progress the story. I found that some of the puzzles were kind of absurd, like use a stick to smash through a concrete slab, but for the most part they are fairly consistent to the world. You will run into puzzles that you might think are completely absurd, mostly the ones dealing with occult rituals, but once you know the story and can decipher the metaphors everything begins to connect. This is what I found most entrancing about this game and it kept me thinking about the story even throughout the day.
Now, I have not yet unlocked the 'True Ending' yet, so I still don't even know everything about the story. But I have received the 'Good Ending' and I am not going to spoil anything, but once you understand the ending, it really is a, "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, kind of moment. Despite still wanting to get the 'True Ending', I am hesitant, since this game gives me serious anxiety. It is not jump out of your seat scary, or will have you screaming in fear. But the whole mood of the game has this lingering malice that is always present, like a evil entity is constantly watching you. There are also hallucinations that sometimes occur which can have some disturbing imagery, or the god-awful sounds, specifically that women dying in the bedroom (you know what I'm talking about if you've played this game) that can really drive you mad.
I laud the Italian dev team for the unique story, and the fact that the more you play - the more you discover; there are details in every corner and each one adds something to the story. The aesthetics are also well crafted and blend with the environment. It really feels like an old abandoned European log cabin in the woods (not the movie). And as a matter of fact Anna has a tone similar to a Grimm fairy tale.
This is not going to be a game for everyone specifically the less patient or possibly the Amnesia fans. I can easily see some players getting bored with the game, to scared to play, or annoyed by having to look up a guide to solve some puzzles (I had to use a guide several times). But I still do highly recommend it, if you are looking for something new and spooky with a rewarding story, then Anna is for you.

Worth what it costs; it costs 2.19 CAD. The most important tip I can give about this game: save liberally. Room 42 does an excellent job at pacing but this comes at the cost that dying makes the player totally replay what they've seen since their last save. (I'd wish for a feature like many VNs have: let me skip or fast forward text and NPC conversations/actions I've already read.)
I did two play throughs then two partial playings to see if I could unlock a third route. My reading of certain events would lead me to believe there is a third route but after two-thirds into the second route, I started getting very tired of a common trope in this game. I don't trust there is anything more to this game than what I've seen.
A pet-peeve of mine is when a character keeps some secret. Even if it is irrational to keep it. (Even if a lie would make more sense than be forthright about keeping a secret.)  Paraphrase of a section of the game: "We gotta leave here right away!" "Why?" "Not telling you" A short while later: "I saw one of those monsters we're avoiding."
There is a lot of secret hiding and not a lot of revelation in Room 42. I find it contrived in media. I  do like thriller, mystery, and detective stories. What I like from them is that eventually there is a satisfactory reveal or a moment of catharsis that made the mystery worthwhile. Room 42 gives no answers in the two routes I played.
I liked most of my time in this game. Moreso at the begining. I'd describe this game as a dime novel: cheap to purchase, worth its cost, and one of many similar cost/value/entertainment games. Just like with novels, books, movies, art, and the threatre, the game industry needs boutique little games like this.

This game is one of the
examples of retro RPGS.
This game features plenty of the classic RPG tropes.
Despite this,
actually feels more original than most Retro RPGs I've played.
To me, it's strengths lie in three specific categories.
Aside from customizing your own character which on it's own is a lot of fun, you can actually use upgrade points to learn special skills such as one-handed weapon attacks, spells and powerups. The best thing is the are absolutely NO restrictions on what you can learn.
Wanna wield a two-handed sword while unleashing fire and electricity at your enemies? Go right ahead! There's no stopping you.
Also, the combat in and of itself is extremely fun as well.
Dungeon bosses are all unique and require a lot of thinking most of the time and timing. Not that menotenous "hit it till it dies" stuff you get from other RPGs.
Now, the story (while simple), is actually easy to follow. You're the son of a collecter, a sort of Ranger who works to find rare and exotic artifacts for study and to better human society. Upon graduation, you're given your own "companion", Bag. Bag works as sort of the parody equivalent of Navi, except instead of giving you useful tips most of the time, you get tips when you lose, making it much more tolerable. He's also more mean-spirited and rude, which I find more entertaining, yet annoying at the same time.
It also pays homage to some of the classic games: Legend of Zelda, Dragon Quest, etc.
This is one of the most beautiful Retro RPGs I've ever seen. The design of the land is 10 times prettier you could make in any RPG maker and the character designs used for conversation are great as well. The dungeon designs are the cherry on top. You're forced to use your brain for a lot of the puzzles you come across and beating them just feels so rewarding.
Final verdict: This is a GREAT game for people who love the old fashion styled games. 9.5/10 Download the demo, and you won't be disappointed.

(Apologies for the rampant BioShock comparisons, I realized these games are rather different but for the sake of comparison and examples I think they work. also I love me some BioShock)
As a fan of BioShock and the environments those games spawned, as well as an appreciation for first person games with a high level of narrative depth, I had high hopes for this game. Overall I found the story interesting and well paced, but incredibly predictable and rather bland. With the exception of one late game twist I was not surprised by any of the various "setbacks" you encounter on your journey, as are common in this genre. Compounding this is probably my least favorite main character of any game I've ever played. He's not funny or endearing, he complains at all times, and he possesses a seemingly below-average level of intelligence when it comes to comprehending the reality of his situation.
Furthermore, one of the things that drew me to this game was hearing that it included interesting and thought provoking moral choices. In the initial stages of the game I found this to be true, though they really weren't choices so much as things you have to do to progress. But apart from a couple instances of this in the first few areas, I found no more apart from a very strong scene near the end.

Another minor complaint was the control scheme felt very clunky and unresponsive, like trying to move in a ball pit or a pit of syrup. I don't think that's so important for a game like this that doesn't emphasize combat, but I felt like I was fighting the game to move around the environments.
Despite the predictable story, lacking characters, and lack of meaningful moral choices, Soma does do some things very well.this game legitimately scared the hell out of me the whole time I was playing it. This game nails tension and the deep feeling of helplessness, emphasized by the total lack of any weapons in the game. This brings up another good point- the items in the world make sense based on the location and setting. Why does BioShock, being set in what is basically a glass box on the seafloor, feature so many guns? A habitat on the seafloor would also realistically need to be pressurized, and as a result guns would be a huge issue. Soma understands both of these things and uses it to build the world further. I was more scared trying to hide from an enemy in Soma than I have ever been dealing with enemies in any other game.
The setting and world is much more believeable and "realistic" than the highly stylized BioShock games, though obviously not as pretty for it. The world design is very well considered overall, and it leads to some really cool atmospheric moments.
Overall I can recommend this game, but I was disappointed by my high expectations. I really thought I'd love this game enough to say I liked it more than the BioShock games, but I just can't say it's overall more than average. It's worth playing, for sure, just don't expect it to change your life. I bought it during the summer sale but I think it's probably worth most of the $30 it normally asks.

I was 3D Worms fan as a kid. Is this game is a childhood ruined or exchanced? I'm on the fence.
This game is more or less an expanded version of old Worms 4: Mayhem. Most notable changes are graphical upgrades and Worms 3D singleplayer campain available to beat. Those are fine additions and the core gameplay is still okay, but there are noticable problems.
Overall art still is a cartoony but normal-looking 3D graphics clash with poor cel-shaded explosion effects - this combination just don't work. Old Worms 3D effects where more eye inviting. Music is completely horrible. Worms 3D (game) and Armagedonn had a distinctive styles: happy-party and grim-doomy respectively. This game is just bland with uninspiring music and no art direction.
Game is slower paced than a 2D worms, which is not a bad thing on it's own. However, overall experience isn't what fun, thanks to the sluggish weapon and utilities physics. Weapons behave very strangely. Some are extremely reliable (constant 50DMG Bazooka shots) or suprisingly unreliable (Banana Bomb). On top of that, AI is still stupid as a Sheep. Team 17 never programmed a fine artificial enemies.
Worms 4 singleplayer missions are uninspired. they are paired with pretty bland story around them. The included Worms 3D missions are more interesting. They are compact, focused and not bounded in half-baked story arcs.
Menus ergonomy and UI needs a complete rework. Hidden important options, difficult navigation, poor visuals.
This game is somethat a fun experience, but you need other people with the same preference to the 3D Worms games as you. With friends, you will have a blast, thanks to the better controls and hilarity of events. You don't have such people around you? Make a pass. You had enough of Worms in 3D (no matter, if in the good or bad way)? Make a pass. I'm still giving this game a Upvote, but it is a close one. I feel really generous today or maybe I feel nostalgic to those original Worms 3D missions?

Playing this game for about 10 hours straight and completing it all in one sitting has left me with some very strong opinions about this game. In terms of gameplay, it's basically Penumbra or Amnesia underwater, but where those games were exhilarating in terms of the monsters and chase sequences, the monsters and the confined enviroments get tedious pretty fast in Soma, especially in a few of the underwater portions of the game. Beyond the hiding from monsters bit, there's also a fair bit of puzzle solving and item collecting, which gets tedious pretty fast, as the game feels artificially padded with all the unfortunate events that seem to happen to your equipment, requiring repairs, usually taking place in a darkened version of the same level. However, where the game truly shines out from it's brethren is in the atmosphere and storytelling. Where Penumbra was Lovecraft underground, Amnesia was Poe and Lovecraft in a big boy castle, Soma is an HR Giger fueled nightmare, taking place underwater in various facilities, and eventually
The setting is fantastic, and the breathtaking underwater atmosphere really pushes the terrifiying depth and horror of the deep, deep sea. The level design is good, and your progression feels natural, except for when you're forced to backtrack, and a few of the levels get very mazelike, with nigh unstoppable enemies
The story is good, but feels muddled, as for a lot of your experience, you're trying to find a means of transport to get to a means of transport to get to some special means of transport to get to your goal, and of course as you progress through this, your means of transports seem to get mauled by everyone but God himself. The story and idea itself are fantastic, and left me thinking for a bit after, but I wasn't impacted by it in the way a lot of people seem to have been. The ending was great, however. Overall, it's a good experience and worth a buy, but don't expect a game with Amnesia spooks or Penumbra puzzles, but where those games lacked in a main story focus, SOMA more than makes up for it.

A charming story told through boring and unneccessarily slow gameplay. I found myself wanting it to end around halfway through it. I would have rather just listened to the remainder of the story and put it away.
The DLC adds a new mechanic (rock throwing; 2 if you count rowing but that doesn't add anything meaningful). The levels are much better designed with actual problems to solve as you progress, but I found the extremely slow move speed, overall lack of action, and no collectibles/reason to (or areas to) explore to be too slow for me. I lost interest before completing the DLC.
PROS:
-Good way of introducing people to an otherwise unknown topic
-A simple but acceptable story
-Graphics are clean and look good, but are VERY simple.
-The fox's motions are extremely well done.
NEUTRALS:
-Use of video clips (esp without the ability to seek) is interesting but questionable in execution.
CONS:
-SLOW. Why is everything in the game so SLOW??? Walking, pulling ghosts, swimming, flying....its all super slow.
-NUMEROUS game breaking glitches. I had to use the "reset from last checkpoint" option several times because things that should be breaking just weren't breaking (esp during the polar bear sequence).
-Very SHORT game. My 3.1 hour is a 100% clear of the main game and about 1/3 of the DLC. If I had finished the DLC I probably would have been just shy of 4 hours total playtime (main game +DLC).
-Very poor level design. Very little use of actual mechanics in the levels (except at the giant, near the end of the game). The vast majority of the game is just moving right with a trivial jump here and there.

TL;DR: The game is fun, it does everything that Dead by Daylight does but better and then some. However 40 dollars is a hefty price tag. Wait for a sale.
So Friday the 13th The game is exactly what it sounds like, a Game that pits 1 player as Jason Vorhees against 7 playing as camp consulars desperately trying to escape his clutches.
The only game i know to compare this to is Dead By Daylight, and in this, it surpasses it in almost every way possible.
Here is a brief synopsis:
-Playing Jason is fun, it is not a chore like the killers in dead by daylight
-There are no sacrificial hooks, you get a person in your clutches you get to brutally murder them
-There are 5 ways to escape/win as a consular
-The consulars can actually fight back, while running is the best option, it isnt the ONLY option
In terms of staying true to the movies, i have to say this game gets it down pat. There are 59 ways to kill people in this game and literally every single one of them was done in a movie at one point or another. The Animations are brutal and amazingly satisfying.
The best part of this game however by far is that is has VOIP (Voice) Chat. Not only can the consulars talk to one another, but Jason can talk to the consulars and vice versa. It turns a generic survival horror game into something else entirely. Its incredible to have a person playing Jason to be beating down the door screaming "HERES JOHNNY!". It allows for some of the most priceless moments ive ever had in a game.
As for the game's "Bugs" ive heard many people complaining about them, but personally i havent experienced anything but a Cosmetic glitch here and there (For example a female consular's hair glitching out and flying all over the place). I havent come across a single glitch so far that broke the game or made it unplayable.
Now unless you are already a diehard fan of the movies, or a diehard fan of Dead By Daylight, i wouldnt buy this game for 40 dollars, its fun but 40 dollars is a hefty price tag. I coughed up the full bill for it and while i dont regret it, i dont feel its worth 40 dollars.
Overall the game is highly enjoyable and has some of the best player made moments in any game ever, but id wait for a sale.

Stories Untold is a game that, at first, feels like a few un-related stories all wrapped in a 1980's visual styling. Tape decks, cathode ray screens and a healthy dose of VHS warping. The chapters each offer a different story: playing a text adventure game, helping an experiemental science scenario, an outpost in greenland and so on.
To put it at the most basic, you're playing a game with a series of slow time events. Much like a quick time event, except you need to seek out the information on how you progress. Unlike a puzzle, which presents you with many possibilities the scenarios presented here each progress linearly. That is you only have one way to progress forward. In many ways, that makes this a walking simulator where you don't walk.
The journey is the destination, as they say. The game is mostly comprised of a compelling story that draws you forward wrapped up in the atmosphere they build up. It's that narrative that keeps you locked to your screen, instead of being a game where you're honing your twitch abilities or puzzle solving skills.
That depends on you. If you're interested in a solid story, then yes. If the idea of a game that's more about being interactive art appeals to you, then it'll do well. If you're looking for a game where you can mute the story and still enjoy it? Skip Stories Untold.

A clunky, delayed, awful control scheme. No way to switch or rebind controls - the game claims there's an "easy control scheme" but selecting the option, going back and forth between gamepad and keyboard, saving and loading, none of these actually do anything. Tutorial signs often describe completely wrong ways to accomplish actions, such as saying to use DPad up when it's actually Right trigger, saying to use left bumper when it's actually left trigger  and faling to describe how to actually drone remote, which must be done in "melee range", with the diver facing the object, using a different button than the tutorial says to, and while pushing the joystick towards the object (and while getting the diver to face the same way, which is a hassle in tiself because the diver can only move up-down-left-right but can move and whose sprite can face independantly of each other, even of your aiming.) Neither keyboard controls nor gamepad controls alleviated these issues. The sub controls like a sub, which is, I suppose, realistic, but the game demands constant and neverending precision and movement to do anything besides move in open ocean. From playing front mounted and bottom mounted crane games to pick up objects (but you can only collect goods from the bottom, sometimes forcing you to awkwardly pick up from the front, carry out, drop, then re-pick up from the bottom to collect), to trying to chase tiny fish with drills, the amount of precision required from your tank like, constantly flipping 2d sprite of a sub is too much.
A robotic, difficult to understand voiceover with no subtitles allowable. They automatically switched off when I went to the options screen, and no matter how many times I switched them back on, saving, loading, restarting the game, nothing worked. Suddenly the voiceover worked for one tutorial sign, and then as soon as I entered the settings to save the game, it turned back off, with no way to turn it back on again. I have no idea how much content, quips, or quest mentions I missed.
Levelup screen steals money, reducing cash but not actually buying upgrades. All menus appear to be active simultaneously, layered over each other, meaning it's possible to buy random supplies while you're trying to use the menu you can actually see - the upgrade screen. The same happens when you're looking at sub selection and supplies, with the levelup screen. I lost 250 dollar slike this, which was pretty much all the money I' collected in the game so far from the tutorial area and my exploration of the first zone.
Fuel system is needlessly punishing - moving uses fuel quickly, having lights on (I will remind you: This is a game about exploring the Mariana Trench. In the ocean. And with a day night cycle where day rarely matters becaue you're in the bottom of the ocean.) drains fuel faster, and wasting limited, hard to acquire cash on fuel means you waste fuel going to and from supply ships on the surface and back to the giant trench where you're actually playing the game. Limited fuel cells can be found underwater, but can easily be wasted if you happen to pick it up too early and uselessly overfill your fuel gauge. But if you bypas them, that means remembering where they are, and being able to get back to it when you actually need it. Then the second backtracking trip to where you were... wasting even more fuel. Explosive barrels are everywhere and destroy everything near them with the slightest bump, including the fuel cells and very very limited ammunition they are often placed by. "dying" and respawning places you back at the start of the level but keeps all objects consumed, which means now you need to try to get back to where you were, but with even less fuel cells underwater than before.
It costs more money to restock on the weaponry than you get by actually killing wildlife, and restocking on limited quantity consumables again cuts into permanent sub upgrades. The game expects you to use the clunky, awkward sub controls to hunt down the likes of tiny seahorses, lionfish, and the like both 1: in a vast, gigantic ocean with no signs to follow, and 2: either by expending limited ammo harpoons, or by attempting to melee a tiny lionfish with a drill 3 times its bodily size, but wasting tons of fuel to do so. Your reward is 5 dollars. Don't even think about exiting the sub as a diver to do so: it takes 2 of your precious 10 harpoon gun ammo, and again, you only get 5 dollars. This doesnt count the time you spent chainingthe sub to  arock so it doesn't float away, waiting for the long exiting sub sequence, aiming to fight the creature, swimming back, and waiting for the long "entering the sub" sequence. All the while, fuel is ticking down. And for some reason, the "Chain harpoon", the only unlimited resource at your disposal, flies through enemies as though they weren't even there.
Database popups fly up and obscure the entire screen for seemingly no reason: I was lambasted by several when the creature in question wasn't even on the screen or in my remote area. They pause the game entirely and ruin the immersion and train of thought you had going. At one point it caused me to lose control of my sub, slam into an explosive barrel and immediately explode the fuel cell it was next to, when I had 25 feul left of 300, and died. Back to the surface. That was the end of my adventure in "Project Abyss". I'd had enough.
Realism isn't an excuse to make your game a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play - and the numerous bugs simply don't help. It's a shame, because the aesthetic and the idea of the game are great. It's just not very fun or enjoyable. I felt like I was fighting the game the entire time.

I don't know what the other reviewers are complaining about, this is a fabulous game. Do I wish it had a bit more content, absolutely. But what is there is at least as good as JA:2. Yes, JA:2 was a bigger game. But in an era where you can't get games like JA built anymore, because everybody's wasting their time on FPS, this is a diamond.  I'm happy I backed it on the Kickstarter, and happy with the end result.
I think that the gist of the complaints are that this isn't as fully featured as JA:2. For example, you can't walk backward, and you don't need to pick any locks because all the doors are already open. I agree, it would be nice to have those things, but they are nice to haves not must haves.
The meat of the old game is there. You pick Mercs, take control of and hold territory, and are always on the hunt for better equipment, and equipment attachments. There are side missions, vendors, and new Mercs you meet along the way.
There are definitely some things missing, but there's also new stuff that I think is pretty cool. First and foremost, this is a new game, built with modern computers in mind and it doesn't crash all the time like JA:2 used to. In some ways it has more strategy. For example, I love the way the game forces you to defend your territories while you're training militia, because you can't have a whole squad of trainers. It's also got a new map and a new mission as well as new Mercs and equipment. The UI is way cleaner and easier to use. The concept of a squad inventory, while less realistic is far more easy to use than having to go hunt for all the equipment drops you left all over the damn map. There's a whole perks system that implements all kinds of useful special abilities like "never accidentally shoots friendly mercs" (granted there were special abilities in JA2).
The bottom line is that it's not JA:2 and as a result the die hards are predictably unhappy. That said, this is the first of all the games that have come out bearing the name "Jagged Alliance" since JA:2 that is actually worthy of it's name. Give it a try, you'll like it.

Project Abyss is developed and published by Tall Story Studios. They’ve had previous experience with Guardians of Victoria, which despite being critically panned, still offered a decent steampunk setting. I’m glad to say that they’ve learned from their past mistakes and continued to release their next Steam game, Project Abyss. It’s very important for indie devs to understand that second chances apply even for them. Far too many developers at the start of their careers, seem to stumble and stop after only one commercial failure.

I really wish there were more submarine simulators on Steam. And not just combat-oriented like the Silent Hunter series, but relatively tranquil sims that focus more on exploration of the ocean floor and shipwrecks. Project Abyss is indeed such a game, even if fully 2D. The submarine game subgenre has a decently numerous following and I count myself as a fan too. Still, I admit that I might have been a bit wary at first once I booted the game and noticed the complex control scheme and hefty tutorial. Project Abyss does take some time getting used to, but it is by no means a time waster. Exploring the ocean depths has its own rewards, beside the loot crates that ultimately fund your expedition. Speaking of means of combustion, you have a fuel cell and monitor equipment which seemed a bit out of place considering that most exploration subs use an electrical motor (in fact all types of submarines use electrical engines when underwater). Perhaps it was just a weird interpretation of the word “fuel”. It’s a finite resource though and instead of a clock, your main enemy will be the fuel depletion which sadly can prematurely end you diving sessions if you’re not too careful and even conservative at times. I do appreciate the attempts at a realistic simulation of finite onboard assets such as harpoons, torpedoes and other equipment. It gives both a sense of urgency as well as resource management since you’ll have to prioritize a set objective or another. The mission structure is relatively open-ended, another aspect I found more than welcoming since linearity has been approached one too many times in video games.
The exploration element is complex, since between you and your path towards loot crates, are all sorts of obstacles from hostile/peaceful sea life (Abyss has nice trivia segments detailing most of them) and even rock/soil/metal that has to be blown away or drilled by case. Your submarine comes fully equipped with all the necessary gear and from time to time, you may have to depart the sub and explore or loot by yourself, in diving equipment. As a diver, you’re more exposed to dangers and shall have to rely on even more prudence and patience since the oxygen level depletes faster than the fuel from the submarine. Luckly you have a trusty drone that can pick up various containers and chests. The gameplay is quite diverse as you can see and if peaceful resolution seemed boring to you, there are some fairly challenging combat sections that can damage your hull quite fast. Even the repair task is left to you, as departing the sub and manually repairing it, is far less time consuming than returning to the host ship. After each successful mission, you are given the option to upgrade various gameplay aspects which will invariably make the game easier. I cannot stress enough how important it is to learn the controls and play it safe. I found myself restarting an expedition far too many times since I risked going further ahead just for “one more crate” or “let’s see where this cave leads to”. Keep an eye on your stats and you should be fine.

Can’t complain of the graphical details since color and sprite variety are right at home. As far as 2D graphics go, you can’t really ask for more. Sound variety though? Yes, Project Abyss is in dire need of more diversity in the audio department. At least the tutorial is partially voiced. Most of the cons I listed below, are related not to gameplay mechanics but to basic game design aspects which I found lacking. You can’t rebind any of the controls and the biggest flaw in my opinion, has to be the lack of Steam Overlay support. Just taking a look at how many screens I took in the past few months, it shouldn’t come as a surprise to anyone when I say that I like visually documenting my game progress through constant screenshots. Sadly, Project Abyss is among the few Steam games which doesn’t let me “fuel my madness”. Such a pity, since I really like this title.

+ Interesting story and setting
+ Complex diving and looting mechanics
+ Elements of economic and resource management
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards
- No Steam Overlay support
- Inflexible control scheme
- Repetitve sounds
Project Abyss is fully worth its asking price and offers both types of Steam auxiliaries, as I like to call them. Achievements and Trading Cards, of course. Add to that, the intriguing exploration and combat mechanics and you have a perfect example of an indie game that fills a subgenre void, left by the relatively few submarine titles in recent years.

- Beautiful visuals and atmosphere
- Charming stories (of the base game and its DLC)
- Interesting storytelling format
- Controls feel rather awkward (aiming with the "Bola" weapon seems more random than anything)
- Bugs/glitches tend to happen, sometimes at the worst possible moments
- Most of the puzzles are too simple
- Extremely short - took just 4 hours for me to beat the whole game and the DLC with 100% achievements (and that includes replaying certain chapters more than once to collect something I missed)
While this game certainly has its shining moments, I feel its flaws weigh them down more than anything. In the end, the $17.99 price tag is simply too much for a few hours of sometimes-frustrating and sometimes-nice entertainment.

What a disappointment!  This game is a poor update of a classic series with little to recommend it to veterans of the previous JAG, Silent Sentinel, Xcom, etc., games.  I disagree with those who say this game is like the original -- it's far from  being that.
The detailed control of your mercs is gone.  You can run, crouch, or lie down, but you cannot walk.  You do not control the attributes of a merc when he/she levels.  You can't hide/unhide.  Weight is no longer a factor, my merc is carrying a rifle, a machine gun, two pistols, ammo for the above, plus several more items.  What the mercs can't hold on their persons is kept in a squad pack (maybe they pull a little red wagon behind them with all this stuff in it).  Your gear is limited by the number of slots.
This is a ONE LEVEL game as far as I can tell, still being early in the game.  No hiding in holes, climbing on rocks, wading into deep water.  Lots of pretty trees, flowers, cows, pigs, etc., though.
You hire mercs from a pool of them that contains some of your lesser favorites from before, and none of your favorites (okay, none of mine).  At any given point, a third of them are "away" and unavailable.  Each merc charges by the day, week, or 2 week period and they are not cheap.  Yet I feel the game forces you to create a party very early in the game because the enemy forces quickly become large (6-8 troops) who are heavily aremed.
This is another example of a solid meaty game being updated by exchanging the meat for tofu.

The first thing I'd like to say about this game is that the amount of work that has gone in to it is so obvious and incedible. No aspect of the game has been left unpolished.
As someone who plays games to relax, this is genuinely one of the best indie games I've played in order to do that. The sound is beautiful, and the way pixel art has been used to create the graphics is really great.
Without posting spoilers, the way the story is told is the right kind of ambiguous, and leaves you with questions you feel motivated to answer.
On the subject of controls, I believe that the developer's original controls are far more immersive, however I've always struggled using/learning new controls for games (even in MOBAs I set my own controls to the defaults I'm used to) so I did set them to the easy/standard keyboard mode, though I'd recommend the original controls for players that don't have this issue.
However, I am impressed at how well the developer responded to feedback about this, and added control options when they were requested.
If you enjoy exploration and survival games I would definitely recommend Project Abyss. I can't wait to play more of it, and it's changed my opinion about pixel graphics. Previously I wasn't fond of them at all, but this game is really beautiful.

JA: Flashback is a game that was barely funded during its kickstarter, and it shows.  It feels like it's still in beta, with several features that should be implemented but aren't, like doors that actually open and close, only ground-level height, and an 'energy' bar which has no real purpose.  There are also numerous misspellings which should have been caught months before release.  Overall it's a barebones, unpolished experience that you are being charged a premium price for.  The devs claim to be updating with additional features, but I'd be surprised if they can turn what was released into anything resembling the previous games.
For prior JA fans, this is not the JA reboot you're looking for.  Getting into the features that were cut would take too much time, suffice it to say the vast majority of them are gone.   For new players, it's a functional but lackluster turn-based isometric strategy shooter.  It does what it's supposed to, nothing more, but there are other games out there in the same genre and style that do everything better, and for a lower price.  Give XCOM: Enemy Unknown a try instead.
p.s. My play time should be about 4 hours higher than what's displayed, it's been reset a couple of times.  I don't know if that's another game issue or just Steam being weird.

Very dissapointing if you are just looking for a deep stratigy game experience, especially if you are a fan of Jagged Alliance. If you're a modder on The Bear Pit, then it's exactly what you expected.
As a fan of previous Jagged Alliance games, I've put more time into this title then I expected to. I did not do this becaues I felt like I was having a good time. I kept playing because I was convinced that if I gave it more of a chance it would grow on me. Almost exactly like how I felt with the older titles, as well the failed remakes like Brigade E5, and Back in Action.
Although unlike the other titles, this game just did not grow on me.
I had picked up the Early Access and gave the first island a shot. It felt simple at the time, melee wasen't even in it at this point, so I knew I was pretty early and so forgiving of the barebone features. Knowing that the game had much further to go, what was already there felt great! I was thrilled that this company was getting the basics of Jagged Alliance down, and I couldn't wait follow the updates as they came.
Except they didn't really come. I remember 1 or 2 monthly updates to the steam early access page, and then one day instead of an update there was an announcement that the game would be released. I was shocked.
Upon release, it still lacked soul. It lacked the many familiar features one can find in most other failed Jagged Alliance remakes. The developers and development community insist that many of these features are either not needed, too expencive, or coming in future patches.
A month later however, the only new feature is ammo types. In the meantime the company has released another project, a re-imagining of their Space Hulk game.
There is a quote from a post their Dev team made on the Forums that reads:
"In hindsight there were so many things we could and should have done differently, be more prepared, produce a playable version and not spend so much time on creating a website. Looking back we really should have spent more time producing solid high level designs to communicate our vision to you."
As a modding platform, it's supposed to be flexible enough so that one day someone at The BearPit might pump out a JA:F 1.13. But that kind of doesn't help the average Jagged Alliance fan who intended to back a videogame and didn't realize they were actually investing in moding utilities.

I've been using Clickteam products since Klik & Play when it first came out. I've always loved their style of drag and drop visual editor and coding, but past products never seemed to be able to handle everything I wanted to do. So they've always been sort of a fun thing to play around in, never anything that can be taken seriously unless it's kept simple enough.
However, after purchasing Clickteam Fusion 2.5 and using it (over 1000 hours), I can honestly say this program is easy to use and learn, but powerful enough to satisfy almost any 2D game creation need. I've been working on a project for the past 6 months in it, and in every instance where I thought I'd pushed the program to its limit again, it handles it like a champ and keeps asking for more.
I won't lie, you're not going to be able to do everything with Clickteam Fusion 2.5. You can't export games to be played on consoles, unfortunately, but for making awesome 2D PC and mobile games, I really can't recommend it any higher. If you've ever wanted to create your own games, but don't know much about coding or programming, Clickteam Fusion is an amazing program that can guide you in and allow you unleash your gaming creativity.

This game is very tricky to recommend, but I feel it's worth a shot for anyone who misses the OLD discovery games. I've been getting flashbacks to the unbridled madness of titles like Lighthouse, and am not sure how I feel about that.
Thus far it took me most of half an hour just to get inside, because I was admiring the scenery and completely failing to find the item I needed to advance the entry puzzle...after that I have fled just to see what happens, then later was kicked out of the house. (Two endings down!)
Puzzle difficulty and exploration difficulty is all over the place, the books help a bit but this is definitely an indie game and the built-in help is there for a reason. I really wish the inserted voices were better, they are bordeline tolerable but a major chance of adding atmosphere was lost there. There is some bad english in places, but it doesn't smell like a fanfic or amateur translation...the most critical story elements got the extra polish they needed and are a delight to read.
In closing I would say that while the game is not very player-driven so much as event-driven, time management and NOT INVESTIGATING STRANGE NOISES are a big priority for me in starting my next run. It seems a reasonable amount of sanity damage may be avoided by not triggering/witnessing supernatural events.
At this rate I am willing to start fresh and attempt to beat it cleanly two more times, then it's time for shameless abuse of outside help.

What

The lightning turns any object into a ‘lightning grenade’ and the automatic targeting will do the rest. Anything else is just style points - lightning grenade is the solution to every fight in the game with the possible exception of the headcrab robots you fight halfway through the game, who always appear in swarms dropping from the ceiling and who often don’t even attack. Hell, if the group is three people or less, you can pick them all up at once and throw them either into a wall or off into the abyss that most levels have.

Worms: Ultimate Mayhem is a mashup of one of my favorite games of all time - Worms 4 Mayhem and the original Worms 3D.
