You might have seen that this game has mostly negative reviews, I'd wager that most of them are written out of a bitter taste in the mouth but, to a degree, they're also mostly justified, and mine might even seem a tad biased too, so take what I say with a pinch of salt.
I'll explain the game a little bit first.
This game isn't badly designed at concept level, it's actually incredibly fun to play on one's own because of the nature of the combat system. The only way I can describe parallels to this game is that it's similar to Dark Souls, except you're more focused on the one-on-one dueling aspect as opposed to rolling around the screen fighting mobs, however, unlike Dark Souls, this game doesn't skirt around the fact that it's basically designed for multiplayer, with the core gameplay focusing around the "Faction War", more on that later though.
We'll start from the ground up, a sort of general what you'll be doing for most of the time sort of approach. Starting on the main menu, you'll have the choice between Multiplayer, where you'll be brought to the Faction map to choose your game mode, Story mode, which is self explanatory, Custom Match, which is also self explanatory, as well as the How to Play menu, which is where all your practice and free modes are based.
I don't want to spend much time on the story, spoilers and all, but it's actually fairly decent to run through a couple times, coupled with the bonus that completing it on higher difficulties yields little rewards for your multiplayer characters. you can even co-op it, if you're so inclined, and the game adds more enemies as a modifier to the difficulty based on how many your have in your party.
The practice modes SHOULD be your first port of call, if you don't want to go straight to the story straight off, since it'll teach you all the basic and advanced concepts you're going to absolutely require if you have any hope of surviving in the multiplayer. You'll be given the chance to test out all of the characters and spar against a bot level of your choice, much like most fighting games do.
So jumping straight into the multiplayer, you'll be at the faction map. When you start the game for the first time, you'll be asked to choose between one of three factions: Knights, Vikings, and Samurai. It doesn't ultimately matter which one you pick if you don't have any desire to invest yourself in the meta game that's going on but you'll earn more rewards if your faction is doing well. For the most part (Assuming you don't have a regular set of people to group up with right away), you'll choose a mode that you think suits you and go straight into matchmaking (I should quickly point out that if PvP isn't your thing, you can still play PvAI). It's at this point that the first major issue people have with the game becomes evident.
For Honor uses a Peer-to-Peer connection system, not dedicated servers. For those that don't understand what that means for you, it means that you'll be piggybacking off another player's connection and using the strongest one as the host. Ubisoft tried to do things a little differently this time around by making it so that EVERY player is dependant on one another for the system to keep them all together, but it doesn't work as well as it sounds all of the time. You will spend some long times waiting for a match especially if you're not a PvP fan, and occasionally, you might even get a random error before you even get matched up, returning you to the main menu once again instead of just trying again, like most other games might do.
Okay, so you got into a match and picked your hero, now what? Well, depending on which gamemode you're in, you're going to actually just end up either running to a zone to capture it, or more likely, you're going to sprint around looking for another hero to duel. This is the part where the next set of issues comes in. Hero balance is very subjective, and highly debated all over the net. I'm going to leave out my own opinions on this matter, but a lot of salt generated around the multiplayer revolves around the behaviour of the players and the heroes and tactics that they use. Fighting against, or even with other players can be a testing experience, I've had times when the A.I. have been teleporting about the screen because of the nature of the Peer-to-peer system. Don't be fooled, you might have fantastic net, but you're bound to have some weirdness happen sooner or later. Scoring in the game isn't particularly important as the final score you have at the end of a match doesn't necessarily mean you're going to do much better or worse at the results screen. For some, you may enjoy just the flow of gameplay itself, for others you may invest yourself a little more into your own personal performance and that's where the second debate of "Honour" comes into the game.
Despite being the games namesake, behaviour in people is wildly varying when it comes to the concept of honour and etiquette on the field of battle, some will go no-holds-barred and attack every target they can for as many kills as they can get, leading to 2v1, 3v1 or even 4v1 situations, others may wait until you've finished with your target and jump in should you be defeated, waiting patiently for their turn, so to speak. The game will not force you to play in any certain way, which is a good thing. Decide which type of person you are early on but be prepared - the community in this game is quite unnecessarily toxic.
After the end of a match, you're given your EXP, a small chance of finding a piece of equipment you can use to buff and customise the look of your character, as well as a small amount of steel (The game's form of currency), which can be used to purchase more gear, emotes, other executions ect. You'll also be given "War Assets" that you can use to deploy on the different regions of the faction map meta game, hopefully helping push your faction's hold further in an effort to win the season, broken up into 5 rounds.
So that's the barest bones description of the sort of gameplay I can offer, now I want to briefly touch on some of the other points that make this a NON recommended game.
I've played this game since beta, and I played the beta constantly until it ended. I didn't get the game for a couple of months until it went on sale, since I knew then and I still know now that this game isn't worth the price it's being sold for. It has quite a few bugs, a lot of crashes and several other issues that make long sessions of gameplay incredibly frustrating, I've heard and seen that these issues are faced by gamers of all types of connection strength and PC specs, frankly, I'm very disappointed in the lack of support for these issues. I regularly crash directly at the end of a match, forfeiting any and all score/rewards for participating completely, requiring me to alt-tab and delete the process in task manager. You might not have the same issues, but it really is anyone's guess as to whether something will affect you or not. Support for this game is NOT very good at all, according to Ubisoft's community support forums. Most people are handed the same generic corporate response you'd typically expect from a company. As it stands, if you have an issue, you're going to have to persist like a man/woman possesed in support tickets in order to get a satisfying result, or, like the rest of us, rely on waiting for the next patch to solve things.
This game looks beautiful, the sound design is lovely and the gameplay for the most part is incredibly fun and, I dare say even addictive. It's just sadly PLAGUED by it's Peer-to-Peer system, a myriad of issues, and now an overall toxic and slowly reducing player base. My final few words regarding this game are this: absolutely watch some more videos, read a lot more reviews to get a general feel for it and by all means BUY AT YOUR OWN RISK
...Unless you can afford to throw your money at expensive Ubisoft titles, in which case go ahead.

Buy it on a sale, play it with ONLY FRIENDS for exactly 1 hour and 59 minutes, then refund it.
Purchased the game on release, got immediately halted from gameplay for 2 weeks due to their failure to handle the (Unsurprising) amount of traffic on release date. Seeing as they're an indie dev, gave them a pass on that, even big names screw that up.
Gameplay wise, mechanics are great! On paper.
Asymettric gameplay with one player controlling Jason, the antagonist star of the Friday The Thirteenth franchise, while the others are unique camp counselors. The counselors work together to repel Jason's attacks, and escape with their lives, or Jason brutally murders each, one by one. Sounds reasonable enough, yes?
Too bad the execution (Hey, puns!) is poor. Animations are wonky, with character hair (mainly on female counselors) going absolutely insane in typical fashion. Clipping is common, and so is items being spawned or dropped into the floor, unreachable by those desperate survivors. Many times has Jason killed a counselor with the car keys, only for their poor friends to find their body, and those keys, submerged into the floor.
Jason is a cakewalk to the point of being boring, with the sole reason being a cookie cutter way to win. "Morph" (Teleport) to a car, use "Sense" to find a player, use the PAINFULLY broken "Shift" to fling yourself into them, and then spam mouse 2 to "Grab". Assuming you have the brain capacity and reaction speed of at least a toddler, you're guaranteed to have a counselor in your clutches. Simply spam away that number 1 key, and you'll immediately choke them to death in an animation you'll soon memorize. Don't be afraid to do this to groups of players, because even if they have a weapon, theres a 0.5 second window between you being able to execute and them "stunning" you and freeing their teammate. Most people run and leave their friends to die, recognizing how poor those odds are.
Pocket Knives are your only saving grace if he grabs you, but only those truely blessed by RNGesus will find 1 of the 3 hidden all over the map. Used to be a perk to spawn with one, but that got removed in favor of useless things like Faster Car Speed (Please note, they couldn't be bothered to properly script Faster Car Speed, so that perk is quite literally useless)
If you do die, pray you're the second one to do so, AND that the first to die didn't already leave (There being no punishment for leaving mid-match), and you may come back as Tommy Jarvis, the Iconic Protoganist of a few of the films! Too bad most people use him to enact revenge on other counselors, with a common sight being a nice big BETRAYED tag besides a dead players name.
Escape methods include a boat, two different cars, or the police radio. Smart Jasons will immediately put a bear trap in front  of every interactable objective, as anyone who touches it will alert Jason immediately. (Unless you're insane enough to want to use 1 of the 3 Pocket Knives to defuse a SINGLE trap.) Even if you manage to get a car, most Jasons will block you easily enough, or a teammate will troll you by throwing himself into its front grill, netting you a nice -1000 XP and making the entire endevoar pointless. Police also appear only at one of two exits, which means Jason will be waiting to shift grab you into the afterlife no matter what.
The Devs have already stated they'll never change the Shift Grab meta, too busy banning random players and anyone who insults their friends. Take a look at the Reddit if you want some good comedy, as they recently had to remove the Developers from the Admin team of the Reddit due to constant abuse.
To reiterate: Buy it on a sale, play it with ONLY FRIENDS for exactly 1 hour and 59 minutes, then refund it.

Mechanically this game is an excellent free-to-play FPS. It's RPG Elements were fresh, to me, and it has done well in areas most other free-to-play FPS games have failed, most notably:
- Ranking systems based on level and equipment which make sense, are intuitive and set you up against players of comparable skill level. Although occasionally a player far to good to be in your tier does slip in.
- The visuals are unexpectedly good, the aesthetic of old and new russian weaponry is very pleasing, the post apocolyptic feel is captured well for the most part.
- The controls feel responsive and intuitive, in moments where they don't such things are intentional game mechanical decisions which make sense and contribute to the overall depth and possibly quality of the game (ie. such as where one adds stat points to improve the inefficiency of that kind of movement. Aiming down sight, running, etc.)
- The game generally captures a realistic and punishing FPS feel without being innaccesible to 99% of the planet like DayZ or comparables.
- Manages to only be minimalistically pay-to-win as of 4/6/2016.
Some random neutral things to note about the game:
- Finding a match can be a bit of a wait (2 minute one average for me, a low level player), but completely tolerable and understandable.
- Matches are 8v8, not on the scale you might expect of other FPS games. This often serves to make matches more personal and most of your deaths will be due to skill imbalance and error.
- I've never handled a gun in real life, can't speak to how realistic the firing of guns are in this game but I do know that many of the guns have a helluva lot of recoil so be prepared.
My largest gripes:
- Possibly not highly optimized (coming from the perspective of only my system in 4/6/2016)
- Lack of gender and race diversity.
- (Correct me if I'm wrong, I will be playing more) The skill system seems to force you down one of two main focuses, either building efficiency of gunplay, or focusing on skills to help deal with a game element known as anomolies, glowing balls of energy that hurt you but can be harvested for superhuman powers.
I'll comment more on the race and gender diversity here because I believe things need to be said of it. First off its one that I have with a lot of games. I found Survivarum's lack of race or gender diversity in character creation to be insulting personally, and unnecesary given that video games are essentially a limitless creative medium. More than just cisgender white men are interested in playing your game devs, and we'd like to be able to represent ourselves in your game space. A purely cisgender, white, male cast is not actually a necessary part of the aesthetic you are trying to capture. Nowadays there is enough awareness that there is no excuse for a lack of representation and presentation in video games and yeah I'm entitled to be able to play as someone other than Grizzly McWhiteDude, thanks.

Never Alone is a very hard game to grade in some respects, but a very easy one to grade in others. As a 2D platformer game, there is nothing special about it. While the dual character mechanic is vaguely interesting, other games have done it better (and many still weren’t very fun). The actual platforming is okay but nothing particularly fun in terms of flow. The funnest parts of the game are the sequences where you run away from monsters or other things, which have a great sense of urgency to them, but many parts of the game are just you navigating various arctic environments which don’t feel very special.
Some folks have complained about the looseness of the controls, but in the end, they are serviceable and work for the game. The real issue is that the game just doesn’t do anything very special gameplay wise.
So what is hard about this game?
Well, it is not just a game; it is meant to be an experience. The Inuit are trying to share a bit of their culture with the player, and they do this both via the story, which is an Inuit myth, and via these little “cultural insight” videos, little mini-documentaries spread throughout the game. The Inuit in the videos are very eager to share fragments of their life, culture, and mythology, and their integration into the flow of the game actually works quite well.
The problem is that, ultimately, it just isn’t all that interesting. The gameplay is meh and I doubt I would have watched the documentaries without the gameplay. Overall, it was an okay experience, but… it just wasn’t anything special anywhere.
Clocking in at about 3 hours and 20 minutes for 100% completion of the base game (I haven’t done the DLC yet), there’s just not that much here.
My advice? Don’t buy this game. But if you already own it, it is a fairly harmless use of three hours.

A well meaning story driven platformer with some flaws.
The stories and the way they are told and narrated is great in this game and by far the strong point. As you progress in the game there is narration of the story in native tongue (with subtitles) as well as unlockable "cultural insights". They are 1 to 2 minute documentary videos of interviews of people explaining the real life lore, culture, and environments that make up the story. I do think they missed a chance to interweave the mini-documentaries in with the actual gameplay but for the most part they were timed phenomenally to coincide with things happening in the game. So even though they were live action videos they never felt out of place and only added to the story telling.
The actual gameplay suffers from what feels like a lack of gameplay testing. The controls aren't exactly tight but that never interferes badly. Also, characters hiccup or get stuck on edges here or there, but never anything "game breaking". The platforming seems ultra casual early as you fall into the narrative but then the challenge sneaks up on you. You soon realize you aren't just running and jumping, there's more to it. The game is quite short (I 100%'d it + 100%'d DLC in 4.4hrs) but the difficulty arc is smooth. Playing singleplayer you switch between your two characters that have varying abilities that get you through easy to average platforming obstacles. I never got stumped from the more puzzle-like aspects, it was just the platforming skill or timing sections that slowed me down. But there is no punishment for death as the respawn points are numerous. Checkpoints are spaced a little further for when exiting the game though.
I will also quickly mention I had a framerate issue after watching some videos where my framerate would plummet, but exiting to menu and reloading the level fixed it and took mere seconds. Never bothered me enough to lookup if it was a common issue. On the subject of graphics, it falls squarely in the "cute" category. I think the animations were done well and there's enough variety. The main game story revolves around a blizzard and has a darker atmosphere while the DLC had a few blue skies and a brighter approach. Both worked. And the sound is solid.
In all, I enjoyed the stories. Wonderful narrative on an interesting subject. And really, that's what you should be here for with this game. The gameplay was lacking and prone to little glitches or hiccups but never enough to ruin the story. But it did surprise me with it's depth to a degree too. I've played story driven games made in the same spirit that quite frankly lack actual gameplay. There is most definitely a game here. The regular price is steep and kept it consistently deeply buried at the bottom of my wishlist since release but it has now found its way to bundles and steep sales. As always wait for one of those. Highly recommended if you want to gather 'round and listen to a good story. Otherwise I wouldn't encourage you too hard or claim its a "must".

SOMA deals with some profound themes and I will be talking about them straight and fairly. We will discuss whether or not this is the right fit for horror fans, Amnesia fanatics, or even first comers to the genre. Ultimately this review should help you decide whether or not these themes are even interesting to you. There will be no spoilers here.
What is this game about, in a nutshell? SOMA is a treatise in some profoundly dark philosophical themes, unlike any that Frictional has explored prior in their roster. The Lovecraftian Horror of Amnesia has been left to the wayside, and the paranoid occultism and even dark humor of Black Plague are nowhere to be found. Instead, SOMA sits you down and asks you to contemplate your conciousness, human experience, connection with others, trust in yourself and what it means to be human. And it does so with some harrowing beats, layering a breadth of worldbuilding to the flanks of a central narration that deals with two characters -- Simon and Catherine.
However, the vehicle that carriers this narrative is cumbersome and often irritating.
Overall: 4/5, Recommended.
Pros:
*Emotionally contemplative story that embelishes the darker side of what we take for granted. Some truly impactful
moments, and a legitimately depressing ending, seal the central narrative as one of their best.
*I appreciated the large pull away from grounded "Horror" roots, even if others may disagree.
*Worldbuilding is astounding at times. The "Impact Event", especially the Coast of Portugal audio log, cast some stark imagery for weeks in my mind.
*Voice Acting is the best it's been in a Frictional title, but it's still not great. More on that below.
*Did I mention the ending left me speechless?
Cons:
*Enemy design is cumbersome and irritating. These encounters truly detract from the experience. I never died in SOMA, on Hard, but that didn't stop them from being a chore.
*Puzzles are less creative than anything put into Penumbra or Amnesia, spinoffs/DLC included.
*Workmanlike level design, graphics, and atmosphere help to elevate the story, but nowhere even in the same spectrum as their other titles.
*Sound design, especially music, is spartan at best.
*I don't know if it's the language barrier or what, but the people they cast aren't that great compared to even other indie horror titles. Some lines threw me for a loop in SOMA, sounding totally disingenuous.
*Game is a little too long. I felt this way with Alien Isolation, too. I feel like these games are padding too much. Amnesia was perfect at six hours. SOMA for ten felt like too much.
*Lastly, the world is too cluttered with nonsense. The same decals, drill items, bottles, shelves, furniture and junk are absolutely crammed into every corner. I love detailed levels, but not when it's the same 25 assets.
---
SOMA starts with you taking control of Simon, who has recently suffered a traumatic brain injury in a car crash. He goes to a doctor for an experimental brain scan to diagnose and cure what he presumes to be his inevitable death, much like his best friend and lover. After a short prologue sequence, this brain scan teleports us to an abandoned research facility in the ocean that is populated by some violent robots and a few friendly voices over the comms. Standard, so far. You are free to explore partially open, mostly linear, hallways and corridors to unlocking rooms, solving puzzles, reading logs or listening to audio entries while occasionally dodging an enemy in a stealth sequence as there is no combat. And that's it, for ten hours. SOMA holds you into a simple four step loop (Explore, Solve, Listen, Hide.) and keeps you there. The intangible asset it holds above competitors is a genius screenplay that adapts some dark, personal themes at its core.
Quickly the game introduces you to the thematic consistency of consciousness. Robots think they're human. Robots are insane, and feel pain. Only the bodies of humans can be found. What happened in this research facility and also the unexpected introduction of a world crisis to pushing them to unknown limits really exemplify the story you're going to be told.
As a contemplative title, SOMA succeeds in all aspects. The story is harrowing and strictly depressing, and even hopeless. Sort of. You'll see. It is however not scary in the slightest. I mentioned that enemy designs are terrible, and they are. They act as time sinks to detract you from the story, often being an asspull into pseudo-stealth and hide/seek elements. This measured formula worked best in amnesia, decently in penumbra, but fails here because Frictional has experimented with too many enemy types and too many AI pattern takes, so that ultimately each enemy feels like a puzzle sequence and not a survival sequence.
The game also leans heavily into the walking simulator department, especially during the useless underwater segments where an awful draw distance and uninspired art direction lull the player to sleep. What is even more puzzling is that there is little to no story exposition, or narration, during these parts. Only the occasional landmark or milestone visual sight build up a fraction of the world during these parts.
SOMA is worth it at asking price. I couldn't have enjoyed the story more, and if you think a contemplative but not scary story interests you, get it. But as a video game vehicle the game loop just simply needs to be refreshed. I've had this main course three times from Frictional Games, but they keep adding more salt on top.

I wanted to find a short RPG and I tried this game.
I finished it in ~ 5 hours and I'm fully satisfied.
As the description says this game is a dark sci-fi PRG set in a dystopian city.
Throught the game you will find yourself several companions and you will solve a couple dozens of quests.
You usually have some choices what to do (who to spare / kill) and those choices affect the game's story (mostly through cutscenes).
The game is made with RPG Maker, so the battles are typical for any JRPG. A big surprise that in this game you can actually avoid most of them by defeating enemies without fighting them (you can disable sentry bots via computers or kill guards using grenades), which is nice since I don't like JPRG battles.
And yes, some of the battles are quite tough. Nothing serious, I didn't die once, yet they force you to use your abilities well.
I also like the story and that you actually have several choices in the end.
Overall, I actually liked this game more than I anticipated.
It was 5 very intersting hours for a very reasonable price.

Project Abyss is a lovely game that captures the essence of underwater exploration and the related dangers. The art style and representation of the ocean creatures is charming and it feels nice when you come across something out of the blue.
At first, the controls seem overwhelming, but this because of the range of submarine and diver tools that are on offer. Moving the submarine itself is done by rotating the propeller to the angle of thrust needed, which gives a very unique and realistic feel to operation. A lot of care is required to finely position the submarine around underwater obstacles. The submarine tools include things like the drill, front claw, underbelly (?) claw, harpoon gun and chain harpoon. I particularly like the claw underneath the sub that moves up/down with the mouse wheel and can pull objects back up.
You can also exit the submarine and explore as the diver, allowing for other weapons and tools at your disposal. It allows for an extra dynamic of gameplay, in terms of exploring inside shipwrecks or repairing the submarine itself from outside. It feels natural to secure your submarine to a rock with the chain harpoon, then explore more closely as the diver itself.
There is definitely a survival aspect to the gameplay, as the fuel on the submarine is limited, along with ammo sometimes running dry. Also the sea itself can be a rather dangerous place. Save when you can and don't waste resources.
From the look of the skill trees and the achievements, there appears to be a lot more content on offer for me to discover.
If deep sea exploration is your thing, then I'd definitely give this a go.

Short opinion:
This is a piece of crap that brings shame to Jagged Alliance series. If you're a fan of any type of tactical turn-based games - avoid it!
Long one:
Yeah, i'm a long time fan of Jagged Alliance games like many others around the world. I don't regret that i was a backer during KS campaign, it was my choice and i was fully conscious about what i was doing. I only regret the final result of this project.
I really don't want to write a book about gameplay, so i will focus on advantages and disadavtages of this game. Here we go:
Pros:
- Graphics, you can love it or hate it, but i think that graphical style that was taken was a good choice.
- Fighting, well, sometimes fight is annoying, but sometimes it can be fun.
- Music, not bad.
- The game is clearly described, you can easily sense what is it all about
Cons:
- Graphics, style is ok, but there are too little details and 3D characters have jest few polygons.
- Sound, i don't mind soundtrack, but sometimes sounds in the inventory are too loud and overdriven.
- Just one save slot!
- Very small quantity of stuff thrown around, so there is no sense in wandering on a map, there are only few containers in which you can find some loot.
- Can't open/close the doors!
- There are no second floors, and you can't go on the roofs!
- There is no possibility to modify weapons!
- Bugged and totally unrealistic weapons. There is no such thing like UZI in .45 caliber, there is no such thing like Thompson with 7, 10, or 15-round clip. Sometimes I had action points, proper ammo and just can't reload the weapon.
- Can't see bloody thing during the rain/storm.
- Pathfinding is totally broken. You can click on a single and simple part of the ground and some of your merc will choose the most complicated and longest possible way to get there (and some of them will probably stay just where they are).
- User interface is not well designed, you can easily click on a random place and accidentally move your merc.
- AI, there are no sophisticated tactics that enemies can use, They just get closer and closer, one by one. Forget about flanking and such things.
- Useless militia, you train them, they lose and so on... There is no possibility to enter combat when your militia squad is fighting.
- Strange mechanics, aim shot is useless and sometimes you can embark into weird "never-ending" shootout. It looks like this: the distance between your merc and the enemy is about two squares, you have rather high hit probability and you just can't shot him no matter what. Another thing: 103, 105% hit probability? What is it? Are devs kidding us?
- No noticeable mercs relationships, They're just callous puppets.
- You can use cow as a cover, the cow is...armoured...
- There is no, absolutely no optimalization!
- What the hell "interrupt" button is doing in UI? Interrupt action should act automatically when given character have enough action points!
- Illegible table of guns characteristic.
- There is a shop of course (in text, not graphical form!). You can buy, but you can't sell your own stuff!
- Camera angles are uncomfortable
...Jesus, i have enough, there are probably quite a few things that i could mention, but this list annoyed me enough. As You see, this game has been practically deprived of the most needed functions. I don't really see sense in existing of JA-ish game which is so neutered. Just look at Silent Storm and even 7.62, or Back in Action. These games have some flaws, but this is nothing comparing to Flashback. This game is so bad that i don't see any potential in it and any chance to upgrage the main problems of it.
People from Full Control said something like this: "KS campaign succeeded with minimum amount of money needed to create Flashback project, and that's why fans and backers will receive minimum amount of content". Pure and simple, 368k $ was practically the lowest amount of money necessary to achieve lowest stretch goals and start developing of this game. This is the point where Full Control made a huge mistake, they should never start developing this game with such a low budget. Some would say: "but minimum budget could not be lower due to low interest in community. If the amount was higher , this game would never have been created!". Exactly! Jagged Alliance: Flashback should not exist!  This is so weak and embarrassing piece of crap that only brings shame to Jagged Alliance brand.
Maybe if FC had more manpower, capabilities, experience, consistent vision and skills to make things right, then they might have a chance to make a really decent game... But they hadn't and they were overwhelmed  by the task which they have chosen, They had to feed their families and stay aflout, we received a game that is poor in almost every aspect. Was it worth it? I don't think so...
I believe that time will come and we will finally receive worthy successor of JA: 2. It doesn't matter how long i will wait, real mercs never die!;-)

The controls are iffy (played on xbox 360 controller), the "puzzles" are tedious with blatantly obvious solutions, and the mechanics are all pretty standard: jump on platforms, climb some stuff, jump off walls, etc. What actually makes this bad is the presence of two characters. Perhaps due to flaws in AI, sometimes the secondary character won't follow you, so you get to switch to them and do half the "puzzles" twice. Other times, they will follow you when you actually need them to stand still for a puzzle (though I've only encountered this once). It seems to me a very simple follow me / stay here system would be infinitely easier. There's room on the d-pad and even more room on a keyboard.
An even bigger issue is that the game's story, it's cultural uniqueness being a selling point, does not transition well to the video game medium. Roughly speaking, the story is a Iñupiaq folktale. The problem is the gameplay itself does not help the story. Around the start of the game, the narrator says the girl and the fox formed a bond. I didn't feel that bond. I just met this fox a few minutes ago, and frankly, for the exact AI reasons I mentioned previously, it was more of a nuisance than anything else. Also, the cutscenes are in a different artstyle, which detracts from the experience somewhat. I can see why, most likely out of deference for the original folktale, but they seem to have taken the original folktale in its original state and then built the game around it, which was a grave mistake. If I wanted to hear a folktale, I could find plenty online, and they'd be just as interesting: I would't feel emotionally attached to the characters but would find the basic story interesting.
One possible reason for my negative experience with this is that I didn't watch the cultural insight videos, for two reasons. Firstly, I didn't want to be taken out of the experience. I understood the story completely, but maybe the novelty is in the learning and not in the game itself. Secondly, much like the folktale issue, if I wanted to watch a documentary, I'd watch one online.

Background in other "smiliar" IDE's: Used Game Maker Studio for 4 years before I touched Clickteam Fusion.
It's really hard to say which is the better tool, since it really does depend on what kind of game you are building as well as what level of control you think you will need to build said game. Honestly, if you're building any kind of 2D platformer, top down jRPG, top-down "Zelda" style adventure game, etc. then Fusion is really all you would need. This is largely due to the sheer number of extremely useful/powerful extension widgets you can add to your project, that do more than adequate work on a number of "heavy lifting" aspects of your development. (You don't need to code things like physics, dynamic animation timing/draw engines, programming for DI/XI controller schemes, GUI's, etc. etc. from scratch, since there is an add-on widget for each of these tasks, and they are all very powerful/flexible.) It took me a grand total of 4 days to completely port the plaformer engine I'd built with GM:Studio over the course of some months, into Fusion, and a good bit of that time was just learning the quirks of the Fusion IDE.
During the testing of objects and rooms, all events that you create are merely interpreted at runtime, not compiled, though you do get to compile your finished project into an .exe for distribution. The thing about interpretation during testing is that you now need to worry about how your event list for a given object is sequenced, since the list will be interpreted (read) TOP TO BOTTOM, during every frame. It's kind of annoying to have to experiment and arrange things so that they work for TESTING, when it probably won't matter how most stuff is sequenced after the compile. The thing this has over GM: Studio, is that you can now test things MUCH quicker, in piecemeal fashion, without having to compile your entire project every single time you want to test anything you did or changed.
Because of the "spreadsheet" structure of the IDE, you are no longer able to write code blocks in the traditional sense. This means no real "if/else" statements, no real "swtiching" statements, etc. There ARE ways to simulate such things within the workspace. One example is dynamically activating/deactivating groups of events as you need/don't need them to run. (Kind of like creating a switching statement, since you can't actually write out a switching statement.) Fusion DOES support the ability to have GLOBAL variables, strings and events, so you don't have to keep copypasting these things from room to room to room. (Example: Player control handling, object variables that need to affect the game world globally, etc.)
Importing animations, tilesets, sound, music, etc. is handled much better in Fusion, IMO. You no longer need to code loops, forced frames and the like, since Fusion is intuitive enough where you can do it all by clicking this or that checkbox.
Now...objects. (Creature objects for example and in particular.) In Fusion, when placing more than one of the same object in room, you are actually placing DUPLICATES of that object, not multiple INSTANCES of that object. That means they are identical in every single way, right down to their event timing. (I.E, 10 hopper enemies: one hops, they ALL hop at the same time, etc.) There is a "ForEach" widget blah blah (UPDATE: There is actually ForEach loop capability built into Clickteam Fusion now, and can be found in the actions menu of any object in your project. Just intialize and run them like you would any fastloop. Testing the potential of these things and what all they can do for you, really does stretch into more "intermediate" territory, but after some good experimentation and watching a few tutorials, it's actually pretty easy.)
Quirks aside, I really do feel like Fusion might be the better option for absolute beginners, and if you're somewhat experienced already and willing to figure out the quirks, could mean MUCH faster prototyping/building for you. (Not gonna lie, the quirks and getting Fusion do some of the more outside-the-box stuff can be a bit frustrating at first, especially if you're reaching for something that's usually so simple to do with raw code. Once you figure it out though, the QoL perks are pretty massive.)

Yes, the game has great visuals.  Yes, it has complexity.  That is where the good ends.  You see, they changed it.
Vega used to be a great game.  Yes, it had problems, but there were many ways for these problems to be resolved.  The makers chose the worst possible method.  Change everything.
They increased the repair for new players drastically, and lowered the repair for end gamers.  Thus, they widened the power gap between the long-time players and new players.
They still haven't fixed the crafting system.  I say "fixed" because they have told us the game is supposed to be about PvP....but we spend all of our time farming for random box drops, that rarely give us the parts we are trying to find, so we can upgrade our ships to do PvP battles.  Effectively, this is a farming game in space.
And now....they are removing the unique quality of speed between the different ships.  So the only real difference between the ships is.....they can hold more "stuff".  All the ship-specific tactics we have come to know and love.....soon to be gone with the next update.
Finally, the new changes make it so that, unless you are willing to spend a LOT of money on the game, you will be looking at playing the game for at least a couple years...just to catch up to where people are AT THIS CURRENT TIME.....not to catch up to WHERE THEY WILL BE in a few years.  Thus....heavy spenders have effectively been given a "god-mode" in game.  So yeah....it's free to play....just not free to win.
In summary....if you don't have a LOT of expendable cash....find a different game.  This one was really awesome, but the devs are ruining it.

SUMMARY:  A love letter, homage, and parody of classic Nintndo-style action RPGS filled with features, character and customization.  Must-support and must-buy for fans of classic action-RPG and crafting.  Even in Early Access, it's impressive.
Let's get the bad out of the way - this game is Early access, and as of mid 2017 I don't expect it to be finished at least until year's end.  That being said, if you love top-down action RPGs with crafting, you probably should be supporting this anyway, but if you want, read my review.
Secrets of Grindea manages a difficult job.  It is a love letter to classic top-down button-mashing action RPGs Nintendo was famous for, but also packs in the "best" features of many games.  It is an homage to all those games, without limiting itself.  Finally it's a parody that's not mocking, but affectionate - and the parody elements even work into the plot.
The best comparisons I've found are Dungeonmans and Starbound, games that took their time, knew their subject, evolved, and turned into something amazing.
In the game, you are a young Collector in the world of Grindea, your aim is to collect artifacts and equipment.  The game offers:
* Highly customizable skills.  You can focus on two kinds of weapons, four kinds of magic, and support skills.  You can also tweak "talents" that affect how abilities and skills function together.  Each of these abilities can also be leveled up, improving and changing how they work.  Build a combat maniac who mashes stuff with a hammer, a summoner surrounded by friends, a dashing and dodging ninja.  It's up to you.
* Simple but effective crafting with depth.  Find enough stuff, make stuff is how it goes, but you'll need to explore and experiment to discover what unknown ingredients are needed.  Fortunately things you encounter that can be used are specially tagged.
* Choose your equipment. Weapons, hats, armor, accessories, and more all affect how your character functions. Power up your magic with a sorcerous chapeau, find boots that speed up your movement while you charge skills, or stick a pumpkin on your head. You can also choose items to be "cosmetic," changing appearance while you benefit from an equipped item.
* Plenty of quests and sidequests and extras.  There's always something to do in Grindea, with plenty of rewards.  Don't forget to return to people you've talked to before.
* The fun of the grind.  If you want to max out your equipment, you're going to mash monsters. Grindea, however, makes it fun, with ways to increase spawns, meet tougher monsters, or refight bosses.  You can even tweak skills and equipment for maximum, fast grind. Farming is actually fun!
* Lots to do.  Go fishing. Raise a pet. Find minigames.  Look for hidden treasure. Up your hat collection with Mister Fabulous. Grindea offers you many things to do depending on goals and mood.
* Your own expandable house.  Have fun building your own domicile as a break from adenturing.
* A great visual style. The world's classic-cartoony not-quite-anime look is charming and appealing, the monsters have personality, the settings are colorful.
* A great soundtrack. There's a classic game soundtrack here that sets the mood and is excellently composed.
* Story and humor.  There's plenty of humor and an actual story (with some great twists) that's not all laughs. The game comes to life as well as making you laugh - then punches you in the gut with pathos.
* Two game modes.  You've got your usual adventure, but also the roguelike random adventure mode that lets you gradually build a character legacy and a town!  It's literally two games in one.
* Optional co-op. On top of everything else, play with friends.
Sound like a lot?  The game's staff also consists of three people as of this writing. It's pretty amazing what they've done since 2011.
Just a reminder as of this writing it's early access.  The game is very fun, there's lots to do, but it's not done.
Now who should get this if you're willing to go Early Access?
* If you love old-school AARPGs you probably should just pick it up now to enjoy it and give feedback.
* If you love looting and crafting and hunting up rare things and playing minigames, get it.
* If the above review interested you.  This game hits a special sweet spot, it just "fits" some people.

SOMA deals with some profound themes and I will be talking about them straight and fairly. We will discuss whether or not this is the right fit for horror fans, Amnesia fanatics, or even first comers to the genre. Ultimately this review should help you decide whether or not these themes are even interesting to you. There will be no spoilers here.
What is this game about, in a nutshell? SOMA is a treatise in some profoundly dark philosophical themes, unlike any that Frictional has explored prior in their roster. The Lovecraftian Horror of Amnesia has been left to the wayside, and the paranoid occultism and even dark humor of Black Plague are nowhere to be found. Instead, SOMA sits you down and asks you to contemplate your conciousness, human experience, connection with others, trust in yourself and what it means to be human. And it does so with some harrowing beats, layering a breadth of worldbuilding to the flanks of a central narration that deals with two characters -- Simon and Catherine.
However, the vehicle that carriers this narrative is cumbersome and often irritating.
Overall: 4/5, Recommended.
Pros:
*Emotionally contemplative story that embelishes the darker side of what we take for granted. Some truly impactful
moments, and a legitimately depressing ending, seal the central narrative as one of their best.
*I appreciated the large pull away from grounded "Horror" roots, even if others may disagree.
*Worldbuilding is astounding at times. The "Impact Event", especially the Coast of Portugal audio log, cast some stark imagery for weeks in my mind.
*Voice Acting is the best it's been in a Frictional title, but it's still not great. More on that below.
*Did I mention the ending left me speechless?
Cons:
*Enemy design is cumbersome and irritating. These encounters truly detract from the experience. I never died in SOMA, on Hard, but that didn't stop them from being a chore.
*Puzzles are less creative than anything put into Penumbra or Amnesia, spinoffs/DLC included.
*Workmanlike level design, graphics, and atmosphere help to elevate the story, but nowhere even in the same spectrum as their other titles.
*Sound design, especially music, is spartan at best.
*I don't know if it's the language barrier or what, but the people they cast aren't that great compared to even other indie horror titles. Some lines threw me for a loop in SOMA, sounding totally disingenuous.
*Game is a little too long. I felt this way with Alien Isolation, too. I feel like these games are padding too much. Amnesia was perfect at six hours. SOMA for ten felt like too much.
*Lastly, the world is too cluttered with nonsense. The same decals, drill items, bottles, shelves, furniture and junk are absolutely crammed into every corner. I love detailed levels, but not when it's the same 25 assets.
---
SOMA starts with you taking control of Simon, who has recently suffered a traumatic brain injury in a car crash. He goes to a doctor for an experimental brain scan to diagnose and cure what he presumes to be his inevitable death, much like his best friend and lover. After a short prologue sequence, this brain scan teleports us to an abandoned research facility in the ocean that is populated by some violent robots and a few friendly voices over the comms. Standard, so far. You are free to explore partially open, mostly linear, hallways and corridors to unlocking rooms, solving puzzles, reading logs or listening to audio entries while occasionally dodging an enemy in a stealth sequence as there is no combat. And that's it, for ten hours. SOMA holds you into a simple four step loop (Explore, Solve, Listen, Hide.) and keeps you there. The intangible asset it holds above competitors is a genius screenplay that adapts some dark, personal themes at its core.
Quickly the game introduces you to the thematic consistency of consciousness. Robots think they're human. Robots are insane, and feel pain. Only the bodies of humans can be found. What happened in this research facility and also the unexpected introduction of a world crisis to pushing them to unknown limits really exemplify the story you're going to be told.
As a contemplative title, SOMA succeeds in all aspects. The story is harrowing and strictly depressing, and even hopeless. Sort of. You'll see. It is however not scary in the slightest. I mentioned that enemy designs are terrible, and they are. They act as time sinks to detract you from the story, often being an asspull into pseudo-stealth and hide/seek elements. This measured formula worked best in amnesia, decently in penumbra, but fails here because Frictional has experimented with too many enemy types and too many AI pattern takes, so that ultimately each enemy feels like a puzzle sequence and not a survival sequence.
The game also leans heavily into the walking simulator department, especially during the useless underwater segments where an awful draw distance and uninspired art direction lull the player to sleep. What is even more puzzling is that there is little to no story exposition, or narration, during these parts. Only the occasional landmark or milestone visual sight build up a fraction of the world during these parts.
SOMA is worth it at asking price. I couldn't have enjoyed the story more, and if you think a contemplative but not scary story interests you, get it. But as a video game vehicle the game loop just simply needs to be refreshed. I've had this main course three times from Frictional Games, but they keep adding more salt on top.

TL;DR:
- The story is the most important part
- Go into the game blind to any information
- Take your time to investigate what happened - There's a mod to disable monsters attacking you, but doesn't interfere with the story and removes most of the horror elements. Use this mod if you feel the horror element causes you hesitation with purchasing the game
- At full price the game is worth buying
---
This is a story-driven game that is thought provoking and challenges your morality at times. I definitely recommend taking the time to learn everything you can about the world around you. The decisions you'll have to make don't have 'right' answers. Seriously. Don't bother looking up what you should do unless you're absolutely stuck. This won't/shouldn't happen often as the game gives hints if you're paying attention and is fairly linear. I say not to look it up because it's very easy to spoil parts of the story that are simply better by experiencing it yourself.
There is also additional content on their official site that contains some interesting parts of the lore and short stories. The coin flip story is my favorite.
Again I say: I don't recommend blowing past all the interesting materials to read and listen to, which are spread around across the levels. You get to experience the story for the first time once. There are stories and information about those that were there before you that are worth the time to investigate.
There *is* a mod available to make monsters not attack you, which changes the gameplay and kind of emphasizes tragedy over horror. I'd recommend getting this mod if you don't want to deal with the horror elements. Avoiding the horror elements allows you to not have to rush parts of the levels, giving you more freedom to explore.
The only cons I can think of is that replayability isn't high; it's equivalent to watching a movie. Another one is that spoilers can really ruin the experience and wikis are rife with spoilers.
I wish I could experience this game again for the first time because it's just so damn good. It's even fun just watching a friend play through it to see what they do.
And yes, we all spent a solid ten minutes fiddling with the stuff around the apartment at the beginning.

***second review***
Fair is fair and the game has improved a lot in the past couple months.  Interface has improved; NPC stores were implemented; stealth, melee and weapon attachments were added.  The game doesn't look nearly as unfinished as few months back... but in the end the big problems are not addressed and probably will not be as they seem to be a part of the design.
On the turn-based tactical level the game is pretty good actually.  You could wish for more destructible environment or say high-grounds system, but in the end the game is enjoyable as it is...
The island map though is just all wrong...
Healing is too fast - in the original getting a merc wounded would put him/her of commision for days, in Flashback chances are they'll be fine by next morning... so there is litle incentive to run a clean mission, as long as merc still breathing by the end of the fight you'll be fine.
Weapons and equipment is too easy to come by making a equipment management a chore where it used to be a crucial considiration.
Money is too easy to get - despensing with the whole fund mamagement component.
Squad inventory means you no longer need to decide what to take and what to leave in the sector - grab eveything, no worries
Militia is useless even on the easy dificulty, you are probably better off just leaving sectors unguarded and recapturing them as needed (map travel times in Flashback seem to be shorten too so you'll get back in no time)
Mercs lost their personality and uniquness - they have voices and background stories but when you have to make decisions about team building, equipment or tactical use - there is no significant difference between Ivan and Grizzly, Magic and Fidel.
And then there are also more obvious problems.  You still can't open/close doors, can't climb to the roof, CAN summon mercs out of thin air, and CAN take cover behind immovable bulletproof cows.
In the end the game is OK, more than OK in fact... but you are still better of playing Jagged Alliance 2.
***original review***
I am afraid I cannot recommend the game as it is now.
The game is a very passable squad-based turn-based tactics, and to be fair it came closer to the original than any other JA wannabes in the past 15 years, but...
It's like someone have tried to replicate your favorite dish.  They figured out most of the ingredients right (team management, strategic map layer, exploration, turn-based tactical combat), but they never got the original recipe so take their best guess to the proportions and processes.
This shows up in a number of way, but first and foremost in the lack of polish.  JA2 sported the incredible level of attention to the details and polish that was trademark of Sir-Tech... Flashback - lack of polish shows in everything from ability to summon merc out of thin air, to clunky interface, to counter intuitive advancement system, to NPC names like beta_thug, to when and what your mercs say, to lack of balance in both strategic level and squad management.
On top of that Flashback is literally unfinished game (several features are unavailable or unfinished)
While the game had "Early Access" sticker on I kept hoping that all those problem would be fixed... in theory there is still a chance (developers promise patches that will do just that)... but until then... I do not recommend paying for this game.
Bottom line: It's an OK game with great potential, but at the moment if you want JA experience you better of playing JA2 (especially with 1.13 patch)

It's hard to find a decent RPGMaker game nowadays but City of Chains hit nearly all the positive marks for me!.
It had a good, captivating story with decent turn-based combat.
The combat is not your typical turn-based rpg system where you would get experience points to upgrade your character, in City of Chains diving headfirst into combat is not usually a good thing since you don't get any experience from battles, instead it works on the principle of giving you 'tasks' (basically side-quests, along with the main quest objectives)  to complete where your squad gets skill points in order to learn skills for combat.
Most battles can be skipped by basically crafting a grenade and throwing them onto the enemy, killing them. This is mainly an almost stealth type rpg hybrid coupled with turn based combat, where charging into battles will nearly always deplete your precious healing items, which are more useful later on in main battles.
This stealth type gameplay fits perefectly in with the story-line, asking you to make the most of your resources along the journey.
Another plus point for me was that there are choices present in the game and also varied endings depending upon them.
My only gripe with it was the music became extremly repititive in the long run (can be forgiven).
All in all a pretty good game, which can be recommended!.

City Of Chains is a dark sci-fi adventure title developed by Astronomic Games and published by New Reality Games. As Holt Allaway, you take control of a small group of escaped fugitives and attempt to lead them to their freedom. Along the ensuing adventure you will have to make many decisions, some of them with far reaching consequences, such as whether to fight or to avoid combat, to help others or to look out strictly for yourselves and finally to show mercy or to kill. Decide wisely because your choices could possibly affect everyone in the city..."A City Of Chains".
Aside from the intriguing story, the superb gameplay is also a standout feature of this fantastic Indie title. Instead of the traditional experience points you earn skill points which can then be used to learn a variety of new skills and useful passive bonuses for each character on your team. From combat and dialogue skills, to explosive and medicinal crafting, there are many abilities at your disposal to enhance the success of your group but choose wisely depending on your particular style of play. The combat is turn-based and strategic giving you time to determine and execute your teams actions then quickly switching to the adversaries turn until one side eventually emerges from battle victorious. As far as the objectives go, there are non-linear and semi-linear locations so there is usually an alternate means to and end. Also remember that choice and consequence matter in City Of Chains as your decisions will have an impact on the world and people around you. For example, in order to escape from some facility undetected do you shoot this unsuspecting guard dead or merely knock him out? And if you should chose the latter and cross paths with him again in the future will he in turn help you or try to kill you? These are some of the moral decisions that you must make throughout the gripping narrative.
Visually, well City Of Chains is a RPGMaker title and we all know what those look like because they typically have a similiar visual style no matter which game it is because that's just the nature of the software. However, City Of Chains is like a RPGMaker title on steroids because it actually looks quite different from any other game in the category that I've come across on Steam. I believe the main difference, at least to me, is that this title doesn't have the "anime" or "cartoony" look of your average RPGMaker title and has opted for a more realistic visual style especially when it comes to character design. Graphically the title is absolutely fantastic and is also without a doubt the best looking RPGMaker game out there hands down. From the set pieces to the character portraits in the cutscene dialogue, everything looks terrific. With that said, the title retains a dark and dreary look color-wise probably due to the bleak nature of the narrative which fits perfectly in my opinion. Also of note, the sound quality is excellent whether it's gameplay, ambient background noises or the dystopian flavored musical score which is superb I might add. In summary, the sleek graphical style and wonderful audio really compliment the great combat and excellent narrative in this title.
City Of Chains is definitely the best RPGMaker title that I've played on Steam even going so far as to knock my previous favorite "Skyborn" off the throne. The dark sci-fi setting, compelling narrative, non-linear gameplay and wonderful turn-based strategic combat come together to create quite the exciting adventure. There are three difficulty modes-Casual, Hardy, Dystopia and given the number of weapons and skills to select for your team as well as the many decisions to be made throughout the story the replay value of this game is quite high. Option-wise there are Steam Achievements and Steam Trading Cards to collect and although the great soundtrack is not available as an extra option you can, thankfully, find the tracks in the game files so they are completely free and readily available. In just a short time I have fallen in love with this soundtrack as it is really good. In summary, I would HIGHLY RECOMMEND City Of Chains to R.P.G., Strategy and Cyberpunk fans as well as anyone looking to go on a great adventure in a dystopian futurisic setting where choice actually matters in the storyline.

Plagued by a sudden and insatiable urge to investigate a mysterious, far away sawmill in a remote, Italian countryside, a man tries to uncover the source of his fevered visions and sense of familiarity with a place he has no recollection of ever visiting, despite evidence to the contrary. His search leads him to unearth a gruesome history of the abandoned dwelling and its past inhabitants, and in particular to the story of Anna, a woman who seems to somehow be at the heart of it all. But to what end?
A first person horror game set almost entirely within a single, modestly sized building, players are tasked with solving puzzles to both progress exploration and to reveal the story related to each room and/or the part the items involved in each puzzle played in past events. But the deeper you delve into the mystery, the more your sanity and reality are called into question as the world begins to change around you and conspire against your efforts. Presentation is stunning as the visuals, sound and overall design are the beating heart around which this games revolves and reason enough to play it through from start to finish.
UI is largely intuitive but can confound on occasion as there's no explanation of its more intricate workings necessary for fully uncovering the story. In fact, that probably also sums up just about every aspect of the gameplay here. Satisfying and frustrating in equal measure, for every part of the game that there is to enjoy, there's also as many flaws as the puzzles and story become increasingly convoluted towards its conclusion. Since quite a few of the puzzles are based around performing rites and rituals, it means the player has no natural process of logic or intelligence to apply to the solution, but instead must pick up on the clues or directions provided by the game, which at times can prove annoyingly obtuse.
But don't let that stop you. Despite its shortcomings (one of the biggest of which is the unneccesary DRM which requires that you create an account with Kalypso Media in order to run the game. A process that feels incredibly archaic at this stage in our chosen pastime), that still doesn't stop it from being a worthwhile and gratifying experience, for nothing else if not for providing one of the singular most startling scares I've had in a game to date (mind how you go in the artisan room!). Anna - Extended Edition also includes the original game released prior to the free update which overhauled a massive amount of the game to include a myriad of new content and greatly expands upon the story and its surrounding lore. In comparion, the extended edition makes the original seem like a skeleton without its flesh and really should only be played after finishing the latest version just to see how far the game has come and how much effort developer Dreampainters went to in order to craft an experience that stays with you long after the credits have finished rolling.

I've played this game since right after it started. Over 3 years. When it first started wow what a breath of fresh air. That was back when it was in Flash and before you could even relocate. Everything was simple then. You researched ships and tech for your base and fought along side your friends against others. Blueprints were introduced and the first event came around. All good still. I still enjoyed playing and felt like the company really wanted the best for the players in balance with still making money off coins. I didn't coin and you could still enjoy the game very much without doing that. Met some great people online and things still were good. Around a year ago their best Community rep left and that's when things went down hill VERY fast. Kixeye started making promises and not following through with them. Things were gettting ninja nerfed and that started making people realize things were changing for the worse. Communication happened with less frequency from the company and then the switch to Unity said goodby to Flash for good.
More new blueprints and features came along (a lot of which the community never wanted) and tweaks to the stats of ships and combat modules started muddling what was once a simple game. Events and mini-events started happening more often and most of the time the prizes were less than spectacular. Mobile was introduced and then things really went down the drain. Kixeye started offering discounts on in-game money and giving crazy bonuses to coin bundles. Alliance features were added a bit before the mobile was but mobile was the start of the official end of this game as I had come to know it. Coin to win had officially taken over the game. I still stuck around because I had been in the game for a while and had most of the ships and tech and had good friends. Events started getting very difficult to do with the enemy dealing out huge damage to those grinding for prizes. Several of the events were so geared towards coining that I didn't even bother. Now "crafting" comes along. So begins the new grinding for parts that were tough to come across and would not drop when they were supposed to. People were getting upset. Answers to our questions were given a in a kind of blanket way and promises were thrown around some to never be fulfilled at all.
Fast forward to a handful of weeks ago and Kixeye informs us that there is going to be a "rebalancing." What that meant was that all the time we had been grinding for parts and making new upgraded ships, was soon to be rendered completely irrelevant. Every single ship was getting changed. Every. One. Shield energy was getting slashed and armor damage repair on heavy ships was about to go through the roof. Not only that, they said every ship class was getting their speed changed to match each ship in that class. So an easily researched ship was now the exact same speed as an event ship you had to grind for (in each class). Mass of items stayed the same but their energy/damage resistance went way down.  Many other similarly ridiculous changes are also to be introduced soon. The community erupted in mass disapproval of course. Overnight dozens of threads in the forums were posted and people were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I've never seen so many thumbs down on the thread Kix released about the changes coming. It was easily 95% negative. So after that the founder of Kix did an online interview where he basically avoided all direct questions regarding how wrong this all was. The community managers haven't properly addressed this yet at all. Negative threads continue to show up dozens by the day and no proper response yet. Nearly everyone in the community hates this idea and doesn't want it. Free players and coiners alike. They don't care. They already released the first part of this "rebalance." Two more to come.
Do not play this game. It looks great and had potential a few years ago but the company only cares about a flood of new money coming from mobile and has no desire to keep vetran players. They have ZERO long-term vision. They ignore the community as a whole and just do what they feel like. What started as a beautiful flower planted in fertile ground has since been dug up and replanted within a field of weeds where it's being suffocated to death. Avoid this company like the plague.

The skill choices aren't limited in any way other than being less effective if you use certain weapons. The skills require a "charge" and unlock more powerful versions once you've leveled up the skills enough.
Story-wise it has some solid moments. A cinematic-driven story with a lot of humor/comic relief. There are some potential plot twists starting to evolve and that may give the story a bit of a turn and spice things up a bit. Overall while i'm not a fan of story/cinema in games, it was enjoyable and not too dramatic or overdone like what a lot of titles do.
Creativity-wise, there is a recipe-driven crafting system. You essentially grind some items and are able to put the items together and figure out what the "unknown item" is. The character's house is being implemented and there is potential that players will be able to add particular items to that house, and perhaps in a certain order. Other than that players also have some room on choosing their combat style. A player may be a meteor summoning "shieldmaiden" that uses a magical spear instead of the typical sword/staff.
Other than that there's still a lot of the game being developed. This review was for a particular steam badge. ;) I'd have written a review upon official release instead of during early access, and likely will udpate this review once SoG is complete.

Because this game is so early in development, this review is bound to change as the developers continue to work on it.
Collision Course does not have much to offer at this stage. It is set in an expansive prehistoric world populated with hostile people and a variety of dinosaurs. The dinosaurs themselves are very well done. The models are outstanding, and the animations and AI work well as threats to the player. The environment is also done well, as it feels realistic and huge. Some areas feel like they are pulled right from an episode of Walking with Dinosaurs. The world is made more alive by the game's dynamic natural events. Meteor strikes and earthquakes happen at random. There are also human enemies in the world, which are alright. Unfortunately, there is not much to do in the game (yet). The only objectives are to survive and collect supplies. Although this has not happened to me, I can see how some people might get bored after a while. (There are, however, certain hidden secrets that you can search for. I won't spoil them here.)
One of the game's best aspects is its potential. The developers have made it clear that this release is very bare-bones. The final product will have much more to do, including a developing storyline revolving around an impending asteroid impact. This is why I recommend Collision Course-the existing product is a great starting point for a fully fleshed-out game.

This game is very promising. It may be early access but don't let that deter you as it has tons of content to keep you interested. If you're a fan of games like Final Fantasy, the Legend of Zelda, Fantasy Life or other similar RPG games you'll find joy here. The 4th Wall is something it likes to smash down quite often as you'll come across many Easter Eggs and reference, one being the Triforce laying on the ground or a character mentioning "/" commands. Secrets of Grindea knows it's a video game and uses that to it's pleasure since it allows it to make tons of jokes. Heck you start out from a town called "Startington".
The characters are also quite pleasing to meet. Your father has a backstory and a driving motive that I find interesting to explore, as you plung further into the game his past is opened up to a point where you realize you aren't the only character of importance running around Grindea. The games controls seemed odd to me at first but I later came to admire how well they work. The arrow keys act as your movement while Z & X are your sword and shield. You have items and skills linked to the A,S,D,F,G,Q,W,E,R,T keys which can each be rebinded. I tried to change them around but I find it much more comfortable to use the defaults.
I definitely recommend this game to any fans of RPGs and in-game collecting.

Now, I'm not the biggest fan of platform games. I used to have pretty much no choice but to play them having grown up with the likes of Sonic The Hedgehog and Super Mario World, but never did have any real patience or skill, 3D platformers made that a lot easier later on, like with Spyro the Dragon and those became bigger favourites, though still far from my most favourite genre (if I can ever decide what that is! I love RPGs, but RPGs can be platformers, point & click, FPS...)
Still, having won this game over at
from a kind user giving away a copy (I've given away well over a hundred games myself too, all different.) I entered a couple of others before winning, as you do, but only enter for games I believe I will eventually play fairly, either to completion or at least invest a few hours, no matter how long that takes.
Never Alone somehow quickly rose to the top of my play list. I'd heard good things about its play style, characters, art style... You name it. In-particular stories from why others had it on their wishlists, which would vary from wanting the trading cards to loving the idea of playing the fox. One person even commented they'd planned to play with their younger brother, but had kept arguing over who'd play who! Numa or the Fox.
Advertised as co-op, I had no idea how would play both characters at once, but the AI was (mostly) top-notch, a little silly at some points, but it was easy to swap between characters, and many of the puzzles were interesting, fun and requiring a little thought, usually just to slow down and think them through. It even kept me interested for the entire time I played, though my heart skipped a beat at one scene
The added short videos are well worth watching too, for they tell the story of the Alaskan natives and how they have survived in that environment. Their culture, history and how they live in their communities, in many respects, a lesson much of the world also needs to learn once more.
In short, we'd break this down into positives and negatives.
Overall, I definitely can recommend the game. It stands out to me as a game suitable for those both experienced and new to the platforming genre looking for something a little more casual yet addicting.

I really like this game. The world looks great and the dinosaurs as well.
There is a lot to explore and some strange surprises I don't fully understand yet.
So far I have found a gun, a crashed pod with some loot such as stim packs, energy cells and a steel bar as melee weapon. The encounters with AI have been scary and intense, especially when I ran into some
Robot guy that was guarding the crashsite (Wasn't able to kill him so I ran away). In the jungle there where humans running around and one of them started shooting at me the second he saw me. But I was able to sneak up on some of them as well and punch them in the face to then take the loot they where carrying. When it comes to the dinosaurs I have to say that they are a highlight for me in this game. In my first few minutes of playing I had a Tyrannosaurus come at me and chase me through the jungle. It was so scary and since then I'm sneaking through the woods trying to avoid the dinosaurs as best as I can.
There are view things that I want to point out as well though: I don't think that Collision Course is for everybody. It has a bunch of bugs and there is a lot of walking around and sneaking involved. People who are a bit inpatient or are looking for a game with non stop action could get bored after a while I guess. Another thing is that there is no real description of how to do things. After two hours of playing I found out how to use consumables and that you can punch crates you'll find in the world to loot them. Personally I like that the game doesn't tell you all the stuff you can or have to do but I have seen some videos of people who got annoyed by that (Items have descriptions when you hover over them with your mouse guys!).
Overall I have to say that I'm having a really good time with Collision Course so far and that I'm going to play a lot more of it. It would be nice to have more items, weapons and stuff like that but looking at the roadmap the developers have posted I am convinced that they will work on that and eventually will make this a really awesome survival/adventure game.

Hands down one of my favorite games that i've played so far. It's very simple, the gameplay isn't groundbreaking, the art style is pleasing, good music and the story is fantastic.
The Good:
+Culture- Not many games bring this into play. This game does an amazing job of representing the culture of the people they based their game off. From the music, to the art style, to narration, to the in-game videos, and to how the entire game is based around the notion of oral history/story telling.
+Music- It has a very beautiful and mezmorizing soundtrack that added quite a bit to the overall experience.
+Gameplay- Works with a 360 controller without any fiddling around, is responsive and very straight forward.
+Graphics- I really like the aesthetic of the game. It's not a super demanding game, in fact I can see this eventually making its way to IOS or Android, graphics are really crisp at 1080p and look good.
The Bad:
-Basic-It's a very easy, straight forward and (sometimes) boring game.
-One Difficulty Fits All- I wish this had different modes or challenges, but oh well.
-No Rewind for Videos- If you miss something in the in-game interview videos, you have to rewatch again.
Overall:
This game is a story and it plays like one. It's not that challenging, the graphics aren't amazaballs, and you can play through it (probably) in one sitting. But the creators did justice to the people they based the story off. The interviews are interesting, the way the story is told is beautiful, the art style (while I still think it could have been better) is really nice and the game is an enjoyable playthrough.
If you're looking for a nice challenging platformer, maybe just skip this one and watch a playthrough. If you're looking for a casual game to kill an evening, and has an interesting story to boot, this one is for you.
