TL;DR:
- The story is the most important part
- Go into the game blind to any information
- Take your time to investigate what happened - There's a mod to disable monsters attacking you, but doesn't interfere with the story and removes most of the horror elements. Use this mod if you feel the horror element causes you hesitation with purchasing the game
- At full price the game is worth buying
---
This is a story-driven game that is thought provoking and challenges your morality at times. I definitely recommend taking the time to learn everything you can about the world around you. The decisions you'll have to make don't have 'right' answers. Seriously. Don't bother looking up what you should do unless you're absolutely stuck. This won't/shouldn't happen often as the game gives hints if you're paying attention and is fairly linear. I say not to look it up because it's very easy to spoil parts of the story that are simply better by experiencing it yourself.
There is also additional content on their official site that contains some interesting parts of the lore and short stories. The coin flip story is my favorite.
Again I say: I don't recommend blowing past all the interesting materials to read and listen to, which are spread around across the levels. You get to experience the story for the first time once. There are stories and information about those that were there before you that are worth the time to investigate.
There *is* a mod available to make monsters not attack you, which changes the gameplay and kind of emphasizes tragedy over horror. I'd recommend getting this mod if you don't want to deal with the horror elements. Avoiding the horror elements allows you to not have to rush parts of the levels, giving you more freedom to explore.
The only cons I can think of is that replayability isn't high; it's equivalent to watching a movie. Another one is that spoilers can really ruin the experience and wikis are rife with spoilers.
I wish I could experience this game again for the first time because it's just so damn good. It's even fun just watching a friend play through it to see what they do.
And yes, we all spent a solid ten minutes fiddling with the stuff around the apartment at the beginning.

Still, I had a hard time doing so, particularly during sequences requiring speed -like while being chased. Also, during that first round it seemed the guy chasing you could KO you from a distance and while the girl was on a ledge, which became quite frustrating... R6 is a REALLY good game with a not-so-steep learning curve and a good wealth of playable operators. Progression is easy and well paced, for example, after playing through situations and 3-starring each one, you are gifted around 6,000 credits which can be used to purchase a good amount of operators to get you started. Or you can use those credits to customise a few specific operators with attachments or cosmetics to show your devotion to those operators. After that, playing through casual games to rank 20 can be a drag but you can use the time to hone your skills and improve your aim and teamwork.
Once you reach ranked, the game becomes completely different. The skill required to compete goes up and you will have to learn and adapt to other teams strategies and playstyles. This, I believe, provides an experience you wont find anywhere else! Besides, this is one of the only games Ubisoft hasnt butchered so yeah, enjoy it for what it is.
I highly recommend buying, strictly because of how fun and well thought out each game can be. Wether you're playing Casual and looking for a quick fix or as a warm up, or playing Ranked and going head to head with Ace players and Crackshots to compete and gain rank. That and Terrorist Hunt isnt too bad and the situations act as a long winded tutorial for the game.

While I do recommend this game, I personally wanted more from it. I think I jumped into this game thinking it was something different.
Episode 1 was stupidly fantastic to me. Gripping story, awesome plot twist and genuenly spooky. I've never been a fan of text based adventures because I always thought they'd be too difficult to play. But I really enjoyed it, I never had too much trouble navigating the house, although I did want to be more thorough.. like looking in the fridge or trying to find the key to the utility door.. but it was a really awesome play.
It kind of reminded me of those old goosebump books, readers beware you choose the scare! where you could pick your own adventure by doing different things throughout your readings. It was always such fun figuring out differnet ways it could end! So I went back into episode 1 to see if I could get a different ending by finding that utlity key, alas, couldn't find it and ended up being the same ending. Thats alright, it was still a good story so I kept my hopes high for something just as good in the second episode..
Unfortunately it fell a bit short for me- it really is my own fault for thinking it was a complete text-adventure. Some of the puzzles became not too difficult, but extremely tedious- I felt like in the first chapter I was so enthralled with the story and the pacing that I was excited to see what happened next. I kept pushing through the painfully dull "click certain things to progress" bits because I wanted to see if the next episode would be better. Episode 3 had me really interested in what was going on at the weather station but I felt a little held back typing in code that I kept having to look back at the monitor to memorise.. I ended up having to grab a piece of paper from my cupboard to write things down- it pulled me out of the mood a bit. The walking section of the game surprised me- I was bracing myself to be thrilled by a plot twist but ehhhh.
I admit to actually just watching the last episode via youtube- because i honestly had lost alot of my hype for the game and wanted to see the ending, to see if the story was any good. I was left a little disappointed.
TL:DR
Game is visually awesome, opening of the episodes was snazzy. But I was looking forward to episodic text-adventures that had awesome plot twists, but somehow interconnected. story fell a bit short and gameplay can become tedious.

TL,DR version: buy the game, it is a good one, but don't expect a Jagged Alliance 2. (30 october 2014)
Jagged Alliance Flashback is a good game, with the potential to become even better when the planned upgrades are finished.
It has been a bit of a rush to get it finalized, it still feels a little incomplete / rough without things like weapon atachments and a polished interface. Still, I like the game in its current state and I am looking forward to its future.
Please note: Flashback is often compared to Jagged Alliance 2 (or sometimes Back in Action), which are bad comparisons. Flashback gameplay feels much more like the "classic" Jagged Alliance 1, it is smaller in scale than Jagged Aliance 2 and offers less interactions. Back in Action was a (failed, in my opinion) attempt to create a Jagged Alliance game with a modern style. I really disliked its "Plan and Go" real-time / pause mode, and think the re-enactment of JA2s story was weird at best.
I am a huge fan of the Jagged Alliance series, I own (and played) all the games, and I do think JA2 and especially the fan-made 1.13 version are the pinnacle of the series - JA2 1.13 is THE one game I would choose for that shipwrecked-on-an-island scenario. Jagged Alliance Flashback is no match for it, but still a good game that I never regretted backing on Kickstarter, and it is WAY better than the bad reviews it is getting right now, shortly after its release.

This is a great idea, performed only adeqately, with very limited diversity in song choices. They had the chance to make this game completely top notch but they settled for much less IMO and are really grubbing of the money about it too. I'm very disappointed that you cannot purchase all of the DLC at the advertised prices. Only the DLC specific to Rocksmith 2014. Otherwise you have to purchase the original Rocksmith ($29.99 right now on Steam and Amazon) and then another $10 tool to import the songs into Rocksmith 2014. Then you have to pay for the $3.00 song that you wanted in the first place. They are just sticking it in and twisting it, coming and going.
They should have had some finger-picking and classical rock songs included but nothing like that. No rockabilly or hot rod sounding rock (like Commander Cody, Junior Brown, Johnny Cash). No real good blues rock either (Gary Moore, Seasick Steve and the like). I mean what artist wouldn't want millions of people learning their songs the correct way? How hard is it to sign up these artists? Well those are the main bad points about the game IMO.
The good? Well it does a pretty good job of recognizing my guitar's notes for the most part although I have to repeat notes sometimes in the arcade games. Many of the songs are also very good and seem to be complete including multiple (dual) leads. There are tons of great sounds and effects for the guitar and lots made up specifically for the featured songs. You can slow the song without changing pitch with the riff repeater, allowing you to really zone in on tough licks. I also really like Session mode which really made me think a lot more about chord tones. There should have been some lessons for recognizing and utilizing them more effectively.
I like the game. It's really more of a practice tool and its pretty effective as that. I have recommended it to friends and other musicians I know. Its just that I believe they could have done the game better and they probably will in the future ( I hope anyways)

As much as I wanna recommend this game (I really support indipendent developers) this is not a game that I will support, upvote, like, share or whatever cool kids do to make games popular.
I played nearly 10 minutes and then I had to restart my computer. It seems like the game froze my system without even closing. It kept running while the whole desktop was just, frozen. Another flaw is its availability for older PCs. Take for example Warface. I could run it in 60 fps with my 2012 laptop. This game ran at 12 fps at minimal settings and didn't even match the detail level of Warface. Now, I can understand that a company such as Crytek can spend more time and money to make such compatibility real, but really this could be better as I can run many many games with a laptop.
When you first start up the game, you will apparently need to... well, install it. I wasn't checking when it was doing it so I don't know if it was an external program needed to run the game, but still, after waiting 20 minutes for the 4 GBs to download and then having to wait 30 more for whatever-it-was do install was a bit frustrating for the 10 minutes that I played.
When you start the game you will be launched into a """character creation""" menu. It's not even character, it's just "Here, choose the face that you won't be able to see for the rest of the game." and that's it. You then get straight up thrown in a match with a simple tutorial on the controls. This brings us to the next part of the review.
Probably 99.9% of the people that downloaded this did it because it says FPS and not because you like post-apocalyptic flowers. Well, the gun handling is awful. I tried using a PPSH or whatever it's called and the recoil was absolutely nuts. I had to slam my mouse down to even hit a single shot.

There are no classes but there are three weapon choices when you die, a PPSH, and Winchester and a shotgun. Not sure what the difference between the Winchester and the shotgun is, tho. I can't know it since my PC crashed 9 minutes into the first match. I didn't challenge my poor Windows again to try and run it.
1. It really bothers me how you just get thrown in a match without even being able to look through the menus and understand what everything does, You only have about 30 seconds to maybe change your settings and get prepared for a match.
2. Anomalies. What the hell are they? As I said various times I only played about 30 minutes of this and don't know any story, if there is. I just know that you should never approach flowers surrounded by a green mystical aura. They kill you.
3. Factions. There are 4 factions that all have different weapons and abilities but I can't really talk about it since the damn game crashed again after mULTIPL- [DATA EXPUNGED]
4. It did it again. Do you know when you're playing an FPS or any other fast paced game and the mouse just pops up? It just pops up and look at you like "Hey bro I'm chilling here can't play now." YES. It happened every 20 seconds and I couldn't do anything but wait for it to stop loading (for some reason it was the loadin mouse icon) until I could be able to play again.
5. Graphics. I don't know. It looks like any other free fps game. It looks like royalty free graphics, honestly.
In the end, I'm sorry for the developers but I really can't recommend this. If you put more time listening to what we want and what we have to say maybe this could become a success. From some videos that I saw the gun upgrades and other features look neat, but I can't get to them if the game crashes my computer every two seconds.

It also doesn't seem to understand prepositional phrases; it first tasks you with finding the generator "around back" of the house, but attempting to type "go to back of house" (it doesn't use north/east/south/west room linkings like most text adventures) has it attempt to open the front door instead. There really is no time or space or cash for a bad text adventure (even with a cutesy 3D shell) in 2017.

Buyers beware, this game is less feature-rich, less entertaining and less professionally-made than it's beloved predecessor, JA2.
It's easy to be critical of series sequels, especially those made by a new company. The fact is that fans of the series were hoping for a new installment in the beloved series which would harken back to the good old days of a stubborn Fidel, broken-language Ivan, cheerfully deadly Scully and mysterious and powerful Magic.
Those characters are present, along with much of the classic cast. The problem is not the characters, but alas, Jagged Alliance is about much more. I played Jagged Alliance upon it's release, and Jagged Alliance 2 years later. Sir-Tech's vision of a modern mercenary group in an XCOM style of gameplay was brilliant, and I didn't even discover XCOM until much later.
Flashback, however, offers none of the strategic delights of roaming a jungle and hiding behind trees, glimpsing enemies for a moment before they fade out and flank you, or sneaking around buildings to approach enemies stealthily and take them out. You move your units in a turn-based manner, you equip them with various weapons and gear you find or purchase in your travels, but that is where the similarities end.
Tactical combat is a joke, with a poorly designed interrupt system which rarely triggers despite having an experienced teamate facing the enemy around a blind corner. ranges are ridiculous, and weapons fall off to a 0% chance to hit at such a short range that early combat takes place within 4 squares by necessity, and marksmen with an 85% score rarely have above a 60% chance to hit a center-body shot even at that range.
The result is a grindy slugfest wherein utilizing good tactics for cover and concealment and positioning and intersecting fields of fire fails to draw out enemy mercenaries into makeshift kill-zones and enable your team to kill them with minor injuries. Perhaps this was intentional, but for me... the tactical advantages gained by good positioning and approach techniques were a big part of the game. Sadly, this is not the only shortcoming Flashback exhibits.
The sectors are largely empty. Gone are the days of finding secret crates stashed back in a corner of a sector, looting it and finding that much-needed lockpick or ammunition of flak vest. Perhaps they have populated some key sectors with these things, but in the four starting areas there's not so much as a single crate to be found - and believe me, I scoured the zones. So while they have filled the zones will all kinds of terrain features to fill up the squares, there is nothing to interact with to make exploring sectors and looting buildings in any way interesting, which was a huge part of the JA series experience.
The UI is clunky and unintuitive, and it fails to offer some of the more interesting dynamic features of JA2 - that is, line of sight cones and rooftop access. The diversity of available weapons - which has no option to raise or lower - simply makes the entire game more difficult, decreasing the likelihood that you will find weapons or ammunition on enemy corpses which match those your party is using. The dialogue screen is almost identical to JA2, which is not a compliment - dialogue was one of JA2's weak points - but falls short of even that in failing to provide more than a very simple and linear dialogue. Where at least JA2 gave certain mood-flavors to your responses, Flashback offers only prewritten script which fails to cover any reasonable range of optional responses.
The English is bad. I realize this is an overseas company who bought the IP, but really... the English is bad, in a finished game product which is supposed to be the professional and legitimate successor to a great franchise. Grammar is where the main mistakes are, but the mistakes are grating when you consider you're paying for a professional product. Using "is" instead of "are" and "them" instead of "it" where appropriate may seem a petty criticism, but my eyes get crossed and I have to reread the already-boring dialogue because somebody didn't do a decent proof-read of their script before release, and it's annoying. Some may not care, but it's still worth noting in a list of the shortfalls of the product.
There are glitches. Sadly, this is to be expected of most modern games, and I won't detail them. They are numerous, but the ones I discovered are relatively minor and akin to what you will find in most games shortly after release.
Overall it seems the company was looking to make a quick buck on a popular franchise, released a comic-sketch version of the mature and gritty mercenary game, and decided to call it a day. Four stinging chapters, one intense story, and a partridge in a pear tree. [/song]
‘I did not see that coming’ I said to myself followed by ‘All right, now this is going to get really good’, and I was only halfway through the first chapter. What begins as a powerful WTF moment in an SF experience in chapter one (echoes of ‘Inception’ the movie) evolves into an intense reality check by chapter four. Caveat Emptor: All will the find the last chapter emotionally unnerving. Embrace the experience.
Story: Am I a hostage in a CIA experiment? Is this a dream or Area51? A dream within a dream? or is my mind failing? What am I hiding? Have you ever been the passenger? I have.
Game mechanics: Text adventure style (imo poor parsing compared to classic z-interpreter games), puzzles based on complex instructions, and some 3D thrown-in for the sake of variety. It comes together very nicely, perfect for my ADD.
The playthrough is short @2 hrs and worth every penny if you need different. The only real negative that I can come up with is a significant part of this game uses 1/3 of the screen for text based entry and reply; if you are on a very small screen like 11 inches you might find this tough.

One of the reviews says "gameplay is perfectly balanced (although a bit hard at the beginning)", this apparently means facing enemies with seemingly 2000+ health when your party has a combined pool of 800 heath. This was on casual difficulty and thats just the leader, not including his lackies. After using all my items, ammo, abilities and reloaded multiple times I still couldn't beat him.
I say "seemingly" cause you can't actually see enemy health, you have to guess which makes combat decisions rather clouded. I couldn't tell if my strategies made any diffirence or if I ever came close to winning, for all I know he has 10 000 health. When all your ammo and items are gone the fight is reduced to mashing spacebar and hoping, or you can try and predict his target and make them "Defend" which only drags out the fight or does nothing depending on your predictions.
There is very little in the way of settings but I didn't really expect there to be. Besides changing the background color there is a resolution option that switches too fast to select the one you want but that doesn't matter cause the resolution never changes anyway. You can remap your keys but since whole thing is played with 2+movement keys that is mostly useless.
At the end of all this I have only one question: How did this game get "Very Positive" reviews?

The story is well made, gameplay is perfectly balanced (although a bit hard at the beginning) and the "levelling" System gives the game a pleasent new touch.
you are beeing taking captive by the police and suddenly find yourself in a prison breakout and while trying to escape make some friends, with the goal of escaping the city.

Avoiding battles is a MUST on higher difficulties, due to them yielding NO XP and just a few coins and ressources, often leading to a loss rather than a reward for fighting, so you often need to think: "should i really fight those, or should i sneak by?", luckily there are many routes and even the possibility to knock enemies out (single) or toss a grenade at them (multiple) Fun fact: you can knock people out by "sneaking" up on them, but mostly i litarly run right into them and they not even notice! XD
you don't get any XP in CoC instead you'll receive Skill points to use after each mission. Normally I don't like games like this. It's got turn-based JRPG-style combat, which I usually hate. It's made in RPG Maker, which in my opinion is a trash-spewing engine. The graphics are in an old school 90's poop-and-vomit color palette.
To my own surprise however I really enjoyed this game. Like I said I don't really play these sort of games so idk, but the controls felt nice and innovative in a way. You could probably play this game with a NES controller as the most used buttons are the arrow keys, Z and X. The way menus are designed took a bit of learning but once you get the hang of it they are really nice to use. The combat system has you queue up actions for your entire party and then pressing 'Execute', which I liked way more than the standard turn-based system I've seen in games like Final Fantasy. The party has an interesting variety of skills and abilities, and a surprising amount of them are usable outside of combat.
The story is decently written, even pretty interesting towards the end, and to be honest what I liked the most was that it's pretty short and all the side missions are in some way related to the main missions.
All in all a tight and focused take at the old school RPGs that even haters like lil' ol' me can enjoy.

For the price, probably the best vertical shmup on steam, but is has some things going for it that deserve extra attention. However, below are my first impressions after one complete play through on normal.
Difficulty: On normal I completed a run the first time I played it with about 4 lives remaining. I'm an average shmup player. The normal difficulty should be manageable for even beginning players.  However, even though I completed it without that much difficulty, I wasn't bored except for a few moments here or there. The pacing and challenge is balanced really well overall.
Pros:
+ Controls (for the most part they are good)
+ Visuals (The promo video did not make that great of an impression on me as it looked a bit bland and stiff. I ended up buying the game based on the reviews. As opposed to many other shmups, you can clearly tell at all times, where your ship is, where your hit box is, and where the bullets are. What seemed bland in the video is actually a judicious design choice.)
+ Variety of unique bullet patterns.
+ Music is pretty good and fits the atmosphere well.
+ Character art is well done.
+ Power up and bonus system is fun.
Neutral point:
- (MINOR) While the controls are good and tight, they might be a tad too tight compared to what people are used to in a Cave shmup.
Cons:
- Limited enemy types and sprites.
Future feature 'wish':
This game would really benefit from a bullet grinding system for points for all characters.
Summary:
Considering it was primarily developed by a single developer, this indie shmup, while a bit rough around some edges, is a real gem and it deserves the attention of die hard and beginning shmup fans. Definitely worth the price.

I played this game for many hours, but that doesn't make it good.
The "servers" are terrible. It's never going to get better, because it's flawed on a fundamental level. It's always going to be peer-to-peer, and that's always going to be a detriment. I've lost duels over it, I've had terrible matches because of it, I've lost entire games' worth of progress because of it, and it takes FOREVER to get into a game even when it's a "very high" populated playlist; all because the system takes a year and a half just to find eight people with decent connection to one another. If someone rage-quits, it will almost always stop you mid-fight until everyone re-synchronizes. That is, if it can reconnect everyone to a new host at all.
Updates are just slow enough to feel excruciating waiting for them to buff the weak classes you want to play, or nerf the class so easy that everyone plays it. When updates do come? It's a minor tweak, a bug fix for a bug you've never seen or heard of, and maybe a few patterns or emotes. The new "outfits" that get added are extremely overpriced bundles of patterns, symbols, a color scheme and an ornament that you can't get any other way. It takes *days* of grinding to get enough currency to unlock them; they're not really worth it but they're about the only thing to grind out the currency for once you get the few direct currency-based unlocks you wanted for your character.
You might see me racking up more hours when new characters get released, or checking out a new map, but I'm in $100+ deep. I DO NOT recommend that you follow my lead.
Second-Season update: The Gear stats are handled better now, but the new characters are plainly better than their Launch counterparts. One of them completely disables the player for long, inescapable combos, and the other literally teleports around spamming unstoppable kicks into free damage. Neither get a great deal of health, but fighting either is excruciating. There's just nothing to be done, if you don't manage to perfectly parry/dodge the Centurion, you just lose a huge chunk of your health. Blocking won't cut it. When fighting the Shinobi, you pretty much need to have precognition in order to get a hit in. It just comes down to luck, whether you guessed their move right or whether they get to take 1/3 of your health with no counter-play.
Somehow, I hate this game even more in Season 2. I desperately wish for my money back, so that I could spend it on literally anything else.
Third-Season update: The Gladiator released in a pretty decent state, or at least reached that point by week 2 when I broke down and gave the game another shot. The Highlander is so  bad it's ridiculous. The mechanical concept of holding Heavy to access a second moveset of Super Heavy attacks is neat, but in practice it's extremely fickle and supremely impractical. Heavy attacks are already the worst attacks in the game unless you can *force* them to connect, so giving a class very slow attacks across the board supplemented by even *slower* Super Heavy attacks is just asking to get whaled on.
As always, jumping into AI matches is fine, if excruciatingly slow from a matchmaking and progression standpoint. It seems they adjusted the rate at which higher-level AI are chosen to populate the enemy team, because every so often one of them will be surprisingly competent. It's made the AI matches a little more fun, even though there's still never any chance that the AI team will give players a run for their money.
If you're waiting for the "turtle meta" to die off, S3 still hasn't made it happen. Every duel with another player, we're either making loving eye contact for an hour or they're parrying anything and everything thrown their way. I guess you can still argue that the matches are *partially* skill-based, but more often than not it doesn't matter what buttons you hit. Characters and combos are chosen specifically to prevent any kind of opposing interruption. If you hit a wall, you *will* eat the heavy, which chains into an unavoidable punch that knocks you down, which allows them to do an undodgeable ground stab, and so on. Throws into charges, people punching or kicking you into an endless state of exhaustion, you name it. That's still For Honor. I think this is my third play-session, and I'm already wondering why I keep booting it up.
Halloween Update: They added a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥-looking masks that activate the same way that idle/execution/emote effects do. You can buy them for 15K ♥♥♥♥ing steel along with yet another set of ugly, busy little emblems to adorn your character. For the two-week event, a special game mode turns all the little soldiers into skeletons that deal very high damage. It's a mildly interesting twist on Dominion, but one match with a "randomly" matched Rep ~10 squad against a Rep 50+ squad killed any enthusiasm I had for playing during the event or for the rest of Season 3.

Man oh man, devolution on a grand scale.
I got Force unleashed 1 for xbox 360 during 2008 or might have been 2009, i liked the game, i knew it had flaws, things that could have been done better, but it wasnt bad. The game was fun, had variety, felt like a god of war clone casted into Star wars mold, both things i absolutely love. Then came news of the sequel, i though that it would be a chance to improve on things, to play through new locations, beat new Star wars characters into submission. Then, the reviews poured in, i was dissapointed, never got the game after that. Fast forward to year of our lord, 2017, bought it from a sale for 2€. Yeah, not much, but still felt like a waste of my money.
Lets do some comparing to the original title.
First up, lenght. I remember Force unleashed 1 beign a bit on the shorter side, something like 9-10h mark, might be a bit more with the DLC lvls that came with it. Call that a short game? i just beat Force unleashed 2 in about three hours. So thats the first obvious problem.
Well, as if that wasnt enough, the game is simplified, stripped of content.
The original game had 7 different location + 2 or 3 from the DLC, you had places like Hoth, Kashyyk, Death star, Jedi temple, Tattoine. Things like that, you know, classic Star Wars locations, more so, they provided variation, one level was filled with snow, another one was a desert, you got the Wookie homeworld and jungles, these location also provided variety in enemies (and bosses)
Instead of using that unending potential of possible locations from the Star wars universe to base the maps in, what do we get? 4 maps, each of them basically a shipping yard, warehouse, assemble area or some other inside location. Filled with about 4 different types of enemies.  The first game also had many boss fights, ranchors, giant tentacle monsters. and some more familiar faces like Obi van Kenobi, Proxy droid of Darth maul, Boba Fett, Luke and other Jedis and the obvious Vader + Palpatine. A bunch of memorable characters. now what does the second game offer us? The Gorog. which is a hulk on steroids, Terror walker which is a robot and Vader. Thats it. The list is short and unmemorable, except for the, again, obvious Vader fight.
Then the combat, Force unleashed 1 had the basic force powers like dash, grip, lightning, the basic works, but it also had a God of War style system where you get orbs from killing enemies, which you can use to buy new combos and attack moves for the lightsaber, you had plenty of different combos, some which used different force powers during the attacks, in the second game you have the same force powers, but instead of different combos, you get light attack and heavy attack.
So, at the end of the day, its bad, disgusting. It makes me wonder what the hell were they thinking? what was the point of this game, i red somewhere that 90% of the people who made the first game were in the team that made this one, how did they not see how much the game went backwards with literally EVERY aspect, well, except graphics i guess. How did they dare to sell this with the full price tag of triple A games. I genuinely feel bad for people who paid more then some trivial sum of a few euros for this game.
If you want a Star wars game where you can run around destroying things with force powers, a laid back, straightforward but entertaining baggage, get Force unleashed 1. But stay away from this one.
Greed is a path to the dark side indeed.

There's a fascinating documentary here, the problem being that it's unlocked by playing a beautiful yet mediocre and extremely frustrating platform game. Said game starts off promisingly; it looks great, it's full of atmosphere, it has a cute fox companion, and the character swapping seems like a promising mechanic. Alas, before long you're close to throwing the controller at the wall because of the clumsy and imprecise controls, annoying camera and very frequent glitches that require you to restart at the previous checkpoint. Again, and again. Shame, because I really wanted to learn more about the Iñupiat, but I just couldn't wrestle any further with the sadly flawed game they wrapped it up in. Having said that, I get the impression this was designed primarily as a co-op game, and perhaps it works better if you have two players, but the AI that conrols the second character when you're playing single player seems determined to make life as difficult as possible for you.

Sure, there are some bugs, sure at the higher equipment levels (matchmaking is based on equipment, not character level) cheaters are more rampant, and sure, some of the balance is whack.
Over all though? I'm having a lot of fun with the game. I'm hoping that VG gets the freeplay/PvE mode up and running sooner rather than later, but over all I really enjoy it.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons would be my recommendation for a similar but more polished and enjoyable experience.

This game really deserves more attention. There are games that have tried various elements contained within this game - text adventures, walking simulators, tactile puzzles/deciphering codes with mysterious equipment, but this has quite a few ways it asks you to interact with the game at different points and it all hangs together very well.
My only warning would be that it starts with the weakest part of all the episodes, that is trying to figure out what it understands in the text adventure, and to play the episodes in order - I won't say any more than that. Even though I love the spectrum loading screen and the old bedroom that you sit in, for someone my age it didn't understand any of the classic text adventure phrases but I soon got used to what it did understand and it doesn't require a lot from you in that respect. It still has some great fourth wall breaking moments in that first episode and is definitely not just playing zork. In subsequent episodes it is doing other things entirely and only revisits the text adventure briefly anyway.
In all honesty about half way through epside 1 I was being dragged through, it wasn't a chore in the slightest as I wanted to see what the hell was going on. It's got great atmosphere, it's full of surprises not just in the story but also in the interactions you make. A great few hours.

To preface, this IS a good game and I have to congratulate the team for trying something really interesting with this one, but after writing my thoughts down, I felt the need to change my recommendation. Here's why.
I played the demo for Stories Untold a while ago, and was thrilled by the concept; a return to a classic text-adventure formula, enhanced by a few modern touches here and there made for a really unique horror experience. It's incredibly unnerving and engaging, especially in a genre currently bogged down with "run around collecting keys and hiding behind boxes" games (looking at you, Outlast). It's also certainly worth the asking price, even if just to support the concept itself, though I would recommend spacing out the episodes (of which there are only four total), so that you don't burn through the whole thing too quickly.
Unfortunately, the game has a series of what I'd consider drawbacks, that after enjoying the demo so much, left me feeling more than a little dissapointed with the full experience. For starters, it doesn't look like much work was done to account for how the player might write certain commands; there were numerous occasions where I found myself fumbling  over trying to reword simple instructions, and being constantly met with the game telling me it didn't understand. Frustrating, but only a minor detractor, and arguably could up the tension for some people, if you've less of a temper than me.
The 'puzzles' themselves can also be more of a chore than a challenge at times, and seem to mostly consist of reading instruction manuals and flipping switches rather than actually figuring anything out, so you don't necesarily feel accomplished in completing them. The main offender here is in Episode 3, which has you reading instructions from a microfilm; even when hitting the buttons to 'focus' the instructions, I couldn't make out what was written, and I'm not exactly visually impaired. Chapter 3 had a really interesting premise, in fact ALL the chapters do, but I spent most of it just feeling frustrated. This is again true in the long, slow walking segment in Chapter 3. It feels really forced, as if it's just there for padding. By that point in the chapter, you can already tell exactly what's about to happen, so it just leaves you waiting for the game to hurry up, or throw something more interesting at you that never comes.
The overall plot is a mixed bag. I'll try to explain without spoiling things. The House Abandon (Chapter 1) is excellent, really creepy and full of intrigue; seriously, play the demo and I'm pretty sure you'll want to grab the full game, as I did. Unfortunately, I think that's really the best the game has to offer. The other chapters are far less interesting, and particularily dissapointing if you went in to them expecting a text-adventure like the demo, the full game simply isn't one for the most part. It just boils down to reading an instruction, and typing it in or pressing buttons; may as well be some sort of office job simulator at some points. The second episode is also a highlight though, in terms of story at least, and present you with a very different vibe to the first, and a very different scare. Even if the gameplay was poor, I was keen to keep going to see what happened next, and was interested to see how/if it all tied together.
Sadly, it all falls apart in the third act. You get another different and alluring premise, but then the gamplay starts and, as I've mentioned, it's the worst of the lot. After a few moments the story of this episode becomes very predictable, and honestly I'd hesitate to even call it a story, since next to nothing happens. By the time the final episode rolls around and you're plonked into the obvious setting that appears at least once in seemingly every horror game, I only kept playing for completions sake, and in the knowledge it'd only take me about 30 minutes. You're given a very dreary resolution (with a few clever exceptions, such as where the title comes from), and some of the more interesting parts of the game end up feeling wasted. Bizarrely, they return to the usually quite liberating text-adventure gameplay for the final portion, which is perhaps the most on-rails portion of the game. I was left trying to find other things to explore, or take other options, but the game just keeps saying 'no' until you reluctantly agree to finish the story. I understand what they were going for here, but it doesn't really feel in-sync with the crux of the story, the 'big twist'. It'd be interesting to take away player agency here if the character themselves had no choice, but instead your character's just a♥♥♥♥♥♥ and now you have to be one too.
I would however, really like to commend the devs on the visuals and sound design. They nail the claustrophobia of being trapped at a desk, and this is particularily evident in The House Abandon (without spoiling, there's some REALLY creepy environmental stuff for a game that mostly has you looking at a screen within your screen). The game clearly wears its Stranger Things influence on its sleeve, and more to its credit I'd say; the 80s vibe is incredibly stylish and the nostalgia for old games and horror movies only amplifies what The House Abandon already does so well. It's really a pity they basically throw it out the window after that. Whilst the rest of the game still looks nice, the visuals and sounds rarley ccompliment the gameplay they way they do in the first episode, and never to the same degree.
Stories Untold should be rightfully applauded for trying some really cool new ideas in a genre in dire need of new blood. As a big horror fan, I really have to thank them for that, and really hope that they improve on what they've done here, because I really think it could lead to something very special. As it stands though, Stories Untold, feels more like an experiment, one that doesn't have it's kinks quite worked out, and from my view, includes some major mistakes that spoil the experience. ABSOLUTELY play the demo. Unfortunately though, it's all downhill from there.

I still have some hope left for this game, since there must be some patches coming even after the release. My hopes aren't set too high though, since the problems of JA Flashback seem to lie deep in the game design rather than in some easily fixable quirks and bugs. is a shooter that continues the story from the first game. Though to be fair you need not have played it to at least have a basic understanding of what is happening.
You play as Jackie Estacado who has become the don of the Franchetti crime family. Reluctant to use his powers granted to him by the Darkness lest they influence him too greatly; In the events occurring in the introduction he is forced to embrace them once again.
The Darkness gives Jackie demonic powers in that from a gameplay perspective results in more or less having two extra arms. However the extra arms are more like demonic snakes than regular human arms.
You can duel wield rifles, grab and slash with your tentacles; throw piping and impale people into walls. Rip car doors off and use them as a shield; before it gives out in usefulness whip it at someone and slice them in half. Basically anything you want or feel like you should be able to do as a character with ostensibly four arms, you can. And it all feels really good and smooth. The guns feel powerful and so do the arms.
The animations are extremely gore-filled. With help from the leveling tree you can earn health regen and ammo recoup from specific animations as well as more basic things like faster reload or increased ammo capacity. Feeding the darkness the hearts of falling enemies doesn't really get old.
, the game is rather pleasing, featuring a cel shaded/comic book representation of its visual assets.
The single player
is rather short (around 5 hours) but it doesn't over stay it's welcome. The game also has some co-op missions in the form of Vendetta missions. These can be played solo or up to four players. Honestly, it has a little bit of a Left 4 Dead vibe to it. Sort of arena with some traditional level design for preamble. There are characters to play as rather than classes. Notably, the one that stood out to me was the shaman. Voiced by none other than Dave Fennoy, though I think he sounded a bit like the character Lee from TellTales The Walking Dead which I believe to be the closet to his real voice (turns out, he is like Nolan North, Tara Strong, Troy Baker level amount of prominence, I had no idea.)
The actor who does the voice of the darkness is also extremely talented; Mike Patton, an in-studio example of his voice can be seen/heard
. These phenomenal voice actors make the story telling that much better.

I bought the Developer version of Clickteam Fusion 2.5 (which includes all the exporters) from Humble Bundle a while ago  and I have spent a fair amount of time on it and it is quite easy to use. I currently use it for college projects and personal projects and it can be stress free at times. Here are a few pros I would like to point out:
> Most of the time, its simple and easy to use.
> There's no need for you to have any coding knowledge.
> Importing objects and frames is stress free.
> Adding soundtracks of SFX is very simple.
> There a broad range of free extensions which makes life easier.
> Good software to start off with if you want to go down the route of Game Development and design.
Don't underestimate the software because there are some cons:
> To create complex games, you will need a great understanding of how the software works...
> Tutorials online are extremely hard to come by, especially advanced tutorials where the conditions are similar or exact to what you want. (There is however, a  set of "starter's" tutorials which come with Clickteam which covers the basics).
> Sometimes, to do a simple thing, you may need a lot of events. (which are conditions inputted by the user which Clickteam "reads" to perform an action).
> Some events may even require mathematics to work otherwise you get the "Syntax Error" B***S***!
> Some text objects (*cough* Counters *cough*) do not anti-alias, so you end up with a poor looking text graphic. You can create your own text however but this up more time and effort.
> To create nice looking graphics, its recommended you create the graphics inside an external program such as Adobe Photoshop, Krita, GIMP or even MS Paint! Reason being is the visuals editor is very basic and isn't very attractive, so its best to avoid it if you want nice graphics.
> Pay £640 if you want everything.
> Limited to 2D graphics and basic 3D graphics.
All in all, its good for starting off but I recommend trying Unreal Engine or Unity as they are free and produce a much more greater outcome.

Absolutely love this game, and I will explain why as both a tool for guitarists and as a game.
Firstly, I have been playing the guitar on and off for a number of years. However, like many people I do not get enough time to practice as much as I would like, and especially rarely get chance to "jam" with others. This game provides a great way of learning songs, techniques and most importantly teaching you to play with the band, as if you were jamming, but so much easier. Yes you can use a metronome, and you can play along with the track, but this is so much easier and more immersive. The visual tab-like but easy to read user interface provides keeps you going and in time. What makes this even more immersive though is how it changes the amp modelling and effects not only for each song but automatically as you move through the song, which is SO immersive. This is actually tedious and difficult to do with a traditional amp / multi-effect set up. Lastly, it also sounds really good, I usually play using an expensive Marshall JCM2000 TSL valve head with 4x12 cab and decent vox multi effect pedal (plus a few seperates i have built).. this game I play through my hifi system, and it actually sounds really good - not quite as good as the Marshall half stack CAN give, but the game makes its  sound right for every song so easily. This game has a tag that says "free-to-play", which is true, it is indeed FREE to play. But what you dont know till you're already inside, is that it is also massively Pay-to-Win.
In my time playing VEGA Conflict, (on browser before the steam release) there are 3 kinds of players; Coiners (spend real money, and LOTS of it), Scripters (cheaters/hackers), and those who actually play for free.
The PRO's of this game;
1) Great visuals, especially since the steam release
2) Gameplay is easy to learn but near impossible to master, meaning that there is always someone out there better than you.
3) Each fvf (pvp fleet battles) is like a game of chess, make a wrong move, your ships go down quick.
4) You are free to customise your ships/base however you want, with a plethora of weapons, armor, shields, and special equipment, and the battles that follow with these ships will be decided by your skill and your fleet's arms and armaments.
CONS;
1) Kixeye (the almighty developer) got greedy, or so allege the great majority of the players, and they keep proving us right with their schemes to get you to spend real money, which the coiners do, and they get WAY ahead of the free-to-play people, and abuse it. In other words, there is HEAVY imbalance of power in this game. In other words, the rich get ahead, and leave you in the dust.
2) The monthly events that kixeye throws at us are getting increasingly hard for f2p players to keep up with, while the coiners simply dish out some money and intant-repair their fighting fleets and just rake up the event points, and get the event ship/weapons which are available for just those few days.
3) The worst thing about this game is something that kixeye wont change, and that is the behaviour of the players. It can be the coiners gloating about the sheer advantage of power they possess over you, or it could be that they just derive pleasure from attacking you everyday, because maybe they feel they have something to prove. Who knows? I've seen too many people use just the most racist, offensive language at you, either because you are new, because you attacked them once, or whatever else. (They often start the fight in the first place).
4) The politics. Kixeye introduced "Alliances" some months ago, and now if the player of one alliance steals resources of the other, a MAJOR dialogue is opened in the game chat between the leaders of both alliances over freaking 200k in resources.
Whats that? Report them to Kixeye? lol you think that does anything? There were rumors floating around that kixeye un-banned cheaters because they started coining before they were banned, or something like that. Do I believe that? I dont know, its just a rumor. But who knows for sure...
This used to be a good game, and if you ask anyone who was playing before Carriers were introduced, most will agree. (not the coiners obviously. Well, maybe some of them...)
Pretty long review, I know, but seriously, unless you are super-rich, the playing field is ALMOST NEVER level or equal. There are dozens of games out there that deserve a download more than this game.

Another thing to keep in mind is that it's SHORT. I played it for 2.5/3 hours before I completed the story. It also isn't highly replayable, at least for me it isn't. An extremely short, but playable, Cyberpunk RPG with a smattering of quasi choice and consequence. It deals with the usual Cyberpunk tropes, so if that particular genre floats your boat you might somewhat enjoy City of Chains.
There's nothing but sloppily implemented combat in this game, and though you can upgrade non-combat skills, you can't use them in creative ways to avoid combat or uncover alternate routes through the various areas. So, if you go into this thinking you can stealth your way through the game, prepare to be disappointed.
There are some nice details in the game: news consoles in each area which give you an immersive look at the consequences of your quasi-choices, as well as some nice background info. There are multiple endings, but you can unlock all of them, I believe, in a single playthrough by simply saving at the right time (not sure if any of the dialogue changes in the endings based on your choices throughout the game) so replaying the entire game doesn't seem to be necessary. I also felt that most of these endings didn't even make sense from a narrative point of view.
The story is predictable and dull. I found the entire cast of characters to be poorly written and uninteresting; they all have the personalities of a stone.  Despite the game page claiming there's choice and consequence, there's none to be found. What it really means is that there's a handful of different endings and a few minor dialogue swaps.
The atmosphere of most areas is appropriately cyberpunky. However, there is little exploration in these tiny, barren areas outside of one or two side-quests in each hub.
All in all, this game isn't worth buying, the quality simply isn't there to justify it. Should you want to go slumming, make sure to pick it up at a greatly reduced price and enjoy a very bare bones RPG.

TL;DR: Rushed release with bugs and missing features you would expect from a game calling itself Jagged Alliance. This is BIA all over again.
First three hours of playing revealed several obvious bugs and simple oversights and simplifications, such as:
After conquering the first small area, I started to train militia in a chokepoint sector. After training four militia, first enemy patrol comes in: 8-man squad, with long range weapons. I had my team in the same sector, prepared to defend with militia. For some reason, you first get automatic combat resolution of enemy vs. militia, and all four were easily slaughtered. After starting the actual battle, my troops were no longer in defensive positions, but spawned in the middle of the map. Defending against long range weapons with pistols and SMGs required very cheesy tactics, only possible because of the simple AI. I managed to train another four mercs before the next squad, only for them to get slaughered again. After one more cycle, with no way to repair weapons, the game will soon be uninstalled.
Enemies don't usually drop weapons, but I understand that as a design choice. I would expect to have some place to buy medkits and repair kits though, the only "store" in first town is a weird dialogue hack, where you can't even see your cash total, or stats of the weapons you are buying.
No manual, especially no information about character creation, status effects, or stats like "reaction time", and even in-game tooltips or tutorials don't cover those. IMP character creation has a random element to what perks you get and in which order, it would have been better to allow the player the option to manually select perks, instead of having to re-roll through the questionnaire. This looks like a feature that was cut short in development, like many others. It seems that the four perks you get at start are not all active until later levels, so it is weird to get locked into that choice at character creation.
Weirdly all mercs from previous games are back to Level 1, and their salaries don't seem to match their skills. I'm not sure if they will change as the game progresses, otherwise you are more or less limited to the starting squad that you train up. They have pretty weird perk choices as well: Ivan, Buzz, Lynx and Shadow all come with a Shotgun-crit-chance perk.
There are some good points, like squad inventory, a movement cursor that shows visible enemies from target square, and simple militia training (unlike having to manually haul weapons to civilians, like in JA:BIA).
This might be playable after a major bug fix and feature update, but until then, stay away. Basically, this looks like early access. Time to reinstall JA2 wildfire...

Loved JA2, was looking forward to someone creating a modern version of that.  How hard would that be, basically create JA2 with modern graphics, and a different campaign.  No problem, right?
Apparently its a huge problem.  Why something that could be done over 15 years ago (JA2 was released in April 1999), can't be done now is simply beyond me.
Almost as soon as I started the gane I was thinking "nope".  They dropped the ball, badly.  I haven't played that long, I will admit, but already its clear the game is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
All the little things that added so much to JA2 are missing; containers, strange things you'd find, different ammo types, mods for your guns (even if some of them were silly), interesting voice overs, strange characters, even the horribly voice acted Ira added something interesting to the game.  And Meltdown, my absolute favourite character of all.  The game had personality!
None of that is here.  This feels very bland and basic, I'd say even worse than Back in Action - and that is a pretty low bar to actually slip under!
JA2 was originally praised for "its non-linear gameplay, freedom of action and variety of tactics, mercenary character traits, story-telling and role-playing, detailed world, challenging opponents and excellent audio."
Flashback is not going to get that praise.
The graphics are primitive (for modern games), but servicable - I can forgive that.  There are few voice overs (I'd say what is there was lifted straight from JA2), otherwise the audio is middle of the road.  The UI is clunky and basic.
And the combat?  Full Control also developed a free game called Frontline Tactics that I played for a while (like all free games they want you to pay for it with microtransactions, amusingly enough the MT system didn't work when I was playing).  I instantly recognized the combat as being that system put in this game with some small tweaks.  Its very basic and repetitive, and the AI is very stupid.
I can't even recommend getting this game on sale.  Unless it gets a major overhaul - and it would have to be such an extensive overhaul that I simply can't imagine it happening - I would have to suggest that people play JA2 instead.

I'd like to think that I'm unbiased as I write this feedback (hoping that it will be a fair warning if you are researching the game) ... but I did really love Jagged Alliance 2, and felt it was a game ahead of it's time, full of personality, decision-making and fun.
I've had a BRIEF play of this 'reboot', and I really struggle to find the motivation to spend any more time with it.  After an hour or two, I've had enough.
The problem is, it's shallow.  I just see so many features missing or glazed over.  At least with 'Back in Action', the game had a pretty robust combat system that innovated on the original .. if JaBia had delivered on it's promise to bring over the personality and substance of the original JA2, and bring with it the new combat, it would have been awesome, instead of a disappointment.
Flashback - well, it's even worse, I'm afraid.  It has fewer features than JaBia, the combat is dull, the AI is pretty much utterly stupid (sorry, to be specific .. you can be shooting at the AI and it will run past you and stand to it's back with you so you and your buddies can kill it).
It has promise, and I really would be interested to play this game with another 6 months of rich development, but my feeling is that the people making it have exhausted all the upfront kickstarter money, and rather than grow a set of gonads and spend their own time and money perfecting the product - to yield the ultimate financial and reputation rewards of creating a wonderful, memorable game - they just launched early and incomplete.
Animations are absent .. like, taking cover seems to be just .. standing there.. there is no corresponding action from the merc (at least that I can tell??) that they've taken cover.. nor can I see any easily accessible stat/graphic/icon or anything that tells me that they are actually in cover ..
It's just .. weak.
It's a weak, disappointing title, and I have buyers remorse.
I regret buying it, and I actually don't give a flying poo-poo about twenty bucks .. I regret buying it because by doing so I'm supporting an outcome that I find increasingly unacceptable in the gaming world - releasing unpolished, feature incomplete, over-promise-under-deliver titles.
I'd recommend you steer away from this game if you are considering buying it, at least in it's present form as at 25 October 2014.
UPDATE:  As at 7 February 2015, I've had a second look and injected some more time into the game (apparently, according to the defenders of the game - some vested modders from "the Bear Pit", you have to have a minimum of 3 hours gameplay to have a valid opinion .... although I can tell if a game sucks pretty much right away, and you'd have to be mental to hack away at something that sucks just to confirm it doesnt suck, right?).  Anyway just to update, several months (and a few patches) later, the game is still quite awful .. it's boring, feature incomplete, poor AI, and as they fix other bugs, they apparently create new ones, like all the females for some reason now like to crawl around on their stomachs... if you're thinking about buying this game - think twice - you can get a lot more bang for your gaming buck elsewhere.

If you like the Darkness comic you'll (most likely) dig this game.
Story: simple at first with a mob/noir tone going towards more horror/fantasy as it goes, engaging enough to keep you playing and actually care about the characters, some (very few) parts really pull the right strings and drag it towards its highest points. The only real downside of it is what to me looked like a terribly abrupt sequel-bait ending, it's not bad in itself but it felt like the development team got the rug pulled from under their feet. All the dialogues span to funny, to ok, to interesting, to meh but the voice acting is always spot-on.
Graphics: very Borderlands-esque but less cartoony, if you're familiar with Marc Silvestri/TopCow style you'll feel home. The game looks pretty in its style and no elements ever looks out of place or ugly, some sceneries may look a bit flat and underworked while others will look fantastic.
Sound: very good voice acting, ok to good music and sound effects, terrific voice/sound for The Darkness itself (no others than Mike Patton!)
Gmeplay: fast and funny, the Darkness super-powers/human weapons mix works very well, often times I wished it was more seameless but overall it's very fun to play and represents the highest point of the whole experience. There's some light RPG elements in the form of a skill-tree to layer the fighting experience a bit and give a solid excuse to hit NewGame+ as soon as you finish the campaign; also there's some choice you can take but nothing that will make any actual difference, beside one (that I will not spoil, of course) that felt like a really hearthfull inteligent idea. Took around 6 hours the complete the main game story (missing a lot of the collectibles, so I guess you're supposed to take things a bit slower and go looking around) and, while it surely felt on the shorter side, it's close to the right amount for the story that it tells, pushing it to 8-9 (with added content, of course) would've been probably better. There's an on-line/off-line coop/solo extra mode based around episodes that happen off-screen in game and it helps pushing the total gameplay hrs count a bit further without getting boring but nothing exceptional.
If you're looking for something easy but not too casual, for something enagaging but short, for something with a disctinctive cool look and feel, if you like the comics then I strongly suggest you to grab this game.

So the trailer makes this game look nearly impossible, but it's actually quite accessible. Unless you're playing on Harder mode, in which case it's... actually still fair!
Wish Project's stages and bosses have cool, varied, and well-balanced bullet patterns throughout the game. I've rarely been caught off guard and killed unfairly. All the patterns feel like they're presented more as puzzles that you need to figure out how to overcome rather than needing to be memorized by repetition. ie, Lots of other shmups have these random fast bullets that make you kinda feel cheated when you get hit by them for the first time (but then you remember them on your next playthrough) - this "cheated" feeling and memorization stuff aren't really in this game.
Controls feel tight. I've found lots of shmups in this style force you to d-pad movement, but full analog control is supported here. It's a 3-button game: shot, special, and bomb. Most "specials" are abilities like freezing bullets or changing your main shot mode. Controls are fully customizable including adjusting how slow you move while the optional slow button is held.
Diversity in playable characters is great - each of the 8 characters makes you approach the challenges a little differently which adds genuine replay value. It also looks like there are 8 more characters to unlock. Character art and sprites are a bit weak though.
Other misc notes: Hit detection is pretty generous, but precise. 2-player mode is fun because the players can use their character abilities to work together. Music is good. Trying to earn a gold medal on each stage reminds me of Star Fox 64. No online leaderboards, but maybe they could be added in an update.
Pros
+ Varied, fun, and balanced bullet patterns
+ Playable character diversity
+ Controls
+ Music
Cons
- Character & sprite art
- No online leaderboards

Absolutely love this game, and I will explain why as both a tool for guitarists and as a game.
Firstly, I have been playing the guitar on and off for a number of years. However, like many people I do not get enough time to practice as much as I would like, and especially rarely get chance to "jam" with others. This game provides a great way of learning songs, techniques and most importantly teaching you to play with the band, as if you were jamming, but so much easier. Yes you can use a metronome, and you can play along with the track, but this is so much easier and more immersive. The visual tab-like but easy to read user interface provides keeps you going and in time. What makes this even more immersive though is how it changes the amp modelling and effects not only for each song but automatically as you move through the song, which is SO immersive. This is actually tedious and difficult to do with a traditional amp / multi-effect set up. Lastly, it also sounds really good, I usually play using an expensive Marshall JCM2000 TSL valve head with 4x12 cab and decent vox multi effect pedal (plus a few seperates i have built).. this game I play through my hifi system, and it actually sounds really good - not quite as good as the Marshall half stack CAN give, but the game makes its  sound right for every song so easily. For someone with a more starter guitar and amp this game will actually be a STEP UP from what they are using no doubt. My ONLY critisism of this game as a tool for guitarists is that it lacks 7 string (or more) support, which means I tend not to use my 7 string for this. Also, as you will change the tuning for many songs, floyd rose bridges with locking nuts are a total pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥for it, this is a limitation of locking nuts, not the game though (if you don't know why, don't worry as you almost certainly dont have one).
Reviewing this as a game is hard, it is unique and clearly aimed at guitarists. I love it, but I am a guitarist. The closest thing to compare it to is guitar hero, which I enjoyed for a bit with friends, nothing more than a laugh like wii sports. But by comparisons to Rocksmith, guitar hero is really just a childs toy, in rocksmith you ARE playing the guitar and learning. I have always viewed someone who practices guitar hero to extent of finishing through the fire and flames on hard to be a bit sad.. because I always thought, why not spend that time ACTUALLY playing the instrument instead? Now, you can do both... Of course non-guitarists will also have to buy an electric guitar.. but if you are one of the few people interested in this game who doesn't play guitar I would recomend you spend the extra money; get rocksmith 2014 and a newbie guitar.

To be fair, you have to have a very high IQ to understand Overcast: Walden and the Werewolf. The terror is extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of Huxleyian philosophy most of the scares will go over the typical player's head. There's also Walden's nihilistic outlook, which is deftly woven into his characterization - his personal philosophy draws heavily from Mikhail Bulgakov literature, for example. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of the scares, to realize they aren't just jumpscares - they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence, people who dislike Overwatch: Casten and the Wolfboy truly ARE idiots - of course they wouldn't appreciate, for instance, the inherent terror in Walden's catchphrase, "Ouch My Eyes Are Bleeding" which in itself is a cryptic reference to Keillor's American epic Lake Wobegon Days. I'm smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Microblast Games' genius unfolds itself on their screens. What fools, how I pity them.
And yes, by the way, I do have an Overbearing: MIchelin Man and Humphries tattoo. And no, you can't see it. It's for the ladies' eyes only - And even they have to demonstrate that they are within 5 IQ points of my own (preferably lower) beforehand.

Worms has always held a very strong position in my opinion. It wears it's heart on it's sleeve: It isn't an A-List game and it isn't for everyone. But for me, it's one of the most passionately developed game series ever.
Things have certainly moved on since the side-scrolling invertibrate slaughter-fest of the first games to the 3D variants of the game. And whilst I did love the 2D games, I have to admit that I prefer the 3D versions. Ultimate mayhem combines the best bits of two great titles: Worms 3D and Worms 3: Mayhem, keeping all the best bits from both and removing the bad.
The customisation is absolutely fantastic: Worms with Pope hats and 3D glasses shooting bazookas at Worms with Bunny ears and disco glasses has to be one of the most hilarious things in gaming.
As I said before, it's turn-based nature and sometimes fairly difficult missions are not for everyone. But if the thought of carnage, explosions, flying sheep bombs, alien abductions, an endless array of hats and voices, air-strikes and a huge concrete donkey even makes you smile, then perhaps you should give this game a look.
You won't regret it.

This is a very short, but also very intense and interesting game. The gameplay, based on point-and-click adventures, is minimal, but the same cannot be said about the content which is actually a deep and even disturbing reflection on human life itself. As such, this game quickly develops into a thought-provoking philosophical experience, loosely based on the classical myth about Sisyphus (who was ordered by the gods to push a stone uphill over and over and over, since it always rolled back at a certain point) with some extra thoughts by Albert Camus thrown in.
Usually, I'd skip through a game as crudely drawn as this one, with only the most basic of artwork. But the texts and the interactions - even though they mostly seemed meaningless to the absurd - quickly grabbed my attention, and I played through it at a leisurely pace. Though the game is very short (I played through it in half an hour, reading everything), it shouldn't have been any longer given its thought-provoking nature. The almost minimalistic sound track does provide the right amount of extra atmosphere at the right moments.
All in all: well done, and certainly worth trying out if you're into games that dig (excuse me the pun) deeper than most. You get a very easy 100% achievement game as a bonus, but that feels completely trivial after playing a game with this kind of content.

This is a game that is difficult to review. While part story, part platformer, and part documentary/education it’s hard to label this game, which ultimately leads to its appeal.
While the art is wonderful, the platform elements are what keep this game from being perfect. Bugged by poor controls and wonky bugs, the game suffers at times and becomes dangerously (like pre rage quit) frustrating. Some of the puzzles and/or figuring where to go next can increase this frustration. On one episode in particular, I had to restart the game to actually get the NPC to do what it was supposed to.
On a mechanics level, quite a few people have complained about the bola mechanics but in my opinion its no different than firing like in a bubble shooting game or even Angry Birds. Those that have difficulty with keyboard controls will ultimately have to resort to using a controller, which is a blessing.
The game really shines in the story telling department as well as the interesting information and history.
Pros –
Drop dead gorgeous
Immersive atmosphere
Beautifully rendered, you feel like you are in a Pixar film
Excellent use of Documentary information
Adorable main characters
Nice blend of story and platform.
Cons-
Buggy game mechanics
Buggy scripting
Some difficult maneuvers
People not used to using keyboard controls may have difficulty
Frustrating difficulty spikes (easy, then suddenly hard)
Annoying recurring themes (like the wind gusts)
Limited replayability
Overall, 8/10. Would not pay full price but when purchased on sale it’s a must own. A worthy addition to anyone’s library and a unique game that belongs in its own genre niche.
If you have difficulty using arrow keys or WASD to control a character on a 2d Left to Right type game and do not have a control, I do not recommend this game to you.

For me, the pluses of the game are
+Sci fi / cyber punk / espionage setting
+"non-Chibi" RPG graphics seen so often in other "RPGMaker" titles
+Music
+User-selected Skill Tree/ Level Up
+Memorable character designs
This is the first actual RPG "RPGMaker" game I have picked up, after briefly playing "The Deed", but I'm glad I have. I'm not a big fan of the overly-chibi style of much of the RPGMaker titles, nor their insistence on completely replicating aesthetics or world environments similar to those already seen in titles of the past on older consoles (namely a seeming overabundance of titles in fantasy settings, though those have their value as well, this caught my interest a lot more not being another "knight, mage, priestess" vs villain in armor and cape setting. As a fan of cyberpunk and espionage it's nice to see both implemented into the storyline and design at large so early in the game, which I imagine will continue as the story progresses. The story is well-written and some memorable characters / villains are present. The battle gameplay itself is familiar turn-based territory, while the music fits the sci fi / futuristic atmosphere.
A user-selected progression of character Skills keeps things fresh, while gated sections of levels offer some replay as far as re-exploring areas after you have unlocked a characters Advanced Hacking / Lockpicking skills, etc...
Based on the quality of this title, I will definitely give RPGMaker titles more praise.

My Friday the 13th: The Game Review
At its core it's a fun game, especially if you play with friends and do some roleplay and mess around with Jason, but there are many things that make this game not fun.
First off the bugs in this game are unbearable. Some games you can grab people from 5 feet away, some games you can't grab them when they are right next to you. There is another bug that happens to me once in a while, where I grab someone from the seat of a car and then someone hits me with a bat and I start flying across the map, even through the map. Me clicking on the road where the car is heading, but spawning on the side of the road watching them pass by while I'm sitting there frustrated. Hit registration is laughable in this game.
The community is where it really stings. People shooting you, hitting you with any sort of weapons. Even to the point of running you over. Bunch of sore losers leave the game when you're about to kill them so you don't get XP. Also glitch abusers, people boosting each other up by being Jason and killing everyone besides their friend so that they both get XP and waste people's time waiting.
Well, since I'm listing a lot of negative things about the game I guess I will list some good things. All the different Jason's are unique and very detailed with its abilities and character design. Every once in a while you get into a lobby where people actually like to have fun and do some games, roleplay, etc. That's about it, heh.
In all, the game is fun if you play with the right people, most of the time you are going to get put in lobbies where people troll or boost other people. For its price I feel like its the middle with me. $40 is lot for a buggy game with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ community. $30 is way more acceptable for a game this size. Just buy this game when it's on sale, or if you want to buy it full price, go for it. Just know what you are getting into once you buy this game.
Thanks for reading my review.

TL;DR: Soma is great, buy it and play it if you're familiar with the genre.
Story: Without spoiling, though it had some periods where I felt like nothing was developing, I was interested and the ending was solid.
Sound: The soundscape is phenomenal, since you have no immediate weapons you have to heavily rely on your ears. Is that a piece of wreckage? Is it an enemy? The sound keeps you focused and informed, and is designed well to allow you to figure out which direction the noise is coming from.
Atmosphere: The atmosphere of the game is equally as good as the sound. It's got neat lighting, there's ocean-walking scenes and a diverse enough environment that allows you to know you're in different areas while still remaining cohesive. Some moments are pretty, some are gritty.
Gameplay: The game relies heavily on sneaking and quick-thinking, as you have no means of offense. Your defense is just moving, listening, and occasional interactive objects that can hold up enemies.
Overall: The ending was great, there's a philisophical theme to the game and I found the writing in the end to really blow me away. At first I thought it would be just another horror game, but this seems to be the exception and not the rule. I firmly recommend this game.
