Don't buy this game. It's a broken, buggy, confusing mess of disparate elements, hastily cobbled together with little thought, ugly mechanics obscured with pretty graphics and buzz-words like "sandbox" and "hardcore survival" thrown around to lure in the unwary.
Pros:
- This is a good-looking game, at least from a distance.
- It sports a fairly large game world which feels lived-in and real.
- Excellent atmosphere replete with background noise, harsh wind and insect buzzing. It pulls off that desolate post-apocalyptic feel better than any game I can think of besides Metro 2033 and Last Light.
- Good overall sound design
Cons:
- It's poorly optimized and chokes even the highest-end PC's and lowering the video settings to minimum doesn't help much. It tries to compensate by un-rendering many props at a ridiculously short distance.
- Confusing everything. You get a "tutorial mission" the first time you play, which explains a few things, but not nearly enough of essential info. Hours into the game, I still didn't know what I was doing. Something's wrong when you don't explain why there are invincible, immobile enemies spawned in clusters throughout the world.
- Enemy encounters are surprisingly rare outside of periodically attacked outposts. That said, when you do encounter more than 1 or 2, you can be killed within seconds. Because AI pathfinding is hard, the enemies always teleport behind you, and warp away when attacked because they're also dumb as rocks, so the devs had to make them as cheap as possible so that they wouldn't be just cannon fodder.
- NPC traders only accept specific combinations of items, so you're stuck lugging around meaningless junk for much of the game.
- Randomly generated "quest" system which is nothing but deliver box A to shop B. This wouldn't be so bad if getting around in this game didn't take an eternity. Oh, and of course they have weight values and clog up your initially tiny inventory. Also, each random quest box can only be turned in at one NPC. This is literally the most half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥"quest" system I've ever seen in a game.
- What makes this worse is you lose everything when you die. That's fine for players who want to feel super hardcore and macho, but that's going to turn off a ton of new players who aren't even given a chance to get comfortable with the mechanics.
- Random health pickups strewn throughout the world aren't enough to keep you alive and health regenerates excruciatingly slowly.
- Only a handful of servers, usually just one per game mode and region, most of which seem buggy as hell.
- Unwieldy, confusing UI. No way to track other players or friends... unless they have to join your tribe first, and in that case, F that.
- This game seems to have been either abandoned by its developer or they just don't care. Controller support has been broken for months, private servers were promised since the beginning and still haven't surfaced, hackers are running rampant and unchallenged, etc. Apparently, they can't even do something as simple as send a forgotten password email... 3 times. I just happened to remember mine or I'd be SOL.

SOMA isn’t so much a game as an interactive story, and I highly recommend it. Honestly, the gameplay elements almost take away from the game. The game is extremely linear, and while you’re supposed to escape from your enemies they occasionally camp you by standing right between you and the one way that you can get to your objective. The only reason this isn’t more of a problem is because the game is extremely forgiving in terms of deaths and heals - SOMA doesn't try to be challenging.

Without ruining anything I’ll just say that SOMA is full of twists and turns and leaves you thinking far more than almost any other game I can think of. If you’re looking for a deep story and a compelling atmosphere this is one game you can’t afford to miss! SOMA is a short experience but the questions it raises will stay with you long after you finish the game.

So you're reading reviews to see if this game is worth your money. Well let me tell you about getting your money's worth out of something. This game is so thought provoking it hurts to think about. So you thought being human means you're actually a human? Wrong. You think that being you means that you are you? Also wrong.  What exactly do you define human? Play this game and you'll definitely be thinking about things for a while. The encounters are all unique and you have to adapt to their settings as well. The atmosphere is excellent and the game is beautiful when the word is applicable. No, this game is not a jumpscare carnival where every attraction is another FNAF rippoff. No, no, no; THIS game is art. Some pros and cons:
Pros:
~Story is very good (requires you to pay attention to dialogue and finding backstory in environment).
~Doesn't force you to explore, could theoretically beat the game in 2 hours or less if you knew what you were doing.
~Graphics are actually very pleasing.
~Environment is astounding.
~Build-up to intense moments.
~Legitimitely scary encounters.
~Sounds in this game are very emersive.
~It feels very optimized.
~There are modding capabilites to expand your playtime even more if you want.
Cons: Not much here, just little things
~No FOV slider, caused some motion sickness at points, also locked at 60 fps. Still very playable though.
~Sometimes objectives aren't super clear, you will occasionally run around aimlessly for a few minutes.
~Sometimes the enemies felt too easily avoided, make your own conclusion there.
~There is only one difficulty, but thats what mods are for.
Also the ending. It made me want to yell in frustration and cry in agony. But it also made me want to yell with satisfaction, but still cry. A lot actually. Mainly from disbelief.

This game is a big improvement on the original and fixes nearly all of the really annoying problems it had. I highly recommend this if you are into guitar or bass at all, beginner or advanced.
The good:
* Session mode is a huge addition that lets you improvise over a customizable band that reacts to what you are playing. This alone is worth the purchase price.
* The tracklist and DLC so far is great and if you own Rocksmith you can import the 50 songs from that for $10
* Large video library with lessons working from the very basics to more advanced techniques
* Master mode will now gradually fade out notes from sections you do well in rather than throwing the entire song at you with no notes.
* Riff repeater makes it easy to stop in the middle of a song and practice a section at any diffulty or speed you want. This is a HUGE improvement.
* The new score attack with leaderboards is a lot of fun once you have a song down pretty well
* The interface is, for the most part, much better.
The bad:
* The game seems much more forgiving on single notes now but can be very difficult to get chords to register completely throughout an entire song. Bends work fine on guitar but the game seems to have trouble recognizing them consistently on bass.
* While the guitarcade games are better than the original's, they suffer from a lack of options and too much downtime after a loss to really be a great tool.
* Still no way to just just study the tabs without playing the song
* Career mode is gone and the game no longer plays back your performance after you've finished.

The Darkness 2 is one of my personal favourites in a long list of games on my steam account. It is everything you could possibly want from a first person shooter that has a noire feeling to it, with light horror elements and an interesting story that will keep you hooked.
The story, without spoiling anything, is a direct sequel for the first part, meaning eveything ties up and the timelines are logical. Basically: you are Jackie Estacado, a young mafia member with dark powers beyond control,that seeks vengeance.The plot gets better and makes more sense as you play through the game. You have choices, tough it's not a primary element of the game and the story and levels are rather linear, choices only representing the question "do you want one more cutscene?", most of the times.
The gameplay is where this game really excels at. You have the basic fps mechanics with a strong emphasis on the signature dual wield of Jackie, which can carry 3 weapons with him- a primary, a secondary and another secondary, with the option to dual the secondaries or carefully aim with them. Besides that, the power of the darkness system is truly a breath of fresh air for the genre. Jackie has, at all times, 2 demon arms besides him that, if controlled right, can do huge amounts of damage just on their own. Tactically combined with the generic fps mechanics, they can adapt to any situation and turn the tides of battle in a second with specific skills. They can slash, execute enemies in exchange for health, ammo, etc, grab objects from the enviroment to use them as either defense or gory offense. Your godly powers go away in the light tough, as the game offers dynamic light gameplay elements, requiring you to think strategically before encounters as you shoot lights out and cut down heads.
The game also has a skill tree system, featuring 4 different skill trees that all branch out from a primary ability and that can be leveled simultaneously. The primary skill adds a new mechanic, eating the hearts of enemies (dead ones, of course) and replinishing health by it and gaining more points towards the purchase of your next skill. Every skill tree has a speciality and any skill you get can drastically change the gameplay and your methods of brutally murdering bad guys, making the end game the most fun of all, as you got so many tools in your arsenal that every situation is your playground. The skills you get also scale with your own, as you learn to further multitask the demon arms while still keeping concentrated on the basic firefights and making the ultimate killing machine out of you. That's why even the hardest difficulty doesn't feel unfair in any way, but challenging and forcing you to sharpen those reflexes make use of everything you learn. It's a masterpiece to be quite honest with you.
Just so you can get the idea of how deep this game can be (story-wise), before the TL;DR, I'll leave you with my favourite monologue of Jackie Estacado: "Time slips away from you. And then, all of a sudden, it's like you're sitting in a theatre, watching a movie of your own life. You're a fu**ing movie star. And you're killing all the bad guys-tearing them limb from limb.And you feel good, you look good. F**k, you ARE good. And then you realize something: everyone else in the theatre? They're screaming, because they're watching a horror movie...and you're not the hero...you're the monster..."
TL;DR: A great atmospheric game, filled with gore and overall dark themes. One of the best story-driven first person shooters out there, featuring great, complex and innovative gameplay mechanics by using the power of the darkness. A solid 10/10 in my opinion, at least for the singleplayer.

Soma is the most recent installment from horror giants Frictional Games. Rocketed into success with arguably one of the scariest games of all time, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, Soma is a wonderful follow up. With better graphics, more voiced dialogue, and convincing characters, Soma does a lot of things right. The scares are there, and most are truly intense moments instead of cheap jump scares.
My only gripe with Soma is that a few instances require rigorous trial and error, which in the end leads to little to no scare factor. I only had two moments like this, but both were frustrating and made the "obstacles" I had to avoid annoying instead of scary.
Overall Soma is dripping with atmosphere much like its precursor. A solid interesting story line, as well as a believable main character along with a fantastic side character really bring it all together. A must buy for anyone who loves this genre.

The game itself is a very stylized first person shooter with the unique mechanic of being accompanied by an entity known as The Darkness. Though it's mostly known for the two snakes sticking out of Jackie Estacado's back, (not his crotch, seriously, that would be weird) it manifests in many different forms. A pimp stick, an axe, a gun and a katana, all possessed with The Darkness.
The gameplay itself is chaotic, you go through level to level swinging around those tentacles like you own the place. As a first person shooter, it's solid, the shooting feels satisfying, the weapons all behave differently from one another, The Darkness serves to aid your firefights, not hamper them, as they don't remove your weapon as you're actively using them, shields, humans, what have you. Overall it's solid.
The thing is, the Magical Ginzo's adventures only last five to six hours, and even with the Vendettas co-op addition, you really won't get a whole lot out of this game. The game is cheap, however, and if you find it discounted, buy it.

The Darkness 2 takes place two years after the events of The Darkness. The series protagonist Jackie Estacado is now the head of his own Mafia organisation and has the darkness under control. Jackie is still haunted by the events of the first game and feels he was to blame. This is where the game begins as Jackie is ambushed by an unknown group he calls upon the darkness once again to save his life. Now he must find out who this group is and why they want him dead.
The gameplay is similar to the first game, utilizing the quad wielding system Jackie can shoot one two-handed gun or two one-handed guns. You can also choose to shoot one one-handed gun for improved accuracy as well. While Jackie is holding his weapons he can use the two tentacles sticking out his back to attack people. This was innovative in that clicking and holding the middle mouse button would result in being able to choose which angle to slash at (in a sort of Metal Gear Rising manner). The extra arms also aid Jackie in eating the hearts of dead enemies to restore health. Gruesome takedowns offer shields, health or extra ammo. Ammo is spare at times and the game encourages you to experiment with other weapons. Using the tentacles Jackie can also pick up weapons off the ground from far away. The tentacles can also grab props in the game, which then become throwable weapons.
The game is gory fun, with a story that is serviceable, compelling enough to get you to the end credits and some interesting sub story sections in the game that I won’t spoil. Some people dislike the art style but I think it lends itself well to its comic book roots.
In conclusion The Darkness 2 was very fun. The darkness powers shake up the first person shooter formula that has been getting stale for a while now. The voice acting is top notch, especially Mike Patton who voices the evil companion of Jackie, The Darkness itself.

Holt Allaway has just been arrested due to his refusal to use his expertise in building military robots for the government: fleeing his cell soon after with a few companions in tow Holt will have to flee the police and find a way to get away from the city.
You'll be following his adventures in this 6 hour sci-fi RPG where you'll battle, hack and charm your way through four different acts: City of Chains has a quite good story and setting and is enjoyable to play despite a few gripes with its UI and combat system.
-decent art style
-the soundtrack is very nice and varied
-an interesting story that slowly connects Holt's escape to importants events in the city
-the dystopian sci-fi setting is done well
-a skill system and the few weapon categories at your disposal help give some variety and choice
-selecting certain skills'll make you able to solve situations using hacking or charisma, sometimes bypassing a danger entirely
-a few difficulty spikes, generally based on whether a character gets targeted too often: enemies can do quite a bit of damage even on normal difficulty and unlucky KOs can feel unfair
-the RPGMaker UI can feel a bit clunky when crafting (as you can't see the amount of materials you have while doing it) or when you want to readily know how much ammo you have left during a battle
-the Morale mechanic felt like an unnecessary aggravation
While six hours might not bet alot for an RPG City of Chains manages to make those hours enjoyable thanks to its setting and a well-paced, effective story: you'll also be able to influence certain events by killing/ sparing people and what ending you get by choosing one of three different missions in the last act. Combat is pretty fun and you'll have a few skills/ weapons to help you even the odds or can decide to use a grenade to kill enemies outside of a battle, if you have one and don't mind not getting any loot. Each character has skills you can unlock using points gained from completing quests and they'll slowly follow archetypes you're familiar with (damage dealer, tank etc).
Combat can also get a bit frustrating at times, enemies can hit hard and bad luck might mean you might get a character near KO quite quickly if you're not careful. KOs will influence party Morale and this is a game mechanic I wasn't completely happy with, while I'm fine with it having an effect in combat I was annoyed at finding out it can also prevent characters from lockpicking/ hacking if it gets too low. You can restore morale using a certain medical consumable but it honestly feels like a gimmick that gets in the way of the fun and made me just reload a save if a fight made it drop too low.
For the most part City of Chains was a smooth ride though and felt like a competent game with a good mix of combat and exploration: it's not overly long and its brand of dystopian sci-fi isn't horribly original but it works well and it's fun to play.

City of Chains takes the foundations of a retro-inspired RPG and attempts to combine them with an ambitious array of modern gameplay mechanics. Does it succeed or is it's scope too broad?
Read on for my humble opinion ...
New Reality Games have brought forward the unique presentation of their sister title Atonement: Scourge of Time and repeated it here, this time with a cyberpunk sc-fi setting. Do you remember your early gaming years when there were still games that intrigued you with their unique look? Atonement: SOT reminded me of those days so I'm glad to see the same overall aesthetics return here.
As an RPG Maker game, there is an impressive amount of custom, 'from-the-ground-up' work evident here. In fact, the entire game comes across as a
unique experience which I doubt you will find in many other places. The town and battle menus are standard and you might hear 1 or 2 familiar default sounds in there, but the character models, animations and scenery have a unique charm to them that I really enjoyed. Combat takes your typical turn-based approach and applies an extra layer of interesting stats and weaknesses. Even on casual difficulty, you'll find yourself considering your turns carefully for some of the boss encounters.
City of Chains incorporates many modern features usually non-existent in these games such as:
The story will take you on a very fast-paced, enjoyable romp through a dark cyberpunk World where you'll meet many characters and make many important choices along the way. A little bit of exploration is allowed and some of the cities are designed really nicely, with shops and apartment building to wander around. While your story begins in rather dark and grim environments, this is not always the case. Music and sounds are suitably dark/cyberpunk and you'll hear new background music almost every few minutes.
I'm very impressed with the range of skills, items and features present in City of Chains, which you would not expect to see in this niche. While they are not deeply developed, their scope is perfectly matched to the games relatively modest runtime (for an RPG) and nothing ever feels like it takes too much of your time away from the action and story. You will be hacking, smashing and shooting your way through the game and leveling up your skills at a really nice pace, everything feels very rewarding and I think the perfect balance has been struck here.

For a game that has been an on going project for this many years there are certain expacations to be made. However seeing it being an early access game made by a very small team some criticisim can be made and some can't. But that's the point of reviewing. You give critique so the creator can be better. The beauty for us gamers is that developers are like wine or whiskey. They are either good and becomes better, they are good but falls hard due to arrogance and godlike complex or they never were good to begin with. The devs of SoG are hopefully the first type.
Now enough of that and unto the game.
The graphics are smooth and fantastic, for being 2D Spirites. That is however nothing bad as they simply tap into a bit of retro or nostalgia, depending on your age. For reference it's nostalgia for me. As I started this game it felt like playing a new Zelda game. A World to explore and you as the hero. The graphics help this mindset as you travel across the land and my god is the scenery gorgeues. Even with the limited graphics of 2D spirites they make everything flow smoothly and with an almost seamless action. The particles created by the various spells and skills as well as the various stages of boss fights make this game very good. During the harder difficult I died once due to the fact that I stopped and had to process I went from a Zelda-esque game to a Touhou level bullet hell. It was beautiful
The sound and music of the game aids the nostalgic/retro feeling and the sound effects made when you cast a spell or use a skill is quite satisfying. There is no lack of audio feedback on what's going on in this game. You will know when the enemy is about to charge you or a boss is starting a massive barrage of onslought. The feedback you get as a player in this game becomes even more valuable as you play on the harder difficulty when the bosses can go from "oh look a large quantity of bullets" to "This went from casual to hardcore bullet hell real fast...."
As for the gameplay and it's mechanics I'm happy to say that it all feels fantastic. The controls respond as expected and the game runs smoothly. It lacks any need to have a beast of a machine. This is a game I have played during lunch hours on my work and those machines could be from last decade. The mechanics are well thought and well implemented into this game. It's easy to plan ahead on how you want to combat an enemy or a boss as the various types of attacks have easy and memroable patterns to learn. The fact that you also can easily switch mid-game on how you want to play makes it a nice setup for various combinations of attacks. It does however cost some money but it's worth it if you want to experiment.
The game truly makes a good claim on old grinding games. It will become a massive grindfeast if you want to. I spent a good 10+ hours farming for various cards in the game, they are used to get passive boosts. The various mechanics in how you grind with combat can go from boring to a meditative set of moves. If you enjoy grinding that is.
Overall the game works so good I really WANT the developers to finish the game but as I mentioned earlier in my TL;DR. This is to be the equivelent of a stock market investment. It may or may not yield profit in the end. Only time will tell. So far however, I've earned back my money spent in hours so for me this game was quite a good "bang for the buck" deal.

OVERVIEW
In City of Chains (taking place in a dystopian cyberpunk setting) you take on the role of Holt, a former engineer who has been arrested for refusing to cooperate with the government on a secret military project. After breaking out of prison with a few fellow prisoners, Holt must evade the police while getting to the bottom of a big conspiracy.
Gameplay consists of completing tasks (quests) such as rescuing other prisoners or disabling defenses to gain skill points and advance the story. Skillpoints can be spent on passive combat bonuses or on other skills such as hacking, lockpicking, or speech (charisma). Interestingly, a lot of fights can be directly avoided using skills you have learned, such as using the hacking skill to disable robot sentries or using speech skills to talk your way through hostile situations.
═══════════════════════════════════
PROS & CONS
Pros:
Multiple solutions to hostile enemies, sneak past them or use craftable grenades instead of fighting head on
Variety of equipment and skillpoints to customize your squad
Clean, smooth animations, and fitting soundtrack
Choices your forced to make that may or may not influence the ending of the game
Ammo/other supplies are limited forcing you to explore more to find them
Interesting crafting system for grenades/medicine
Cons:
Lack of a map
No health bars for enemies
Secondary characters don't have much backstory
═══════════════════════════════════
SUMMARY & FINAL RATING
This is a unique RPG Maker game that contains elements from games such as Deus Ex or the Shadowrun games. If you like tactical games set in a dark and dystopian setting this is the game for you!

This game is a good game.
This is a good game because it does its job as a game; it speaks to the player, the observer, in the artistic manner that is exclusive to games as a medium. The same experience could not have been had via a movie, book, or oral storytelling.
communicates not only the uniquely-human philosophical conundrum of purpose (in the form of the question "Why do anything?"), but does so in a way that makes the player ask the question themselves. In a movie, images and sounds are simply absorbed by the viewer, and in many cases that is the most effective way of moving them artistically. As a game, however,
moves the player via interaction, by making them decide for themselves, by their own reasoning, their acceptance or rejection of one philosophical stance or another. By the end of it, the player has been tricked into thinking, which is exactly what good art (and good games) ought to do.
The game is free (as some believe art ought to be). You've got nothing to lose but less than an hour which would likely have been wasted elsewhere. Give it a shot. Tell others to do the same. You might just learn something about yourself.

I wanted to write a quick review since this game is getting a lot of hate (some of it rightfully so).
Pros:
-The gameplay is fantastic.  Very responsive, fresh and new, and once you get past the learning curve and really learn the combos, counters, and tricks it becomes a lot of fun.
-Graphics are gorgeous and the animations are phenomenal.  I love the armor designs in this game, and the ability to create your emblem with basic shapes is a great addition.
-Duels.  I absolutely love playing 1v1 and 2v2.  Don't have to worry about gear class and can have some intense matchups.
-Being able to pick your faction and still play any class from other factions is a nice bit of freedom.
-Lawbringer.
Cons:
-It's a bit of a dead horse at this point, but server issues.  Personally I rarely disconnect from games, but I have ridiculous grade internet.  There are many matches, even after the most recent patch, where people are disconnecting midfight and rarely do I go a game where someone doesn't drop, or I don't get the 'processing' loading icon that freezes the match.
-Steel.  It's the currency system in this game, and while they're taking steps in the right direction, it's still ridiculous the amount you need to spend to get gear and cosmetic pieces, especially if you want to play multiple characters.
-Revenge.  This mechanic is frustratingly annoying, and while it's better after the most recent nerf, it's something that can break a well played duel.
-Matchmaking.  Constant matches against people with gear ten times higher than mine and who have prestiged a good nine or ten times compared to my one.  Very offputting when you're trying new characters.
-Toxicity.  This community is ridiculously toxic, and constantly whining and complaining in chat.  I was yelled at in a match earlier for being HONORABLE because I didn't gank someone.  I have been yelled at for 2v1ing someone.  Ledge throwing, playing Warden, playing Lawbringer, using my combos, being a tryhard.  Brace yourself for constant ♥♥♥♥♥ing and toxicity (though what game doesn't have this now a days).
Overall, I am going to recommend this game, but wait until it's on sale.  I've had a lot of fun with it, and while I refuse to give Ubisoft any money for Steel, I still plan on playing the game.

“Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna)” is a platformer that takes you on an adventure through the Arctic as Nuna and Fox seek the source of an eternal blizzard threatening their village's future.
The game itself is much more atmospheric and story rich than you'd expect. What seems simple and basic turns into much more as you move along and the difficulty jumps are tuned almost perfectly. Perhaps the biggest highlight is how the game presents the culture of the Iñupiat, an Alaskan native people. The collectibles, if I may call them that, are cultural insights found throughout the game by finding owls perched away in the levels. These short videos provide a great deal of knowledge and background of the Iñupiat culture. From storytelling to lifestyle to climate change, you learn so much without realizing it. This along with a well designed environment and great music provide a truly unique experience.
Pros:
- Strong storytelling and very engaging. An underrated aspect of this is how the cutscenes in-game are in the Iñupiaq language (don't worry, you get subtitles).
- Beautiful design; the environment and music create a wonderful atmosphere.
- Strong co-op play, eliminates many frustrations over a subpar AI in single-player.
- Insightful and informative. Presents the Iñupiat culture in a very creative way. You WANT to keep watching the videos and learn more.
Cons:
- Controls can be hard to get the hang of at first. And even then, they seem to get buggy every now and then (I noticed it mostly with the gusts of wind).
- Short. At a comfortable pace, you'll likely finish in 3 hours or less. The DLC is a very nice addition if for nothing else to experience the game more.
- AI in single-player is not the brightest. There will be times where you die or the AI dies because it decided to go against all logic and do something silly. Accept it and try again, at least nothing in the game is naturally aggravating like this.
I bought this game thinking it would be fun and different. That may be an “Understatement of the Year” nominee. This is a very immersive experience that I thoroughly enjoyed. I highly recommend the DLC, “Foxtales,” as it is also fun and engaging, but short as well. And after watching the cultural insights, I see how they tied the rich history of the Iñupiat people into a game with superb storytelling; a real treat that makes me appreciate this even more. The price is a little high for a short game in my opinion, but I also believe this to be a game well worth experiencing. Either bite the bullet or look for any kind of sale (I purchased during the Christmas sale for around 9$ I think).
Verdict- This game gets an
and could be higher if it were not so short or if the controls/AI were more reliable. I highly recommend you adventure through the permafrost as Nuna and Fox and immerse yourself in this deep game.

Obscure is a survival horror game that follows five students caught up in a mystery surrounding their school. Disappearances of the students have become more salient over the years and it just so happens that this little gang of Scooby Doo wannabes is here to close this caper. Can you unravel the horrible secrets behind these closed doors?
As far as survival horror goes, you're looking at a fairly predictable (almost carbon-copy) of the Resident Evil series. Sure, there are a few things scattered about the gameplay that make it different, but the same concepts apply. Search rooms, gather items, shoot monsters. One could argue that the only thing changed here is the setting, but I think most are willing to look past that.
Although I give this game a good rating, I believe that your enjoyment with Obscure will be heavily reliant on whether or not you played survival horror in the past. Honestly, I think the entertainment value hinges almost entirely on nostalgia trips, as this game is really nothing to look at nowadays. Still, some times it is nice to see where we came from and Obscure should certainly keep you occupied if you even have the slightest bit of curiosity about this gem.
With that being said, let's talk about a few things.
Since you have the ability to choose from five different characters at any point throughout the game, you should know that each character has their own advantage. One can hit harder with melee weapons while another can pick locks faster. It adds a certain depth to the game that can really make you strategize your next moves.
To add onto this, all the characters are mortal. Unless every one of your characters die, you are never met with a game over screen. You simply go back to your next available character and start all over. Having the characters be able to die is really interesting to me, as it made me feel more connected with some of the characters. It makes every health pack important and every room a nightmare if you're low on health.
Another cool thing about controlling characters is that you can control your partner. While it doesn't have as much depth as controllable AI today, it is neat that you can tell your character to stay put while you scout ahead or have them follow and back you up. Again, just that extra layer of strategy that the game adds is very enjoyable, at least to me.
The dialogue is great too, but I can see why some people might not like it. If there were ever characters to personify the early 2000s, Obscure's characters would be it. A lot of the cutscenes are laughable and the character interaction is just as neat. At any rate, it is cool to see what was really in style years ago in comparison to how we are now with our games.
Also, I have to say this. The soundtrack is damn-near phenomenal. People might be interested to know that the same person who made the soundtrack for the new horror game Get Even, Olivier Deriviere, is the same person who made the soundtrack for this game. Seriously, if you don't want to buy the game, just look this OST up on YouTube and please agree with me that it's fantastic.
Lastly, I think the gameplay is just all right. I had troubles putting the general gameplay in the positives or negatives because there are times where I was incredibly frustrated with it, but other times where I was pleasantly surprised. If you burn through ammunition and health packs, you'll probably get irritated quick. Otherwise, the gameplay is actually pretty engaging and fun.
Maps are pretty great in this game, but only last until you reach the end level. Without spoiling anything, the end map is seriously frustrating. Corridors, doors, and chambers all over the place that can leave you wondering where you're at spatially. I had a hard time navigating some of the rooms near the end because I kept entering the same place. So, traversing that area was a big pain in the rear and took me way longer than it should have.
The story is lackluster. Like I said in the preface, this game is really reliant on nostalgia. You won't be getting a grade-A story here. It's going to be very odd and almost laughably silly. I can't imagine that anyone finds the story to be good nowadays. Maybe back in 2005 when this was considered scary as all hell, but not today. If you buy Obscure for the story, you'll be disappointed.
Characters are disappointing. Their abilities are cool, don't get me wrong, but anything that allows you to feel empathetic about these people is void in Obscure. You have some very slightly interactions between them, but there's no personality to latch onto. They're just the typical High School cliches: the jock, the geek, the promiscuous, etc. It makes beating the game feel sort of lame, if I'm being honest.
Also, just had to add this in.
When you first start the game, you meet up with two of your friends in a classroom. The janitor comes by and locks everything up and your goal is to stay after school, sneak around, and find your missing buddy. What's the first thing you have to do? Pick up a bat and smash a window in, steal an item from said room, then pick the locks to escape. I mean, the school goes absolutely bonkers anyways, but come on.. That's grounds for expulsion, right there!
Looking for a trip down memory lane at a fair price? Go ahead and buy this sucker. The story is mediocre, but it's at least entertaining enough to keep you playing. Gameplay is pretty decent and, while it doesn't stand up to Resident Evil or Silent Hill, it still earns its spot for die-hard fans of survival horror.

I have quite a few things to say about this game and while this review might be long, I hope you'll hear me out to the end, since this game does have a lot to offer. Firstly, I want to note that I watched this game for a bit before I bought it and from what I've seen and experienced, there have been a lot of positive changes to it that have helped it succeed. This game is far from perfect, but it has been improved upon since it was initially created and went from a nearly miserable state, to a condition that makes it playable and enjoyable.
The gameplay itself is exciting and rewarding should you succeed. You won't necessarily be terrified or afraid all that often, but there will be moments that get you and every close call with Jason that you survive will feel great. Some of the best feelings in this game include escaping Jason with a last minute juke, going back to successfully rescue a survivor and escaping, and of course, working together to kill Jason Vorhees to send him back to h-e-double hockeysticks.
However, what really sold this game for me was the community. I met a solid group of players early on through a micless random I had encountered in a match. These individuals are by far one of the best groups of gamers I've met through online gaming. Many of my hours in this game have been playing with them and honestly I don't know if I would've played as long as I did without them. We've created a steam group and discord outside of F13 and have begun to play other games together. This experience alone is really what made the game for me. I'd encourage you to buy this and find your community within the game, because as many other reviews have said, the people in this game really do make it what it is and if you can find a fun and respectful group of individuals to play with, you will tremendously enjoy yourself playing Friday the 13th: The Game.
I'll give the game itself a 7.75/10 (due to its occasional bugs and launch issues) and the people I've met there a 10/10 and easily recommend it.
(Disclaimer: I'm not saying everyone who plays this game is amazing and respectful, as that would just be untrue, but there are some amazing folks who play this game and finding them makes sifting through the bullsh*t worth it).

Never Alone is a captivating 2d platformer based off the story of "Kunuuksaayuka;" a traditional tale of the Iñupiat, an Alaska Native ethnic group. You play as both a young Inuit girl named Nuna and an arctic fox who go on a journey through harsh weather to find the source of a perpetual blizzard threatening the lives and homes of the girl's village. It's a casual and informative game that's nice to pick up on a lazy afternoon.
The game is simple and linear, and the graphics are pretty. Nuna and Fox are both adorable and strong characters to become easily attached to. The game devs did a pretty good job adding diversity into the puzzles (while still keeping it relevant to the story and the Iñupiaq culture) and slowly amping up the difficulty of solving them as the player progresses throughout the story; however, the mechanics can be a bit wonky at times (especially jumping and using Nuna's weapon), and the game is prone to some bugs. Some stages require quick thinking to switch between Nuna and Fox, as they both have different abilities and can't always travel the same paths/jump onto the same platforms.
"Cultural insights" are scattered throughout the game, symbolized by owls. They are one to two minute videos showcasing interviews from multiple Alaskan natives. They give the player more knowledge about their culture, from their values and traditions to their mythology. This part of the game makes it more documentary-like, which may discourage some, but it enforces the original purpose of the game; to spread and preserve the Iñupiaq culture.
Overall, this was a game I heavily enjoyed, although the mechanics made some rage-enducing moments.

Well boys and girls, I've put nearly 350 hours into this game (at the time of this writing), and I have to be honest; I feel this game is what you make it.  If you've had "technical issues", then I certainly do not blame you for smearing it all over the reviews.  However, there seems to be a fairly large number of people who don't have as many of these issues.  The game is "buggy"; startup issues, "nether.exe stopped working", server crashes, collision issues, etc.  During the pre-release days, we all lived with these issues due to it's status.  Once it released though, the problems continued.  Most of us had adapted to the problems and continued to play.....because it was fun.
The game began to take it's toll on me when the "cheaters" showed up (I don't call them "Hackers"...they are not deserving of such a title).  My friends and I would often team up against them and get killed....oh well.  I quit playing the game after several months of struggling to survive, regardless of my efforts to be friendly.  I had only 12 player kills.
The PVE servers renewed my interest in this game.  I've played nearly as many hours since their release, as I played in the first 8 months without them.  Yes, the game still has problems; but If you can deal with them, you may find the game is quite fun (assuming you can get signed in).
As far as graphics, they're not too bad.  Sometimes it's nice to stand and admire the lighting against the post-apocalyptic Chicago silhouette.  The graphics do seem to be poorly optimized though.  I talked to several people with decent rigs who had frame-rate issues.
I thought the 64-bit requirement was a little odd.  It didn't pose a hinderence for me, but I'm sure it did for some people.
So, would I recommend this game?  I suppose it depends on what type of person you are.  If you're willing to look over a few issues, then you may find it very enjoyable.  However, if you're looking for a highly polished, perfectly functioning game, this may not be the game for you.
By far, the biggest issue with this game, is the development team.  The best thing to do is assume they don't exist.  That's how they treat the players.  Don't look for support from anyone other than players.  Steam doesn't care and PUREbs, Phosphate, or whoever, go with the 'ol "Cash and Grab" way of doing things.
Take it for what it's worth!

Jagged Alliance Flashback feels to me like the first true and genuine attempt at making a new Jagged Alliance game since the original two. Right from the start it's clear that the people making this game are fans of the original and that they're truly trying to re-capture the gameplay. The map, its sectors and the way you move on it are all faithfully recreated. Movement in the game itself has been modernized a bit by using larger tiles, but the game honestly benefits from it. The addition of very clear indicators that not only show your cover but the angles towards your enemies is a fantastic one. There's no guesswork in whether or not a piece of cover works at an awkward angle, the game straight up tells you before you move. Not only that, but it tells you this in regards to every enemy visible to your guys.
The gunfights feel satisfyingly lethal as well, and with added polish will no doubt match the brutality that I came to love from JA2. Your mercs can die and often quite easily, if you're not careful with them, and it takes little to make them bleed. The blood effects are fantastic as well, with battlefields quickly becoming spray-painted in red, splattering onto walls, objects and the ground in fantastically exaggerated ways. There's no realism in it, but this is one front where realism truly is neither needed nor wanted.
As with any early-access games, bugs are to be expected before its release, so no points are taken from their existance. Only just ecchoing the ever present warning that if you buy this game during early access, you're getting it as is. What I played was satisfying, fun, visceral and deadly, and it's no doubt the closest thing to a true and real Jagged Alliance game we've had in over a decade.

Jagged Alliance Flashback is a test that Full Control used to guage how Kickstarters work.
*UPDATE* Final Version Review:
Not much has changed since the last review, unfortunately. You can create your own merc now, which presents you with a screen crowded with uninspiring text that honestly looks very uninspiring. The entire game using 1 font that isn't very pleasant to read large chunks of text with. The inventory and character screen all look the same with some really simple text boxes for info and filter types.
The game feels very rushed at no real surprise, because it is. Full Control decided to put a year of work into Jagged Alliance Flashback during and after the Kickstarter with time for vacations and to get through a large bug list for their other game, Space Hulk. Unfortunately it really shows in the game, as it looks messy and rushed from the start.
Old review:
With one update left to go before the final version, things don't look good for the new game in the JA series. Even this 'late' in development (only 18 months) the game feels like it doesn't know what it wants to be. Touting itself as a spiritual successor to the very popular Jagged Alliance 2,
seems to forget its roots and a lot of the time, what made those games good. It's uncertain what will be in the final game compared to the early access version we've been playing, but the devs attitude towards the game recently make it sound as if they'd just like to be done with making it. They went to Kickstarter without a plan, and upon being funded, quickly realised they were out of their depth. They spent most of the time making the website and assigning community officers and their game suffered because of it. Already they are implying core features will be added after the game has actually been released, but I find that hard to believe with their obvious lack of motivation to continue on the game.
The game plays like a basic isometric turn based shooter. You can target head, bodies and legs with your weapon. Up until recently, you couldn't choose the amount of AP you took on the shot and had to keep 'rolling the dice' to try and hit someone. The UI is unintuitive and hard to comprehend at the best of times. It's colored with a flat gradient and unflattering font. Mercenary portraits and interactions are limited and static. Inventory management might as well have been removed because clearly they don't understand what made it good in JA2 (pockets of various sizes for different items etc). The art style isn't consistent; some areas feel totally out of place due to their pallette.
For what it's worth, this game does
things right, just generally the things you wouldn't attribute to Jagged Alliance. The cover system is nice, and hitting enemies in the head with a low-percent chance to hit is satisfying, it just makes you wonder if this game would have benefited if it wasn't tied to the source material it loosely bases itself off of.
Jagged Alliance: Flashback is an empty experience that just kind of exists. People will get this game confused with Back in Action. At this point, if you want to play Jagged Alliance, you'll be playing JA2 with the 1.13 mod. It's sad but teaches you a thing or two about Kickstarter!

Stories Untold is a fun little game with a world and visual style patterned after Stranger Things. I recommend playing through the entire thing in one sitting, which I did (without any guides) in about 2h45m - so about the length and price of going to a movie.
Structurally, the game has 4 distinct chapters, which appear unrelated at first but start to converge as the story progresses. The game begins with a fairly traditional text adventure but quickly introduces new puzzles and gameplay elements. The visuals, audio, voice acting, and plot are all well done and engaging.
Some of the common complaints have to do with the text speed and parser during the text adventure portions. The text speed was a bit annoying, especially as transitioning back and forth between areas causes the game to repeat the same description - hopefully the developer will add a minor quality-of-life feature to allow users to hit the spacebar or something to instantly complete the text, but as it stands it was only a minor annoyance for a few minutes and not game breaking. Similarly, I didn't have much issue with the parser - it's fairly rudimentary, but as the game progresses less time is spent doing the text adventure stuff in favor of other types of puzzles.
The only significant issue I had with the game involves a section where you need to listen to and transcribe a series of numbers delivered in Morse code. If you're not playing in a quiet environment, have good headphones, or are remotely hard of hearing, this part can be extremely frustrating because the beeps and chirps of the audio are delivered so rapidly that it's hard to discern the dots and dashes.
I'm unsure how much work it would be, but I'd encourage the devs to add an option in the game to slow the Morse code audio down to make the dots and dashes easier to differentiate and possibly add some kind of visual element (like a small light) that would blink on an off in relation to the Morse code audio. As it stands, if you have any of the aforementioned issues with either hearing or quality of your listening environment, you'll likely just have to look up the solution online.
One additional recommendation is that you play the game with pen and paper available. The third chapter (the same one that contains the Morse code bit) requires you to receive and retain strings of numbers and codes that are easier done if you have them written down.
Aside from those relatively minor issues, I absolutely loved the game, its setting, story, and presentation. If you've seen and enjoyed the show, Stranger Things, it's definitely a worthwhile experience that costs and lasts as long as going to a movie.

A very clever experiment but not a very good game.
There's great art direction on display, voice acting is believable and there are moments where all the different gameplay elements genuinely work together to create a chilling atmosphere and put the player right in the centre of it all.
Unfortunately, none of those individual gamelay elements are done particularly well.
Text adventure bits are very bad at recognizing commands.
What little puzzles there are seem to be designed to test your patience rather than challenge your intelligence.
1st person walking bits are weirdly clumsy and unresponsive.
But I could overlook all of that if it wasn't for the story.
First three parts are quite intriguing, each for its own reasons. But when the Big Reveal comes in part 4, it retroactively invalidates most of what you've done up to that point. Even if the plot itself is sort of legit, the fact that none of what you've been doing really matters leaves a bad aftertaste. It just doesn't feel like time well spent.
I wish there was a "middling" review option available. I hate to give this game a thumbs down, but simultaneously I can only recommend it as an interesting experiment, not an experience worth having. Then again, it's not an expensive game and I definitely hope we'll see this particular style of adventure games evolve in the future.

As a whole, I thought the game was definately worth 79p, and I did like it, despite suffering from some issues.
It is an odd one. It's concept and style is one I really like, and I think it had potential. However, it's issues were that it's gunplay was awful as aiming was perfetic with nothing but a slight zoom to increase it. It's story (espcially towards the end) was just senseless and didn't feel like it really cared for itself. The game has an insane amount of blur and film grain, that it is sometimes impossible to see anything. Animations sometimes literally don't happen! And most importantly, it is SO DAMN HARD. Trying to hit anything often fails and reloading is a long pain. The enemies are way to overpowered and kill you in one hit, and they often come in large numbers at high speeds. You'll often be replaying these levels, learning the enemy's attack patterns and spawn areas to get an advantage, which just becomes repetitive.
Not to mention, the jumpscares aren't appreciated.
However, the game did do somethings right. For example, it's enviroment and artstyle is beautiful. Never have I seen a game create such a vivid and dark world. It's music is very fitting for the story it's telling and it's sounds are outright creepy and well costructed. Level design isn't bad, although not knowing where to go next was a common thing to happen. The game creates a great atmosphere and becomes immensly creepy when it wants to, unfortunately, this is often followed by a terrible, cheap jumpscare. In fact, this game has possibly the worst jumpscares I have ever to experienced. They're just a loud noise with a bright light without warning, and it's scary, yes, but not appreciated. At least  jumpscares from a game like Outlast were well done.
So why could I possibly be recommending this game? Well, if you can overlook it's flaws, and yes, that'll be harder than the bloody game itself, but if you can, it is a scary horror game with good pacing, and a brilliant atmosphere. For such a cheap price, I can only recommend this just so you can make your opinion on wether you thought this game was worth 79p.
It tries, and does what it can to impress you. It may not be a masterpiece of horror, but it's well worth the GB of hard drive space and your hard-earned 79p.

If you're like me and you read game reviews before buying a game, you might be wondering why a lot of people are so massively frustrated at the lack of timely updates to this game. After playing the game, I can understand why. Secrets of Grindea is really, really good. Every single area in the game is polished to a diamond sheen. It's just a huge shame it isn't "finished".
+Great Animations and Soundtrack: I really am a fan of the animations here. While the character portraits are, in my opinion, a little offputting, the animations of the characters and enemies are top-quality and show action surprisingly well. The soundtrack is very well-made and fits the areas of the game well.
+Fun Combat/Character Building: There's a lot of flexibility to the leveling system, and you don't have to fall into the Warrior/Mage/Rogue trope like many other games. The combat is fluid, and surprisingly challenging sometimes, even on normal mode.
+Surprisingly funny satire: The narrative of Secrts of Grindea plays out like a satire of genres ranging from classic Legend of Zelda-likes to MMORPGs and Roguelikes. Unlike a lot of satire, however, it does this really well. Stick with the story, and don't pass it off as another edgy attempt at satire.
-Updates all over the place: From what I can see, development time is slow. You can access the beta, and the content in the beta is just as well-made as the rest of the game minus a few sound effects here and there. This, however, is not a lot of extra content, and the current beta maybe adds an hour-and-a-half to total gameplay time. I find it hard to be too critical of this considering the polish of the game, however.
-Sometimes a bit too challenging: Some areas of the game can get hard. Like, really hard. That isn't necessarily a bad thing, but due to some boss and enemy patterns, it can come down to rng more often than not. Skill will get you past it, but sometimes it can et annoying.
Overall I would suggest waiting for the game to fully release, but if you're like me and don't care too much about early-access, I would recommend it.

Primarily a Mobile player, level 32 at time of review
MMORTS, Far better than most MMORTS's, good base building mechanics, real time tactical ship battles, relatively high rate of customization to ships (stats and equipment only, appearance customizations are severly limited and are more a side effect of certain upgrades),decent variety of ships.  A great game to play on a variety of platforms.  Active development team.
Level 1 to 20: Relatively fast paced with a little effort, you won't, however, matter much in the grand scheme of things.  You're small and will likely only be accepted by recruiting factions and factions looking for people to click the "help" button and speed up wait times slightly.  It's a good learning period though, and you won't have much to worry about.
Level 20-30: The game starts slowing down about here as wait times start occuring more frequently and the ships you can possibly field start getting more expensive.  It's here that PvP becomes "a thing" and while you won't likely be much of a threat, people will try to pick fights with you occasionally.  This period of time is the "awkward puberty" stage of the game.  It's basically a very "tough love" learning period that lets you see if you really want to play this game.
You will need to play for long term goals that won't come to fruition for days, weeks, even possibly months depending on how active you are, the goals you have, and how much experimenting and "messing around" takes up your time.  It will be a bit grindy.  You will face hardship (as much as you can from a game that is) and it will take a bit of time to get through unless you pour literally hundreds if not thousands of dollars to speed through the waiting periods.
Level 30-34: Pre-high end PvP.  Anything level 35 and up is at the mercy of anything else above level 35.  There is no longer protection against anything higher then 5 levels attacking you at level 35.  As such, you will likely spend your time researching and upgrading your fleets and defenses until you believe you can handle being at level 35 and above.
Level 35-40: If you're smart, you won't call too much attention to yourself, either way, you're going to likely be a target more often as level 45-50 basing fleets try to steal the resources you have or even just try to scare you off so that you won't be competing for resources and parts.  by now you know the importance of farming vega fleets to upgrade your ships and you'll know that if everyone is farming, it becomes harder to farm at a solid rate, hence why people attack enemy farm fleets.  More resources and upgrades for them, less for the enemy.
Level 40-50: Typical PvP level.  I haven't reached this point so I don't know what to really tell you about how you're likely to be spending your time.  Most of what I see is farming in sector and warring for domination over other factions.  Events are much easier now and the real threat is rival players.  Supposedly wait times take weeks at this level unless you are willing to dump large amounts of money into instantly getting past them.  Time is now, by far, the measure of success in war.  It's constantly a struggle to ensure your enemy's fleets are out of commission for longer than your own.
At the time of this review, an update is officially announced that will change the entire way repair time and refit builds work.  This will rework several strategies and alter the way the game is played substantially.  In fact, the entire focus of the game will likely shift towards a much more agressive style of play due to repair times being completely based on the defensive values of the ship (outside of ship upgrades)
As of this moment, I recommend this game.  You can play it on your PC, then play it on your phone.  It's not perfect but it is worth spending the time to see if you like it.

I wanted to write a quick review since this game is getting a lot of hate (some of it rightfully so).
Pros:
-The gameplay is fantastic.  Very responsive, fresh and new, and once you get past the learning curve and really learn the combos, counters, and tricks it becomes a lot of fun.
-Graphics are gorgeous and the animations are phenomenal.  I love the armor designs in this game, and the ability to create your emblem with basic shapes is a great addition.
-Duels.  I absolutely love playing 1v1 and 2v2.  Don't have to worry about gear class and can have some intense matchups.
-Being able to pick your faction and still play any class from other factions is a nice bit of freedom.
-Lawbringer.
Cons:
-It's a bit of a dead horse at this point, but server issues.  Personally I rarely disconnect from games, but I have ridiculous grade internet.  There are many matches, even after the most recent patch, where people are disconnecting midfight and rarely do I go a game where someone doesn't drop, or I don't get the 'processing' loading icon that freezes the match.
-Steel.  It's the currency system in this game, and while they're taking steps in the right direction, it's still ridiculous the amount you need to spend to get gear and cosmetic pieces, especially if you want to play multiple characters.
-Revenge.  This mechanic is frustratingly annoying, and while it's better after the most recent nerf, it's something that can break a well played duel.
-Matchmaking.  Constant matches against people with gear ten times higher than mine and who have prestiged a good nine or ten times compared to my one.  Very offputting when you're trying new characters.
-Toxicity.  This community is ridiculously toxic, and constantly whining and complaining in chat.  I was yelled at in a match earlier for being HONORABLE because I didn't gank someone.  I have been yelled at for 2v1ing someone.  Ledge throwing, playing Warden, playing Lawbringer, using my combos, being a tryhard.  Brace yourself for constant ♥♥♥♥♥ing and toxicity (though what game doesn't have this now a days).
Overall, I am going to recommend this game, but wait until it's on sale.  I've had a lot of fun with it, and while I refuse to give Ubisoft any money for Steel, I still plan on playing the game.

This is a very well thought out and carefully developed game. The developers are transparent with their project and unfortunately this isn't their full time job. If you're not the type who is:
A) Interested in game design from a developer's point of view via blogs
B) Interested in providing imput and feedback on a game in development
C) Patient enough to wait as long as it may take for updates or full release
Then Secrets of Grindea may not be for you, probably best to wait for the full release because you may be disappointed. Don't get me wrong, what's been already released is great. But you'll be left wanting more, like getting a three course meal and extra long for the entree.
Development issues aside, Secrets of Grindea is a combination of several action adventure titles, made into a unique experience. There's a lot of heavy influence from Secret of the Mana, but there's some Legend of Zelda, and Monster Hunter thrown in too, but in a way that meshes well to create something fun and engaging within itself.
One of the best aspects is not having a class restriction. There's three skill trees: One Handed, Two-Handed, and Magic. You can focus on one, two, or a combination of three to create your own character, fully customed to your playstyle. Throw in the three passive trees: General, Melee, and Magic and you have ways to relly make skill combinations shine. So far the favorite build I've made is a Berserker that gets a magic attack bonus from less than 50% MP that randomly deals burn damage on attack and gets a physical attack bonus on burning enemies. (There are different types of support magic, but those are still in development)
The story is engaging for what's there so far. Plenty of overused RPG tropes, but done in a humorous way that pokes fun of the genre or even some twists on what you would expect. A handful of pop culture references mixed in too for lampshading purposes. It's short, sweet, fun but still a work in progress.
The real draw of the game is the Arcade Mode. Pretty much a Roguelike system where you run through randomly generated dungeons with whatever kind of build you want to try. This is probably where you'll be spending most of your time after "finishing" story mode. It feels like a roguelike, plays like a roguelike, and is as fun/infuriating as a rogulike. Good stuff, just make sure you go through story mode to avoid any spoilers.
6/10 for what's on the table now. Most likely would get a 9-10/10 when fully released. Buy if you're interested, definitely follow it if you're curious. Just keep in mind that it's only three people with full time jobs making this game. Updates are pretty slow when compared to standards you may be used to with other Early Acess titles. Not a bad thing, just a lot of care put into development.

(NOTE: I've been playing the GOG version, which is why my playtime on Steam is so low.)
The added scenes in the Director's Cut are welcome, and flesh out the story a little, but the new sections at the beginning of the game where you play as Nico feel a little padded with unnecessary puzzles to extend the playtime. Ironically, a few things that were in the original game are missing here, like some pieces of dialogue and an option that used to result in a death and game over. Nothing very significant is gone though, much more has been added than has been lost, and some things were cut for good reason, so it's not a problem unless you're a purist. The Director's Cut has the same graphics, resolution and sound quality as the original, but newly recorded lines are of higher quality; which actually makes the rest of the sound much more jarring, as the old lines of dialogue are very low quality in comparison. The UI is slightly different too, and there is a hints system which gives you clues (and eventually a solution if you prod it enough) to the puzzles, allowing the player to set their own difficulty as they wish, so I find this a great addition. The most noticable difference of the Director's Cut, apart from the new scenes, is the fact that little boxes appear on screen with characters faces during speech, which animates the dialogue a little more.
For those who aren't familiar with the game at all... Well, two things make a good adventure game: story and puzzles. On the story side, it's a globe-trotting kind of adventure about finding ancient clues, exploring ruins and mausoleums, uncovering murder plots, and a little bit of magic and mysticism. Although it sounds quite serious, it's actually a pretty vibrant and light-hearted game with some good humour and exaggerated characters. It's charming, but pretty grounded and rarely laugh-out-loud funny. The story makes me think of a mix between Indiana Jones and The Da Vinci Code. On the puzzle side, it doesn't indulge too much in the typical "adventure game logic", puzzles usually make sense (with a few exceptions), and you don't have to roleplay MacGyver that much (again, with a few exceptions). So overall, great. Not every puzzle is entertaining though, and some are a little obtuse or long-winded.
As a P&C adventure where you spend a lot of time just looking around a static screen and talking to people, visuals play a fairly important role. The art style was always good (for the most part anyway... Characters can look a bit "off"), but this game does look aged, and I'm not just talking about the resolution. Characters can clip through each other or through objects on the screen, some sprites are badly aliased; and when George is walking at an angle, his positioning and size relative to the environment around him can look embarassingly bad.
Overall though, a great game that spawned a great sequel and... some other ones.
PS. I forgot to mention the music. I love the music in this game! Very atmospheric soundtrack, kind of minimalistic but soothing, and always fits well with the scene.

These are actually the charms of these types of games, but they arent for everyone.
Subjectively, i'd give this game an 8/10 Objectively, it'd get something around a 4/10. Theres a huge disparity between what a general modern gamer is looking for, and what specific kinds of people like. Type of Game:
Third Person Turn Based Tactical Action
Version Played:
PC version through Steam
Similar Games:
XCOM, The Original Jagged Alliances, and to a lesser degree Final Fantasy Tactics
The Good:
- Combat and gameplay is just as well crafted as the original two, which is a huge leap in enjoyability over the lacking Back In Action game
- The enemy AI is actually formidable in Flashback, which really pushes you to make the right tactical decisions at every turn
- Fog of war returns to this version, which creates a much better environment for strategy and challenge
- The overall humor to the game is very tongue-in-cheek and, again, harkens back to the original Jagged Alliances
- The difficulty level is very high and can create some very tense moments
- For example: Being pinned down with only one squad member left knowing that exposing yourself to cover would be your doom, but being forced to do so in order to take a decent shot at the last remaining enemy. Shooting at his torso would increase your chances of accuracy, but would only wound him. Instead you aim for the head and go for the killshot. You miss and immediately pay the price with your life. Restart mission.
- Even as Early Access, the game has an active modding community that makes full use of the Steam Workshop. This could greatly increase your playtime with the game while waiting for its full release.
- There are many systems in place that haven’t been fleshed out yet, but show great potential.
- These include things like: XP skill progression system, equipment loadouts, and numerous weapon types
The Bad:
- The game does not have a decent User Interface yet, which leads to confusing directives and less than intuitive menu navigation
- Bugs, as expected, are numerous. Some examples:
- Inventory management screens that won’t disappear after you leave them
- Buying mercs that don’t show up on your next assignment
- Stuck on a mission that won’t progress even after its objectives have been completed
- There isn’t a full-fledged tutorial yet, which means I spent a lot of time trying to figure out the mechanics. I imagine I still haven’t quite figuring out the proper way to play the game.
- This may just be my personal preference, but the camera is very difficult to manipulate. The default setting does not move with the arrows, but first needs to be rotated correctly. Not a game breaker, but a pain the butt none-the-less.
- The depth to the game just isn’t there yet, which will turn away many that are looking for a deep Jagged Alliance experience. The story isn’t complete and the missions are not all implemented. Storylines are completely flushed out and characters aren’t fully developed.
Can you play it while the children are awake?:
While the game doesn’t have the most realistic graphics, the blood and death are still present. I would not allow my children to watch me play it, but I imagine it would be fine for some that are more mature.
Did I make time to complete it?
The version played was not complete, but I played what was there. The gameplay, as I mentioned before, was very enjoyable. I don’t imagine I will be firing it up again until the game is out of Early Access, however, because I definitely found myself wanting a deeper experience.
Redlight or Greenlight?
This game is currently at a redlight.
Jagged Alliance: Flashback is a great starting point for a long awaited reboot of the original Jagged Alliance games. However, the content that is currently available just isn’t worth the $44.99 asking price. At this point I can guarantee the game will be worth the wait when it comes out, but only purchase it at full price if you are willing to support developers that will do the Jagged Alliance brand the justice it deserves. Do not purchase it expecting a fulfilling gaming experience.

Eight months ago I went to their website to create an account and saw quickly that the website had not setup any security at all. When you create (and login) an account you have to do that on an unlocked page and they 'mandatory' wants you to fill in all your personal data (they even want your phone number, MANDATORY). If you don't fill in all the data you can't create an account there.

I have told the dev on the Steam forum about the security issue and he said that he will forward it. Eight months later the pages on their website are still unlocked and unsecured which gives me a bad feeling about the company. I don't like companies that wants to know everything about you when you create an account, but does not take the privacy and security of their customers seriously.
This is pretty much unacceptable in 2016, any company that operates on the internet should have at least some basic security setup and have locks on the sensitive pages to protect the privacy of their customers.... or simply don't ask for so much personal 'mandatory' information on the account registration page if security and a safe account registration is not a priority.

It is also not very clear why they want so much personal info from me when I create an account, why do they want my phone number exactly?

I really have to give a big thumb down on that aspect and as a result the whole review will get a thumb down... till the time they take the personal data of their customers seriously and have redone the account pages on their website.
And pls note that the thumb down is not due to the product/software itself, I am pretty satisified with how the software works.

Just an upfront preamble before the actual review. The company who made this game, Image & Form Games, sent me a free copy of the game and requested that I make a YouTube video covering it. They did not request a review be written, I'm doing that on my own accord. My video covered first impressions of around the first thirty minutes of the game, and is linked below:
The game itself is a 2D platformer where you use a pickaxe to mine ever deeper into the Earth in search of a lost friend. As you progress you acquire new abilities, such as a bomb launcher to blow up things, and a hookshot to allow you to pull yourself to walls, ceilings and floors. You will also acquire upgrade cogs, that will allow you to access extra functions for the abilities you unlock, such as making your pickaxe do more damage to enemies. You will find gems that you can sell to make your abilities overall more powerful, like making your pick axe mine through blocks faster or giving you more bomb launcher ammo. There is also a levelling system in the game, and each level makes your gems sell for more money, and allow you to further level up your abilities. The game is littered with dungeons, smaller areas that serve as a place to challenge yourself within the game and find upgrade cogs and artifacts. There are also a number of secret areas to find throughout the map.
Overall the gameplay is fun and engaging. The game in general is very easy, outside of one or two sections that can pose a challenge. The secret trials unlocked at the end of game by collecting every artifact is also a welcome challenge if you're looking for it. Besides a (kind of) boss at the start and the final boss, there are no other major enemies within the game, just minor enemies to serve as obstacles as you make your way through the game. If you're looking for a game to really challenge your abilities, this game probably won't do it. But if you're just looking for a fun platformer that you can enjoy progressing through and exploring for secrets, then this is the game for you.
There is a story, but it doesn't get incredibly in depth. The basic story is that you are Dot, a robot in search for her friend who went missing after he defeated Vectron and saved the world in the previous Steamworld Dig game. You quickly find a new friend to join you on your journey, as you dig further down into the mines and discover that a sinister plot is unfolding. The story is pretty interesting, but it doesn't really seem to be the focus of the game. It serves more as a reason for you to keep exploring and moving through new areas of the game. But in that respect, the game does do a very good job of making sure you know where you're supposed to be going by making sure it is marked on the world map.
I played enough of the game to beat it with all artifacts collected and access the hidden trials at the end of the game. Having played it all, I can fully endorse this game to anyone who enjoys 2D Metroidvania style games. If I had purchased it for $20, I would have felt it was money well spent given I enjoyed all 12 hours it took me to fully complete the game.
