I originally was interested in this game solely because of its beautiful graphics. The artwork looked so beautiful, I wanted to see what this game was all about. Once it went on sale, I bought it to give it a try. This game gives you roughly 3 hours of game play, with the option of purchasing a DLC which obviously extends the story. I however did not buy the DLC, so my review will only reflect the actual game.
Never Alone is a story-telling platform that gives you the option of playing in co-op or individually. Not only is this game a piece of art, it gives you insights into another culture you may not have known much about. The game switches between two different art forms in order to tell the story of a young girl and her new found friend. These two friends are inseparable through their journey to protect the girls village. Although this game can be difficult at times, it is an enjoyable puzzle game, that you will use trial and error as well as your problem solving skills to get you through.
I suggest this game to people with all levels of gaming. I especially recommend this game for pairs of friends that have varying levels of gaming, because it allows you to help each other through the puzzles and platforms in many different ways. I myself do not consider myself to have high gaming abilities, but even I was able to help my partner with parts in this game. It has a little bit of something to offer to everyone that plays the game.
One last interesting thing that this game offers that I thought was unique are the "cultural insights" built into the game. Similar to the achievements that you will receive while playing through the game, you will be awarded these cultural insights. In the main menu, after you complete the game, you are able to view all of your insights and click on ones you find interesting to watch. These insights will give you more cultural background and extend the games premise if you really enjoyed it. Learning more about the events and stories that helped mold the frameworks of Never Alone is a great bonus for real fans of the game.

A classical adventure point and click game in which you play as an American tourist on vacation in France. Just so happens that a bomb explodes inside the cafe at which you were having a coffee. Needless to say it's enough for the main character to investigate and get tangled inside the Templar story.
So the game is a bit cheesy. Has that 90's vibe as well. But that's actually quite refreshing nowadays. And I enjoyed it quite a bit. The story is a standard Templars story - there's a conspiracy, they want something to rule the world, you're up to stop it. Simple but quite entertaining. On your adventure you'll get to visit France, Spain, Ireland and Egypt. The characters while feeling a bit cliché are still pretty interesting and the dialogs are pretty fun.
Visually it's still very lovely looking. Hand drawn locations are varied and pretty - although in a bit smaller resolution. It still looks good. And the animations remind of older French animation films. The sound is also well done - all dialogs are spoken so no reading necessary.
The puzzles are pretty nice - there's nothing too abstract and they do make sense for the most part. Only on few occasions you get the full map with no clue where to go next. For most part the next step is obvious. The interface used is a standard point and click - but instead of picking sentences to speak you use the icon of the topic or item you want your character to talk about. Pretty neat if you don't like reading all the possible questions you might want to ask.
Overall this game is pretty fun - even after all these years. Interesting characters, well designed and drawn locations and most of all entertaining story makes this a must play on any point and click enthusiast list. Highly recommended.

I have to admit that I was not the hugest fan of Frictional's breakout hit, Amnesia. I enjoyed it, but I found it rather overhyped. It took me a while to check this one out as a result. But I have to say, it fixes all of my issues with that game and adds even more to love with a fantastic story.
It has a much better variety of enemies. You only spend a short time facing each monster, but that keeps your time with them all the more memorable. There's a lot less time to be numbed to each monster, something Amnesia suffered greatly from IMO. It also adds a welcome touch of variety to the run-and-hide horror games that have been so common since that game stormed onto the scene. Each enemy requires a different strategy to bypass. They're all rather simple, but they keep things fresh while adding something a little more immediate to a very story-heavy game.
As I said, the story is brilliant. When I hear about games with good stories, I'm often a little disappointed. Many just seem to be trying to impress players by being philisophical (which has a tendency to feel forced) or by throwing a wild twist at them, but aren't really fully developed stories. Soma is not one of those. This is a game that poses big questions about the nature of existence, but the characters keep it grounded, giving you that emotional connection that really makes you care about the questions it's asking. There are choices that actually made me turn the game off so I could reflect on them for a day or two. I can't recall the last time I've done that. Even the side-characters get some moments to shine and pretty much the full gamut of the human condition is on display here.
Highly recommended. Must-play for Sci-fi fans.

Never Alone is a puzzle platformer about a little girl and a spirit fox trying to find the source of a blizzard. I played through this game with my 3 1/2 year old daughter and overall it was a positive experience. She didn't find the story all that interesting (it moves very slowly which makes it hard to follow for younger children) but she still felt tension and excitement during the more "urgent" sequences. None of the platforming sections or puzzles are all that complicated and of the few that were, it was simple of me to switch to single-player mode, beat them, and then return to co-op.
Now my gripes with the game. CO-OP is basically drop-in/out which is always nice but for some baffling reason it's impossible to switch characters between controllers. The little girl (Nuna) is always P1 controller and the fox is always P2 controller. So whenever my daughter wanted to switch and play the other character, we'd have to swap controllers. Not a huge deal, but still a design oversight.
Secondly, the whole idea behind this game is to honorably represent a minority people's culture, right? And yet the game features a female protaganist when it's clear the original story features a male protaganist. Inbetween levels there are excerpts of the original story from the original storyteller. They all refer to the main protaganist as "he" and "the boy". So it begs the question of why they made the protaganist female. I don't think you get to sit on a high horse of "culturally representive game" if you decide, feminism > minority cultures.
This strangeness continues in the Foxtales DLC which begins talking about two friends who live in different villages (both infered young boys) but the player characters are....Nuna and the fox again. It doesn't really make any sense and I can only presume that they didn't have the budget to model new characters and mechanics.
All in all this is a great co-op game to play if you have a youngin'. But I wouldn't recommend for an adult playing by themself as it's a bit too simplistic for a seasoned gamer.

It got super glitchy for me to the point where I seriously considered uninstalling in the last chapter of the game.  The primary glitch I saw was where the video would sort of freeze, switching rapidly between a couple of frames, but you could tell from the audio that the game was still going.  Alt-tabbing fixed this most of the time, but some of the time the game would crash.  And it takes a few seconds for it to tab back in, which really destroys the momentum in what is supposed to be a fast-pace game.  This happened to me at least half a dozen times in the final boss fight, as well as, I think, two crashes.  There were also some pretty stupid video glitches with the boss where (s)he would just wink out of existence in a transition cutscene.  Really took all the fun out of it.
Crashes happened at least once per chapter, usually when a cutscene was supposed to start.  Once I knew things were screwy when a bunch of enemies were just standing still around me--the next cutscene caused a crash.
The gameplay could be fun in a mindless hack-n-slash kind of way.  The RPG elements were very limited, but I think it would all work together if the port was better.  Do not buy this game expecting anything seamless or even remotely bug-checked.

A great concept marred by bitterly pityful execution.
What starts out to be a promising logical puzzle horror adventure game turns out to be a completely irrational, illogical set of clicks and attempts by the player to try to guess what the developers intended to happen with little or no feedback at all. Even the in-game hints system is vague at best.
The controls for inventory and using items is very annoying and lacks fluidity. The forced walking speed is an annoyance, especially when there is a fair amount of backtracking throughout the game involved.
You also can not describe this title as a horror survival either, as its not possible to die.
Some nice touches of horror brushing through the gameplay but very weak and suspense is not sustained properly in-game, which causes the scares to be cheap jumps rather than actual in-your-head horror. Not very obvious but there are 3 different endings which is always a nice touch to implement into any game.
I'm a fan of this genre so its great to see games like this get developed and out into the commercial world, especially by independant developers but if unpolished titles like this were released out often the genre would be soon dead and forgotten.
Worth a couple of quid in the sale and you have an interest in horror type games, but avoid paying full whack.

This game is fantastic and is a must-buy if you play guitar. If you don't play guitar and are curious, it's actually good enough that I'd still recommend getting it. It is far and away my favorite music game on the market.
Be warned that it's more of a guitar practice tool than a game. But that's exactly what it should be: a practice tool that has just enough game-y design to keep it interesting, but not so much that it gets in the way of practicing. The only linear progression the game has is in the form of "missions" along the side of the menus that encourage you to try different things. You can ignore them entirely if you want, but sometimes they are very helpful (especially the ones associated with the Session mode, which teach you bits of relevant music theory). It's a well-designed experience.
The interface is very slick and the game has no loading time or lengthy transitions between browsing and playing songs. This is great news because the interface was the main flaw in Rocksmith 1. "Riff repeater" phrase rehearsing options are integrated into the pause menu, so you can drop into them on the fly while playing songs.
The soundtrack is excellent. It has hits (Knights of Cydonia, Paranoid Android, etc), more obscure music with fun guitar parts, and even a few tracks from small indie bands I have never heard of. The song Stay In by Jaws is one of the indie songs that stuck out to me. And it's very worth it to import Rocksmith 1 songs -- they have had their tabs updated to fix inaccuracies and to use new features in the new game (RS1 DLC songs have be updated as well).
The game has a Session mode, where you can load backing instruments, jam, and have them follow along with you. It's alright. It's implemented well and has a ton of options, but I and other friends find it odd that it follows you, rather than maintaining a constant rhythm for you to improv over. Your mileage may vary with it, but it's a welcome addition.
There are also a number of Guitarcade mini-games that focus on various guitar techniques. They are a distraction for when you're bored with performing songs, but some of them are pretty amusing. There is even a House of the Dead 2 spoof where you play chords to shoot zombies.
I'm an amateur guitarist, but it's thanks to Rocksmith that I've kept up with practicing as frequently as I have. When learning an instrument it's easy to get bored when it turns into a grind and you don't know what music to try. You need some structure. Rocksmith is that structure, and it makes it easy to practice.

A venerable Warden main since the first closed alpha session of December 9th, 2016, I loved For Honor.
Played it whenever the alpha tests were live, and the following closed and open betas.
I normally don't support Ubisoft games, but the Beta tests were fantastic and I'd had enough experience with the game to warrant my Gold Edition purchase. I was a little suprised at myself.
Somehow on release, For Honor was a broken, unbalanced mess.
Many connectivity issues,
Developers not meeting their own weekly content goals,
Extreme balance issues that go beyond a character style, and into bugs that made moves more powerfull than intended,
Issues with many mechanics in the game like Revenge, Guardbreaking, etc
All of this with no communication from Ubisoft at an outraged community.
I was disapointed, and stopped playing for a while. Most people stopped playing. The game went from 40k players at launch to a 5k daily average.
Only after a community organized boycott of the game, did the For Honor dev team respond.
They promise weekly update vlogs, weekly content, fixes and balancing for all the gameplay issues.
So far, they've been delivering as promised and the game is in a somewhat playable state again.
I'm enjoying For Honor like I once did, but with connectivity issues still rampant, the game has a long way to go.
However, with the continued support of the Development team, I'd say we're not far off from the promising game we almost had at launch.
Here's a thumbs up to the development team, and hope that the game will continue to move in the right direction.

Anyone with a brain (and access to the Steam Store) can plainly see the sheer volume of free, independently developed games available to play. Wade through the chest high sea of titles and major trends start to pop out: bad copies of iOS games, badly executed "free"-to-play games, and the ever present "art" game. With many reviewers adamant that "this game isn't even a game" and "lol French new wave level of pointlessly esoteric dialogue", one is tempted to relegate Sisyphus Reborn as one of the other walking simulators touted as "art" games. That assumption is false. Sisyphus Reborn is an actual art game because it does what vast majority of similar titles fail to do: it makes you think. While a bit on-the-nose at times, make no mistake, Sisyphus Reborn is the most well thought out interactive interpretations of existentialist philosophy there is. Through a barely twenty minute campaign, the game enables the player to experience Albert Camus' concept of the modern Sisyphus, a human who recognizes life's innate meaninglessness, and forges their own path based on their choices in spite of it. I especially reccomend this game due to the way it drastically lowers the barrier to entry of existentialist philosophy. It simplifies Camus' extensive meditations regarding suicide and the true meaning of life (or lack thereof). In the future, I'd like to see this game developer's interpretation of other philosophers (Schopenhauer's perspective on sex, perhaps?).
Game is good. Makes people think.

It must have been nearly twenty years since I've played the original Broken Sword for the very first time. Literally this has been the big bang of my adventure love, the origin where everything started, encouraging me to play a nearly countless number of point-and-click games up to the present day.
The more it hurts to give a negative review. My criticism concerns the Director's Cut and not the original version of the game, which - while never reaching the quality of the very best LucasArts games - can be considered a classic and should be played at least once by every serious adventure player. For being superior Broken Sword suffers a bit too much from its dull stereotypes and jokes at the expense of others for my taste. That aside it is a good game and a staple of the genre.
What flips my review from blue to red are the changes the publisher did in the Director's Cut. For sure I've read other negative reviews regarding these changes beforehand, nevertheless I decided to give this version a try, thinking it can't be that bad. I was wrong. Well, it is always difficult to replay a childhood game, the risk of breaking the rose-colored glasses is nearly hard-wired, but it has not been the game itself that spoiled my experience. No, it rather happened that I felt in love again with all the things I enjoyed in the past and felt familiar with. It's the deviations from these familiar things that broke the magic and in all honesty and objectivity, none of the changes Revolution Software did in the Director's Cut does the game any good. If I want to say at least something positive I would say that the added portraits partly feel felicitous. On the other hand these additions don't fit the graphical stlyle of the game and are as redundant as all the other changes in the Director's Cut. I've been prepared to worry about the new mandatory mouse-over hotspot 'feature', which is a pile of junk treating me like a moron, unable to solve anything on my own (other recent games provide keybinds to enable/disable hotspots) but it is far more than that. The whole new Nico chapter is redundant, feels out of place and adds nothing interesting to the game. Even worse this chapter replaces the phenomenal flight over paris intro from the original game. Furthermore there are a lot less hotspots and hence less comments in the game, making it super simple and less intriguing. The famous goat puzzle is totally ruined (in the past solving this puzzle was somehow special - even for new players it is 2 seconds now), same as every single scene where your character was able to die in the original game. You simply can't die any longer and every option that would have lead to death has been removed without substitution. And the final cutscene... come on guys, nobody needs that.
I'm not dissapointed because my childhood game has been changed somehow. I'm dissapointed because my childhood game has been changed somehow in a bad way and it's messed now. It would have been way better if the puplisher just had rereleased the original game as it is.
Verdict. My whole playthrough was a rollercoaster of cozy memories and extremely bad 'OMG, what have they done?' moments. Nevertheless even this Director's Cut sprays some Broken Sword charme. So if you've never played the game or if you've played the original game without having close affiliations with it, it might be ok to play this version with scaled down expectations. However if you've played the original game in the past and felt in love with it, avoid this version by all means.
9/10 (original game, released 1996)
5/10 (Director's Cut)

Amazingly atmospheric, far better than most horror scifi games. It's like someone combined System Shock with Bioshock, then took the guns out and poured a hot sauce of existential dread over the result. Never before have I seen a video game tackle the Mind-Body Problem this well. Recommended for fans of psychological horror, regular horror and cyber philosophy.
I do agree with the sentiment that you could remove the monsters and still end up with the same game, though. There is a bit of a disconnect going between the strong narrative that the game tries to tell, and the classical gameplay from Penumbra and Amnesia. However, without the monsters... There wouldn't be much of a reason to be scared. Atmosphere will only carry horror so far, at some point there has to be an actually scary thing to make all the times when there is no scary thing but there *could* be a scary thing that more frightening.

Published by Devolver Digital and developed by No Code, Stories Untold is a collection of four short tales that comes with a retro theme based out of the 1980's. Everything from the music to the objects that you interact with have a genuine 80's aesthetic to them that just can't be shaken, and this ambience enhances the mood of the episodes, which are filled with horror and sci-fi elements.
As revealing any portion of the story would be to unveil the master craftsmanship behind the entire plot, let's leave it to be said that this is a title that you should experience for yourself. During episode one, "The House Abandon", you find yourself in front of an oldschool TV, complete with retro keyboard, playing a text adventure. It all starts out normal enough, but events soon take a macabre twist. Each of the four episodes have different settings and atmosphere, giving them a new and fresh feel during your first time playing through them. Most of the gameplay is made up of easy-to-solve puzzles, or instructions that are as simple to follow, especially during the second and third chapters.
The gameplay does leave much to be desired, though some players who find solving any puzzle a challenging task my find themselves more enthralled by Stories Untold. Rather than relying on jumpscares or frightening enemies, the real horror here comes from the unknown and the unseen. The first three episodes are excellent, but the fourth and final entry where everything comes together is ultimately what causes this title to fall apart; some may even refer to it as a cop-out ending to the anthology. It would've been best to leave the player guessing, and the horrors unrelated.
For its hour and a half of longevity, Stories Untold is a fairly sturdy and substantial horror game. It's not all text-based adventure, as some may think given some reviews and a good chunk of the first trailer, but the title would benefit from more of this type of gameplay. There's little to no replay value, so once it's finished it will just sit in your library for the upcoming aeons. However, if you enjoy yourself a good dose of chilling 80's inspired sci-fi horror, you will thoroughly enjoy the small amount of time that you get out of it.

Untold Stories is a 'episodic' thriller that uses the UNITY engine in remarkable ways. It's incredibly hard to get anyhting across about this game without spoiling the entire plot behind it, so bear with me.
Each episode is a daunting, creepfest of atmosphere, and mostly that, only atmosphere. If it wasn't clear, there's no combat to be had in the game. Mostly by puzzle solving will you unravel each story, but don't turn away if you -really- want to try out this game over that. The clues are in the game and become readily apparent as you experiment with this and that, make sure you check help menus when they're presented, and if all else fails? Don't get angry. Walkthroughs exist, and if you are absolutely positively stuck at some part, don't feel like a failure for looking it up. Some things can get a lil abstract.
I really can't say much without spoiling except to say, this game is short, sweet, and worth every dime. Each episode, despite your seemingly limited interactions with it, contains plenty of spine chilling narrative that feels not unlike reading a incredible horror book in the middle of a storm. You won't glaze over anything present. If you're a fan of horror storytelling, you absolutely have to have this game.

This game represents something amazing, it was a brilliant survival game, the mechanics and idea were all brilliant. However now little progress has been made in around 2 years. If you don't find a good group/server to play with the community is immensly hostile, with packs of apex preditors forming on server after server and killing everything that moves. I can however reccomend Pangaea, as this server operated by some truly brilliant and dedicated people is the only reason i keep playing the game.

-some truly impressive and brilliant comunity groups out there with a nice atmosphere and a balance between rp and competetive play
Cons:
-core mechanics, such as scent and growth, not at all implimented but started years ago.
-devs distracted by making sci fi versions of various dinos and humans/cannibles before these core mechanics are sorted
-rude attitude of devs towards early access participents.
-lack of progress
-majority of servers have a bad comunity

I promise this now, if or when the game is progressing meaninfully I will re review, and when this game is done I cannot reccomend it enough. But for now the devs should not be rewarded for their currently progress. I will continue to play until then and may change this in the very near future. Fusion 2.5 is the next in the line of event-based software development, stretching back to Click and Create in the 90s. It's the successor to the Multimedia Fusion and The Games Factory - and it shows. The UI is dated with some of the editors being almost unchanged from the 90s. It looks like an early 2000s Windows app. It's slow and clunky. The event editor is a mess. Basically, it feels like a Win9x app at times - because Clickteam have slapped a terrible outdated Visual Studio UI onto tools that were around in The Games Factory.
While it's one of the more flexible of the event-based game development systems, and there are a load of extensions and commerical games made with it, it's still a mess of a program to use. There's a good idea and amount of flexibility buried here, but it's significantly hampered by the atrocious UI and Win9x thinking that Clickteam are clinging to. If you want to make games there's better software. Construct 2 is a highly competent and modern event-based app which is much more user friendly and cheaper (although it only exports to HTML5). If you're serious about making games, get GameMaker Studio and learn to code.

The Darkness 2 has passable gameplay with about 10 weapons, half of them being what I would consider upgrades of a lower tier. It has a low replay value with not much to do after beating the Story and Vendetta/Hit List Missions (about 9-10 hours altogether). The best thing it has going for it and why I recommend the game is the single player Campaign portion of the game.
There is very little stalling in the plot. The game starts with the reveal of a new enemy and has about 3 objectives that are logical to progressing before starting the arc with the big bad guy. To me that is very efficient at getting to the point. I was nervous every time a sentimental moment happened, worried if the game would do a cheap jumpscare. It compelled me to care about what was going on and that is a rare feeling for me to have with dramatic stories like this.
Each time you can go back to your base, the other characters have different things to tell you that aren't always related to what you are doing, such as the story told about eddie when Jackie and Vincent are catching up. If you are into playing a game and exploring the subtle changes, you will be rewarded for your time. The plot constantly attempts to mess with your judgement of the situation and makes every chance for a choice an uneased gut check.
Check the game out when you have the opportunity to pay attention to the dialogue and really grasp the story. It was inspired by a comic book series and plays like reading an interactive graphic novel.

There isn't a whole lot to do, so if the thought of simply being a dinosaur and interacting with other dinosaurs doesn't interest you, you'll likely get bored.  However, the devs are constantly working on the game with updates and new content and game mechanics are on the way.
All in all, I will recommend it so far, as even with such minimal content ( no humans, limited game modes, lack of mechanics such as scent, AI, collision, trample damage, etc )  the game is still a gem.
Who doesn't want to be a dinosaur?  Come on.  Get the game now before it it goes up in price because I think this is going to really blossom into something spectacular.

A venerable Warden main since the first closed alpha session of December 9th, 2016, I loved For Honor.
Played it whenever the alpha tests were live, and the following closed and open betas.
I normally don't support Ubisoft games, but the Beta tests were fantastic and I'd had enough experience with the game to warrant my Gold Edition purchase. I was a little suprised at myself.
Somehow on release, For Honor was a broken, unbalanced mess.
Many connectivity issues,
Developers not meeting their own weekly content goals,
Extreme balance issues that go beyond a character style, and into bugs that made moves more powerfull than intended,
Issues with many mechanics in the game like Revenge, Guardbreaking, etc
All of this with no communication from Ubisoft at an outraged community.
I was disapointed, and stopped playing for a while. Most people stopped playing. The game went from 40k players at launch to a 5k daily average.
Only after a community organized boycott of the game, did the For Honor dev team respond.
They promise weekly update vlogs, weekly content, fixes and balancing for all the gameplay issues.
So far, they've been delivering as promised and the game is in a somewhat playable state again.
I'm enjoying For Honor like I once did, but with connectivity issues still rampant, the game has a long way to go.
However, with the continued support of the Development team, I'd say we're not far off from the promising game we almost had at launch.
Here's a thumbs up to the development team, and hope that the game will continue to move in the right direction.

You know, I like action games, the rush of trying to not die and make through a level, the fear of having to restart your perfect run due to some mistake you made, that feeling you get when you defeat a boss without any potions left, I really enjoy that. But on the other side of the spectrum, I also love puzzle games, and adventure point-and-click games from the 80's and 90's, in my opinion, reign supreme on puzzles. I've been playing them since I was a kid, I've played through the Monkey Islands, the King's Quests, the Space Quests, Grim Fandango, Day of The Tentacle, and several others, and if any of you read my Introduction, you know I'm a big fan of Ben ‘Yahtzee’ Croshaw, but I actually got introduced to his work not through Zero Punctuation, but through 5 Days a Stranger and the Chzo Mythos, back when he used to make adventure games.
But still, it's been a long while since I played adventure games, and it is a colossal change of pace from my more recent rogue-like and acti on-based masochism experiences, but I'm glad I'm getting around to try one of the adventure game franchises from the 90's I never got around to play.
Broken Sword 1 is a cookie cutter adventure game from 1996, still, almost every game at that time was like that, so not really a criticism. Now, of course most of you know what a adventure game is and how to play it, but I have to drown out these reviews, you know.
In said game you point to something to interact with it, either collecting it or gaining some information, and with said items and information, you move forwards through the story. Done, see? I explained it in a short sentence just for you.
On a more serious note, I actually really like this game's puzzles, they are mostly well thought out and make sense, Cthulhu knows I've suffered through some badly designed and downright insane puzzles in several adventure games. “BUT SHOES, GOAT PUZZLE MAN, GOAT PUZZLE.” Yes, yes, it's from this game that the infamous goat puzzle was born, I personally didn't find it too bad, but my research told me that it actually makes sense in the Director's Cut (the steam version), so that criticism is basically gone, still, by what I read, that puzzle was just sadistic.
The story in this game is really good, it's really gripping and interesting, a bit cliche though, but that is forgivable, most of the characters are really well developed and likable.
Nicole Collard, a bold French reporter who got this great interview with one of the national heroes, but when she got to his house, he was murdered by this serial killer she wrote several articles on, The Costume Killer, and after some investigation, she discovered that the murders were all connected to some sort of cult conspiracy, and after writing her paper detailing all that, she received a phone call from her boss ordering her to stop writing and never talk about this business again, until a mysterious phone call directed her to meet a man in a café.
George Stobbart, an American touring through France found himself enjoying some latte in a café, until he noticed a strange and suspicious man entering said café, he paid no mind to it, but after a while a clown with an accordion rushed inside the café and left without his accordion, but a briefcase, the same briefcase the man was carrying, and after a while… EXPLOSION!!! The whole place was blown to smithereens, and so George feels it's his civilian duty to find this killer clown and help the authorities, until he met pretty reporter Nicole, who told him about the whole conspiracy. And so, together they must find this assassin and put a end to this madness.
The writing is pretty good, I give the game that, and there is a quite nice bit of mystery and intrigue, as well as some well done twists, it's a pretty enjoyable ride.
The graphical design is well done, the cutscenes are really well drawn, downright breathtaking at times, they also somewhat remind me of the Don Bluth cartoons, which I really enjoyed. That said, the in-game graphics looks kind of odd, the backgrounds are nice, but the characters seem a bit off, I can't really tell what it is, but still, not bad at all, considering when this game was made. The music on the other hand is really good, it gives the vibe of mystery and conspiracy, it really is ear candy. Back to the other hand though, the voice acting has some issues, and it really is noticeable, not experience-ruining, but still, you can clearly notice when they used different microphones and when they recorded on different locations, because at times the voices sound really good, at others it's just awful, but it isn't on the actor's fault, they do mostly a good job, a bit cringeworthy at times, but nothing too bad, the problem really is the microphone. 1996 though, so I'll give it a pass.
Overall, the game is great, I definitively recommend it, it's a well done adventure game, the experience is definitively worth the time. It's got good characters, a good story, and good design, if you're a adventure aficionado you've already played this, so I don't know why I even brought that up.

7.5/10 - Never Alone is a powerful hybrid between game and documentary. Included in this game are short, in-depth vides comprising of interviews with Inupiaq people complemented by beautiful footage. These videos are unlocked as you progress and do a wonderful job of giving a cultural context into the game mechanics, locations, etc. which you have just come across. While most games would dismiss these types of short explanatory videos to a sub-menu or as a DLC, Never Alone places them at the very forefront of the game.
Indeed, they are more central to the experience than the game itself. Never Alone's gameplay is fairly standard and uninspired for a platformer. Nuna can toss a weapon and drag a box whereas Fox is able to scale walls and summon spirits that serve as platforms for Nuna to use. Never Alone is therefore for the well-versed gamer, relatively simple and not particularly challenging. However, I must point out that I personally would prefer this to a more challenging but frustrating game. Keep in mind that Never Alone focuses on a cultural story moreso than the gameplay itself. The gameplay's features also tie well with the Inupiat culture. A blizzard becomes a game mechanism and emphasises the Inupiat belief that all things have a soul - even sila, the atmosphere. Although I've only played the game in solo, the AI is pretty well done and I found no major issues with it.
In many games, Nuna's cultural heritage would be a convenient way of rounding out her character, but Never Alone injects that culture into every crevice of the world she inhabits and the game that you play. Never Alone provides the player with the ability to walk around in that culture, to face enemies and traverse environments shaped by that culture's struggles and stories that really helps the information shine. Additionally the game looks beautiful and sounds great, dotted with a sparse score and a gruff narrator speaking in the indigenous tongue. It's clear that great respect was paid to the Inupiaq culture. Never Alone has an genuine desire for you to learn about these people, their way of life and their ways of storytelling - and by the end of the game you walk away with an appreciation of all three.

Stories Untold is not a very long game. From start to finish, I spent maybe 2.5 hours playing through the four episodes available. And yet, those 2.5 hours were some of the most unique and experimental in gaming I've played in years. It's not a title I'd recommend to everyone, but I'd imagine if the trailer, or word of mouth, has led you to reading reviews on Steam - you are likely going to enjoy what is on hand here.
The primary method of interacting with the game is via text commands as each section of the game eventually comes down to typing in commands. You'll spend lots of time typing in 'look around', or 'go to [location]' and reading the output from those actions via a computer terminal. However, each episode has it's own take on this interaction - from having you decode Morse Code, and using microfiche, to following step by step instructions in how to operate lab equipment. These allow each episode to feel unique while still feeling part of a larger whole.
Which, without spoiling anything, is mirrored in the overall story. While each episode tells a unique and unsettling story, they are all part of a larger narrative that explains why these particular stories were chosen to be told. It feels similar to watching a few episodes of the Twilight Zone - or watching a horror anthology such as Creepshow. Everything is seperate until you take a step back and look at the bigger picture.
Stories Untold also nails it's retro 80s vibe. As much as it tries to evoke 'Stranger Things' from it's opening theme - it earns that right based on how effective the rest of the games settings and mechanics are used.
I really enjoyed my time with this one, and hope that we get to see more from the developer No Code in this vein of story telling.

Obscure is like a B horror movie, with all it's downsides and advantages, only that it's a game.
The advantage a good B movie has is the ability to turn something really dumb and forced into an enjoyable experience. Obscure is doing this 100%, the plot isn't there to tell a story, the plot is there to force characters into situations where they must fight monsters. By the way, the characters are basic high-school teens and they have zero character outside the stereotypes you can see in any american show/movie whatever which features high school life. Hell, they don't even talk to each other outside the usual "WE WERE WORRYING ABOUT U GUYZ" or some♥♥♥♥♥♥
About the monsters, it's dumb, the concept of them being vulnerable to light is good, but the game has no explanation WHY ON EARTH ARE THEY VULNERABLE. Since the monsters (it's not a major spoiler, but it's a detail which isn't obvious, you decide)
.
So now that we have the grasp of what kinda feel Obscure has when you think about it, we can move on to how it feels when you don't. Just like a B movie should feel, you can laugh on the logic bumps and "weird" execution or cringe on them. Mainly I was laughing, the whole game just screams "don't take me seriously pls".
Outside of that the gameplay was actually fine. The fighting could be a little bit more complicated, outside of the final boss you're just lighting and shooting at random creatures. The best mechanic is that the game has perma death, if one of the five characters die it's not game over, the character just dies, no coming back, it adds to the feel that people usually DIE in horror themed stuff. There's also a part where you can basically kill one of your teammates by being an inattentive prick like me, that was super cool, I felt bad after that.
Also, you can combine items. Maybe back then it was a huge thing (I don't think so) that you can combine items, but I feel like that's not a big deal, not that big at least as people emphasize that. Your options are limited as hell, no reason to pee your knickers just because you can tape a flashlight to a handgun or a shotgun. You can also play co-op, but I didn't really care about that, I like my horror alone. But if you want to pop a beer and laugh while you're participating in some B horror action then Obscure is probably one of the best games for that.
I shouldn't like this, but I had fun while playing so I don't care.

Well this is disappointing, I had The Darkness II in my library since 2014 and thought it would be an amazing game. Oh boy, how wrong I was...
+ Beautiful comic book art style. Of of the best besides Borderlands and The Wolf Among Us.
+ Some levels look really good thanks to the art direction.
+ A dual wielding system where you can mostly mix and match, meaning you can carry a Desert Eagle in one hand and an UMP 45 in the other one. Or two UMP's in both, two Desert Eagle's in
both, etc. This is very welcoming since this is rarely seen in FPS games.
+ Quite decent voice acting.
+ The Vendettas (COOP levels) are quote fun, much more fun than the SP campaign even.
- The story is worse than average, you won't find anything new or exciting here.
- It took me only 6 hours to complete the main story. There's some extra stuff and a new game option, but it's nothing but unnecessary padding. To think that this game costs $30 is appalling.
-  I mentioned "extra stuff", it's a tagged on COOP campaign. They're selling a Four Pack for $90 on this very Store Page and you'll be able to get 2 or 3 hours of gameplay with your friends, now if this isn't value for your money, right? /s
- The gameplay feels just like your basic CoD clone. Hitmarkers? = ✓ Huge crosshair that forces you to use ADS? = ✓ Heavily scripted gameplay? = ✓ Cutscenes every few minutes? = ✓ 3 Weapon carry limit? = ✓ Regen health? = ✓ Jumping is useless because of invisible barriers? - ✓ Useless AI? = ✓
- The soundtrack is extremely boring, it's your typical Hollywood music that's supposed to sound "epic".
- The darkness powers are meh at best, you can slice enemies in half or behead them, though you'll be seeing the same exact animation every time. I haven't counted them but there don't seem to be more than 4 or 5 different kill animations.
- The game is almost entirely composed of corridors. I wasn't kidding when I compared this to CoD, hell, the few CoD games I played actually had more open areas than this game.
- I've mentioned this before, the AI is beyond awful. Enemies will take cover right next to you. Enemies will yell "Don't get too close to him", while running towards you or standing right next to you. Some levels have  friendly NPC's to back yo up, but they don't actually do anything when an enemy gets close to them. The enemy will also fully ignore your pals, they're only fixated on you.
- Talking about enemies, the entire game uses them same enemy models over and over again, just with a slightly different skin.
- The enemies are extremely annoying to the point of madness. There are enemies who will blind you so that you can't see anything whatsoever for a few seconds, your darkness powers won't work then either, enemies who have huge shields to protect themselves, they'll shoot you from a distance and when they get close they'll knock you back a large distance, enemies who can literally throw a magical lasso at you that will steal the weapons your currently carrying, then there's the teleporting enemies which teleport themselves all over the map. All of these enemies are also huge bullet-sponges and you'll run out of ammo all the time because the game tries to force you to use your darkness powers.
- The boss battles are like this: Huge bullet-sponges that can usually teleport and send waves of enemies at you.
- Talking about waves of enemies, a lot of the SP campaign consist of you being locked in an arena type of level while enemies swarm all around you. You have to kill wave after wave and then the game allows you to move on. Rinse and repeat.
- The graphics look better on the Store Page than they do in the game.
I hate to be so negative about a game, especially a game with such a beautiful art style, but that's just the way it is.

I have a love-hate relationship with this game. At it's core I love it. I love the concept and the features. I like where it's going and remember fondly where it's been. I've sunk so many hours into this game that I can get back into it and pick it up as if I'd never left. Fighting and hunting and hiding as if I'd always been there. Well, not that I"m the best fighter in the first place. Anyways, I do recommend the Isle. There really isn't quite anotehr game like it and I want to see more out of it. Good graphics, good sounds, a constantly improving UI. I recommend the game and I implore you to watch videos on it and learn about it before your purchase it. Get a feel for it.
Some days just playing as a dinosaur is all I need to make me feel happy. The fact that you are this ancient creature and have to hunt, fight, etc to survive is great. The fact that there will be even
things to play such as humans excites me too. The game is enjoyable, with or without company, though at the moment can get a bit tedious.
And, if you can, just avoid the community unless you can find a very friendly server. The biggest reason i don't play anymore is that the communities for gaming become so toxic (not neccessarily the Isle in particular). This game is best played with friends you trust, and stuck to that, rather than playing with giant groups of people or on servers with absurd rules, etc. The game itself is great, but it is a multi-player game. Just, advice on what to watch for. Find a decent server with good non-corrupt staff and invite a few friends and you have the recipe for a good time.
Generally the game is well maintained. Some bugs will go ages without being fixed but it is due to the developers working on more important things. The developers are not the kind to sit back and let you railroad them with your petty BS either - either give good constructive feedback that helps them somehow or keep your mouth shut because you aren't helping, you're wasting their time. They have a game to build; they don't need to hold your hand along the way. Be patient and enjoy it for what it is. The developers are a lot more open with the Isle than any other game I've seen
So yes, I do recommend this game and I'll be getting back into it as time allows.

Alright, here's the shakedown for this game.
Pros:

1: Game has beautiful graphics
2: Concept is amazing.
3: Actually well thought out mechanics.
Cons:
Matchmaking. This game is solely multiplayer, which i thought at first was pretty cool. You start out with people of your level and it goes from there. I was totally wrong. Every game after "The first battle" that you're thrown into (as warned by the game), you're consistantly matched with opponents that are better equipped and much higher tier than you. Often you're matched with a team of a consistant equipment tier that you are, leaving all the upper tiers to the enemy team, making it honestly near impossible to play. The past ten games i've played have been like this, with before the ten being a single "Research mode" and the starting game. This single con, all by its self, ruins the aspect of the game for me. The reason being due to the fact that, spawn camping becomes extremely prevalent, and don't even bother saying "Oh you can just leave the game", "Well the pros outweigh the cons", or even "It's beta, give it a break". A beta game usually has its proper matchmaking system together to make gameplay consistant and balanced, where as this game just throws a huge amount of people together, quite often with one side heavily stacked, and leaves it like that. <---- this to me is game breaking
With these in mind, another con, is the weapon balance. You could say "Well it's like real life, some weapons are stronger than others, and this game is trying to be realistic.", but to be honest, an SMG style weapon VS a sniper rifle, I should be able to spray at close range (iron sighted in) and easily remove the threat, while compensating for recoil. But instead, the scenario turns on its head, and i miss most of my shots due to either a bad server connection, or enemy armor that outmatches my gun. <---- This needs to be balanced
Again, with servers in mind. This game is heavily Russian influenced, and i wouldn't be surprised if most of the player base was russian (or people from that area). Which leaves people like me (your average white guy) with a terrible ping, and gameplay to go with it. <---- that needs to be fixed
So to wrap up, the graphics and game idea, as well as the menus, are made amazingly, but, the matchmaking system, as well as the weaponry, really need to be re-balanced if not overhauled before i even consider coming back to this game. Thank you for reading, hope ya found this useful

So... There you are, sitting at your computer, expecting to be taken to the cafe, when suddenly, you find yourself thrust into a new beginning, where murder, a mime, and a familiar French photojournalist of notable repute, find you delving into a realm of new puzzles, and an intriguing little mystery of its own. And what about the poor American tourist who has to travel across Europe to solve the more bigger mystery? Well, he's still got his own story, albeit with a few improvements aimed at engaging your brain a bit more. Thought you knew the story well?  Well someone felt a little extra work to solve the mystery of the costume killer and the secret of the Knights Templar was in order.
The Director's Cut is just what you expect - an updated classic given extra content and a few more puzzles. While the danger of death is no longer there from making a mistake, it's still remains a nice, calming title to play. While the main story and puzzles you need to solve remain unchanged, the side story involving Nicole is a welcome look extra, and the puzzles added in on both her story and George's are a nice little touch.  This Classic remains a fine example of the Point-and-Click genre, and the updated version just cements how good a game it still remains.

If you think learning how to play a guitar would be fun, this game is worth it.  However, you have to be prepare to learn how to play guitar, not how to play Rocksmith.  This is not easy, but if you are at all compelled to pick up the guitar, pick up Rocksmith.
Giving this game a 'star' rating would be really tough.  What Ubisoft has managed to do with Rocksmith is amazing.  The ability to get the timing right between the guitar, the song, and the noteway is remarkable.  This technology has more potential than I can even begin to imagine.  I hope this continues to grow.
In that respect, it's 5 stars all the way.  However, Rocksmith 2014 is not without some issues.
First of all, the elephant in the room: UPlay.  I like the idea of a global leaderboard and the other community things that come with UPlay, but man, does UPlay suck.  Rocksmith is good enough, I'll forgive them, but I wouldn't buy another product that required UPlay.
Somewhere between Rocksmith 1 and Rocksmith 2014 they messed up the tuner.  This is a really important part of the game.  Especially now with so many different tunings in the songlist.  The worst part about this is the lack of any real response from Ubisoft about this issue.  This literally drops 2 stars from the product.  I have to believe it's fixable though, if only Ubisoft would communicate what their plans are around this known bug.
The UI is still poor.  Rocksmith 2014 has a much UI than it's predecessor, but it also couldn't have been worse.   Even really simple things like not properly doing key repeating in the riff repeater.  It still feels like a console UI ported to the PC, which generally means the UI sucks.
Minus 1 more star for the poor UI, and we're down to 2/5 stars.  I really think both of these things can be fixed.   If you're in doubt, maybe wait to see if Ubisoft fixes the known issues.
Keep Rockin!

Before we get into this let me just say that I love Broken Sword. The original Broken Sword. I have probably completed it more times than I have other games in my library. I especially go back to it now and again to experience its world, its characters and its humour.
So you can imagine my excitement when finding this "Directors Cut" edition on Steam.
Unfortunately I simply could never recommend this version to anyone who wishes to experience Broken Sword and see what all the fuss was about back in the day.
If you really want to play Broken Sword nowadays, there is a "Broken Sword Trilogy" DVD-based package that you can buy on Amazon or EBay (ie. a non-Steam release) and it includes a perfect working version of the actual original Broken Sword and it will work with modern hardware and OS. So go for that.
As for the problems with this version? There are so many to talk about...
- Missing dialogue which affects the humour and even misses vital plot points.
- MIssing animations (NPC characters no longer have a talking animation, the flags no longer flutter in the breeze at the Hotel Ubu).
- Missing interactions with certain objects throughout the game (such as just about everything in the museum, you can't read the patients medical records in the hospital, you can't read the historical information on the boards at Montfaucon).
- Missing cut scenes such as when you first enter the castle in Ireland.
- Missing interactions with entire characters in some locations (such as the guy in the middle bed in the hospital).
- Sound glitches whereby I heard Lady Piermonts piano playing in other random locations (amongst other problems).
- A clear difference in recording quality between the new dialogue and the old dialogue (especially noticeable with a headset).
- The additional scenario as Nico offers nothing to the game as a whole and then just abruptly ends and is gone.
- Some puzzles have been simplified to a ridiculously simple level (such as the goat puzzle).
- The game is now 100% linear - you can't go to Montfaucon before completing the hospital section, for example.
- The diary is a pointless addition and the text within it is far too basic - almost childishly written. It also somehow knows vital plot-related information before these elements have been revealed through dialogue.
All in all if you want to rediscover Broken Sword for even play it for the very first time - I simply could never recommend this version of the game. Find a working copy of the original and play that. It's a far superior experience and you won't be missing out on so much material either.

A thrilling, good written classic point and click-adventure with some "deepness and seriousness" i miss from other adventures today.
The game starts with an assassination in a cafe in Paris, where the american George Stobbart unfortunately decided to chill on his travel. He survives it, and starts together with a female journalist, Nicole Collard, to investigate about the assassin. The more they find out about it, the more they get involved into a thrilling, murderous Story about the old temple knights, assassins and a secret society.
The original version of this game from 1996 is one of my favourite point and click-adventures, unfortunately only the Director's Cut-Version  is available on steam. The DC-Version got new content included (1-2hours of story and riddles with Nico) and a help system. "It got new content, and still you like the original version more, why?" you ask ? Here is why:
- new content doesn't fit in (new graphics mixed with the old graphics, same with the audio)
- content got cut out from the original version: Scenes where you can die are cut out; dialogues who are not fitting for children; some hotspots are not clickable anymore.
That takes a huge portion of the thrill and entertainment away from me.
Any way, one of the best point and click-adventures that you should have played, if you like the genre. But better get the original version!

I played the demo through, sat on it for a day, and decided I absolutely should buy the game.  It seems inspired by games like Link to the Past (one of my favourites) and has a similar feel to it.  I like that there is a lot of depth to characters, though if you go for a plain 1h or 2h fighter you'll probably end up with a sort of samey character as you level up all of the 1h or 2h skills.  That said, there are tons of options for combinations with various kinds of magic and skills, though I would like if leveling up skills had more of an effect than 1-2% at a time for most of them, to further increase character diversity.
The depth is very good in that there is a lot to do with your character, but not in a confusing way.  I was surprised when I found out you can also level up pet skills to further increase stats, and collecting monster cards also gives solid bonuses.  Looking back, it doesn't seem very complicated now that I've played through the current game a couple times, because it's easy to understand.  If you want to play through the game just mashing the attack button, that's fine (it will be really hard though), but you also have the option to level your skills in such a way that you can set up crazy combos and blow everything up.  The combat later on gets exciting enough that it's fun even to grind mobs looking for the card drop, both against the easy mobs and hard ones.
If you like the demo, and are willing to pay for a promising early access game, I recommend it.  The game feels very polished, it's just a tad short at the moment (~8-10h to get through the story mode)

THOMAS WAS ALONE (but he really isn't) is a platforming puzzle game that borders on tedium as you guide a few block 'characters' to their respective exits. Everything is a block or cubes, straight out of what would look like Atari, but with modern improvements so you don't notice the lack of textures. Things like lighting, good simple, yet dynamic backgrounds and the fact that the level always looks to be at a slight tilt. While it might not stand out visually, the game has good mellow and trippy background music that is just soothing to complete each level. There is also a well voiced narrator that just talks over a few parts of the levels to give the characters life when really, they're just blocks. There is quite a lot of fan art for these 'characters.'
The controls are really as simple as they can be. So simple, you don't even need a controller. Arrows to move the character, a jump button and buttons to switch to the next or previous character.
Its all nice on the eyes and the ears, the only real problem is this is just tedious. Each character has their own unique style. Some are short and can fit where others cant. Some are tall, some float. You can use characters as stepping stones so they can make it up ledges and this is where the game hits a tedium. Imagine to make it up a ledge, you need to use 2 characters so that the short character can make it up. Then do that 5 times and 5 more times before the end of the level. Sure its not every level, but it really feels dull having to switch between 3 characters, get them in position just to ensure 1 of them gets to his exit. It gets into the realm of being a chore. Sure it doesn't take that long to complete each area, nor is it difficult, but it just feels slow having to use 3 characters to make it the slightest bit further. I don't feel any sense of accomplishment getting to the next level.
To make up for that though, the game has frequent checkpoints.... especially right before dumb deaths. Deaths that might have 1 character standing on top of a floating character, but when you jump out of the water as the floating character, the character on top flies into a bed of spikes. Well, luckily the game knows this will usually happen, so there's a checkpoint right behind it. Another plus that the game has is instant respawn. It keeps you going like Super Meat Boy. This helps the game a lot.
You won't find any enemies in Thomas, only friends to aid you... and instant death traps like water and spikes. The game is very straight forward, jump and avoid death traps. Use friends to get to different areas, hit switches to change areas.
Thomas is a game full of easy achievements. Maybe an hour for 15 achievements and 2 or 3 hours for the entire game to be complete. There's no real replay value here, the collectables are out in the open and easily obtained.
There are other platforming puzzle games that are better challenges, that feel less like a chore to complete. However, because of the music, narrator and the simplicity, it is a very soothing stress reliever to play.

As someone who plays a fair amount of horror games, I really wanted to give ObsCure the benefit of the doubt. And in many ways, it shines. Creature design is great, the underlying premise once you get past the "disposable teens" veneer isn't bad, and the variety of puzzles manages to keep things interesting while keeping in theme with the school campus setting. However, there are a lot of drawbacks to the game, to the point I'm not entirely sure why it receives such high praise.
In general, ObsCure seems rather player unfriendly. The UI itself is pretty solid, with the relegation of menus to the shoulder buttons on a controller proving fairly intuitive. Ammo and healing item scarcity seems reasonable, for the most part, and while there are some tough enemies, you're usually well-equipped to take care of them. Emphasis on "usually," which we'll get to shortly. However, the game seems to have overlooked something rather major in that there's no listing in the controls section as to how you can pass items and weapons on to your partner if you're playing single-player. I was several hours deep and frustrated by a long run of deaths before I finally found what button combination handed things over thanks to a FAQ, thus arming my second character with a second weapon in case their shotgun ran out.
The item scarcity also became an issue when boss monsters entered the picture. Rather than giving you the chance to maybe stock up on a bit more ammunition or healing items than normal before a big fight, you're left to pray that you've hoarded enough and that your last save disc was used somewhere not too far back. If you get far enough in, this can be game-ending, as you end up with less than adequate firepower to survive. I got so frustrated with what I think is the 2/3 point of the game that I sacrificed two of the five students in combat, just to keep the ones I actually liked having around going.
ObScure also gets cheaper and cheaper as the game wears on. The most egregious example I made it to occurs in the Dormitory area, late in the game, where hidden holes in a hallway floor result in instant death despite there presumably being a floor to land on, albeit with injury, beneath. This is the first instant death situation I can remember in the game, and it comes out of nowhere after everything else just smacked you really hard at worst. It just feels like a really unfair leap without any precedent. If it makes any difference, all of this was encountered on the Normal difficulty level.
I'm tempted to give this another chance, maybe on Easy, just to see how the story resolves, but I don't recommend that anyone else suffer through it. Save yourself the frustration.

I first played an hour into the sequel of this game (Obscure: The Aftermath) back when it first came out 8 years ago, without knowing it had a predecessor. As soon as I found out, I stopped, and promised myself I'd play the original Obscure before delving into the sequel any further. I fulfilled that promised just now.
Most of the game's shortcomings, few and far in between as they may be, can be attributed to the team's seemlingly low budget and humble technical capabilities at the time. Despite those handicaps, however, they managed to create a spectacular experience with what they'd got. Their ambitious approach to a Resident Evil / Silent Hill-esque experience is certainly unique and engaging. though not without flaws.
For instance, Resident Evil 3 had me jump through hoops, retrace my steps, carefully calculate my ammo and herb usage just to gain some progress, which some frown upon, but I find to be vital survival horror elements. I this game, however, I rarely felt this. I always knew where I was supposed to go next, and what to do there. This gave the game an almost linear feel; consequently, I almost never felt scared or lost. But that's just me.
The co-op system is thrilling, but having a partner when playing solo can be cumbersome; they tend to get in the way and you lose the true ending if they die, which they happen to be fond of doing quite often. If you're playing alone, I strongly recommend you command your partner to wait at the gathering point in the middle of the school, where they can be safe and not get in the way.
The story appears to have only existed as a means to an end: to let you know why the school has gone to hell. There are no "obscurities" or profound revelations, nothing that really counts as a twist, and as soon as you pick up the first couple of newspaper clippings or files, you will most likely have figured out the whole conspiracy. As a storytelling enthusiast, I found that to be a bit of a letdown, since it had the potential to offer something far more grand.
All in all, I savored every minute of this game and the aforementioned issues did not really get in the way of my enjoyment; I liked it with all of its flaws, just like I like Resident Evil's terrible voice acting.

The gameplay is different from similar games because it puts the focus on PvE, something that most games of this genre, well, the might as well not even include for all the good it does them. This game also is kinda boring solo, but you can join a faction and find some really nice people. I've been playing less then 5 hours, but I've already had people outside of the faction I joined give me everything from guns to health items. The community is pretty nice from what I've seen.
Next, I've seen a few posts about hackers, and I can say that I've yet to run into one. They are either really nice people, and don't shoot noobs, or they just don't exist anymore (likely that latter). I know that I don't have much time in the game, and only about 2 hours in PvP, but that is usually more than enough time to get sniped out of nowhere when there are hackers, especially after being given an uzi and a sniper by some random guy.
All in all I'd give this game an 8/10, and it would be 10/10 if the bugs were gotten rid of, they are sometimes fun, but they can also be distracting.

If you think learning how to play a guitar would be fun, this game is worth it.  However, you have to be prepare to learn how to play guitar, not how to play Rocksmith.  This is not easy, but if you are at all compelled to pick up the guitar, pick up Rocksmith.
Giving this game a 'star' rating would be really tough.  What Ubisoft has managed to do with Rocksmith is amazing.  The ability to get the timing right between the guitar, the song, and the noteway is remarkable.  This technology has more potential than I can even begin to imagine.  I hope this continues to grow.
In that respect, it's 5 stars all the way.  However, Rocksmith 2014 is not without some issues.
First of all, the elephant in the room: UPlay.  I like the idea of a global leaderboard and the other community things that come with UPlay, but man, does UPlay suck.  Rocksmith is good enough, I'll forgive them, but I wouldn't buy another product that required UPlay.
Somewhere between Rocksmith 1 and Rocksmith 2014 they messed up the tuner.  This is a really important part of the game.  Especially now with so many different tunings in the songlist.  The worst part about this is the lack of any real response from Ubisoft about this issue.  This literally drops 2 stars from the product.  I have to believe it's fixable though, if only Ubisoft would communicate what their plans are around this known bug.
The UI is still poor.  Rocksmith 2014 has a much UI than it's predecessor, but it also couldn't have been worse.   Even really simple things like not properly doing key repeating in the riff repeater.  It still feels like a console UI ported to the PC, which generally means the UI sucks.
Minus 1 more star for the poor UI, and we're down to 2/5 stars.  I really think both of these things can be fixed.   If you're in doubt, maybe wait to see if Ubisoft fixes the known issues.
Keep Rockin!

First the disclaimer:
Whatever time shows up on my playtime stats, it's considerably lower than the truth. I've actually been playing a pre-Steam-release version of Surfasaurus off and on since last summer (2016), so ignore the time stats.
I was also given a Steam key as a courtesy to my support of this game in the past. But I would've paid for my copy anyway!
Now the facts:
This game is great, but you need to consider a couple of factors before you choose to buy it (and let me just say that you should choose to buy it, but I digress...well, no I don't; you should buy it, but still...)
1. This is not the kind of game you can just binge on. Well, you can, but not without cheating. Let me explain.
-Surfasaurus is designed with mobile play in mind. No, not that stupid pay-to-play freemium stuff. None of that here. No, it's designed as "potato chip gaming," in that you only need to play about 15 minutes a day to get the full effect of what this game is. I'll explain more in a moment.
2. You should play the mobile version if you haven't already, but the Steam version is bigger. No, not longer with more features. I just mean you can see the screen better. Unless you're playing on a six-inch monitor. Then maybe the phone is better. You should really get a bigger monitor.
3. It's designed on the OHRRPGCE, which means that resolution is limited for now. Suck it up. It's a fun game.
4. The price is way too low for its quality. I keep trying to convince the designer to raise the price to $4.99 or higher. I don't think he'll do it. Take advantage of the low price! It's worth it.
5. This game fits in the same world as the designer's other games, including one that's already on Steam, called Mr. Triangle's Adventure. I haven't reviewed that game yet, but I will. It's also worth playing. You don't need to play Mr. Triangle's Adventure to appreciate this one, but it does help if you want to "get" some of the references.
You get the idea.
Now, the way this game works is that you play the game in real time, which means, if you're playing on a Thursday night between 5pm and 9pm, you can visit the cafe in the game to play its Trivia night. The game "lives" parallel to our own world and time, so the game exists at whatever time and day you're playing in real life. That's both a positive and negative.
The positive is that you can plan your gaming time around the events that would happen at the same time in the game. In other words, if you're playing on a Sunday, then you can probably visit the kiosks and buy costumes, since the town's vendors show up on Sundays. Same thing with trading cards. Want to listen to one of the island's special guest bands at the cafe? Play on a Friday or Saturday night, instead of going out to the bars and clubs with your real life friends. It's cheaper.
The negatives are basically identical to the positives. If you have Thursday night commitments, for example, you might miss out on Trivia night. This is why the mobile version is more accessible than the desktop version, even though it's smaller. At least you can play trivia with gorillas and parrots the same time you're doing whatever you'd normally be doing on a Thursday night. It's a bit harder on the desktop, unless you have some useful way to lug your desktop around everywhere.
Or you could have the best of both worlds and play it on your laptop. Tnat works, too.
Gameplay is simple. You just talk to townies, pick fruit, collect trash, and interact with others in order to collect bonuses, buy things, trade things, etc. There's also a social element, where you can learn about the townies through trading card collection, and find out their likes, dislikes, and birthdays. Knowing these things improves your social standing around town. You can also visit the gym to make yourself stronger, but you have to make sure you visit it consistently. Don't treat it like your own gym, the one you have a membership for but haven't visited since last August. You need to actually show up at this one consistently if you want to get far in the game.
Oh, and of course, there's surfing. Eh, you'll figure it out. It's easy, but important.
So, on the surface this game doesn't look like much, and if you expect to play the whole thing in one sitting, then you're not going to get much out of it, especially since playing the whole thing in one sitting will mean playing for a month straight--I hope you don't have that kind of free time. But, when you think of it as a lifestyle, and a consistent adventure (use your imagination), you'll find that there's a lot to mine from this little gem of a game. All you have to do is play a little here, play a little there, then get back to the grind of real life.
Or, you could just mess with your computer's system clock and marathon the thing. Do what you want.
Just get the game and give it a chance. It's smart. And it's grossly underpriced. Take advantage of that. One of these days the developer might actually take my advice and raise the thing to $4.99 or higher. And pick up Red Triangle Games other titles, too, if you want the complete experience. All of his games exist in the same universe, so you'll get more out of each if you give each a chance. You can get the whole series for hardly anything.
Oh, and just for trivia, this game is a contest winner. Look it up.
I could say more, but I don't want to ruin any surprises.

Apparently, from what I've been told and read, that this game has been in development for 5 years.
I come back to the game a year after I beat the content of the game and all that's been added is a few pages of dialogue and a new "dungeon". Took me about an hour or so to bust through the new additions, then I spent some time in arcade mode.
So... Let's do some simple maths ('Cause I don't know how to do much else concerning maths);
~1 hour of story content = 1 year of development.
Game looks to be about 30-50% "complete" in its story. Wouldn't be surprised if the devs skimped a bit just to release a "full product" in a few years.
Let's take a look at, say Cave Story. Took a guy 5 years (during his spare time, also in college and working a full time job) to make this game. Game's a masterpiece in its genre. Polished and perfected.
Let's also assume that the 3 devs (I dunno if they hired anyone else, doubt it though) are also on this same schedule. Spare time working on the game only. 5 x 365 = 1826. 1826 / 3 = 608.733333~
That's just shy of 2 years in development for a completely finished product if 3 people are on the workload in an an equal capacity. So why has it taken 3 people 5 years to do the same amount of work as 1 guy? Why is the development of this game so slow and awful?
I shall pose an answer for you in the form of a question; Say you pay someone upfront, the full price of the cost to put a roof on your house. What is the motivation to actually do the work? What's stopping this company from driving in a single nail per day and then calling it quits? They already have your money, why continue with the job at all?
Early Access is just... A bad business model in its current form. It's not bad for the business, that's for sure, as games like Starbound and this one will attest to. It's bad for the consumer, and for some reason the consumer just laps this garbage up like it's some sort of ambrosian nectar of the dev-gods. There really needs to be some sort of time-limit (One year at the most, 30 days after the deadline to clean up) for games to either finish their development and release a full product, or start refunding all purchases completely.
As it stands, there's absolutely no reason for anyone to ever pull "Early Access Game" from their pages it's basically free money for a tech demo and a couple of lines of "story" to sate the spasms of frothing, ADD-rattled fans.
Gaming has fallen so far, and I hope for another crash.

A solid game, considering as of August 2016 it's in Early Access. What do you get for 10.99? You get a modern retro looking rpg clearly inspired by the SNES era, with the option to play solo or with up to 3 friends with either keyboard or controller (I recommend you use controller). The gameplay is captivating: the boss battles especially are well crafted and not to mention very challenging. These battles do a good job of incorporating the co-op aspect although the battles are almost as fun solo, albeit slightly easier.
The world has a variety of locations and each is unique both in visuals and inhabitants. The music and sound effects are excellent. The story is funny in parts but not the main attraction. Where the game really shines is with its weapon and class systems. There are lots of attacks to use whilst in combat using a range of melee weapons, magic and specials. The game constantly allows you to level up skills and gain new ones. Like in most games from this genre, you have the choice on which skills you'd like to focus on more, for example making your character's health high so you can act more as a tank, rushing into swarms of enemies whilst a friend attacks from afar with magic or a bow. Improving your attacks is rewarding and, in my opinion, is one of the most enjoyable aspects about Secrets of Grindea.
Quests involve puzzles, exploration and quite a bit of reading (obviously, although cutscenes can be skipped). Overall it is a great game that is easily woth its price.
The only negatives would be: it has a mediocre story and missed the oportunity to make pets aid your character in battle (instead they just follow you around and that's it).

The platforms are tedious, the enemy waves are immune to your force powers most of the time, limiting creativity, and the quick time events are out of control. There's just nothing fulfilling about this game. Get it on sale and play it on easy. Otherwise, you're not missing much.
